So, Warframe. Let me tell you about how this game goes.
It starts simple enough. It says "Check out this space-ninja thing."
Then it says "But you can change 'class' by getting new frames"
Then it says "Did we mention that we have a few guns to try?"
"Oh, and by the way, you can level up your mastery rank by completing things by variety. Try it all!"
sweet and holy. OH. And it's FREE.
I was skeptical. I thought, free? Ehhhhh, it can't be that good. It is. It really is. It's upfront about the grind. That's what this game is. Make some goals. Short term. Long term. make a big list so you have some focus, but most of all, enjoy it.
It's truly free in that you're never going to actualyl HAVE to buy platinum. Other people will buy parts of prime pieces you get from certain missions. So if you have spares, you can engage in that.
On top of that, the community is pretty great. I'm not saying that it's entirely sterling, I've had a few bad apples in random groups, but overall, everyone seems to be willing to help you get the most out of your experience, and help you out when they can.
Do it. Try it. You have nothing to lose but countless hours of enjoyment to gain.

When I was growing up, I enjoyed the original Sonic games on the Sega Genesis very much. For me,  two games in particular were the pinnacles of the series: Sonic 3 + Knuckles and Sonic CD.
So after years of no Sonic, I found out about this game and once I tried it, I found the game I had wished for ever since I was a kid.
Sonic Mania is a true sequel to the original games on the Genesis. We have a combination of excellent platforming, a sense of speed rivaling that of the ''blast processing'' days and a killer soundtrack. The excellent music in particular is so good, that I actually feel a little frustrated that I cannot buy the soundtrack here from Steam.
So if you liked the original 2D Sonics and wish to get the best overall package that the series has arguably ever had, look no further. This game shows that despite all that has been going on, the blue guy can still have an excellent game with the right people.
This game is a love letter to fans of Classic Sonic, plain and simple. If you havent played it yet, give it a shot! It's worth it.

tl;dr: Addicting and fun shoot-em-up. Okosan would be proud.
QP Shooting was a delight to finally see on the Steam store. While it's price is high compared to other shoot-em-up's on the market (eXceed for example) I'd say it's justified with it's many varied play styles, graphics, etc.
It's gameplay is like your typical bullet hell, but with some visible charms added in, the biggest being formations. Formations allow you to change the style your firing your bullets at, allowing you to hit more bullets in a certain area, switch your bullets to hit enemies from behind you, etc. You start with 3 of these, and can purchase up to 28 (Yes. 28 formations!) of them as you play and progress in the game. Another thing available to you is the play style, which affects how your hyper works. This is very helpful for those who are still practicing the swing of things or want a certain way to fight during hyper mode.
Past that, there is a good variety of (strangely cute) enemies and bosses, of which some designs may even provide a small chuckle or a questioning "Why is a tree attacking me?" as you continue on your conquest with pudding.
First off, for those who played 100% Orange Juice: Look at QP in her full vectored glory!
The graphics are nowhere near top-notch, but for what they are: they are good. I think the coloring choices and graphics are perfect for the style and attitude that this game attempts to portray, and definitely give a cheery vibe as you go on your quest for the elusive pudding.
One thing I have to comment on though is the background scenery you see as you play through stages. It gives a 2-D in a 3-D environment feel, and as soon as I saw it, I instantly got nostalgia of Ragnarok Online. This touch definitely gave it a much more connective feeling towards me, personally, but I'm sure we all can agree how enticing 2D-in-3D always seems to look.
I'll try not to give a very biased view on this. The music is catchy, it's cheery, and it fits the mood. While I personally like it, it may not be for everyone. That doesn't mean you can't easily mute it, though.
The music gives an exciting pace to the gameplay, but it is very, very short. Most of them seem to sound like 20-second loops, so if you plan on playing this game for a long period of time, I'd recommend turning it off if you value your sanity.
Wait. Scroll up and read the quote at the beginning of this review. Yep, that's the story. Carry on.
In a more serious tone... While it is a incredibly childish storyline, with not much of plot twistery to boot, it still gains some momentum thanks to the graphics and music. It does feel like a cheery stroll to find the pudding, running into friends, beating the love out of said friends, etc. and as my broken record says, the mood says it all.
Don't play this game for story. Play it for the gameplay. It's fun.
It's a good game. It's a fun game. Throw down your bucks and gain a ton of hours in return. If you must, wait until a sale. Use your card-farmed monies. Whatever you have to do. If you like shoot-em-ups, you WILL like this game. With it's many different play styles, modes, and stages, it's sure to keep you entertained and give you your money's worth in exchange.
Now go and get that pudding.
EDIT: Forgot to mention. Buying this game also gets you QP - Dangerous!! in 100% Orange Juice. Which is pretty nice.

A seemingly typical doujin shooter in which bullets are almost always cancelled when their source is killed. In this way, a little extra emphasis is placed on accurate shooting and offensive play. To help, you also have a swarm of "R-bit" guns orbiting your ship which you can re-arrange on the fly in a number of patterns. It's only through the skillful application of these patterns that you can dispatch enemies before their curtain fire reaches you, uncluttering the screen and keeping your anime friend alive. In addition to your hyper mode functioning as a shield in desperate times, extends come fairly easy in this game, making it forgiving in spite of its difficulty.
Its oddball style will undoubtedly make some players feel alienated while others roll their eyes. However, for the thoughtful STG fan who can embrace (or look past) its quirkiness, this is a robust and flavorful offering with a great soundtrack and a subtle bite in its mechanics.

There are a few things that I like with RADical ROACH. First, the setting, post apocalypse world with lots of mutant animals and you, as the rad roach, flying along killing them all, although the roach (you) doesn't care much about what is happening around him. The story, the art, and the music are all great.
You can play it in three difficulty modes: HARD, HARD, and HARD. I choose HARD.
My biggest disappointment with this game is that there is no achievement. A game this hard, should at least try to let the player to achieve something, to feel satisfied, to brag. You win the game, so what? Your friends will never know--unless there is an achievement for that!
If you like challenging games with insane difficulty, and old school style kind of game, this is for you. If not, you will rage quit and cursing a lot playing this game.
Personal score: 5/10

Crusader Kings II is an addicting strategy game. In the base game you play as a Christian ruler as early as 1066 and attempt to keep your dynasty alive till the mid fifteenth century. This is not a game about a country but a dynasty you can let your kingdom collapse in ruin as you abandon it to win a crusade for Arabia, the only real goal is to keep your dynasty landed. The dlc list may seem monsterous but that comes from years of expansions (the community got the devs trapped in a one more expansion state (the last expansion was suspose to be 4-5 expansions ago but keep being move back because of the demand for content.) Each expansion does it own thing adding new features, start dates, and/or religions. But the base game feels like a complete game by itself and in a way feels like a totally different game from when I started to play it.

So I have played this before on a friend's computer and was finally able to buy it because of a humble bundle sale. This game is fantastic. If you enjoyed Endless Space, as well as other 4X strategy games like Civilization as well you will love this game. There is a lot to it and the fantasy theme to this is very unique and beautiful. Beautiful is also the perfect word to discribe the art and music of this game which the Endless strategy games seem to dominate in this respect. For newcomers to the Endless strategy games I believe this game is a bit easier than Endless Space even on the easiest difficulty however even then, at least for me, it is still a challenging game. In each game the fantasy world is randomly generated and each time it is generated, it's always quite beautiful. I would easily rate this game 10/10 and honestly can't think of a negative aspect of this game.

Incredibly fresh and interesting take on the 4X genre with beautiful graphics, unique races, phenomenally simple and effective UI (right-click to go back; c'mon Civ, get it together) and tonnes of replay value. Ever played Civilization and thought to yourself "I wish x was a feature" or "feature x should really be expanded on" this game has filled all of the gaps where Civ hasn't. This game is much more intutive than Civ and also much more fun. Hopefully the next Civ game will borrow heavily from this title or I may not even buy it after the ♥♥♥♥ing shambles that was Beyond Earth.
Pros:
- Combat is fun, involves actual strategy, and feels more plausable than Civ.
- Minor factions can be interacted with properly and all have unique units, they're not just cities you can conquer.
- The regions system is amazing because it makes the borders of countries look real and you don't have the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ snaking borders and no mans land in between factions that Civ has.
- Unit stacking.
- Quest system, each faction even has a main story quest, far better than Beyond Earth's quest system.
- Things constantly change so the game doesn't become repetitive like long Civ games.
Cons:
- Research system is strange, its not objectively bad, its just that Civ's version is better. It is however innivotive.
- Much like Endless Legend some of the factions feel very uninspired.
This game is 100% worth paying full price for and Amplitude are well known for how involved and receptive they are of their community. 10/10 would conquer Auriga again.

In my opinion this game could be awesome. But the amount of bugs, glitches, broken and missing systems outweigh the positives, and that is why im giving it a negative review. Its like a computers game version of a 'tease'. "Here is all this awesome stuff...that i will fail to deliver." The AI makes single-player play only a short term option.
Breakdown:
Positives:
+ Each Faction has unique technologies and unique playstyle
+ Each Faction has unique units (changing factions forces you to change combat style)
+ Each Faction actually feels distinct and plays differently
+ Beautiful world design with unique concepts
+ Detailed Civilization Statistics easily accessed during the game.
+ Customizable Races and Units
+ Customizable Maps
Neutral:
+- Unique map system that is cool but doesnt allow you to see the whole world at any one time
+- Quest system, while a positive at first glance, is poorly done and alot of quests 'break' easily, quest count is low which leads to lots of repitition
+- Unique 'Winter' system, while a positive at first glance, effects everyone the same and only slows the game down
+- No naval system for people that like water maps. I just turn water levels way down.
Negatives:
- No Key Rebinding and limited shortcuts
- Lack of documentation. Tutorial/Wiki only give the broad information on how to play the game. Indepth game mechanics are not explained. There is no internal game library (like Civ) to explain these details either.
- Bugs are addressed each patch. However there are still a few annoying ones that havnt been addressed since January.
- The diplomacy system is better. Flavor text makes sense most of the time. Trade values are still iffy which leads to easy exploitation.
- While each faction has a backstory, it is harder to work through some factions then others. Others can ruin your play if you try to follow them (as Drakken, try to take that one city all the way across the map, of the Ally you have been friends with since the start of the game)
- The battle system IS unique. But in a negative way. Lack of unit control and poor programing lead to frustration. You give commands at the start of each battle round. Issues occur when your units cant follow your orders (which is often). The AI takes control of your units and sends them places which dont make tactical sense. (HINT: Make all of your units "Stand Ground" to avoid the crappy AI moves)
- A full unit stack (6-9 units) can kill (literally hundreds) of weaker units and take tons of cities without taking major damage. There is no 'fighting your way back' in this game.
- Taking cities is waaaayy to easy. You can easily take a close neighbors city within the first 20 turns.
Major Negatives: ***AI is still pretty terrible.
- It cant fight in battles. Once you get the hang of the battle system its easy to trick.
- Makes no diplomatic sense. Never fights empires that are threats. Easily bribed.
- It cant build 'strong' armies. It doesnt upgrade units early/often enough.
- AI technology selection doesnt make sense (Dust based civilization skips 3 dust boosting techs). They also routinely skip "unskippable" techs.
- Kinda stops playing if they lose majority of empire. Never see more armies from them or any switch from horizontal to vertical gameplay.
- Doesnt play to victory type. Playing conquest victory? Every AI empire is fine playing an economy based game as one empire slowly takes out empires one by one.
Final Statement:
The game is in much better shape then when i started playing in November. I last played during th beta release of the expansion pack. AI still needs work.

Open world, no hand holding dinosaur hunting game. Even though its still being created and updated, it has a nice level of polish. Animations look great, and the enviroment looks nice. Dinosaurs are scary, due to how easy they can kill you, but also scary in a  realistic sense because they dont always find you. Join a player vs. player server and basically play "Hunger games: Dinosaurs are here too"
Some of the most suspensful moments in this game are the moments when you dont even push a key or move the mouse, and  a T-Rex is walking 6 feet away from you. Do you move away, or hope it passes? You only have 6 arrows and 4 magnum rounds. Its choices like these that really are special with this game. Your not overpowered with machine guns, and you move like a human carrying gear.
Throw some headphones on, and you can really sink many hours into this game looking for better gear, and hunting.
However to call the game a hunter game at times can be tough, might as well call it "TheSurvivor" because you feel powerless at times. You usually start off with a bow and arrows but their is almost no way to tell were the arrow flys when you shoot it until you see the little "smoke" effect it makes hitting the ground. Making it a bit frustrating to use at times unless you like 10 feet away from a raptor. Obviously if your 10 feet from a ratpor with a bow, your a dead man if there are 2  or more raptors which is almost the case, so prepare to die a lot.
Likes:
-Dinosaurs! (Only 3 for now, but its the most requested 3 I would say)
-Open world
-Not an easy game
-Multiplayer! Play with up to 16 people as teams! Or play against other players! (2 types of enemys!)
-Player vs player mode really is scary with both threats everywhere, only using your ears and eyes
-Your little screen device will give you subtle hints on dino locations, but not enough to feel overpowered
Dislikes:
-The Bow is not well designed. Aim and fire and you dont see the arrow in the air, only were it hits assuming you hit ground and can see the "smoke" effect. Makes you say "Were did the arrow go?" a lot. Especially since this is a starting weapon, it makes it frustrating when the game also spawns you near 4 raptors. Would be nice if it worked like a crossbow with some kind of indicator of distance and being able to see the arrow fly to adjust aim.
-Sound design can be better. Its not sounds themselves, but were the sound is coming from. The Trex stomping is an awesome sound, but it seems like it just plays, with little sense of direction. A lot of sounds could use a better sense of direction. I can tell its coming from behind me, or in front of me but not to the left right or center.
-There is too much walking with not enough reward. The best loot (Weapons) are only at specific camps marked on maps while there are random pick ups across the map but they always have decent stuff. Why cant the randoms have good pick ups? Makes me only want to check out camps.
Overall if you like dinosaurs, and dont mind open world games, I would for sure reccomend this game! It will require patience as it is set as a hunting game. So dont come in expecting dino kill streaks, since every kill counts in this game.
Grab your headphones and prepare for dino suspense that you cant buy anywhere else.

Pretty fun game. If you're familiar with bullet hells, you should get used to it. The main gimmick is the R-bit system, which allows customization of 3 of your shot patterns any time you start a game/profile. You can unlock and buy more in the shop as you progress in the game, so that's quite a bit of replayability there. It's not so broken by any means either. Another small gimmick is a Hyper system, which is akin to Suguri only that it simply makes your shot stronger, and you're allowed to take an extra hit without penalty.
One more thing to mention, is that it includes a "Conquest" mode, in which you play the entire game but with the ability to save progress inbetween stages, so you can retry as much as you want or just practice a stage (You cannot change your formations when you're still attempting to complete the game, so keep that in mind.)
While decently short, and being completely non-serious about everything besides it's difficultly, this is definitely a shump you should pick up on steam, if only because it's really fun.
The controller support is pretty nifty and works well, and there is options for scaling your window size if you're worried about that. The general enhcancements, I currently don't have any problems with it so far.

Crusader Kings II is an addicting strategy game. In the base game you play as a Christian ruler as early as 1066 and attempt to keep your dynasty alive till the mid fifteenth century. This is not a game about a country but a dynasty you can let your kingdom collapse in ruin as you abandon it to win a crusade for Arabia, the only real goal is to keep your dynasty landed. The dlc list may seem monsterous but that comes from years of expansions (the community got the devs trapped in a one more expansion state (the last expansion was suspose to be 4-5 expansions ago but keep being move back because of the demand for content.) Each expansion does it own thing adding new features, start dates, and/or religions. But the base game feels like a complete game by itself and in a way feels like a totally different game from when I started to play it.

This game has a very nice-looking hex-based map with a well-polished effect for transitioning between a highly-detailed view of the terrain an an abstract map with borders between regions. That's really the best part of the whole game. On the other hand, I've been dissatisfied because:
1. The game crashes all the time.
2. It's the blandest combat system out of any 4X fantasy or medieval game I've ever played in my life: from early games like Master of Magic and Lords of the Realm, to Dominions, Warlock, Eador, Stronghold, Total War, Age of Wonders, Disciples, even Civilization in the early ages - they're all better combat systems, where I get to build at least some units that I enjoy fighting with.
3. There are many neat-looking special locations on the map, but they all just give some resource to whatever city you build next to them, and you end up ignoring most of them because each region can host only one city. In the end there a few different kinds that are all interchangeable.
4. The research feels unbalanced and fairly game-y: the cost increases with each previous research item you get, so you can never use your superior research power to clean up the simpler items you've skipped. It's somewhat like an RPG where the enemies always feel the same because they're scaled to your level. Meanwhile many late-game techs are inferior to early game items. It costs so much production to build late-game buildings that it seems more effective to stick with the boring early game tech.
5. There isn't anything exciting to research for your military - just +2 swords to replace your +1 swords basically.

Not sure what I was expecting, but this wasn't exactly it (more "meh" than "positive" review)...
The visuals are probably gorgeous (which would be one of the major selling points), however, my computer isn't built to handle this at its finest; that being said it does run smoothly on the lowest quality filter and still looks pretty.
The city building aspect of this game is simple, but effective. What killed this game for me is the combat... it just plays so clunkily. You tell a unit to hold position and then they run two spaces away into range of the enemy, but not into their own range? I don't really understand anything except that I can't control my units how I want to and it's cost me more than a few victories in my limited play time. That and there's no way to disengage from a battle, so if you happen to click on an enemy party that displays 2 units and they have 12 units of reinforcements, you can't back down. Good luck surviving six turns of reinforcements.
The units and mini-factions are even more diverse and unique than the major factions; I would argue that the strongest selling point of this game is the ability to experiment with so many different unit (through various faction assimilations) combinations. However, the individual major factions, to make up for all this diversity, really only give you three units each, which is a bit disappointing. The heroes for each major faction (thankfully you can recruit outside your faction) are essentially all the same, too... also disappointing.
It's worth dinking around with if you're a big RTS fan, but nothing every gamer must own. Game plays a little too slowly for me, even for an RTS. It's probably gorgeous, if graphics attract you, but the combat is awful and hard to control. Oh, and the clicking in this game drives you bonkers after awhile. Have to click on things four to five times occasionally to select it.
EDIT: There is a retreat button, but it only seems to appear if you have a distinct unit advantage... at least, that's the only time I've seen it. Also, the soundtrack is pretty, but gets repetitive quickly.

It’s certainly been an interesting year, we’ve seen many greats crumble, we’ve seen many diamonds in the rough and so as this year comes to a close I got to review one last 4x empire strategy game (unless some other 4x empire strategy game hits the radar before 2015 which will make this rather awkward).
As well as being a 4x empire strategy title, this title by Amplitude studio also shares similarities with another sci-fi civilization game (cough cough).
However while many would be guilty of taking one glance and simply dismissing this as yet another Civilization-lookalike, even on the surface Endless Legend is in fact a very different take on the genre that has rarely seen much change in recent years.
Already Amplitude have shown they’re no strangers to thinking outside the box with Endless Space having you manage planets then more recent Dungeons of the Endless concocting a mixture of dungeon crawling with tower defence and Endless Legend is not the title where they plan to stop.
In fact it should be noted that if you didn’t notice the similar naming conventions here, that Endless universe is a rather spectacularly vast narrative to take in, as Endless Legend ties in both previous titles lightly yet the link is there and serves to truly paint the scale of the stage.
The stage being set on a small chapter in comparison in the form of the planet Auriga, a boiling pot of varying faction and races after the mythical Endless left their mark on the universe before becoming one with the stars in the cosmos.
And believe me when I say that the factions are a boiling pot of variability,
with eight very diverse factions each as unique as the other you’ll be amazed how much choosing one faction over another will completely change the architecture of your campaign.
Honestly I don’t know where to begin, there’s the Necrophages, an insectoid hive mind that need to be at constant war in order to sustain their need to propagate and feed which is integrated into both their lore and gameplay mechanics. Almost on the opposite side is the Drakken, an ancient dragon race that preceded even the Endless who see themselves as the peace keepers of the planet so they start off already knowing each faction as well as their location and are even capable of forcing treaties and peace with these factions. My personal favourite are the nomadic Roving Clans, a merchant faction who are masters of the marketplace, capable of seeing and benefiting from all transactions as well as being capable of moving their settlements in order to increase profits; they however cannot declare war directly so they have to play a very manipulative angle by banning factions from the marketplace or even profiting by selling units to both sides of a war. While the Roving Clans can move shop whenever they feel like it, the Cultists are limited to one city. A community designed faction, the Cultists of the eternal end are a faction who were relics created by the Endless who were driven mad and now their sole objective is to spread their belief, that of the eradication of all remnants of the Endless. These guys are incredibly unusual yet awesome to grasp, since they’re limited to a singular settlement they have a preacher unit (as opposed to a settler); these units go about converting minor faction settlements instead of typically pacifying them. A converted minor faction give the Cultists a constant stream of units and gain resource points surrounding the village back to the player.
Now you’ll see already the previous paragraph is huge and I’m barely scratching the surface of the overall depth Endless Legend has in store; there’s still a bunch of over factions each playing widely different from the above mentioned and you can even create your own faction if the endless replayability was endless enough for you. Now of course you will get bored reading about all the differences between the factions and the vast lore available for each and you might just actually pick one, once you start though it must be said that you should leave your understandings of Civilization behind (the game, not actual civilization) as Endless legend does drop off a lot of the formula in favour for some new blood.
For one veterans of Sid Meier’s Civilization series or indeed many strategy titles of similar nature will notice you cannot simply begin your settlement wherever you please nor can you just rapidly expand by cranking out settlers.
Even just as you’ve started a campaign choosing the right spot to begin your faction’s rise to power is crucial; you see as EL plays on a hexagonal based tile grid you’ll find that each tile can produce each of the four main resources (food, dust, industry and science) as well as several of the unique strategic and luxury resources. While science and dust are import it is crucial for a city to with food and industry, food for obvious reasons and industry points will dictate the speed of your production whether it be units or buildings and should you make the crucial mistake of placing a city down where there are no industry points then you’ll be hitting that restart button. Another part of this very distinct formula is how the game handles settlements, you see once you place a city down you will in turn gain a section of land which your influence spans. These sections of land are known as regions and once a region has a major faction settlement no one else can settle there unless they raze or take over that region’s settlement; this can be rather harsh on newcomers (seeing as how little the tutorial actually explains) especially when you actually start to expand and realize your region is already surrounded. However once I familiarized myself with these I found it so much more enjoyable, as it means the player is likely to pay more attention to their settlements and I found myself caring a lot more when it came to maximizing my resources and such.
Surprisingly enough for a 4x strategy title the visuals in this game are fantastic, while it does mean you’ll probably lose sight of your units at some point or the other the map is sight to behold.
There is a ludicrous level of rich detail painted into every tile that helps heighten the sense of immersion as you explore this familiar yet alien-like world that only stops being glorious when you realize that the magnificent transition into a winter wonder land means your units won’t be conquering nearly as fast as you had hoped. While on paper it sounds like a really simple mechanic the changing of the two seasons, Summer and Winter (nobody likes Autumn anyways), can and will drastically change the current flow of your campaign whether it’s buying you some more time from the impending war or slowing your production to a grinding halt.
While at first the interface will arguably appear very unfamiliar with the several sub menus for trading, diplomacy, managing your armies, managing your heroes, research etc etc and pop ups tend to really get in the way (ie. getting told my cities have finished building when I’m in the middle of talking with my neighbouring faction) however as I found myself completely at home with the UI after my first few sessions the gameplay comes second nature as I begin my 3rd playthrough already.

Only 1.5 hours in but here's my impressions so far:
PROS:
Graphics, nice and moody with a great draw distance (think recent far cry games)
Sound: AMAZING!!!  from the music to the ambient life so far it's very good.  *see below for my first dino encounter where sound played a big part*
Controls:  So far it feels good to walk and look around.  weird not having a jump button though.
Location:  Excellent so far.  Vast island with forsests, swamps, mountains, beaches, and I think a volcano (wasn't never able to climb up to the top to find out for sure but once again the excellent sound design tipped me off that something was going on up there).  Found a few locals so far.....an old beach log barracade fortress called "Raptor Bay (I think) and an old concrete tower with some small 3 walled cells around it.
BUGS SO FAR
First one was I was getting constant "lost connection to server errors".  I was playing in a solo world but I'm thinking that means you're connected to a single "hive" a-la DayZ.  I ALT-TAB out to find out windows was blocking some of the online features so I allowed it access.  and restarted steam but still constant disconnects continued.
Got stuck in a hollow tree that was next to another tree.  With no jump button I couldn't get out.  Gave up after five mins....quit to menu and restarted and thankfully it started me back near spawn.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
I can't wait to see what this game turns into as it's development cycle goes on a bit further.  My first life ever led to one of my best gaming moments of the year.  I logged into the world and was awestruck and immediately pulled in by the excelent sound design and setting.  I myself love vast open world exploration games and the setting of the island had me hooked right away.  I wandered about with my GPS and found a loot container and arrows.  I followed the edge of a swamp set deep in a basin with mountains and forest all around.  I felt somewhat safe because I could see for a good distance in most directions.  Then I decided to climb up and out of the basin.  As I got further up the mountain I noticed some large trees with hollow trunks.  Thought to myself "hhhhmmmm gotta remember where this is in case I need to hide".  Hadn't gone much further when I heard.....something...... wasn't sure what it was.  Staring to get a little nervous I pressed on.  Then I heard something else......sounded menacing......sounded close...... ok now I'm scared.  Was this just an ambient sound I hadn't heard before?  I crept onward now looking over my shoulders in every direction.  Then I heard it........OK OK THAT HAS TO BE BAD....I then started backtracking to my hollow tree.....the only safe place I knew of.  As I headed toward it I heard the sound again.   I got to my tree and went prone in the ferns inside.  I then heard a loud pronounced dinosaur call on my left.  Then as immediately heard an answering call off in the distance.  My mind raced....ok this must be raptors.  Then I heard another call and multiple answers...... silently I began to pee my pants.  Each set of calls got closer and closer.  I crawled prone as far back as possible into my tree.  Then i began to hear footseps.  Then snorting and sniffing.  Now I'm in panic mode.  Peering through the dense ferns I was prone in I could barely see outside my tree truck.  I saw a shadowy figure flash by.  Then another.  Then a third.  The forth one was close enough to make out a distince outline.  That outline also was accompanied by a text box that said UTAH RAPTOR.  Ohhhhhhhh  Crap!!!  I figured that they were hunting me.  As I saw the figures moving by I thought I had given them the slip.  Nope.  One stopped right outside my tree.  Then a second.  Then a third.  After an eternity of about 15 seconds the 3rd one saw me and attacked.  Trapped inside the tree with nothing to defend myself and nowhere to go I didn't last long.
I was that encounter that will go down in one of my all time gaming moments.  It was so perfectly set by the hostile undiscovered world I was exploring.  And made perfectly terrifying by the excellent sound design as I heard the dinos calling to each other.  I know that at this early point in the games development there's not a whole lot to see and do yet but if this is any indication of what's to come I'm all in for this adventure.

Until there's a means to play an offline, singleplayer game I really wouldn't recommend this.  Though access to the internet is not a problem for me, I am not a fan of purchasing a game and then being unable to play it because an update breaks the ability for the game to connect, or similar nonsense.

Currently there is no true single player game here, as you are still required to connect to a server even when playing in a world confined to one participant.  Connection loss is a real pain because apparently, things like supplies and items' positions are dictated server-side, meaning while you may end up reconnecting to the game should the connection falter, whatever items were in your immediate vicinity (like, for instance, a crate of supplies I spent a good 30 minutes trying to get to) will disappear.
Hopefully updates come along which enable more consistent play.  As it stands I am too frustrated with losing my sense of progression to keep playing.

At the time of writing this review, I've clocked a mere 10 hours on this game, but it has been a stellar 10 hours. I still can't believe that this is a free to play game. I actually feel like I want to buy one of the Pinnacle Packs, just to thank the devs for such an awesome experience.

The bugs that I've encountered so far are extraction points that don't work and enemies that are unresponsive. While these can be irritating (especially the extraction points), I'm confident that these problems can be easily addressed through a few hotfixes. Also, I wish they'd give a bit more love to the stealth approach.
Among the good things are the co-op missions, an immersive single player campaign and lore, rewarding grind experience and a good amount of support for players who wish to keep playing for free.
Warframe is a Co-Op game with a lot of heart and variety, and I sincerely recommend that people give it a try.

An interesting game that is best played with friends, Interplanetary puts you in control of a planet pitched in a fierce battle against the other players (And the developpers hinted AI may be coming soon) by shooting at eachother with railguns, missiles, lasers, and superweapons. This sounds easy enough but you'll find that when you need to shoot your opponents, your railgun will be facing the other direction due to your planet's rotation. Your lasers don't hit anything but air and empty soil because your opponent has worked on counterinteligence, and your missiles were brought off course by the gravity well of a passing gas giant. He takes the shot, but misses you just barely. And the gravity well of your planet redirects those railgun shots right into the orbit of a third player.
I did not expect it, but it is surprisingly challenging in your tactical and strategic choices. Do you build everything nearby so the early game railguns will do barely any damage at all, with everything you have fitting nicely under one defence structure... or do you spread out everything so a superweapon can't hit everything at the same time and destroy half your buildings with one well placed shot? Who do you aim at first? That guy who keeps shooting railguns at you and is obviously out for blood, or the guy who is peacefully building his war machine with mines and data security centers? The list goes on, but it has more than enough variety to allow for plenty of experimenting while it avoids having a single strategy that will always come out as the best.
It is certainly worth giving a try, with plenty of decisions and choices to keep you thinking, but fast paced enough to get through a game without spending your whole day on it. (Average, casual games I played with friends lasted about 1-2 hours)
For 10 euro, I would say it's worth it and recommend giving it a go. If you're not convinced, keep an eye on this one for when it goes on sale

So with just the 1.5 hours I have, I wanted to share what I experienced with this game.
I'm a long term Sonic fan, in fact grew up with the Sega 16 bit, so Sonic was my Main game. Sonic 3 and Sonic 3d were the most fun for me. Anyways, going back on topic.
As the years progressed, Sonic changed. They started using more heavily CG edited stuff, added voices, and....kinda killed the Sonic I knew.
You see, the old Side Scrolling Sonic was the best because you PROGRESSED AT YOUR OWN PACE. You could go as quickly as you wanted, and as slowly as you wanted. You didn't Need to speed blast through stuff, but if you had the stages memorized, you could TEAR through them, and show off for friends. That was part of the thrill, exploring the stage, being able to show that one friend where the secret they kept missing was, stuff like that.
Sonic along the way stopped being the game that drew in so many fans, that MADE Sonic the icon he is today.
Mania brings that nostalgia back in a great way. This is a Sonic game that I was missing for so many years. It is worth the money. It brought me back to when I used to ride my bike home as quick as I could, so that I could get some Sonic time in.
tl;dr New sonic game that feels like the old stuff, had blast playing

"SEGA should hire these guys!" - Every Sonic fan in response to Sonic fangames
Well, it happened. Not much to say that hasn't already been said but I figured I may as well add my two cents. This is a game by the fans for the fans and is a passion project to its core.
Pros:
-Classic Sonic gameplay perfected. Sonic Team has struggled to replicate the classic gameplay in past attempts such as Sonic 4 and Sonic Generations' Classic Sonic and could never get the classic physics on point. Mania does it right and well with momentum-based gameplay and proper bouncing physics, with additions such as the drop dash.
-Beautiful visuals. Like many have said, this is what 2D Sonic would probably have looked like on the Saturn. Animations look clean and the sprites for the environments and characters are detailed while retaining the classic feel.
-Great soundtrack. It doesn't try too hard to sound like classic music but still has a nostalgic/retro vibe. Listened to some of the composer's music prior to this game's announcement, so when I found out he was doing the music I knew for sure it would be good. Then again, it is a Sonic game we're talking about; the music is good 99% of the time.
Cons:
-Boss fights. Personally I don't think many of them are well designed. Not sure how to explain it without spoiling individual bosses. I guess to put it broadly, some of them can be clunky. You may find yourself getting hit constantly without really learning an attack pattern (at least that was the case for me, maybe I'm just bad.)
-Rehashing. It may sound like a bit of a nitpick, but I think it's a justified argument because
There are also a lot of classic gimmicks used throughout the game even in new stages, though to be fair there are also numerous new gimmicks to complement them. Normally I'd be fine with rehashes here and there, but this has pretty much become a staple for the franchise for nearly the last decade. Games like 4, Generations, and Forces rely heavily on rehashing to the point where it starts to diminish the value of having something new as opposed to something that's filled with too much nostalgia. Not to mention, the first two stages are
Meh... what I'm saying is we've been down the road of reusing old ideas for the sake of nostalgia numerous times. Ideally I would've liked to see all new stages in the game to help facilitate the idea of this being a "new" classic game.
Nitpick:
-I think they should've based the designs off of the Sonic 3 sprites. Personally I think they're the best looking ones, and it makes the most sense since this takes place after Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
In conclusion, Sonic Mania is a great game and reminds us why Classic Sonic is better than Classic Mario (okay, that's subjective, but you know it's true.) Though I do think it does a lot of unnecessary nostalgia pandering, it doesn't take away from the positive aspects and probably won't be a problem for most people. Whether you're a Sonic fan or not, there's a lot of enjoyment to be had in this game and I definitely recommend it.

Let's get a few things out of the way: DRM and Denuvo
This game has them, and if you do not like that, get the Switch/PS4/XBONE versions instead.
...
But do get this game, oh please get this game and do not let the problems with the DRM dissuade you from getting it.
It's it's sincerely a return to form for Sonic and it goes beyond just being a "decent sonic game"
It's fantastic and stands among the best the franchise has to offer.
Developed by former fangame developers, Sonic Mania is an incredible love letter to the classic era of the series which manages to understand its gameplay and fundamentals in a way only passionate and talented developers can.
Gameplay wise it's about the same you would get from the classic sonic titles from the 90's with momentum based mechanics and that's entirely a very, very good thing. While most of the stages in this game have been taken from Sonic 1, 2, 3&K and Sonic CD, and only four stages are entirely original, the level design in these old stages give new life to them to the point many feel like new zones in a way. Overall, the level design in this game is beyond superb and does with some of the problems the original titles had.
In terms of visual presentation it appears as something straight out of the 32-bit era and dresses itself as the long lost Sonic game the SEGA Saturn never got with some of the best pixel artistry ever seen on the medium. The character animations are crazily fluid and look fantastic.
Most of the soundtrack consists of remixes from previous games with a good chunk of original content in there. But even so, I can easily consider the game's soundtrack to be some of the franchises best as the remixes are incredible (special shoutouts to Stardust Speedway) and the new content is delightful and fits right into the classic series as potential new iconic tracks.
I think I can say Sonic Mania is easily the best Sonic game released since Sonic 3&K.
Get this game and support it; this is the kind of quality we should be getting more often out of the series.
it's an amazing omage to everything that made sonic 2D games fun, with new stages and gimmicks thrown in to make it a totally unique experience.

A must have game for any bullet hell fan! QP Shooting Dangerous!! charms with it's cheerful style and tons of gaming customization options!
The game has 2 play modes - the classic arcade one, no continue allowed, and you play the levels in order, or the Conquest Mode, that saves your progress and allows you to progress one stage at a time or practice a stage over and over, so when you go arcade you can rack up the highscore!
The most important game mechanic for me is this : when you kill an enemy, all it's bullets on the screen become stars, that you automatically gather and they fill your Hyper bar. So most of the time your best chance of survival is killing everything on screen in a timely fashion :p Once you get hit ( you start with 3 hearts, enough for 3 hits) all the bullets on the screen disappear, but new ones are there in no time and you have like a second or 2 of invulnerability. Another major mechanic is the Hyper ability - it get's filled with you gathering stars and when you activate it all bullets on screen turn into stars, all stars turn into yellow stars (more valuable than the normal green stars) and you get extra damage. Around the hyper ability there are 3 gameplay styles - Orthodox, Defensive or Aggressive style. Orthodox is the balanced one, Aggressive gives you more damage in and out of Hyper mode, but the length of the mode is significantly reduced, and Defensive mode - the opposite of aggressive. I played the aggressive one when I progressed, but I think the orthodox is really the one I had the most success with.
The way you shoot is determined by the formation you choose - and there are 3 you can "equip" out of 28 available / unlockable. You get points to unlock further formations by playing the game and achieving highscores. I have not experimented or unlocked enough formations, but I like the default ones - you pretty much need a focus fire in front of you, one for a spread that you'll use most of the time, and one with reverse shooting direction, so you can take care of backstabbing enemies.
Don't kid yourself, the game looks cute and the story is hilarious ( PUDDING!!1), but the levels are pretty tough even on normal difficulty settings. The controls are tight, there is full controller support and you can even rebind not only your keyboard controls, but even your gamepad keys - I love this!
The best part for me as let's player is the fact, that once your game is over, you're presented with the option to save your run, so you can watch it later - I find this awesome, as commentating while playing a bullet hell is a damn hard task :p
QP Shooting Dangerous!! is a pretty well rounded and cute looking bullet hell, a must have for every fan on the genre and with 4 difficulty settings to chose from, maybe for newcomers as well. Add steam trading cards to the low price tag and this becomes a really easy recommendation!

Uncomplicated but challenging Bullet Hell game that doesn't take itself too seriously, sporting a good soundtrack and quirky characters.
The mechanics are pretty easy to get accustomed to, but hard to master - this game uses a Chain system for scoring, gives you the ability to engage a Hyper Mode that is important both for survival and for scoring, and allows you to pick three shot types per run that you can switch between on the fly.
Clever usage of the right shot type in the right situation can make the difference between nightmarish bullet walls from all sides and a mostly empty screen, so some strategy is required - you can't just rely on the basic Front shot type all game and expect to win.
That said, the game is never unfair - for instance, you're given advance warning when enemies appear from locations you might not expect them to appear from, a gesture that some other Bullet Hell shooters today still don't seem to deem necessary.
Overall, a quite fun game. Fans of the Bullet Hell genre will probably feel right at home. For people that are new to the genre, the game offers a "Conquest Mode" in addition to the standard Arcade Mode, allowing you to take on one stage at a time rather than all five in one run, so it's probably also a good entry title.

It's pretty much what you'd expect from a bullet hell game (that's a good thing), and I don't think I have to comment on the visual style since you get that from the screenshots and video, but the Rbit system does deserve some attention.
Rbits are rabbit... bits that fire bullets to supplement QP's firepower. What makes them interesting is that you can choose how they fire. That is, in front of you, behind you, to the side, rotating, and so on. In any particular play you've got a set of 3 Rbit formations you can switch on the fly. This means picking a few bullet patterns to handle different enemy and boss patterns. There's a total of 28 different shot patterns that QP has access to, but only 5 of them start unlocked. You can unlock more as you play the game more, and these unlocks are persistent through plays, giving the game some permanant progression without making QP objectively more powerful (as opposed to something like Danmaku Unlimited's upgrade system). You may or may not want to pick a new set of formations really, since the starting ones are the standard suspects that you'd be used to. Maybe you want to try something crazy? Try getting the trap formation (which doesn't shoot, it places the Rbits down in a spot for as long as you're using the formation, and the Rbits do damage to enemies that collide with them), then place that where you know a boss is going to be sitting. Certainly things like the trap formation are very situational, but that's fine since you have access to three that you can switch between with the press of a button at any time on any given play.
The Rbits certainly don't revolutionize the genre or evern change it very much at all, but still, they're a very nice touch.
The only thing I could really bring up as a negative is that I'm not particularly into the music. The music isn't bad, but it's certainly not something I'd listen to outside of playing the game. That's not a huge knock by any means, but when it comes to bullet hell games I've grown accustomed to loving the sound tracks, so it sticks out when I'm not absolutely in love with the music.

tl;dr:  Divinity OS2 is one of the best RPG's and one of the best Co-Op games out right now, and quite possibly the best game I have played in years.
A friend of mine got me this game as a Christmas gift, and I have not been able to put it down since. I enjoyed Divinity OS1 before, but this game manages to outdo it in most aspects still.
The story is amazing. It truly makes you feel like every small decision you make matters, and changes both the course of the game, the way your characters personality forms and how they interact with party members and the world in general(and obviously how they react to you as well).
Most if not all dialogue is fully voiced by great voice actors(including the narrator), the sound track is atmospheric and immerses you straight into the fantasy world, and the graphics and world design are gorgeous.
When I played the OS1 for the first time the slow-paced combat kind of turned me off at first (I thought it was quite hard to survive, and kind of confusing), but once I got more into it I grew to like it, and with Divinity OS2 all my doubts about the turn based combat have vanished. It is a lot of fun to plan out your next moves with your friend. The game wants you to be creative and tactical in combat, so you better not try to run head first into every fight, or else you will probably end up dying many times.Rather you will often use the environment to your advantage( which reacts to pretty much anything you do ) applying status effects, luring enemies away to overwhelm them in numbers and combining elements with your party members to cause havoc.

The companions have rich stories, are fully voiced and quite interesting (I had a hard time picking a follower because they're all quite cool).
That's pretty much all there is to say: if you like (Old-School) RPG's and don't mind the slower paced more tactical combat system, this is probably the best game out there right now.
Best Game Of 2017 so far

Dang, this has to be one of the greatest RPGs I've ever played. That's saying quite a lot due to my *ahem* EXTENSIVE RPG experience. I regret that I waited way too long to purchase this game. If you played the first Divinity: OS game and enjoyed it, then this one will more than likely tickle your funny bone.
Right off the bat the game had me hooked at character creation, with something extremely simple; the ability to choose between 4 instruments that will be the lead in the music that plays during the game. Of course, there's more than just that in the character creation. Such as creating your own character from scratch, choosing to be a charismatic dwarven melee powerhouse that can talk their way out of sticky situations. Maybe choose to be an elven lone wolf ranger that can assassinate targets from stealth and talk to animals. Perhaps a undead human throwing out massive spells that obliterate entire fields of enemies from the safety of your oversized lounger while you sip on warm tea. (pip-pip) You may, however, find it difficult to obliterate many enemies on the two hardest difficulties, Tactician and Honour, both of which are the same difficulty, but the ladder only allows one save, not my cup of tea for a massive content RPG, but to each their own.
There are 6 attributes in the game that you can choose to level, and this is a game that you most certainly don’t want to focus on ONE attribute.
Strength: Boosts damage of your strength based weapons (e.g. swords, maces, axes) and increases that amount of weight that you can carry in your bag.
Finesse: Boosts damage of your finesse based weapons (e.g. daggers, bows)
Intelligence: Boosts damage of your intelligence based weapons (e.g. spells, wands)
Constitution: Boosts your base vitality per point spent by 7% (every class needs a little love from this attribute)
Wits: Boosts your initiative (turn order) and critical hit chance
Memory: Boosts the amount of spell slots you have so you can use more spells. (VERY important for most spell casters)
Gameplay is your classic turn based gameplay. Turn order is determined by the amount of initiative that each character has. There’s a plethora of status effects that I’ll quickly skim through the most common ones. Burning, inflicts damage at the beginning of each turn of the character effected. Stunned, skips effected character’s turn. Silence, unable to cast any spell. Charm, makes effected character fight for charmer’s side. Decay, take damage from healing abilities. There’s also ally status effects that can be quite powerful. However, in order to cause any type of status effect, you first have to get through the enemy's armor and magic resist shields. Armor prevents damage from physical attacks/abilites and magic resists prevents damage from all magic based damage. Once you’re through the shields, you can start damaging their vitality and this goes for you as well. Combining spells is also a thing in this game that can turn the tides of battle greatly… Or horribly. For example, cast a fire spell on the ground to light it ablaze, then cast a rain spell, now that there’s steam from that rain spell, cast a lightning spell on the steam and you’ve created a lightning cloud that will stun enemies that pass through it. Or, you know, just have a character sneak around throwing oil barrels around the enemy then cast a fireball at the oil barrels and watch as the enemy is engulfed in a fiery inferno. There’s plenty of options to choose when you’re in battle, you just have to be imaginative enough to use them.
The story, in my opinion, is leagues better than the first one. I didn’t really enjoy the whole time weave source hunter mumbo jumbo from the first game. But, this one sets you on a journey to become a Divine. A Divine is a person who is chosen by the seven gods to become a powerful being of death and destruction! Mwahaha *hack*. Or not, if that’s like, not your cup of joe. There’s romance in this one, which is a plus in my book. I was aiming to romance the red headed jokester with a big secret, Lohse, I was giving her all the right signals until I did a 180 about 70 hours in and decided to go with the deadly and mysterious long nec- I MEAN elf, Sebille. (You’ll get the joke when you make an elf character). She was pretty bummed about it too. Speaking of bummed, if you end up picking up the Pet Pal trait that allows you to speak to animals. Be prepared for some of the most depressing crap you will ever read. My word, Lorian, what is wrong with you. You brought my emperor of death character to his knees in tears, you monsters... The game has PHENOMENAL writing though, I was actually invested into many characters. I grew to hate some characters that I would go out of my way to cause them pain. So I did just that actually, by killing everyone they loved. 99% of the characters in this game are killable. You think that person is important for the story? Well, throw a fireball at their face and see just how important they really are. The dialogue in this game isn’t overly long in some places. The first game had some real bad cases of over complicated dialogue. I don’t need to read a 1000 word essay on why the void needs to be destroyed. “We gonna die!” will sum it up quite nicely.
All in all, this game is fantastic. First game in a long while that I was actually constantly excited to play. Wishing that I didn’t have to go to work. Waking up early to play. Felt like a wee lad in the days I’d use to get up hours before school to play Runescape. Shoot, I’m not even done with the game yet. I want to try making a Lone Wolf Dwarven ranger and killing everyone that’s possible to kill. No, I’m not messed up inside.

Great 4x fantasy game.
Pros:
+ The art direction is
and the factions and their lore are awesome. The factions get their own questline and their own intro videos. Many, many unique tiles that give their own yields really sell the fantasy setting. The overall universe that they've set up is really great.
+ High amount of customization for your military units. You can pick various armors and weapons that have their own advantages (Higher chance for successful attack? Higher damage? More defense? More movement points? You can mix and match to your hearts content)
+ The factions have highly unique abilities and units. One can use spells on its units in combat, one doesn't use food, another can force other factions out of the marketplace, one can turn dead enemy units in food supplies, and more. Also many minor factions (like city states if you have played Civ V) that all have their own unique unit and benefits.
+ A tech web that forces you to debate on what to unlock. There are many options and after a (short) amount are unlocked, you unlock the next chunk of techs to pick from (called eras in game). This means that there will be many techs left from the previous era that you can still unlock, along with this new era stuff you just unlocked, making you choose between many beneficial techs. There is also a rising cost of all techs, keeping you from flying through 5 techs in only 7 turns.
Cons
- The game crashes. A lot. I think I've had around 30 crashes in 50 hours of playing. Lowering the settings seems to reduce the occurrence of crashes
. Fast loading times and autosave every turn keep this from turning into table flipping rage, but players still shouldn't have to put up with it.
- There is a steep learning curve and the game is in
need of a better education system. It has a tutorial yes, but when you are done with that there is no "new player" option to add to matches, something to bridge the gap between brand new player and someone who knows all the systems at play. It has an encyclopedia that you can open, but it is bare bones and really needs much more content (also, it alt+tabs you out of the game and open it in your browser. Come on, put your encyclopedia IN the game). You'll pretty much have to do your own research with online guides and google. You'll struggle through your first couple games due to a thousand little things that you haven't learned yet.
- A couple "nitpicky" cons: There is this thing in diplomacy (all diplomatic actions cost a currency called influence) where you can give a faction a compliment or warning to decrease the cost of future friendly or hostile diplomatic actions. I can see how this is trying to lean players away from making quick and abrupt changes to the relationship between factions, but in my experience it is very small decreases in the cost so I just never used it, instead paying small price increases just to do what was more convenient.
- The battle system is...well it isn't
but I don't particularly like it. When two armies fight it turns into a turn based battle lasting 6 turns (these 6 turns are within the battle system, so the battle will finish within 1 turn outside of the battle system). You can make precise decisions within the battle, like have my 2 archers attack this guy, have the pikeman mob the enemy leader, have my support unit heal my leader, etc. Except it can actually be pretty hard to make your army do what you want it to do. You and your opponent give all your units orders first, and then all those orders play out. This means you can have sometimes up to 10 or 12 units all going out and fulfilling their orders one after another. This means that if something unexpected happens, someone lands some critical hits and an enemy dies quicker that anticipated, your units won't be able to fulfill the orders you gave them and they will decide what they should do instead, which never seems to line up with what I would have wanted them to do. You can also just quickly auto-resolve battle without doing any fine details if you don't want to go into a long battle, but you take some risks with doing so.
+/- Multiplayer. I have not played ANY multiplayer in this game. It might work flawlessly or it might be a broken mess. You'll have to get that information from another review.
Although it seems I dragged on with some of the cons, I love this game and fully expect to get hundreds of hours out of it. The art direction/lore is phenomenal and some of the best I've seen in a game, and there are a lot of systems at play that allow for experimentation and that you can sink your teeth into. I would have happily paid a full $60 for this so whatever price it is selling at now, it's worth it.

Still a more sportlike experience than anything EA has to offer, and no loot chests.

Imagine Endless Space combined with a fantasy-style civilization and you'll have this game.
There's going to be a lot of comparisons to Civilization here. The largest and most obvious difference happens before you even start the game. Instead of "customizing" your civilization a la Civ:BE, or just randomly picking one from Civ 5, you have the option of picking a prebuilt race or making your own using a point-buy system. The differences are huge and actually define the race, instead of being restricted to a unique unit or hardly game-changing mechanic. You can play as the dead dudes who are sealed inside their armor who live off of dust, granting a huge bonus to income and negating the need for food, or play as the wandering merchants who can literally move their cities around the map if needed.
Once you fire up the game, you start with a military and a settler, much like Civilization. The difference, however, is the fact you are restricted to colonizing a "region" instead of just placing a bunch of cities in a crazy pattern to try and min/max your coverage. Strategic and Luxury resources don’t even have to be inside your city limits. Instead you build a building on them, no matter where they are in the region. Instead of harvesting and "having" x resource, you now harvest a certain amount of x resource a turn. This makes it extremely hard to go back to Civilization because I like this system so much better.
The armies in the game are exactly the same as Endless Space. You have a limit based on your technology on how many units you can fit into an "army" and you can assign a hero to guide them. Combat turns into a miniature battleground like a stage from many other games, and has a miniature system that is serviceable and interesting in its own right. Units themselves are interesting. Instead of having a crazy large selection of units (civilization), every cavitation has 4-6 units. Each unit can be customized greatly, though, by choosing weapons, armor, and accessories depending on your level of technology.
All in all I'd definitely pick this one up if you're a fan of the genre, and I'd recommend it twice as much if you loved Endless Space and wanted to see a land-based version.

Though recommend 'yes' with a few caveats.
Let's get the easy ones out of the way. It looks very nice. The zoom controls seamlessly run from a overview-from-orbit kinda map to 'hey look, that soldier actually changed his sword on that upgrade' close ups.
The UI is well thought out, easy and intuitively. I would have liked a few more overview screens (like, in what region can I find what resource/minor factions/number of villages) and it works - which is a nice change from some games.
The backstory is okay - I am curious enough to find out more, yet it isn't something thrilling like SMAC had. Still, it's cool enough, different enough, but nothing that stands out.
There are a few things I find lacking. Not 'don't buy it' lacking, but more curious-raise-eyebrow lacking. For instance - why are there different movies for introducing each faction, but no ending movies for the various ends?
Now - to the caveats.
At first glance, I thought that the different factions played REALLY different and was pleasantly surprised. I started the game with the Broken Lords and the the Necrophages. I liked how I as a player was more or less forced to adapt a game srategy that 'came with' the faction - more or less. But, I now have tackled all but the Cult - I am rethinking my earlyer observation. As it turns ou, almost all factions with the possible xception of the Necrophages can just use the same strategy - focus on dust (the currence of the gameworld) and buy your way out of everything. The faction differences are very minor. Roving Clans move their cities. WHy bother? The pillars of the Mages - influence on the game minimal.
Handling the minor factons too - first I ran around doing all the quests, only to find that razing the villages gave me more XP, was quicker and less of a fuss. On account of all factions being able to use the same strategy, chosing which minors to incorporate into my empire becomes a no-brainer. + dust (Delvers) + regeneration (Sisters of mercy) + loyalty (Eyeless Ones) and expansion can be doen at its fastes - or I found. Picking a fight wiht a minor factin seems to have NO effect hwatsoever or those reamining on the map. They do not become more militant - so there is no consequence of an agressive policy ot ethnic cleansing.
The techtree - I seem to find a few issues with it. For instance - there is too little advantage in the military units you can field - improving them through research is not really an option. Level them up is much, much more effective. Sure, there is the different gear, but there is little use for the various ones made of different materials. And with strategic resources being not that rare when (remember - focus on Dust) you can just buy them off other factions or the marketplace, it's not a real 'weighing of options'.
There are AI issues too. Why does any AI faction completely ignore the ruins/ Why, after I have taken 80% of their regions, do they still (all of them! refuse flat out a truce, unless I pay them a massive amount of resources/tech/whatnot? Thta's just stupid.
Why do all AI factions rush into peace, treaties, map exchange and whathave you only to retreat from those without any obvious provocation? If an AI faction is stated as being 'terrified' of me because of its lacking military forces, how on earth does that compute in "hey, we had peace, we had trade and research treaties - this means war!" and that's always. I purposefully tried to remain at peace with all but no matter how I placate the AI, war is the end result. It makes no sence.
Am am ignoring the few remaining bugs - they are nothing more than a nuisance and will be solved anytime soon, so that's not the issue here.
All in all - I think this is a work of love, it has potential out the wazoo, the combat system is nifty, but consider this if you are looking for your next 4X fix.

Updated April 1st Release:
This is NOT a full release of a game.  It should be labeled as being in BETA at best.  Models and environment are top-notch.  Dino attacks still need some serious work.  Simple things like a drag-and-drop inventory aren't finished yet.  And most of all there's still no realistic interaction between the dinos, i.e. dinos preying on other dinos.  But its a lot better than it was.  It's getting there.  It has SO MUCH potential.
This may be one of my all-time favorite games. But its not for everyone. It's like being a cop, I suspect. A midget cop in a barbarian cannibal universe. Armed with a big ♥♥♥♥ing gun. That you don't always have ammo for. So you hide in a trash can and watch them eat your friends and neighbors and wait for them to leave. So you can get the ammo left on their fly-blown corpses. So you can track those barbarian cannibals down and explode their livers. Then you take selfies with their dead bodies.
Early Release Review:
I will say up front that this is a hunting game.  You can spend a lot of time where nothing happens.  Ammo can be feast or famine, as it
be in a survival game.  The game pays off for those with patience and persistence.  You can sprint around so long as you hear nothing.  When you hear raptors, you have to slow down.  Move away.  "Make like a hole in the water."
Despite its myriad of disastrous alpha bugs and severe lack of content, I LOVE this game.  The environment is best I've ever seen.  There's a real feeling of terror when you hear a pack of raptors and have 2 shells left.  Or you're solo armed modestly with a Tyrannosaur  20m that has your scent.  Surviving encounters like this and the eventual vengeance exacted through patience and planning is exhilarating.  Teaming up and taking down a T-rex is fantastic fun.
Weapons are at the settlements.  Download a basic map that shows the settlement locs and you'll have a gun in no time.  Ammo is found randomly in the wild.  Then find someone you can tag along with and work with them to get camo and ammo.  Once you've done this, the game really opens up for you.  Shoot for the heart/lungs/spine.
.  Work for a clean LOS to the target and reveal yourself at > 10 meters so they come straight at you, exposing their chest for a killshot.

Discovered this game when a popular MMO I play went down for an extended maintenance. Me and my guild were looking for something to pass the time and this was a cheap and hilarious distraction. 100% Orange Juice is a board game combining elements of Mario Party, Sorry! and Sonic Shuffle (remember that?) infused with the personality of characters from publisher Fruitbat Factory's various other games.
The object is to go around the board collecting golden stars and winning fights with mobs, bosses and other players. Once you have met a specific goal (# of stars or # of wins) you can land on a home space to obtain a Star. Do this 5 times and you win! Travel around the board is done via dice rolls and the occassional warp space, and battles are done via cards. The battle system is actually quite deep for a game like this; you have ATK, DEF and EVA stats to consider, ability cards to play and a unique "Defend or Evade" mechanic which allows you to try and dodge an attack at the risk of taking the full brunt of it.
While the mechanics of the game are satisfying enough, they aren't perfect. For example, there is no tutorial that I could find; you must simply dive in and learn. Sometimes this can be fun, but others may be frustrated by this. The terminology is also confusing as you want to obtain golden stars, which are like currency for meeting goals, and the main stars used like victory points. Changing one of these would make games easier to understand.
My big problem with this game is its longevity. This is a multiplayer game at heart best played with friends or in an online party. There is a campaign, but from what I've found the CPU is just too overpowered and 'lucky', There's also a wealth of content to unlock like extra characters, cards, and miscellany, but almost all of it is too expensive. Only the serious diehard is going to earn the ridiculous amount of in game currency to buy items. Don't forget the obscene amount of DLC characters, all displayed in the game's store.
Story - 1/5 Each character has a little mini story for the campaign, but good luck beating the CPU.
Graphics - 5/5 Adorable art style that never gets old.
Audio - 5/5 Each character has theme music that plays when they score, keeping things fresh.
Gameplay - 5/5 Once learned games become addictingly fun. Battle mechanics are in-depth too.
Replay - 2/5 Most content is locked behind in-game or real currency.
Overall - 4/5 Grab some friends or join a public lobby and prepare to get stuck in to this addictive board game. It's really a 'one more match' type of experience that could be all the better with better access to content.

>Better sense of direction: compared to previous titles oblivion tends to hold your hand a bit more in telling you where to go.
>Guilds: the questlines from the guilds in this game are insanely good, especially the dark brotherhood.
>Mods: lots of ones out there that do all kinds of cool things which are easier to install with a quick internet search thanks to the massive community for this game.
>Voice acting, a lot of people complain about it but to me it is a breath of fresh air as coming from morrowind which was very text intensive I was greateful for words to be spoken
>Fast Travel!!! need i say more? XD
>Game interface has been made a lot more user friendly as well compared to previous titles in the series.
>Expansions/DLC: They are epic!!!! A secret pirate cave, a vampire manor, the knights of nine!  aswell as the new shivering isles  to explore. (yeah...the horse armour sucked... especially when it would change the beloved shadowmere horse :()
Mixed:
> Graphics are pretty decent except for the model faces, which look bloated and ugly. Decent Mods out there though fix this (blockhead) etc etc
Cons:
>The Main story: To be honest this is the only fault i had with oblivion, i felt the main quest line was very boring and dull especially when you have to constantly close oblivion gates all the time, it got very repetitve regarding this which then made the game feel like a chore for a bit. Also the characters involved around the main quest line did not really have any impact apart from the king.
Overall I feel oblivion made massive improvements to the series in all aspects apart from the main story which just sucked in my opinion, maybe i have been spoilt by how good the morrowind story was, meh who knows. Apart from this the game is a complete gem and all elder scrolls fans should give it a chance :D

Pros: World is massive.
- Sounds are fantastic, and scary. Gunfire sounds extremely well in this game. You can hear a fellow hunter over 800m away fire round after round as he is swarmed by raptors.  Raptors sound great and you can hear them close in on you.
-Terrain does what it should, the forest and different areas are very dense with foilage. So raptors can get real close to you without you seeing them. Stealth is a MAJOR part of gameplay.
-The community seems very friendly and willing to help you or talk with you. Almost every game ive joined ive left adding a friend on steam.  Hunting together is extremely fun and has saved my life a few times being in a larger group. In that same note, ive seen 2 t-rexs tear up a crowd of players in a valley i was attempting to join up with.
-The actual hunting can be really fun, as these dinosaurs can be tracked across the entire map, provided your skilled enough to keep their trail. It looks similiar to what i believe evolve is going to have for tracks. You can use dino calls, you scavenge for your gear like a dayz game, but your customizing and inventory is like an old school resident evil. Not much to it yet, there are scopes and different weapons but not many so far. 1 bow, 1 pistol, 2 rifles, 1 shotgun. different rounds for them liek the shotty has buck and slug.
The cons:
-DINO AI..(sometimes)......it needs patching but potential is there. A dinosaur can hear you, see you, and even track you. The raptors work in packs and can provide an issue because you do seem to get attacked by them from multpile directions. However, sometimes they charge past you, or walk right by you even tho your not hidden, they walk funny up hills, they sometimes aimlessly make wierd turns,The trex seems to have a few malfunctions aswell. Theres only 3 dinosaurs at the moment, with what i assume is ALOT more to come. SOmetimes dinosaurs stand there or get stuck and you can take them down easily. Other times, you get killed and never even saw it coming. Due to the small amount of species in the game thus far, their interactions from what i have seen are minimal. Smaller dinos run away from the big one. I would love to see the world become more alive in future updates. Maybe come over a hill and find a pack of raptors attacking a herd of herbavores or a single trex. I wish the raptors necks would turn to acknowldge you, the seem very rigid at times. other times its fine.
Conclusion
Its in alpha, and its already as solid as the carnivors games we had on pc in the early 2000s. Even with the bugs, that we all know alphas must go through, this game is a blast, and i do recommend it alsong as you dont get mad easily and can undertsand there will be problems as the game polishes out. I am having a blast though.
