Defending reduces the damage by the number you rolled while evading totally cancels the damage if your roll is higher, if not you totally lose fight and stars . You can also use Hyper Cards at fights if they're available. Hyper Cards are different for all characters. At the start you automatically needed to collect stars but after you've done that you can choose your own missions. Those are called karmas. You need to done five karmas and you win. This game has a near infinite amount of replayability, and a near infinite amount of play styles. Sometimes people will bombard your planet with railgun shots on the second turn, and sometimes no shots will be fired until somebody calls in an asteroid. The tech tree fits the length of the game perfectly, as well as it is almost 100% balanced. The new upgrade feature really adds another dimension to the optimal play-style, as it allows for more energy and materials to be produced in a smaller area. The array of weapons that you can arm your planet with is grand, be it with pinpoint accuracy lasers or homing missiles. One of the best, but most complicated parts of the combat system is the gravity of the planets and the sun. You could aim a shot so that it looks like it will be spot on, but then the planets will orbit and gravity will throw the shot out of the system. All in all, this game was definately a 10/10, I hope to see many new features in the future.

My "blind let's play" video of my first game:
You'll need to consider a few things before buying the game close to the early access release date:
1. Early Access here means that - it's very early days yet. There's lots to things to do, but not much depth. Just exploring the one island won't take long, but you can spend as much time as you want building and drawing etc.
2. The drawing element is essentially an in-game paint programme, with the ability to add basic animation frames if you want. Right now you can edit/draw anything you're holding in your inventory (if you have picked up the Witch Brush), plus you get to draw your character when you first start playing.
3. There'll be bugs - unoptimised graphics, a couple of  spelling mistakes, features that don't seem to work - but they'll get fixed. No full crashes, but did have to reload quite a bit to clear any built-up lag, though.
4. The building isn't as intuitive as Minecraft, with (simple) menus to select shapes and so on, but once you get the hang of it you can build blocky structures easily. You can alter the default cube to stuff like ramps, arches and flat bits too.
5. You don't get given all the building/colouring tools at the start - you need to go out and find them in the world on scrolls. Plus, everything you build requires energy, which uses up very fast and then slowly fills back up again. You can find items that increase your max energy, but at the start of the game you're very limited (This applies to story mode - I don't know yet if sandbox mode will have this limitation).
6. Fighting is very basic. You start with fists but I recommend finding an axe!
Sketch Tales is already a lot of fun and shows amazing potential but right now it's very rough around the edges. I recommend it, but I'm most interested in what's to come. Multiplayer, when it happens, should be a riot.

Having nearly reached 1000 play hours I figured let's make a review.
Let's start with the vanilla game. Even without any DLC's there's a steep learning curve. Tutorials are very basic and some factors are simply left out, so even if you would play each tutorial a million times until you get it, you're still left with things that simply aren't covered. But if you don't mind starting over and over many times, you'll eventually get it.
There's many complaints that the vanilla game is basically a demo version of the full game. Given the insane amount of DLC, this is certainly true. However even without DLC there is enough to this game to play for many, many hours. You'll just be stuck in Europe. If your character reverts to pagan or islam, or has a tribal culture the game will stop if you do not have the correct DLC to play these. This can be seen as a cheap way to force players to buy the DLC. I think I had about 100-150 hours into the vanilla game before I bought my first DLC. So it's not necessarily true. There's enough to do, even if you can only play Christian rulers with Feudal cultures.
Personally I consider the Swords of Islam and the Old Gods DLC to be essential DLC's. Because it allows you to play Pagan and Muslem religion, and tribal cultures everywhere, thus opening up 95% of the world as playable territory. You can get the India DLC if you really want to play in that part of the world but I have to say after 1000 play hours I can't really say I miss it. Then I have Charlemagne, which I think is great because you can start in 769 where the world is far less developed, with more smaller realms and thus making it easier to carve out your own empire. But I would not call it essential. Finally there's the ruler designer, which one can argue should be included in the base game, but nonetheless I have to say it's nice to be able to customize your very first ruler, but I would also not call it essential.
Those are still the only DLC's I have so far and still I'm playing this game over and over again. Of course, it is all a matter of opinion and for you it might be different, but what I'm trying to say is don't believe that in order for the game to retain its replay value, you are forced to keep buying DLC.
To me the best part of this game is that you're not forced to do anything. You might be someone who believes gaining an enormous empire is what it's all about. I have certainly done that many times. And many times it failed halfway through, or broke apart at the seams after a few decades. Other times it thrived. But it can be equally interesting to play a count with just one or two lands, or a small-time duke, and going full out intrigue, trying to get your family members into positions of power by marriage and assassination, and then let them be the king while you are in the background not being an interesting target to anyone and just hunting and feasting each year. Or it could backfire hilariously and you lose everything your family build up in the past 200 years.
I would recommend this game to anyone to whom the idea of having half the world as a playground and then just starting the timer to see what happens is appealing. In my opinion there is some DLC you will require but most DLC by far is optional and well, if you have enough money, just get them if you really want more diseases or more random events or more options for your council members or more music or etc etc etc

THE SKINNYYY (FOR TL;DR)

+Diplomacy for the most part makes sense

-A bit of learning curve with having to learn the delicate intracisies of Feudalism and Norman French/Latin jargon
-RNG/Percent-based Roleplaying can be hilariously unforgiving - take your chances well!
-No Naval Battles
-Pesky Vikings....pesky, pesky Vikings
-So...much...DLC!!!
-AI During Wars can be a little weird and predictable
-Certain Gameplay features like de jure drift can be very finnicky and require careful planning
I was a long-time Total War fan before I stumbled onto this game - I still am a fan of the series - but holy God what can I say? How can I start with this game???
First of all the whole gameplay about it is EXACTLY what I wanted in Medieval II: Total War, it has a nice blend of Grand Strategy, RTS and Roleplaying elements all in a perfect little blender - it really does incorporate many genres into one and it does it really, really well!
However I will come right out and say this game will cost you a pretty penny, although I can't really think of any DLC that is totally useless, almost every DLC comes with some nice gameplay bonuses that flesh the game out unfortunately the fact that getting all the DLC will amount to something ridiculous like $120 total! That is just outrageous, but the game just on its own or with a few of the DLC - not all of them is good enough! For example I do not own the Sunset Invasion DLC and the game is just perfect as is.
This game really is almost like a Game of Thrones simulator and unlike in other previous Total War titles Diplomacy and decision making at a slow pace really do matter - you can't declare war for no real good reason - everything has a Casus Belli, every piece of land is de jure attached to a Duchy - and that Duchy to a Kingdom's demesne - you will really have to get the Norman French and Latin words down, honestly when I first started playing I had no idea what I was doing and even after utilizing the Tutorial I still had a very feeble grasp of what I was doing, not only that but the focus of the game is NOT to conquer the World but to see your DYNASTY thrive and stay alive throughout the generations!!!  So...
This game is very GUIDE heavy! You NEED to read strategies, guides, ask questions to the community's veterans, good thing is no one is toxic on the Steam Community so you can happily ask away questions no matter how stupid they may sound!
Once you get over the learning curve however the game is smooth sailing from there, and the fact that you can start the game from any specific year, month, day (except for the Charlemagne and Viking Age starts) is also refreshing too! Adds a nice little cool factor when you get the chance to play as your favorite historical character at whatever stage their life is - wanna play as Llwelyn ap Gruffydd just as he was starting his offensives against the English? You can do it - wanna play as Robert the Bruce right after he reclaimed Scotland's throne? You can do it, wanna play as the Independent Duchy of Brittany? Or the Kingdom of Jerusalem? You can friggin do it!
Paradox have an almost perfectly, historically accurate game, anything though from the Charlemagne or Viking Age start is more like 70% historically accurate - but that's just due to the nature of record keeping during those turbulent times rather than a lack of effort on Paradox's part.
If you are a grand strategy fan that loves a bit of rping seriously get this game and you will lose whatever social life you already have to begin with, it's time to muster the banners, get those useless Barons working and write a letter of assistance to that useless double-chinned King that you married his ugly daughter just for that political alliance - you've got Crusading to do! DEUS VULT!

Those who don't remember the classics and salivate at the prospect of creating their own character in Sonic Forces, and then those who remember the platforming prowess it took to take on flying battery zone in an actual game.
Sonic Mania is for the latter.
Sonic Mania is for the true believers who never gave up on the blue blur releasing one more platforming hit backed with 90's electronica. I've played about two hours of this game and, when I realized I had to be awake for work in 5 hours, managed to pull myself away for some pesky sleep. I am already thoroughly enjoying the game, despite the many frustrations of hunting massive, nearly unstoppable killing machines. I have yet to take down a Tyrannosaurus or a Triceratops, but can effectively defend myself against a Utahraptor or two.
I'll say this, keep in the front of your thoughts that this game is in EARLY ACCESS, which translates to EARLY DEVELOPMENT and the people behind its creation are still hard at work on it. That said, I have faith that we'll continue to see updates as regularly as they can manage and anything they do, at this point, is going to improve the playability/enjoyment.
There is a steep learning curve here. It really is a brutal, primal hunting game. You're not meant to walk into a world ruled by giant, flesh-hungry reptiles and come out an hour later not having been repeatedly mauled with a T. Rex head on your trophy wall. It's unrealistic to purchase this game and expect to kill everything you set your sights on.
You start with a bow. Arrows do not penetrate dinosaur skulls.
If you want a serious challenge, then opt in and support these folks and help make the game better. If you buy it, hop in and being killed often frustrates you too greatly, just come back in a month and see what's changed.
Some notes on possible improvements (which I'll submit as Feedback in the game, as well):
- For a dinosaur hunter, stamina is in short supply. I'm pretty sure if I was being chased by an eating machine, I could run  while longer than these poor saps.
- Ammunition stacking is a MUST (Everyone has mentioned this, I know).
- Swimming sure would improve my chances of not being dinochow.
- Being able to jump would be an excellent benefit.
- A starter knife would be excellent.
- "Harvesting" would be much improved if we were harvesting useful materials from dinosaurs we've killed.
- Retrieving arrows when "harvesting" would be great.
- Traps would be really great to see.
- Character customization.
I'm sure there will be tons more suggestions, but you all keep up the great work. Thanks!

My first impression of the game was how amazing it looks, and the sounds get you really into it. Finding my first crate wasn't hard thanks to the map piece you spawn with, and soon enough i killed a couple utharaptors. The constant struggle to track animals and don't get killed make it both a hunting game and a survival game, but i think that's cool. The dinosaurs look really good, and if you've been lying in a bush and looking at a T-rex close up as many times as i, you know how terrifying they are. Just hearing the footsteps of the t-rex is enough to awaken all senses and make you hide in a bush to localize it. The way the T-rex and Utharaptors act is awesome, they track you if you run, or if they hear you walk normally, and follow your smell if you're not careful. However the Triceratops act a bit strange in my opinion. The guide said they might be agressive, but after MANY encounters both from far away and the point when they step on you, they all just run away, and then they run. Far. Really far. other than that the world is pretty cool, awesome with the volcano in the middle and bases that's been destroyed. Been playing the game with a friend for a whole weekend + 1 day after school (maybe 20 hours) and even though i get the best guns and gear, i have to be careful not to get overrun by a pack of raptors, which has happened a few times when i get cocky. Luckily i just have to go back where i died and pick up my stuff again (if nobody's stolen it, i played on a server with just my friend). Now we've done most of the things although we haven't cared to run across the map after a triceratops that's been hit, and only managed to kill 1 T-rex, but 20 hours of gameplay and more to come is more than you get from many other games that costs more. Now we're just waiting for the next patch with new dinosaurs. I recommend this game for anyone who likes survival games and wants a game for the weekend packed with scary moments, traces of adrenaline at times and beautiful graphics sprinkled on top.

When I started reading reviews calling this "the greatest RPG ever made," and even "the greatest GAME ever made," I had to  try it. Then I played the game and I felt kind of disappointed. It seemed extremely difficult and I wasn't used to getting the cold shoulder from a game. By that I mean compared to most games this one does not hold your hand, you won't get arrows pointing you in the direction you need to go, everything you need to know is actually in the dialogue and/or read in notes and books (and sometimes a rare hint from the narrator). I kept feeling confused on where to go and who to talk to and the quest system seemed kind of clunky and hard to understand at first.
I'm ashamed to admit, I asked for a refund at about the hour and a half mark. Then I went a couple days thinking about the game and that I couldn't believe I couldn't get into it. And then I thought about it again and again and realized that something was nagging at me and I couldn't stop thinking about it.
So yeah... I bought the game again. I looked up tips this time around on which characters people like in their party and which skills really help early game (Lone Wolf changed everything for me). I started to appreciate the detail and get into the story, and I have to say, the story is absolutely amazing. Well, there is way too much to say about this one. I’ll try my best to do it justice. First, I’d like to say that I’m quite happy to see a cRPG receive as much attention as this one is getting. I only discovered this genre of RPG fairly recently through a friend. So I am by no means an old-timer or anything like that, and to be honest I brushed this genre aside up until a year ago. Only then did I realize just how vacant the genre is of games. They started making a comeback  since around 2014-ish with the first Original Sin, Wasteland 2 and Pillars of Eternity. But before then? The genre was pretty much dead silent with virtually no games that gained any traction whatsoever. The old and eulogized Infinity Engine games casting a looming shadow over the genre probably didn’t help all that much too. What I can say though is that Divinity Original Sin 2 has rejuvenated the genre for me. It has outdone and even outclassed some RPGs and most certainly today’s AAA standard for what RPGs should be like.
Divinity Original Sin II allows for actual roleplaying, not only that, it also encourages it. Now you might say, “Oh, so what? You’re supposed to roleplay in an RPG.”  In which case you’re right, but unlike most RPGs of late Divinity Original Sin 2 does not need players to constantly remind themselves that they are roleplaying... in a Roleplaying game. Divinity Original Sin 2 perpetually imposes roleplaying onto players. Now this might not be anything new to the cRPG genre but it definitely isn’t a common design in the popular RPGs of the last decade or so. If you find this to be an exaggerated claim, then I can only urge you to experience it for yourself.
So now that I’ve ineptly reaffirmed a key characteristic of the cRPG genre so that we’re somewhat on the same page, we can finally get to the part where I over-elaborate. I will now tell you why I like this game so much.
The game encourages players to learn its systems and mechanics and solve all sorts of conflict in creative and unusual ways, whether it’s in combat, an NPC interaction, or finding the next clue or way forward in a quest. The first area in the game does a great job at properly introducing players to all these systems they’ll be using and to what they will be doing for the rest of the game. The combat is turn-based and usually plays out like a puzzle that requires players to apply their acquired knowledge of the systems and rules to beat the odds. The game rewards the player who is proactive in their strategies before battle and one who can shift tactics in reaction to unpredictable circumstances. And trust me, there will be an excessive amount of these unpredictable circumstances and scenarios that neither you or any other player could possibly account for. So prepare to load older saves a lot. Divinity Original Sin II will ask for a lot of trial and error, and I can see how this can put some people off. The first playthrough I played was with a buddy and it was riddled with retries and going back to older saves to try and undo mistakes we made. It was really hard to account for every possible fail state or every possible decision that might change the outcome of some quest or somehow influence an NPC’s attitude towards you.   Sometimes we would try to save a certain NPC or restore an occurence but realize that reloading the save file might result in too much progress lost.  More often than not, predicaments are too far gone to be salvageable and so we ended up mostly just rolling with the mess we were making. Larian Studios has excelled at creating an emergent narrative for players, and I can attest to it. Divinity Original Sin 2 makes the player aware of their very strong role in determining the outcome of the story that unfolds. As you play, you become aware of all the possible choices one might make, and you realize the level of authorship that is given to you. The choices, the reactivity, and writing that avoids simply pitting good versus evil, all help accentuate the flexibility the game gives to its players and incites them to contemplate their alignment on matters in the game. But while the player might have a surprising amount of agency over the story, I lost track of how much control I actually had. I sometimes didn’t know what would influence what, but I vaguely knew that my decisions would influence something in some way. Some decisions I made or decisions I didn’t make led to causing a development I had no idea would occur. The writing doesn't make it any easier. It's really hard to pick sides, as factions are constantly shown in a different light (they are never all good or all evil), and some choices result in equally grim situations. It’s tough to align yourself to be either good, lawful, or all bad. I suspect most players will probably end up being some mangled mixture of hero and bad guy, rather than one type of alignment. Of course, this isn’t bad or anything but it sure is taxing and tiring to just stay afloat in such a sea of chaos. When I would lose track of certain quest developments, I would refer back to the cryptic quest log, only to quickly close it before it had drained me of all certainty. And it’s not like the game just constantly dumps tons of exposition onto the player that overwhelms, but rather it’s the sheer amount of story developments, decisions, character progression, where to go, and what quests are semi-done or are done but you didn’t notice, that make some aspects I need to take note of become seemingly imperceptible. It’s intense. This sometimes would come into conflict with how I wanted to align my character.  There would be times when I accidently got lucky and did something I would have done if I knew what was at stake. A good example that comes to mind would be when me and my buddy had to venture down into some sewers(One important thing to note is that we were trying to be evil and villainous at every turn, absorbing souls, choosing the villain dialogue option whenever we had the chance, straight up killing any NPC we didn’t like, and so forth. It was a lot of fun). So we end up killing the entire population of a city, accidentally.  We weren’t paying attention. Yes, we definitely are to blame for our negligence. The game told us that person X was smuggling Deathfog, but we read that in a letter or something in Driftwood 20 hours prior to all this, and only now it gets mentioned? It kind of didn’t sink in until my dwarven party member turned the valve. Of course, this was totally in line with our evil intent on the world, so we just went along with it. It made sense for us. But what if we were trying to be the good guys? That might not have gone all that well. I guess that’s the beauty of it all, right?
As for the other stuff:
The music is fantastic and can really set the tone for the different areas.  The game has some great areas with a wide array of environments ranging from jungles, farmlands, beaches, inter-dimensional planes, and so on. The combat is great, I really had a lot of fun with it. I don’t really share the gripes other people have with some aspects, such as how the armor works, maybe because I have not played the first game. From what I’ve seen, most people have a problem with how it has changed the pacing of combat but maybe it’s just different, not necessarily worse. But once again, I don’t know what changed so I guess I’m exempt from giving Original Sin 2’s combat too much praise.
So to conclude, Divinity Original Sin II is one of the best RPGs I’ve played. I highly recommend this game. It might not be the best choice if you’re new to cRPGs but it’s definitely one you should play at some point. I would have recommended it for newcomers to the genre. The ease of use and great introductory first act all count in favor of this, but I felt like the game might appear too cluttered in later areas with too many pieces to keep track of. Tyranny would be a better start, in my opinion.

tldr; I'm recommending this game, but only if you're a fan of Avalanche Studio's other hunting sim, theHunter, and games with roguelike death mechanics, like DayZ or Dark Souls, and only if you'd like to support the development of the game. It's at a point that I would consider very early development.
After only playing this game for a little over an hour, I can say it's extremely challenging in it's current form. If you're adverse to dying a lot early on in a game, then this isn't for you. Unlike in theHunter, everything in these hunting grounds is in reality hunting you, and it's your job to avoid them as best you can, at least until you can get a better weapon than the crappy bow you start with.
When you first spawn, you're presented with the all too familiar tracking/GPS tool you use in theHunter. In this it's called the Settlersmate, the premise of the game being you're a convict, banished to an island on a planet called Primal Eden, and tasked with "cleaning up" the island of it's wild life. In front of you is what appears to be the pod you are dropped onto the planet in. It contains an improvised bow, 10 arrows and a map fragment. That's your starting kit, but don't expect to be taking down a lot with it. It does very little to most of the inhabitants of this paradise, other than to serve to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off. The map fragment uncovers a small, random portion of the map, which is mostly blanketed by a 'fog of war'.
From then on, you're pretty much on your own to roam around the map. Keep a sharp eye on your Settlersmate, because there are supply crates that can contain ammunition, possibly weapons (although I've only ever found the starter bows), and occasionally new items of clothing scattered about, and a few POIs you can stumble across that usually have loot crates, and even a little bit of lore.
If you're
lucky enough to come across any dino activity, it works pretty much the same as in theHunter. You get an audible queue from your Settlersmate and you can left click to analyze the sound or track marks.
This game mixes the hunting simulation of theHunter with roguelike elements of games akin to DayZ (if the zombies were gaint eating machines that can run at 30mph). You die, you respawn in a random location on the map (which looks to be quite enormous), with the starter kit.
Pros:
Cons:
Extreme levels of challenge makes this a game not everyone will like, but if you're a fan of Avalanche's other hunting sim, you might enjoy the reversal of roles.

I am impressed with Endless Legend. Looks great. Plays well. Easy to get into (for a 4X game).
The UI at nearly every level is clean, crisp, and informative. Every bit what I've come to expect from Amplitude.
I love the factions. Not only are they colorful, but have distinct gameplay. It isn't just a "take basic race, add 1-2 bonuses" formula. You have one with movable cities, another grows population with corpses, and another uses Dust (currency) as its only food source. Plus each faction has its own tailored Quests to complete, which further drive the story behind them.
Of course, if it is a 4X fantasy then there have to be Hero units to hire for leading armies and governing cities. EL heroes are generally what you'd expect. One thing that is different is how items are handled. Hero equipment is treated like upgrades. So if a hero finds a powerful sword, he doesn't actually get it. The find just unlocks the upgrade. You will have to send him back home and pay to equip him. Annoying in short term, but a boon long term; if you got the resources, all your heroes could have the upgrade.
I like the minor factions. If you're a Civ5 player, think of these as a cross between a barbarian camp and a city-state. They spawn hostiles. But if you pacify them, you can someday get them to start working for you. There are a lot of different minor factions in the game, most of them typical fantasy monsters.
The world map is beautiful. The artwork is colorful and special spaces distinct. It has a tactical boardgame design to it, which I do appreciate. The fact that hexes can have different heights creates some interesting maneuvers. Flying units are even more valuable here.
The tactical turn-based combat is not as in-depth as a game like Age of Wonders III. I am okay with that, to be honest. EL is not as reliant on warfare (though like any 4X it is a big part). And what EL offers for combat is very well designed. Units can vary widely. Terrain and elevation matters. The combat AI is exceptional at suggesting targets and automatically re-targeting in mid-combat (say, if the first enemy is killed), rarely making mistakes. I wish more games had this kind of combat AI.
Research is pretty straightforward. Instead of a tree, you have a group of techs to choose from. Research enough techs and you unlock the next tier, giving you another collection to pick from. Ever wanted a game like DEFCON except in space and with giant planetary railguns? No? Well apparently these guys did and it's awesome.
This game is like DEFCON except if M.A.D. wasn't a thing but instead people had no idea how to actually hit each other nor what to actually hit in the first place. You be launching giant, hypervelocity masses towards the enemy planet only for it to fly way off course and hit the next planet over, or be blocked by a giant planet between you and the enemy planet, or slingshot around the sun, and miss your own planet by inches. Its equivalent to launching nukes to Russia only for it to hit South America instead, and getting one nuke to hit the targeted country out of the hundreds you launched, not even being sure if you hit anything remotely important.
You also have to manage the resources just to fire said giant, hypervelocity masses, and build and research other weapons with their own advantages and disadvantages.
Could definitely use a better interface but at the same time could be much worse, and being it's early access it's probably on the radar.
If you liked DEFCON it's a definite buy.

And be warned about the asteroid superweapon: it only fires from ONE point in the asteroid field, so its usefulness varies with where in the system your enemies are in relation to it.

One of the best games I've ever played from a new developer. It takes a few minutes to really understand what's going on and where to go, but once you grasp the concept of how it's played, the rest comes naturally. I suggest it to anyone who's in the mood for a challenging game without a whole lot of committment.

"Only If" I knew what was actually going on.
Only If is, at its core, an "escape the room" game while at the same time deviating from the "find the item(s), move to next area" model. Its approach is unique, but there is quite a bit of work to be done.
The good: Barring the lack of subtitles to completely understand what's going on, being trapped by the disembodied voice of a maniac was way funnier than it should have been. The dialogue is nonsensical at certain points, but I appreciated the banter between the protagonist and his capturer. As I mentioned earlier, it's not a game where you have to collect an assortment of items and mix and match to move onwards so I appreciated that. Even though it was a bit disorientating sometimes, the surreality of it was also a big plus for me.
The bad: The main issue is the lack of "game elements". By this I mean that the game is played solely by ear, so to speak. There are a few instructions, like c to crouch and shift to run, but other than that you have to figure out the rest on your own. While experimenting is fun in and of itself, it is a little frustrating when you have to utterly guess at what to do next. One instance is the fact that at certain points in the game, you must type out an answer but there is no indication anywhere that keystrokes are being registered and recognized as a "typed answer". The platforming level is unintuitive.
There are other things I forgot to note as I played the game, but these were all the glaring pros and cons in my eyes.
I am actually glad I played this, but I wouldn't forward it to my friends as it's a bit, "out there"? However, for a gamer looking for something different, then you found it.

review:
AIPD is a rogue-like shoot-em-up game in which you have to survive waves of ever more intimidating enemies to make the game a whole lot more difficult on yourself and select a challenge. These include things such as: enemy powers upgraded, forever decreasing multiplier, you lose the ability to fire your weapons under certain circumstances, etc. It’s a simple idea but executed very well. You feel in control of your ship, it makes you really feel you are to blame whenever you die, unlike in many other games. Graphically it’s quite impressive, basically, everything has its own effect or whatnot with a bloom effect.
Basically, it’s what you’d expect from a rogue-like game. You play in a tight arena with ever increasing amounts and difficulties of enemies. Over time, you will get some crazy multipliers and unique weapons/ships, each one either adding or nerfing to the gameplay. Personally, I found some combos of weapon-ships to just be flat out over powered. Such as a quick nimble ship using a highly damaging weapon. I can quickly get out of trouble wether it’s by shooting my way out of there or flying away.
Pros:
Beautiful soundtrack
Amazing on-screen effects
Progressively challenging
Lots of ship-weapon combos
Can help reflex/action times
Fun
Cons:
Not really that many ships or weapons
You get to design your own scenario, but you will still need to pick all the challenges in the end.

As an expert in the field of paleontology I have a vast knowledge of dinosaurs, in particular the velociraptor; so therefore, I feel that I am in a strong position to express my thoughts on the hunting grounds of Primal Eden.
I arrived on this planet having agreed to fly over it for a small fee as a tour guide (of some sort). At no point did I believe that these people were remotely crazy enough to land the plane. I woke up on an abandoned runway having been knocked out via a blow to the head. The distant sound of a man and woman shouting at the top of their voices filled my entire body with dread and fear as I came around. I knew this was now a fight for survival!
As I moved swiftly and quietly through the thick, dense and foggy bush I hoped that I would find signs of life such as camps left over by previous people who dared venture to this ludicrous planet. Perhaps I could find some sort of radio or telephone that I could use to call for help. By now the valley around me filled with the unnerving sounds of various carnivores. The roars piercing my heart and sending tremors straight through my spine. There was no hope.
As I laid helplessly in a thick set plant I felt the horrifying thud as the ground started to shake. I then realised it was the same terror I had experienced some years ago in Jurassic Park. The thunderous sound began to get louder and louder. I then ran as fast as my legs would allow over the valley hill and found an abandoned camp called Sir Arthur’s Folley. To my delight and amazement I found a .700 rifle and 2 bullets. I do not like guns but I intended to survive this island as I have done twice previously. As I loaded the bullets the tyrannosaurus rex came crashing through the trees behind me…...I knew what had to be done.
I tried to throw a stone to distract the foul beast but to no avail. His head raised into the air as he then let of a rambunctious growl before charging at me. I immediately ran behind one the compounds concrete walls in fear of what was about to happen, with adrenaline pumping around my body I looked around the wall at the oncoming charge. I raised my rifle and shot the creature in the head! Nothing happened... I then ran back behind the wall where I realised my health was low from when I dropped down the small cliff into the camp. I sprayed myself with magic spray that made me feel revitalised and full of energy. The mighty head of the beast then clipped straight through the corner of the wall scaring the s**t out of me. “How the f**k can you do that” I angrily yelled at the beast. It then stood still so I took my shot, BANG, I hit the animal in the upper chest just below the neck. He let of an almighty howl as I punctured the left lung. As I aimed down the sight for one last time I pulled the trigger….nothing happened. I had no ammo.
I then thought LEG IT, so I ran down the hill until my stamina had deserted me. I laid down in a bush hoping the foul creature had not seen me. My heart was thumping and sweat was pouring from my entire body. The footsteps crashed down the hill behind me. I laid there motionless. The T Rex then stopped not knowing where I was. I had done it, I had got away from the beast when I then heard footsteps to my left. I looked to find a guy in a bright yellow shirt and orange trousers standing in my bush. I then slowly looked around at the T Rex as he then spotted me, charged me and then ate me. NOOOOOOOOO! The guy in yellow and orange clothes then proceeded to steal my gear and disappear into the night.
Hmmm, maybe I get into character a little too much when I play this game….It is an epic game especially when played with other people. Getting ambushed by raptors or five people running from two T Rex’s is sooo much fun! Awesome game that you must try.

I guess I'll write a few things about the game. TL:DR version at bottom, even that is long.
First things first, this is an EA release which means its full of issues and is incomplete as far as content goes. Visually it looks very good, and the sounds are good though there are a few glitches, especially when standing near someone who is trigger happy, or about to be eaten.  The issues I have no doubt will be ironed out but their release target of early March 2015 is rapidly approaching.  And as far as content, if this game ends up getting the same kind of attention to updates and additions as theHunter has, then we will not be wanting for different critters to hunt, or varying types of gear.
As far as the gameplay goes this is one of the most fun games I've played in quite a while, and doubly so when playing with friends. And you do need to play with some friends or at least make some and travel around in a group, as your suvival chances are very slim with no allies.  The only thing that becomes an issue when in a large group is ammunition, as there is usually a shortage for everyone, not like that is better for solo players however.
The problem here lies in the loot tables, or rather the amount of loot/ammo whatever that shows up in each box. The boxes need to have at least double the ammo available if not more, and there really is no point in having a stack of 1 round that you cannot merge into other stacks, same with healing sprays.(Fixed! You can now stack ammo and stuff, GJ Devs!)
Players shold be able to jump, and possibly climb low walls and rocks.
And lastly, as with theHunter, there really needs to be dedicated servers for this game, as the host/client connection issues that plague theHunter are present in this game, with players timing out or crashing every few minutes, it can become frustrating just to play for a few hours.
TL;DR version
Pros-
Amazingly fun with a group.
Good visuals, some of the scenery is quite beautiful.
Good sound, the sound of a T-Rex stomping near me makes my whole house shake with the sound turned up!
Great potential
Cons-
Incredibly high learning curve.
Exceptionally difficult almost futile to play solo, turning some gamers away, and others to hacking/exploits.
Obvious glitches and bugs that would cripple a live release (I expect they will fix this by release)
No Dedicated Servers, and with the crappy hosting/client system this will keep many players from fully experiencing the game.
Tiny pool of creatures to hunt (Obvious that more will be added)
Small pool of weapons (also expect this to change soon; WTF no .50 BMG? SRS GIEZ)
No combining stacks of ammo or healing sprays? (Fixed stacking now works!)
Very low loot tables, crates need at least double the ammo/healing loot if not more.
No jumping, climbing or swimming, cause these trained dinosaur hunters haven't learned that, and they can't even run very far.
Any idiot can hack the game, at the very least, hosts need to be able to ban players from their servers, as one bad experience can ruin the game for people.
Takeaway: Great fun with a few friends and easily worth 20 bucks.

Pros:
Intuitive combat system makes for interesting gameplay, especially when reinforcements are involved.
Summer/Winter shift forces the economy to remain dynamic, and winter turns can be difficult to struggle through.
AI Diplomacy works pretty well, though the values of tech/resources could be rebalanced.
Very customizable game settings: no two worlds will be the same (unless they use the same seed)
Research/Tech tree is expansive, and enables for longer paced games if needed
Unit customization is awesome. You can create new units from the templates of the old ones, but with new gear. It's cool.
Cons:
Occasional crash issues (will update review when resolved)
Not as much unit variety as I'd like to see. Sure you can create new versions of old units, but I want to see more variety in class.
Not that much variety in quests. A lot of them are just "Maintain this level of production for x resource for y turns". Gets kind of old.

Endless Legend is a beautifully designed 4X game that has potential to seperate from a genre who's template is bereft of value for most experienced gamers. Amplitude Studios introduces several clever mechanics, which, at first, will quell many 4X gamers' need for an experience beyond the rotting corpse of Sid Meier's Civilization.  After gaining a basic understanding of the mechanics and races introduced, which is a thoroughly enjoyable experience, the game quickly loses it's unique complexity becoming formulaic in execution and soulless down the stretch. Endless Legend does, however, display a promising foundation that could trancend into a redefing example. This possibilty is contingent upon the correct areas and weaknesses being addressed, mended, and expanded upon effectively before the inevitable reinvention of the genre.

It's everything Civ: Beyond Earth should be, and yet also a few things it's lucky to not be. It's not a perfect game, not by any means, but if you're a 4X fan then it's probably worth your time. If you're really craving a fantasy-themed Alpha Centauri-style game, this will fulfill that need. I'd recommend buying it on sale, personally, but if you really gotta scratch an itch, it'll be worth full price then.

This game is very fun and easy to get into. You control one of about 20 awesomenauts in a 3v3 match where you have to push through lanes by defeating droids and turrets, all the way to the opponents base. You have tanks, pushers, healers, harassers, and so on so every kind of player will find at least one character they will like.
Essentially, it's a 2D MOBA (think Dota and League of Legends) with a heavy emphasis on casual play, as well as co-op.
The game is far from dead and is reasonably active, but most of the people playing it now have been at it for quite some time. So if you're new and you're going to play this at an odd time (like the middle of the night), matchmaking could place you in a very one-sided game. Though that should change for at least a week or two after a sale, when there's an influx of new players to balance out matchmaking.
If you see this on sale, BUY IT. I guarantee you'll have a blast, especially if you're playing with friends. I'm personally picking up the Starstorm when it's next on sale.

Warframe is one of those games that you can tell the developers, Digital Extremes, really poured themselves into.  I'll try and do this game some justice in my review, kicking off with the good stuff.
First off, it is exactly what it sells itself as.  Space ninjas.  It is a crazy power trip, you are the definition of overpowered, and you can definitely feel it.  Over the shoulder camera views, run and gun, very fast paced as you carve a path of destruction through your enemies.  You travel around the solar system on your personal ship, running missions and gathering resources to expand your capabilities, arsenal, and Warframes.
Warframes themselves, are basically the classes and powersets you can pick.  They all follow some particular theme, and there is massive amount of customization available there as well.  All have an array of four fairly fantastic abilities, essentially "space magic!" and also a passive ability.  These abilities can range from outright damage, crowd control, support, and almost all of them feel pretty impressive.  The number of Warframes is also constantly increasing, as the developers just love to introduce new Warframes on a regular basis.  I can guarantee there will be several Warframes that likely fit your particular playstyle.  Every Warframe can carry a pirmary weapon, a secondary, and a melee weapon into combat, as well as one companion / pet.
Combat is very solid, though the AI of the enemies is not impressive.  Most of them basically come at you in horde mode, with a few variations.  What counteracts the repitition of fighting off constant enemy zergs is the obscene amount of customization available in combat.  Want to fight with a bow?  You can.  Want a machine gun?  There are dozens available.  Want to just ghost around murdering things with a katana while invisible?  Yeah, you can.  The arsenal you can lay your hands on is massive, and constantly increasing as new weapons are introduced to the game.  Some of these weapons are lackluster in their basic form, but even then, you can go on to modify their characteristics to your individual taste.  Other weapons are just outright incredible implements of murder.  Either way, you can tailor to your wants.
You want more dakka, you can have it.  Easily.  Same as the Warframes themselves, you're bound to find something to your taste.
Movement takes a little getting accustomed to, but its very fluid, and you will feel like a ninja as you vault flip and bullet jump through the world.  Speaking of the in game world of Warframe, most of the games missions take place in randomly generated tileset maps.  Most missions won't follow the same pattern as the last, even on the same node.  There's some variety in your mission types, though you'll see a lot of the standard tropes in use.  And here lately they've started into the territory of open world environments, with the Plains of Eidolon, which is also a hell of a lot of fun.
Story and lore are, surprisingly, pretty detailed.  It might not seem so off the bat, but given time, the game has some really good background it drops on you.  You've just got to stick with it long enough to get there.  And don't let anyone give you spoilers toward it, it is, frankly, far to badass when you encounter some of it to be ruined.
Last out of the good stuff, this game is both Free-to-Play and has a pretty decent microtransaction economy going in it.  There is literally no need to spend any money, at all, as you can get your hands on every Warframe or weapon without dropping cash.  The trade system can let you farm rare "prime" parts to sell off and acquire in-game currency from other players.  About the only thing the game really forces you into buying are Warframe and weapon slots, and frankly they're pretty cheap.  And this game drops freebies on you like crazy.  Honestly, its got one of the best economies going.  I'm pretty damn happy dropping money on them to grab cool cosmetic skins and armor sets.
I guess I gotta have the pro / con going, so... Here's the things I'd say are negatives.
This game is a serious grind.  It can take a lot of time to get to some of the rarer items.  Flip side of that, it doesn't -feel- like a grind.  You're always going to be picking up something useful to you, resources, mods, something.  But still, it takes a lot of grinding, so if you mind that, you're gonna be put off.
Tutorial might be the most lacking part of the entire game.  Warframe has a collosal amount of customization and an equally massive number of systems to get into some of that customization.  The tutorial really doesn't do the best job of introducing you to the complexity of it all.  Even story wise, the tutorial is pretty basic.  If you can power past that, then you're solid; plus the community is a good one and if you ask for advice, you'll probably get an answer.
Archwing.  Ok, so, this is basically the flying in space combat portion of the game.  Its not terrible, but I can't say its good.  Its really just something a lot of Warframe players just kind of groan and endure through.  Fortunately its not forced onto you to much.
And thats about it.  Frankly, I love this game.  The community rocks, the Youtube commentators are good, Devstreams actually try to engage and -listen- to the community, and the in game mechanics and economy are all just great.  And its updated incredibly often with new content and gear.  I've played the other triple A titles, Destiny, EA's wandering mess of shooters; and I swear none of them do as good of a job as Digital Extremes do with Warframe.  I highly recommend this game.  At least give it a spin, I mean hell, its free!

Paradox Games have a unique formula filled with complexity and strategy, and CK2 is no different. This is also somewhat of a problem. They are all beasts of a game and are effectively a genre of their own.
From the perspective of a newcomer not willing to dive into and dedicate towards such a radically different formula, it's extremely convoluted and requiring exceptional dedication to learn. And yes, I'm not recommending a game because it takes too long to learn.
Additionally any non-specialist game with over two hundred dollars in DLC should have a double take before buying just out of ethical concerns.

This is my favorite game of all time.
Sid Meier famously said that a game is a series of interesting decisions.  Using that premise as the basis of my review, games do not get more interesting that Crusader Kings II.  I am a long time player of strategy games; it is easily my favorite genre.  I have spent a lot of hours playing everything from the Microprose classics of the early/mid 90s, the first to Warcraft games, eariler entries to the Total War series (as well as the newest one), and a great many other titles in between.
What sets CKII above every other game I've played is that the number of tools at your disposal to solve a problem are staggering, leading to an infinite number of "interesting decisions."  The goals you set are your own: do you want to "paint the map" with a min/max powergame or do you want to see the Norse Gods spread to the four corners of Europe/West Asia?  The goals you set for yourself will dicate your problems (though angry vassals and ambitious heirs will create more than their fair share as well), and the tools you have at your disposal to solve those problems allow you to truly be creative.  Have a son that is just a real pain the in butt?  Make him a commander and send him off to battle to (hopefully) die gloriously in combat.  Have a wife who has suddenly decided to swear a vow of chastity when the realm desperately needs the two of you to get busy?  Get in good with the Pope and divorce her.  Or create a plot to... you know... or find some willing coutier to make your very own Jon Snow.  Of course that could lead to other problems.  It is a game unlike any other in that you can truly be creative in your approach to problems and you can role play or powergame to your heart's content.  The game doesn't force you down one path or another.
The many choices and problems stem from the many systems the game has in place.  This is an important point: this game is not easy to get into.  Understanding the nuances and the vocabulary of fuedalism is a hurdle - more than once I tore my realm apart when I promoted a vassal to a duke when I was little more than a duke myself.  All the hard work I had put in to taking those counties was lost in a second due to a dumb mistake on my part.  But you learn by doing in this game.  And the UI is actually really strong and polished.  There are tooltips for everything.  Just play it and it will come to you.  Once it does it opens like a flower and will blow your mind.  You'll know it when you get to that point.  I would NOT reccomend watching youtube tutorials.  Stick with your own efforts to blunder through and look up concepts in the wiki that aren't clear to you.
As far as DLC goes, it has gotten quite a bit out of hand, certainly for these older paradox titles like this and Europa Universalis IV.  I am reluctant to comment on that.  With the hours I see myself putting into this game, I have to feel that the value I'm getting for the cost of the DLCs and the on-going development is worth it.  Not only that, but there are an insane amount of high-quality mods for this (definatley reccomend the game of thornes mod as well as the heavenly map mod) that will keep you playing this game well into the next decade.
I try to go back and dabble in other games like Total War, Civilizaiton, etc., but I just can't.  CKII has ruined them for me.

I grew up on the Myst Series and love first-person puzzle games so I'm always on the lookout for interesting new additions to the genre.  When I came across Only If I thought - it's free, I'll give it a try.  After playing it I'll admit I wasn't 100% disappointed but I was about 90% disappointed.
There are a few redeeming points where the "levels" were truly mind-bending or the visuals were truly beautiful.  Clearly there was some serious intelligence and creativity somewhere in the development process that generated these striking moments and I’d love to see some of the more interesting concepts fleshed out in larger, more involved games.
Unfortunately all this is overshadowed by an
storyline.  Only If manages a dialogue that is, at best, annoyingly confusing, while at the worst moments, extremely juvenile.  At its lowest points the dialogue is offensive – while some players may have no problem with the language, developers should remember that the gaming community is not entirely made up of 20-year-old straight males with classically frat-bro senses of humor.  Prepare to spend 50%+ of your in-game time listening to this dialogue usually during while trapped cut-scne while staring at a completely black backdrop.  Near the end of the game I was so checked out of the story and so sick of listening to the characters’ voices that I’d leave the game running and work on something else.  Dialogue aside, the game certainly makes an attempt at being an interesting story-focused puzzle game but simply falls short in execution.  Indecipherability is not a substitute for depth.
And the ending is absurd.  It’s as if at the very end of the game the developers actually realized that all the story “depth” they had been working at had missed its mark and then, in order to save face, suddenly decided to pretend it was all some silly joke.  A bit like a slap in the face for the player.
Finally, there are a few issues with controls and maneuverability in the game – be prepared to “die” often – but nothing I wouldn’t expect from a free indie game - in fact on the whole the mechanics were decent.  I’d also recommend playing in “fast” rather than “beautiful” mode – the change can mean the difference between life and 10 straight minutes death on repeat.

AIPD is an arena based shmup that's tailored to provide a specific kind of score attack experience. There are only 15 waves, a few types of enemies, one boss, one life and a big health bar. Your goal is to get to the end with as high a score as possible, that's it. In terms of raw content, some might find this lacking and I can't blame you if that's so. However, if you are a fan of score attack and particularly, one you can customise the challenge of, there's a lot to like here.
You have a variety of weapons and secondary abilities at your disposal. Most are locked off initially but you can unlock them all in less than an hour of play. You can use combinations of these, along with various powerups and superweapons you will acquire in the stages themselves, to take out enemies as fast as possible. Defeated foes will drop tiny shards that will increase your multiplier and you want to get as many of these as possible. Taking damage will lower your multiplier but not reset it entirely. After each stage, you're presented with two challenges that you must pick one of before proceeding and which stack as you get further in the game. These challenges will either give you a handicap or your enemies an advantage but they also come with an instant multiplier boost that is higher for more difficult challenges, encouraging greediness. You only have one life and can't regain health but your starting health is very generous. Once you either die or defeat the boss, your score is added to the leaderboards.
Up to 4 players can play together locally and in addition to that, there are other modes available with different sets of challenges activated from the get go, plus three custom profiles where you can pick your own sets of challenges and thus, starting multiplier bonus. There's a lot of ways to customise your experience and challenge which is really refreshing to see and I wish more games like this did.
The one major bummer about AIPD is the leaderboard implementation. There is only one leaderboard for each game mode (including the custom design mode) and every difficulty level adds to the same leaderboard, meaning that if you're playing on a lower difficulty or playing the custom mode with less challenges enabled, you have an unlevel playing field with higher level players. There are two schools of thought on this. Some like it because it encourages people to get better and play higher levels but personally, I like each difficulty to have its own leaderboard so those that don't have as much time or just aren't as skilled can still feel like they're competing for a top slot. Personally, I'd like to see each difficulty get its own leaderboard, as well as each combination for the custom modes. A minor gripe at worst though.
AIPD looks great (even on low-end hardware), plays great and really gets what makes a good score attack experience. This isn't going to be for everyone but if it's the kind of shmup you dig, the price is well worth it.

In this game you are air dropped into a world inhabited by dinosaurs where you try to hunt and kill them for sport.
You start off with a bow and a handful of arrows and must make your way on foot using a hand-held computer to find better weapons and gear, as well as track dinos.
There are currently 3 types of dinos in this game: Raptors, Triceratops, and the T-Rex.  The other threat are poisonous plants.
As far as I can tell - you do not craft or build anything in this game.
Pros:
- The map is massive - I'm guessing it's probably about the size of Maui.
- The flora is nice looking.
Cons:
- The bow is almost worthless.  The odds of taking out a raptor is very slim.
- If you sprint - you run out of stamina after 20-40 yards/meters.
- If you exit the game, you will lose all of your weapons, ammo, and other gear.
- you cannot cross water that is knee deep (or deeper).
Overall:
In this game:  You walk thru the jungle.  When a raptor attacks you, you shoot at it with whatever weapon you have on hand (only vital shots count).  If you killed it, you scan the kill in your computer (yay points).  If you did not one-shot the raptor, you die.  If more than one raptor attacks, you die.  If you encounter a T-rex, you die.  This is a walking/hunting/dying simulator.

Interesting game! I highly reccommend "Only If" for those who have a knack for story-based games and solving puzzles. It also incorporates decision-making skills in terms of choosing which path/scenario for Anthony (that's you). Black Pawn Scenario or White Pawn Scenario. So this game has a replayability value here.
The story unfolds interestingly enough -- Anthony goes to a party and he partied hard, apparently, that when he wakes up the next day, he finds his female companion missing and he's in a strange house. What happens next? You decide. ;)
The graphics are pretty good. I love the details like the carvings on the wall, the mounted paintings, the knob on the safe. Voice acting is superb. Some expletives here and there, but it's cool. There might be places where it's too dark to see, though. But later on you'll be provided with a flashlight.
Sure you'll die a lot. But by dying in the game, you'll figure out which is the correct path to take; should you stay or should you just run? You'll ask yourself, "Is this real?" or "Am I truly inebriated that I'm hallucinating this stuff?"
In a nutshell, play this game! Surprisingly good for a free-to-play game. Thumbs up to the developers! :D

It's a MOBA for people who aren't versed in genre stalwarts like Dota or LoL, but do know 2D platforming. It'll teach you the core elements of the genre in an accessible way, but experts will still dominate you. This one goes on sale for cheap quite often, definitely pick it up then, though its current price can give you hours of fun.

Gameplay 9/10
Fast paced 2D MOBA, easy to understand, hard to master. Has some competitive potential and there are a few tournaments. The controls are great and the game rewards skill and teamwork. The game has some small balance issues, but they are constantly working on in it.
Graphics 8/10
The cartoon graphics are really nice. The effects are ok, but they are polishing them. They got much better over time.
Sound 10/10
The music, the nauts' theme songs/lines and the sound effects in general are awesome.
Matchmaking 7/10
Well, this is the main issue of the game, but I don't think there's much to be done if the playerbase doesn't grow. There aren't enough online players in each region for good matchmaking and lag free games. However, some small improvements could be done, like creating the teams after the six players needed for a match are found. This way the best players won't end up in the same team. Also, a pre-game lobby where players could talk and decide what nauts they pick would be great.
Misc
Some characters are quite original, the theme songs and lines are funny. The game is constantly updated and improved. They are adding new features, new skins, new characters and a new map is planned. The community is pretty great and they've done some great things, like websites where you can check the leaderboards, upload and download replays or where you can check, create and share naut builds. They are also organizing tournaments from time to time.
Anyway, I strongly recommend this game, it's one of my all time favourites.

That said there's not much passed the basic gameplay cycle, so what you see after the first few levels is what you get for the game. Luckily there's a few modes of play to spice things up.

You are in a circular arena and shoot waves over waves of enemies while you can move to a different direction than you shoot. After each stage you can choose one of two randomly chosen modifiers (there are a lot in total!) making it more challenging and you can even build your own difficulty with them in a free mode.

It seems keys are given away pretty often for this game, and you don't have to play long to understand why.
Let's start with the difficulty options: Hard, Hard, and Hard. There are three buttons, but they do nothing. Oh look, it's an attempt to be clever, or troll the player, or whatever the purpose was. Okay, I get it: No choice, expect rage-quit difficulty.
Except I wouldn't call the game hard. At least the core of it. And I don't normally play these kinds of games. Hell, I beat the first 3 stages just by idling in the same spot on the screen, holding LMB to fire, and occasionally using the special laser attack (RMB), which mows down enemies for a good 5 seconds or so. You can activate a shield with Space, but it doesn't make a difference. If you get hit you lose a life (3 per level) whether you're shielded or not, so I don't see why it was even included. (Maybe another 'hah, we're making this difficult' jab?) Both "abilities" are only usable once per level. They reset when you die.
You're constantly moving forward (WASD adjusts your relative position), shooting stuff that comes flying at you and dodging repetitive obstacles like bugs carrying shields, wrecked bicycle wheels, ground canons, etc. It felt like a cartoony version of those old "fixed shooter" arcade games. Or maybe a weak "runner" game, just in the air and with a couple of weapons at your disposal.
The obstacles are the same in every stage, and in the same locations. Their patterns can be memorized via trial and error. The different swarms of insects are more annoying than difficult. Just stay to the left and keep firing constantly to clear the way, saving your laser attack for the more unpredictable types. The most difficult aspect is probably figuring out the hitbox of each enemy/obstacle/projectile, so you know just how far to nudge to avoid getting hit.
Each level adds a new obstacle/enemy or two, but the overall object is the same: shoot swarms and avoid predictable hazards till you reach the 'end' of a level. It gets boring quickly, because all you're really doing is correcting your errors until the whole level is burned into your brain. It's like the video game equivalent of memorizing a really long and pointless string of numbers. You repeat it over and over and over and over, and eventually you get "good" at it by pure rote. But getting to that point is anything but fun, and there's nothing rewarding about it other than bragging to your friends, who are just gonna roll their eyes at you for attempting it in the first place.
Overall, I'm glad I didn't waste money on this. If you score a free key by all means try it out for yourself (or for the cards), but otherwise there's no point. There are no achievements, the 'plot' and minimal dialogue are hollow and uninteresting, and there's really no incentive to beat the game whatsoever. Save your money.

Watch a few gameplays, and see for yourself exactly how a game plays out. I got this game as a gift from a friend of mine a while ago, and it was a nice surprise since I’ve been wanting to play
since it was released on Steam. It’s a short visual novel about a genderless MC named Olea and two mysterious girls: Flori and Llima. Her fates became intertwined because of a tragic past event, and that changed their lives a lot in the following years.
The main goal is getting “fragments” by choosing certain answers, and that will unlock new endings and CGs, leading the player to the “true ending”. Each gameplay takes about 30 minutes, and you’ll have to replay a few times until you get all the fragments. This can be frustrating since a few scenes and the transition effects cannot be skipped, and you’ll probably need a guide to help you with the missing fragments. The art style is beautiful and I especially love the painting. BGM is good too, sometimes it stops out of nowhere and things get very silent, but that wasn’t a problem to me. The story was nice, nothing amazing but it wasn’t bad either. I liked the characters even if we have little time to know them better because of the fast paced narrative.
6/10. Overall, I recommend this game when it’s on a good sale and if you’re feeling like solving a mystery, even if it means that you’ll have to replay a lot of scenes.

Natural-Beyond Nature- is a visual novel in which you take on the role of Olea, who is on an introspective journey to discover him/herself, to find purpose to their life.  As Olea is on this journey, he/she meets two girls, Flori and Llima, and discovers that they are best friends tied together by a common fate.  Olea feels that they know them even though Olea has never met them before going on this journey.  (As Olea is a genderless character, I'll refer to Olea as he/she or they.)  Also, the dreams that Olea has are tied to these two girls somehow.  Depending on who Olea ends up meeting first, he/she will end up getting on either Flori's or Llima's path and thus get to know her better.  There are a total of 6 different endings you can get, depending on how much friendly points Olea has with either girl as well as how many nature fragments are collected.  Each option that Olea can choose, regardless of whether it earns them friendly points, will earn a fragment and there are a total of 30 fragments.  If you collect all 30 of them, then you can get the last two endings, depending on friendly points.  (I say friendly points rather than affection points since Olea can't start up a romance with either girl.)
Now that I've summarized what the game is about, it's time for the review.  ;)  I really love Zeiva's games and this one is just as wonderful as her other ones.  The art is beautiful, the story is lovely (even though there were some grammatical errors in certain sentences and such that I felt could have used some polishing-the use of vocabulary has improved, though), and the music pieces are wonderful.  I thought that the ending theme song was absolutely perfect for the game's theme and message.  I liked the idea of obtaining nature fragments although I felt that doing so could be repetitive at times since you would have to replay certain paths and pick different choices to get another fragment.  Also, for one playthrough, I'd say that it might be 1 to 1 1/2 hours.  I didn't time it so I can't say for certain but this might be somewhat short for those who are used to playing longer VNs.  However, for the price, I felt that it was fine for the paths to be on the short side.  In addition, I loved how the additional features, such as the side story, character gallery, and author's notes, were unlocked after getting the true endings.  I always love these features in VNs and before I forget, I should mention that some of the side characters appeared in Voices from the Sea, a sort of prequel.  For those who have played Voices from the Sea, you might especially recognize Cantus and I loved that the side story was about him.  ^^
Overall, I truly enjoyed Natural-Beyond Nature- and felt that for the price, it was worth playing.  There are no Steam achievements but the game itself is quite good and there are plenty of in-game features to unlock so it's worth checking out.  If you like VNs and are especially a fan of Zeiva's work, then check out Natural-Beyond Nature-.  :D

I just bought this today since I was in a VN mood and I wanted something short. I read <sin>'s negative review and how he mentioned it being 3 hours at max. Unfazed by the negative review, considering that I wanted a short game to kill the afternoon, I decided to get it anyways to kill the afternoon. I am happy to say it was a good decision.
The story, while quite short, is nonetheless interesting enough to hook you to want to see the 'true' end. The art is gorgeous. The music's not half-bad, but not such a strong point as the art.
For such a short story, one negative point is how often you have to run through the entire game multiple times to get to the different choices. I would have liked an option that included an auto-skip rather than, "Hold the down arrow."
But otherwise, it's well worth the price; though I payed a bit less since it was on sale. I will keep myself updated on the new games released by this studio.

I love Voices from the Sea, but this game does not quite live up to it's predecessor. There are about 3 hours of content here (being generous) but each "run" is only ~30 minutes long. I found it annoying to need to replay the game this many times to see subtle differences.
The music is good but gets cut off frequently before the track can finish. The most notorious time this happens is during the "Day 2" title card, which awkwardly divides a tense scene in half. In general the pacing is a bit wonky.
I believe there is a "true" route once you collect all 30 fragments, but I haven't been able to find the last one. The game offers no hint as to what scenes you are missing, and I've almost exhausted my patience.
The story is good, but I would have honestly enjoyed it more as a properly paced kinetic novel. I hope Zeiva can learn from this title and mature as storytellers.
Verdict: grab it during a deep sale.

Voices from the Sea is my favorite visual novel of all time. When I heard that there was another game similar comeing out, I sat through every delay and got it the second it came out. I can honestly say I'm not disappointed. Natural -Beyond Nature- is my second favorite visual novel. It's not quite as good as Voices from the Sea, but it's still amazing. However, it's not very much like Voices from the Sea. It takes place on the same island and has similar supernatural being in it. But overall, it's not the care free and happy story that Voices from the Sea is. Insted, Natural -Beyond Nature- is rather gloomy. It has a serious story with multiple endings. While Voices from the Sea made me feel happy, this made me on the brink of crying at the end. Unlike Voices from the Sea, the choices you make in this game actually do something. Which could really make a lot of people like it better.
Since the story isn't quite as good nor as welly told but has better visual novel gameplay, I'd give Natural -Beyond Nature- that same thing I gave it's predecessor.
Natural -Beyond Nature- earns a 9/10.
The story is still great and still welly told, just not as great or welly told as Voices from the Sea.
This is the better visual novel, not the better story.

(It should be noted that I easily have hundreds of hours on this game and other ES titles)
Yes, over Morrowind, Daggerfall, and especially over Skyrim.
Morrowind brought to the table some of the best lore and content of an RPG at the time, and if I had to play 1 and 1 only Elder Scrolls game for the rest of my life, it'd probably be Morrowind, but still it flew under the radar for a lot of people. A lot.
Its 2006, Bethesda are looking to branch out on to a new generation of console and a growing base of PC players. They are trying to appeal to a wider player base.
The biggest way they arguably done this, was with getting rid of the RNG combat that previous Elder Scrolls titles had, and introduce a new style of dealing with foes. When you hit something.
(As spammy and clunky as the combat might be) This opened up the marketability to a lot more "softcore" type of players, who wouldve been turned off the dice roll that was the combat in previous titles. This doesnt mean the game is completely unrecognisable to its previous, there are still some big things that Oblivion keeps that make the ES games so iconic. Fantastic quest lines (Thieves guild and The Dark Brotherhood), a great amount of lore and overall a world with a lot to explore. Thats not even mentioning the addition of great voice acting in this game. (Even if it may be silly at times)
You may not be reading a load of dialogue from every NPC where you would in previous games, but there is still a lot to be discovered, through books, NPC's, quests and even to the simplist of rumours from most NPC;s in the game. The game still offers a lot to someone who wants a more deeper experience.
The game may be a tad dated compared to other RPG's on todays market, especially in regards to graphics, facial animations  and a world that seems empty at time. Not to mention, the main story can easily be called a let down, especially compared to Daggerfall and Morrowind. What im trying to say is, ofcourse, Oblivion, has its flaws. Like all games do, but it is still an iconic game and one that opened the Elder Scrolls door up to so many people and I think any fan of RPG's, a vast amount of lore and certainley fans of the Elder Scrolls series, should play this game. You may not love it, in fact, you may hate it. But it is a game that is a must play for me.
This game for sure is not perfect, but it should be experienced, even in the state it's in nowadays.

The Elder Scrolls is a franchise that we are all familiar with to some extent I think. The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim is one of the most critically acclaimed games of all time. The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is its predecessor and to many people, a better gaming experience. I personally agree whole heartedly and here's why.
Questing:
TES IV: Oblivion has incredible diversity in its quests. Both in stand alone quests and in depth quest lines. The Thieves Guild is a riveting tale that you become an unlikely hero in. The Dark Brotherhood is a tragic story of rise and fall with the eventual discovery of your importance in their faction. In the Arena you watch yourself go from underdog to grand champion to win the love and adoration of the thousands of inhabitants of the Imperial City. Questing in TES IV feels much more alive and immersive than the cookie cutter repeat quests of TES V.
Customizable Experience:
The path you take is entirely yours to choose, as in all TES games. Oblivion stands apart in my opinion because of your innate ability to succed as a player even if you choose to completely ignore seemingly essential quest lines. Not only that, but your character skills are a direct result of how you play, not just what you feel like grinding at the time. Customizable spells and enchantments make each character a powerhouse in their own regard.
DLC:
From the Knights of the Nine to the Shivering Isles, every item of DLC for TES IV is extremely high quality. Brand new stories that provide new pieces of lore and a way for your character be an unlikely hero in a story he doesn't belong in. Even the DLC housing is incredible. Abandoned castles and magical towers hidden in the mountains, there is something for every type of player. Storage options are limitless and the houses feel like he have history to be discovered within them.
The Main Story:
The daedra are a pretty big part of every TES game. Oblivion has a huge involvement because of the main story. It provides a lot of insight into what the daedra are doing when they aren't causing havoc in the real world. Oblivion gates are opening everywhere and someone has to figure out why and how to stop them. Why not you?
In conclusion, the game has an indescribably fantastic feeling of progression and uniqueness for each playthrough. The game itself was ahead of its time in most regards including the size of the world, the variety you have available to you, and the addition of large amounts of lore through immersive DLC.
Overall 10/10 game. Highly reccommended to any RPG lover.
