I picked this game up on a whim and have been very pleasantly surprised with how much I'm enjoying it. You play as a small hovering rescue spaceship venturing deep underground on the planet Apoxus Prime to rescue colonists from…something. To be honest I'm just over 2/3rds of the way through at this point (or so I assume), so I haven't fully worked out the story—according to what the survivors I've been rescuing say, it has something to do with the colonists/scientists there trying to drill deep in the core for energy or treasure or something. Anyway, they dug too deep, and now something's out to get them (either the planet or the different, invariably hostile creatures that live there). It's a simply but effective story (the real focus is the gameplay and it doesn't try to overshadow that) and I've enjoyed getting additional scraps of information from each stage as I descend.
Anyway, the actual gameplay is pretty simple, but in an elegant way: you fly your little spaceship around, and can either shoot missiles (more on this in a second) or fire a short-range retractable grabber arm on a rope that will auto-target survivors or treasures (or a few other bits of interactive level items). Your health is represented by a temperature gauge; if your heat level fills all the way up your ship melts and you need to restart the level. Normally you can fire missiles as fast as you can hit the fire button, which will fly straight forward and explode on contact (thankfully you don't take splash damage from them, but it
totally possible to kill the very survivors you're trynig to save). Holding down the firing button howver will switch you to firing a barrage of homing missiles at the cost of quickly heating you up if you don't feel like aiming. It's a simple system but I found it to work pretty well in practice, allowing me to be lazy about aiming sometimes at the cost of making it much more likely I'd die if a projectile hit me (one projectile normally fills the heat bar 3/4ths full).
Most of the game's real meat, however, comes from its fluid simulations. Levels have a number of different fluids on them: starting out you'll encounter water (cools you down, can be life-saving) and lava (melts you almost instantly and will still heat you up if you're just in the vicinity, combines with water to create soft rock which you can blast away), but later levels introduce ice (melts from lava, can freeze water to replicate itself), explosive gas (which rises, and explodes if it touches lava or electricity), and some weird black oily stuff that I've just reached (reacts with water to form explosive gas, heats you up slowly but also slows your movement to a crawl, and seems to be almost magnetically attracted to you[??]). There's also various bits of rock that can be destroyed, usually to allow one fluid to mix with another to allow you to progress. Some levels have upgrades that do things like let you spew infinite amounts of water or lava in order to solve the level, or make water hurt you while lava heals you. This helps keep the gameplay fresh, even though I never got bored with the core gameplay conceit mixing different fluids together to accomplish something.
The actual gameplay reminds me a lot of Vessel, another 2D game based around fluid physics puzzles (though it's much more peaceful). The setting for some bizarre reason really reminds me of the old LEGO Rock Raiders game, though the gameplay is NOTHING alike. (I guess it has to do with exploring caverns deep underground with lava and ice…)

Endless Legend is the 3rd game in the Endless series, and as they say, 3rd Time's the Charm!  Though my next words won't really convey that well.
This game is unfinished.
Everything feels pretty loosely connected (that was the only way I could describe things).  The UI feels weak and seems too small.  Sometimes enemy armies will come out of nowhere and destroy your city in one turn.  These are problems that can be patched out or updated.  (The camera doesn't move to show you important things like enemy movement etc., so you can feel like you're being left in the dark to vitally important things.)  Also, randomly the game will say a huge error has occured, give you a feedback log for you to do nothing with, and then continues running as normal (unless it then decides your next turn will never start, but a quick Save/Reload solves this).
However, despite these faults, compared to Beyond Earth, this is the better game.
The 9 factions are all fantastic, look wonderful and have great, unique effects, and each one feels very different!  From the Necrophage which are quite literally incapable of learning any form of peaceful diplomacy and feast on the flesh of the living to the Drakken, draconic beings who adore peace and start the game knowing everyone (and everyone knowing them), it's truly wonderful.  You can even make your own factions from scratch!  Of course, in old Endless-4X style, you can customise your armies with equipment that improves over the course of the game (making your units take longer to produce to compensate), it all balances out very well.  Minor Factions you can assimilate into your army also make for important choices on which lands you take and which places you destroy, for each grants you a passive bonus along with a new unit for you to make (and considering each army can only make 3 different military units, this is vitally important).
This game is good, you should buy it, but it does have some rough edges, but nothing you can't fix or get over.  Get ready to learn a lot of new stuff and have plenty of fun!

Endless Legend is a 4x turnbased strategy game with that plays similar to civ5. Just because it plays like the basics of civ5 mean it is civ5, there is in my opinion many more things that this game has then civ5 does. Each faction is totaly unique and plays completly different then the others, they each have their own lore and each unit looks and acts different from another. Each faction has 4 unique units that have different strengths and weaknesses. Also players start with a "hero" which is basically a general from civ5 but that does way more then adding a buff to a unit. There are tons of heros from each faction and each one looks different(heros from same faction has small differences but have different uses) and plays differnetly, one may be used for leading a army by giving it +2 damage while one could be used to govern and town and give it +6 industry. Also every unit can be customized with different equipment to make them stronger as the game goes by, this is simmilar to civ but instead of the unit become a differnet teir(as a musketer becomes and rifleman) the units in this game stay the same except their equipment changes and you can see the difference in appearance do to this change. Also like civ5 there is small factions that are ran by ai, you can add these to your empire by either attacking and defeating them, bribing them, or by completeing quests given by them. Once they join you then you can assimilate them into your empire and then produce their unit that can only be used by assimilating them. The unit is based off that small faction and its appearance is completely differnet to any of the playable factions, there are lots of these small factions that can be conquered by the player. I recomend this game to anyone that loves the Civ games, fantasy or just 4x turnbased strategy game in general.

I’ve been playing this game for quite some time now. I’ve recommended it to pretty much all of my friends at this point. Most of them bought the game immediately after giving it a try.
So here’s a quick list of things I like and dislike in Awesomenauts.
Things I like:
-	Easy to learn
-	Regular patches
-	Many characters with unique play-styles
-	Less serious than other ‘MOBA’ games
-	Funny character voices and well suited soundtrack
-	Big fun with friends
-	Split screen functionality
-	You can turn a game around at almost any point in the game
-	It’s cheap, even without a sale
Things I dislike:
-	Lag issues spoil the fun from time to time
-	Patches and new characters can bring some imbalance (gets patched out most of the time though)
-	AI is too good or too bad depending on the character (sometimes better than the player that left, turning the game upside down)
-	Unfair matchups are not uncommon (especially with premade teams from different leagues)
Conclusion:
The folks at Ronimo did a really good job at adapting the MOBA genre to work as a 2D platformer. They’ve created a game that really made it to the top of the list of my favorite games of all time (and that’s saying something, I’ve played A LOT of games). I’d recommend this to pretty much anyone.

Don't let labels fool you though. This game is more of a liquid physics and environmental puzzle game than "shooter". Liquids include water, lava, and slime/sludge. There's certain rock, smoke, and ice that come into play as well. They all interact predictably. Sometimes your ship gets certain upgrades on certain levels to deal with these obstacles as well. And yes, you will be shooting some baddies along the way too. You're objective is to get by these puzzles and baddies to save seven lost fellers every screen (panning). Five screens make up a stage. Five stages make up a level. Three levels make up the game.

I love a good first-person puzzle solving game. I grew up with games like Myst (and its sequels), the Journeyman Project series, etc. I hadn't had a good first-person puzzle experience in a while and I stumbled upon Only If.
I was thrilled! It seemed similar in tone to the Stanley Parable, but involving more interaction and puzzle solving.
Sadly, my excitement was soon crushed beneath the heal of this awful awful AWFUL game.
First off, the game itself is incredibly buggy. In the Parlor where you pick a pawn (thus determining the course of the game you play), it initially didn't matter which one I chose as it always gave me the black pawn route. I thought this was a design choice until I later found out it wasn't and that the damned game was broken. Later, after using the code to get to the white pawn path, essential graphical clues don't actually appear where their supposed to. At least, they don't all the time. Oh, they sometimes will when they feel like it, but don't expect the damned things to do it every time. Lastly, in the black pawn route, I was able to walk right off the map and fall into the oblivion below. I couldn't even restart the game! I had to close the window manually to even try again!
So, this game is buggy and broken beyond actual enjoyment.
But that's not all!
When the game DID work, it didn't make it any more enjoyable. No, the "puzzles" they want you to solve are sometimes impossible to figure out without a walkthrough. OR an objective has such abstract or imprecise conditions that you could be at it for an hour and STILL not get to the next step. "Start here and run for 6 seconds. Turn Right"?? What determines what is six seconds?! Me?? You?? Do we go with the standard "1 Mississippi 2 Mississippi" or a quick "1 2 3 4 5 6"??

Been looking forward to this game for a long time because I loved the previous Divinity titles. I love the combat style, the humor, the dialogues, but sadly the game has become completely unplayable due to the worst optimalisation I've seen in years.
Even on a relatively new PC it´s completely unplayable after Act 1 due to long loading times and stuttering. It´s a common problem which hasn´t been patched as yet. The game demands an unreasonable amount of processing power. My PC has a i5 processor and a GTX 1060 graphics card, which should be well within minimum requirements, yet it's still a massive slideshow even at the lowest graphics settings.
It´s a real shame, because I really enjoyed the game at the start. Act 1 was great to play, with a lot of winks and nudges towards the other games in the series. But as soon as I got off the boat in Act 2 the game became completely unplayable, taking up to 5 minutes to load a savegame and half a minute to pick up a single item. Updated my graphics drivers, got rid of old savegames, set all graphics settings to very low, but nothing helped to ease the demands on my CPU.
I had to abandon the game after really enjoying the first part :(
Don't leave your fans hanging, Larian Studios, please patch this game!

First, I play only a few single-player RPGs recommended by friends and I haven't played the previous Original Sin. Prevoius turn-based game I played was the Baldurs gate series. Been playing with focus on huntsman for a while now.
+ The voice acting is absolutely superb!

+ Lots of fun combat tactics, dialogue/choices, areas and side-quests to explore!
+ Even as a casual RPG player I found it easy to get started.

* My frieds complain that the leveling is a bit uneven and also that Initiative doesn't work as you'd expect on Hard difficulty. However, on Normal difficulty I find the progression balanced.
* I'm not sure what to feel about the magic/physical armor system. Perhaps I'll get frustrated with it when I try playing with Hard(er) difficulty.
- Camera control. I struggle sometimes when peeking into areas with large depth/height differences or searching for loot in cramped spaces.
- The UI experience is good overall but strangely awkward in the Runes section - or is it just me? I'm a bit of a hoarder so sorting on weight or value/weight would also be nice (playing unmodded - I'll check the mods later). I personally like sortable listviews in general.
Conclusion: This game is a magnificent creation. Quite obviously there is a group of particularly dedicated people behind this. Well done, and keep up the good work!

* Story:
Amazing story, well written fully voice-acted characters that you care about (for the most part).
* Graphics and Presentation:
Great on both, the graphics are nicely done with few or no issues noticed, and the presentation, menus and such are very good as well. Interface and gaming experience customization was ample.
* Soundtrack:
Excellent Soundtrack, love the music and it goes well with the game and various settings.
* Customization:
There's too much here to comment on but basically with GM mode and mods you have a lot of ways to customize your gaming experience. Could be a good amount of replay here.
Cons:
* Combat:
This isn't really a con but more a personal preference, I am not the biggest fan of turn based combat, but I will say (even tho it's technically in the "cons" section) it's manage well and keeps a fast pace which is nice.
* 4k Support and Mouse Cursor:
So 4k has been out for like forever but these guys missed the mark on that one in a small but key area, the mouse cursor. I have to play the game in 1080p so my mouse cursor doesn't dissappear. Hopefully they fix this or someone creates a mod for a custom cursor :)
Overall, like I said, one of the best games of 2017.

The Cons:

2. Balancing. This game suffers from total chaos. Mechanics are brilliant standing alone but clash with eachother.
3. AI. Battling in a tactial format the AI takes over. All 'Tactial' battling is lost to poor AI grouping for CPU opponents to wipe out your army with AoE attacks.
Other Thoughts:

I am not usually compelled to write reviews, especially positive ones, but this game is pretty great. I expected something awful, or laughably bad. The translation is a little Engrish and some parts of it lack polish, but it's a genuine, full fledged game. It has a bit of fanservice that isn't too bad, the character art is absolutely adorable. It looks like a more High Res Luminous Arc, but plays a lot more complex with class changes, dodging, and all kinds of things. There are secret quests, the story is surprisingly not awful. All in all it's very worth the 8 bucks I paid for it. Had I known this game was this good, I would have paid the full price for it.
If you like tactical RPGs it's not going to be as hardcore or in depth as Fire Emblem or Disgaea, but it's easily as fun as FF Tactics A2 or Luminous Arc 2. Sadly there are no cute boys, but Frida may be the cutest thing I've ever seen.
My only 2 nitpicks so far are that I'd like if there was a way to show characters in their default costume and not class costumes (Fridaaaa), and to pan the camera up and down instead of just zoom in and turn. There may actually be ways to do those things. Controller support wouldn't hurt. All in all though, I'd actually recommend this to my friends and already have. I went from joking with them about how terrible it would be to convincing them to play.

If there is such a thing as a "Casual" sRPG, then Empire of Angels IV is it. Taiwanese developer Softstar has delivered a truly great, fully featured strategy role-player here that works really well for quick hits of strategy gameplay goodness. Its very polished and loaded with content, but the battles are very pick-up-and-play, which I'll be honest, is a nice contrast or palette cleanser after playing
strategy games with missions that can take a half-hour to an hour (or longer).
Now don't get me wrong; EoA4 isn't dumbed down. Whether you're looking to outwit a wide variety of enemy units that challenge you differently, promoting characters to new unit types and giving them new skills, splitting up units into different groups to tackle multiple objectives, etc. Empire of Angels brings it. Its just
here is more compartmentalized. Levels are smaller and missions are pretty quick, for the most part, being doable in less than 15 turns. Less than 10 if you complete secondary objectives of doing them quickly. Because of its straightforward controls and fast-paced battles, this is honestly one of the most fun strategy games I've ever played.

Speaking of Presentation, EoA sports a vibrant, cartoony aesthetic complete with super cute, chibi-style anime girls. While it won't push your PC or show up id Software any time soon, it
really polished and very well done. Its super cuteness stands out even against other eastern sRPGs like
or
too. Sometimes, strategy games like this can look incredibly cheap, and just plop their no frills, grid-based levels into a void; not so here. These levels look fantastic with lots of props (some destroyable) and a nice draw distance that definitely suggests everything is set
. Also, despite being something of a mobile port, the GUI and menus (with their relatively big, touch-friendly buttons) still manage to look great on a monitor and work well with a mouse. Everything here genuinely looks
.

The controls too are extremely polished and mapped intuitively to keyboard & mouse, thankfully. There's camera rotation and zoom on right click+drag and scrollwheel respectively, and keyboard shortcuts for things like trucking the camera across the map, etc. A simple radial menu interface lets you decide actions for the girls during a turn, and of course simply clicking on squares to make them move or attack there. This feels like it was made for keyboard play, from people very familiar with playing PC games.

Heck, the polish even extends to the script. Props to the writers for the game; there's a decent amount of Engrish on the Steam Store Page for EoA4 (to be fair, this
"full-time vocal and funniest 3D game"), but
in the game itself. Surprisingly,
Not only is it Engrish-free, its genuinely pretty cute and funny. All the voices are Chinese though, of course. Its not THAT localized :) All the girls sound appropriately cute though, so no problems there!

Finally I just have to re-iterate how
everything is and how friendly it is for "Quick Hit" gameplay. There's a lot of "Quality of Life" things, from having the tutorial messages easily accessed from the pause menu in case you forgot your keyboard shortcuts or various mechanics, to being able to save any time, to having the option of undoing any character's
before Ending their Turn - even going back to, and replaying a mission from,
. Its already super pick-up-and-play friendly, but this is all incredibly welcome and just makes Empire of Angels even MORE playable. You won't have to dedicate a few weeks of your life to play this like, say, an XCOM 2; EoA4 says "You're totally cool to just play us whenever!" Its really nice.

Besides the minor issue of seeing no way to speed up enemy turns (which, like the rest of the game, go by pretty quickly anyway), I literally have
to talk about. It's honestly one of the highest quality games I've seen for just $15. This is one the best surprises I've found on Steam and is super enjoyable any way you look at it. This is an incredibly easy recommendation for fans of sRPG's, RPGs, anime visuals, cute things...

Do you like games like Fire Emblem? Empire of Angels is essentially FE light... if all the characters were female, and lived in a biologically impossible world populated by ONLY females, and everyone wore sexy clothes... all the time.
The game is a lot of fun. The story is serviceable, light-hearted for the most part, and doesn't interfere with what we're all here for, the battles. Two things really stand out for me. 1) The game essentially allows you to, very organically, choose your difficulty. Maps give you three optional objectives in the battle that you can either choose to complete or ignore, with two often making the battle a little bit harder/more intense should you choose to pursue them. If not you can simply breeze through a lot of the maps with minimal difficulty. 2) The game rewards you completing these optional objectives, but doesn't ostensibly punish you for not completing them; anything you earn through working harder during battles can also be earned through grinding, which is a nice compromise I think.
Admittedly the translation isn't perfect- at times it is more a transliteration of the native Mandarin rather than at true Western translation i.e. some metaphors and idioms come off as awkward or incomprehensible because they are transliterated rather than rewritten to something more identifiable to a westerner. There are occasional misspellings and odd syntax as well, but all of these things are minor, in my opinion at least, and I don't feel anyone should be completely turned off by it. Also the game can be a bit grindy, and even encourages it. I've been mainlining JRPGs since birth so I break out into a cold sweat when I can't watch numbers incrementally rise over long repetitive sessions of play, but for those who don't grind up JRPG's a snort them through crisp rolled up dollar bills regularly this may be a bit of a turn off.
All in all this game is a bit of a hidden gem, and certainly a credit to the Taiwanese game industry

In my humble opinion, this game is like the "childhood game of my dreams."
An RTS game with the ability to jump straight into the action in the first/third person control is like nothing I've experienced before. Based on gameplay mechanics of Men of War, this game allows players to take into account the importance of flanking and infantry tactics.
When engaging a position held by rebels, split squads up, keep some in the back for long range support, keep the close-quarters men for the battle. Then take up defensive positions and call in a tank, take control and use its heavy weaponry to wipe out the enemy reinforcements at long range.
Playing with friends is even more exciting! While your allys IFV rolls along through war-torn streets, take command of your soldiers and clear buildings of enemy RPGs while your ally guns down that HMG up the end of the road.
And if you own the full version, give the editor a try, make your own custom battles and missions, you're only limited by what your computer can handle.
The game is quite balanced in my opinion, when you lose troops, you slowly get back the manpower that was lost, and can easily jump back into the fight.
I've honestly found that this game offers plenty of replayability, and when the DLCs are released after the game is officially released, I'm sure players will have fun getting their hands on new equipment. It's a shame that alot of people are impatient and don't seem to understand that like most things in life, "you can't rush perfection"
The devs really don't get the much recognition that they deserve, especially for indie developers, which unlike larger companies tend to listen to their community.
I'd like to point out, that this game may not be for everyone, and the devs have solved this by allowing you to "try before you buy". Though as I write this review, remember that this game is not quite finished, and for those who are reading, I beg you to be patient and simply wait for any issues or bugs to be fixed.
For RTS fans who want something unique and exciting, I'd recommend this game.

The Term: 'Conversational Landmines,' applies.
The lack of questmarkers makes every quest a puzzle, reading the journal and looking around for your objective prevents the immature 'where da arrow point at, boss?' It lets the player figure it out, and not spoon-feeding us like a necrotic geriatric.
Combat is turn based, no need to pause every few seconds to dish out commands, or the Diablo style 'run around and spam your four spells.' Every encounter must be thought through, and can sometimes completely avoided. The magic system is fresh, like your local farmers market, you can combo different elements to create things such as smoke which can be electrified, poisoned, and block line of sight, ice can be made by creating water and freezing it, making friends and foes alike to slip:
Multiplayer is a lot of fun, I recommend either four or two players. There's a talent called lonewolf that buffs parties of two or less, it's like snorting Mt. Everest if the snow was cocaine instead of... you know... snow.
Loot is randomized, from quest rewards to what you pulled from inside Craigg the Innocent crab you heartlessly murdererd. Traders carry the same items, and unique items drop in every playthrough.

Cons:

There is no save button, which means that during survival mode, a game lasting several hours will have to be trashed simply because you can't play any longer.

So Empire of Angels IV is a game about a bunch of grills on a quest to collect the four Lord Souls Whoops did it again. You collect the four Menhir (or attempt to anyway, spoiler) and you have zany adventures along the way. The plotline makes little sense, even when it's explained to you and I can't figure out how the characters wind up in the situation that they're in. I feel like several situations were disastrously contrived. It's almost like the developers had a checklist of things they wanted to shovel in. Here's your rival, here's your betrayal, here's your feels trip, the list goes on. And as noted before, they don't connect well. On top of that, it was hard for me to invest myself in the characters and I think that may be because of presentation. There wasn't really much of an underlying story to connect me to them.
There are some fantastic CG shots that I just absolutely adore. Holy smokes, they're beautiful. While the CG shots are beautiful, the rest of the game is far from it. Its graphics remind me of Tales of Symphonia in which the characters could make only one face. Granted in this game, the characters can make a surprised face, the graphics still look incredibly similar. Not to say that I didn't enjoy the class upgrade screen in which the already scantily-clad women became even more scantily-clad.
The game also thinks that it's Fire Emblem but is a little worse for combat. Every attack has an element (even basic attacks which I found to usually be fire type) and if you happen to... I dunno, fight a fire type enemy, you're going to have a bad time. The elemental triangle is up to the player to discover. There are many components of combat that had limited use. The lockpicking skill is used... four times(?) in the game and three of those times were in one level. There's also a change terrain skill which is only really needed for like three levels in the game. It helps in the later stages when you're in the volcano levels (because of course that's where the finale takes place) but other than that, kind of a waste.
The level scaling is rather annoying, and you should expect to make a few grind stops later in the game. And I complain about this because my allies were level 35 (even with some grinding) around the time that the level 40 enemies started showing up. And it ramps up drastically over the last few story missions.
As you complete story missions you can upgrade your characters to advanced classes. As noted earlier, there's a bit of eye-candy when that happens. However, referring back into battle, some classes are just useless. There are two types of mages, which for the purpose of this review we'll call the lightning mage and the fire mage (I call them this because these are the skills I used the most often on them). Well, lategame enemies are fire type, so that sucks. And the third offensive skill on the fire mage is more situational and very difficult to use effectively. So why bother with it? Just use the lightning mage which ultimately was the better DPS. Units overall become incredibly powerful lategame, able to kill in two hits or with huge AoE that destroys enemies. It's beautiful.
So what's my call on this? Humph. I think the game drags on a little bit longer than it should, and I can't actually invest myself in its story. I can't invest myself in the characters. And maybe it's my fault. This is the fourth game in the series (presumably) so I wonder if that investment I can't come up with comes from those games. But that's not really much of an excuse. I think I'll have to give it a pass despite the fanservice. Certainly not for full price ($15 at the time of writing).

Well, finally you get to play as a bug. And no, I do not mean Battlefield 4. Radical Roach makes you play a..Roach, and this game is typical shoot-em-up - you fly from one side of the screen, to another, obliterating your enemies.

Big fan of shoot'em ups? Yeah, me too! So I made the mistake in getting this game because I thought it would be fun but man was I wrong.
This is a shmup for kids. There is no challenge what so ever and every level is exactly the same as the last.
The "Options" menu (or lack of) is a joke, you can select between difficulty "Hard", "Hard", and "Hard"...no..I'm not joking. You can also turn "HiDef" on or off (whatever that means). There is no sound options so enjoy the loud music that you can do nothing about :)
The game has controller support but for some odd reason they decided to only enable the D-pad and not the Thumbsticks. I bet every gamer was just dying to play a shmup with a D-pad...
The game also has no score system and no achievements so there is really no point at all to killing/missing anything. If you get hit twice and didn't kill a single enemy throughout the entire stage and I never got hit and killed every existing enemy, we both pretty much have the same skill level because the game rewards us the same (which is with nothing).
Bottom line, never buy this at full or even sale price. If it is ever bundled and there is another game you want and this game happens to be in there grab it.

Speaking on FPS mode, it can give you a good edge in a spot but you should really play the game at Hardcore settings, realistic fog of war and the highest ManPower output you can for a true "War" experience.
The Rock Paper Scissors aspect is annoying at best, the best counter to say an Abrams is either spamming TOW at it or just bum rushing a squad at it where they throw a molotov and it insta kills your Abrams; Fielding any sort of aircraft is a death sentence. It'll just get mowed down almost immediately without fail. Your super salty squad that is max experience will get wiped in a matter of 1 second because ONE Boot that just comes in and sprayed everything in sight.
The Game is Janky in short. Best played while its F2P and furthermore, played with some friends where you can either sit in dispair or work the AI's quirks and loophole it into a victory.

A nice shoot 'em up with some a very good aesthetic, a nice soundtrack, and some clever puzzle design, set in a distant planet where a scientific team has ended up stranded, and it's up to you (and a friend, if you have someone to play local co-op with) to rescue them.
The gameplay is simple at first sight, you move your ship around shooting at stuff; however, the goal isn't to kill everything in sight, but rather to rescue all the scientists stranded in the planet. Even if you fail to save one, the game grants you several "lives", which are consumed upon the death of a scientist; if your ship is destroyed, you simply restart the current level, you can even restart by yourself if you failed to save a scientist; however, your lives remain the same. There's also different pickups which grant extra lives, or protection against the different hazards, including liquids like water, lava, and a magnetic goo. Another thing is the different skins you can get during a level, which grant you either new weapons, or change the way your ship reacts to the different liquids.
The soundtrack is very nice, too. It keeps the relaxed mood of the game, and it never feels out of place. As far as the level design, from the puzzles to the environment itself (background, theme, etc), it's very good. The puzzles aren't very complicated, but they still require some skill to solve. There's also secret areas with treasure hidden among the different levels, so you'd do well in exploring.
Well, to conclude, I'd say I recommend this game. It's a fun way to pass the time, and it's not too stressing; in fact, I'd say it's quite relaxing.

Oblivion has not aged as well as I thought it would, it’s a very average game that has a lot of issues. Playing Oblivion again made me realize how broken the game really is. The biggest issue by far is the level scaling where all the enemies level up with you. You start out fighting mud crabs, rats and goblins and by the end of the game you're still fighting mud crabs that have leveled up with you, but the rats and goblins have mysteriously disappeared to be replaced with ogres and trolls. You start out finding iron and steel swords and face bandits with fur and leather armour. You finish by finding countless ebony weapons and face superbandits with daedric armour. It’s crazy how bad they f*cked this up. Your character could be level 50 that has the best gear and all his stats maxed out and every enemy in a new dungeon you enter will be ogres that are also level 50 and kill you in a few hits. There is no sense of progression and that kills the game in a big way. The fixed enemies in Morrowind for example added tension and reward to the dungeons and the world exploration because you are never sure how strong the enemy will be when you enter a new area which creates a tense atmosphere. But in oblivion there is always the reassurance no matter where you go that the enemy will be on the same level as you which makes all the enemy encounters boring and very dull. I’ve tried multiple mods that attempt to fix the scaling but none of them were balanced or stable like the way some of the Skyrim overhauls are. Pretty much all of Oblivion is filled with inconsequential npc’s that have nothing to say and the writing in general is not very good so I don’t like the idea of spending many more hours in this game with an overhaul that requires a bigger time investment in a world that doesn’t have interesting characters.  The visuals have aged very well for a game that is over 10 years old now and graphical mods with an enb makes it look stunning. However a big problem with the visuals is the draw distance because you see trees, grass building just pop in and the game has very low quality textures and detail when looking into the distance. It takes you out of the immersion very frequently and there isn’t any mods to fix the draw distance without it being heavily taxing on your system. The combat is very bland, basic and generic. Sword fighting lacks visual feedback making the combat feel very floaty because it lacks impact. This mixed with the very unbalanced and awkward game mechanics or lack there of (like the leveling system and lack of combat mechanics like dodging) creates very boring and weak combat. All the dungeons in the game was designed by one person and it shows, they are very repetitive, only use a few templates and they lack variety, the dungeons overall feel very procedurally generated. These repetitive dungeons mixed with the bad combat makes the dungeons a complete chore as well as the oblivion gates which are also very tedious and repetitive. I didn't have any fun with the dlc and the expansion shivering isles because my character hasn't made any progress in over 40 hours of gameplay. I purposly decided to cap my character at level 18 because i had no reason to keep on leveling and i've been doing the same generic button mashing combat for even more hours so i was just asking myself what is the point of playing all of this. The story and setting for shivering isles is decent but that didn't help make the experience any better at all. I find it hard to recommend Oblivion to newcomers. There is nothing the game does very well. The story is ok, cyrodiil is portrayed as a generic fantasy land, exploring the world is not a whole lot of fun especially with the flaws I brought up. Some of the guild quests are pretty cool but it’s undermined by weak characters. Out of Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim Oblivion is by far the worst of the three for me.

The game you've waited so long to play you forgot you were even waiting.
The level design is stellar; the bosses are a lot more interesting and harder to cheesily bounce on than in the originals (you know what I'm talking about); the new levels are creative while being true to the classic aesthetic... It's a beautiful thing. So if you like Sonic, play it. If you like platformers, play it. If you don't like either of those things then, well, if anything's gonna change your mind it might be this.
Sonic fans, don't be put off by the "recycled" material. They've done new and wonderful things with all of it. Honestly it feels a heck of a lot less derivative than any of the more recent, ostensibly non-throwback type 3D Sonic games that have come out since... let's say Adventure 2.
If I have one criticism, it's a pretty obscure one that pertains to the game more as art than as a game: the tone is really different than that of the older games. It feels a lot lighter, a little sillier, and more low-stakes than the originals, especially S3&R. One of the things that was special about Sonic as a character was that he was this Mickey-esque cartoon character but in this grim, doomed world. Like, toward the end of S2 and especially S3&R, there was really this end-of-the-world vibe; it felt totally epic, kind of dark, and very high stakes. Robotnik seemed almost to have already won. So that was cool, and I miss that. This game feels like a lighthearted side-story in comparison. But what I'm really, really hoping, is that the very savvy and capable creators of Mania are just saving that kind of epic vibe for the next game. So, yeah -- let's all buy this game and give it great reviews, and if we're really lucky, Sega will get the message and keep hiring these guys and putting out excellent games like this one.
P.S. You probably won't even notice the DRM.

I do not know how this happened, but the creators of this series appears to have out Civilized, the civilization series. While some of the base mechanics are akin to the Endless Space series such as the use of dust and heroes, others are reminicant of the newer Civilization games such as the map layout. I think what strikes me most is the battle mechanic. Its a refreshing new take for a strategy game that truly is workable for TBS games. Rather than having a 100 unit "stack of Doom" ala Civ II or being stuck with 1 unit per square ala Civ V - you can create armies of a limited size (that grows dependant on army leaders skill or tech) but still maintain a reasonable cap. The best part is the actual fight where it utilizes the area of the skirmish like a chess-board but incorperating the enviromental elements for each square. So now its vastly past the scale of one unit on grassland looking up at a foe on a hill, you now need to take into account several hex units out which adds a very rich level of battle that the TBS series sorely needs.
Fraxis, take note of this game.

This is a great, great game.  It's worth it's meager price tag of $40.  (Meager in terms of major games, which always have a baseline of $60.)  Put it on your wishlist and snatch it up when you catch a price break.
It's all about the factions.  Unlike in Civ 5, the factions play very differently from each other.  The Wild Walkers kind of focus on expansion, exploration, and harmonizing with the planet, while the Cultists focus on forcing everyone else in the world to join their cult.  This is far from the minor differences of, say, one faction getting +2 food in the capital, as opposed to +1 industry on water tiles like you would see in Civ.  The faction differences in Endless Legend are about PHILOSOPHY, and not about mechanics.  The Cultists are only allowed one city, the Roving Clans are not allowed to declare war, the Drakken can force other factions into peace and alliance treaties.  These are game-altering differences that lead to different game experiences and interesting cross-faction interactions.
Every little part of this game has been fleshed out and thought through.  Every little part of it makes sense.  It won't be the easiest thing to pick up right off the bat, since the guys at Amplitude Studios think just a little differently than you're used to, but they also like to reward you for your efforts.  The more you play, the more you see the big picture, and the more you realize just how perfect each piece of the puzzle is and what a beautiful picture it makes.  Somehow this game is more polished, more interesting, more diverse, and more fun than Civ 5, in which I've got a couple hundred hours logged.
The tutorial is excellent.  It brings you into their way of thinking without patronizing you like you've never played any kind of civilization game before.  The artwork is different and interesting, all the way down to the way the interface responds when you scroll in and out of the map.  The music and sound of the game somehow enhance the whole effect that they are trying to create.  Before you know it, you'll have hours and hours logged and wondering what you ever played before.
There are a few minor issues that keep this game from being a 10, but as it is a new title, I expect those things to be ironed out as time moves on.  For instance, if you accidentally (or intentionally) get ahead of yourself in the tutorial, and even sometimes in a created game, you could end up with a quest that you cannot complete.  Overall, this is usually no big deal, since you are given LOTS of quests during the course of your adventures.  However, if the quest you cannot complete just happens to be a faction quest, then you are effectively cut off from the rest of the storyline for your faction, short of resorting to a save state.
Also, there's not much in the way of naval combat.  This is a really minor gripe for me since about 96% of the time I never used my navy in Civ 5 for anything other than a deterrent, anyway.  But if you're a big fan of naval forces and/or combat, you may miss it here.  Quite frankly, I was many hours deep into this game before I even realized that there was no navy.  Somehow it feels like they told a complete story without it.
I expect a DLC sometime in the future that will probably handle some sort of naval units and a few more factions, although there will never be a glut of factions like in Civ.  Each faction is so fundamentally different I imagine it would be difficult to maintain any kind of balance (or even to come up with a plethora of ideas) if there were endless factions.  (See what I did there?  I might have just named the DLC. )  I mean, unless you're playing Venice, there really isn't much difference between the 300 factions in Civ, anyway.
As it is, though, I am very happy with this game and highly recommend it to anyone who has that 4x itch, that civ itch, or anyone who just wants to play a really good game for a change.

Larian turned gold to lead, but this game is probably worth it, provided that you know what you do.
First off, choose wisely your play level. I chose tactician as a veteran of RPG. I was well served. Indeed, tactician it is! But it doesn't say that you should also scratch every single little advantage that you can (steal as much as possible, stack on potions etc.) in order to be well prepared for the last fight. It also doesn't say that you shouldn't expect your characters to be heroic! Indeed, in many situations at that level you will have to resort to cheesy tactics such as some characters fleeing the combat to recover skill timers, heal, then come back while the combat has been frozen because you left one character or invocation hold it... Or by reloading consistently because you were not prepared for a nasty surprise in a combat and had nothing left to deal with it; so you reload, come back with smart prepositionning and the combat will go smoothly. I remember a fight against some outrageous horror -helped by numerous cronies, all of them more powerful than my characters despite being one level above-, which I easily lost head to head, then won after reloading, placing my characters far enough, engaging with invocations and keeping my characters far enough -actually out of combat- that I could always cast a new invocation when one died. I finally won that fight without a scratch. Smart ? sure. Pleasurable ? Hardly.
So unless you like going very slowly, always moving like there is a fight at the next step (or reloading often), managing inventories to be sure each character has the absolute best equipment, has the necessary consumables,  and so on (i.e. total micromanagement), skip the tactician level. At normal level, the game is going to be challenging enough for most players. Especially the last combat, which I never finished -I have done quite well in the first part, but am hopelessly outnumbered in the second part. I probably know what is wrong, but I won't be going back batching the potions that I am missing, respecing my characters to more useful stats, traits and spells, changing runes for more useful ones etc. you get the picture for tactician level.- So, I won't know the end of the story line I chose, and I won't change my storyline just so the last combat is easier. That's a bit sad.
And NO: YOU CANNO'T CHANGE THE DIFFICULTY LEVEL DOWN!
That's a real shame!
Also, there is no excuse for larian in turning an excellent character development/combat system into the mediocre thing that it has become. In that respect, Original Sin 1 was way better. The current system has clearly been designed in order to foil the player and outrageously favor the opponents. You cannot inflict secondary effects (blinding, stunned etc.) as long as the target has magical or physical armor (a new protection that comes above your hit points.) This means that the first rounds of combat are always going to be damage dealing: you won't have any crowd control coming until you've done some attrition first. Worse: the system favors teams which choose a damage type and stick to it. I made the mistake of wanting a balanced party: the result is that I am too weak for the last fight. Actually in some fights, I had characters standing aside, watching the combat go because they did not deal the right kind of damage...
After all this has been said, I still recommend this game because the story looks good, the world is well developped and generally speakig as RPG go, it stands on the top if you don't fall into the trap where I fell.
EDIT: I finally found the courage to do what I said I wouldn't do, and of course finish the game. As expected, I had to respec my characters, and decided to go for lone wolf. The advantage in lone wolf lies not in the power of the characters (they indeed are stronger, but you have overall less firepower), but in the fact that you don't have to bother about the survival or such and such character, as well as reducing the drain on your consumables (you use two instead of four for a similar effect.) The fight was easy [SPOILERS (light) AHEAD] mostly for use of the special tea sold by Mrs Kremm, combined with at least +50% full elemental protection potions and five star dinner -i.e. all elemental damage did heal me, which both let me remove most healing spells as well as use my own offensive spells for healing-, the pawn and duck duck goose (for good movement, not mentioning spells.) Other talents which I thought would help did not (guerilla) [END SPOILERS] ; I changed my main character from pure mage to hybrid melee (fighter) / mage, helped by an archer/assassin ; as explained above, this was a choice to favor physical damage over magical damage, choice made necessary by the difficulty of that fight. I of course had to spend considerable time to prepare the characters and the consumables, buy or craft the required potions and books as well as redistribute equipment. The trouble is that in that fight I did not recognize the character(s) I played consistently from the beginning (no respec before the end), which is annying (to say the least) for a RPG! The other trouble is of course that I could not have to feeling that the hero was well above the other contenders to deserve my victory. Indeed, the stats of all other human opponents were consistently above those of the hero. Understand who can!

This is a shoot 'em up that, in its entirety, is only a mediocre skeleton of a shoot 'em up - you scroll horizontally and shoot at enemies with a time-regenerating shield and a once-per-level super laser. There is no scoring mechanism (which for the life of me I can't understand in a shoot 'em up), no lives mechanism (if you die, you just restart the level), and no differing weapons mechanism of any kind (you only ever have the stuff you start with and none of it can be upgraded).
Also, the game is... artificially difficult. I mean yeah, the game is difficult, and really I don't even knock it for being difficult, that's fine. But it's stuff like randomly removing your super laser from some levels, with no explanation other than "well we just wanted to make this level harder" or something, I don't even know. What kind of shoot 'em up does that? And I'm talking like, level 2-2 in the middle of nowhere, just the next in a series of horizontal scrolling levels, no boss or anything... if you're going to give me a super laser, let me use it. And it's not that I can't beat it without it - I did - it just feels forced.
Yeah, to me, there's nothing really that attractive about this game. I'm not saying it's a horrible game - it has some entertainment value if you like horizontally scrolling through levels shooting enemies and dodging terrain traps, yeah, it does that, and it does it alright. It's difficult, yeah, it's got that going for it. But... that's really
, seriously. There is nothing else besides proceeding through levels shooting enemies and then a boss after a few levels. No other little incentives or mechanisms anywhere... *shrug* It's only so interesting.
Not an awful game, but not really one I recommend spending very much time on.

RADical ROACH is an horizontal  shoot 'em up game that stands neither on the bullet-hell side, nor on the more traditional Gradius-like type of shooter.
You're a mute cockroach in a post apocalyptic world, apparently dominated by fleas (and other insects and creatures), all trying to put a stop to your renegade run.
It's your job to keep going forward, through 4 different areas, each with a certain theme and enemies.
First off: the developers warned the players that the game is hard. Well... it certainly is, but not for the right reasons at all. It's not a good challenge. It challenges your persistence and patience rather than your skill and reflexes. I'll talk more about level design and difficulty later on.
Alright, let's begin with its
, as usual.
As you can probably see from the screenshots, the game looks pretty good!
It has a bold, hand drawn, cartoony style, and to be honest, it fits the silliness of the game's story.
Everything has a personal look to it, and the bosses are also interesting, in their visual design. It feels like it was made in Flash, and that's fine. The problem is that it plays like it was made by an illustrator with very limited knowledge of how to design the game (other than its visual style).
The animations can be dodgy, at times, without solid transitions between each other. Specially for the bigger enemies, they just vanish into a far smaller explosion sprite when they die, which looks a bit awkward.
All in all, every animation seems to have fewer frames than it should, not really feeling fluid enough. But hey, it's not too bad, it just could have been more polished.
This is a side scrolling shooter, so expect a heavy amount of parallaxing with quite a few layers, that actually looks pretty cool. Despite being a fairly simplistic way of doing it, I actually liked the way the backgrounds passed through, well done on that!
A problem with it, was that you could see the repetition on it, if you look close enough. Slightly larger backgrounds wouldn't have been bad, but it's just a minor concern.
How about
?
Well, both felt off, to be honest. They didn't really fit the theme..
The music itself wasn't bad, but again, it just felt generic, and didn't complement the game's visual style in any way.
One big problem I've had with sound design, was that the music just restarted whenever you died. Instead of just continually play, keeping the flow of the game up, it stopped, and started from the beginning. Maybe this isn't very obvious for most people, but it actually makes a huge difference when playing a game, specially one that requires multiple tries and restarts.
Just another criticism, that isn't quite directed at the game, but I'll just leave as a future suggestion.
There were times when enemies threw projectiles at a rhythm, which helped me get more "immersed" into those sequences and felt great. The problem is that it wasn't sync'ed with the music, and ended up ruining the moment. I realize it was most likely not the intention, but I think the game would have benefitted from more rhythm oriented sections.
Another very annoying thing, was the lack of options. It didn't even have music/sound effects toggles. It was just♥♥♥♥♥♥poor.
Sometimes, I like to just put on my own music, and that wasn't an option at all. Even for lowering sound, I had to use the Windows' Sound Mixer. Big no on this. Come on, how hard is it to put a couple of separate sliders into the game?
It had "Fullscreen" and "HD Mode"(Whatever that was) and another 2 other options that I didn't really need.
Oh... and it doesn't have a Pause Button. If you press escape, you're taken to the level select screen, which will, of course, start you from the beginning of the level. And, if that level happens to have a cutscene, you'll have to see it again, since they're all unskippable.
The menus were just awful from a navigation standpoint, without consistency at all, sometimes using Esc, other time having to click it, ... It was awful. And it makes a more negative impact on the game that could have easily been avoided.
Let's get on with gameplay.
This... is going to be hard. It's mostly awful... with a few glimpes at good ideas, and a couple of good levels.
Your objective is to survive for X amount of time in each level, essentially. There will be different phases in each level. While the phases are fixed, enemy movement within those is a bit random.
Radical Roach implements what's known as "quantity over quality". In almost every single level, there is a huge amount of enemies, cornering you into a place where you'll definitely take damage. The most effective way of playing it is actually just shooting straight and not movement, for the most part.
Another huge problem, is the hitboxes. Specially the player's. It really big. It's not like a bullethell, where they let you dodge bullets efficiently. No, no, no, no, no! Not here. Here, you'll just have to find the sweet spot, and stand there for as long as possible. And pray that the game doesn't spawn enemies in places that will be impossible to dodge.
The game is pretty straightforward, and there isn't much innovation here. There are a couple of cool enemy designs, with patterns that you must learn (and I really like that sort of design!), but then, they're just mixed with the awful amount of other enemies spawning randomly, and leaves the player really frustrated.
Another impediment, is the way the parallaxing has foreground layers, with obstruct the vision, and some of the enemy projectiles get easily mixed with the background colors, rendering the screen a freaking mess.
The difficulty in this game comes from bad level design, exclusively. Big hit boxes, some awkward collision detection at times, too much flash, bad choice of colors, etc. etc.
And almost every level is like that, unfortunately.
In the first world, the screen was fairly big, giving the player space to maneuvre (except for the amount of enemies on there...). But in the second world, you're on a cave, that highly limits where you can go...!
Most of it makes no sense. It's just a bunch of ideas thrown together, without the concept of pacing.
There is no difficulty curve at all. The game starts and ends at roughly the same difficulty. (Well, the last levels were actually easier).
You also have a shield and a special projectile (first it's a laser beam, then a triple shot, a black hole, etc., changing with each world). The problem is that the game strips you off of it at will. In some levels they're available, in other levels it's not...
Then, the shield is badly implemented. It pops whenever you touch a spike (which occurs awfully frequently, as your hitbox gets bigger with the shield), and it also has like a second of delay... So, if you're in a pinch, you're dead. It's not like you can use the shield at the right moment...
BUT, there was hope! The Bosses were actually quite fun, at times (despite creating a few almost impossible dodges at times), and there were a few levels that were far more structured, and thus, less frustating. The penultimate level was a good example of that. It was tricky, certainly. But you could plan ahead, and then avoid everything with skill and reflexes, rather than luck.
Unfortunately, those good moments were few and far between.
It had potential. But it's the perfect example of artificial difficulty.
It's not that people don't like hard games, it's that hard games nowadays do it wrong. They're about randomness and trial and error!

Oblivion has not aged as well as I thought it would, it’s a very average game that has a lot of issues. Playing Oblivion again made me realize how broken the game really is. The biggest issue by far is the level scaling where all the enemies level up with you. You start out fighting mud crabs, rats and goblins and by the end of the game you're still fighting mud crabs that have leveled up with you, but the rats and goblins have mysteriously disappeared to be replaced with ogres and trolls. You start out finding iron and steel swords and face bandits with fur and leather armour. You finish by finding countless ebony weapons and face superbandits with daedric armour. It’s crazy how bad they f*cked this up. Your character could be level 50 that has the best gear and all his stats maxed out and every enemy in a new dungeon you enter will be ogres that are also level 50 and kill you in a few hits. There is no sense of progression and that kills the game in a big way. The fixed enemies in Morrowind for example added tension and reward to the dungeons and the world exploration because you are never sure how strong the enemy will be when you enter a new area which creates a tense atmosphere. But in oblivion there is always the reassurance no matter where you go that the enemy will be on the same level as you which makes all the enemy encounters boring and very dull. I’ve tried multiple mods that attempt to fix the scaling but none of them were balanced or stable like the way some of the Skyrim overhauls are. Pretty much all of Oblivion is filled with inconsequential npc’s that have nothing to say and the writing in general is not very good so I don’t like the idea of spending many more hours in this game with an overhaul that requires a bigger time investment in a world that doesn’t have interesting characters.  The visuals have aged very well for a game that is over 10 years old now and graphical mods with an enb makes it look stunning. However a big problem with the visuals is the draw distance because you see trees, grass building just pop in and the game has very low quality textures and detail when looking into the distance. It takes you out of the immersion very frequently and there isn’t any mods to fix the draw distance without it being heavily taxing on your system. The combat is very bland, basic and generic. Sword fighting lacks visual feedback making the combat feel very floaty because it lacks impact. This mixed with the very unbalanced and awkward game mechanics or lack there of (like the leveling system and lack of combat mechanics like dodging) creates very boring and weak combat. All the dungeons in the game was designed by one person and it shows, they are very repetitive, only use a few templates and they lack variety, the dungeons overall feel very procedurally generated. These repetitive dungeons mixed with the bad combat makes the dungeons a complete chore as well as the oblivion gates which are also very tedious and repetitive. I didn't have any fun with the dlc and the expansion shivering isles because my character hasn't made any progress in over 40 hours of gameplay. I purposly decided to cap my character at level 18 because i had no reason to keep on leveling and i've been doing the same generic button mashing combat for even more hours so i was just asking myself what is the point of playing all of this. The story and setting for shivering isles is decent but that didn't help make the experience any better at all. I find it hard to recommend Oblivion to newcomers. There is nothing the game does very well. The story is ok, cyrodiil is portrayed as a generic fantasy land, exploring the world is not a whole lot of fun especially with the flaws I brought up. Some of the guild quests are pretty cool but it’s undermined by weak characters. Out of Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim Oblivion is by far the worst of the three for me.

I'll try to keep this simple. If you are into world building games like Civilization then this is for you. I'll admit it does try to pass itself off as much more complex than it really is, but adding some of the DLC can improve the game from it's bare bones content. That being said it's still good for hundreds of hours of gameplay, or even just 50-100 which is a standard RPG type. Be forewarned that may only be ONE playthrough of the game however. Since you might want to try different religions, cultures, or starting as a King, Duke, or from various areas of the map - all of which grant you different benefits and drawbacks - that will mean 100 hours of EACH playthrough so that is where the depth comes in. Of course, you can always find yourself outwitted, surrounded, poisoned, left with no heir, have your wife cheat on you the plot to kill all your children that aren't her natural born (especially if you've used concubines), and leave you totally screwed in more ways than one.
Personally, I haven't found any trouble expanding my first playthrough. I did the tutorial as King of Leon. I murdered my brother, took Portugal, murdered my other brother, took Castile, and began merrily about my expansion for glory. I was left with no sons at one point but Queen Maria was up to the task & I married an English Prince to secure a truce from the powerful northern invaders so I could focus on the evil Muslims to the south. Upon her death my Kingdom was split and from that point on I was seperated from Castile as her line and their English blood allowed English invaders to take half of Hispania while I took the other half. I finally was able to get a cadet branch off into Andulusa and even Scotland as allies and had my eyes on England itself but my cousins to the East in Aragon gave me trouble and even though I'd driven the English out of Hispania I could never fully regain power for myself. My allies with my family name were attacked by Muslims and I was constantly fighting their wars for them because I wanted that land safe - thinking I could more easily marry myself or execute them to gain it back rather than fight off a Muslim horde on my own. In the end the lack of expansion left my own Kingdom small, but my family name fairly well known and the clock ticked down on an average score for a first timer.
My 2nd game - now in progress I went full tilt and bought many DLC's. Charlemange, Way of Life, Conclave, and a few more. I chose my 41st real life great-grandfather Sigurd - Ragnar Lothbrok's father. Much life real life I easily expanding out, took over Finland, Sweden, Norway, landed on the English shores, and later founded the Empire of Scandinavia. I reformed the Pagan religion and became Falkyr in less than 250 years. Then I declared holy war on the Muslims and took Andulusa - that same place that screwed me in my 1st game. After a bitter war against an enemy 3 times my size that lasted 5 years (and over 6 months in real time) I finally won and gained a whole Kingdom in one shot. I was 33% bigger instantly and now was a top 5 player in the world. I handed out 110 titles to win over my subjects and figured I'd be popular and rich. 60 gold a month is nice right? I passed laws making it so I didn't need permission from my counsil to do anything. Within a few years while I was waiting for peace and my armies to build up, factions began to form for gavelkind succession, law changes, independence, and even to remove me as ruler! HOW DARE THEY! Don't they realize I MADE THIS LAND WHAT IT IS TODAY?! I'd never lost a war yet so I fought the first one and was winning until the 2nd one declared on me, then the 3rd, and I started to get chipped away at. I began to let the smaller states go independent, sure I could snatch them back up later after the war, but it was all happening too fast. So I tried to jail a few - popularity dropped, and then at last I was faced with perhaps stepping down from the throne and giving in to some demands... and that my friends is where I currently sit. So even when you are the biggest, baddest, most feared man on the planet, you are literally seconds away from losing at any point. Each click matters and hundreds of years of work can literally go up in smoke. Quit now and be the #1 dynasty... or try to overcome the odds, play for 300 more years and see just how much of the world I can take?
1) Battles are automatic - you can't control them except if there is moving speed attribute or a siege attribute basically. Everything else is very hard to predict. A few things like "Heavy infanty bonus 30%" works if you have 60% of your troops as heavy infanty. Otherwise... forget figuring it out. I'd like to see them add a "choose tactic" option for each of your commanders in the battle with a list of the tactics they know, and the available terrain in the area. A "narrow flank" "by the river" or a "defensive bonus" "in the mountains" would be nice to use different situations against other commanders who are good at "morale damage" and "routing the enemy" "in the forrest." They could fight the battle out as they saw it before it happens.
2) Plot % don't matter. 100% doesn't mean 100%. You're going to get found out. You need at least 300%-500% if you want to get the job done, and even then you might succeed but you might get found out in the process. Be warned.
3) Understand your culture and laws. I've been playing as Elective Gavelkind and having 10 babies when I should be having 1 all this time. It took me literally hundreds of hours of gameplay to figure this out. Having to constantly retake lands after they've been divided up after the death of your liege is quite annoying. Don't marry, have many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, legitimize the best one. If you are playing under different rules - KNOW THEM!
4) Certain things in the game never work in your favor. Mercenary companies early on, being a child's guardian, etc. Also, some of the game events don't seem to happen enough. Children events - like raising your 1st born heir to be King - it happens once, you'd think this was a big deal and/or it would have a much more major effect on him. I don't think I've ever actually had "grooming an heir" work and him actually become heir - let alone a good one. The finer points of the game almost seem to be lacking and need polishing. To be fair they do seem to update a lot but it seems to be "wider" not "deeper" updates. Fixing what's there instead of adding new shallow content would be better.
5) Wars are hard. They are incredibly expensive. Take forever to complete. You get precious little territory and everyone hates you for it. By the time you win one, if you get attacked and need to raise levies again - you are so unpopular you are likely to have ruler after ruler begin to take advantage of that weakness and you will see a snowball effect. 1 war will turn to 5 wars in a second. Never go broke, always have tons of gold on hand if you can, always try to win wars quickly and decisively, and don't let anyone see weakness. You will need to take risks, but be warned, they will come for you, and one little bit of bad luck and it's game over.
Overall it's not that expensive a game and you'll get plenty of playtime out of it. You can come back to it from time to time, it doesn't require that you babysit it or anything. The constant pop-ups of 100's of characters and micromanagement can be annoying, but I'll give it an 7/10. I shouldn't have to go 400 years between finding a rare item or a key and then a chest. Merchant lanes should open more, etc. There are many flaws in the game that simply make no sense and it will drive you crazy, but there are so many other things - like the time my lunatic King went crazy, named his horse to the Council as Chancellor and "Glitterhoof" had to be removed... but the option to take my horse as my concubine was there... so I did... and I could umm... mate... with my horse. Well... that was funny? Then I killed my concubine. RIP Glitterhoof

Max Gentlemen is a lame brain game. The objective is to stack as many hats as you can while avoiding any obstacles that are thrown at your magnificent stack. At first, I thought this game was about gentlemanly brawling. Boy, was I surprised when I saw that the game was about who could stack the highest stack of hats. There are basically 2 modes, an infinite stacking challenge and a verus stacking mode. Keys are simply WASD and Spacebar to jump.
In the infinite challenge, you ride a moving carriage while trying to stack hats and avoid birds that are aimlessly crashing into your hats. You press Spacebar to jump the hats on your head and collect more hats. You use the W and S keys to select the upper hats or lower hats to jump.
In the versus stacking mode, you pick up random beers that come from the bartender which reward you with an additional hat. Then you jump hats to avoid the incoming thrown beers and boomerangs all the while watching a fist fights go on in the background.
Conclusion, you can skip this game. Hat stacking is totally nonsenscial. However, for the top hat afficiando, 5 minutes will let you know if you ever want to play a hat stacking game ever again.
Note: Done by The Man Who Wear Many Hats, Ryan Wiemeyer and Michael Block, Chicago. Supposedly, these guys made too much money off Organ Trail (a spinoff of Oregon Trail?)

I have played TheHunter: Primal For about 20 hours now so here is my review. For a early access game the graphics look really good, and the map is huge and the forest looks really amazing.
It does lack a little bit of life though, so far they only have 3 dinosaurs, Utahraptor,Triceratops, Tyrannosauras Rex. These dinosaurs have there own traits and habits, for example. The Utahraptor raptors usually will hunt is packs, so you have to be carful not to get flanked by them. The Triceratops is usually a none aggressive dinosaur of course dont provoke them or they will fight back. The Tyrannosauras Rex is probobly the most scary and toughest of the 3, usually when he is around he will let out a big rour, when the t-rex get's closer you will start to hear big thumping sounds of his feet. The A.I for these dinosaurs i find quite good. Also dinosaurs have certain weak spots like heart and other vital organs, dont go for the head.
You start the game off with just a bow and some arrows , you must explore the island for boxes which might have weapons, outfits, or health canisters. You will also have GPS type device called the settlemate, it will help you locate these boxes and also help you let you know were the dinosaurs are.
The game does have multiplayer up to 16 players online, the online is really fun!.......when it works. there is no dedicated servers yet which is really disappointing. To play with friends you have to open ports to your router and it's a big pain and sometimes does not always work. When you join other peoples games sometimes the players your with dont have good enough connection which will cause a black screen, it seems to happen quite often on servers, and it's really annoying. I hope they will fix this soon because the game is really fun to play with friends.
Overall

+Cool dinosaurs
+Big map
Cons
-Online needs fixed
-No ammo stacking
-Sprint Does not last long
-No real story

OMG!!!! I hate and totally love this game. It is by far the most intense, at times, game I've played yet. It does have some drawbacks though which I will address in a minute. First, i'd like to congratulate the dev team that worked on the sound and graphics. Some of the settings are absolutely spectacular. My brother and I just bought it today and I found myself staring at a couple of sunsets and a triceratops roaming down by the ocean. They're so life-like.
The utahraptors...don't get me started. They were so hard to deal with in the dense forest I finally quit trying to get my stuff back. I was almost there once. I was traveling a little gully and saw a pack of them ahead of me say 50 yards away. Too late, I've been spotted. I laid down and worked my way over against the side of a rock wall as they approached. I can hear them hissing and that weird growling. One just walked right by me.  My God, they're everywhere. I can see their tails. Okay, my screen is red and I'm am feeding them with my entrails. I love this game.
The pros are the intensity is insane. There are long stretches when nothing happens, but the never knowing when something is going to happen, especially at night makes the intensity more enthralling. The sound and graphics are top-notch. The utahraptors actually herded us up a hill where we had no choice but to take a stand against them. Very real feeling of dread. Between my bow and my brother's .308 scoped hunting rifle we won. My brother ran out of bullets. I'm going to cut this short because he's back and we're going to play some more.
The minuses are the stamina. It runs out wat too fast IMO. Should last a little longer, but not too much. There's not enough wildlife yet. There should be a crafting system to build a place to make a homebase. Or perhaps a structure that can be used as one. That's it for now.
If you like survival games, some long stretches of just looting and exploring followed by stomach twisting moments of chaotic mayhem where hours of hard work can be extinguished by one bite...this game should not be missed. Twenty bucks and my brother and I are hooked. In the immortal words of Axl Rose, welcome to the jungle baby...you're gonna die!
Challenging and Terrifying!!

At the time of writing this, I have played 184 hours on this game, from when it was first released to most recently.
Overall, this game is very fun, but it has its ups and downs, but the downs that it has are most likely fixed or polished in a very timely manner.
This game offers something that I have wanted for a long, long, time. Which is simple, yet innovative, since it hasn't really been done yet. This game offers something incredible, which is simply this: being able to take control of a soldier in first person. Of course, the mechanics for it aren't superb, but that's to be expected from a game focused on real time strategy not shootin' up the bad guys in first person rambo style. It's still fun to play around with, though, and I thoroughly enjoy playing around with it.
For the moment, as of November 27th, 2017, there aren't that many factions and that many vehicles (excluding mods) to play around with, which causes the game to start getting dull. But, whenever an update comes out, I go and check it out and slam another 5-10 hours into the game and maybe some more if a new mod is out.
Multiplayer is pretty solid and so are the maps, but if you want to create a scenario all on your own, you can just hit up the editor and make it in 20 minutes or less (depending on what scale of a scenario you're doing.)
This game offers workshop support, custom scenarios, custom multiplayer games, first person aspects, and strategy.
Although, there are cons, like lack of factions, lack of smooth first person combat (basically Fallout 3/Fallout New Vegas first person gameplay), and overall gameplay issues concerning the fps with slower computers, these will more than likely be smoothed out.
On another note, there are many reviews calling this game awful for petty reasons, one of the most recent is about the boundry fog, which is so petty and atrocious to give a game a bad rating because of the fog. That whole review is completely absurd. People are also complaining about it's lack of content and how bad it is compared to MOW:AS 2. Which one thing you should consider, MOW:AS 2 had a game before it: MOW:AS  This allowed them to polish up the textures and graphics of that game, and then add more units, items, missions, maps, and fixes to it in a more timely manner.
I hope the devs keep up the good work with this game, and I appreciate what they're doing.
