Oblivion has not aged as well as I thought it would, it’s a very average game that has a lot of issues. Playing Oblivion again made me realize how broken the game really is. The biggest issue by far is the level scaling where all the enemies level up with you. You start out fighting mud crabs, rats and goblins and by the end of the game you're still fighting mud crabs that have leveled up with you, but the rats and goblins have mysteriously disappeared to be replaced with ogres and trolls. You start out finding iron and steel swords and face bandits with fur and leather armour. You finish by finding countless ebony weapons and face superbandits with daedric armour. It’s crazy how bad they f*cked this up. Your character could be level 50 that has the best gear and all his stats maxed out and every enemy in a new dungeon you enter will be ogres that are also level 50 and kill you in a few hits. There is no sense of progression and that kills the game in a big way. The fixed enemies in Morrowind for example added tension and reward to the dungeons and the world exploration because you are never sure how strong the enemy will be when you enter a new area which creates a tense atmosphere. But in oblivion there is always the reassurance no matter where you go that the enemy will be on the same level as you which makes all the enemy encounters boring and very dull. I’ve tried multiple mods that attempt to fix the scaling but none of them were balanced or stable like the way some of the Skyrim overhauls are. Pretty much all of Oblivion is filled with inconsequential npc’s that have nothing to say and the writing in general is not very good so I don’t like the idea of spending many more hours in this game with an overhaul that requires a bigger time investment in a world that doesn’t have interesting characters.  The visuals have aged very well for a game that is over 10 years old now and graphical mods with an enb makes it look stunning. However a big problem with the visuals is the draw distance because you see trees, grass building just pop in and the game has very low quality textures and detail when looking into the distance. It takes you out of the immersion very frequently and there isn’t any mods to fix the draw distance without it being heavily taxing on your system. The combat is very bland, basic and generic. Sword fighting lacks visual feedback making the combat feel very floaty because it lacks impact. This mixed with the very unbalanced and awkward game mechanics or lack there of (like the leveling system and lack of combat mechanics like dodging) creates very boring and weak combat. All the dungeons in the game was designed by one person and it shows, they are very repetitive, only use a few templates and they lack variety, the dungeons overall feel very procedurally generated. These repetitive dungeons mixed with the bad combat makes the dungeons a complete chore as well as the oblivion gates which are also very tedious and repetitive. I didn't have any fun with the dlc and the expansion shivering isles because my character hasn't made any progress in over 40 hours of gameplay. I purposly decided to cap my character at level 18 because i had no reason to keep on leveling and i've been doing the same generic button mashing combat for even more hours so i was just asking myself what is the point of playing all of this. The story and setting for shivering isles is decent but that didn't help make the experience any better at all. I find it hard to recommend Oblivion to newcomers. There is nothing the game does very well. The story is ok, cyrodiil is portrayed as a generic fantasy land, exploring the world is not a whole lot of fun especially with the flaws I brought up. Some of the guild quests are pretty cool but it’s undermined by weak characters. Out of Morrowind, Oblivion and Skyrim Oblivion is by far the worst of the three for me.

The Game plays like any Classic Sonic Game, 2D Platforming, Good Stage Design and a few Gimmicks in some Levels.
The Characters Play like they were in the Classic Games, Sonic (Along with a Dropdash) can wield many Abilities only exclusive to the No Save Mode, Tails can fly and Knuckles can Glide.

I'll try to keep this simple. If you are into world building games like Civilization then this is for you. I'll admit it does try to pass itself off as much more complex than it really is, but adding some of the DLC can improve the game from it's bare bones content. That being said it's still good for hundreds of hours of gameplay, or even just 50-100 which is a standard RPG type. Be forewarned that may only be ONE playthrough of the game however. Since you might want to try different religions, cultures, or starting as a King, Duke, or from various areas of the map - all of which grant you different benefits and drawbacks - that will mean 100 hours of EACH playthrough so that is where the depth comes in. Of course, you can always find yourself outwitted, surrounded, poisoned, left with no heir, have your wife cheat on you the plot to kill all your children that aren't her natural born (especially if you've used concubines), and leave you totally screwed in more ways than one.
Personally, I haven't found any trouble expanding my first playthrough. I did the tutorial as King of Leon. I murdered my brother, took Portugal, murdered my other brother, took Castile, and began merrily about my expansion for glory. I was left with no sons at one point but Queen Maria was up to the task & I married an English Prince to secure a truce from the powerful northern invaders so I could focus on the evil Muslims to the south. Upon her death my Kingdom was split and from that point on I was seperated from Castile as her line and their English blood allowed English invaders to take half of Hispania while I took the other half. I finally was able to get a cadet branch off into Andulusa and even Scotland as allies and had my eyes on England itself but my cousins to the East in Aragon gave me trouble and even though I'd driven the English out of Hispania I could never fully regain power for myself. My allies with my family name were attacked by Muslims and I was constantly fighting their wars for them because I wanted that land safe - thinking I could more easily marry myself or execute them to gain it back rather than fight off a Muslim horde on my own. In the end the lack of expansion left my own Kingdom small, but my family name fairly well known and the clock ticked down on an average score for a first timer.
My 2nd game - now in progress I went full tilt and bought many DLC's. Charlemange, Way of Life, Conclave, and a few more. I chose my 41st real life great-grandfather Sigurd - Ragnar Lothbrok's father. Much life real life I easily expanding out, took over Finland, Sweden, Norway, landed on the English shores, and later founded the Empire of Scandinavia. I reformed the Pagan religion and became Falkyr in less than 250 years. Then I declared holy war on the Muslims and took Andulusa - that same place that screwed me in my 1st game. After a bitter war against an enemy 3 times my size that lasted 5 years (and over 6 months in real time) I finally won and gained a whole Kingdom in one shot. I was 33% bigger instantly and now was a top 5 player in the world. I handed out 110 titles to win over my subjects and figured I'd be popular and rich. 60 gold a month is nice right? I passed laws making it so I didn't need permission from my counsil to do anything. Within a few years while I was waiting for peace and my armies to build up, factions began to form for gavelkind succession, law changes, independence, and even to remove me as ruler! HOW DARE THEY! Don't they realize I MADE THIS LAND WHAT IT IS TODAY?! I'd never lost a war yet so I fought the first one and was winning until the 2nd one declared on me, then the 3rd, and I started to get chipped away at. I began to let the smaller states go independent, sure I could snatch them back up later after the war, but it was all happening too fast. So I tried to jail a few - popularity dropped, and then at last I was faced with perhaps stepping down from the throne and giving in to some demands... and that my friends is where I currently sit. So even when you are the biggest, baddest, most feared man on the planet, you are literally seconds away from losing at any point. Each click matters and hundreds of years of work can literally go up in smoke. Quit now and be the #1 dynasty... or try to overcome the odds, play for 300 more years and see just how much of the world I can take?
1) Battles are automatic - you can't control them except if there is moving speed attribute or a siege attribute basically. Everything else is very hard to predict. A few things like "Heavy infanty bonus 30%" works if you have 60% of your troops as heavy infanty. Otherwise... forget figuring it out. I'd like to see them add a "choose tactic" option for each of your commanders in the battle with a list of the tactics they know, and the available terrain in the area. A "narrow flank" "by the river" or a "defensive bonus" "in the mountains" would be nice to use different situations against other commanders who are good at "morale damage" and "routing the enemy" "in the forrest." They could fight the battle out as they saw it before it happens.
2) Plot % don't matter. 100% doesn't mean 100%. You're going to get found out. You need at least 300%-500% if you want to get the job done, and even then you might succeed but you might get found out in the process. Be warned.
3) Understand your culture and laws. I've been playing as Elective Gavelkind and having 10 babies when I should be having 1 all this time. It took me literally hundreds of hours of gameplay to figure this out. Having to constantly retake lands after they've been divided up after the death of your liege is quite annoying. Don't marry, have many ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, legitimize the best one. If you are playing under different rules - KNOW THEM!
4) Certain things in the game never work in your favor. Mercenary companies early on, being a child's guardian, etc. Also, some of the game events don't seem to happen enough. Children events - like raising your 1st born heir to be King - it happens once, you'd think this was a big deal and/or it would have a much more major effect on him. I don't think I've ever actually had "grooming an heir" work and him actually become heir - let alone a good one. The finer points of the game almost seem to be lacking and need polishing. To be fair they do seem to update a lot but it seems to be "wider" not "deeper" updates. Fixing what's there instead of adding new shallow content would be better.
5) Wars are hard. They are incredibly expensive. Take forever to complete. You get precious little territory and everyone hates you for it. By the time you win one, if you get attacked and need to raise levies again - you are so unpopular you are likely to have ruler after ruler begin to take advantage of that weakness and you will see a snowball effect. 1 war will turn to 5 wars in a second. Never go broke, always have tons of gold on hand if you can, always try to win wars quickly and decisively, and don't let anyone see weakness. You will need to take risks, but be warned, they will come for you, and one little bit of bad luck and it's game over.
Overall it's not that expensive a game and you'll get plenty of playtime out of it. You can come back to it from time to time, it doesn't require that you babysit it or anything. The constant pop-ups of 100's of characters and micromanagement can be annoying, but I'll give it an 7/10. I shouldn't have to go 400 years between finding a rare item or a key and then a chest. Merchant lanes should open more, etc. There are many flaws in the game that simply make no sense and it will drive you crazy, but there are so many other things - like the time my lunatic King went crazy, named his horse to the Council as Chancellor and "Glitterhoof" had to be removed... but the option to take my horse as my concubine was there... so I did... and I could umm... mate... with my horse. Well... that was funny? Then I killed my concubine. RIP Glitterhoof

More so than anything I've played recently, Endless Legend scratches an itch for a 'different' 4X experience.  From the robust questing mechanics, to Amplitude’s unique take on city management and expansion, there are enough interesting and fresh mechanics here to intrigue even the most jaded 4X player and a lot more besides.
Highlights includes the combat system and unit manager, which improve heavily on the highly numeric ‘rock-paper-scissors’ feel of the Endless Space system, while retaining the detail-oriented feel.  With control over unit equipment, passive abilities and even attack style, Legend offers a strategy-heavy, crunchy combat experience, where unit massing is rewarded, but not as much as having the right equipment to take down the specific foes you are fighting.  The difference between frontline bruiser units and backline snipers or support mages is visceral, visual and satisfying, as are the battlefield system and reinforcement mechanics.

Quests feel important and motivated by discovery rather than by necessity.  While some rewards are underwhelming, like the unique weapons and armors for Hero units, others are vital to good game progression.  The ability to unlock research, acquire significant strategic resources, or new unit types make the questing process much more important to mid and late phase gameplay.
Cities also feel more responsive, with specialist-like production direction from the very first citizen and a growth mechanic that rewards different expansion styles in different ways.  Need a manufactory?  Expand to occupy as many hexes as possible.  Need a scientific hub?  Focus on building a tight cluster of a city with as many level 2 districts as possible.  Automatic roads, no workers and tile exploitations make broader city management easier and less micromanagement focused, leaving you with the time and focus to plan expansions and manage larger armies.
The starting factions also provide a huge boost in replayability.  The unique faction traits, as well as units and technologies, lend themselves to dramatically different playstyles.  In contrast to more Civ-like games where strategy is determined more by game-level mechanics and your starting position, each Legend faction has obviously more viable strategies and approaches to the victory conditions.  On the flip side, the factions don’t feel truly balanced.  The differences in starting units alone bias the game early on before players have had an opportunity to research effective counter units.  Some races are even locked out of whole aspects of the game.  Necrophages can’t engage in diplomacy, the Broken Lords don’t interact with food and the Cultists can’t build cities.  While major deficiencies are ostensibly balanced by other advantages, the lack of faction balance discourages diverse multiplayer, while simultaneously boosting single player variability.
While all the differences and new system mechanics can seem overwhelming, the key to Endless Legend’s success are the myriad little and big differences.  It’s an extremely enjoyable foray into new spaces in the 4X genre.

Divinity 2 is an unexpected gem that probably you would never find alike these days. Given that nearly all RPGs today have hack'n slashy action and braindead dialogues in them, you must miss old RPGs right? Well I'm pretty sure Divinity 2 will keep you busy for at least 100 hours. Why?
I'm never much of a strategy player nor I like turn based♥♥♥♥♥♥combat. BUT, turn-based combat can't feel so good in any other game except this one. You're going to LOVE combat system in this game.
Diplomacy and your choices MATTER. Dialogues and actions to be taken by the player are not just random♥♥♥♥♥♥ you feel the game's environment and characters interact with each other depending on actions.
Dialogues are fun! Larian team apparently spent months on dialogues as they are aptly written. Don't forget extra dialogue windows can be opened depending on your character's traits which also can be chosen or gained in the story.
Blessful soundtrack and voice-overs! Divinity 2's soundtrack is just amazing! Even the character's actors must have given so much effort that all the dialogues feel intimate.
It's a HUGE world. If you are like me and love to discover, to leave no stone unturned, you are going to like it. Although it is probably not possible to do 100% of the content alone (due to choices, traits, talents or simply lack of discover) it will keep you busy and you'll enjoy it.
---
BUT my friends & I kinda didn't like some things about Divinity 2. These are:
The story is... a bit weak. Or at least it feels like it after you advance through the game. I don't want to spoil it but it feels like as the developers proceed through the game they may have rushed it until the end in terms of story.
The inventory & crafting sometimes make no sense at all. It is amazing that how diverse the crafting system is yes, but as you get used to the game and progress a bit, you feel it is not really necessary to do crafting because you're not going to need the items that come out of it whatsoever.
It's still SO BUGGY MAN! Especially the last map, Jesus! I still remember restarting game hundred times because either my character looked naked, weird skillbook glitches happened or the AI controlled character stopped working?! There are hundreds of bugs still, but they don't interfere with the game that much. Well, not always...
All in all, buy this game and play it with your friends. I think it's one of the best games of 2017 and I'm looking forward to a DLC. (God King muthafuka)

Divinity Original Sin 2 is the kind of game you stay up til 5:00 am playing because the story and world are so engrossing.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is the kind of game where you can customize your party's skills to a crazy degree and, in theory, play any way you want.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is the kind of game where every character has a story to tell and where the game world feels truly alive.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is also the kind of game you can end up in a game-ending fight because you misclick on something and have to reload an autosave from 40+ minutes ago.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is also the kind of game that gives you very vague pointers to a quest that you can fail simply by picking an unmarked dialogue option or by not speaking to some unmarked person in an unmarked location whose name is some unrecognizable fantasy mumbo-jumbo listed in a horribly unhelpful journal system.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is also the kind of game where you can tab out, grab a glass of water, then tab back in and the eight enemies with twice your stats you're fighting so you can progress in the story still won't be done TPK-ing you.
Divinity Original Sin 2 is also the kind of game to give you five different dialouge options and have the outcome be the same no matter which one you pick, even if you simply attempt to walk into the room and blow the person you're talking to up.
Of course, it's pretty obvious I'm just bad at the game, but ♥♥♥♥ me for wanting a game I can play on normal without cheesing it, right? I've put hundreds of hours into isometric rpgs (NWN, Tyranny, Baldur's Gate) and I've never encountered one so paradoxically annoying as this one.
The "story mode" makes the game a joke, yet the classic mode requires more build metamancing and AI exploitation than actual tactics to beat. The game gives you horribly vague breadcrumbs that you're supposed to follow for quests in a pointerless open world, yet sometimes railroads you into doing things while making you think you have a choice. It's absurd. It's simply not fun for me.
Clearly it's a subjective and unpopular opinion, but I don't reccomend this.

This is a dota-like 3v3 2d-side scroller. Only game of the genre, and it is also well executed.
The good:
The styling and theming is incredibly top-notch. The character theming is good enough to rival pre-hatfest TF2.
All the different Awesomenauts are quite different from eachother, and while the balancing is never perfect, it is alright, considering the nature of the genre.
Seriously, this is a 2d arena game where you have different moves at your disposal, and due to the size of the character pool, very few fights are ever going to be the same.
High skill ceiling. You will see many people with many hundreds of hours put in this game. They are continuing to improve.
The neutral:
It is highly recommended that you get a friend or two to play with. Solo queueing is still completely viable and you can do great things, but friends will absolutely improve your experience. Lone wolves will get less enjoyment out of this game, social gamers will get more.
The bad:
No dedicated servers. Laggy hitboxes are a problem. If you hit somebody on your screen, it's pretty much guaranteed to be a hit, which also means that on the person's screen who is 120ms away from you means that it looks like they dodged it but they didn't. With skill, you can just try to anticipate 120ms away with your dodging, but this is just coming to terms with a real problem.
Matchmaking can be fairly tricky. It has significantly improved in 2014, since I last played in 2012. At its worst, it's usually a stomp fest of a premade-3 vs a team of scrubby solo's, but as of late, I've had more fair matchups than not.
Summary: A low-cost multiplayer arena title that is revolutionary and cool, but has a couple large mountains to climb that prevent it from being great.

(As a note, while this is a thumbs-up review because PixelJunk Shooter is a good game, you shouldn't buy it! Buy PixelJunk Shooter Ultimate instead, it contains this game with a graphical overhaul plus its sequel for one dollar more.)
PixelJunk Shooter is a twin-stick shooter/puzzle game with some neat liquid physics. I found it very reminiscent of indie puzzle platformers, only based on a twin-stick shooter engine instead of, well, a platformer engine, with some tricky levels and fun boss fights at the end of each of the three chapters.
The only real drawbacks are that it's a bit on the short side and, when it comes to finding all of the treasures and secret areas, the game often turns into Pixel♥♥♥♥♥ Shooter, with you needing to flail your grapple around in corners, destroy all the soft rock in large levels, and try pushing your ship into all of the dead ends in order to get 100% completion. That's... not quite as entertaining as actually playing the game for progression.
Still, it ends up a solid enough game to earn my recommendation.

Newer Review:
28 hours in and I can say Legend is not my favorite 4x (500+hours in CIV V and I have major issues with THAT game) and it is not my least favorite (Moo3 anyone?)
I had major issues on my old machine and playing on this new and shiny machine (still not insanely better mind you, just more ram and cpu power mainly) I find Legends to be a bit more playable. But I also am finding it to be a bit boring now. It might just be that I played it a bunch slogging through the lag and mouse problems and UI stuff when it wasn't working so well, that now I have an aversion to enjoying it but I am finding the game to decidedly bland. It isn't horrible and I want people to know that it could be tons worse.
Some pros:
-- Based on the Endless universe it has terms you will be familiar with if you've played Endless Space at all (A far superior game imho.)
-- There is a faction editor. You are not stuck playing some opaque and perhaps hard to play if you are  beginner, faction with weird abilities. You can make your own. (Though I suspect most newbs won't until they have at least some idea what is going on.)
-- This is certainly a genuine 4x game. You need to explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate in varying degrees (depending on how you choose your settings.) And every element of this has a distinct Endless branding to it. Though some of it reminds me strongly of CIV and Alpha Centauri. That's not a bad thing as both games are classics.
And cons:
-- You need ram to play this game. The min requirement specs are just wrong. 12gb seems fine.
-- The hoops required to accomplish goals in this game are not fun to complete. They don't feel organic or interesting to me.
-- I mention above the opaqueness of the factions. This is 70% flavor 30% mechanics I think, but I have ended up avoiding the weirder factions (for now) and just sticking with my own edited ones that perhaps aren't as capable but feel better. This is one area that did not port wel from ES.
-- The faction editor has less flexibility than the faction editor in ES and this might be a balance issue (as in the game designers saw that ES's custom factions had some game breaking issues?) But it feels like like a nerf.
I really, really wish Steam had 3 ratings for games (at least) or used a 1-10 rating system so we could express both concerns about the game and pleasure for what it does right and not merely cater to "Pass/Fail" model it currently has.
As such I am changing this review to a thumbs up BUT I still feel it is caveat emptor as you may not be getting what you expect in terms of UI and performance if you have a semi low end or older machine. (Despite what one commentor said I found 4gb is not enough and 12gb is.)
If you have troubles I do recommend fiddling with the settings as that does help.

Mechanically, this game will be familiar to those who have played Mario Party in the past. The only catch is that there's no minigames determining who wins a battle, but instead you literally battle with dice rolls for attacking, defending, and evading.
You can use cards to aid you in battle, allow you to progress further using the latest metal gear technology, and to buff yourself for the future battles. Not only that, but you can force events, and activate you're character's Hyper, which is their ultimate.
Each character revolves around this Hyper Card, and their stats which may or may not determine the playstyle. It's a surprisingly deep game with counter-pick logic and strategy which keeps you coming back to play it.
This game is best, and I mean BEST with friends. Get this game for some pals and go ham.

Well, I just finished PixelJunk Shooter after ~11 hours of gameplay, and I can say that every minute of it was enjoyable.  It's part shooter, part puzzle game, with elements of gameplay that remind me of Ikaruga (without the ridiculous level of difficulty), a 2d sandbox game (for use of elements, not a customizable world), and the Zelda series.
Each level is well-designed, visually entertaining, and the addition of new gameplay mechanics comes at just the right pace to keep you from getting bored.  The basic gameplay is 1) fly around, rescuing scientists with your grappling hook, shoot a few (easy) enemies before they kill you, blow away rock to find secret rooms/gems and use new ship "suits" and their powers to manipulate the elements to solve puzzles.  The boss design is cute, and challenging enough that you probably won't beat them on the first try or the second, but you won't become frustrated, either.  You life meter is very different from most shooters; instead of a couple hits killing you outright, damage (environmental and enemy) causes you to overheat, and you either need to cool off by plunging into water, or take a time out before you blow yourself up.  This was a very refreshing take on damage for a shooter, and allows one to make a couple foolish mistakes and impatient attempts without being penalized too heavily.
My favorite part of the game was the interplay of the elements in the game:  lava, water, ice, explosive gas, dirt, and a corrosive + magnetic fluid.  When lava hits water, it turns into dirt (and gets cosumed in the process), which you can use to dam up areas, or create an umbrella over yourself for safe passage, and it can also melt ice, or ignite the explosive gas!  Passing through the gass slightly overheats your ship, and is dangerous, because something else in the environment may ignite it while you're in the cloud, killing you.  Water turns to ice when it hits other ice, which may trap and kill your ship, or be ripped down with the grappling hook to clear it away, or deliver water to other areas.  Water also turns the black magnetic fluid into explosive gas.  The magnetic fluid is drawn to your ship, so don't fly to closely over it, as it will rise up to meet you, and quickly causes damage!  It can also be attracted to other magnets, which are usually controlled by a remote switch, playing very similarly to the water dungeons in Zelda.
To further interact with these elements, there are several suits your ship can wear, which are accessible via landing strips in the appropriate levels.  There's a water suit, which swaps your ship's missle launcher for a water hose (don't forget to shoot above yourself and let it rain down on you if you're overheating!), and uniquely, has a grappling hook which can grab and rip off chunks of ice, since you no longer have a weapon that can blast anything away.  The magma suit operates similarly, exchanging your missles for a lava hose, but don't assume you're fireproof!  The inverter suit doesn't change your weapons at all, but switches the gameplay mechanics so that water "overheats" you, and lava "cools" and heals you, allowing passageway through areas you couldn't previously reach, as well as added dangers.  The magnetic repeller suit keeps your missles, but instead of attacting the magnetic/corrosive fluid, you repel it, which can be used to safely traverse pools of it, as well as deflect it away into enemies, or to fill containers that act as switches.
All in all, I'm VERY satisfied with this game, especially for the $1 or whatever it cost in the bundle deal (PixelJunk's tower defense game is HORRIBLE, don't even install it!).  It's simple enough for early teenagers to play, and fun/creative enough for adults as well.  It's a game I'm proud to have in my library to support the developers, and was entertaining all the way through.  I'd say this game is worth $4.99 on its own, and anything less than that is a steal.

Specter of Torment is an expandalone prequel to Shovel Knight. It offers much of the same platforming elements while adding a bit more definition to the characters and backstory.
Shovel Knight pogos on enemies, Plague Knight throws bombs, and the new Specter Knight dash slashes through airborne enemies to gain height.
Every level from the first to the last caters to the unique movement, which requires precise timing. If you attack a target while they're below you then you thrust yourself down--you have to wait until gravity pulls you below your next target before you strike.
Every level is available to you from the start, play them in any order. While you do have an expanding assortment of alternate weapons, I only ever used two. A far cry from the original Shovel Knight which had me alternating all my abilities actively per each level. Too many of these new alternate weapons were gimmicky and saw zero use.
On top of the already impressive library of art assets available in the earlier titles, the developers went all out in adding plenty of fresh new content for me to soak my eyes into. Shovel Knight and it's DLC proves that pixel art can be beautifully tuned if you put in enough work.
Virt reprises his role as the lead musician, composing new unique material for EVERY single stage. Anyone intimately familiar with the original soundtrack will notice the new themes all bear leitmotifs from the original songs. Certain tracks are remarkably improved, while others suffer from only having been tweaked slightly and are worse off for it.
The earliest game in the timeline, you've been conscripted to track down elite knights to form the Order of no Quarter. Campy, humorous overtones prevail throughout the story, save for the somber flashbacks. This is the perfect volume of plot for a solid platformer.
Having already experienced most of the bosses prior, the impact is a bit lessened this third time through. I'm still impressed by the background assets and I love seeing the fresh angles depicted in certain levels.
Recovery items are plentiful enough that you won't find yourself dying outside of instant kill pits or to the errant spike. Checkpoints are frequent, and just like the earlier games you only lose a portion of money which you can recollect.
You're given access to all the stages at once. The inevitable accumulation of hp expansions will trivialize the difficulty of any late game enemies and bosses. You'll still have to be on guard against the occasional instant death trap.
The final boss, while very impressive to look at and in concept, is a bit too simple.
If you've already purchased Shovel Knight (you should) then this DLC will be inside your base game as a free update. I appreciate the effort that Yacht Club games put into their updates, so I threw ten dollars at them even though I didn't have to. Good work should be rewarded. Good games should be played.

STORY: Gotham City Impostors story is about two teams fighting for Batman, or the Joker. This game doesn't have a story, or even a single player. Which it doesn't aim for. It aims to be a fast paced online FPS and nothing else.
GAMEPLAY: Gotham City Impostors plays like every other FPS of today, but it puts it's own "fazazz" to it. Adding ridiculous weapons and items that doesn't give people an unfair advantage. Everything is well rounded and great to use.
LEVELS:  The levels are large, arenas based on places from the Batman comics. Most levels and open and large, giving people great places to hide, or to run and gun. Every level fits with the gameplay and doesn't feel broken because it doesn't fit.
PROBLEMS IN MY OPINION: Back in 2012, this game was HUGE, but now (by the time I'm writing this) it's almost abandoned. Making it hard to find a game at times, and sometimes when you find a game, it'll be almost empty. This game is still great and I wish that more people would play it.
My final rating for Gotham City Impostors is.... 6.2/10. It's a fast paced, fun FPS but it's almost dead and there's almost no community so you might not play it much.

I was a huge fan of the predecessor to this game simply titled "Alien Zombie Death" which was released exclusively on the PSP as a "MINIS" game. It was an overly addicting portable title that played with the feel and charm of a classic arcade shooter. I found it to be one of those rare games with simple controls that anyone can watch and instantly know how to play. "Alien Zombie Mega Death" is an entirely re-worked game revamped from the older version but made for the PC and consoles. The game plays exactly the same but has updated the visuals with higher resolution graphics and provided additional gameplay features. The addicting arcade feel and atmosphere that the predecessor had still remains and makes this version a must own for anyone with a Steam account. If this game were made in the 70s it would have been historically known as a fantastic skill based arcade game.  (a la ... Pacman, Space Invaders). Although each level has challenges that you must complete to advance and open up more levels, I actually consider this to be in the vain of old school high-score games that have no real ending. (ie, Tetris, Tapper). This is a must buy for any fan of retro arcade games. I can't believe how many people have never heard of this game.  Whether you are playing for a high score against friends or trying to complete all of the levels and their challenges, this game will provide gamers with countless hours of pure gaming fun. I consistently come back to this game as my "go-to" when I want to put on some music through steam and play a game that allows me to get lost in the mix. It is a real gem and one of my personal favorite games of all time.

Alien Zombie Megadeath is a throwback to the simply-premised arcade games of yore. You've got a blaster, things want to kill you, kill them first. Difficulty and strategy enter the picture as platform layouts on each level increase in size and complexity, new obstacles enter the mix, and (of course) more and more waves of aliens get lobbed at you. There's not much in the way of depth here, but Alien Zombie Megadeath doesn't really need it. The game straddles the line between survival drive and score chaser, and is better off for not deviating from it.
There's a fair amount to do in Alien Zombie Megadeath even with the rather basic concept, with a huge pile of levels to plow through, and some new outfits to unlock as a reward for your efforts. It's also really easy to just pick up and play here and there, be it as stress relief or to knock your friends down a few pegs on the leaderboard.
Alien Zombie Megadeath may not look like much, especially for 2011 (I honestly thought it was older), but it's still pretty fun and worth snagging.

If you're a fan of stealth mixed with survival / scavenging, then this game is perfect for you. T Rex's are perhaps the most terrifying thing you will ever try to run, hide, or even fight, as even hiding silently they can randomly find you within dense foliage, or inside a hollow tree trunk.
There are a few problems with the inventory such as 1 buckshot round can take up the same amount of space as 5 buckshot rounds for example. It's like ammo is sorted out into individual groups, and once you run out of shots in an "ammo group", then you have to go into your inventory and place new group into the active slot, which would be tedious during a big fight.
The game is very slow paced, as the player must allways take care when traveling from outpost to outpost. Sprinting randomly while traveling can leave the player in dire situations. I haven't been able to play multiplayer yet, but when I do I will update my early access review. Overall, the game has a "hardcore" feeling to it, and I have enjoyed the game so far.

Controls are super intuitive: WASD for movement and mouse to rotate. Left click fires, right click shoots out a grappling hook to pick up scientists and grab things.
You'll find yourself manipulating the environment by shooting rock, and directing lava, water, ice, gas, etc to open up different parts of the level. This is a typical PixelJunk game, unique and fun. Easy to spend a few minutes here or there or get sucked in as the complexity slowly ramps up.
Easy recommend. On sale? A no brainer.

This game is an innovative twist on the good-old just-one-more-turn 4x strategy genre. It has a science fiction feel with each of the eight races being distictly different and interesting. I played my first game as the Drakkens and won before I could finish their quest line. It was interesting enough that I want to play as them again just to see how their storyline ends.
The map is beautiful looking and zooms in and out between the fully rendered terrain hexes and a more tactical oriented map that shows the separate provinces. Not only is in easy on the eyes to look at, but it's also easy to navigate. In fact the whole game is easy to navigate.
Endless Legend has one of the best, if not the best, interfaces I've ever seen in a game. Information is delivered clearly and concisely so you can spend your time playing, not hunting for menus. The reminder prompts at the beginnning of each turn made my first play through a breeze.
Minor gripe: (and it is very minor) I would have liked to seen a larger unit roster for each race. Only four racial units per faction feels a bit limited. You can upgrae them with better gear as you play, but you still only get the four basic models to work with. The minor factions can help diversify your army a bit, but I'd still like to have seen at least a few more racial units per faction. I hope they consider adding more in an expansion.
If you like 4X TBS games Endless Legend won't disappoint. I'm glad I bought it.

The in-game help is not as informative as it could be and both the manual and the wiki are very sparse. Upgrading troops is a bit of a chore since there's no "upgrade all" button; each item has to be individually replaced and when you do, sometimes other items are unequipped for no very clear reason. All in all, beautiful and atmospheric enough that I give it a recommend despite the annoyances.

There are many new and interesting gameplay mechanics here! The only thing I do not like is the semi-automatic control of units in combat. I understand they did that to simplify multiplayer, but for me this is a singleplayer game and full control would increases the immersion.

AWESOMENAUTSSSSSSSSSSS!
Is it just me, or does that sound like an old kids show? Probably just me.
Short version: I recommend this game, but perhaps not if you don't like MOBA's. But it depends why you don't like MOBA's.
Long version: I recommend this game for the following reasons.
Awesomenauts is a MOBA, but a MOBA a 12+ year old could also play. The pacing is far faster than that of Dota or League of Legends.
My personal favorite thing about Awesomenauts are the amounts of characters you can play, and guess what? It's not pay to win! You unlock all the characters by leveling up! Woohoo, I never thought I'd see the day in MOBA history! (Although there are going to be 8 characters in the paid Starstorm DLC, Penny Fox is much stronger than most free Awesomenauts which is a bummer.)

Anyway, back to the characters. You can play as many characters, and they're still being made till this day. They all have unique playstyles and amazing voice acting with backstories that are actually worth it to read.
The combat in Awesomenauts is, like I said before, VERY fast paced compared to a normal MOBA. It's also got an explosive sense of humor.
However, although there are so much good things about this game, where do the negative things come in? Well, Awesomenauts can get repetitive with the small maps, limited amount of items for each character and fairly basic combat. The combat is just left click, right click and middle mouse button click then run away/teleport away if needed.
Also, the respawn times are very annoying. As the game progresses in time, the respawn time becomes longer and very irritating for people who take risks like me.
However this game is very recommended for the low cost of £7 or your regional equivalent. It's an exciting, fast paced MOBA with an amazing art style and a great variety of 'Nauts.
Another flaw would be some balancing issues, some characters being much stronger than others which can ruin some games.
The final verdict for Awesomenauts is a... 7/10. Good multiplayer fun with no singleplayer campaign whatsoever but can give you 50 or so hours of gameplay. Recommended for those into fast paced multiplayer teamwork MOBA games and perhaps anyone else.

Let me get the "flaws" out of the way before anything else: first, the game freezes every now and then, for several seconds (loading textures and whatnot as you go, I assume, since loading-screen times are rather fast for a game like this). In time -- and specially in Arx, the game's biggest city -- this gets
annoying. Second, you get lost during some quests, not knowing what you're supposed to do next. You wander around freely, and end up doing what should be "Step 4" on a quest with, let's say, 5 steps, by sheer accident, and then you have no idea
, story-wise, you did that, or the motivations you should have to do "Step 5"... or, sometimes, even what this one is.
With a decent computer (in USA/EU standards) the first issue should be no problem to you. The second they could have avoided by making it clearer where you should head first, where to start things. But it's no big issue -- you can still get everything done, and make sense out of it.
Now to the game itself:
If you've played Dragon Age, the first Divinity: Original Sin or any other similar game, you know what this is about. D:OS2 is an RPG, with huge maps, lots of quests, plenty of different skills to use, turn-based combat, several possible different builds for your characters, random loot drops, some really challenging battles and, jesus, it's
. It took me almost 120 hours to finish it -- which is great, because it was an enjoyable experience all the way through. Some fights are impossible when you first reach them, but you can level up elsewhere and come back to it later -- I played in Tactician difficulty (the hardest, after the "Ironman" one) and never really got stuck.
The story is good, the writing flawless. The graphics are gorgeous, and the soundtrack excellent (I caught myself whistling along with it quite often, which is something I'm pretty sure never happened to me before).
Now, if you're like me, and can barely move unless you're positive you've created the perfect char (or close enough to it), here's something you should know: after finishing the first part of the game (Fort Joy) you can freely respec all of your characters as many times as you want, whenever you want, by visiting the Mirror in the lowest deck of your ship. So don't worry too much if you're not happy with any of your characters' initial build... I lost some 10 hours trying to put the perfect party together before I learned I didn't have to do so right away.
I read some reviews during EA in which people complained about the combat, about too much use of Crowd Control or Surfaces (in case you didn't play Divinity: Original Sin, you should know you can create water/oil/fire/blood/ice surfaces in this game, then cast some other kind of spell on them to have a certain effect). Spellcasting and surfaces are quite messy indeed, but they also make things more interesting, and don't really ruin anything, so... it's not really a problem. There's a lot of CC in D:OS 2 -- true as well -- but as long as you make good use of yours, you'll be fine. There's nothing wrong with the combat, it's pretty cool.
Put simply: if you're an RPG fan, D:OS2 is a must have. Certainly one of the best out there, and totally worth full price. Oh, and I guess it's safe to say it's bug-free, since I got none after 117 hours.

Endless Legend is a classic 4x with some unusual and inventive mechanics.  Running on the same system as Endless Space the game uses the 'FIDS' food/industry/dust(money)/science used in Endless Space, another critically acclaimed and frequently expanded and improved title from the same developer.
Instead of space 4x this version is one planet 4x fantasy with a twist that the planet undergoes frequent horrible winters that has caused the myriad of unusual cultures living upon it to have to adapt.  In the single player campaign you will receive a unique set of quests related to each of these cultures and how their story evolves.
I particularly enjoyed how the individual cultures have their own approaches and inner strengths in addition to having thorough and well worked back stories, e.g. the Broken Lords who do not consume food, but dust to grow and are internally conflicted about consuming the life of others to stay alive or the Vaulters who lived underground until a disaster which forced them to the surface while discovering they are settlers from space.
This game also enjoys a much more meaty hex based combat system when compared to Endless Space with its 'roll 3 cards to win battles' system, instead with individual units being controllable.
I would recommend this game at any price to 4x strategy fans; on discount I would recommend it to all buyers to try it.  With the currently daily deal at 50% off you can't lose and you are unlikely to find it any cheaper on the christmas sale.

This is my first game review.
Endless Legend is a 4x game. So there is a lot of expansion, killing people, hexagon map structure, and fairly poor diplomacy. But no 4x has good diplomacy. Now the closest comparisons for 4x I can find are Civ 5 and Civ: BE.
The similarities:
-Civ BE and EL both have only ~8 factions, whereas Civ 5 has many.
-Typical 4x strategy
-Hexagon map
Differences:
-Uses a province system
-Cities have much more strategy in shape
-Pesky roads are automatic (THANK YOU!)
-Soundtrack is better than the others
-Technology tree: EL uses tiles, Civ 5 uses a tree, Civ BE uses a web
-Unique items for units
-Special leader units that have skill mapping
-The 8 factions are very unique and have more than just stat differences
-You can form alliances
-Market place with supply and demand
-Every unit is unique to eachother (Every. Single. One!)
-The map has height
-Strategic resources and luxeries are strategic
-The game has its own unique lore tied with 2 other games
Don't take this too seriously. This was just my first stab at a "review". Just thought I should list some stuff that people should know about the game if they don't already. Have fun!

Awesomenauts is a spectacularly well made game.
Playing it is a terrible experience.
I don't play a lot of MoBAs. Why? The fundamental idea of a group of people you don't know being your locked-in teammates for an entire (fairly lengthy) game come hell or high-water tends to lead to some... unfortunate social situations. People get mad when the design of the game forces them into situations where their team is letting them down, and I understand that. That's not something Awesomenauts has a responsibility to change because it CAN'T be changed. That's simply the format and I don't think it's fundamentaly a bad one.
Ronimo DOES have a responsibility, however, to do what it can to keep people from feeling bullied or harrassed as much as possibly while trying to play the game. Other games in the genre do this with report features, eliminating chat altogether, or LoL's interesting player-handled report feature (are they still doing that? I don't know). Awesomenauts has none of this.
Awesomenauts has mute buttons. That's it. Now, mute buttons are a tiny step in the right direction, but what of players that get muted nearly every game they play? What of players that specifically refuse to fight to try to make their own team lose? I actually never saw the mute button in-game. I had to Google it (for thos who are wondering, press the TAB key to bring up the in-game score table to locate the blank square button on the right side of the pane, mouse over it to see to mute icon). Although there is a support email address that one could theoretically send incriminating screenshots to, they would contain no gameplay data (making them completely useless, as players can change their own names) and pausing to take screenshots in-game only subjects the player to more abuse.
So why doesn't Ronimo do this? Well, they're small. An indie studio working on what I believe is their first game hardly has the budget to keep a person or people on staff to sift through user reports all day. They can't even afford dedicated servers, let alone dedicated community support personell. I understand.
I don't think the game ever should have been released.
A game of this type REQUIRES comprehensive and present policing of its community. Without it, games of Awesomenauts for me without friends that I actually know have become untennable. Every pick-up game that I play seems to devolve into a stream of racist, homophobic, sexist, and ablist slurs. Threats of sexual assault abound. Sportsmanship is half-hearted, almost afraid to show its face.
In a game with an aesthetic based on saturday morning cartoons and gameplay based on cute side-scrolling children's platforming games, hatred, intolerence, and toxicity have been given free reign to an extent that outpaces every other toxic community in the genre that I know (which is all of them, by the way).
I play videogames to have fun, and I certainly haven't enjoyed over 75% of the matches I've had. As the game stands now I would never recommend the game to a parent with children of any age; their children would absolutely be subjected to vicious personal attacks and be encouraged to attack others. No one who plays this game for more than two hours in online play will NOT have racist, homophobic, or ablist slurs used against them.
If you're a mature adult, and you're sure you can handle a culture of routine anger that far surpasses rudeness, get the three-pack. DON'T just buy it for yourself. Find some nice friends and play it with them beforehand, because you won't be finding them within the game.
Obviously this review isn't about the gameplay, but there are plenty of reviews that discuss the the gameplay at length. For what it's worth, I think the gameplay is superlative, fairly well balanced, and above all loads of fun. Apart from a few cringe-worthy stereotypes in the voice-acting, the characters are all colorful, fun, and great to play as. The soundtrack is one of the best game soundtracks I've ever heard, the level design is inventive and exciting, and the graphics are consistently gorgeous.
Please don't buy this game. Please.
Not every game has such a bad community. Not every game does such a bad job policing it. This is NOT the universal videogame culture unless you allow it to be. Thanks for reading.

Spoilers:
I was doing one quest, whether this was a main quest, Idk, but it was linked through so many encounters that it was hard to avoid. Firstly I heard about a character named Griff, who despite wearing a source collar, was the top dog in this area. I heard about him through an encounter that I could of missed aswell, would made this all the more interesting. One of the characters in this encounter told me to go to a cave, after saving her from a follower of Griff's. I decided to go there On the way, I picked up a main character, this character is a vessel for a spirit that is trying to control her;
this was random, and had nothing to do with the quest I was about to do, but she managed to interact with the quest line somehow along the way. I went to the cave, and found out that Griff can't control this area of the map, so it's a nice hideout for people who want to get away from his reign. Apparently the person people go to for wisdom is a blind women who can see, and can see things others can't. This is when my spirit controlling follower asks to talk to this women, when letting her, you find out they both are vessels of spirits, but my follower can't quite control hers well. She goes beserk in this encounter, losing control of the spirit, and you have to knock her out. I thought this was weird, but also cool that it happened, as it was out of nowhere, and would't have happened if I didn't add her to my party. I talk to the blind women, and she tells me of a man, who can help us escape the island, as we are magical beings, that might be exiled, or released of our magic. We find out that Griff has locked this man up, who goes by the name of Amyro. Amyro is locked up because Griff described him as a thief who stole oranges, and you decide to come to an agreement that you will find the oranges, and on return, Amyro should be released, Griff agrees to this. I go and find the crate next to a dreaming Lizard man. I talk to this guy, and another party member that I got on my party (because the blind women said a red lizard would be of importance to me) says he wants to dream with the dreamer. He sees that he will rule as a leader through this mans dreams. This was again a random occurance that wouldn't of happened if I didn't take this Red Lizard with me as a follower. I decide to accuse the dreamer of being a thief, and he admits, while also saying that Griff is a smugglar, who uses the crate of oranges to smuggle a dreamers drug, that lets you control dreams. I try to persuade him, but he would not give into my persuasion (I had low persuasion points) to give me evidence, and not rat him out. I decide to kill him instead to get the evidence off him, and give it to Griff. I give it to Griff, and I have the option of taking money instead of releasing Amyro, accusing someone else of stealing the fruit, saying that it was the dreamer, and the I dealt with him, or I could of maybe killed Griff and tried to free Amyro (I could of done this from the start aswell). I decide to say I dealt with the thief, and get Amyro released; and the quest leads into helping me escape the island (I've heard that there is more ways to escape).
If by reading this you thought of many other ways I could of done this quest, most of them would actually be possible. The way I did it, could of not involved any interactions from my followers if I refuted them from talking (lowers likeness from them to you) or not having them in my party in the first place. I also could of saved Amyro many other ways if I chose other text options. I could of found the cave and this quest despite not finding the fight in town, by not talking to anyone in town. Did I have the strength to kill the dreamer with out a party? Could I have added more interactions, or opportunities to this quest? Idk, and that's what I'll eventually have to find out through other playthroughs. How was I mean't to find away to exit this city? I had 2 other npc's that could of helped me from what I saw, but turned them down in favour of my other party members. What I'm trying to convey to anyone who read this far, is that this game has so many opportunities, ways to do quest, random encounters that could happen, the amount of possibilities almost seems endless, and this is just one quest line...
To add to all this, the game will not hold your hand, no quest trackers, quest guides, no arrow pointers on map, no explanation mark to say there will be a quest when you talk to someone. You need to use your wits, and information from talking to people, and without talking to someone, you won't know if they're holding a quest for you, or if they have any relevance at all, a random character could have the best quest, but you won't know until you talk to them.

DOS2 is a game that puts the emphasis of enjoyment on the player, rather than the in game story. It has one of the most liberating gameplay mechanics in any game. But it does sacrifice a lot in order to make this work. The weakest aspect of this game is without a doubt its narrative and storytelling, which is in part because of the gameplay mechanics, and in part because of terrible story writing.
Stories will go unfinished, an action you perform that may shut down completely significant or interesting storylines down the road. At the expense of not shoehorning the player into any one particular decision, you are given a million what-if scenarios. This game gives you one major directive and just lets you explore the remainder of its storyline, as a result, it is not as cohesive, tight, gripping or emotionally charged as many other intersting stories. In this aspect, it really is quite easy to get immersed into the story, but it is hard to become attached to anything you do.
This game attempts to create artificial moral difficulties by pulling out last-minute justifications for actions of its characters which destroy the character and narrative that it has led up to. It is so jarring and unsatisfying to learn that every villain you know is somehow actually trying to reach the greater good. Every good person is actually a psychopath. Everything that has lead to untold suffering up to the point has been the better option. It is a cheap way of subverting expectations.
When you couple this with the fact that important, integral plot points are removed if you naturally play the game (it is unavoidable), you are left with a confusing mess of a plot. You don't know where to go or what to do, so you meander around to accomplish things, and somewhere along the lines you'll check your journal and realize that you've completed your major questlines and have no idea that you've done so. That is why the endings are unsatisfying, and that the resolutions feel hollow. It feels as if the end has come too quickly.
This game should be taken with a grain of salt. If you enjoy deep immersion, gameplay freedom and the ability to customize and alter the world to your liking with what you have, this is absolutely a great game to own. If however, you enjoy games for deep storyline, like the Baldur's Gate series, or Planescape Torment, then you will find this game to be narratively lacking in comparison. Just take it with a grain of salt, and realize it's not trying to make a literature masterpiece, but a fun and liberal experience

Positive:
-This game is the follow up to the legendary series of Men of War games. This brings your favorite game to the Modern times !
-A brand new campaign, modern weapons and equipment, vehicles and gameplay.
-The ranking system for multiplayer is the same as in the previous Men of War AS 2. Many things in the menu and controls have not changed so its a good thing for an experienced player.
-New game modes are plenty of fun, especially Combined Arms where you bring your Abrams backed with an Apache.
-Overall the game is like a refreshment from the previous Men of War game.
-EPIC MODDING POTENTIAL
Cons:
-The same engine as the previous game. Not much graphical improvement was made although I did notice a performance struggle compared to the previous game on my PC. Some new graphical options were introduced but still the base engine is the same.
-The developers decided to do a First Person Shooter style control scheme for individual soldier controls. This is my own opinion, I just don't like it and don't see how it fits this Real Time Strategy game. Sure its fun to blow up a tank with an RPG that you aimed(!!!) but it just doesn't feel immersive enough like Battlefield 3 , for example . It tries to lightly touch the FPS world but it kind of fails due to the lack of feedback you get in this game due to its developmental limitations.
-We are near release. Honestly I do not feel this game is ready for release in the near months.
-Lack of units. In this game, you do not have artillery units. An answer I got from the devs was that the current map sizes do not allow for logical artillery units, which I can understand, ALTHOUGH map sizes in Armored Combat or Combined Arms *could* allow for artillery , but also the devs can re-make or extend their own maps .
Also in Men of War AS 2 (previous game) the map sizes weren't that much different, if somewhat some maps are a little smaller even, but still you have artillery either vanilla or from mods like RobZ realism, and it works somewhat great.
-Reused resources from previous game. I understand this is the same engine and its easier to port stuff from the previous game and add alongside some new stuff like new sounds models prefabs etc.
But you're selling a brand new game for full price. I expect new stuff from scratch, or at least re-worked reused resources. Many buttons and functions are CTRL+X CTRL+V'd from the previous game and I hope those will change at or before release.
==Overall:
I would reccommend this game as I still have belief in this developer and hope they will not disappoint.
This game is overall a fun RTS with modern units and content is only expected to improve.
I really hope to see controllable fixed-wing and rotary aircraft show up in this game unlike previous Men of War games and new artillery units.

A true labour of love and a welcome addition to the classic Sonic series, even if it has been 23 years since the last game.
Sprites have been updated to take advantage of a wider colour palette and have been granted a greater number of frames of animation that work well with the 60FPS performance. The levels are bright and beautifully designed - even if most of them are taken from the older games, they've been tweaked and modified to the point where many of them may as well be considered new levels entirely, especially in their second acts, and the new stages are more than worthy additions. Virtually all of them have multiple paths (with the exception of one), and are a joy to explore.
The music is on point, including new tunes, as well as classic tunes with remixes in the second acts, and all of it is deliciously retro.
All three characters have their own unique movesets designed to make exploring the stages a fun and different experience each time, that make it well worth playing every character in the game. The game is just the right length too, being similar to that of Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
The Chaos Emerald special stages are easily the best in Sonic games yet, it's just a shame that are only 7 of them. Blue Spheres - the special stages that people either love or hate - also makes an appearance in order to earn bonus medals for all you completionists out there, but these are entirely optional if you fall more on the "hate" side of the spectrum. If you love them, there's a whole Blue Spheres mode you can play, as well as a "Mania" mode that makes a few new additions to the formula.
If you keep an eye out, there are more than a handful of easter eggs in the game too, as well as a number of unlockable "cheats" to keep things interesting.
If you've played a classic Mega Drive era Sonic game before, and loved it, you should play this. If you haven't, you should still absolutely play this.

If you've played The Hunter (no I'm not going to type it like this: theHunter), then this is basically The Hunter but with dinosaurs, and if the idea of that floats your boat, then by all means give it a go.
If you've not played The Hunter before, then basically it's a hunting sim with dinosaurs. You get a large tropical volcanic hawaiian style island to roam and explore at your lesuire which looks fantastic. As with The Hunter they've done a great job on making the environment feel very natural and believable. Fancy a quick break somewhere nice in the sun? Then go for a hike around this island. Of course you won't be able to completely relax because the place is also inhabited by dinosaurs, which you can either try and avoid or hunt down. The current premise behind all this is that you're a prisoner/pioneer in the future who has been dumped on this planet and tasked with clearing it of dinosaurs. Evidence of previous pioneers is still littered and dotted around the landscape in places.
To aid you in hunting you get a sort of hunters mate. A little electronic PDA style device that you can use to scan foot prints or scat or even dinosaur calls to help give you a idea of their directional location. It's not always 100% on the ball so you have to use a bit of your own judgment as well. By default, evidence of dino tracks are highlighted with glowing red markers making them much easier to spot in amongst all the thick vegitation. You can turn these markers off and rely only on your own abilities to spot the foot prints and mounds of dino poo. Trust me, even without the glowing markers, trying to spot even a 3 foot mound of poo is tricky, let alone a foot print in the grass. The PDA however will still chirp up and notify you when you do stumble over some evidence of dino tracks.
So what weapons and gear do you get to hunt down these dinos? Well it's an odd assortment considering it's set in the future and that you have been specifially tasked with hunting down dinosaurs. You'd think they'd give you a suit of armour and a gun that could knock down an elephant, but instead you start dressed in a t-shirt next to a pod that contains a bow and a tiny clutch of arrows. Yes, they gave you bows and arrows to take down dinosaurs. I guess the folks in charge back on earth must have been reading the Turok comics in order to formulate their dino eradication strategy. As you move around the landscape, you will come across crates with other weapons, items of clothing and medi kits. Mostly you will find more arrows and bows, but there are also shotguns, pistols and rifles to be found. Annoyingly you won't always find the ammo with the gun, meaning you will have to decide whether to haul around a dead weight with you in the hope of finding some ammo for it. All items affect your overall weight, which in turn affects your movement speed and how long you can sprint for. Clothing items currently seem to offer no bonuses, it's just fancy dress right now. Another issue is that items will not stack at the moment either. So if you have 5 arrows and you pick up another 3, they will stay as two separate amounts in your inventory. Fortunately inventory space is not a problem right now anyway as there is almost no way you could fill it with the current weight limitations. However when you equip the 3 arrows it won't automatically then use up the bunch of 5 after you've used the bunch of 3. You will have to then equip that bunch of 5 manually too. All simple issues that will get sorted in time I'm sure.
The weapons themselves for the most part handle well. The bow is a bit of a pain, as you need to aim it before charging it for firing and you can't do it in quick succession. Meaning if 3 raptors get on your trail and all you have is a bow, then you're dead meat. You might take one, but the other two will get you for sure. A shotgun fully loaded with slugs will even up the score some what. As with The Hunter all the beasties take location damage to things like heart and lungs etc and even if they do a runner they can still bleed out and die later. If like me you have no idea of the internal anatomy of dinosaurs, then taking them down with shots to the vitals will be more about luck and guess work. Currently there are only 3 dinosaur types in the game, the Triceratops, Utahraptors and the T-Rex. The dinos are not omnipotent and you can generally sneak up on them with reasonable ease if you stay low and stick to cover. They can of course also sneak up on you. A few times as I've been strolling along I heard a rustle from behind me and turned around to see a raptor sneaking up on me. If you see 3 snooping around behind you trying to pick up on your trail, then get worried. Avoid the T-Rex. Triceratops is a herbivore and is the best one to actively hunt down yourself without worrying that it's going to eat you instead.
I haven't tried playing it with other folks yet, only "singleplayer", so I can't tell you how good the network code is etc. To play, you have to create a game and set the usual things like how many other players you want to be able to join in and give your game a password. So currently to play it single player just set the players to 1 and password it. In the 3 hours I played last night, I did not encounter any major show stopping bugs or crashes. It all seemed pretty stable to me. Playing it on an i5 with 8 Gb of ram and a GTX770, all on max settings and it all runs just fine.
Right now the game is a bit content thin as previously noted. Only 1 island, 3 dinos, a small smattering of weapons and not a lot else. However of course I expect that to change as the game is delveloped. What is currently there though, is in a very playable state, and if hunting and exploring are your thing then this should provide you with a good few hours of enjoyment even at this stage. The Hunter is currently the best hunting game out there (shame about the microtransactions), so this game already has a good foundation in that respect. It's more or less really just going to be a case of waiting for them to develop the content with this one.
What would I like to see going forwards? More islands with different biomes like windswept deserts and dunes, arctic areas, temperate woodlands and plains. More dinosaurs of course and interactivity beween the different dinosaurs, as I haven't really seen any evidence of that yet. More kit and perhaps a bit of minor base building maybe. All stuff that I'm pretty sure we'll see eventually anyway.

This is a quick initial review after spending my first 1.6hrs in game, all opinions are subjective to change as the game updates as it is in Early Acess State.
I had initially heard of this game from a youtuber by the name of DevilDogGamer, listening to him talk about it immediately peaked my interest. The thought of being dropped in a distant land full of dangerous prehistoric predators with the sole intention to turn the hunters into the hunted.  Dinosaurs have always been of interest, an while currently limited in the species type this game did not fall short of delivering an immersive experience.
PC Specs - MSI 890FXA-GD70 mobo, AMD Phenom 2x6 1075T cpu, XFX 6870HD gpu, Gskill Ripjawz 8gb ram, WD caviar black 2TB HDD, Onboard Realtech HD audio
Rating - 8/10
Pros:
1) The game is beautiful minus a few graphical glitches I noticed here an there, nothing major however. Sometimes I would notice a few white slivers here an there as well from textures that haven't loaded. However with that said my GPU is dated an it still looked gourgous for the better part.
2) Sounds/ambience - The audio for this game has so far been done in extremely good taste. The nature of this game forces you to constantly be vigilant and paying attention. You are being hunted after all, An with time the 3 different dinos become easily distinguishable between them. There is also the atmospheric background noise, as well as the terrain/movement sounds.  There was one sound I feel could use some improvement, which would be when the raptors are coming up on you. To me it sounds like a record player playing static and it keeps skipping, It's by no means a game killer but it does get kind of annoying after a bit.
3) Each individual dino looks amazing and unique, I love that the devs took into account that many believe modern day birds evolved from dinos ( I agree with this but if you don't to each their own ). It's evident in the designs as portrayed by the feathers particularily on the raptor which raptor in itself means bird of prey.
4) Tracking is easy for anyone, Your not going to walk up to a dino sign an sit an wonder for 10 min what it was. Each animal has its own individual sounds and tracks, it's very important to be able to decifer what exactly your chasing... or whats chasing you for that matter.
5) Loot crates stand out, they show up nicely on the pda as well. With a bright orange color, an audio que and the pda dropping you rite on top of it they're hard to miss. I also found plenty of them, an while most had decent drops in it I'll get into my thoughts for improvements on them later.
Areas of Improvement
1) First an foremost to few weapons, I haven't found a single firearm as of this post within the amount of time I have played. I get the survival with limited resources aspect an that this game isn't supposed to be easy, But with the number of crates I opened something other then another bow would have been nice. I did however find enough arrows the T-rex probably would have chocked on them if it wasn't ultimately a pack of raptors that did me in.
2) Non-stackable items - I ultimately died from running out of arrows with my bow, not because I didn't have any but because my stack of 8 had run out and in haste switched to my stack of 3 which is no bueno with 3 raptors chasin ya down.  Pick a number and allow us to stack it up to that, doesn't have to be big i'ld say 8-10 if you'ld like to keep it limited.
3) some dino suggestions for the future - Stegosaurus, Ankylosaurus, Allosaurus, Pteranodon ( more so for ambience then to hunt ), Archeopteryx ( again for ambience ), Baryonyx.
All in all it was an enjoyable experience and I look forward to playing it and progressing with it as it updates. This is the game many of us have been waiting for, and tho this is just the first lick of the spoon it's already hit my sweet tooth.  I would recommend playing with a friend, tho it could work against you as well depending on the type of experience your seeking.
I will continue to update this as improvements and changes are made, this is just an initial review an thoughts of the game in its current state.

PROS:
1. World and Atmosphere. This game couples amazing sound design with stunning visuals creates an amazing immersive world. You can hear T-Rexes stomping around from miles away, and spot Quezalcoatluses flying in the sky before they have a chance to see you. While this does add to the immersion, it also rewards attentive players who can see a threat before it even knows they exist.
2. Weapons and Damage Models. The weapons of Primal are very grounded in reality. All weapons match to their respective ammunition types and every weapon looks, sounds, and feels like an actual weapon. Firearms are loud, bows have believable ballistics, and everything feels very solid. Coming from someone who is very experienced with firearms, I can attest to the realism of this game's weapons. Also, being based on a realistic hunting game, Primal's damage models are very precise. Heart shots are king, while general body/gut shots will not instantly drop most of Primal's beasts. Overall, the guns are good.
3. The Actual Gameplay. Primal's gameplay is very intense, You can go from walking through a peaceful field to being chased by Utahraptors in mere seconds. This isn't a casual game. Deaths are punishing while kills are immensly rewarding. Even with high level gear, carelessness is often punished with death.
CONS:
1. Bugs. While the games stability has been immensely improved, the game still has lots of bugs. It wil crash every so often, and movement is very finicky. Also, the only servers are hosted through other player's internet connections, resulting in high pings and short lived servers.
2. Developement. Until recently, this game had been declared dead by most. The developers of this game are very invested in other projects and seem to view Primal of a sort of hobby on the side. On the up side, they have issued a survey for players to take and have also decided to try and tackle some of the bugs. Even though the game has officially released, they still intend on giving it regular updates.
CONSENSUS: Primal is a great concept, but it is still in the making. While basic gameplay is good, there are still things that need to be ironed out and content that should be added in. While I understand some negative reviews, I believe that many of them portray this game in a bad light. Many people simply expect things from the game that it simply cannot offer. There isn't crafting or base building (as of yet) because the game is developed and marketed as a dinosaur hunting game. But, in the end, it is for you to decide. If you enjoy challenging or intense games, this is for you. If you're looking for another Primal Carnage of Orion: Prelude, then you will be dissapointed.
