I've been following this game for some time, and I have to say this might be my favorite 4X since the Civ Series. The Visions of The Unseen "Patch" fixed my biggest gripe with this game and finally added some flavour to the dialouge when interacting with the A.I.
In no particular order, the pros and cons:
+ Fanatstic aestethic that provides a fantastical world which feels fresh in a sea of generic fantasy worlds.
+ Factions are interesting, diverse and fun to play as and against. There are Vampiric Ghost Knights; Pacifist Dragons; Deranged Slavers who rebel against the god-like creatures who made them; Mages who draw magic from pain, and more.
- They are however, a bit too specialized.
+ Most factions have incomparable gameplay, for example the Broken Lords don't need Food, but use Dust (Money) instead; the Cultists have only one city, but can take over Minor Factions outside their territory; The Roving Clans can move their cities; so on and so forth.
+ Unit customization is great, allowing you to choose what gear your soldiers have.
- Faction Creation, however, is basic at best. You really just give an already existing faction a new name and some new bonuses, you still have the same units, heroes and even quests.
+ Developers give players a lot of input, holding votes and contests to determine what to add to the game.
- They rejected my Faction in the contest. But I'm totally not bitter about that...
+ All their games (Endless Legend, Endless Space, and Dungeon of the Endless) fit together and form a story, but you don't need to play the other games to understand what's going on.
All in all, I recommend this game. It is definitively worth the price, and I would recommend the Emperor Pack too, as the extra goodies make it all more interesting.

I wont add to the numerous reviews of the gameplay. You can see that on others. Its so damn good it will ruing every RTS game for you as they will seem shallow after playing CK2.
Most of the negative reviews you will see are not related to the gameplay but the DLC policy, and how much you will pay for the entire package. Honestly this is a little unfair for several reasons:
1) The game was released in 2012 and is still having content added (5 years later at the time of this review). Most of the industry would have had us rebuying sequels at full price (and then buying DLC on the sequels). We would be on CK5 at this point, probably with less content than we have currently.
2) Look at the other reviews time played. You will see that hundreds or even thousands of hours of gameplay. Put that in context. Many AAA titles are £40-50 and have 10-20 hours of gameplay.
3) You dont need all of the DLC to play. I dont have all of the DLC and am having a blast at 200 hours as things stand at the moment.
4) About half of the DLC is cosmetic. Dont buy it if you dont want it.
5) Bringing us back to the games age. Yes the DLC is expensive to get in one lump, at full price.... guys this is steam, do we pay full price for anything? CK2 and its DLC is on sale regularly. Be patient, wait. The negative reviews all quote around £200 for everything. Steam sales will reduce that to around £100 for everything (uncluding the cosmetics). Thats around the cost of a normal title plus a season pass (shall we say with an average lifespan of 2 years). I am not arguing that the game is cheap, its price is average.
6) The flow of DLC means this game remains constantly supported. Features are added regardless of DLC, the game is well polished, bugs are rare. Other than MMOs with a regular subscription of premium features, how many games are supported and updated 5 years or more after release?
7) Lastly for those considering buying it: Dont consider it like your average game where you NEED the DLC to get up and running. Buy the base game and maybe 1-2 of the DLC. Add to your collection as later sales come up. I dont have all the DLC yet, but given that my current game has lasted me 2 months so far (and im nowhere near the end yet), I dont feel in a particular hurry to expand the game at this time.

As appears to be the PixelJunk formula, this game takes a basic concept (twin-stick shooter) and makes something unique out of it. PixelJunk Shooter is a shooter, but also an exploration game and a puzzle game at the same time.
There are 15 levels and each is pretty decently sized, with numerous hidden gems and secret rooms to find as well as 35 survivors to rescue. Or maybe not, because they are very fragile and one shot or one drop of magma can kill them, costing you a life. Yes, lives are how many survivors you accidentally kill, instead of your ship itself having lives. Generally though it's actually pretty hard to game over unless you're trying to, aside from the few instances where survivors can die just because of bad placement (there's only like 2 or 3 of these, but they're really annoying :T)
There are three main worlds and each has several gimmicks of its own. The first world introduces all of the main mechanics, the second introduces ice mechanics and alternate suits, and the third introduces oil, switches, and all sorts of mechanical devices. This keeps the game fresh in each new world, and each world also ends with a pretty nice-sized boss that tends to be somewhat of a puzzle boss as well. The shooting is generally well-executed, enemies are fair and you have several methods of killing them all; normal shots, homing missiles, and environmental kills all come in handy depending on the situation.
The health system in this game is also fairly unique; it's entirely based on heat. Being near lava heats your ship up, as does being surrounded in gas. Taking a shot gives you a fair bit of heat. And touching magma is almost always instant death... but you don't die unless you're already on fire AND you touch the ground, so you can be saved from near death by a conveniently placed pool of water. It's a reeeally neat mechanic and one I've never seen before, and it's executed really well (and eventually, inverted... ehehe, but the inverter suit actually makes no sense, to be honest).
The gameplay is pretty smart, the mechanics are pretty original, the length is fairly decent, and it's generally pretty fun. Twin-stick shooters don't tend to be a genre I play much but with how interesting they made this one I ended up liking it a fair bit. I might even play PixelJunk Monsters at some point even though I dislike tower defense games because, hey, I'm sure I'll get an interesting experience out of it regardless. Q Games really knows what the hell they're doing and it's a shame their games don't get much buzz.

So, Primal.
What can I say about Primal.
Well in what other games are you forced to hide in a bush for half an hour with you buddy, whilst cowering from a T Rex?
Honestly though, quite a good game, ill go over some pros and cons.
Good:
The atmospheric nature of the game is great; both the sounds and graphics are quite pretty.
The core game play is actually pretty nailed down despite it being early access, you can shoot Dinosaurs and throw rocks and what ever, what more do you need?
Despite there being little in game right now, it's actually quite fun grouping up with your buddies and treking through the jungle, surviving and all that jazz.
Bad:
The game lacks some content, I mean, we could do with some more guns, maybe some dynamic events. Base building would be great in this game. Then again, early access so what ever, no big deal.
Run speed at the current gesture comes in two catagories: Faster than light or extremely slow. It would be nice to get a happy medium.
The lobby/hosting needs some work.
The Dinosaurs can be quite stupid sometimes, then again, they had small brains right?
All in all, I reccomend this game, especially if you want to waste £15 and possibily have some fun doing it. I mean, its not the greatest game in the world, you'll find out how much patience you have and you will be in a bush for 80% of your game time, but even that being said, it's oddly addictive and way more fun with others.

I have thousands of hours logged into the Elder Scrolls series, but out of all the games I always come back to Oblivion. This is the greatest Bethesda RPG not because of the amount of content or setting, (although those are outstanding) but rather for it's in-depth questing, enjoyable gameplay, replayability, and focus on player leveling. In Skyrim, there are no major skills and minor skills which leads to a lack of focus when it comes to building a character. In addition, the crafting skills in Skyrim can be maxed at a very low-level giving the player gear which out-classes even the best quest rewards. Oblivion bypasses this by not including such skills, and instead giving you loot based on quests and RNG. This system is much more preferred as it carries player development and leveling into the end-game. Not to mention Oblivion's quests, which far outclass the quests of any of Bethesda's works thereafter.
TLDR; This game is better than Skyrim in every way, except for graphics.

-AoL  is not one of those too-complex 4X games where even the most basic features require research
Slag
-I’ve experienced a fair few bugs, lots of late game chugging, and one crash
-At a certain point complex battles do not have a manual control option, leaving you only the ability to auto resolve
-I don’t like that changing your troop AI to “offensive” or “defensive” doesn’t alter your victory estimate
Verdict
After winding up disappointed with Endless Space, I was leery of Amplitude Studio’s newest venture, but when Sam told me he was having a good time I decided to give it a fair shot. At this point I’m happy to say that was a good decision, as it is really scratching my 4X itch.

Let me start by saying, if you're getting this game to only focus on getting/using a set few weapons or Warframes, speeding through content, or only do quests, you're probably going to have a bad time. That said, it is an awesome game with hundreds of hours of content ranging from an expansive array of weapons and Warframes to hoards of enemies to lay waste to with an insanely robust modding system.
Now yes there IS grinding but if you're grinding the same resource for hours you're probably doing yourself a disservice. Get some friends and just enjoy wrecking armies and plowing through the solar system and you'll find you'll collect all the resources you need for the next weapon along the way anyway. Same goes for weapons, don't focus on that one overpowered endgame gear, it's endgame for a reason and trying to power your way to it is not going to be a fun experience.
As for the premium currency (platinum), money is NOT the only way to get it. Platinum can be traded between players, usually for rare drops. Got lucky with a Prime blueprint but can't use it anytime soon? See if anyone is buying it and then go treat yourself to some badass decor with that sweet Platinum. Many things in the store are also available through alerts, events, clan research and drops so don't assume it's always going to be locked behind paywalls.
Other things to note:
- The true meta end game is Fashion Frame
- Mastery Rank doesn't necessarily determine skill. it's more like equipment usage
- Warframe is constantly getting free content updates for more things to do
- I'm nearing 400hrs and I'm still only about a 3rd through the content...

I loved Men of War Assualt Squad II, it was one of my favorite RTS games of all time, so naturally when I saw a new game by the same devs, I had to get my hands on it. But when I first got this game awhile back, I was very disappointed in it. Not because it was a bad game but because the game would play very poorly, making it unplayable. And I was unsure what the issue was. Sometimes games will try to use my intel graphics instead of my Graphics Card but I would select my GPU in settings and it would still play with a max of 5 fps even on the lowest settings. I tried very hard to locate a solution but couldn't find anything on how to fix it so I just uninstalled it and went on my way. But when I saw it got a major update, I hoped that it would finally work for me. Man am I glad I gave this game another chance. The modern military setting is nice, the graphics are very well done, and the gameplay is even better/smoother than it's predecessors. I love how when you move up infantry they will move in a line and not jumble up like a bunch of idiots. The gunplay is great, and the direct control is incredably fun and also has a lot of detail for those more precise shots. There is plenty of variety in units for both sides as well. I also have to say that I really appreciate the Hardcore mode which increases damage significantly and makes it so I don't have to download a mod to get more realism. The story is simple and straightforward with simple objectives (pretty obvious for most rts games but just in case) which is fine for some but might be disappointing for others so if your getting this game for a story then I'd look somewhere else cause this game is more focused on the multiplayer battles and skirmishes. However that does not mean it is not enjoyable as I have had a blast playing attack/defend and other objective based missions along with some very unique missions that add to the fun. Also, I really like the improved AI skirmishes, they are a lot of fun and the AI really have gotten an overhaul. Overall, if you liked the MOW series or multiplayer rts games, then this game might be for you.

I was a big fan of DigitalMindSoft. They created their own genre and are continuing to experiment with the RTS genre -- a genre that many have proclaimed dead. Their previous releases were reasonably priced and full of quality content. Assault Squad 2 started this down-hill trend with its DLC, which should have been free. Yet, I did not mind paying -- as I enjoyed the game and wanted to support my darling devs.
Yet, currently, DMS has fallen -- and hit every branch down the bad practices tree. Now this quaint RTS gem is wrapped in never-ending Early Access, season pass, microtransaction and F2P gimmicks. To add to that, this game only has 2 playable factions -- one of which isn't even a real country. Considering there are screenshots of other, more interesting, factions on the preview, they have obviously been axed out for DLC.
No. Don't buy this. Wait for the complete version (bundling the DLC) to come on sale. Tough love, DMS.
Edit: Alternatively, you can wait for the modding scene to pick up. DMS still continues their excellent tradition of mod-friendly games, so you can expect many high-quality free extentions made by the community.

Anybody with even an ounce of nostalgia for the retro Sonic games absolutely has to play Mania. Christian Whitehead’s oversight has previously brought the Mega Drive Sonic titles up to scratch with the excellent mobile ports. Sonic Mania has gone a step further and brought the Sonic game design paradigms up to 2017 standards.
The all-star team of Sonic super fans who produced this work have shown an incredible amount of admiration and respect for their source material. This should come as no surprise; most of the devs behind this game have intimate knowledge in what makes Sonic
and this experience has been drawn from making ROM hacks and other fan titles purely out of a labour of love. To be making choices for what ultimately was to became a real Sonic game must have been a dream come true for them and it shows in the final quality of what was produced here. This is a game where the “Press Any Button” text on the title screen is a reference to a programming oversight on the original 1991 game! That’s how far the attention to detail goes!
The flow and physics of this game are absolutely perfect. The zones, both old and new, have settings and setpieces which don’t feel like somebody imitating the zany fever dream of a 90’s mascot platformer; they feel like they truly belong in that era. Each zone has been polished to perfection and after just a few playthroughs you will find a sense of flow in them that even the old titles never reached, especially after mastering the drop dash. This is where Mania exceeds the quality of the games it stands upon, we have had close to 23 years to analyse where these games faltered and here you can play the full efforts of that analysation. You don’t need to be a superfan to appreciate a game that’s just straight up fun.
You also don't need to be a superfan to apprechiate how ace the soundtrack is. It's the best a Sonic has ever had. Everybody I show "Ruby Delusions", the first boss theme in the game, is blown away. It's just groovy!
I hand my fullest recommendation to anyone who grew up with a Mega Drive in the home. To those who were on the side of the NES I still feel confident telling you to buy Mania, it is a fantastic game if you are, or aren't, wearing nostalgia goggles. Just keep in mind some of the deeper references that are giving people like me a huge smile will probably go over your head.
My only gripe, and I hope we get a sequel that will alleviate this, is that the new zones are so good that the remixed ones don’t feel necessary. Although they offer cool twists on the original concept it’s clear that the team was talented enough to put the whole game together without needing to rely on the past so dramatically. Give these dudes full creative freedom next time, they can reach great heights.

This is my first review on Steam, maybe the only I'll ever do. I hope that shows how much I appreciate this game. I first played this game really late relative to most other gamers: around just before Skyrim's release, but I don't regret it one bit. My record probably says I played this game for about 100 hours or so; that's just the PC version. I played the game on the PS3 for around another 300 or so. Thematically speaking, the two aren't so different.
Anyways, the review! I've played a bit of Skyrim just this morning so I can understand why people would say Oblivion is sort of dated, but the modding community fixes that a great deal. Frankly, modded Oblivion would break the ranking system as I simply cannot think of any flaws for it (except perhaps it might get a little taxing on your computer as a modded Oblivion might require higher specs than you have, although the worst that has ever happened to me were a handful of crashes that were unrelated to my LOOT order). So I'll talk about vanilla Oblivion instead.
The most obvious con (I prefer to start with cons first as they're very few in number): the graphics and animation are indeed somewhat dated, but you're not looking at Doom 3 or GTA: San Andreas running. After Skyrim, combat seems a little lacking in quality but the underlying structure is far more vast (by which I mean the greater number of spells, etc.)
It might also get a little repetitive for some: beginners might realize that fighting quickly devolves into keeping your shield up and sneaking in one or two swings while the enemy's swing bounces off your shield. I'm not going to hide from that criticism: it is true, but only for the prototypical SnS (sword and shield) characters. Two-handers and archers and rogue-types (sneakers who aim for the backstab) and even people who try to bypass fights by sneaking entirely add fun gameplay. For instance, the first character I began playing on the Steam version after playing literally every possible build under the sun on the PS3 version was a hand-to-hand Nord priest (really a monk) from Whiterun's Temple of Arkay. I would beat up everyone and when they "died," I pretended they were really only unconscious. Extremely frustrating playthrough but it forced me to realize the limitations of a hand-to-hand build and made me think of ways to actively resolve issues without fighting impossible odds, something I think my priest would have done anyways. It was particularly fun playing the Shivering Isles DLC, thinking about what a priest might do amongst all of this Daedra politics. Knights of the Nine was obviously right up the priest's alley. I went on this entire tangent to show one point however: due to all of the immersion of this character's playthrough, I never once complained that my combat style amounted essentially to throwing the same 3 or 4 (if not just 2) punches at enemy shields.
Here's my big gripe with the game, one that I won't bother redeeming. The leveling system is abysmal; you should look it up on the wiki page but essentially, monsters level up with you. This is common for some genres of games (such as some rougelikes) but the problem is that the leveling system is designed in such a way that unless you keep records of which skills you're leveling up, you're unlikely to level up "efficiently." I won't bother explaining what that means as it'll take too long (ironically, I only just realized how long this review is getting), but understand this: if you level up inefficiently for too long (and my first several playthroughs as well as some others scattered throughout my love tryst with this game fell victim to this) monsters will start to get stronger than your character. This includes "pests" such as mud crabs and so on, who can eventually stagger you and chain hits killing you in only a couple attacks. Mud crabs should never be that strong when you're at level 20+ and whatnot; Skyrim fixed this with level caps (among other things). If you buy this game, I recommend you try it out (I've heard that some like it but I think the consensus is that it necessitates too much notetaking which detracts from the experience) and if you don't like it, definitely mod the leveling system as there are much more friendly alternatives.
The pros? Literally everything else. I played this around the time I played Fallout 3 and this game's main quest shined whereas Fallout 3's main quest was almost unplayable. But as with most (at least contemporary) Bethesda games, the side quests are amazing. My happiest moments are stumbling upon sidequests where I didn't expect them. The real question is: does the game let you have fun in between the quests? Mods make this question an easy yes, but for vanilla Oblivion I'd give a more tentative yes. Grinding is a pain in Oblivion, which I mean not only to level up but also to accrue gold and items so on. Don't grind, explore naturally. If there's a cave you want to check out, don't just rush in eager to complete it and move on but let it mark itself on your map and go to a town where you can stock up and return. Let the game immerse you, in other words. You can do this with mods, sure, but also by sticking to character scripts (like my h2h priest Laknr) and self-imposed conditions (Laknr only uses healing magic and never strikes woodland creatures, even the hostile ones). Some people say Skyrim is a casual's Oblivion, suggesting that Oblivion requires some sort of dedication to play. Often this is meant in terms of the game's mechanics, which is true for the leveling system but complete BS otherwise. I interpret the saying as arguing that Oblivion requires one to immerse themselves much more deeply to enjoy the game. That gap between playing and being in Oblivion, that process of immersion, is definitely tougher to bridge for Oblivion than Skyrim, but Oblivion rewards you so much more for it. Of course, it helps if you geek out over fantasy RPGs like me.
Edit: Just wanted to also say that the modding community is still thriving! Enjoy the game!

TL;DR: I would still recommend this game after 500 hours of play. This is not the early access/beta game, alot has changed.  It has a friendly community and requires team play. There are regular bug fixes, patches, and in-game and outside of game events. New content has been slow coming (expected in Jan), but the official release was only 4-5 months ago. There is plenty to do without a new content.
Come join us! There is no monthly subscription, and it is well worth the $14 I paid.
---
The game is not the same as it was in early access/beta. So don't watch old youtube videos or read wiki articles when deciding to play. I did not play back then, so all of my hours have been since the official release. The game has a very friendly in-game community, which is essential for a game that is so team oriented.
You must join a guild to succeed in this game or have friends to play with you. The skill system is designed to require team play. This may be a positive or a negative depending on the type of game you are looking to play, but established guilds are always looking for new players to join them.
There are 3 factions from which to choose, but it has no affect on your character other than where you start the game. You can only master 6-7 skills of the possible 15 main skills and 6 weapons. You start out shipwrecked on an island and begin crafting weapons and building your base/guild - going from stakes and barricades to large castle walls with cannons, arrow towers, and ballistas.
Many reviews complain about high-level players constantly attacking novice players. It doesn't really happen anymore. It doesn't encourage new players to stay if we beat you down before you get started. If you leave the novice area to build your guild, you will eventually get attacked. PvP is part of this game. If you start out and strategically build you guild in the novice area, you can survive there without being attacked until you are ready to move on.
Some reviews say there have been no game improvements. This just isn't true. Sure there are still lots of things that could be improved upon, but saying we haven't had any fixes is false. Here is a list of things that have occured in the last 2 months:
October 25/26: Pumpkin Festival
- New skins and festival mount
- New permenant mount for purchase
- New Game Launcher
- New Decorative Crafts using Pieces of Shrubs
- Bug fixes.
Nov 2: PvP Tournament
Nov 9: Patch
- Minor changes and bug fixes.
Nov 11: Treevia Event
- Skin rewards.
Nov 23: Patch
- Anti-Hack Tool integration
- Hidden Tent Event
Nov 24: Treevia Event
- Skin rewards.
Dec 1: Winter Festival
- New skins and festival mount
- Improved chat features: Whispering and an In-game text translator
- Warden Tree system adjustment
- Removed undead from novice zones
- Fishing, Carpentry, Healing/Bandage adjustments
- Increased novice resources
- A few new recipes.
Dec 9: Robinson’s Odessee Event
- Item rewards and a server buff.
- A backstory was created through hidden diary entries around the world.
-

Dec 16: Fishing Contest Event
Dec 20/21: Patch
- Improved chat features: friend list
- Weapon mastery skill adjustments
- Bandage/Healing improved
- Crops cosmetic change
- Bug fixes
I hope this helps some of you decide if the game is for you. It has great potential, and it is steadily getting better every patch. It is a lot of fun building up your guild, mastering your crafts, and exploring the world. Hope to see you exploring Vegonia with us.

I was gonna write this long post about what basically ruins this game for me. Again, my opinion, don't get triggered. I think this is the most overhyped and poorly made cashcow of a game ever. The devs were so lazy in making the quests that even murdering every NPC in all of Rivellon doesn't even matter, they just respawn in each act with crippling alzheimer's syndrome making them forget it all. I dropped a deathfog crate in act 4 on top of all the paladins and they just kept walking into it giving me that sweet, sweet EXP. Then some random paladin woman asked me if I was behind the murders, which of course I denied, being a lone wolf character on the hardest difficulty and having maxed out finesse because stacking archers in this game with finesse + wits is entirely broken in every way conceivable, especially when Fane can just grant himself another turn after the first and always be first because wits = initiative. And I succeeded in convincing her that I was, in fact, not behind the murders of her ENTIRE PALADIN ORDER because I had 5 in persuasion, basically the only stat you need to max out every time. This kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥happens throughout the entire game, with most NPC's literally being useless and lifeless with no character traits whatsoever. Combat is a complete joke, rogues/summoners/necromancers don't even need to exist. Polymorph needs 2 points to access every broken spell in the game. The entire game's story has these insanely stupid plotpoints that are supposed to be shocking, like Dallis being Fane's daughter (foreshadowed exactly nowhere and cared about by exactly noone). It's like they are missing 50 pages of text in this game. I have so many examples of the bad or straight up missing writing in this game, it's like the devs used most of the budget to go on pool parties or something.
So basically, combat sucks on any difficulty (with tactician + honor mode basically being "ENEMIES HAVE 50% MORE HP" sort of lazy, typical♥♥♥♥♥♥that you should never find in a carefully crafted RPG such as this one). The story is a sad, unfunny joke, with few redeeming characters that actually make you care about them (only Lohse and Red Prince to my knowledge have proper endings to their stories, both being decently written. Beast's story can actually proceed without him being alive and end the exact same way it does if he was.) There are far, FAR too many characters that are interesting at first glance but, woops, look at that, some pages went missing! Too much effort to find those it seems! From Lucian himself to basically an entire camp of EXP fodder characters with barely any story related to them or ways to finish quests related to them without just straight up KILLING them. But oh, this game was definitely carefully crafted and wonderful, especially the part where I could teleport NPC's while talking to them with one character and make most fights an even bigger joke than they were initially. And finally, gear in this game is the most pathetic attempt at skipping work I have seen. They basically just put RNG loot everywhere and didn't give two flying ♥♥♥♥s about making more custom weapons or armor that are actually worth getting BECAUSE OF THE RNG LOOT EVERYWHERE. I also love it when talents become useless past the point where they clearly stopped trying, which is basically act 2, because they just couldn't be asked to  write anymore quests that are worth a damn (R.I.P Pet Pal). And let's not forget the always useful and prefered talents such as ambidextrous, which is great for when you want to do a grenade only playthrough with a one handed weapon only! Oh wait, that sounds tedious and stupid? Well, sucks for you, most talents ARE tedious and stupid, with no real usage over obviously better ones (Bigger and better). This game is only truly likeable by hardcore fans and people who tend to be bad at RPG's. Also those who like to delude themselves they didn't buy a crappy product that clearly has way less merit than people brandish it with.
TL:DR Combat sucks, story sucks with some small exceptions, class and talent balance sucks, difficulties suck, detailing on the world is poor gameplay wise and nothing you do has any impact on the ending and most, if not all of the game, including purging all of Rivellon for EXP GAINS is entirely viable and goes unpunished in any way. Voice acting is amazing though.
Final thoughts, do not buy this game if you like good story, a real, fair challenge or have played basically any other RPG with above toddler level difficulty enabled.
Buy it if you have already managed to find the missing 100 pages of backstory and quest dialogue, as well have an idea how to patch the game into some form of balanced state where I can't oneshot the final boss in two turns on the hardest difficulty. Or, you know, if you just really like good voice acting.

Warframe is a fantastic example of a game fully supported by the devs for a long, long time. I first tried it back when it came out and didn't really like it, so I reinstalled it several years later, after the Plane of Eidolon update. And boy, was it a pleasantly different experience.
There's so many things to do it's mind boggling, and it will take some FAQ and tip-list reading, as well as playing for a while until it all "clicks" and you understand what it's all about. And it's about magical-tech space ninja in the far future! There's story and quests, and the ability to replay completed missions for more experience and loot. And it's all for free- there is a premium currency, but you can easily trade stuff- easily obtainable stuff!- with other players for that.
You can play solo, or with up to three friends or go public matchmaking. There's also PVP if that's your thing, although the game is 99% PVE.
The community is also the most positive bunch of people I've ever seen, it's really hard to believe for someone coming from Dota and Overwatch.
Also, the game looks FANTASTIC. The visual style is well defined and I really like it.
I guess it's to be expected from the developers who made my favorite Unreal Tournament :)
I fully recommend this game- give it a try, it costs nothing!

PixelJunk Shooter is a short yet very enjoyable, straight to the point, exploration game with a bit of shooter action.
The charming Shooter is very easy to playthrough and the bosses are interesting.
I think that the most special thing about this game is the fluid simulation and the mechanics that magically emerged from it. The developers did a great job at picking that as their main feature and explored all its different aspects (attract, repel, solid, gaseous, etc).
The development direction ended up with a simple and short game but quite rewarding.
In fact, it is rather understandable and probably key factor of success the developer put together a short experience, since it brings a good all around polished product.
Even though it is categorized as shooter, I find the exploration part of the game the most notorious one.
The shooter aspects are not very challenging at all. They just fill up some spaces in the overall game design.
Level design and art style are both great. Music also fits in smoothly.
Do play it!

Here we go...
Gameplay 4.5/5:
As you can probably see above, its a board game, since most things are said above, I'll focus on the cards. Almost all of the cards in the game have a unique effect,  so you'll barely find any cards that seem similar (hence the word unique).  There are four different types of cards: Event Cards, which affect everyone playing; Boost Card, which instead of boosting your combat abilities, most of the time it'll let you gather more stars, heal you or move around faster; Trap Cards, which as expected give negative effects to who ever steps on them; And finally there are Battle Cards, which'll give you an advantage (in most cases) in one stat, at the cost of another.
Now I'll talk about battle. In battle, you have three different stats: attack, defense and evasion; Each of those stats will add or subtract the number from your dice roll, and whats partly unique is the defense and evasion system. Defense will subtract thier atk roll from your def roll and that'll be the damage (with a minium of one damage); Where if you successfully evade, you'll take no damage but if you fail, you'll take all the damage.
Now for the victory conditions or normas as it calls it. There are two ways to win: the first and most used is to gather 200 stars , while the second is defeating 14 opponents. There are five levels to have to pass, each one costing a different number of points to pass, for example to get pass level one you'll need 10 stars, lvl two 30 stars or two defeated enemies, and the cost rises from there. You'll need to get past level five in order to win.
Characters 5/5:
A bunch of characters from Orange Juice's other games are included in this (similar to super smash brothers), with three of them being unique to 100% Orange Juice. Even if you haven't played any of Orange Juice's other games, you should still be able to pick this easily. (This is what acutally got me to buy Orange Juice's other games)
Computers 3.5/5:
Once you've played awhile, the computers become extremly predictable, but for this it appears they're given higher dice rolls (especially Tomomo).
Multiplayer 5/5:
As said above, the computers are easily predicatable, so you'll get bored of them pretty quick and seeing how this game was built around multiplayer it'd be a waste not to use it. While I've only joined a few ongoing games, I've hosted my own server for hundreds of games and almost everyone whos come to it is talkative and friendly. I haven't noticed any cheaters throughout my games either.
Boards 4/5:
There are about 22 different boards, each with it's own layout,  field events and background animations.
Sound 5/5:
Each character has thier own theme song for when they level up, most of which sound very good and reflect what that character is like. The sounds of picking up stars is pretty good, but the battle noise is just a generic punch sound. The warp noise is pretty unique as well, or at least I haven't heard anything similar in other games and finally theres a noise when you lose stars on a drop panel, which just sounds like a generic bang noise. Aside from the voice actor saying whats happening on screen I can't think of any other sounds (without the voice dlc).
Graphics 5/5:
Every character has five different animations to them, for which they just spin around into their new animation but don't be mistaken I like the character's graphics alot; but the real shine in graphics are the card's pictures, each one drawn expertly and with at least four different artists for the pictures (though I'm sure theres alot more then that).
Story 4/5:
I'd have to say the story mainly follows Marie Poppo, who steals an item from every character she meets. Shes also the one who starts the story by stealing Kai's (whom the game considers it's protaganist) wallet and continues through each level all the to the final one. While the dialog is changed for each of the four campagins, they each follow the same story of chase Marie Poppo.
Overall 4.5/ 5:
This is one of the few steam games I can recommend you purchase while its not on sale and even purchase without dlc. Another thing to say is that most of the pictures on the steam page are really outdated and while I haven't downloaded the demo, I'm guessing it's very outdated as well.

Looks flashy on the outside. Has no depth. PvE is the same from beginning to end, gets stale pretty fast. No endgame PvE. PvP is nothing but running, running, running. Must have at least 5 players to max out all skills, which means if you want good armor, weapons, medicine, food (for buffs), a strong base, you need at least 5 dedicated players. If you don't like playing games with groups of people this game probably isn't for you. Weapons break way too fast. It's a constant grind, craft, break, build, repeat--and I have had my fair share of grinds. From beginning to endgame and forever after that, you better get used to cutting down trees and mining ores every single day.
There are videos from the devs showing a big chest of gold, this doesn't exist. Their website has a drawing of a rogue-like character dual wielding, this doesn't exist either. 95% of the dev posts from the forum responding to player requests and complaints are one of them saying along the lines of "We will look into this, I cannot promise anything will be done." Devs aren't doing anything worthwhile to the game, instead they make cosmetic items like shark suits and cute bunny ears.
The game is really fun when you start. You start to level your weapon crafting and armor, and carpentry. You get to see your base come to life--if you have the friends to help you with it. The game is relaxing if you just want to turn your brain off and cut down some trees. Beyond that, after putting about 100 hours into this game I cannot recommend it. The game ultimately feels empty, there are no rewards for killing other players than hoping they drop something nice (which you only drop 1 item out of your inventory when you die). You kill a low-level player, they drop a rock, and then you get a 10 silver bounty on your head and every enemy can now track your movement on the map.
Now the devs are doing some bland diary-search quests for some NPC named Robinson. Diaries are hidden across the map and you find them and they tell you something. Maybe it will lead you to the big chest of treasure in one of their videos from months ago that still isn't in the game? They aren't making improvements, they are just doing what they want to do and not listening to the community.

Awesomenauts is a MOBA with WASD movement and mouse aiming.  Also there's actual gravity, because the game is a platformer.  Essentially, Awesomenauts is the happy medium between a DotA style MOBA (I'm including LoL in that category) and a shooter game.  Without the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ RTS controls which so many other MOBAs have, Awesomenauts's gameplay itself ends up with a lot of technical depth (and anything which a script can handle doesn't count as depth).
One thing which is a plus to some and a minus to others, though is that Awesomenauts has very simple character growth.  Each character can pretty much only double in strength before maxing out, and there aren't even that many options with which to max out.  IMO it's a plus.  I think they got it just right.
Of course, the Awesomenauts community is kinda small, so matchmaking ends up being very variable, even within a single tier.  But I normally play FPSs, so I'm used to it.

With it's sleek graphics, smooth gameplay and balanced weapons, Warframe is sure to be the best F2P game out right now. With its non-pay-to-win style, its going to dominate the market.

While initially fun, diverse and intricate, Warframe isn't a number shooter I'd recommend for continuous play. A large amount of bugs, poor optimization and the ever-dreadful crashes will quickly grind down your enthusiasm into bitterness about wasted time. Moreover, the developer has an affinity for questionable gameplay and balance changes - in the most unfortunate case, you'll spend time, effort and (hopefully not) money to find a way that you enjoy this game best, only for all of it to get removed several months later. DE isn't particularly familiar with the culture of "inconvenience compensation" or the term "player convenience" in general, and looks down upon whatever it qualifies as "harsh" criticism, which makes the sudden gameplay changes even harsher for the user to process. In general, there's a stigma against veteran players, reinforced by constant introduction of new resource-gring timesinks and nerfs based on popularity (If something is used by 99% of the players due to its efficiency, it will be nerfed until it's not worth it). The updates, while technically common, often introduce only new weaponry and cosmetics - which can be rather disappointing once you familiarize yourself with the game.
A particular point I'd like to make is the game's movement system. While it boasts speed, fluidity and 3-dimensionality, majority of the maps are designed in a way that do not take advantage of either of the three, and most of the time the additional acrobatics one might employ during firefights result in nothing but a sense of personal satisfaction and the player's model stuck through the level's geometry.
While I can't claim that I am familiar with the development's team vision of the game's story and plot, I feel cheated, in a sense, when I inspect in which direction the story has been progressing. While initially more ambiguous and mature, allowing the player to enjoy the role of a mystical space mercenary, the plot quickly degenerates into the same old story of special teenagers/chosen ones/etc. fighting for the forces of good and peace against your average caricature villain of the week. The predictable dialogues, unskippable "cutscenes" and simplistic plot choices feel slow and bloated, and the occasional quips of the "Oh-so-funny" sidekick become infuriating after the fifth time you hear them (The option to turn them off, understandably, appeared only four or five months after the introduction of said companion).
Overall, beware. This is a great idea in the wrong hands, and will leave you disappointed and yearning for something better.

Don't believe the hype: this is a fairly terrible entry in the 4x genre. The developers have provided a single innovation: a new way to provide bonuses for the AI. This "innovation" prevents the player from fully controlling his units during a battle, which leads to incredibly sub-optimal unit maneuvers.  Attack orders are issued at the beginning of each round for all units, so if your unit's target dies during the round, the unit will choose its own battle plan, which is invariably awful. Rather than attack a nearby unit, yours will pick an absurdly distant one and have to walk around the absurdly common obstructions that litter every battlefield. This phenomenon is most noticeable and insufferable when playing a faction with slow moving 3rd tier infantry against an AI faction with flyers: the opposing flyers will isntantly relocate next to your squishies while your  titanic morons ping pong across the battlefield.
As for the "changing world" that everyone keeps talking about: you will experience the occassional winter, which slows movement and all types of production. Yeah....uh...amazing...or  something.
For a fantasy 4x, this game is terribly light on magic, which is disappointing since magic typically provides the tactical variations in these games. Any "spells" your units have are little more than auto-attack or auto-defend animations.
Your roster of troops is limited to 3 units plus various mercenaries. The units you do have are typically uninteresting with little in the way of tactical options. Attack or defend, that's it. Oh, the choices!
Perhaps this developer will soon make an audacious foray into another genre by providing us "Endless" tic tac toe bereft of the Xes.

Endless Legend is a 4X (explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate; Sid Meier's Civilization is an important example of the 4X-era) turn-based fantasy game.
It's really difficult - for an old strategist like me - to find something wrong within the game.
+The visuals are stunning,
+the soundtrack is harmonic and match the turn-based gameplay,
+the combat system is simple, yet interesting,
+a modern transparent UI,
+Customizable race and units and
+Mod support.
(Also the lore is quite fascinating)
But! - like every pro - there is critic:
-Like in other strategy-games, there's a lack of AI-performance. If you turn up the difficulty, it will just provide higher buffs (like more money, more science etc.) for the AI. It could simulate a challenge for someone, but for others it's just cheating and unfair. (I will deny my own opinion in this regard)
Overall, good stuff. Not bad for an Indie-game. This game tried some new ideas and implemented those successful.

The Positive:

+ The possibility to make custom races based on pre-existing ones.
+ Every race has their own, interesting storyline.
+ More victory types than in Civilizations V
+ Beautiful graphics style
+ Amazing music with a unique sound to it
+ The pace of the game is quicker than in Civilization. You do not have to wait for ages (literally) for just a monument to be built.
+ Immersive fantasy-world
+ Unit customization
+ The game has in-game quests that grant you rewards upon completing them. Also, each faction itself has its own main quest and they are really rewarding since the benefits they give you can be quite large.
+ The combat system is interesting and actually challenging and although it may feel you have little influence at first, there is really a lot you can do to influence it. It is more like telling your units what to do instead of controlling them perfectly.
+ Made by a developer that continues to add new content. For free. Yes. Here, you do not have to buy a ton of silly downloadable content or expansions to make the game more fun. *Winks to Firaxis*
+ Good city building style and management
+ Conquered cities do not lose 75% of the existing buildings like in Civilizations, the same with population. Because of this a conquered city still has value. Also the cities that are founded later in the game are not necessarily behind in the development, because you can buy buildings from the early game for a relatively low price and so the new city can quickly go to the same level of  your older cities.
-+ Science. It is interesting and also non-linear. But it feels a little weird for me. Also, most researches are often focused on just one type of advantage. So, things that purely give you more food, or more Dust (= money), or purely militairy things.
Some negative:
- May be overwhelming in the beginning. Because it can be a little complicated and the game itself provides few explanations.
- The game can get a little laggy near the end of the game. Especially when the winter comes.
- If you compare waging wars in this game to waging wars in Civilization V, then I must say that in Civilization V it was better. Because an army was not a single entity like in this game. There was also nothing more satisfying than rolling several catapults supported by a ton of swordsmen and archers up to an enemy's city and than bombarding the hell out of it. It was rather satisfying. Although sieges in Endless Legend are also good (and I like the idea with units being granted extra health points for defending in a siege) it is simply less exhilerating.
- In continuation of the above. War music. Declaring war on someone and then getting to hear adrenaline-filled songs may be one of the reasons why I always ended up being called the ''warmongering menace'' in Civ V, unfortunately these war/peace themes are not as present as in Endless Legend or do not exist.
- Small variety of units
- No naval combat. The seas are not used for anything more than transporting troops.
I cannot think of more negatives.
In short, I would say that this game is rather innovative and beats Civ Beyond earth any day in the history of mankind, or the future for that matter.

Now for a more serious review.
As you can see at the top ^ I do have a decent amount of time put into this game, thus I do have a decent amount of experience.
Let's start with the positive sides of this game, as this is a positive review:
- price: 2 euros and 50 cents in all sales, and the only 'real' dlc "starstorm" is usually also on sale and fairly cheap
- for a MOBA this game is innovative as it is a sidescroller, which makes the feel completely different
- the theme: all the different nauts have a very detailed theme (with backstory, theme song, killing spree song and excellent voice acting)
- there’s a lot of variety in the different nauts, which all have different playstyles and builds to learn
- the game is constantly getting updated by the developers by adding new nauts and maps, improving the balance and providing news about new dlc and tournaments at the start screen
- it's a game which has a fairly high learning curve, which makes you feel like you're never done learning strategies
- there is a decent competitive tournament scene with prizemoney which is exciting to watch
- strategies and team compositions are important so coordination is key
- fun to play with friends (to be fair all games are, but coordinating with your friends does make it more fun than queueing with randoms)
- close community: at the higher skill end of the playerbase basically everyone knows each other and there a TeamSpeak servers where you can just hop on to queue with some people you know won’t disappoint (like some randoms ;-; )
Now for the negatives:
- lack of gamemodes, as of right now there are three actual gamemodes: normal mode, team deathmatch and randomnauts. Only normal mode can be played by queueing online
- the playerbase isn’t very big, with around a thousand players online on average, this makes that lower skill player sometimes get matched up against more experienced players and that more experienced players get matched up with a team of a lower skill level
- soloqueueing after the period of getting to know the game isn’t very enjoyable, so I recommend to buy a 3-pack with two other friends when this game is on sale, so you aren’t alone
- getting friends into the game once you have a decent amount of hours (like me) might be tough, as your skill levels will be radically different (a solution to this is to make a second steam account, and use the family share option with your main account so your friends don’t end up in games where everyone outclasses them
- the angry players, these are players who constantly rage at balance; teammates; the matchmaking system and most importantly you. These players are mostly rampant at the medium tier level of play, so don’t expect to encounter them too much when first picking up this game.
As I can’t think of any other points to discuss I will end the review here.
I hope you, the reader, found this review helpful in your decision of whether or not to buy this game, or if you already own the game and you will now get a little less salty at people you don’t know for no real reason. PJSalt

Original article with a hilarious picture of a dino with four arrows sticking out of his head here:
I’ve been playing theHunter for quite some time. Once a year, I throw in my yearly subscription and it allows me to pick up a gun or bow and go patiently wait for deer, bears, elk, and more to come close enough to shoot. Other than the fact that you’re shooting animals, it’s an almost calming experience. A relaxing, slow simulation that still allows you to feel accomplished over the course of a single hunt.
As you can imagine, I was pretty excited when I saw theHunter: Primal. theHunter is already a great hunting simulation with some impressive AI and gorgeous scenery. It’s also regularly updated and, even now, is still getting new animals every so often. There’s also not much risk in the base game, though. Sure, a boar could maul you but you can jump right back in with all your stuff intact. You don’t die. You’re just “injured.” This new edition could very easily have become the prehistoric Cabela’s Dangerous Hunts of the series.
Then I read the store page a little more. Worry set in. Rather than being a new edition of theHunter, the game seemed to want to take the core gameplay and underlying technology and make something closer to a futuristic version of The Stomping Land, sans dino-wrangling. PvP was the first alarm. Then I read about “survival” and “permadeath” features. It was starting to sound a bit like something I didn’t really want.
Fortunately, it isn’t as bad as it may sound. It is still very much theHunter. theHunter with a bizarre, vague story, futuristic setting, and dinosaurs thrown in, but theHunter, nonetheless. I didn’t personally try out PvP so it would be hard to give an opinion on how that works – I didn’t even come in contact with Kat during the time we were playing – but the basic gameplay is there. I would be surprised if it weren’t. There’s an acclaimed game that it’s being built on.
You can tell, too. The basic AI behavior is there. Raptors hunt in packs, with the occasional raptor scouting ahead and then returning to the group. Tyrannosaurs shake the ground as they walk, and will often pay no mind to you unless you make yourself very obvious. Triceratops are generally more peaceful and won’t bother with you.
It isn’t all there, though. I experienced a number of problems with the AI, mostly pertaining to raptors. I mean, triceratops paying no mind to the tyrannosaurs that are coming right at them, shaking the ground as they go, and then bolting at the first sign of your tiny human self makes no sense to me but it’s more of a design flaw than an issue with the AI, and one that was probably carried over from the more peaceful creatures in theHunter. I was even used to animals that hopelessly walk into rocks repeatedly, hoping to finally get past them, having experienced many issues like it in the original game. No, my problems run deeper.
Raptors work perfectly fine – until they become aware of you. Then they break. Not all the time, mind you, but they are broken pretty easily and there have been several ways in which I’ve experienced them breaking. The most frustrating is when you’re being chased. They do this awkward thing where they will attack you and then stop, wait for the animation to finish, and continue to sit there, as if “getting their bearings.” They can’t attack you and move at the same time. They don’t jump at you in any sort of way or pin you down. They just run up to you and come to a full stop when attacking. As if this didn’t break immersion enough, with raptors repeatedly falling yards behind you only to suddenly start running after you again, if you save your stamina until you’re attacked bolt towards the nearest brush without looking back, and dive into it, there is a high chance you can escape a raptor. You know, a raptor that is faster than you and was chasing you.
That’s not all that is wrong with them, though. Sometimes, when you are in areas with a lot of cover, and you dive into cover, raptors will still know where you are – sort of. They run at you…and then proceed to stand over you, turn at a ninety degree angle to you and just sit there. If you move, there’s a 50-50 chance it will fix them and they will kill you. If you don’t move, there’s about a ten percent chance that they will lose interest and walk off. Yes, you read that right. Raptors that know you’re there will sometimes randomly walk off rather than killing you. However, the most hilarious encounter I had with one of them occurred when it knew I was there, so it ran around an entire group of trees, sideways the entire time, making me think I was safe before showing up right next to me, facing a different direction without moving.
It’s not like you can really take advantage of this, either. The bow is very, very hard to use, requiring exacting precision in the right places to take anything down. No, headshots don’t work. I’ve tried. I should have known better, being someone who plays theHunter, a hunting simulation, meaning you should, as you do in real life, aim for the lungs and heart, but I tried anyways. The result was a hilarious four arrows sticking out of the raptor’s head as it sat there, not killing me.
However, the biggest problem is hinted at in the article title. Right now, it’s just a bit of an amorphous blob of awkward game design. More like a mod for theHunter than anything, a testing bed for ideas as they throw dinosaurs in and try to figure out how the community wants them to do things. It’s very much theHunter. Other than losing everything when you die, which doesn’t exactly feel like you’ve lost much currently, it is very much not a survival game. Not yet, at least. At the same time, though, just enough has changed to make it feel less meaningful than theHunter. By introducing survival aspects, it’s not about killing the biggest dino or having the most successful hunt. It’s about survival. But theHunter isn’t and, right now, at least, it’s sitting in this spot where just enough has changed that it doesn’t scratch the same itch as theHunter but it isn’t changed enough to warrant not just playing theHunter.
It’s fortunate, then, that the game is buy-to-play, rather than a hybrid of subscription and free-to-play models. You can buy Primal once during Early Access and never have to worry about any other fees. If you’re an existing fan of theHunter, regardless of what happens, you will probably get your money’s worth through the joy of hunting dinosaurs using their existing hunting model before inevitably going back to theHunter while you wait for them to sort everything out. Don’t worry, you can turn off PvP and make it a dino hunting marathon. If you’re a fan of survival games that incorporate PvP, however, I would wait a while. The mechanics to make it one aren’t all there yet and it’s a bit unclear of where they’re going to go from here. It shows promise for both ends of the spectrum but it needs a bit of time to find itself first.

After playing this a couple of years ago this game has really come a long way ! With any game like this there's the obvious comparison with Company of Heroes. I only briefly played Men of War which I never liked. Call to Arms is not quite as slick as CoH but can more than stand up in its own corner. From the beginning the music in the main menu fits. Voice acting is not embarrassing. There are already major mods in development for it including a Star Wars mod (as yet unreleased). While MoW represented a more technical approach to real time RTS, Call to Arms is at least fairly accessible now for those more used to thing like CoH.. But there are some problems with the controls. Selecting units could be a lot easier (why not follow tried and tested control schemes ?). I found myself getting frustrated learning control techniques that seem to be unique to Call to Arms but I guess any game has a learning curve. But with a bit of perseverance, and along with wracking up the sound effects volume, its possible with Battle mode to quickly get into an AI Skirmish game. Soldiers tend to look after themselves as long as you use cover properly. Once the firing begins the thing that stands out for me is the sound engine in this game. Really nice ! Weapons sounded nasty and dangerous. The environments are well put together with a large selection of maps. Buildings are destructible. Performance is good although I've only fully played the smaller 1v1 maps with 50 population cap so settings might have to be scaled down a bit for some of the huge tank warfare maps. So Call to Arms, for a free beta at the moment, is worth checking out. But be warned it's not an instant jump in and understand what's going on kind of deal. It actually closer to something like the ArmA series (and yes you can jump into an FPS mode) but maybe not quite as punishing with the simulation and control complexity that ArmA has. However I did feel rewarded for persevering with and understanding the game. Definitely a game not to discount too quickly.

The Bad:
Too much focus on free "expansions" which in itself is a long stretch to call it expansions at all and too little focus on fixing the state of the game. Also shameless advertising for Endless Space (a different game) on updates regarding this game is starting to get really stupid which should not be in the updates/news of this game.
Huge amount of desync errors in large multiplayer games, giant red alert windows with error reports spamming your gameplay (but does not cause the game to crash) which you have to dismiss every turn, AI errors using diplomacy and will greet you 8 times pr turn non-stop, AI randomly overtaking real players in multiplayer environments at random forcing reload after reloads, quests that spawn armies that you need to hunt down just to see them disembark and being on a boat permanently (where you cannot attack them)
The list is very long but those are the most aggravating ones that comes to mind.
And I have not even gone into game tuning like what the game would be like with naval combat, more interesting siege mechanics etc., in short this chunk was just the mechanical errors.
The Good:
When you are lucky at the majority of errors either do not manifest or are at intervals long enough separated for you and your friends to have a good time, the game is great.
Beautiful graphics, amazing UI, great faction variety, nice music, artwork, in short really loaded game.
The Considerations:
The fact no quality assurance has been given to the games development before release is astounding. Most of these errors are very consistent and reproducible yet was not only released but we are at the "second expansion" release and they are still not addressed.
As a result, despite how much potential the game has and how much I like it when it works (which granted is not often) I have but no choice to give it thumbs down.
I am simply tired of the contemporary standard defending shoddy craftsmanship as an "industry standard"

What is it?
2d sidescroller, controlling a ship to solve puzzles using water, lava and a magnetic liquid to save your crew members.
The Good:
+ The game's main premise has you navigating the enviroment, destroying the environment so that water and lava can mix forming new terrain for you to destory and progress further along. Keep in mind this is a simplified version of the game, as you progress the game introduces some new mechanics and ships to keep things varied.
+ Combing the different liquids together is really cool and adds a fresh new gameplay idea, combining different liquids together provides different results.
+Graphics fit the enviroment nicely
+ Some cool boss battles
+ Achievements are easy to get and shouldn't provide too much trouble.
The Bad:
- The game doesn't really take its ideas far enough leaving a very easy game.  The game doesn't get that much harder as you progress either. I was a bit disappointed when I beat the game.
-Roughly 3 hours long, 5-7 hours if you go for achievements.
Conclusion
Although I had fun, I felt the game was a bit basic for my taste. I would have liked the game to be a bit more challenging especially in regards to the puzzles as the game does introduce some cool elements later on in the game.

"Changed Religion and now I can't play because I need dlc"
Before I get on with the review I want to respond to this, changing ones Religion in this game is a very difficult thing to do, and in my over 800 hours playing this game I have not once had it done by accident, maybe they changed that recently but I sill have yet to see something that can change my characters faith without my consent. And even changing characters faith by choice is rather difficult and requires a lot of planning. Not to mention the amount of autosaves this game provides means this particular "issue" seems remarkably easy to avoid.
On to the game itself, it is simply put a lot of fun, you play as a dynasty, not a nation, and you rule through the feudal methods of the time. Because you play as induviduals not nations, it allows for some increadibly enjoyable storytelling in the game, every holding, from counties to barony's has their own character. Its very possible to see those Barons you had under you at the start of the game rise to become your rival kings, or watch as splinter groups of your dynasty come to rule entirely seperate and rival nations, I've managed to get my Imperial Byzantine family sitting on the throne of Poland and later the Holy Roman Empire. The feudal mechanics also means you have to worry about the opinions of your vassals, you can't go around executing every one of them that annoys you becuase then you set yourself up for rebellion. The Politics in this game and its rather lifelike (in some areas) mechanics means fourtunes for yourself and your rivals can change on a dime to very entertaining and/or frustrating effect.
You will be limited by the laws and traditions of whatver nation you play as, a Byzantine Emperor will have a lot more control over thier subjects than say a French King, and the feudal system and the mechanics they use to implement it can make controlling a large nation rather difficult, as your vassals can become very challanging, its easy to fight a glorious war of conquest against those muslim infidels, and then find a rebellion break out among your subjects as you lose too many soldiers fighting the heathens.
The goal of the game is ensure the power of your dynasty (though this is a very loose goaln and you can chose any goal you like) and this means things like ensuring a good heir and sorting out your succession so they don't end up fighting a massive civil war once you die. Of course there is a lot of randomness and other events that can completely ruin your plans, much like life, disease could wipe out your family, ranadom luck and/or clever planning could lead one of your vassals to inheriting half of your duchies and gaining an army larger than your own. Your son could become fierce rivals with the son of your most loyal vassal, leading to later hatred between the two whent hey inherit and a wealth of problems. And you'd better hope that Jewish doctor you hired doesn't sacrifice your amazing firstborn son to cure you of the flu (true story). This randomness can get frustratibng at times, but it does make for a highly entertaining experience if you can roll with it, as well as some hilairious stories
Finally I want to talk about the dlc policy, I got this game when it was reletivly recent, so I've ended up buying the dlc rather dispersidly when it comes out, so I n ever really faced the wall of dlc that people buying now would. That said the base game before the dlc was still a lot of fun, and even paying full price for the dlc, I've easily gotten my moneys worth in again, over 800 hours of playtime. that said I do understand that the dlc can be rather dautning and a lot to pay for something you don't know if you'll like, so I'd point out that the game goes on sale rather often, and bundles like the Five year anniversary edition can get you the dlc thats really particularly important. So its not too difficult to get this game for a reletivly cheap price, and I think its definitly wotrh it.

First of all another great game by Amplitude (Dungeon of the Endless and Endless Space), props to them.
If you like any 4X games then I'm sure you will find this game enjoyable to say the least, and even if you don't I would say definitely give this game a try. I was skeptical about buying this game in that I wasn't too fond of 4X games, but boy am I glad that I did. At frist this game may be too much to handle with all the information that needs to be taken in (esp for me who haven't played 4X games before, like me) but after 2 or 3 games you will get the hang of it. Graphic wise it's 10/10 for me, esp considering that this is an indie game, it's just the right amount of goodness without the lag. Soundtrack is also very good, I mean it's not amazing or anything, but it definitely is what I exepected from Amplitude (all their games have great soundtracks).
Pros:
The great thing about Endless Legend is that it has everything that a standard 4X games will have plus more. This game was very refreshing for me in a sense that I have been playing games for as long as I can remember and that no new games have really impressed me of lately. Instantly I knew I would be hooked on this game for awhile in the fact that there are total of  8 factions you can choose from. Each factions are unique in their own way with their own sets of "main story quest", perks, units, and heroes. One small thing that sets Endless Legend apart from other 4X games is that heroes have skill trees (even though it's all passive) which I thought was pretty cool. There are also total of 14 minor factions or so that you can take over, which allows you to make different units that is apart from any major faction units. So all in all you can say this game is pretty much like CIV except just better with additions as I have mentioned. (Plus other many cool things that I won't mention, hopefully you will buy the game and find out yourselves :P )
Cons:
So far I have been very happy with how the game played out other than how the battles played out in that it's pretty standard click and click to move/attack. I guess you can say that it kind of gets boring after awhile? There isn't much you can do with it and most of the times I find myself just "auto battling" and moving on. I just wish there were more ways that I, as a player, can affect the outcome of the battle more and that maybe it could be bigger in size. One other thing that I also found a bit lacking was the fact that each faction only have 3 units to produce from, which is kind of fixed by the fact that you can have minor factions, but still I wish there were more to choose from. Also, it would be cool to have some kind of defense mechanism near your city other than just having extra fortification, such as towers or catapault of some sort. Other than the battles I really don't see anything wrong with the game and considering that this game is decently new I'm sure they will improve on it even more near future.

TheHunter: Primal is still quite clearly in early access.
There are several issues with the game at the moment, not least of which being the AI, as a lot of people have noted before me. I will give you a short list of the things that are a bit weird/bad in this game:
- Raptors are unable to attack you from behind if you simply walk away from them
- Raptors act in very weird ways when you have your back faced against them, such as do not attack you, will try to, but are not able to or will just stand next to you and do nothing
- Ai pathfinding is quite bad in a lot of cases, causing you to find triceratopses climbing mountains or t-rexes stuck in trees.
- Pathfinding is especially an issue when the dinos are chasing you, stopping randomly and making 90 degree turns out of the blue or running around in odd patterns and not directly coming straight at you.
- Raptors sometimes absolutely ignore you, even if you are literally standing right next to them.
- Dinos often completely ignore the fact that they are being shot at and will not notice you until you have shot your 10th arrow into them.
- The dinos will often freeze if you just hide in a bush and they come looking for you, causing them to get stuck into their idle animation indefinitely until you come out of the bush.
- Multiplayer barely works.
And here is a list of just general things I've noticed in the game:
- Weapons do very little damage, HOWEVER this is not a problem and I hope the devs do not buff the weapons, at least not too much. This means that actually killing things requires you to know their weakspots, often this is not the head. This means that you really can't really mow down dinos with guns and have to instead wait for a good moment when you can get a clear shot at their heart, for an example.
- Sprint is horribly short and the cooldown for it is horribly long. You can run for about 30 meters and you have to catch your breath for about a minute.
- It feels very silly having to stand still for 20 seconds when you run out of ammo to let that raptor you shot claw you to death, maybe the game could use some sort of melee weapons, anything to make it feel like you are actually fighting back, even being able to use your fists would be nice, just give me something to make it feel less like I always just silently have to accept my fate whenever I fail to kill something and run out of ammo.
- dinos do not attack eachother. Since when did t-rexes let triceratopses just chill right next to them?
- Inventory stuff is a bit broken. You cannot stack smaller stacks of items to create one bigger stack. 1 bullet weighs as much as 20 bullets.
- A HUDless mode would be nice, there might be one in the menu, but if not, adding one would be really cool. Although the current HUD is very unnoticeable, which I do appreciate, a HUDless mode would be even better.
- You can lose all your items if you suddenly lose connection to the game server, which sucks,
Even after all of that, I do really like the game. The sounds are excellent and it is very intense to hear that t-rex stomping behind you while you are hiding in a bush. The game manages to make some really memorable moments happen in its random world almost constantly and I mean that in a good way, not talking about just glitches. If I played this game in junior high, I think this would have been one of those games where me and my friends would just talk about all the crazy stuff that happened to us in this game during lunchbreaks. The gun sound and feel phenomenal, I don't think I have heard better guns in games before, granted I don't know too much about guns, but the guns actually feel like they pack a real punch and aren't just cap guns. The tracking mechanics work great and it is really cool to track down that raptor you shot and which is now running away. The world, albeit a bit bare, looks beautiful.
However, even after all that good, I will say I do not recommend this game at its current phase, even though I have myself enjoyed it immensly. This is due to the fact that it is not right now a very good game, due to the bugs and balancing issues, a fun game (in my opinion) maybe, but a good one it is not. However if you are able to look past all the bugs there is a great game in here with an even greater atmosphere where you can easily lose yourself for hours.

Currently the most played game in my Steam Library, 100% Orange Juice is certainly one of the most unique games I own. 100% Orange Juice hosts a great mix of chance, choice-based combat, surprises (good and unfortunate), and humour. It's a great game to play with your friends, the only issue being a maximum of four per game. The community is also incredible to play with. The game's roots are simply a combination of an online board game, anime, and spiked orange juice, but you'll find yourself in a different situation every time.

For as weird as this game is, I was not totally dissappointed with what all it can give. 100% Orange Juice may look complicated at first, but once you get into it, it becomes one of the simplest (and most luck-based) board games ever. Also, before you go off on your own, this game is really more enjoyable with a group of friends. Going online on your own can be fun, but this game is one of those games that's ALWAYS more fun with friends. ...Or enemies. Pick your poison.
Also at first glance, there's a lot of DLC. Now, the DLC packs that I think every player SHOULD have to have somewhat of an upper hand are the card packs. It's a bit unfair to make better cards locked behind a paywall so that the players with less money to spend won't be able to enjoy the full experience. So, if you have a little bit of money, and maybe some patience, wait around to when the pack DLC's are on sale and get them. Or, get them when you buy the game.
For the character DLC's, they aren't necessarily pay to win if you don't know how to use them. Some characters can be classified as better, but overall, they really aren't too much more than the characters the game lets you have upon purchase. So, that might seem like they aren't worth it but, if you like a certain character from Orange Juice's lineup, there's no shame in buying them as DLC.
All in all, the game's fun and should DEFINITELY be played with friends, but the problem I have with it is that I feel like TOO much stuff is behind a paywall. If Fruitbat or Orange Juice would make at least a few of the DLC's free with the game, it might be a better game so everyone isn't on different levels just because one person has more money to spend than the other. ...like me. But that's besides the point. Enjoy the game for what it is, and it is a very enjoyable game, I believe.
