Endless Legend is an amazing achievement, breathing new life into the genre that was established by Civilisation.  The biggest attraction is that the different empires to choose from have genuine differences in gameplay. Notably, the cultists can only ever build one city, while the necrophages cannot be at peace with their neighbours.
There's a lot going on in Endless Legend, but it always feels like you're making decisions, rarely like you're pushing units around to support a decision you made a long time ago.  (Roadbuilding is a fundamentally different experience than it is in Civ, in a very good way.)
The learning curve is steep, although it's not off-putting in the way that Endless Space could be.  The battle AI can be a bit crazy and baffling at times, and sometimes my units felt stupid.  If you've ever been disappointed in Civ, then try Endless Legend.

So far I have been a HUGE fan of the developers ever since I first played Endless Space. Now with this 4x strategy game theyve done it again.  The game does have the usual 4x elements but this game is something else completely. The Combat  is a MASSIVE change from what earlier 4x strategy games have done (COUGH* CIV COUGH*). You can actually equip your troops with better weapons, though each faction only has 3 troop classes. The battles in this game are unlike any 4x strategy game Ive played, It actually makes you strategize for battles and enemy engagements. The research tree style is also very unique. The game itself is freedom. The ability to make custom classes even in the vanilla game. This game has a REALLY unique storyline element, which gave playing alone tons of replayability as you try to finish each factions unique storyline. Never have I felt so much fantasy RPG elements in a 4x strategy game. I give the game a 10/10. I highly reccomend this over Civ titles.

One of the most original and innovative 4x games to come out in years. Eight wildly varied factions (each with their own unique, expansive plotlines), a host of really interesting, unique mechanics (only one city per district, no tech tree). Most of the mechanics are very intuitive, but offer some pretty significant depth.
This came out at the same time as Beyond Earth, but it's been much better received, and the reason for that is simple- it has personality. Playing with each of the factions is like starting a different singleplayer game, and the faction creator is very flexible. Like its predecessor, Endless Space, the game also has fantastic, understated art and music.
The only problems are that some of the more advanced faction-specific mechanics are poorly explained, and that the AI can sometimes be poor at defending their cities. Amplitude have patched this, but some more work remains to be done.
Overall, the most fun I've had with a 4x since Alpha Centauri.

This is without a doubt at the top of my list for best strategy game of the year.    Once again Amplitude has turned out a solid product, and the developer continues to support and improve the game long after release.
The game is one of the few 4X titles to find a workable and satisfying solution to the strategy of spamming cities, and the lore in the game combined with the perks of the factions in the game give each faction a distinct and interesting flavor.
The combat is a semi-controlled tactical battle, where you can control where a unit moves or who it targets, but without detailed control about how the unit gets there.  The combat is probably the least satisfying element of the game to me, but is still decent.  The rest of the game is simply excellent, and easily worth the full price of the game.

Divinity: Original Sin 2 contains a level of depth and attention to detail that is becoming increasingly rare in modern games.  Every element of the game feels purposeful and well designed.  The game never feels "grindy," every combat encounter presents a real strategic challenge and either moves the story forward, opens up areas of the map, or offers interesting loot.   The unique armor and elemental systems add a significant level of strategy to the game.  Strong planning and improvositation wins fights, not superior stats (not that stats are meaningless). Although there is plenty of "junk" to pick up, most weapons and gear you come across will offer interesting trade offs to the gear you are currently using, forcing you to constantly make important decisions about which gear to use.  Every single line of dialogue is voice acted and the music is phenomonal, but never distracting.  There is also a good bit of humor which occasionally feels a bit out of place, but is generally well executed if not laugh-out-loud funny. There is so much more I could talk about, but just do yourself a favor and buy this game, even if you usually aren't a fan of turn-based RPGs.

This is pretty much a game that shows, IMO, a lot of what's wrong with today's prentious attitude concerning games as a story-telling environment. I don't have any experience with this genre, so I can't tell if everything is this crappy, but this particular game is really, really bad.
I've played about half-an-hour of this game and it's irrelevant if you now tell me that, later on "it becomes the best game eva!!!1!", because the beginning is descouraging and one of the worst thing I've "played".
These guys did manage to create a decent horror atmosphere, but why is this a game? Would it take too much writing skill to make a movie and throw it into the immense pool of mediocre horror films that spawn every year? At one point, I was in a burning field, moving slowly in an irksome way (why would I want a game to be deliberately frustrating?) and, occasionally I had to press E to not die. Why? What good does that make? Is this what people think that a game's "interactive" part implies? I could've watched a movie and just mess around with the volume knob and you wouldn't call that a "game".
Another thing that bugged me is that whole "Save the black pawn thing", then a chessboard appears giving you the option of picking a white or a black pawn. It doesn't clarify whether you pick it for "saving" it or "not saving" it and that's another thing that I consider deliberately frustrating.
Maybe I would've watched this as a movie, even though I'm not a horror enthusiast, but I wouldn't bother to press "E"  from ten thousand different positions just to pick a key in plain sight that seems to be reluctant of me picking it up. I think games today have this problem when they try to be just movies for people with ADD, occasionally requiring you to press a key to show the next cutscene or play the next line. The interactivity aspect of a lot of games today seems forced and unneeded, "Only If" is a perfect example of this, so, unless you like movie-like storytelling but can't sit for two hours without clicking some buttons, I'd recommend you stay away from this "game".

Okay, I will admit at first I HATED this game... But I will also admit I was bad at it. Really bad. The game has a bit of a learning curve. But now, I like it. I wouldn't quite say I love it, but I'd say it's worth the $10.. even though I got it for 99 cents. :D
It's basically a base/tower defense game with 2D cartoon aliens.
I think there's like 20 different characters now, and that's exactly what they all are, different. Each and every character is unique. There are no 2 characters where you think "Hmm, this one is kinda like that one" They all look different, and they all have their own special abilities. Pick up solar(games currency) or gain it by killing, and you get to upgrade those abilities.
It definately helps to either read up on all the characters abilities, or have an experienced friend to play with you. What you don't know, kills you... Over and over and over.
Overall, it's really a good game. I only have one problem with it. Leon. Leon makes me sad. No matter what character I am, no matter how upgraded I am, he finds me, pops out of nowhere, and out-DPMs me no matter what I do. Of all the deaths I have in the game, I'd say 90% are Leon related.
Get the game, it's worth it. Not sure? Wait until it goes on sale. But before you make your judgement on whether or not you like it, play every character. That's the secret, you have to find the character that you like and do okay with, then continue to learn and progress from there. Don't just try 1 character and say you hate it, because that's what I did. Learn from my mistakes.
P.S. Leon OP, please nerf. 9/10

Great to not having to swap discs when traveling from one island to another!
Well, what can I say that hasn't already been said? It's a classic point-click adventure that's been modified to run on Windows 7 and maybe above. Yes, there are bugs in this version, and I will focus on those for this review. Now, I don't look at these bugs as a broken game, but rather an older era game being pushed to run on current systems. Really, it's impressive that those games even work at all a lot of the time. Naturally, the graphics aren't HD but it looks just as ~good as it did back then (it picks a smaller resolution while playing).
So if you've played Riven before, and want a copy that you can play again, this is it. (or until Starry Expanse finishes realRiven). If you are new, the puzzles are tough but fair, the world is quite attractive, and it's part 2 in a 5-part series (6 if you include Uru), so there's lots of lore to be had.
Anomalies you may experience in the Steam version of Riven:
- Some buttons do not have animations, but still function as normal.
- Sometimes it felt like a sound effect wasn't playing, like the Maglev door opening/closing, but that only happened on the observatory (smaller but not smallest) island, in the lower level.
- While on Jungle Island and approaching the village from the forest path, the lookout post plays it's whistle but didn't animate for me.
- All animations/movies are 1 or 2 pixels lower on the screen. At the beginning this is very noticeable but as you run around, the effect is easily ignored.
- Movies are a different quality than the still images. Again, noticeable at the start but easily ignored.
*** - If you save your game and later the game freezes, it may seem like your save was deleted if you are no longer able to select the Load menu. It is still there! Just start a new game, Save, then try the Load function and select your previous save file. Also, there is no Autosave, so remember to save often!
- Book pages flip 2 at a time, but if you hold the button then they will flip more. So hold it just long enough to get 3 pages to flip, then click back a page once.
So to go from pg.1 to pg.2, go to pg.4 then back once.

I bought this game because it had so many good reviews, but after several hours of playing, I can't figure out exactly why. Some reviews compared it to Civilization V, but that's not a fair comparison, in fact it's downright misleading. The strategies for each game are completely different, and whereas Civilization V has a wide range of units and buildings you can research, this game doesn't. The games pace is also extremely slow, almost painfully slow. This is one of those games, where if you don't build armies, you don't win. Arms race is the name of the game. This will be a problem for those who like to explore and build new cities, simply because if you devote your time to this, you will most certainly lose. It's not a bad game, but I certainly wouldn't recommend it when there are so many other fantasy strategy games out there that are much more polished.

Overall an excellent fantasy 4X strategy game that has a lot of polish and interesting ideas to it, and well recommended to fans of the genre (Civ V etc).
Settle cities to gain control of regions, pacify the local minor factions and assimilate them into your empire for unique bonuses and combat units.
Recruit heroes to lead your armies and govern your cities and customize them through talent trees.
Research (or find) equipment to improve the stats and abilities of your units.
8 playable factions so far, each with their own traits and playstyles. Each faction has their own questline that will give you various tasks to accomplish and keep some semblance of a story going, and more quests can be obtained from searching the numerous ruins scattered across the map.
Battles are done on smaller battlefields on top of the world map where your army stacks (usually 4 to 8 units plus a hero) spread out and have 6 rounds to declare a winner.
AI is probably the weakest point of the game currently, in particular I feel they're a bit too passive when it comes to diplomacy and their army compositions can be less than optimal. The developers do seem dedicated to tuning and adding to the game, so hopefully we'll see some improvements in this regard. See the Steam and Amplitude forums for post-launch plans and feedback requests.
Visually the game looks really good, perhaps the graphics are a bit too detailed too at times when you're trying to spot the really good tiles when settling a new city. Zooming out will give you a simpler map of the regions and strategic resources, and most of the game can be played from that view if one is so inclined.
There's naturally multiplayer, and fortunately it doesn't seem like an afterthought as you get the exact same game and interface as when playing alone. For diplomatic actions and trading players are required to spend "influence points", possibly to dissuade human players from being too generous to eachother.

New armour system makes combat a tedious chore, encounter design is terrible with constant "sucker-punch" attacks often from dialogue (seriously, ♥♥♥♥ you Larian) and it's absurdly level-locked. There is still nothing in the design that encourages the use of the innovative surface interactions in combat. The surfaces mostly just make a total mess of the screen in combat forcing you to play them in overhead view just to see what is going on. Oh, and the initiative system with rounds that reset everybodys position in the queue every time they rollover is just bad and feels broken.
The items are also rigidly level locked with huge number bloat, creating an unending loot treadmill with bland equippables and an avalanche of useless items on the side. I completely ignored the crafting system and just sold everything and still spent a ridiculous amount of time managing my inventory.
For class design, you can just be every class and take every skill, same with all the enemies you'll face, plus there are consumbles to cover every skill so expect guard dogs to attack with fireballs and poison darts and fighters to possess powerful magic and status grenades as well. You'll get all your interesting skills within the first few hours, and then it's a hard slog all the way to the end of the game. (Yes, you get source skills, but source skills are tied to a limited resource.)
Attributes do very little (+5% damage! +1% critical chance!) and thus aren't much fun to play around with.
The storyline attempts to be more serious than the first one, but still comes off as amateurish and painfully r3tarded without having the lighthearted tone which at least redeems the first games story in a small way. There is just nothing relatable about the quest for divinity, the characters in the story or about killing voidwoken. There are a few interesting plot twists here and there, but the story is highly skippable. I had no issue with the narrator, personally.
NPC cast is 99.9% forgettable. If I ever played this game again I would design my own crew and kill all the NPCs.
The game is too long for it's own good, Arx was a pointless lump and a slog that only exacerbated the problems with the tedious combat, weak story and added a pacing problem to the games many issues.
This is not an improvement over the first game, and it fails where it attempts to address the issues from the first game. Hopefully mods can make something out of this, but I'm not sure the basic design mistakes like level-lock rigor mortis, item overload or the tar-baby of the armour system can be fixed at all.

Firstly, it took a little finanglin' to get it to run on my windows 10 machine. This wasn't really that hard at all, and I am not particularly computer savvy. I had to run Riven in compatability mode, which meant I had to click the .exe instead of launching through steam for each launch. The other thing was setting "affinity" through Task Manager (something about how many processors the game runs on, if I understand correctly, all one does is right click the process and click "set affinity", then make sure only one CPU is checked) which amounted to ~4 mouse clicks per launch. Without doing this, I would experience crashes. Finally, I had to use the "alt" key menu for saving and loading games.
These modifications took about 5 minutes in total to understand, and added perhaps a few seconds each time I played Riven. To complain about these issues while knowing/remembering that this is a very old game not designed for modern systems is not necessary in my opinion.
Technical issues aside, I very much enjoyed this game. I'd like to fancy myself an averagely clever person sometimes, and it took me a while to figure out many puzzles. When I eventually did, (occasionally with the help of one or two UHS hints (UHS is a spoiler-careful hint website)) I was either shouting at the monitor that this game is enjoyably clever or simply smiling at how cool the game is. However, I must say that some puzzles seemed a little out of the blue in my opinion, which is to say that perhaps 2 or 3 times I was saying to myself "how would anyone think to do this/figure this out without walking around for hours or without hints or UHS!?"
In terms of story, I very much enjoyed the plot/story/worldbuilding of the "Myst Universe," if one can call it that, albeit with some minor detail confusion/dissatisfaction.
TL;DR, it's an at-times difficult but absolutely rewarding and very fun experience unlike any other games I have played up until this point. Perhaps it's the "honeymoon phase" talking but I would rate Riven a 7 or 8/10. Undoubtedly would recommend.

My current review:
Alright lets start with some things I see commonly come up:
-There is no Micro-transactions, it is a one time purchase.
-People seem to worry about it being abandoned like The Stomping Land. Avalanche Studios would have too much to lose if they ditched the game so do not see that happening. They are the ones responsible for the Just Cause games, I do not see them being willing to ditch a game to ruin sales of their other major games.
-Yes there is bugs, it is early access.
-Yes there is a lot of walking and patience required at some parts, this is hunting not a run and gun war game.
So far I am quite enjoying this game even at it's beginning state, from the amazing visuals to hunting and being hunted by dinosaurs.
There is currently 3 types of dinosaurs, 2 more planned during Early Access phase before release. You start off next to a pod in which you will receive a bow, arrows, and a map fragment, these items are quite weak (but can kill if used properly) and after exploring and surviving the dinosaur inhabitants you will stumble upon encampments and chests in which you can find loot. This can be anything from ammo, camo, health right up to guns.
If you are not careful you could wind up in the jaws of a T-Rex or ambushed by a pack of Raptors. Stealth is your friend when hunting these creatures. T-Rexs are not really advisable to hunt alone as they are extremely tough to take down but with a group of fellow hunters you can take them on. Raptors can track you and even plan to flank you, plenty of times some will creep up on you without you even noticing keeping you on your toes a lot of the time.
Your items go with you after you relog or switch servers, they are with you until you die at which point if you want your items back you will have to run back to where you died to reclaim your items if someone has not already looted your items. PVP is an option for servers to have as well.
Some people do complain about the damage of the weapons against the dinosaurs but the thing is, they're dinosaurs, not thin skinned humans. They have thick skin, thick skulls and small brains, you want to aim for vital organs such as the lungs/heart for the maximum effectiveness. A well placed shot will take down a Raptor in one shot, a T-Rex can be taken down with several well placed shots although if you hit in a not so vulnerable area it will take a lot more to take the mighty beasts down. Animals if hurt enough will bleed out over time as well, so do not just automatically expect a fleeing animal survived. Even the mighty T-Rex may flee if hurt enough.
I do not want to give much about the story of the game away, but there is a bit of a storyline behind it which you will discover while playing if you keep your eyes peeled out for such things.
As for bugs, there is a few and I have crashed a few times but not enough for me to really complain.
I could go on but this is already long. Overall if this is your type of game and do not mind supporting Early Access titles I would recommend it, if that does not sound like your thing, then wait it out.

So, when i saw this game, i did not had much option other than to just buy, a game so similar to the hunter being pay it only once with no micro transations? I'm in!
About the game> This is The Hunter on steroids, you are stranded on a wild planet, you've been sent as cannon fodder before the colonization, even though the lore is as basic as the Avatar movie, it is enough to get you going. You start off with just a bow and a few arrows, and you have to scavenge drop boxes left around the planet if you want to survive, and, while you do that, you get to hunt dinossaurs.
Hunting dinossaurs is a bit different from hunting wild boars, the carnivores won't hesitate to have you as their next meal, and they don't lack the ability to track you down. Most of the times, it is best to just let your prey go than to engage in combat, if you lack the element of surprise, this is not The Hunter, this is Be Hunted. You will find yourself lots of times listening closely for clues about your foes as you crawl away through the dense foliage, not for the faint hearted.
Exploring is just awesome as the world feals really life-like, with a awesome science-fiction touch as you see yourself orbiting another huge planet exploring a planet that highly resembles Earth. Bonus points for hunting with your friends, you won't forget the first triceratops you'll put down after a lot of teamwork, yes, the bow may not be the best weapon for hunting such beasts, but it surely can get the job done. Also, this comes to another point: can you play it offline? Yes, you can, but unlike The Hunter you WILL need some help taking down the larger animals and surviving the dinoes that hunt in pack, find some friends and do it together!
Also, as this game is based off on The Hunter, a hunting simulator, you can expect long walks and some frustrating situations,, but that is part of the features, if you don't like it, this game might not be for you.
Of course not everything is great, and, for now, probably we can blame early access for it, sometimes the interface gets clunky, or there might be some technical errors. I am not mentioning the lack of content, as there is way too few dinossaurs and guns to keep you interest for a long time, but it will probably get only better with time.

PixelJunk Shooter is a twin-stick shooter, with a very big focus on physics (specifically fluids). While exploring the underground caves of a planet, you'll have to interact with lava, water, liquid metal, ice and rock in order to save the scientists who are now trapped.
The story is basically that. You're in a ship, trying to save every scientist. And also collecting hidden gems. Whole it may seem a game about exploration, it didn't quite get to that point, in my opinion. But more on that later.
Let's start with presentation.
The
is very minimalistic, with soft colours, and yet, it looks great, in my opinion.
It certainly looks unique, and the fluids especially, give it a a special look.
The enemies have a mechanical feel to them, but it fits, along with the Boss Fights.
The
was less of a standout for me, but it was certainly not bad. Just a bit more faint than I'm used to, staying in the background for the most part. It helped with the light-hearted exploration-y atmosphere, I think it was well chosen for the game they were going for.
The sound effects were in the same vein.
How's the
, then?
First off, the game is divided into 3 areas, each with a few levels. Each level also has about 4 (I think) areas to explore, each of them self contained, and fairly small.
The first area is more vulcanic, the second, deeper, is full of ice, and the third, the deepest, has an industrial feel to it.
Each of them has different mechanics associated with the physics. These are all connected to the area it's set in.
You control a little space ship, propelled by thrusters. The movement feels quite great actually, with momentum very notable in the ships handling. It feels great, even though there aren't section to challenge your pilloting skills. It's still good that the tight control is there while you're just flying around.
Then, you have a Hook/Tractor thing to pick up the gems and the scientists you find, and you also have missiles, to destroy rocks and your enemies.
There are also several different types of ships. You'll find modifiers in specific points of the levels. For the standard ship, lava with overheat you, while water will cool you off. Each time you get hit, you don't instantly die, but your heat will rise substancially. To survive, you can either back away, or dive into water.
Besides, you'll find ship modifiers around the levels, for when you need to actually progress the levels.
There is a Magma ship, that shoots lava, a Water ship that shoots water, and can pull ice with is hook, there's an inverted ship, that is hurt by water, and can dive on lava, and there's also a Magnetic ship that repels the liquid metal. These sound, and play really well, but they're highly limited to the levels. You'll only have access to them in the exact section that you need them, and there's no action from the player in discerning which ship he needs for the given section, unfortunately.
In each level, you'll try to find the
. You have to deal with all of them in each area to unlock the next one (either save them, or kill them). Every time a scientist dies, you'll lose a life. Your limit is 5, but you'll gain another one each time you collect 100
(these are spread around the levels, and also dropped by the enemies).
You also try to find
, that are used to unlock levels, or just for achievements. Unfortunately, these are very easy to miss by mistake, and you'll have to replay the whole level if you want to 100% it (it is NOT needed, though. I did some thorough exploration the first time around, found every
, and still missed a couple of gems in many of the levels. I never had the need to replay levels to proceed though, so the game was designed to keep you going naturally, saving these for the completionists. That's really good, in my view!).
There are also
that you collect in your Gallery (yeah, not creepy at all), and these will talk to you, giving you a bit of backstory into their expedition.
The base of the game is out of the way, now.
This game reminded my a bit of Waking Mars. Besides both being about exploring the caves, both are very focused about combining elements (in WM, it's mostly interacting with the creatures, in PJShooter, is with the fluids). While Waking Mars gave you a real feeling of discovery, learning about each species and all about their lives and interactions, that isn't very present in PixelJunk Shooter.
PixelJunk Shooter is a very straightforward game, and also not very challenging. It's something to enjoy casually.
The level design was pretty good, in my opinion, providing good areas to experiment with the fluids, and learn new mechanics without a wall of text. While that was all there and great, the whole game felt like a very big tutorial, in a way. Everything was subtle, but not challenging, and specially not giving the player much freedom.
You'll have everything delivered into your hands when you need it, there's no puzzle solving, or anything, which wasn't what I was expecting. So, if you're looking for an experience of discovery and learning, go play Waking Mars.
If, on the other hand, you want a laid back twin stick shooter with cool physics, give this one a try.
The Boss Fights were the funnest part of the game, for me. They weren't very hard either, as you were pretty comfortable even after getting hit (as long as you were careful). But that comfort gave you the time to learn the Bosses patterns without it feeling frustrating, and led to interesting fights.
I found the game enjoyable, certainly, but in a way that I wasn't expecting. It's very, very linear. There isn't trial and error to understand the fluids, or anything. It's not about learning the mechanics, and then applying them into more complex puzzles. It's mostly about learning on the go, always with simple puzzles. And to be honest... that's fine.
It may not be what you're looking for, but it's good that it exists, for people who do. And it's a very well done game for its purpose.
It's also very cheap on sale and you can easily get it. Go ahead and give this one a try if it sounds appealing!

I love the way these games are crafted, I love how they actually create the illusion of strategy, without actually having complicated, and difficult to learn, elements.
I love that anyone can play these games and if not enjoy them, then at the very least understand them.
Love it.
The games follow the same logic of the type of series of games that have been developed by Microsoft Games, Age of Empires, Age of Mythology, etc.…
You pretty much have to gather resources to then create buildings that grant units, as well as other improvements, for both the gathering of resources, as well as for the combat mechanics.
These games nail the progression of your empire, the growth of it, both superficially as well as mechanically.
And it feels incredibly rewarding, and in that side of things I have no problem with, even if it has been something of a formula that the “RTS” games that Microsoft have created over the years, it works, and it does just enough both aesthetically, as well as in the games tactics, in the way they change, and in the way the add stuff that’s different to these games, to make each entry always different and enjoyable.
One might say Rise of Nations it’s a bit more of a complicated, and deeper strategy game than say Age of Empires, with the similarities being simply in the fact that both games deal with war, and diplomatic, strategies that come in the middle of both, and in the growth of an empire, that goes through the years.
Difference being that Rise of Nations takes that a step further and creates these grand games, that can last for hours, all with the same emphasis but whilst sharing more of what you’ve come to love, and expect from Microsoft’s “RTS” games.
The only problem that I have with it, its that, no matter how much depth, and rewarding gameplay mechanics these games have, the biggest problem I’ve been having has to do in regards with the way the game handles a lot of its mechanics, and gameplay enhancements.
I cannot tell you how much I dislike that the campaign makes alterations to the core gameplay design up to a point in which it destroys it, I understand they’re supposed to be scenarios that are already created, in which you only need to take part of, but I dislike that usually the strategic, and minimal layers of illusion the game manages to create start being undermined by a set of poor requirements for completing each mission.
Some sections in this games turn the wonderful creation of the empire, into a redundant chore of taking a group of your combat units and pinning them against your enemy, all of which happens at times in missions, without the joy that it is to even gather, and create that army.
Upgrade it, and “breed” it from the start.
Admittedly there are custom game modes that you can create which respect the games systems, I enjoy that, and I would say that’s probably the main reason as to why you’ll be playing any of these games.
If I had to say anything about Rise of Nations its that in a way it’s the Age of Empires sequel I never came to expect, because really, up until some years ago when I got into pc gaming, It was the first time I heard about this game, and I (foolishly) actively, and deliberately, tried to avoid playing it, because I thought it would strafe off far from what I loved from previous entries in Microsoft’s set of “RTS” games.
Lucky, we are, that now we can play all of these games at higher resolutions, and framerates, whilst staring deep into the beauty of a lot of our memories.

Got this game from a Humble Bundle ages ago, never paid much attention to it.
Decided to give it a try after a friend asked me to.
0 Regrets.
So much depth, so much RNG, so much salt.
Going into depth:
The game has a very solid, polished boardgame base that, while it could be described as "Mario Party without the Minigames", goes much further than that.
While extremely RNG-based, each character has a distinct playstyle that benefits certain patterns, and combined with the shared card deck, no match ever feels the same.
The game rewards you for just playing it, so losing isn't much of a problem either, sometimes you're not even in it to win the match: The fun you had from making a losing play is rewarding enough. Daily quests are available to give you means to farm Oranges(currency used to buy cosmetics), and while not necessary to complete them every time, you'll find yourself wanting to leave your comfort zone often and playing varied styles of characters.
Many DLC are available, but they do not imbalance the multiplayer aspect: A new, dlc-less player can compete on an equal level with a veteran, although more limited in character choices.
Also, on a completely personal note, I absolutely adore the game's cute, simple aesthetic, the community and the memes.

Crusader Kings 2 had a very negative opening experience for me. I bought the collection on a sale a year ago only to see it didn't actually come with the full collection. It excluded Charlemagne so the first hundred years or so were cut off from me. (Luckily now they fixed that and the collection is actually the collection.) Went on the tutorial and had no idea what I was doing then joined a friend's multiplayer game and was even more lost. I refunded it, thinking of Paradox poorly (which I still do, the greed of this company is insane, but I can't stop loving their game). Months later another friend decided to buy it for me and I gave it another chance, and I'm happy I did. Crusader Kings 2 is probably my favorite strategy game of all time, and for good reason. Every playthrough is it's own individual, unique, quirky, and randomized experience. Just go through the positive reviews and read people's stories, they are quite outrageous and memorable. The connections you make with your player character and other characters is amazing, the dynamic quests and decisions and etc are all so good. And the actual strategy is quite good as well, but that isn't the focus of the game. It's the character and story building, this game is more of a history simulator or story simulator then a strategy game. I would recommend buying this game just for the stories you can make.
Side Note: Paradox is an insanely greedy company and I do not support them or their marketing and business practices. In fact I find them very deplorable.

The graphics are vastly improved compared to the original Myst, and in fact, I think they hold up surprisingly well even today, despite the tiny resolution. The worldbuilding is also much richer, and the story more subtle. The game takes place mostly on one single, bigger world, which feels more like a real place with wildlife, people, and curious technology, than the barren, tiny Rube Goldberg-islands of the odd-numbered Mysts. I recommend this game. There are obvious problems with it, however:
One has to wait long durations for animations to complete that needn't repeat, for example, at the Moiety cave access wall, or the Whark totem, or the maglev terminals. No doubt if these animations could be skipped the game would lose its immersive grip; nonetheless, I should like to navigate across small chasms if those are narrow enough to jump. Meanwhile, some movies do not play, for example the switch on the waffle iron puzzle and the grate on the drain. When linking you must watch the movie before progressing. Every time you want to open the dome you must enter the code, which is only challenging the first time and tedious every time after that. Differently coded domes might pose that challenge, were the codes conveyed inexplicitly.
The pre-rendered graphics are gorgeous; no two places look the same and accordingly each place has its own mystery to observe. Some have remarked that with point-and-click adventures the limitation on your movement is not clear. Asking oneself whether a frame looks open enough to allow my passage is distracting, if an interesting puzzle in a way. The limited perspective also debilitates me in understanding space and how the islands are arranged. Any recreation of the game I hope achieves a higher resolution and a seamlessness panorama as the player turns.
For clarity those props with which you can interract to achieve some end are the only props with which you can interract. If in Fredddy Fish games the player can expect reaction from any click then surely that is not liable to confuse adult players, and would distract from felt impotency. Places on Riven defy exploration by denying a ladder or somesuch thing. I wasted a lot of time trying to find access to the higher levels of the village because I felt that a clue might lie there, and well it could have, or rather there be some evidence of the villagers beyond that given. Magleving to Survey Island shows a forest that was once accessible but was removed for some reason. Riven, small as it is, invites you to scour every nook; it seems cruel for the game to elide expectations that it established.
These problems hardly hinder the game, which is exceptional. You will struggle to have a more rewarding gaming experience than on Riven.

I wasn't sure about Endless Legend.  I love 4x, but I thought Endless Space was bland and uninteresting.
But let me make this clear: Endless Legend is an incredible game that I strongly recommend.
Art design, music, and worldbuilding are all fantastic.  Game balance is great considering how distinct the factions are, with many difficult decisions (unfortunately, still a lot of no-brainers as well).  There is a strong focus on war, with a chess-like wargame minigame that has incredible potential-- AI isn't quite up to par yet, but updates are promised.
This is the kind of game that has design written across it in boldface with indelible marker.  I started out scratching my head at some of their choices, but as I played, it became clear that every mechanic was carefully considered.

This is a 4X game with some interesting new mechanics, which mostly work well. For me it's basically the Sword of the Stars (1, not 2) of land-based 4X. The things that I enjoy most are the city management system and that you don't have to go wide to win, though there certainly are advantages to rapid expansion. I beat the game on the hardest difficulty with the one-city-only faction.
If I was giving it a score I'd probably say 8. It isn't as polished and well-rounded as Civ V, but I find it to be more fun and interesting.
- Looks much prettier than Beyond Earth.
- Lots of people praise the music. I wouldn't say it's the greatest, but it is solid.
- All the factions are interesting and different. Each has a gimmick, though they don't all suit the playstyles that the developers intended.
- The hero system can be annoying at times, since some heroes are just completely better than others, and it is random chance which ones you'll be given access to (though starting heroes are always the same).
- As with many 4X games, it suffers from the fact that the victory conditions can be pretty meaningless. Literally the fastest way to win a diplomacy victory is to continually break your alliances and reform them each turn. Also, once you start winning, you may as well just kill everyone else immediately rather than waiting to get a science victory or whatever.
- Combat can be very tedious; I recommend increasing the combat animation speed immediately. Also, do not underestimate the importance of initiative in combat. Each unit only gets one attack/counterattack, and the default counterattack overrides all except one of the special attacks.
- You have to work out a lot of the mechanics for yourself. This game does not hold your hand. Reading a guide on city leveling/building is almost mandatory.
- Harder difficulties are legit challenging.
- Quests system is robust enough, but some of them are fairly stupid and/or impossible.
- Strategic and luxury resources all have meaningful differences and advantages.
Some basic info so you can work out if it is the game for you:
Hex-based movement. Out of combat movement is in army stacks with movement of slowest unit, but combat is in a 6-turn battle/encounter where the units split into one-unit-per-tile. This encourages you to build armies which complement each other out of different unit types.
Cities work differently to most other games of the genre. The population is essentially all "specialists", to use the Civ term, where each unit of population can be used to create (base) 4food/4industry/4science/4dust/2influence depending on your priorities that turn. Food, industry, etc. on terrain adjacent to the city is automatically collected, and you can expand the city by building districts in adjacent hexes to increase the area being passively collected from.
The world is divided into regions, and you can only have one city per region. This makes city placement be really important, and leads to important decisions as to city expansion.
Units are upgradeable with equipment. Each faction has three unique base units, and you can assimilate up to three minor factions to get a faction-unique buff and their factions unit. eg. assimilate the Haunts to get 5% to science per Haunt village in your territory, and build "Ended" which are flying ghosts with a chain lightning attack.

Sonic Mania is a throwback to the 16 Bit era where Nintendo and Sega were the biggest games (no pun intended) in the industry, 3D graphics required extra hardware, controllers were (usually) wired and everyone still had a CRT TV.
It has been lovingly handcrafted by Pagoda West, Christian Whitehead and Headcannon Games to portray what could have been if there had been a main 2D Sonic game on the Saturn, and it NAILS it!
The physics are spot-on, the graphics are beautiful, the bigger stages that are either all-new or twist and bend the stages we all love to simultaneously tickle our nostalgia while making us anticipate the next new thing, and the new stage gimmicks work handsomely.
This is Sonic 4 as we truly imagined it, and it shows that it was made by the Mania, for the Mania.

This game is everything a Sonic fan could hope for. Fast, fluid gameplay, expansive maps, challenging but rewarding gameplay, if there weren't so many stages from past games, it would be practically perfect.

Has been playing this game most of the day now. If you like a realistic hunting game with dinosaurs, then you will like this. It looks good and has the right atmosphere, that make u feel that u are there. It also makes you sneak around a lot. The "cons" in this game, seems to be minor bugs that will be fixed anyway and the "pros" has already been mentioned. As soon (and they will) as more life is put into the game, I can't ask for more. Here is what I to see:
1. That species roam specific areas, that are realistic to them. So you don't meet the same all over the map.
2. I hope to see some function, that makes you feel you have an objective. Like to hunt a specific dino or with a certain weapon.
3. Veteran or Alpha dinosaurs, with a nickname. Killing this is like killing a boss. It has to be rare. (1 per server).
4. Hunger/Thirst/Temperature/Wounds <- Else it is not a survival.
5. Dinosaurs has to be affected by other dinosaurs. A raptor has to flee from a T-rex. Triceratops from all carnivores and so on.
6. Meaningless critters and insects. I know they're there, but we need more. The more life, the better the feeling.
7. Herbivores that is just there for the viewing and gigantic size, like Diplodocus or such.
8. The ability to make shelter, a fire and roast the meat, that u also has to be able to harvest. <- I know this one might sound a bit far fetched, but that would really upgrade everything and give u a purpose for the hunt.
9. The simple ability to JUMP! Even if it has no purpose, but the psychological feeling of having that freedom really boosts the gaming experience. Imagine if you didn't have the ability to reload (like in old games), but by giving u the option to suddenly choose and reload at the right time, changes the game a lot. So a simple jump would do.
I can't really say anything bad, as all my need has been fulfilled, even in alpha. The above is just hopes and wishes. The negative stuff I can say is just bugs that will be fixed anyway. I have waited since childhood for someone to make a god damn game like this, and now I have it!

Honest and non-misleading gameplay:
Comparing this to The Stomping Land and Beasts of Prey, this game easily beats both. When you enter this game you can instantly see a lot of work was put into it, with the huge highly detailed island, with the dinosaur models with textures done so well and the very nice ground vegetation which give the game such a great sense of realism.
As a hunting game, the AI needs a lot of work, they are not buggy but rather dumb, like zombies in DayZ, and if they spot you they are close to impossible to kill, which in some cases can become frustrating. The mobile tracker device works perfectly, but I feel as if the original game deserves that credit.
As a survival game I get a nice immersed horrified feeling, the aspects of this game can really come off quite scary, as the forest tried so hard to do.
So far I can say that it is worth the money, the game shows hard work by the developers, and I have hope they can maintain creating a more realistic primal hunting game.

I'll go over a few things that got me all giddy inside and things that make me kinda ticked.
Pros: There's defiantly qute a bit to this game and it has a lot of nice things to it.

-Visuals : The game is pretty, it's gorgeous and the dinosaurs look cool too.

And you can use it to put waypoints on the map as well, and I found out that if you're playing with a friend and they got a map fragment that shows a closer settlement thing, they can set a way point and you can see their waypoint they set so you can meet up.
Cons: There's quite a bit that's kinda bad about this game, but they're fixable.

They're fragile yet strong creatures. they should not be able to take a small army's worth of ammo to the head and keep going. No!

IDEA: Might add to it.

If you liked Men of War, and want a modern setting, you will LOVE Call To Arms.  The same wonderful destructible environments that we all love with this engine are still there, armor penetration mechanics, cover systems, etc.  Now featuring a new first person direct control, which actually makes combat inside buildings realistic for the first time in a MoW game!!!  No longer will your men run in and stare at the enemy until they decide whether or not they want to shoot each other, you can (and should) do it yourself!  Tank battles across open desert in first person view really improve the immersion.  This view allows you to realistically guide ATGMs and do whatever you want really.  Weapons have their own realistic sites/optics/whatever they have attached in first person view, realistic zoom capability, etc.  There's much more content on the way too.
If there's one thing that I really would like improved upon, it's the armored vehicles.  I believe they are working on an ERA system which is great, but some sort of armor modifier for different warheads such as RHA equivalent protection vs KE, RHA protection vs CE, etc.  The penetration and armor values we have in game for the biggest and baddest tanks currently in the game (M1A2 TUSK and T-80U) seem quite a bit off as well.  The heaviest armor listed on the M1A2 in game is 600 mm.  It's not much trouble to penetrate it frontally.  I think the armor values and armor system need tweaking.  But please don't let that stop you, it's still a great game.

It's a long game, but a good game. II just finished my first playthrough at 110 hours. I didn't complete EVERY quest but I did come to some sort of resolution for most of them. Divinity Original Sin 2 is a rich and beautiful world to explore with an explosive and exciting turn based combat system. The game has a very intersting story that is 99% voiced which goes a long way in immersing you into this world. I never knew that I needed games like this to be voiced and to have a narrator. Take note Pillars of Eternity 2. It gives you this sense of going on a real Dungeons and Dragons style adventure. It conjures up feelings of Baulder's Gate 2 while being very modern and engaging. This is the divinitive CRPG experience in gaming today. I firmly believe it will be a classic like the CRPGs of old.
The game isn't without it's flaws though. Firstly the last two acts slog a bit. There are still tons of interesting things that happen and a few jaw-dropping moments, but some parts I struggled to boot my PC up and play the game. This comes right into the second flaw, the game is a little too long. You definitely get your money's worth. This game would give you good value per dollar even if it cost $100, and it only cost $45 US. It's a freaking steal. However, when it takes 100+ hours to beat a game while seeing most of it's content sometimes you just burn out a bit. Finally there are some flaws with the actual gameplay a few times. Some of the puzzles are unecessarily difficult, sometimes it feels like the enemy gets 10 turns for every 1 turn you get, and it has performance issues in a few spots.
However, overall this game is the best game of 2017. It's an absolute steal at $45 and the game tells you a story you won't soon forget. Easy reccomendation to anyone even slightly interested in CRPGs.

The amount people♥♥♥♥♥♥on Skyrim's magic as being weak I expected to be able to fly about one hitting everything in Oblivion. Hours later, maxed magic skills and attributes sitting in the Arch Mage's quarters and I'm wondering what sort of juice people were taking. The magic is godawfully weak and after casting about 5 spells I'm straight out of magic and the enemy's health is down a quarter. Oh, you want to heal? Every restoration spell crafted or otherwise costs about half your magic bar for about 10 points of health. You want to put on a fire cloak or ebonyflesh for defence? Those spells don't exist. Okay, maybe I Fus Ro Dah nope, wait, you're some random pleb, you have no special powers.
Okay, maybe I can fix the game with mods. There's a few decent ones for improving the faces, but as for the confusing ♥♥♥♥ing UI and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ levelling system? No can do bud. There's a few out there that make small changes to levelling like giving +5 instead of random numbers or more magicka so you can actually cast spells but none of them truly fix it.
There's DarnUI but that just makes the UI smaller and gives you a larger inventory, it doesn't change the way the UI looks so you can figure out where to find what the ♥♥♥♥ you're looking for - you still have to mashclick the various tabs trying to figure out which vague symbols represent the thing you're looking for. The inventory itself is larger, but you still have to spend half an hour scrolling to find what you want - or you can get a mod that makes everything into icons. Unfortunately the icons are ♥♥♥♥ing tiny and half the items in the game are identical so you're still ♥♥♥♥ed if you're trying to find Random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s Letter to Other Random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Which brings me to the dialogue and story aspect.
Instead of meeting, for example in Skyrim "Hunter" in the woods, you get to meet "Blyjan Thundercunt". Most NPCs have names and schedules and do more than just stand around all day doing nothing which is one of the few things I liked about the game. However you don't want to talk to them. Both you and them only have generic dialogue and in the rare occasion you have a quest that requires talking to them you end up finding that they change their accent halfway through talking to you. The biggest offender of this I found was the beggar npcs that exist for the Thieve's Guild questline. Speaking of which, the Thieve's Guild were presented well, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t contracts for Maven ♥♥♥♥♥face, but there's very little of worth to actually steal. The vast majority of houses have zero items of worth, occasionally a potion or two if you're lucky. Shops can sometimes have a few items of worth, if you're willing to haul the 100 weight steel swords around so your fence can give you a third of the item's value. Oh, yeah, if you thought selling items in Skyrim to level up Speech was tedious you'll just love Oblivion. At the time of writing I've probably sold about 40k worth of items yet my Mercanitle is at 16. Speech is seperate and is levelled using a boring minigame whenever you talk to someone, but aside from a few occasions it's not really worth the time it takes to level it.
After completing the Thieve's Guild questline and getting the stupid looking Cowl that is far too big for my character's head, I went on to the Mage's Guild, which is one of the most tedious and boring thing's I've ever done in a video game. You have to go to every city in the game, there's like 6 or 7 of them, and go into that city's mages guild. Then you have to do a favour for whichever incompetent asshat they put in charge. Usually this means doing a lot of waiting around and then going into a generic cave and killing Necromancers, the most irritating enemy ever as a Mage as they constantly run away from you ducking and weaving so you can't hit them with projectile spells and can't catch up to them for touch spells. There's about five Necromancer filled dungeons you have to complete as part of Hannibal Traven's chores - by the end I wanted to join Mannimarco - Okay, let's be honest, I wanted to join Mannimarco from the start. Then Hannibal out of the blue kills himself and makes you Arch Mage. The story's about on par with Skyrim's College of Winterhold so, if you've played it you know it's not great. I never got to do the main storyline because my character is so weak he's unable to kill the Dremora in the Kvatch Gate, but I expect it's more of the same.
Thinking more about the game, I figured maybe the reason I didn't enjoy any of it was because I was spoiled by games of today like Skyrim, GTA V and, well I was about to say Fallout 4 but that's a real matter for debate. But really, it's not that the graphics or the UI in Oblivion are low texture quality, it's that they're terribly designed. It's not the textures on faces that make them look ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's how they're shaped. It's not that there's a lack of easy perks to get what you want in the levelling, it's that levelling is confusing and doesn't feel rewarding. The game is a whole bunch of poorly executed concepts that could have been awesome like spell crafting, but ended up being pointless and disappointing.
But hey, people say Morrowind was everything Oblivion wasn't, so I guess that's next on my list to try out with some graphics mods.

Don't be fooled by my time played. In order to get this game to work, I had to buy and install it from Steam, but then use the Steam files in a separate engine.
If you try to run Riven without tweaks, it WILL crash on you, unless your computer is a relic. However, you can find a solution here:
I have Windows 10 and this fix worked for me. I grew up with this game and it's one of my all-time favorites. I was so happy I almost cried, haha.
I absolutely adore this game, but it's not going to appeal to everybody.
Pros:
1. The atmosphere. All right, if you're the kind of person who loves exploring a game world, trying to figure out how the culture works and getting immersed in the unique flavor of a dimension all its own, get excited. Riven gave me an experience I have been trying to repeat with other games all my life. The world is truly unique. You know how Peter Jackson made Middle Earth feel like a real place with history, rather than just another fantasy world? Riven has that sense of authenticity, sprinkled with a good dose of mystery and unease.
2. The puzzles. Honest-to-goodness, these are THE best puzzles I have ever encountered in an adventure game, hands down. The puzzles truly correlate to the world. You aren't just running into random crap you have to solve that breaks immersion. The puzzles all tie into the story, and then they even tie into each other in a way that makes them art. It's beautiful.
3. The characters. At various stages of the game, you'll find a journal kept by each of the three main characters. If you're prepared to do some reading (okay, actually a alot of reading. It's worth it, but you do have to be prepared to sit on your butt and read for a good twenty minutes in the case of Catherine's journal.) you're going to find some unique characters. (You don't have to read through the journals to beat the game. They contain necessary clues, but you can skip to those pages.) Catherine, Atrus, and Ghen have more individuality to offer than your average character in games. Also, if you're into the whole reading thing and you like this game, you need to get your hands on a copy of The Book of Atrus. Just throwing that out there.
4. The design. Holy crap. As far as maps and puzzles go, this game is gorgeously designed. I can't say much about the mechanics, as you're basically just pointing and clicking the entire time, but one could argue that the mechanics are the puzzles. It's elegant. I hadn't played this game in about ten years, and the beauty of the design really stood out to me when I finally got it to work on my laptop.
Cons:
1. Mobility. I was going to put "graphics", but honestly I find this game to be stunning. It's old, of course, but the point-and-click interface allowed for images that are beautiful and photo-realistic, though admittedly low-res (you can get an idea from the screenshots). The flipside to this, of course, is that there are only a few places you can look. You interact with one frozen screen at a time, and, on top of that, there aren't a lot of animations to liven things up (the water doesn't even move). There are also a few places (I can only think of two) where it's difficult to tell which direction you're going to go based on where you click on the screen. You also have to wait for every single animation to COMPLETELY finish before you can move again, and that does get a little irritating after a while.
2. It will not run on most computers without workarounds.
3. It's pretty short.
4. You are going to find yourself backtracking a couple of times. It can get a little tedious, especially since you are so isolated in the game world. That's part of the atmosphere, but you may find it feeling empty at times.
5. Even with the workaround, I did come across one glitch (in the prison by the sacrifice/execution device). It isn't game-breaking, but the glitch makes it incredibly difficult to solve the related puzzle if you've never played the game before. I recommend looking up a solution at this point (you'll know the glitch when you come to it).
6. If you haven't played Myst, important parts of the game universe will not be properly explained to you except by inferrence, and it's better to know these things early on. All you really need to know is that there was a race of people called the D'ni who lived deep underground on Earth. They could write descriptive books that would create a "link" to the world they described (basically a teleporter in a book), but their civilization was destroyed and almost all of them died. In-game, Ghen and Atrus are descendants of that race, the last known surviors, if you will. Also, deceptive versions of "linking books" can be written where it looks like you're travelling to the world described but you're actually getting trapped in limbo between worlds.
Overall, if you love adventure games, games with strong atmosphere, or even just if story is the main priority to you when you play a game, pick this one up.

AoW doesn't have the unit customization that this game does. However, the combat in this game is much less detailed, though not as bad as that of Endless Legend where you select three cards and that's it. In this game you select Attack, Defend and Stand in place. You then also have to point a unit at what you want to try to attack. So, you basically have to front load all your choices and wait to see how the initiative driven turns play out. I personally prefer to make my moves as a unit's turn comes due.
Spellcasting is also largely missing from this game, or at least I haven't encountered it yet in my brief stint.
The maps seem much more interactive in this game, and I do like how battles play out on the main map, with all its terrain elevations and features instead of a subset. You really know what you're going to be battling on in this game.
Overall, I will certainly continue to play the game, but the actual battle mechanics themselves, while a step up from Endless Space, are still not all that great.

The game is kind of neat, but the developer did the sort of thing that you'd expect white knights to do in a forum.
It was pretty cool to see the change into a third person control that lends some very interesting layers to the game, but as this happened, at some point people requested some additional animations that were lacking in Men of War in order to smooth everything over in terms of movement.
The developer response was "we're not doing animations yet" time and time again at the early point in which this feedback was given.
As it goes, how most of these stories go, release is apparently around the corner and some of the most obviously necessary additions to the animations are lacking. Addition, really, it's just one teeny, tiny thing that really drives the nail in the coffin of the feel of this game. Animations have been updated sort of, but there's not really much difference you can see from Men of War.
So what that leaves us with is... A first person unit control (quite interesting, imho) that is hampered by a complete lack of smoothness in one critical area: the ability to
and
. You can go prone and crawl around, you can stand up and walk around. You can aim and fire during the latter, but you
crouch walk.
I don't know, maybe it's a little bit too much to say I just can't get past this, but the developer wanted feedback, and they said do it in reviews, so this is what I have to say: this game is... pretty neat. I like it, I want more of it, I understand it's terribly niche though and a lot of people didn't really buy into it or go for it, and that if I wanted to change that, I should probably recommend it.
But man, something so simple and stupid really creates so many frustrating moments with the game that I just can't past it. Sorry. :(

A review from someone who played Skyrim for 3000 hours before forcing myself to play this.
Protip: Don't. You can't fix this game with mods, it's so hilariously bad in every aspect. I tried so ♥♥♥♥ing hard to like this game since the fanboys in TES forums keep harping on about how it's god's gift to mankind but ♥♥♥♥ me there's barely anything to like about the game.
First TES game I played was Morrowind on the OG Xbox, but I couldn't get over how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it looked and how little direction the game had so after about 10 minutes I ended up putting the disc back in the case and there it has remained. Some time after that a friend recommended Oblivion, so I tried that on the PC. The premise sounded good after watching the intro and listening to the great music, and then I got to character creation. You, and everyone else in Cyrodiil has down syndrome style potato faces. I didn't want my character to look completely ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like everyone else in the game so I chose Argonian as my race as they're not meant to look remotely human and don't have much potato face.
I ♥♥♥♥ around a bit with the Emperor killing rats and getting smacked around by the mythic dawn and then I level up. What a ♥♥♥♥ing mess. I just can't. I cannot within words describe just how awful the levelling is, it's just something you have to experience for yourself. Level up a few times and try to figure out what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on there and good luck because I had no ♥♥♥♥ing clue. That was about where I gave up.
Years later Skyrim's coming out and after my experience with Morrowind and Oblivion I have exactly zero desire to play it, but my friends in college keep encouraging me to give it a go. Oh hey, they fixed the faces. Oh, the levelling system actually makes sense? Whaddyaknow, I might actually enjoy this. 3000+ hours later I figure maybe I'll give Oblivion another try.
Well, I got around 40 hours in this time, completed a few guild questlines but never managed to do the main story. I figured I'd be a mage since it's fun as♥♥♥♥♥♥in Skyrim blasting lightning with impunity and ♥♥♥♥ing about with Telekinesis. ♥♥♥♥ me that was a huge mistake. The amount people♥♥♥♥♥♥on Skyrim's magic as being weak I expected to be able to fly about one hitting everything in Oblivion. Hours later, maxed magic skills and attributes sitting in the Arch Mage's quarters and I'm wondering what sort of juice people were taking. The magic is godawfully weak and after casting about 5 spells I'm straight out of magic and the enemy's health is down a quarter. Oh, you want to heal? Every restoration spell crafted or otherwise costs about half your magic bar for about 10 points of health. You want to put on a fire cloak or ebonyflesh for defence? Those spells don't exist. Okay, maybe I Fus Ro Dah nope, wait, you're some random pleb, you have no special powers.
Okay, maybe I can fix the game with mods. There's a few decent ones for improving the faces, but as for the confusing ♥♥♥♥ing UI and the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ levelling system? No can do bud. There's a few out there that make small changes to levelling like giving +5 instead of random numbers or more magicka so you can actually cast spells but none of them truly fix it.
There's DarnUI but that just makes the UI smaller and gives you a larger inventory, it doesn't change the way the UI looks so you can figure out where to find what the ♥♥♥♥ you're looking for - you still have to mashclick the various tabs trying to figure out which vague symbols represent the thing you're looking for. The inventory itself is larger, but you still have to spend half an hour scrolling to find what you want - or you can get a mod that makes everything into icons. Unfortunately the icons are ♥♥♥♥ing tiny and half the items in the game are identical so you're still ♥♥♥♥ed if you're trying to find Random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s Letter to Other Random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Which brings me to the dialogue and story aspect.
Instead of meeting, for example in Skyrim "Hunter" in the woods, you get to meet "Blyjan Thundercunt". Most NPCs have names and schedules and do more than just stand around all day doing nothing which is one of the few things I liked about the game. However you don't want to talk to them. Both you and them only have generic dialogue and in the rare occasion you have a quest that requires talking to them you end up finding that they change their accent halfway through talking to you. The biggest offender of this I found was the beggar npcs that exist for the Thieve's Guild questline. Speaking of which, the Thieve's Guild were presented well, no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t contracts for Maven ♥♥♥♥♥face, but there's very little of worth to actually steal. The vast majority of houses have zero items of worth, occasionally a potion or two if you're lucky. Shops can sometimes have a few items of worth, if you're willing to haul the 100 weight steel swords around so your fence can give you a third of the item's value. Oh, yeah, if you thought selling items in Skyrim to level up Speech was tedious you'll just love Oblivion. At the time of writing I've probably sold about 40k worth of items yet my Mercanitle is at 16. Speech is seperate and is levelled using a boring minigame whenever you talk to someone, but aside from a few occasions it's not really worth the time it takes to level it.
After completing the Thieve's Guild questline and getting the stupid looking Cowl that is far too big for my character's head, I went on to the Mage's Guild, which is one of the most tedious and boring thing's I've ever done in a video game. You have to go to every city in the game, there's like 6 or 7 of them, and go into that city's mages guild. Then you have to do a favour for whichever incompetent asshat they put in charge. Usually this means doing a lot of waiting around and then going into a generic cave and killing Necromancers, the most irritating enemy ever as a Mage as they constantly run away from you ducking and weaving so you can't hit them with projectile spells and can't catch up to them for touch spells. There's about five Necromancer filled dungeons you have to complete as part of Hannibal Traven's chores - by the end I wanted to join Mannimarco - Okay, let's be honest, I wanted to join Mannimarco from the start. Then Hannibal out of the blue kills himself and makes you Arch Mage. The story's about on par with Skyrim's College of Winterhold so, if you've played it you know it's not great. I never got to do the main storyline because my character is so weak he's unable to kill the Dremora in the Kvatch Gate, but I expect it's more of the same.
Thinking more about the game, I figured maybe the reason I didn't enjoy any of it was because I was spoiled by games of today like Skyrim, GTA V and, well I was about to say Fallout 4 but that's a real matter for debate. But really, it's not that the graphics or the UI in Oblivion are low texture quality, it's that they're terribly designed. It's not the textures on faces that make them look ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's how they're shaped. It's not that there's a lack of easy perks to get what you want in the levelling, it's that levelling is confusing and doesn't feel rewarding. The game is a whole bunch of poorly executed concepts that could have been awesome like spell crafting, but ended up being pointless and disappointing.
But hey, people say Morrowind was everything Oblivion wasn't, so I guess that's next on my list to try out with some graphics mods.

While Myst was a bit claustrophobic in its small island worlds, Riven drops you into an island archipelago.
This is not an easy game, and I highly recomend having a little notebook to take notes, if only to decipher the alien numerals. Avoid online walkthrus if at all possible, the real joy of this game is figuiring it all out for yourself... eventually...

Go to Riven age if you are brilliant and brave and patient and big hearted. On Riven they are not. They are nasty to you, take your things, run away, and play the wailing, rotating Kazoo from towers when they see you come. Then they hide. There is nobody to hold your hand. You will face the Myst-mystery rehashed many a time: what the xxxx is this? What the xxxx is this then? Or this. It is all turned off, of course and needs to be turned on, buttons, levers, dials. You are the repair man. Nobody answers you. Nobody pays you. Somewhere in there you encounter a book that rants and tries to explain. Maybe it is meant as an apology by someone who cannot be coherent, who hallucinates, imagines all sorts of people that are not there. Maybe you can guess a thing or two, too: the guy in white runs away because he is ashamed that he cannot pay your salary. You cannot eat his nuts. They are unclickable.
There are difficulties in places which will maybe yield by putting together two and two found in other places, if you look carefully. You don't know when you have the two and two, or what you have. Should you? You have a book. It is useless.
Like the mind, your age is scattered about. You explore two-dimensional projections of a presumably three-dimensional age! Sometimes you have more projections surrounding you, sometimes less, to account for what is there. You click your controller to find out how many directions you can look today, to switch from projection to another! Your mind reels trying to connect the dots and establish in the minds I the true three dimensional age from these slices you are allowed to see. A walkway leads somewhere. Where does it lead? Where does it come from? If only you could rotate the head in a smooth, elegant fashion and 360 degrees, so much would become clear. But clickety click, your age is disjoint and made of whiplash. Sometimes you can click left, right, sometimes only back. The world has become a constrained manifold with unintuitive metrics. Sometimes you have to think to close doors to explore more. Why would you close doors, the manifold is so constrained already? You want an open age. You cannot even climb on rocks. Your eyes start to tear at the glaring pixels from a past age. It is a slideshow with moving parts that once came on 5 rotating disks. The five is a very significant number and exists as number of points in a star too.
Sometimes in this senile delirium the age has a hickup and freezes altogether. You have to exit the age beforehand to fix, and immerse yourself in Myst of Task Explorer and Affinities of Processor Units. Then, one day you find a jail cell. There is somebody there! But he vanishes. You discover teleportation after a dark tunnel, by click you return to place that makes no sense to be there. In any case then you have permanently lost your submarine and can no longer go to school. To earlier time fragment you go, if you can.
Such ages shouldn't be written, neither sold. It is an age past, belonging to museum.
It is sometimes said all problems are human problems. In Riven, humans disappear and leave their problems to you, like so much garbage.
To modern age we go.

My thoughts on this game are mixed. Cartoonish yet charming visuals, with a whimsical feeling to everything. The grind - oh dear heavens the amount of grinding to accomplish the most simple of tasks. The grinding in this game makes you pump the brakes really fast. If you're not in a dedicated guild or with a very large group of friends all dedicated to a particular task, you're not going to get very far. I'm not saying that you shouldn't work for something, but when the grinding is mind numbing, it goes from being a game to a chore real quick.
If the grind wasn't as bad, this game would be a no brainer - it has so much appeal! Build a base with your friends, have your friends branch off in different professions, but at the end of the day, it all comes back to murdering thousands of trees for hours on end. Hopefully they rebalance the progession system that doesn't have it so focused on grinding, and more on exploration, building, and finding. When 8 people grind for 7 hours to murder trees to make a halfway decent fort, nobody feels like "continuing the adventure" after that. Also, the curve for leveling up tradeskills is a little steep. and only furthers the needless grind.
Despite that, I will still "recommend" this game. It can be fixed, its just a numbers game for the developers to mess with at this point. They could have something great on their hands.

If a several-years-old action game with "Overwhelmingly Positive" in both time categories doesn't convince you to at least give this Free to Play game a try, I guess you're still looking for a testimonial.
I raided in Warcraft for more than a decade. I played Destiny and Destiny 2 both on their releases, and raided to the cutting edge on both games. Both franchises have their highlights, and both franchises have aspects of the day-to-day that could be considered fun if you can tolerare the grind. You'd probably play Patrol on Destiny if you liked the gunplay and the semi-open world. You'd probably do World Quests on WoW because they have changing rewards even though none of them was remotely challenging. Both franchises had ceilings you hit quickly in terms of gear progression and combat. Fights are over in seconds. You might think you're okay with this.
I encourage you to give this game a try for no reason other than to get a fresh taste of what proper action combat should be. Warframe is not a game that is out to limit how powerful the players feels. This game helps you relish the feeling of mercilessly, relentlessly using an endless selection of Warframes (what are essentially classes for mmos, or heroes in mobas) and an endless selection of weapons and mods (customizable gems/materia/talents options.) You can level everything up in this game, from your gear to your mods to your collection of warframes. And not unlike one of the only good things Bioware did in their multiplayers is that you can choose to reset your level for a given gear/warframe to give it a slight buff to its base stats, making its next level-cap iteration even stronger than before.
The best weapons, gear and warframes are obtaining through a pretty clear path, and require no real money to acquire. I've been playing about two weeks now, and have my first Prime crafted, a berserker melee goddess called Valkyr.
In Warcraft and Destiny, I sometimes loathed the grind that I endured because the grind was a means to an end reward. In Warframe, I thoroughly enjoy the combat part of the grind, and barely notice time go by after trying my hand at a fistful of warframes with playstyles I liked.
You can play the game entirely without paying money, and it has a support staff and community who are more friendly to new players than any game I've sampled since high school.
And if you're like me and you enjoy customizing the appearance or transmog of your characters, the meme known as Fashionframe is very much a thing here. Endless shader options to all aspects of your frame, their weapons, their armor and attachments, even different skins submitted by the Steam community -- all color customizable.
This game helped me realize how bad Destiny is becoming, and how blind I was for years in settling for a mediocre time investment after work. Please, do yourself a favor and at least try it, especially with Public matchmaking. I hope you enjoy the game as much as I am.
