Now my first main problem with the game is mouse button 4, who in their right mind binds that to back in a game, I use it as PTT, so every time I spoke it would prompt me to exit the game or leave my hosted or joined session, to top it off, you cannot unbind it in the controls.
After rebinding what controls I could to suit it more like MOWAS2 I find that some of the contols you cannot unbind at all. I have no problem learning new controls but  you still have locked contols in a game, all controls should be eligible to be rebound by this time, its 2017 not 2000.
Jumped into a CO OP session with a friend and first thing I try is the FPS addition to the game and boy is it beautiful, always something I felt was needed when clearing buildings in MOWAS2, it makes for a very nice addition to the game. Just having a different perspective on the battlefield makes it a new and interesting dynamic, weather in vics or on foot it adds a whole new type of gameplay but unfortunatly thats all Call to Arms has going for it. After that it drops to a worse game.
Dont be fooled by the steam release date, this game was not released in Nov 2016 it was released in Mid 2015, leaving 2 years of development time to produce a bugfest, copy pasta sounds from MOWAS2, and lazy work.
Lets start with the bug, Sitting on the main menu, my friend randomly crashed to desktop while waiting for me, literally not doing a thing, just sitting waiting on me and he CTD for no reason, hey, crashes happen I get it, but usually have a specific fault because the player was doing something at the time, but he was literally doing nothing.
Start game and after being in short lived awe of the FPS system implimended into the game, I was disappointed to hear the many sounds I recognised from MOWAS2, I was hoping for a fresh take with Call to arms but weapon sounds and enviroment sounds being the same I was slightly saddened with the Copy Pasta. I get it, many Devs reuse assets from old games, and there is usually no problem but a Modern war game sounding the same as a WW2 game leaves little to enjoy after 250 hours of hearing it before.
Another sound issue I had was that 2 years of Dev work and their is zero voice acting, I mean none. Their are mods with more enthusiasm shown in their work than what Call to arms campaign had to offer, which was bland subtitles and not very many of them.
Down to the lazy work, I mentioned the copy pasta main menu and the reused sounds so I will just mention a few more, the assets on the map in game were little difference between meaning the same house over and over just facing different ways and the (terrorist?) enemies all wearing the exact same kit, Its either they are an organised army and decided amongst themselves to be different from civies or more likely copy pasta lazyness. The realism is non existent, Reloadable AT4's, Humvees destroying H barriers by just tapping them, make them completely useless to what they were designed to do. Like what? When you reload a weapon, weather its an M2 .50 Cal or an M203 40mm GL, you hear the audio of them both relading then nothing for 3 or 4 seconds, after that you can use it. It just comes across as lazy, really.
What finally did it in for me was playing the start of the third mission of the campaign, within two minutes of launching the mission, my co op buddie recieved the dreaded out of sync error which has only ever happend to us before when playing modded games in MOWAS2, from a little digging the only way to fix is wait for a dev to find the bug and release a patch or uninstall and manually delete the game folder, then reinstall the game. I've had this game since its release back in 2015 and I've seen it go through a lot of changes.
Perhaps the most drastic change this gagme has over the Men of War series, is the fact it has gone free to play. Most people would be against this change, but it helps boost the player numbers, and the micro-transactions that have been put into the game do not make the game pay-to-win from what I've experienced and the gameplay remains the same as its always been. However, one thing I will point out, is that you need to pay full price for the game bfore you can use mods, which is a big let down due to how big the modding community is for this game.
The modding community for this game is outstanding with you being able to use the workshop as well as other platofrms such as ModDB to get mods into the game, as well as it being incredibly easy to make your own assets for the game.
Combined with the editor that this game comes with, it allows for countless lost hours where you can create your own mini battles, your own singleplayer missions, and your own multiplayer maps, which can then be published onto the workshop for others to play.
Overall, I do recommend this game to those who are on the fence about it, even if its just the free version to play multiplayer. And if you aren't convinced still, then I highly recommend watching YouTube videos on this game

"Makers of PixelJunk Racers, Monsters, and Eden and just like all their other installments, Shooter specializes in simplicity, familiarity, and over all fun. The music was composed by Alex Paterson and Dom Beken. Anyway enough of the back ground lesson let us dive into the actual review of PixelJunk shooter!
Story: The story is quite simplistic to say the least, to put simply there are scientists who are trapped underground and need rescuing. Your character pilots a twin shooter subterranean vehicle built for blasting through the rock and mud as well as a pod for picking up the stranded scientists along the way you encounter a verity of different obstacles as well as monsters and you’ll be so happy they equipped your tiny ship with guns (very insignificant weak guns but they get the job done….eventually)..."
Read the full review on Broken Analog:

Pixeljunk Shooter is a fun little 2D shooter with some pretty impressive fluid physics.  You fly a small ship through an extensive cave system rescuing scientists and fighting hostile creatures on your way to figure out what's happening on the planet.  The levels are all self-contained however rather than being a more open metroidvania-like experience like Insanely Twisted Shadow Planet.  Each level contains multiple individual caves in which you must either save or kill all scientists in order to progress to the next.
Your main enemy is heat with being hit by enemies and hot objects and just being near things like lava increasing your heat meter.  Once it reaches maximum you lose control of your ship and usually crash, though if you're lucky you will land in water and be saved.  The system is designed very well and helps make ship positioning important to gameplay.
Throughout the game you will be introduced to new enemies, obstacles, and interactible objects as well as different ship mods which let you interact with both solid objects and liquids in different ways.  They are all well-constructed and add some nice variety to the gameplay.
I have only played two Pixeljunk games so far, but I found this one far more enjoyable than Pixeljunk Eden.  It has much better pacing and better-designed game mechanics.  Definitely recommended for people who like 2D shooters or just like playing with liquids.

PixelJunk™ Shooter is a bit hard for me to categorize but lets call it a physics based Puzzle/Shooter thingy. While I am not a fan of the shooting in the game I don't mind the exploring or puzzle parts of the game and the few times the shooting/fighting shines is during the few boss fights in the game.
A pretty straight forward list of achievements mostly being for collecting the various scientists and gems in the levels which can be fairly challenging to find (at least the gems). The game also has an achievements for finding all secret areas so exploring is recommended. There are really only two achievements that might take some extra work and that is the big kill grind (1000 enemies) and an achievement for collecting 100 coins in a single spin. The later might take a few tries but can be made easier by using a guide to check out ideal spots for it.

If anyone wants a true D&D-like video game this holiday season, I highly recommend Divinity: Original Sin 2.
I finally finished my first playthrough after 88 hours according to Steam, but would love to pull together a party of up to 3 other friends to go through it again. It's easy to see that it will be an incredibly a different experience every time you play. Everything depends on what quests you find, how you resolve them, and what your party make up is. All in all an unbelievable amount of content, fully voiced with one of the best casts I've ever heard, and as of this writing it's still being polished regularly by Larian. There are some kinks here and there with the quest logs and inventory management for item hoarders like me, but nothing so severe that it took away from my immense enjoyment of this game.
My main warnings: the themes are very dark/mature, the entire game is morally grey at best, and it expects you to be a smart player.
By this I mean there is a LOT of gore (e.g. their elves eats the dead in order to preserve the memories of the deceased), you will be faced with choices where there is no 'good' option or you aren't skilled enough to take the 'good' option (persuasion is not a dump stat in this game), and the answer to many quests involves reading and paying intention to your environment rather than quest markers. If you are playing with the pre-made Origin characters as companions, you will also be forced to balance their personalities with your own ideals, and they may leave or turn on you should you not fall in line with their motivations.
Likewise, this is a game that isn't afraid to kill you. If you find yourself thinking "that looks dangerous" or "huh, a lot of people are warning me about going this direction" it probably means you're going to get destroyed should you attempt it. And when I say 'destroyed' I mean it - the combat has multiple difficulty levels with ebbs and flows but overall remains challenging. You can respec at any time to 'fix' your build once you get to the second Act, but you'll still find yourself unable to fill every potential role with 4 people - you have to pick and choose the best way to solve a problem with what you have.
If you prefer handholding in games for objectives, skipping dialog, take pride in always playing games on the highest difficulties, or don't like reloading when you try something risky, this is not the game for you.
If you like taking your time to observe, working out puzzles in creative ways, tactically challenging combat, relying on trial and error to learn, and moral ambiguity in your stories, you should give it a shot. It is a gem in its genre.

Nominated for "Game within a game" award for the darkly entertaining toy in the village classroom that teaches children (and the player) the D'ni number system.  What a great way to seamlessly integrate puzzle information into the world and storyline!  It's what this game does best.
Riven has great replay value because the puzzles are so complex that I forget their solutions after a couple years and can experience them all again like new. ;)

In my opinion the best adventure game of all time. Of course I loved Myst (which you should play if you want to understand the story of Riven), and I also enjoyed Exile (storywise half-baked, but very good on gameplay and graphics for the time). The storyline is great, the puzzles are difficult but solvable.
Storywise, I've never seen a game come close to this level. Yes, this is one of the few games you spend a substantial time reading people's journals in - but it's worth it. There are a number of bad or semi-bad endings that are actually quite fun to try out, but only one really good one. If you want more story (I did!), read The Book of Ti'Ana and the Book of Atrus - they really help to understand the background of Riven and show just how much thought Rand & Robyn Miller put into this game.
Graphics-wise, the game is low-resolution but still well-made for a game this old. I would love it if they did a remake like realMyst, but that might also take away the mysterious feeling from the game. I like to come back to Riven from time to time and relive the experience, I wish they still made games like this.
Oh, and the music is perfect to enhance the feeling.
It's a classic.  I'm still waiting for REAL Riven.

Overall a fun (but difficult) puzzle game that needs a little extra work to get working (the anti crash mods were a godsend) but if you're willing to put in the extra effort the game, in my opinion is certainly worth it.

No, you don’t have to play Myst before this one. The vast majority of what you see in Riven is new or was just mentioned in the previous game of the series.
---
With that out of the way, you’re probably still wondering what this game exactly offers. Gameplay wise, it’s Myst. You point and click, solve puzzles, see small cutscenes, have people talk at you, and interact with them, leading you to the good ending, or one of the
or so branch offs.
Scenario wise, I loved it a LOT. More than Myst. Riven reminds me of my childhood (I grew up in a very green island in the middle of the Atlantic so there’s that). The cutscenes for the trams are amazing, if you can handle the low resolution. With headphones and in my dark room, I felt like I was really there, a pseudo rollercoaster over (and sometimes under) the sea. Spying the villagers from afar was a nice touch, a distancing from the emptiness of the Ages in the previous Myst.
The lore and background story is given mostly by notebooks and the like that you occasionally find. Even the small things in the scenarios tell you small stories of their own.
I didn’t like the way puzzles were structured. Riven is more of an open world, while Myst was quite linear. Some clues seemed so scattered around and senseless I had a hard time connecting the dots.
Also, beware unskippable cutscenes. Many of them. They are small and you repeat them often. Any cutscene where the animation is off-screen, welp you can’t skip it. Also, that long speech
. Ya, you can’t skip the longest part of it. Oh and the game pauses when you alt+tab, so you really have to watch it.
---
Overall I liked it. The premise is simple but enjoyable. Having real people talk to you in this surreal but photorealistic place really helps with the immersion, as well as the simple soft soundtrack and the ambient sounds.
I wish I could visit Riven
.
PS: Fans were making a realRiven of sorts, it’s called The Starry Expanse Project. It still has a long way to go but it does look great.

I've been a fan of classic Sonic since I first played Sonic Mega Collection on my Gamecube so the announcement of a new 2D Sonic game like this caught my interest. I got this about a month after it came out and I was not disappointed. Sonic Mania has become one of [and possibly] the best Sonic games I have ever played, All of the levels are beautiful designed: both the remixed and new ones. However, it's a bit disappointing that only a few stages are entirely new. These new stages were so good (specifially Studiopolis and Press Garden) that I actually want a new 2D Sonic game from the same team that made this to make a new game like this but with only new zones. I still enjoyed the majority of the stages and the bonus features the game came with as well. However, there were some odd choices in terms of what was brought back like certain stages or the bonus game, Blue Sphere which I previously didn't like. But after getting all gold medals in Mania from Blue Sphere, I guess I kinda like it now? The new bonus stage is alright as well. Only $20 is a solid price for a game of this size and with the amount of content in it, it's easy to come back over and over. If you like classic Sonic, this is a must buy.

You have already heard all the praise for this game, so I'll just point out the pros:
- Awesome Music by Tee Lopes: remixes on returning levels are awesome and new songs are just a blast to listen to.
- The stage layouts are very large and very well made. The design is just a beauty to look at and fun to play through.
- Many unlockables and extras: Some unlockables will give this game a good replay value. One in particular is the Competition Mode, in fact, we play that A LOT.
- NOSTALGIA: Classic Sonic Fans beware. You will scream with joy. Lots of references and it's just cool to notice them, so if you're a big time Sonic fan, there's no reason to avoid this game.
Okay, now there are a few things that bother me a bit. They're not really cons, but things just to be aware about:
- Denuvo: Not going to go in depth with this, but if the DRM bothers you, I suggest getting Sonic Mania for Console or something. Just from experience, I haven't experienced any problems regarding my own computer.
- Difficulty: I found this game to be relatively easy compared to Sonic 1, 2, and 3&K. It wasn't so easy or too hard, but I guess it's just right. I was a bit disappointed that it wasn't as challenging as the Genesis games.
- Pacing / Levels: One of the major problems I have with Sonic Mania is the pacing or rather the missing difficulty curve. It doesn't get progressively harder. The level difficulty is around the place; one zone you spend 6 minutes then suddenly the next zone is only 2 minutes long. This causes some levels to feel out of place, but regardless they were all fun to play.
- Cutscenes: If you remember Sonic 3&K, those cutscenes between zones gave this awesome feel of how each zone was connected. Sonic Mania mimics those, only to an extent. There are indeed those kind of cutscenes, but there are times where those cutscenes aren't present. And it throws you off. Like, couldn't the Christian Whitehead and the other developers make a 2 second transition between X and Y zone?
- Short Game?: I guess the first playthrough is very quick. I don't remember how many hours I had before completing the entire game, but it probably took less than 10 hours.
Long story short, if you're a long time dedicated Sonic the Hedgehog fan, this game is a MUST-HAVE. If you're wanting to try out the sonic series, play the Genesis games (if you haven't already) to truly feel the nostalgia and improvement Sonic Mania brings. They're 5 bucks each on Steam (and less on sales).
It's somehow a wild and colorful callback and callfoward the Sonic franchise. If you friends ever say "Sonic was never good" So them this.

Endless Legend is a decent addition to the plethora of 4x games that abound.
It takes staples of the genre, borrows some ideas heavily from Fallen Princess, and smoothes out all the lumpy bits into a very seamless experience.
The UI is a tad clunky, and I would have preferred reserving areas of the screen for specific things, rather than having a kind of nested information system, but that's a minor complaint as the UI overall is quite functional.
The game definitely has the "just one more turn" appeal that will keep you glued to your chair for hours, however the AI is very passive, and I'm yet to feel actually threatened or concerned with its progress in a game. Which is a bit of a shame considering the slow pace of the game more or less relegates it to single player, unless you have some VERY dedicated friends who are willing to sit down to game with you for a very long while.
Overall I've enjoyed Endless Legend, it does a lot of things right with a minimum of frustration. Worth buying if you're into 4x games.

I've been avoiding early access recently, too many games on there that feel like a 2nd year computer games students university project floated on steam to make some undergraduate a little extra beer money, too often left buggy and unfinished, all that promise, and my cash, gone.
Fortunately then, for theHunter: Primal that isnt the case here, and the game is in development by a studio that I've known and come to trust for a number of years now, who are commited to working with their community, and have a good solid history of regular updates and not abandoning their projects.
Since I picked up the game on release yesterday, I've already seen 3 updates to the game pushed out, just off the back of tweaks the team realised were necessary from the early initial reports, which to me is suggestive of a good team.
Built with the same avalanche engine that powers the games "older brother", theHunter: Primal builds on the back of a good solid hunting simulator and adds dinosaurs and survival to the mix.  Armed with nothing more than a bow, a handful of arrows and the clothes on your back, it's up to you to seek out better equipment and to try and survive.
As it's early access, the types of dinosaur are limited at the moment, with plans to add further animals as the development moves on.  Sure there's some kinks to be worked out, and some balancing issues to make the game enjoyable for the widest audience, but it's fully playable and highly enjoyable now.
My favorite ingame experience so far?
It was midnight, it was dark, and a badly timed trip had left me at the bottom of an open valley with trees on the slopes to either side of me.  A kilometer up ahead, the grasslands gave way to rock, and open country on the side of the islands volcano, a safe haven for me, if I could reach it, where I could hide amongst the crags with a clear view and wait out the dawn.
But that was a kilometer away.  Much closer, the heavy footfalls and roar of a T-Rex reminded me I needed to keep moving.  Somewhere nearby the strange, laughter like chittering of a raptor let me know I was not alone.  Was I hunter, or prey?
Carefully I moved through the undergrowth, hoping to sneak away, every sound seeming amplified, and fear running her icy fingers down my spine.
My character brushed up against something toxic and coughed, the noise so unexpected, caused me to freak out and jump out of my chair, before logging out and then laughing at myself for it.
Would I recommend the game to others? Absolutely.  If you enjoy hunting, dinosaurs or survival style games, then it's definitely worth a look.  As a caveat, however, this thing is in early access.  Expect a few bugs, balance issues and for things to change, but if you can live with that, it's really worth it.

The problem with this title is that it tries too hard to be something, anything at all. You can really see through it cracks that is was a project of experimentation, without clear goals. Environments and scenery -gorgeous as some of them are- are a clear example of disjointness. A rather clever joke ties this nonsense, but I wouldn't call that a story, not even writing of any sort. Puzzles are frustrating and illogical, and gameplay somewhat buggy.
So no, I wouldn't recommend this one even though it's free.

PixelJunk Shooter is, as the name suggests, a shooting game. You control a yellow ship which is sent to help out some scientists on a planet in which after alot of digging something went wrong. The story is told when you rescue certain survivors, colored ones, which upon pickup will show up a text screen telling something that happened previously during the excavations. You progress through the game by picking up gems and survivors which will then unlock new areas for you to play. Gameplay wise the ship control is really smooth and satisfying with a some pretty decent shooting, your ship has 2 standard attacks, one that shoots projectiles if you keep tapping the attack button and if you hold it down you'll launch homing missiles. The level design and the visuals are pretty well done, considering it's a 2D game and as you progress to later levels the difficulty really ramps up at a fair pace keeping the game challenging even when you already master the game. Besides having to kill enemies on each level and rescuing survivors and gathering gems you'll find yourself most of the times trying to solve some sort of puzzles in which you need to manipulate various type of terrain either it is ice or rock and liquids such as water and lava or even gas or deadly black goo. Overall PixelJunk Shooter is a pretty fun game to play when you're bored or if you're looking for something casual, you can easily beat it in around 6 hours or so and it's a pretty good time. If you're a fan of PixelJunk games you'll probably also enjoy this one and if you do enjoy this one but haven't played Monsters or Eden you should totally check those two.

The Elder Scrolls series is one of the best and most well known rpg experiences available, and it's difficult to pick a favourite. But if I did choose a favourite, it would have to be The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion. Oblivion has better gameplay than Morrowind, better quests than Skyrim, a better story than Arena and better accessibility than Daggerfall.
Of course I enjoy every Elder Scrolls game, but Oblivion made some bold decisions and came out on top, and for that I applaud it. Morrowind had a captivating environment filled with fascinating quests and lore, but the gameplay was annoyingly bad until you reached a good enough level. Skyrim had great gameplay but monotonous, repetitive quests and characters. Oblivion is the compromise: it introduced the fun combat gameplay we all know and love, but still retained most of Morrowind's depth and complexity.
The presentation is fantastic. Oblivion may not have Skyrim's graphics, but the rich colours and forests make Oblivion's game world a lot more pleasing to the eye in my opinion. The soundtrack is second only to Morrowind's, and the whole thing came together to provide an awe inspiring backdrop to all the adventures you would have. On that note, let's talk about the quests. Oblivion's quests are better than Skyrim's by a country mile, and are some of the best in the series. I'll never forget that fighters guild quest when I got high on Hist Sap and destroyed a whole village, or that time I had to fight bandits who had hijacked the ship I was sleeping on. Few quests from other Elder Scrolls games can hold a candle to what Oblivion has to offer. Fans of the Dark Brotherhood will know that Oblivion's Dark Brotherhood questline is the best in the series, and the main story can stand on its own two feet.
If you like RPGs, or if you have played other Elder Scrolls games, you really need to play Oblivion, as in my opinion it is the best of the bunch.

What’s up with all these awesome indie games coming out of nowhere?   Embers of Mirrim may just be one of the best platformers I’ve played this decade and before last week I had never even heard of it. While I hate to describe a game by using other games I will quickly throw it out there that this is a unique blending of Ori, Brothers, Entwined, and Ikaruga. If you have played any or all of these games then you’ll have a point of reference as I try to clumsily describe this masterpiece with my inadequate words.
When Embers of Mirrim begins we find ourselves in this giant cavern as packs of dark and light cat-like creatures called Mirrim assemble before a god-like being who looks a lot like Grumpy Cat with deer antlers. After a mystical ceremony complete with visions the creatures split in opposite directions.   As you take control of the dark Mirrim you start running to the left – a jarring experience for platformer veterans who are used to always going to the right- and you can revel in the graceful animations and silky framerate as you run, jump, and ground-pound your way through a level full of cliffs and raging white water that is clearly designed to get you comfortable with the controls. Soon, you will take control of the white Mirrim, and this time you are running to the right, enjoying the same mobility as well as an extended jump with a glide mechanic that will prove useful almost immediately.
After these solo levels the Mirrim will fuse together into a single creature, not only enjoying the abilities of both but also able to split apart into Embers, disembodied spheres of green and purple energy that can float for short periods of time before reassembling. This is where the fun and the real game kicks off. You can only stay in ember form for a few seconds, but there are glowing orbs that will reset that timer and also color-coded energy meshes where you can remain in ember form indefinitely. All of these elements as well as a neutral orange mesh where you can only exist in Mirrim form all combine to create an ever-increasing set of environmental and navigational platform puzzles that will put your multi-tasking skills to the ultimate test.
For those who played Brothers and are familiar with controlling two independent “characters” simultaneously with twin analog sticks, you already have a head start on the mental discipline required to play this game. Embers of Mirrim does a fantastic job of easing you into the increasing challenge of the binary puzzle designs. At first you must simply pass through colored wall meshes or traverse large gaps by using sequences of green and purple orbs to keep your ember form active until you reach the opposite side. But all too soon you’ll find yourself going through mazes where you must keep your embers within a certain proximity while simultaneously navigate different maze corridor patterns for each color. If you get too far apart or your ember time runs out you reassemble at the start of the puzzle and try again.
The level of creativity is borderline genius. Early on you are running across a giant waterfall and these huge hollow tree trunks start spilling over the falls forcing you to go into ember mode and slip through these color coded patterns of orbs and meshes; basically standing in place but moving side to side as the tree passes falls around you. And it only gets more brilliant from there. There are even secret areas with constellation-like patterns that must be revealed by moving your sticks in equal and opposite patterns. Given the nature of the game design and the near constant demand of dual controls, a gamepad is required.
The game keeps gradually adding in more demanding use of your binary skills, forcing you to sprint, jump, then quickly shift to ember form, pass through an energy field then glide to a leaf then quickly leap from it before it curls up only to pass through colored orbs in ember form and quickly return to Mirrim form before you touch the orange mesh protecting the final ledge. Fail any portion of that and you do it all again. There is a potential for frustration, but the game seems to ramp the difficulty with your natural adaptation of the necessary skills to complete any given puzzle with one, two, or three attempts.
The brilliant game design is made even better thanks to some gorgeous visuals that keep getting better and more original with each new level. The camera moves in close one second then pulls out to where your Mirrim is a mere speck the next, providing an epic sense of scale. Textures are richly detailed and the colors are exquisite and the framerate never faltered, even at 4K resolution on my 1080ti card. Complementing the visuals is an outstanding score that provides an energetic and adventurous theme throughout the entire game and some nice environmental sound effects.
Embers of Mirrim is easily one of the most inspired platformers I’ve played on PC or console since Brothers back in 2013. While that was primarily an adventure game it is refreshing to see just how well this twin-stick mechanic can be integrated into an energetic platformer complete with mind-bending puzzles, thrilling boss fights, and white-knuckle escape sequences. If you are ready to split your brain and try to control two characters at once then you definitely don’t want to miss Embers of Mirrim. It’s a platformer like no other.

This game is fantastic, but I must issue a warning:
Player creativity and practice is an absolute requirement.
Some people say the game gets old quick, and that it's too simple to squeeze enough enjoyment out of it to make it worth the money, and that d!ck jokes aren't funny. Those people are wrong.
When I picked it up, I liked it, and it made me laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off for a bit, but I wasn't quite hooked. Then I played a match with someone who was REALLY good at the game, and it showed me the potential for hilariously rewarding gameplay and growth through raw skill. It actually exercises your brain because you have to figure out which keys you need to push next, and in which order, while you're helplessly rag-dolling through the air.
Sometimes it can be a little buggy, but honestly, that's part of the fun, and the bugs don't break the game by any means. And even if you don't get very good, the real reward comes from the awkward, flailing movements that still, after 60+ hours of play, occasionally make me laugh helplessly.
What I've learned is that this game has two crowds. One crowd, who picks the game up for an hour or two (or less), and decides it's kinda okay, but too simplistic for their sophisticated tastes, and who still laughs at d!ck jokes anyway? And then there's the other crowd who gives it a chance, really learns how to use the mechanics, has a total blast and falls in love.
Now, there are obnoxious jerks who play online, that think they're funny, and waste your time slapping your tender bits until the timer ticks all the way down. But just use that as motivation to get good at the game so you can beat all those jerks, and eventually they'll go away, because chances are, they're part of Crowd #1. And anybody you like playing with, look up on Steam and add them, and after a bit, you won't run out of people to play with.

If you'd like a review that is about the game, and not a complaint about DLC, here's mine.
A basic summation: Crusader Kings II is a grand strategy game where the player plays as a Middle Ages monarch. The overarching aim of the game is to keep your bloodline's descendants in power over something. When I say something, it might be a single county in Ireland, or it might be the Kingdom of England. Your line of succession is one of the most important facets of the game: as long as you have a viable heir your game will not end even on death, because you will be reassigned to play as that heir. If you ever fail to secure an heir of your bloodline, your game will end.
Which brings me to a description of the game's freeform nature: you cannot "win" this game, because there are no victory conditions. The player's goals are their own to try and achieve. What the game does have are a variety of game over conditions that should be avoided, such as being defeated in war and deposed or the aforementioned lack of an heir. As long as you avoid game over, you're free to do whatever you want in your realm and in the world. If you'd prefer to play as a humble vassal to the Holy Roman Emperor, you can do that. If you'd prefer to try and overthrow your liege via war or intrigue, you can do that. If you want to skip the trouble and simply choose to play as Holy Roman Emperor, you can do that!
That said, the game presents interesting and realistic limitations to whatever you do. As I've mentioned, family is a large part of the game. Having viable, capable heirs (not inbred or sick and well-taught with good traits) is a must and you must be careful how your holdings are distributed. Nothing feels worse than spending a character's lifetime conquering a massive dominion, only to have it split in two on his death because his two sons share the inheritance via Gavelkind succession. Speaking of conquering, a player cannot simply declare war - he must have a casus belli, or a reason to do so first. Whether that reason is a courtesan with a weak claim on some faraway land thanks to a slightly-noble birth, or holy war, or even a false claim generated via intrigue, there must be something to claim when sending troops abroad.
Another massive part of this game is dealing with reputation and other people. Your reputation, especially with your subjects, is ever-important. Your nature (and traits) and your actions both affect your standing with every person in the game. Everyone from the Pope to the Earl of Nowheresville has an opinion of you, and they matter! If you are a long-tenured, brave, just, pious monarch, your subjects by and large will admire you and very few will be significantly opposed to your rule. But if you are more cruel, arbitrary, and a bad person, many people will come to hate you. As a general rule, many people (particularly of religions other than your own) will hate you and it doesn't matter much, but it's much worse when many powerful people who desire your throne detest you. Revolutions in your land from angry subjects or ambitious vassals will leave you treading carefully.
I'll note that this game is very much like life: often very fun and interesting, but frequently difficult and punishing, with a knack for dealing a blow and then kicking you while you're down. You will have your best ruler ever die of a sudden illness at the age of 32, to be succeeded by his idiot son who himself will live to 80. You will have an opportunistic revolt while you're overseas crusading. You will have treacherous relatives and complicit rivals, and at times it will feel like the game is overwhelmingly against you, because it often is! Just remember that like in life, bad things happen, but with some perseverance all can be overcome.
If this wasn't already clear, this game is incredibly complex. The amount of actions and micromanagement possible is simply astounding. This gives the game a steep learning curve and the in-game tutorial is near useless. There are a number of very helpful YouTube tutorials which can be watched to help learn the game, and I'd recommend spending some time there before diving in. Once the game "clicks," it's easy to follow, but learning all the systems and actions is daunting without outside help. I'll say this: this game is not the sort of game a person can buy on sale and leap right into for a few hours of good fun. It's the sort of game you spend some time learning, and then gameplay becomes incredibly immersive. It takes some effort, but it is also very worth it.
I'll conclude this review by commenting on the DLC policy that has generated such revulsion in recent months. This game is 5 years old and is priced at $40 for the base with $200+ in DLC that many people will claim are necessary otherwise the game is empty or broken. My rebuttal is simple: firstly, the game is excellent and incredibly enjoyable without any DLC. I bought and played my first playthrough in the vanilla base game, and it was great! The basic experience is to play as a Catholic ruler of a European nation in 1066 or later. The DLCs add a variety of functions: start the game earlier in history (769 or 867,) and play as other religions and nations outside of Europe. Sword of Islam predictably allows one to be a Muslim, Rajas of India an Indian, and so on. DLC features are not necessary if one is not interested in what they allow. My personal thoughts on the game/its DLC for new players: this game often goes on a good sale where the base is $5 or $10 and the DLC are all around 50 percent off. During a sale, one can purchase the game and every worthwhile DLC for less than $50. Given that these sales happen frequently, it does not take very much patience to have this great game for not a lot of money.
Lastly, for reference, what I'd consider my "essential" list - these can be purchased together on sale for around 25-30 dollars total, and by themselves give an immersive and brilliant experience:
- Base game
- Legacy of Rome: adds many interesting things for the Romans, but it's mostly for retinues which allows the player to form a standing army, very useful
- The Old Gods: allows for play as Pagans and gives the 867 start date, but importantly also makes revolts much more threatening and interesting
- Sons of Abraham: allows for play as Jews, but also includes many improvements for Catholicism and makes holy orders (Knights Templar, Hospitallers, etc.) far more interesting
- The Reaper's Due: adds the Black Plague/minor epidemics, but also entirely reworks disease and makes it much more interesting

I've played this game once or twice, and I can say with certainty it's pretty good stuff.
You play as a magical space ninja terrorist murderhobo and you commit genocide against several different factions because a disembodied woman's voice tells you to.
There are quite a few different ways you can go about committing said genocide.  Whatever sick, twisted fantasy you have can probably be indulged with the tools available.  Things like rifles, shotguns, swords, pistols, hammers, sticks, sticks with points on the end, sticks with blades on the end, whips, rocket launchers, bows and arrows, magnetic bows with explosive arrows, disgusting pustules filled with toxic fluid you throw at people, a hammer with a jet engine taped to the back,  launchers that throw spinning buzzsaw blades, laser beam rifles, a gun that plops out small singularities, and a whole lot more besides.
You also have a large variety of frames to choose from, which sort of act like classes with their own abilities and strengths and weaknesses and roles to play.
The game is very, very grindy, but to me it never felt like a downside.  The basic gameplay loop of select mission, murder a ton of "people", then finish mission and look at the loot you  earned is very satisfying.  There's always new weapons, frames, features, mission types, etc., being added to the game so there's almost always something to do and a new goal to set your sights on.  Warframe's free-2-play model is also one of the best I've seen.  The only things locked behind paying platinum (the in-game premium currency) are cosmetics and slots for additional weapons and frames.  There are ways to earn platinum in-game, however, by trading with other players.
Lastly, there are some really neat quests in the game and I feel like DE is getting better at creating them with every one released.  Upcoming quests actually have me pretty excited to see where the story goes!
tl;dr, this game is neat, lots of good reasons to play it, there's a reason I have this many hours played

Last night I started into a free puzzle adventure/platformer game called "Only If." It's very well done in most respects, and all I've seen so far have been mainly positive reviews from critics. It's about 1-4 hours of first-time gameplay, depending on your ability to analyze situations and think carefully; subsequent playthroughs are faster.
You take on the persona of a college student named Anthony, who spends a seemingly long night of partying (with drugs and alcohol involved) at the house of his romantic partner, Samantha. He awakes in someone's bedroom, alone and slightly hung over. Things take a quick turn for the worse, as your only course of action drags you into a psychological thriller that bends your perception of reality. An antagonistic man named Vinny reveals early on that he is related to Sam, all while playing a game of cat-and-mouse with the hero in an attempt to break him using a series of mind-bending tests that turn physics on its head.
This game had me drawn in from one of the very first challenges, as I repeatedly failed to understand the fundamental concept of breaking the rules. It requires you to pay close attention to everything from the beginning of each area - missing something almost certainly curses you to have to figure things out the hard way. Granted, some puzzles are timed, and failure often brings you back several stages in the story, giving you an opportunity to catch any important pieces you might have missed.
Probably my favorite area in the game was in the flower garden/park, as the puzzle design and visuals really complemented each other. It even felt like the area relieved a lot of the built-up stress from previous puzzles.
I had some issues with the lighting and the sound - they ran perfectly on my machine, but there were no ways to adjust settings using in-game options. In far too many places, the lights were too dim to see where important puzzle pieces are, and the main character likes to mumble to himself a lot, which makes you want to really crank your sound up in hopes of hearing what he's thinking - ultimately a recipe for disaster when you start hearing head-ringing noises like you might expect from being dazed and hung over.
But the thing that really grabbed me and effectively forced me to want to review this particular game was its ability to make you think... "WHAT THE F***!", each instance being more of a headache than the last. When you think it can't possibly get any worse, it does, and by a certain point which will remain undefined (blatant advertisement), you can't help but laugh at it. And believe me, laughter is what they are going for here.
Two words: THAT. ENDING. (blatant spoiler aversion)
I give very high credit to Raymund Vincent Ferrer, the voice actor for the villainous Vinny, who played his part impressively well, especially in places where believing his motives and reasons would be questionable. Every line he spoke was done to perfection, and I regret to say that as a result, the flaws in /Anthony's/ voice acting were all the more noticeable. Shout out to Raymund, wherever you are, you amazing, definitive, everlongingly forgiving bast*rd. :)
The controls throughout the game were clean in almost every aspect, though there was a lack of hitbox consistency (ie. objects glitching through and bouncing off of one another inappropriately). There was quite a bit of colorful language (trash talk), which is to be expected from drunk college students. It only left me wanting more when it came to freedom from the linear plot.
Score: 5/5, 91/100
I strongly suggest getting this game to all of my computer gaming friends who enjoy a good mind-bending every now and then. It's not anything scary, though it often gives the impression that something unexpected might happen. Keep in mind that you're getting into something that can be frustrating at first and, when you finally succeed, may leave you baffled about how or why it worked. Test your limits, and prepare to be unprepared for THAT ENDING.

Fun/gameplay: Compared to similar games (civilization and others) this game will feel very slow and empty; absolutely nothing will happen for 100's of turns unless you initiate wars. Also even on hard it is very easy, yes there are a few pitfalls which you have to learn to avoid, but these have nothing to do with a clever AI, merely unexplained mechanics.
The quests are the best bit of the game, however you will soon have seen them all and even they become repetitive.

Stability: Runs fine in early game <100 turns ,but after that will crash very often, sometimes every turn for many turns.

PixelJunk Shooter is a dual stick shooter that is a joy to play. The controls are simple. Left stick for movement, right stick for aim. Right trigger for shooting, holding the trigger will unleash missiles. The catch is that missiles will overheat your ship. Cave ship. Not a space ship. The left trigger sends out a grappling hook to pick up stranded miners, which is the objective of the game.  When you get the stranded miners, it opens a door to the next level. Each 'stage' has a few levels in it.
The real selling point of this game is the incredible interaction that you have with the environment. You can destroy soft terrain. Your bullets will take out chunks and not the entire terrain / wall. There is water that is fluid and dynamic. It will also cool down your ship when it overheats. There are enemies and lava. The lava flows just as the water, makes your ship overheat and when it meets water, they bond together to form soft terrain that you can destroy. Its such a nice dynamic.
There are powerups to keep your ship cool from the lava's heat. There are objects that you can grapple and tow around, such as a water bomb, good for drowning a volcano. There is a watercan object that you fill in water or lava, and when you take it out, it showers whatever liquid you have in it. Again, there is a lot of interactivity in the game.
This is a game that rewards and encourages exploration. If it looks like there is a way off screen, that's probably a secret area with the game's main collectable diamonds. Well you need diamonds to progress past a certain stage. You will have to go back and play each stage a few times in order to collect enough hidden diamonds. While it might seem like a downer to replay stages and levels, its all fun. Nothing seems like a chore. Its soothing, relaxing, nice to look at and with the incredible interactivity that you have with your environment, no playthrough is really the same.
On top of it all, the game sets itself apart with its art style. Its a beautiful, simple style instead of typical dualstick shooters that overload you on bright visual effects.
It is well worth the price and you can probably pick it up in an indie bundle. I've also got the sequil on PSN and personally, I think this it better.

A few years ago PixelJunk Shooter first appeared on the PS3. Still one of the best games on the Playstation network it has finally been made available to PC gamers. Now you can find out what all the fuss is about as you pilot your little ship through a host of physics and element based levels.
The plot, such as it is, has you sent in to rescue your crew mates after mysterious goings on while mining on the planet of Apoxus Prime. To do this you have to fly your craft around tight underground caverns while using water, lava and magnetic black liquids to your advantage. It’s reminiscent of Thrust with its inertia and gravity based gameplay but your craft will stay still if left alone. Your also won’t die from hitting walls (which is a good thing or it would have been nigh on impossible).
The game is a 2D styled shooter where you manoeuvre your ship around a section of an enclosed map. Normally you will have to get water to turn lava to rock or lava to melt ice or some other combination of dropping one liquid onto another. You’re doing this because you need to get to and rescue all the lost crew members in each area. If too many of them die you have to start the level again. It’s wonderfully inventive and a whole lot of fun and there are hidden areas and diamonds to collect along the way as well.
The level design is nigh on perfect throughout the game and the difficulty curve is just about right. The huge boss monsters found at the end of each world may cause some frustration but they provide tense and heroic showdowns of David and Goliath proportions and once you work them out shouldn’t take too long to get past.
Shooter is split into three main areas each consisting of five levels. There are the initial outer rocky areas, the ice caves and then the mine. Each individual level is split into sections which require everyone to be rescued before a bulk head opens to the next.  Each has its own tricks and traps and will keep you on your toes throughout.
You will also need to think quickly as the game has a wonderful way of getting you to forget what you’ve just learnt. For instance, for the first area you are trying to keep away from lava (overheating causes you to crash), but then in the ice caves you’ll come across and inversion suite which makes lava cool you down and water heat you up.
It’s a game that keeps throwing new ideas and things at you to keep you interested. The water suit and lava suit are just the start and you’ll soon be switching around and dealing with freezing lakes and clouds of gas as well as the usual lava and water. The key thing is that everything stays fun and creative throughout. Once you’ve completed the game you’ll probably want to dive back in to further explore the levels and find all the missing diamonds and any crew you missed along the way.
PixelJunk Shooter is a game we’re still playing on the PS3 to this day. The fact a whole new audience can now pick it up is great and this really is one of the best games of its type. Q-Games have crafted something special here and the years have done nothing to diminish its appeal. It’s perhaps a shame that the PixelJunk Shooter 2 wasn’t included as well (as it is pretty much part 1 and 2 of the same game), but we’ll be first in line to get it when it arrives.
This was always going to be a certified hit with us as long as nothing had gone wrong in the conversion and from our experience this offers all the fun of the original. PC gamers really need to play this as it’s simply a masterfully executed, great little game packed with more invention and ideas than most massive AAA releases can even come close to.
Overall 9/10

I have yet to play this with friends, but this game is fairly addicting. Puzzle game players will love it. Pixeljunk has become a company I follow now because of their unique games and wonderfully light-hearted art style. Keep up the good work!

The Elder Scrolls series is one of the best and most well known rpg experiences available, and it's difficult to pick a favourite. But if I did choose a favourite, it would have to be The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion. Oblivion has better gameplay than Morrowind, better quests than Skyrim, a better story than Arena and better accessibility than Daggerfall.
Of course I enjoy every Elder Scrolls game, but Oblivion made some bold decisions and came out on top, and for that I applaud it. Morrowind had a captivating environment filled with fascinating quests and lore, but the gameplay was annoyingly bad until you reached a good enough level. Skyrim had great gameplay but monotonous, repetitive quests and characters. Oblivion is the compromise: it introduced the fun combat gameplay we all know and love, but still retained most of Morrowind's depth and complexity.
The presentation is fantastic. Oblivion may not have Skyrim's graphics, but the rich colours and forests make Oblivion's game world a lot more pleasing to the eye in my opinion. The soundtrack is second only to Morrowind's, and the whole thing came together to provide an awe inspiring backdrop to all the adventures you would have. On that note, let's talk about the quests. Oblivion's quests are better than Skyrim's by a country mile, and are some of the best in the series. I'll never forget that fighters guild quest when I got high on Hist Sap and destroyed a whole village, or that time I had to fight bandits who had hijacked the ship I was sleeping on. Few quests from other Elder Scrolls games can hold a candle to what Oblivion has to offer. Fans of the Dark Brotherhood will know that Oblivion's Dark Brotherhood questline is the best in the series, and the main story can stand on its own two feet.
If you like RPGs, or if you have played other Elder Scrolls games, you really need to play Oblivion, as in my opinion it is the best of the bunch.

Riven picks up right where it's famous prequel Myst leaves off. Atrus has just returned from Myst island and he asks the stranger (you) to travel to Riven; a world gradually falling apart, where his wife Catherine is imprisoned. While Atrus makes hasty edits to Riven's master book to hold the world together you must find out what happened to Catherine and imprison Atrus' corrupt father Gehn.
Riven was the pinnacle point and click adventure game, one of the best games of the genre. It's puzzle design, world building, and storytelling complement each other seamlessly. As you explore you will encounter Gehn's various ploys to govern and awe the Rivenese, you will penetrate the systems he devised to keep himself safe from intruders, evade his henchman who want to capture you, and discover the underground resistance that will aid you.
Riven has aged extremely well in both it's visuals and mechanics. its an unforgettable world that tells a minimal, tight story through it's images and puzzles. The year after Riven was released Half Life burst on the scene and made action game the hot new thing. If Half Life represented the birth of a new type of game Riven was the last act of the old guard, a final masterpiece polished to a mirror shine. This game took advantage of new technology to perfect its genre and as the last great adventure game before their decline it's too good to miss.

Good ol Clasic sonic He’s had his fair share of ups, downs, and loop-de-loops, but Sonic has proven to be one of gaming’s most beloved and enduring icons. With Sonic Mania, Sega brings Sonic back to his classic 2D sidescrolling roots, taking direct inspiration from the 16-bit games that originally propelled Sonic and friends to superstardom. Sonic Mania is proof that no matter how much time passes, great gameplay is always in style.
Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles are back to fight Eggman’s forces the best way they know how: running, jumping, spindashing, flying, and gliding their way to victory across twelve zones. You’ll see classic zones from Genesis-era Sonic games, like Chemical Plant, Stardust Speedway, and Lava Reef, alongside all-new areas like Studiopolis and Mirage Saloon. These new zones are particularly impressive: the theming and level design in each is colorful and creative, and I was  eager to run around and explore, finding all sorts of challenges (and easter eggs) within. Take, for example,  the glittering neon lights and electronic contraptions of Studiopolis, an area themed after a television studio in a big city. One route might have you thrust into the guts of a popcorn machine after being beamed around like a satellite signal, while another will send you speeding through the city’s underground subway passages.
But even the old zones are packed with plenty of new tricks. They’re bigger, more elaborate, and filled with traps and gimmicks both old and new that tickled my nostalgia bone and surprised me. Sonic 2’s Chemical Plant Zone was always been a fun romp filled with high-speed tunnels and ramps, but with the addition of chemical jelly goop that bounces you around and lets you cling to walls, it feels fresh and fun in a whole new way. “
Even the old zones are packed with plenty of new tricks.
The zones aren’t the only things to get an overhaul, either. Reworked Sonic stages look more beautiful than ever, packed with vibrant color and dazzling visual flourishes, while the new zones’ artstyle meshes perfectly with the 2D pixel art of classic Sonic. Everything, down to the smallest of background elements, is more detailed and features more movement than ever before. That goes for the enemies, too -- Eggman’s new “hard-boiled heavies” are depicted with lots of quirky personality, making them interesting and unique villains without speaking a shred of dialogue. The soundtrack is also top-notch, packed with remixes of classic Sonic tunes alongside all-new compositions.
Sonic Mania has all the the crucial elements that go into making a great Sonic adventure: big, elaborate stages, responsive controls and movement physics, interesting and engaging tricks and traps, lots of hidden nooks and crannies to discover, and hazards that challenge you to stay alert and act fast. I replayed many of these stages over and over, finding little nuances and secrets that eluded me the first, second, and even fifth time around.
And there is incentive to replay these stages, as there are numerous hidden special levels you’ll need to conquer to collect the Chaos Emeralds and see Sonic Mania’s ‘true’ ending. In special levels, you chase a UFO through a 3D landscape by collecting speed-enhancing blue spheres and rings. It’s a fun concept, but it can be tough to see barriers that block your way on the ground, and collision detection on some objects seems off. Making matters worse, colliding with a bomb can start a chain reaction that sends you careening uncontrollably into other sets of obstacles, which can make otherwise good runs turn bad very quickly.
Also returning are bonus stages from Sonic 3, which you’ll find at the checkpoints scattered across the zones. These stages don’t unlock emeralds, but do unlock bonus features once you’ve completed a set number of them, like a sound test, a debug mode, and even hidden sub-games. They started out easy, but grew satisfyingly challenging, and completing them all perfectly took quite a bit of time and practice.
Not every throwback to an old Sonic game is welcome, though. Chances are that if there was something you saw in an old Sonic game, it’s in Sonic Mania somewhere -- even if it wasn’t a particularly good element of an old Sonic game. For example, it’s neat to see a callback to Sonic 2’s Sky Chase Zone, but let’s face it -- the forced autoscrolling and wonky controls in Sky Chase Zone were not very fun then, and they’re still not great now. And that incredibly annoying “keep the lights on” mechanic from Sonic 3’s Sandopolis Zone remains just as incredibly annoying  23 years later. “
Not every throwback to an old Sonic game is welcome, though.
And while the game’s boss fights are generally pretty cool, some of them have a tendency to drag , like the Studiopolis midboss and a revamped version of Sonic 1’s end boss. I know old Sonic games didn’t have checkpoints between multiple bosses, but it wouldn’t have hurt to have added them to Sonic Mania. And finally -- Sonic’s new drop dash move? It’s a little  weak and slow, and actually pretty hard to use - I stuck mostly to spindashing. (Annoyingly, you can unlock options to use the Sonic CD speed-up and the Sonic 3 instant-shield technique instead, but only in a mode that doesn’t save your progress.)
The Verdict
Still, even when Sonic Mania stumbles a bit, it’s only on little speedbumps in the road. For every issue I had, it didn’t take long before I was enjoying myself again, eagerly anticipating what sort of wacky wonders the game would throw at me next. It truly is the classic throwback longtime series fans have been clamoring for, but there’s plenty to love here even if you didn’t grow up with a Genesis. Sonic Mania is a stellar example of a retro revival done right.
My FInal Rateing is 8.7 out of 10 -Sonic Mania is the classic throwback longtime series fans have been clamoring for.

Sandbox Crafting and Building with friends. That is what the trailer and game description promised.
I played during Early Access, Loved the graphics. Enjoyed the fact that I am (very slowly) putting together a base, building by building. Saw the potential in the game. Hated the chore I have to go through to get anything and everything done. I was very disappointed and since it is Early Access, I was hopeful.
When it was officially launched, I came back to see how the finished product is like. It is still the same. Clumsy, unintuitive UI. Tedious chore of building anything.
This is not a game crafters and builders will like.
TL;DR
*Crafting UI is clumsy, unnecessarily complex and unintuitive.
*Building is monotonous, tedious and boring.
Fallout 4 is a better base building game than this. Do I need to say more?
Long version
Minor
- The UI was clumsy. Very clumsy. The only way to use items in your backpack is to equip it to your quickslot then select it then RMB. Can you imagine in real life, you are thirsty and decide to drink water from a bottle in your backpack. You take the bottle from your backpack and put it in your Batman belt pouch and only then you can drink and put it back to the Batman belt pouch. Then you keep it back in the backpack. Realistic? Yes. Unnecessarily tedious? You decide after doing it 50 times.
- Interact with almost everything using RMB is creative. I like that. But why do you have the RMB menu for food when the only option ever is to eat it?
- Leveling up takes very long and gets longer.
CRAFTING
Crafting UI is non-intuitive and very difficult to use. This is the part that annoys me the most. Especially when crafting is a major part of the game. If you want to craft Raw Wood at a Workbench, just follow the following simple steps.
1.Walk up to the workbench, RMB and select Interact. Look for the recipe for Raw Wood from a list of all recipes highlighted red. They are red even though you have all the required materials with you. They are highlighted red because the required materials are not in the workbench and it doesn't matter to the workbench if they are on you. Oh, as you get better at crafting the list will get longer. Did I mention that all the recipes are highlighted red for no good reason other than the workbench is empty?
2. Look at your backpack for the items required as stated in the recipe. If you do not have enough, go and get it now and then return to the beginning of Step 1. Put all the required items into the workbench.
3. Look through the list again to find the recipe. It is highlighted green now. How nice. Click on the recipe name and boom. You have one Raw Wood. Click 7 more times if you need 8 Raw Wood. If you run out of materials along the way, go and get it now and then return to the beginning of Step 1.
4. Rejoice in the crafting experience. The crafting UI is specially designed to be extra tedious and unintuitive and unhelpful as possible to let the user enjoy the thrill of being able to craft something despite all that. What a nice sandbox crafting game.
BUILDING
Buildings are SUPER tedious to build. I have a feeling that this is specifically designed this way to prevent players from reaching endgame. Because there is no endgame. There is nothing to do when your skills are all maxed and your base is nice and big, other than trying to destroy another guild's base (which involves a lot of running around since everyone is out of stamina.) Please follow the following steps to build one wall section. I repeat one wall section. Not that kind of wall in AoE where the game will give you walls in between when you put down 2 columns. You need 20 wall columns if you want to build a wall 20 squares long. Let's do just one together, shall we? Then you can repeat 19 times by yourself for the North wall. You can work on the other 3 walls the rest of this week.
1. Get a wall upgrade pack at a Drawing Table and carry it to the position you want (at a snail pace. The reason why a piece of building plan is so heavy escapes me. But it is alright. Bases are specifically designed to take up as little space as possible. This means the wall is not far from your Drawing Table. And your vaults) and unpack it. Make doubly sure that it is in the correct position.
2. You have just laid the plans on the floor. You wall project has just started! Let's see what we need.
3. Rock and Log. Hmm... They are not in your backpack. That's right! They are not. These items are dropped when you mine big rocks and chop trees respectively. You carry them at a snail pace, one at a time back to your wall project, which can take 2 mins at a time because big rocks and trees don't like to spawn near your base.
4. (15mins later) You have completed moving the rocks and logs. Good job! Now you just need to add Firewood, Stone etc to the wall. We have them in our backpack. Move the firewood to your quickslot, RMB and put firewood into wall project. Move firewood out of your quickslot, move the stone to your quickslot, RMB and put the stone into the wall project. You get the idea. Repeat as required for other materials.
5. For higher level buildings there will be a stage 3 for the building. Not for this wall section! We have our wall! Completed! A piece of it. Now get cracking on the remaining 19 sections of the North wall.

So I think it's about time I provide a detailed review on my journey of Tree of Life since 2015. As I have quiet a bit of experience with the game during a number of different stages.
Firstly, it is a great game but poorly designed with little to no end game. So if you are looking for something to do in the long run this game isn't for you.
The launch of the game on steam in 2015 was to help fund devlopment of the game and progress it through the stages needed to do a release. As of September 19th 2017 the game has been "released" but it feels more like a Beta 2.0. A lot of the released item's don't function properly for example you can cook food but the buff's don't work as intended. This should have been fixed before release.
The development team went from early release to launch with a completly different game engine without working out the issues. So basically the old engine was thrown away and a new game engine was used. But, there was not enough testing for bugs on the new engine before release. So in short the "launch" of the game was a CASH grab to help fund development and pay employees while providing a game not ready to be officially launched.
If you like long grinds, cash shop items that provide no real bonus to the game, and not P2W this game is something you may want to try. As of right now there are a ton of bug users, duped items, and more happening in the game so the economy is in a flux right now. Again why this game shouldn't have been launched till the bugs got fixed.
So 500 hours into a game where the developers don't care enough to take the time to finish a product before launching is a bad business model. Just means you are in it for the money and careless about the community and the game itself.
The game isn't worth 20 dollars let alone 10. But, I go on the concept if I can get 100 hours of game play per 10 dollars of a game it's worth the investment.
In short if you want to play a have done game buy it and realize it wasn't worth it and get a refund. If you honestly, want to just run around and do what ever while watching netflix buy it.

A game that should cater to the true sandbox PVP niche falls very flat. Since I don't get paid for professional level reviews, I'll just toss out a few quick points.
It was descrided to me as a Shadowbane "light" mixed in with some DAOC and splashed with some Fantasy Earth Zero so I was fairly hyped. Sadly, it is nothing more than a setup for a future cash store grab.
Characters:
The skill cap per toon is far too small so dedicated PvP'rs will not get to see many aspects of the game unless you piggy back off of a crafting guild.
Controls:

Six hotbar slots are usable for holding items. There are no "spells or abilities" that do not come from direct character control.
(EX) Two handed weapons can use a power attack by holding down "SHIFT" and waiting for the ability to charge up. Shield users can charge a shield attack that will stun on hit.
To "use" an item, be it food, potions, or any other consumable you must have it on your hot bar, press the corresponding key, then right click on the screen to open a radial menu, then mouse to the radial menu section to use said item. It is very clunky.
Base Building:
The base building is very half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and superbly grindy.

The time to build vs time to destroy a base is ridiculously unbalanced and with offline raiding mechanics incorporated it's not very rewarding.

Combat:
The combat mechanics are utterly atrocious with no flow to it at all. The action style combat which should be a massive sell point is very poorly implemented.
Having all toons capped at 250 stamina turns the game into nothing but never ending open field chases with the winner usually being who does not run out of consumables first.
Just a few small points without taking up too much of my morning time.

I prepfer the fantasy setting of the game to the real-world setting of Civ, myself.
The factions are varied and interesting, and actually do have differences between them as far as they play. (IMHO, many 4x games have only minor differences between the races/factions whatever and its mostly a cosmetic thing). Yes it does have some flaws, but they are minor and overall, its amazing
The 4x genre has been suffering in recent years, but I think this game's going to end up as classic as MoO2. And it deserves to be.

A great little addition to the twin-stick shooter clan, this game is very much deserving of your monies.
The gameplay is solid with excellent physics which are thankfully not entirely tied to your movement which makes the controls quite responsive. There's a variety of enemies with different types of attacks though most of the actual threat comes from the environments themselves. You have to dodge the lava, the black goo and the exploding gases and carefully but quickly wind your way through the mazes, rescuing crew members. The different suits you can put on in certain levels certainly shakes up the gameplay quite a bit. The secret treasures are also fun to look out for. The crowning glory are the 3 bosses. Each require very different strategies and defeating them is indeed a challenge. You have to look out for the weak spots which usually glow but as with the rest of the game, the real challenge lies not in hitting the spots, but dodging the environment and the other enemies.
The graphics are good with a very colorful style. The colors were chosen with great care though since you very rarely confuse the foreground with the background. the colours also help in identifying the types of surfaces which greatly aids in knowing exactly where you want to go.
Special mention goes to the soundtrack which is a mix of many different and weird styles with lots of random sounds and speech bytes for added measure. Makes for a nice atmosphere.
The one con would be that the story ends very abruptly and is primed for a sequel.
If you;re a fan of twin stick shooters, make sure not to miss this!

100% Orange Juice is essentially a board game with a battle componant attached to it. You can battle other players, NPCs, or Bosses depending on the space you land on. There are two ways to win the game: stars and wins. Both have their advantages; Stars are easy to collect and easy to lose, whereas wins are always a fixed number and will never go decrease. Cards can also be important whether you are trying to win using star or wins.
This game has both pros and cons. As far as the cons go, I'm a bit annoyed that winning could be completely up to random chance no matter what strategy you use, but that is the way board games are in real life, so it's not necessarily a negative. Another con is that campaign mode is very lack luster; the story lines don't really make sense and can't be skipped through. There is also no real explaination as to who the characters are or what their strengths and weaknesses are, which I feel is a missed opportunity in this game. The pros of this game are that it's fun. A game will never go the same way twice which keeps things interesting. It also easy to pick up and learn. I did not read the user guide that the game offers, but was still able to quickly pick up this game and understand what is going on. This is a game I could see myself playing with friends even after completing campaign mode, however I wish there was local multiplayer available and not just online multiplayer.

100% Orange Juice is a curious case. To put it simply, if you think games mostly determined by RNG aren't fun, unfortunately I don't think this is the game for you. Your movement is determined by a dice roll and, while this is actually mitigated somewhat well by most maps having lots of forks in the road to choose from, it's still a factor. The dice mostly come in with battles, where your attack, defense, and evasion (you either take none of the damage or all of it if you choose to evade) are all determined by the dice. Once again, this is somewhat mitigated by a whole host of characters having different stats that add or subtract to the die roll (for example, if you don't like dying, maybe a character with + Defense is preferrable). However, untimately, there are six numbers you can get that are out of your control.
Lots of other reviews say that this game is entirely RNG (either in jest or frustration), but I disagree. Of course, I already mentioned how you can choose direction and character, but there's a general awareness of the game that can give you an edge. Knowing who to fight and when to do it is important. Taking gambles to go a possible unoptimal route play a part. And, of course, the cards (1/4 of which you choose to put into the deck alongside the other players) are huge in determining the outcome of certain scenarios.
And, while a good chunk of the game is based on RNG, I don't think that's entirely a bad thing. The RNG makes the game fun. You don't have to play it too seriously and get mad when you're losing because it can be blamed on the RNG a good amount of the time. Plus, it's a great game to turn your brain off to and just play for the reason. I've enjoyed playing this game online on the side while watching streams, for example. And the battles being influenced by RNG plus some potential "trump cards" means the tide of the game can turn very quickly when the person in the lead loses a battle and thus half of their stars. Plays like that are what make 100% Orange Juice as fun as it is.
I think the only thing I have to complain about this game is unlocking characters (and stages/cards, but moreso characters). You get one free character at the beginning of the game, then to unlock the rest of the non-DLC characters, you have to play through that story campaign and some change (or beating all of it for one). This is a multiplayer game at heart, and I've had a good chunk of friends who have been reluctant to play the story mode because AI isn't as fun and it takes time despite being stuck with only one character. It's made less of a drag if you use Shift to SUPERSPEED the game, though, so it could easily be much worse without knowing this. But once that hurdle's over, the game's diversity really shines. Each character has their own unique gimmick or twist, and only a handful are considered weaker or more powerful than the others. And I don't believe 100% Orange Juice suffers from Pay 2 Win despite how many characters there are to buy. The characters that I think are some of the strongest come with the game.
So, overall, if you're planning to get this game, be advised that it's rather RNG-dependant and you have to do single player to unlock characters. If those don't sound like problems, then I really can't recommend it enough. It's silly fun down to its core, and it's filled to the brim with characters, stages, cards, customization options, and updates from the developers despite looking like it's just a simple Flash Browser game on the surface.

The objective of this game is to race against 3 other opponents to be the first person to complete all 5 objectives in a game. You roll a dice and you either lose stars, gain stars, fight monsters, earn a card, or randomly warp to another location.
For objectives, you are given two choices; gained a certain number of stars or beat a number of enemies. To beat enemies you're first given to attack. If your opponent still survives, he will attack you in return. You have a choice of defending or evade. Once a player's HP reached 0, you or your opponent will be under KO'ed. In order to revive back to the board, your dice must be above a certain number written on the screen.
There are boost cards, trap cards, battle cards, and event cards. Buy them through shop based on your stars earned in your previous matches. There are customisable characters, unlockables, and more to discover inside!
