The Elder Scrolls series is one of the best and most well known rpg experiences available, and it's difficult to pick a favourite. But if I did choose a favourite, it would have to be The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion. Oblivion has better gameplay than Morrowind, better quests than Skyrim, a better story than Arena and better accessibility than Daggerfall.
Of course I enjoy every Elder Scrolls game, but Oblivion made some bold decisions and came out on top, and for that I applaud it. Morrowind had a captivating environment filled with fascinating quests and lore, but the gameplay was annoyingly bad until you reached a good enough level. Skyrim had great gameplay but monotonous, repetitive quests and characters. Oblivion is the compromise: it introduced the fun combat gameplay we all know and love, but still retained most of Morrowind's depth and complexity.
The presentation is fantastic. Oblivion may not have Skyrim's graphics, but the rich colours and forests make Oblivion's game world a lot more pleasing to the eye in my opinion. The soundtrack is second only to Morrowind's, and the whole thing came together to provide an awe inspiring backdrop to all the adventures you would have. On that note, let's talk about the quests. Oblivion's quests are better than Skyrim's by a country mile, and are some of the best in the series. I'll never forget that fighters guild quest when I got high on Hist Sap and destroyed a whole village, or that time I had to fight bandits who had hijacked the ship I was sleeping on. Few quests from other Elder Scrolls games can hold a candle to what Oblivion has to offer. Fans of the Dark Brotherhood will know that Oblivion's Dark Brotherhood questline is the best in the series, and the main story can stand on its own two feet.
If you like RPGs, or if you have played other Elder Scrolls games, you really need to play Oblivion, as in my opinion it is the best of the bunch.

Crusader Kings 2 is both a great and terrible game: it can give you some of the greatest gaming experiences you'll ever have, but it can also be a crushingly frustrating mess of a game; here is the verdict.
The Good: Addictive and in-depth gameplay, a huge array of obscure/famous historical nations to play as, an enormous timeline spanning across just under 700 years, a vast array of options and progression methods allowing for many different playstyles and approaches, a huge amount of entertaining random events and quest-lines, the game focuses on your dynasty and character, allowing you to become attached to your leader and their progress; a very unique and rewarding experience.
The Bad: The combat system is lacking and relies almost entirely on the number of troops, an infuriatingly unpredictable morale system, terrain, and leader skill, some areas of the map feel scripted, with some nations 90% of the time following the same path or course of action, 3/4 of the nations are locked behind DLC, leader opinion seemingly makes little to no difference on factions or plots, tribes get very cheap abilities that mean they can often steam-roll large kingdoms.
Misc.: It's very fun to start as a minor tribe and form a kingdom, slowly changing your government and growing your nation into a  feudal state, a lot of the large powers can actually be very challenging to play as, the game includes wikipedia pages for non-fictional rulers.

Tree of Life looks like a casual sandbox RPG game with faction wars and base building. However, that's only how the game advertises itself. In reality, it is a game caters and rewards hardcore players who join large groups while inadvertently punishing guilds in small numbers (3 or fewer). The game revolves around constant deterioration of equipment and supplies, in addition to a mandatory tax that is paid weekly in real time, which makes it too time consuming for solo/duo players to keep up.
The game provides 21 skills (called masteries) to gain up to 50 levels in, while allowing 320 total levels spread between economic (living) and combat. This means you can max out 6 skills only and combat will require you to level 2-3 of these skills, leaving you 3-4 economic skills to choose to max out. While this sounds like a great thing to encourage interaction and a living community, it means soloing/duoing is essentially impossible. Arrow/Cannon towers require carpentry to build and blacksmithing/tinkering to maintain. Your armour and weapons will require blacksmithing, tailoring, and tinkering. Those skills alone means solo players will have zero combat skills if they wish to build their base, and that means they can not kill the enemies required to get the materials.
Weapons and armor constantly break, which is a good thing to keep the economy moving. However, because they break so often and quickly, you will likely go through 2-3 weapons in the process of gathering materials to make another 5, not including any hits you take to your armor and bags. Armor is difficult to maintain and you usually can only afford to maintain the lower level suits, and sometimes not even those. As you level up to higher levels, you will be able to maintain them  better and longer, but will still find yourself farming 5-6 hours to counter maintenance in order to have 2 hours of actual fun playtime.
There are three factions that you choose from when making your character. These factions can attack other factions, but can't attack their own. There is a faction chat in game, but even on the American server it is usually dominated by French or Chinese and getting a response to a question or discussion in English is actually a very rare thing. If you're a small guild or group, don't expect to  rely on help from others in Faction chat as they likely will not understand you, or you will not understand them.
The game has a heavy advantage to those who are willing to pay for in-game items in the premium store. $25 will get you a mount that you never need to maintain other than feed. You can get a mount in game, however it will not have the built-in light source that premium mounts come with and will die after a set number of uses, forcing you to gather materials for another one. If you're not a rancher player, then you will never make your own mounts. Bags can be purchased for $10-15 and provide extra inventory space that doesn't break. Bags crafted in game will degrade just like armor and weapons. What makes this dangerous is if one breaks while holding items, all of the items spill out. This is not a concern for the player who pays real cash.
Overall, Tree of Life is not a game I can recommend. I have put in a great number of hours hoping the game would get better as many online games do. Sadly, there is no end game and the grind never changes.

This game is fantastic, but I must issue a warning:
Player creativity and practice is an absolute requirement.
Some people say the game gets old quick, and that it's too simple to squeeze enough enjoyment out of it to make it worth the money, and that d!ck jokes aren't funny. Those people are wrong.
When I picked it up, I liked it, and it made me laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off for a bit, but I wasn't quite hooked. Then I played a match with someone who was REALLY good at the game, and it showed me the potential for hilariously rewarding gameplay and growth through raw skill. It actually exercises your brain because you have to figure out which keys you need to push next, and in which order, while you're helplessly rag-dolling through the air.
Sometimes it can be a little buggy, but honestly, that's part of the fun, and the bugs don't break the game by any means. And even if you don't get very good, the real reward comes from the awkward, flailing movements that still, after 60+ hours of play, occasionally make me laugh helplessly.
What I've learned is that this game has two crowds. One crowd, who picks the game up for an hour or two (or less), and decides it's kinda okay, but too simplistic for their sophisticated tastes, and who still laughs at d!ck jokes anyway? And then there's the other crowd who gives it a chance, really learns how to use the mechanics, has a total blast and falls in love.
Now, there are obnoxious jerks who play online, that think they're funny, and waste your time slapping your tender bits until the timer ticks all the way down. But just use that as motivation to get good at the game so you can beat all those jerks, and eventually they'll go away, because chances are, they're part of Crowd #1. And anybody you like playing with, look up on Steam and add them, and after a bit, you won't run out of people to play with.

You can either decide on building a ”tower” (vertically) or ”bridge” (horizontally) with human bodies in different color and styles that you decide on before the game. The turn passas around between the players each getting a body to control. Then you need to get that body as high up or far as possible on a joint construction and if you're unable to pass the farthest/highest body already there, you are out of that round. There is also a timer... of course.
Each limb is controlled by a different key on the keyboard or buttons on a pad if you use that (I do!). And the akward moments when you fail with the controls will bring everyone to a laugh, even you.

This is such a stupid game, yet I actually had fun with it. Me and my friends got many good laughs from this game seeing the other players fail on reaching the top of our naked-body-construction. I remember Pixeljunk Shooter being good fun a few years ago when I played it on the PS3. But playing it now it managed to annoy me sometimes. Some of the deaths are annoying, sometimes even cheap, resulting in you having to replay entire sections because of one tiny mistake. And no, the sections aren't all that big and can be completed in just a few minutes. But it's frustrating when you're almost near the end of a level.
It's also the only thing that annoyed me, because what you have here is a cute looking, physics based, twin stick action game (it's not really a twin stick shooter, so naming it that would do it injustice) where you save trapped workers and try to find as many gems as possible. Why is the last one so important ? Because you can only progress until you have a certain amount of these gems. Still, it's not that time consuming, because the game can easily be finished (not 100%)  in 3 or 4 hours. There are 3 worlds and they consists of several levels each, and each levels consists of several sections. At the end of the world there'll be a boss fight. Those can be a bit difficult, but collecting enough stars allows you to earn extra lives. You'll rarely have to replay an entire level. Anyway, the environmental puzzles are fun to solve, and it's cool to look for secrets (I don't know if you can really call them secrets, though).
Ask me if this is the best Q-Games/Pixeljunk game and I'd have to say no. That honor still belongs to Pixeljunk Monsters. Shooter is a close second, though.
But ask me if it's worth it and I'd say yes.

This is my favorite PixelJunk title.
The game controls similar to most twin-stick shooters (Smash TV, Geometry Wars, Beat Hazard) with the left stick moving your ship, and the right stick changing which direction you are facing. Shooting is done via the right trigger, and the left trigger lets you grapple people or gems into your ship.
There is a central mechanic of liquid physics at work, with early levels having water and lava. You often have to lead the water where you need it to go, while trying not to lead the lava places you want to keep safe. The water can be directed to lava to allow you to clear it out, and some maps have earthquakes that happen at certain times, releasing one or the other fluids from off screen. This can either be helpful, or very harmful. Triggered lava can cut off secrets if you take too long, or lead to death.
Rather than a life bar, you have a heat gauge that fills up when you take damage, get too close to lava, or fire missiles instead of your little pea shooter. Getting away from the action will allow you to slowly cool down, or you can fly into water to speed up the process greatly. If you over heat, which trying to fly through lava will certainly do, your ship will stall and you will die.
The music and animations are also well done. Moving or turning your ship makes it's tiny fins and boosters move and fire, rather than just rotating some plain sprite. A lot of neat little touches went into this game that other developers would have just not bothered with.
It's a really fun title, and well worth the price.

To be honest, I thoroughly enjoy this game, especially in this price range. The physics are nice and the adventure so far is entertaining. There are some quite polar opposite tattributes for the pros and cons though.
The pros are obvious; who doesn't like a magic/medival game with so many paths? The unique and interresting hole of the game had me hooked for a real while. The races and character customization had me at the very beginning. The magic that is allowed here is helpful and interesting, but you don't even have to use it! You can just be a berserker or an archer. The music is well-done and tells me of the mood I'm supposed to be feeling. The enemies are more than just reskined zombies and actually talk or give the choice to fight.
The cons aren't very far from view either; textures are repetitive, but not much should be expected from that, as it is quite old. Hit detection is poor. I can sit for a few minutes at a time trying to snipe a rat only ten meters away only to run at it in frustration with a knife in the end. Weapon sound effects are overly reused with only about two different noises for swords and knives and one for a fireball. Animations are quite robotic, but that should be expected. The same gossip can be heard from every single NPC. The side quests completely distract from the main quest (I've played for a while and still haven't got the time to deliver the jewel to the guy I'm supposed to.) Trying to complete some quests is impossibly hard. I can't do a lot of quests without checking the wiki. The repurcussions of some quests are too severe to simply do the quest to see. If you're a guy like me who likes to do it right the first time around, then the wiki will have to be open every step of the way. It's not fun to spoil how some quests go if I want to make few serious mistakes. Some of the buttons can be confusing. I played for over three hours without knowing where the map was in the menu. A word from the wise; pick your traits with extreme consideration, because you might end up getting stuck with a trait you can't stand having. Before you play this game, or go too far, let me say this; vampires, and vampirism. This hugely annoying, frustrating, burden of an illness has stopped me from giving the whole-hearted thumbs up. Oh? What could be so bad about vampirism? One thing, you can get it anywhere and anytime you sleep. Boom. If you want to level up, but don't want to get bit, then too bad. You have to sleep to level up. The thing that balances it out though, is that once you get it and cure yourself, you can never get it again. Convenient? Yes. Well, now how do you get rid of it? Heh. Hehehe. Ha. Simple thing. Are you a nice guy like me? Well then you can't. Even if you were a terrible person in this game you'd have a hard time moving on. Because guess what's the hardest quest yet? Curing vampirism. 2 steps. Not that much? Sure, but guess what? Well, first thing, it needs FIVE grand soul gems. Easily the most expensive consumable item that you will get in the first fifteen hours of this game. Saving up for something else? Well not anymore. Grand soul gems cost five hundred gold. Now, not sucking blood will cause you to become very vulnerable to sunlight. Guess what? Shop hours are only in the morning. It's rigged that you CANNOT cure yourself without sucking blood. There's not enough time to begin with in order to cure yourself during the initial sun-resistant timespan. Not knowing about this will cause you quite the headache. You just go along saying, 'oh, it's ok. I can resist sunlight right now. I can live with this,' well, you can't. Traveling by night gets very upsetting.  Trying to get the soul gems by dungeon delving? Good luck, because there are only 3 you can get free from dungeons. The rest you have to pay for or steal. Before you go ahead and accept that you have to bite people in order to get the soul gems, let me tell you, victims can sometimes wake up and call the guard. Save before you enter their houses. Now you get to the NEXT annoying part. After you return to the witch after scouring for soul gems day and night, saving all your worth for the greedy merchants, (or you simply took a stroll to her basement and stole some of the ones there,) you come gasping at her feet saying 'is it over?' well, the lazy witch then says that you have to get a list of ingredients for her. Some are common and obvious, but others? The blood of an Argonian, amd bloodgrass. The first one you can get from Argonian thieves which you may or may not encounter, or from a certain Argonian archer in the arena, or if you're evil and just ran at a poor citizen and stabbed him/her. But the next, if you haven't gone far at all in the main quest, it'll be a pain. Searching merchants from far and wide if they have any, and, no suprise, shop hours are during daylight. Before you say, 'ok, ok you've made your point that it'll be next to impossibe. I think I'll stick with skulking in the shadows,' you see, if you don't drink blood after a certain amount of days, you get a disease ten times worse than vampirism where you HAVE to drink blood EVERY DAY or else you die. So either just be a jerk to everyone and be a criminal, or do yourself a favour and save before you sleep.
All in all, this is a great game for it's time. I liked it (until vampirism ruined my game). My ratings are:
Quest(s): 6/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Overall Clarity: 4/10
NPCs: 4/10
Uniqueness: 10/10
(I won't include graphics for obvious reasons)
Leveling System: 6/10
It's a great game. Try it for everything except vampirism.

This is a review of Riven (the sequel to MYST) Steam version. I say this first because i've already played the game originally in 1997 and certain things had changed for this review (alltough the game essentially is the same from 1997 just compiled to dowload online).
I loved the game when i first played it (almost 20 years ago by now). It was a very interesting sequel to Myst and added many things to the story (in fact, it had a story!) You meet ghen, catherine and again Atrus.  There is something going on at least! that is the main thing i guess.
The game came out in 5 cd rom discs wich was pretty notable for that time, lots of data and videos. More than 3gb of data for 1997 was a heavy thing.
The puzzles are very hard, it is still hard now,but, even if you use a walkthrough it still is rewarding to find out how the world works, how the story of atrus and his family and the linking books unfolds.
The music is the best. Pretty much half of the experience in this game (the first one and this one in fact) is the music. Totally amazing, complements the graphics so well and what happens on screen at times. The graphics by the way, were so amazing in 97 that, still, to this day in some places,  they still seem to be made last week. Of course, in general they've became old, but still, this is a 20 years old game!!! Is like watching a movie from 1996 and thinking that the special effects are not so bad...
Now, that was my review from the original game. Now to some things from actual steam/gog version i am reviewing and why i post a negative review.
While i was happy to be able to have a newer build of this classic game, wich i can download from steam and install in modern OS everytime i want. i did encountered certain problems, wich are not acceptable even if it is an old game.
First, the game crashes in certain contexts, certain situations. Like for example clicking too fast when moving around (wich of course didn't happen in the original version) While i know that if i don't click too fast i will probably avoid these crashes, still is something that should be taken care of. Specially knowing that the creators and the company of this game (cyan) still exists and should be made aware of this and take care of the problem. Second, in certain situation when saving, your game can crash, during the saving screen... (if you don't use the save buttons).
Also, third, and most catastrophic, there is a scene in game, where you have to turn on a light in a passage. When you do that, and you turn around, either the game crashes or takes you to a previous screen.... this is unavoidable. There is anyway, a way to continue through the passage after turning on the light (without crashing) so i finished the game luckily, but i already knew what to do there, i don't know what i could have done if it were my first time playing it, and didn't knew what to do there. This is something that happens at least in a win 7 64 environment and should be fixed, if not they are essentialy selling you a broken game. This is why i will not recommend this game, at least this version on steam and gog (the same). It is a shame, there was an interesting game...somewhere, there, but now it is too old, and its broken in someplaces so... (you could say that, ironically,  the game, the same as the fifth age in riven, have become full of fissures everywhere....how sad...)

Should I be knocking on this door?  Bothering the natives?  Is there a point to it?  Do I have to sneak up on those weird dodo/seal things?  Why do none of the buttons or switches have labels? Still, you should buy it.  It's dope.

Hey Everyone!
Now I don't normally write recommendations, however his game is worthy of it.
To begin, people who don't enjoy Civilization would struggle to enjoy Endless Legend, as they are the same type of game.
However, as opposed to guiding humanity through history, Endless Legend allows you to craft your own civilization in a futuristic fantasy world. Futuristic Fantasy you ask? Well there are demons, as well as high tech exploitation of resources. Cool stuff if you ask me.
The game looks absolutely fantastic, and is probably one of the best looking strategy games I've played. Further, the download is under 2gb! Gameplay is deep, and rewards forward thinking and planning of city positioning.
The A.I. is pretty good, more predictable and more realistic than the Civ A.I., however it seems a little too passive and generally won't engage in a war unless provoked or absolutely necessary.
Leading onto that, the combat system in this game is very unique and while a bit odd to come to terms with, is very intuitive and ultimately fun.
Some negatives are it is a hard game to pick up. The tutorial isn't bad, and does a good job and teaching the basics but it took me a few games to fully understand how to play the game properly and well. Furthermore, the endgame seems a little messy and it's difficult to understand what needs to be done to achieve victory, but again this will come to the player who spends a few good hours tinkering with the game.
Overall, a very solid game and one every strategy and 4X fan should look into!

I got this editor to create Quake 1 levels for my own enjoyment with the comfortable layout/control scheme of Hammer/Worldcraft (an editor that I am very used to). I'm really happy with I've gotten out of this editor in only about 2 hours.
It's very easy to quickly iterate on brushes and realign textures. There is a UV grid feature which I absolutely love, and lets you align your textures as perfectly as you want. It's cross platform too, meaning you can (potentially) save brushwork and use it in another game.
If you are like me and you don't like leaving the comfort of the Hammer editor, but want to make levels for retro games such as Quake - then this is the editor for you.
If you are new to level design or have more experience with modern editors, then I would suggest checking out Trenchbroom and see if that satisfies your needs.
Overall it's a great product, and has renewed my motivation to create levels for retro games!

A constant love-hate relationship characterizes the gameplay of pretty much everyone that has played awesomenauts competetively. Scanning the game's official forum tells you why. This is a beautiful game that is marred by some flaws. A 2-D side scrolling moba with an array of characters greet you when you play this game.
Pros
- Beautifully drawn characters and environment.
- New updates every 1-2 months.
- 19 awesomenauts to choose from.
- 4 maps and different game play modes.
- Replay system / Tournaments.
- Great for casual play in leagues 3-9.
Cons
- Horrible matchmaking.
- A disconnect will drop you 200 ranks.
- If you're in a premade with good team members you can pretty much stomp everyone.
- If you play solo you'll get to league 2 or the bottom of league 1 and matchmaking will eventually drop you a couple of ranks.
- Sucks for competitive play.
- Those who play on the worldwide network (like me) will be matched against those that want to play within their region. This causes a lot of friction in the community. Most Asians can deal with the lag but others cannot.
The reason I stopped playing this game was because I was tired of facing only 2 possible outcomes
1. You play in a premade and no one can stop you. Stomp Stomp Stomp.
2. You play solo and you get matched against duo or premades and your teams mates are in league 3-5.
The game is awesome and you should check it out. As long as you do not take it seriously / competitively you'll love it. Fair competitive play is only possible with manual matchmaking.

This is a balls hard classic point and click puzzle game. I used to sit around the computer with my family and try to figure out the puzzles. We never could get the best ending.

1. Start the game
2. Alt+tab out and open up the Task Manager
3. Under the 'Processes' tab, find Riven and right click it
4. Select 'Go to details' on the right click menu
5. Right click Riven again
6. Select 'Set affinity'
7. Set it to run on only one core by unchecking all of the boxes except for one
This should solve the problem of it crashing after a few minutes of play, but you will have to do this every time you start up the game.
Besides that, there's not much else to say. Riven is a great game, there's a reason it's considered a classic.

Honestly, Riven was probably my least favorite entry in the Myst series. What I enjoy most about the Myst series, is the prospect of walking around through beautiful, exotic, semi-abandoned worlds. Riven is the Myst game that least fits that description. And since it has been many years since I read the Myst novels, I found the exact plot of Riven rather confusing. And some of the puzzles are just annoying. Like, throughout the game there are doors that you can open with a click, and you can also close them with a click. Normally, this is a completely useless feature, and you assume it's just there for completeness. But exactly twice in the game, there are hidden passages that you don't see unless you close a door after passing through it.
With all that said, being my least favorite entry in the Myst series still means it's a pretty great game. Gehn's character is great, and the sun-drenched isles of Riven are beautiful to walk around, and to figure out the economy of how they all fit together.
And of course, if you're going to play the Myst series, you've got to play Riven anyway.

Bought the four pack to play with 3 others I knew.  We started the game, and the tutorial quickly told us to chop down some trees.  We were instantly yelled at by several people in game for "not replanting the trees."  You can replant trees?  The game said nothing about replanting.  We were told we were going to be reporting for being bots (which we clearly answered back that we were not), and proceeded to be stalked by several people in game while we were trying to learn what was going on.
Eventually, after some time, we managed to finish the tutorial only to find out that our own self-made guild tree (your own Tree of Life) would EXPIRE after 6 days if you didn't pay in-game funds for "rent."  What does that mean?  Did that mean all of our in game assets would suddenly become public if we didn't log in enough to pay the rent?
OVERALL...
It seems like the game could be good, but it has a built-in system designed to force you to have to play in order to keep any progress you made.  There is a series of micro transactions which can increase your travelling speed and/or inventory slots, which is annoying.  Money is required to keep your guild alive, but takes up actual inventory space...  The tutorial is HORRIBLE...  Badly worded...  occassional horrible misspellings ("survey" is not spelled "suvery").  Swimming is slower than just jumping across the water's surface...    Many resources seem to be more limited than they should be, and as a result, players tend to yell at each other for doing things the game tries to tell you to do.  This game is just BAD and has a severe lack of direction.
EDIT:  I understand the game's need to delete out unused assets to allow gamers to not be overburdened on finding free locations. Sooo, I really enjoy 4x strategy games, and since I liked Civ V I bought Beyond Earth, yet it really disappointed me. Then I read somebody saying that Endless Legend did, what Beyond Earth more or less had promised to do, though not being sci-fi themed, which made me give it a chance... and boy! I'm enjoy this game so much more! I like the whole feel with it and really looking forward to the modding community to make some awesome maps and other stuff in the future!
If you like 4x strategy games and Beyond Earth left you with a "meh" feeling, then you should buy this :) Or at least try it!

Accessible to those who enjoy the Civilization series, but breathes its own unique ideas into the 4x formula and executes them very well. The game has strong graphics, beautiful music, and well written lore. The factions play very differently from each other with their own mechanics, which adds a lot of variety to your strategy and play style. A surprise hit for me this year that I'm greatly enjoying!

Endless Legend is a solid take on the 4X strategy game in the same vein as Civilization. However, it isn't a clone of what's been successful in past games with different graphics. The game does a fantastic job of weaving in the quest system and its story line to make playing the game a refreshing experience that goes beyond the need for just one more turn to win the game. It makes you want to actually see how your efforts have turned out and where some of your decisions have led you. I'm definitely looking forward to what the future can hold for the Endless series of games.

Amplitude Studios is on a roll with this and Dungeon of the Endless. Endless Legend really sucked me in whereas I bounced off of Civ 5 and Endless Space for the most part. With EL they've made the world really come to life. Their use of faction quests, writing, and lore is brilliant in the way it marries a traditional campaign mode with your standard random map skirmish mode. The combat is one of the better approaches for 4x games - just enough player input and control to make it interesting and it never drags so much that you feel like auto-skipping all of it by mid to late game. There's also lots of RPG elements in levelling up and perking up your heros and kitting out your troops with advanced weaponry, items, armour, etc. Tons of customization options.
The factions themselves all have their own unique story and playstyle - some of them, like the Cultists and Roving Clans play radically different than most 4x factions. The economy and tech tree and city management has huge depth. Tons of strategic possibilities and paths to victory. It is a bit of a slow burn but the music and artstyle and UI all make it a place you don't mind losing hours to.

It was a toss up between buying Endless Legend or CIV Beyond Earth, I can say that I am 100% happy that I went with Endless Legend. This game is everything that you could possibly want from a strategy game. It has a ton of features that I have never seen before. The lore is really good, the combat system is unique and strategic, the diplomacy offers a ton of options etc. I could go on and on about this game and why it is one of the best games I have ever played. Each faction or race hase a unique spin that gives the game a huge amount of replayability, you can also create a unique faction to play as. Heroes and individual units can be upgraded and augmented with discovered or researched tech.
I would also like to note that the graphics, especially the world map are gorgeous. If you are a fan of turn based games or the Civ series of games Endless Legend is a must buy!!

From the makers of Endless Space comes a stylish fantasy 4x. For anyone who has watched the intro to The Game of Thrones, the art style will be familiar, a quite unique look that I dont recall seeing before,
The gameplay is fairly familiar to anyone who has played a lot of 4x, with a few interesting mechanics to throw in there. Empire planning every few seasons allows you some customisation for your empire, allowing you to focus on say dust production (game resource) or reduction in costs to recruiting units. Strategic resources located within your territory enable you to create armor, weapons and equipment for your troops as well as provide mid to late game bonuses which again provide some nice customisation.
You are able to customise your units to some degree creating 1h shield or 2h for the basic infantry units for example. Further customisation in the material the weapons and armour is made from allow for further bonuses such as stuns and sweepback strikes (aoe).
The only problem I have encountered stability wise is the need to run the client in 32bit as suggested by the company on the forums as it was prone to regular crashing. I have had no problems since doing this altho it will crash on exit every time now, (will update if this is fixed or changes)
Overall I would recommend this as a nice addition to 4x library.

Alright guys, first things first. Yes this is an early access game, remember that. Always when buying such games. Lets get into this.
For an early access game this game is in quite a good state and stands on very promising ground to deliver an exceptional title. I love my survival games and ones with dinosaurs, vast maps and huge forests just grab my attention. This is definitely the best survival dino game I've played. There is definitely limited content to the game atm. There are only three dinos in the game atm and as of this moment I'm still unable to play multiplayer. Depspite this, god I've had some fun. Yes that first little letter is some roleplaying but that is honestly my first experience in the game. I survived for quite a while, imo anyway lol. This game is very beautiful, absolutely huge and completely terrifying early on. You're so insignifcant its not funny. You're hopeless against their attacks so all you can do in sneak and slink around gathering supplies and creating an arsenal. So during this time you explore much of the terrain, see much of how the dinos act as you sit there and watch. You survive. Barely.
So rather than blabbering I'll list some pros and cons.
Pros/Awesome stuff:
Dinosaurs...big ones
Huge and I mean huge map that is intricately detailed and beautiful. Love it.
Presence. This game has presence. It has atmosphere. You're so small and helpless and you know it. This is done through the environment, the detail of it all, the atmospheric sounds of you creeping through the bushes, the call of all the dinos and the terrifying attacks of the dinos.
Tracking a wounded dino...pretty fun in such a hostile environment. Killing it is even better.
Its muliplayer capability is huge, I can't wait to get into some games. To track a T-Rex with a team and take down such a beast, definitely looking forward to it.
The fact that your not the hunter, your the hunted. Never forget that, everything can change instantly.
The enormous potential this game has. Giant sauropods roaming through the forest, a stampede of herbivores as they are chased by a T-Rex, the potential is just endless.
Theres more and I could go on but you get the idea.
Cons:
I think weapons are a little too weak. Shot a raptor 4 times in the head with a bow, didn't die. Five shots with a shotgun...this game isn't meant to be played solo, the damage is proportional for groups of players not solo players. Remember that always.
Not too much to do atm. I don't see this as a con as this is early  access its to be expected but people need to be aware of the state of the game atm. You need to be informed of such a thing. Not much to atm BUT down the road, ♥♥♥♥ yea.
The stamina system, your like a morbidly obese person. Can't run much and you can't run far. Needs to change. Trust me, if you had a T-Rex on your♥♥♥♥♥you'd make Usain Bolt look slow. Btw you can't outrun one lmao
Thats all I really have a problem with if you could call it that. Just things that you WILL encounter and perhaps need some changing.
Things I'd like to see though:
More dinos
Crafting of any sort. Weapons, backpacks, houses, !!TRAPS!!! like deadfall traps etc etc, would be cool.
Ability to capture dinosaurs. Would be cool. To capture a dinosaur. On the island there is what used to be a base surrounded by wooden spikes with two towers...I'd make this place into a dino arena. Thats just me lol
I'm unaware as to the variety of weapons available but perhaps a larger variety. Tranq guns, lmgs, flamethrowers.
In the crafting systems have skinng possible, ability to use their carcasses.
Yes I know this is a title from a company that makes hunting games, yet this game can be turned into something a little but more than a 'hunting' game. If that is simply the end game scope for this game, simply bagging kills then that would kill the game for me. It would be such an anti-climax. This game has huge potential. Please don't waste it.

The map is large but not infinite, allowing you to reach other players if you can survive the trek. It can be scary at times, when you're crouched next to a bush hearing something far off coming closer. Trying to guage where it's coming from. And how many they are. Very tense moments, like the first time you see a Rex from far off.
The game does change a bit once you find a gun or two. I know it's a hunting game but when all you have is 5 bows, you aren't hunting anymore. You're fleeing to the safety of other players and the slim chance of good luck along the way.
There are things that I love about this game. The 8 year old in me that still loves dinosaurs more than anything else loves the bejesus out this game. But there are some issues.
The crashing is still bad. That is going to need to improve quickly. It's hard to develop a rhythym when players are constantly getting dropped. I'm on win8.1 and I'm not lagging. But it still crashes all the time.
The other big issue and I swear it's not because I'm bad, but the aiming mechanism is awful. Bow"hunting" is nearly impossible. The guns are a lottle bit better because you don't have to draw them back but it still ain't great. The game gets choppy to the point of death. And then you respawn all the way across the map and have to sneak, crawl, and walk a good 4000m to reach the other players. The game has a way of spreading you all out .
So. It has amaing potential but right now, developers, this has to get better. Like, $20 better, if you catch my drift. Please don't let this die.

Like so many people, I tried Warframe about 3 years ago for 8 hours (or so my steam profile claims, I have only the vaguest memories of the experience). It didn't grab me. As I said, it's been so long that I don't really remember what I thought was wrong. It could just be that some other good game came out and I concentrated on that instead.
Forward several years and my gaming PC died suddenly, and I was left with PS4, that I didn't want to sink in much money. So I tried Warframe, just because. That was before or during the time War Within came out. So I played it quite a lot, and enjoyed myself. Even decided to sink in some real money because I felt I had gotten a game's worth of money out of it.
I stopped playing it at some point, I did Second Dream, but that's probably when I stopped because life got in the way.
But I lately started playing it on the PC, and I have to say that I am continually wondering if I really saw all this stuff that I've seen so far when I played it on PS4. Because man, I feel like there's way too many things I don't remember now in the game.
Some hardcore player-whiners, I notice tend to say "questionable stuff in Warframe" that has been added lately, or that has not been addressed, or whatever.
But ♥♥♥♥ me, man, this game is free to play and the very few and very minor limitations (inventory space for over three warframes and weapons) that are behind paywall are cheap as ♥♥♥♥, and the game comes with some free platinium. Also you can earn that through grinding and trading stuff.
So I honestly don't understand those people.
Do they honestly feel that they should be getting whatever they want from a game, always, forever, and for free? Also, if it's not a perfect game (it's not) neither is any other game. This game has come so far in four years, and has changed so radically that the future is truly bright.
The game could go to♥♥♥♥♥♥ especially if some key people leave and it becomes pay to win hell, but if they keep their heads this seems to be a journey that's going to be a game that's truly worth playing for years to come. My only recommendation for new players is to save platinium for inventory space, sell blueprints/stuff on market to get plat for the inventory space and stuff you don't want to grind for.
But most importantly, pace yourself, enjoy the game and don't burn out on it. This seems like a game that's going to flourish for years to come, and it's a very good idea to take your time and enjoy it so that you can come back every six months or a year to experience the latest version of the game.

is a great and simple puzzle game, with just as much personality as the main games have. While the game may feel short at first, since it took me about 2 hours to complete the base 25 stages under the time limit for each "Star", I was surprised by another 25 EX stages. At that moment I knew I had to tell the world about this game.
The challenge is there for those who want it, with the previously mentioned "Stars" in each level, in case you complete them under a certain time. If you just play casually you can still have fun, but the thrill of shaving off each second from your previous best time while trying to get each "Star" is a superb feeling.
The music is great in my opinion, it certainly made me feel pumped even while facing hard stages and I caught myself humming some stage themes a few times.
I do have one complaint, and it is the control. This is a port of a mobile game, and it shows. Dragging the blocks around can be a little iffy at times, and you must make horizontal or vertical moves only, if you by mistake try to move a block in a diagonal (even if you have space for it), you may end up not moving the block at all. This can be an issue while trying for better times, leading to frustration.
And I haven't found a 'gallery' option in the game to check the cool pictures you get after each completed set of stages. Bummer.
Even with the controls being a little annoying at times, I still recommend the game for its price. It's a great pass time and challenging too.

Mighty Switch Force - Hose it Down is from the Mighty Switch Force series. This time around, its a puzzle game of the Slide Puzzle/Oil Spill variety
Once again you control our mighty Firefightress, but she doesnt do much moving - you control plumbing blocks within the buildings, moving and flipping them to reach and extinguish the fires.
the Stages are each 5 puzzles long with the 5th being a "rescue Puzzle" where you have to extinguish all fires and rescue a person from the grid by building a path to the ground level and have her exit right.
Each Stage introduces a new Item/mechanic, such as flippable pipes that turn 90 degrees and cant be moved, Mud as a destroyable obstacle (similar to fire, but not needed to finish the stage) or Neon Pipes that only show what pipe they are when in contact with water.
There are 5 Stages in the regular campaign as well as 5 EX-Stages (5 levels each) for a total of 50 Puzzles
the music is neat and pumping, but has some little knacks here and there, such as bad looping (song started over and then immeadiately jumped to a part in the middle)
the game is rather short but for the price, I would say its worth it

Surprisingly good for 5 dollars.
What really makes this game is the control scheme: unlike Super Meat Boy, when this game's loading screen says it's best to play with a controller, I actually disagree. Super Meat Boy was a platformer, where a controller really was an upgrade... but here? Here, I sort of think it works pretty well to use keyboard and mouse.
The controls are 80% of the game. The rest is learning the physics and planning where to put each figure.
Mastering the controls is the real game here. And it's a challenge, but for the right reasons. It's strangely fun, at least for me.
And you can pick a safe-for-work mode if staring at mostly naked men climbing each other somehow isn't for you.
Ultimately, this is another of my recommended 'minute' games, where you can play and get something out of it in the few minutes between having to do the next chore or bit of homework. Not a complex game, but the simple challenge of the controls and climbing physics is enjoyable, and there's more to this game than the silly title and nearly-naked characters would lead you to believe.

I played now for a while and this is one of the games, where a neutral button would be nice.
It is a repetive grind game, where the whole goal is to grow together to gather more and better materials - maybe raid the enemy faction - and that is all about it at the moment. There is other greater goal, but if you are aware of that, it can be quite fun, if you have a group of people, who also enjoy of doing so - and if you have none, there are plenty guilds that will give you a home.
Very important to note is that it is not ment to be played alone, you can only maximize 6 of the skills (mixed between living and combat skills). So in a familiar or newly found group setup it really can be relaxing - just to give an idea about it, just my first experiences - in a short way.
Start: new character, tutorial pops up and leads you through most of the basics, like cutting few trees, crafting, up until your own base - I found it best to play all the tutorial before joining, so I know how it is setup and how the basic of the different jobs work.
Base setup: after wandering around and your inventory gets more and more filled up, you will look for a place to settle down - not just placing huts, since everyone can just use these makeshifts (therefore taking the place resources) - so also according to the tutorial you place a warden tree and setup stakes around it to mark a complete ste of teritory, which makes your buildings inside only usable by your guild - so after a couple of trees chopped, the base layout is created and you start to setup the first buildings, look more into the possibilites of the skills and wander around
it will not take long until you realise, that the base gets pretty small with all the structures and that it is nearly impossible to do all the stuff on your own - like setting up fields, taking care of animals, chopping wood, mining coal/copper, fishing or grabbing all the other resources - so you start packing up everything and look for a guild
Finding a guild: plenty of guilds, chats help to see who is recruiting or just simply ask who is looking for people (chat in general was very helpful so far) - just decide what you like, power guilds that are most likely very advanced or smaller guilds that grow with you - or something in the middle - also important where they are, since at the beginning you will like to stay at one of the earlier areas
apart from that it does not matter, I found myself shoveling for dirt, chopping trees, mining copper and all the other first resources during the whole time, as they are always required by someone - only things you will always have seem to be twigs and stone so far - but twigs can be used as fuel and well stone walls are also a thing.
Daily doing: I just do some farming, chopping a few dozen trees and exploring/gathering further away stuff like iron, big leather, mineral/sparkling water, pumpkins, tomatos - and that is it - all to make some coins to get the tree to grow for more space and so we all can develope, so we can gear up better and improving our home - thats is, and there is not more about it - so I guess if you are cool with that, then it can be fun (even though it should still have beta status imo) - if you do not like just mindlessly farming stuff over and over again (it is a bit like a coop farm game from FB in better graphic and with monsters), then maybe better leave it
if you want to play, still general my opinion would be to wait for a discount, to give it a try
just one thing: the wiki is heavily outdated and online resources are very sparse, which makes it a bit harder to get used to a few mechanics

What happens if Endless Space has an orgy with Civ5, AgeofWonders3, Warlock, Fallen Enchantress and HoMM5. You get Endless Legend: a gorgeous SciFi/Fantasy 4X with a lovely soundtrack. There is a huge array of systems inherited from Endless Space and also from the other 4X games (I'm not a geneticist). You could say there is too much choice and too much variety, *gasp*. That sounds weird until you notice your choices are not cosmetic, but are 2-steps-forward-1-step-backward type choices.
The 1-city-per-zone is OK because city building is complex, sprawling (in size and depth), and a constant battle of tweaking optimizations for your workers. The optional AI governors are odd with their building production choices and they have no output balance (they will max out one particular output).
Heroes and Units can be upgraded ala Endless Space (this time they are "items"). You can also have up to 3 different allied subrace units which also give empire bonuses(captured by attacking, bribing or quests). Battles are played out on the world map and your commands to the your units are interpreted & executed each round in a strange competitive initiative ranked system. This made sense in Endless Space for your units to be only indirectly controlled, here it can be frustrating.
A little buggy at the moment but none of the bugs have killed a game for me. An absolute must for all 4X fans.

Endless legend is perhaps the best strategy game that I've ever played. It's easy to pick up, but difficult to master.
Each faction is wholy different from one another in terms of looks and playstyle, requiring you to change your playstyle to suit them rather than the other way around. Their questlines are all unique and well worth completing, as it offers insight into their mentalities, history and culture, as well as incredible boosts to your empire. No two games are the same, as each one of the playable factions offers its own challenges that change depending on the world.
The world itself also plays a great part into the game. The everpresent threat of winter forces you to change your tactics in accordance to the seasons, and as the game progresses and the winters get longer even the mightest of empires start to collapse in on themselves.
Gameplay wise, it's fantastic. The UI is sleek and refreshingly easy to navigate, and any information you might need concerning your empire is just a few clicks away. While only being able to unlock 3 units per faction may seem a step down from other strategy games, the synergies between them and the level of customization that the game offers to you are simply incredible.
The Combat is challenging and at times even frustrating as the terrain has a massive impact on the battles themselves, not to mention that both friendly and enemy AI can be finicky in how they move and who they attack, often requiring micromanaging when they are not being autoresolved. The lack of a naval combat option remains a sticking point, but hopefully that is something they will add later. The city building aspect is also great, and while it can certainly be improved there it's already many steps ahead of anything that most other 4X games offer. The games themselves are far shorter than most strategy games, in a good way; There's always something to be done and in this respect the game does a great job at keeping you engaged.
And then there's the graphics. Endless Legend is absolutely gorgeous to look and has to be seen to be believed.
There are pleny of other aspects that I could go into about why I love this game, but honestly, I don't think I can really do it justice.
TL;DR
Beautiful, deep game. Great UI, great factions, Tons of replayability.
Edit:
I recommended this game once a few years ago, but now that all of the downloadable content has come out, I have to revise that review. The addition of global gameplay elements such as espionage, dynamic winters, cooperative and competitive quests and naval combat has made an already fantastic experience truly superb. Each of the new factions brings something new to the table, and encoruages the player to re-adapt their previous strategies in order to put them to use.
If you have the time and money, you can't go wrong with Endless Legend. I strongly advise that you purchase all of the DLC, as it really does alter the game experience in the way that old-school game expansions might.

On the whole, this is an excellent game. A complex but not overwhelming civilization mechanic, challenging gameplay that forces the player to juggle resources and priorities, and (most uniquely) a quest system that actually makes you feel like you're progressing through the game rather than picking up some extra cash to fund a quick expansion. Another thing I really like is that all the different factions have severe differences that completely change the way you manage your empire rather than just giving a bonus to your favorite game mechanic; I started off as Vaulters, but got bored before finishing. I started a new game as Necrophages and have found it absolutely gripping. It's unfortunate, then, that there are only a handful of differences between each faction's tech trees, but that's just a matter of "I like this, and I would have liked more".
The most obvious comparison would be to games like Civilization and Warlock: Master of the Arcane, but I think the more relevant comparison is the other "Endless" game, Endless Space. Both games have very tightly designed empire-building systems, fantastic graphics (for a game genre that doesn't really need them), and a variety of fantastic factions. Also, neither game seems to know what to do with the combat. In Endless Space you gave your fleet pre-set orders in a sort of cosmic rock-paper-scissors game, and then watched as whatever faction researched the best guns demolished the other, because each tier of weapon was way, way more powerful than the last. Endless Legend puts a lot more effort into the combat, but I can still tell they just don't "get it", so to speak.
It's a turn-based system on a hex grid, but there are only a few different sorts of terrain that seem to make a difference. The most complex and thoughtful things get tactics-wise is when you put your ranged units on a cliff where the melee units can't reach them, and plug away. It's good, but it could have easily been better. And the missed opportunities keep piling up; with a game that has such a vast variety of races, including a whole host of minor ones like daemons, ghosts, and hydras, you'd expect to see lots of unique and fantastic abilities on the battlefield. Not so much. There are a few units that to interesting things, like the Necrophage proliferator and the drider healing cocoon, but the vast majority of the units simply hit things or shoot at things, with slight variations in their mobility and target preference (so we're back to rock-paper-scissors). Each faction only has a handful of unit types it can field, and the game taunts you with an utterly useless unit design system. Because you must use an existing unit type as a model, your "new" unit will have the exact same gear options as the unit you already have and have probably already updated to make use of your best equipment. Want those Scavengers to wield bows or crossbows? Sorry, no. They can only wield axes or claws, and there honestly isn't enough difference between the two (or what material you decide to make them out of) to be worth making two unit loadouts and taking one of each with you. Many times I was nervous about attacking an enemy that had an attack bonus against my unit types, only to find that whatever cocktail of other stat bonuses I threw at them was still beating them easily.
So the combat is not the best, and at times it's honestly mystifying. I'm really not sure what a city's defense level does or why I should take the time to knock it down before butchering the city's militia and capturing it. As far as I can tell it might provide a stat bonus to the militia inside the city, but there are a dozen ways this could have been implemented more visibly and creatively.
But despite my complaints, the combat at least never got boring for me, despite my doing it as much as possible. And although the team making the Endless games completely failed to make a combat system with great depth and appeal, I can tell they're really trying. With the level of polish around the rest of the game, I can forgive them this.

I'm writing this review because I'm new to 4x games.  I've never played Civ, the prior Endless games; I have the latest XCOM but haven't played it beyond the demo.  So you get the impressions of someone who's not experienced in the genre and is just relating their own viewpoint untainted by expectations.  I'm also not intending to play competitively or with strangers.
Endless Legend is a beautiful game that is fairly deep but relatively easy to learn.  While it will take time and experience to become good at this game, the tutorial is sufficient to get you started.  With the tutorial under your belt, you'll be able to conduct a single-player game against AI and learn the mechanics and intricacies.
As a turn-based 4x game, Endless Legend asks you to explore the world of Auriga while building your empire.  You must manage relationships with neighboring empires and "minor factions", a wide selection of fantasy races that inhabit the game world.  There are two types of resources - those that are generated by your population and those that are gathered from the map.  By building cities you will automatically generate food, science, productivity, dust, and influence; the quantities of each are determined by the placement of your city and the way you assign your population to work.  These are used to increase your population, build buildings, research technologies, buy stuff (dust is currency), and perform diplomatic actions.
The gathered resources are split into strategic and luxury categories.  Strategic resources are mainly used to upgrade your armies and luxury resources are used to provide stat boosts to your city.  These resources are collected by building mines or farms that generate a fixed quantity.
When it's your turn, you're going to do three primary things:
1) Move your armies around the map, exploring, fighting, and founding new cities.
2) Adjust your cities' resource generation (through worker allocation) and building queues.
3) Queue research, conduct diplomacy, upgrade your Heroes (special military units), and review your empire's policies via the menu screens.
The skill and strategy in Endless Legend come from how well you do these things in response to the pressures that Auriga (and the other players) put upon you.
I'd imagine if you put a time limit on turns, that would generate a little bit of pressure to make some snap decisions.  But turn-based games are naturally quite lengthy.  A 300 turn game with 4 players, at 5 minutes per turn, would take 100 hours to complete if it played to the turn limit.  Of course, you can win the game in many other ways - by military conquest, geographical expansion, scientific advancement, diplomacy, or building "Wonders".
Players choose to play as one of 8 civilizations; each civilization has its own strenghts and weaknesses.  Understanding the civilizations will give some clues as to an opposing player's strategy, and help a player build their own.
It's possible to go through an entire game of Endless Legend without fighting any of the other players or invading factions, but it's really unlikely.  I've called out combat outside of the gameplay section because it really does feel like the weak part of this game.  Before I purchased this game I read many complaints about the combat system, and I would have to say that I agree.  However, the rest of the game is so strong that I don't consider this a deal-breaker.
When a battle is initiated, the map zooms in to focus on the terrain region that will make up the battleground.  Multiple armies can participate in battles provided that they are within this region at the time that combat starts.
You're presented with an opportunity to move your units into more strategic locations than where the game logic drops them.  Then, you give them a target unit on the opposing force, and click to fight.  The game than simulates combat for you, making battles fairly boring.  They don't last very long and are animated beautifully, which is a blessing, but it's still sort of hands off.  The math behind the fights is presented on each unit - you can click any unit in the battle to see their numbers in terms of defense, offense, initiative, abilities, and so on.  So it's fairly clear who will win each fight based on the army's composition - you are not going to be able to pull off some brilliant tactical moves and sneak out a victory against an opposing force.  You just kinda kick back and watch your guys attack the units you told them to attack.
The Endless Legend world map is brilliant to look at.  The map is absolutely crammed with features - even the grassland tiles, as the game's most boring or featureless, are still pretty.  I've spent a fair amount of time just scrolling around the map, zooming in and zooming out and checking out the incredible artwork.  When winter arrives, the map takes on a perfect seasonal hue, making everything feel cold and rugged.  When summer comes back, the contrast is noticable, making the world seem lush and vibrant again.
I've docked Endless Legend half a point because it's almost too detailed.  You zoom in and out of the map using the mouse wheel; although zooming in close is tons of fun because it's beautiful, it's also impractical and difficult to get anything done at that level.  Zooming out eschews fidelity for a territory-based version of the world map, which is great for understanding the bird's-eye political view.  However, you can't really move your armies well at this level because the objectives and terrain considerations are only rendered when you're zoomed in.  Consequently, you will spend most of your play time at a middle level, which still looks great, but is busy as heck.  You can opt to turn off the hex borders and resource markers, but the incredible level of attention to the visuals has backfired in that it makes the world map a little difficult to decipher.
You could probably tone it down in the settings but it would be a shame.  No serious complaints here, it's a beautiful game.
I'm very impressed with Endless Legend's interface.  As a completely new player, I found it intuitive and simple to navigate between the world map and the various menus.  Although there are dozens of screens to learn, I was able to understand and manipulate most of them within only a few hours of gameplay.  I could count on one hand the number of times I've wished I could redo something.  My only complaint is that you can't seem to undo a move order once given to an army; since this is a turn based game you should be able to wind it back before committing.  It's possible that you can, and I don't know how, since I'm still a fairly new player.
I have not explore hotkeys so can't comment; these would be important for highly skilled / advanced / competitive players.
I could sit for hours and listen to the bundled music.  The music is phenomenal and the gameplay / interaction sounds are all immersive and perfectly done.  It's peaceful and gets you into a zenned-out state of mind; the down side is that it's easy to lose track of time.  This is a matter of aesthetic opinion, but this is one of the strongest point of the game.
There are so many nooks and crannies to.  Endless Legend is conceptually fairly easy to get your head around, but digging deep lets you do lots of stuff to tweak your empire's performance.  You can upgrade equipment for your military, develop a marketplace to purchase resources and military units, finesse your diplomatic relations, pacify and assimilate minor factions (and consequently build assimilated units), and much more.
This is a beautiful, relaxing, challenging but intuitive game that will keep 4x fans busy for hours.  Well worth the full price of entry.  I'm looking forward to playing and learning more.

I recommend this game to almost anyone!

If you are having troubles with the game crashing randomly all the time, try this:  Run the game normaly, tab out and open task manager with crtl-alt-delete.  Go to the processes tab and select riven.exe, right click it and choose "Set Affinity..." Uncheck all the CPUs except for the first one, which should be CPU 0.  This will fix any bugs that are related to the game not being programmed properly for multi-core processors, so basically older game.  I've also found this works well for Sim City 4.  The game was crashing on me every 2-4 minutes before I did this and hasn't crashed at all after doing it.  Unfortunately, this needs to be done each time you run the game, which is annoying.
For reference, I am using a Windows XP PC, and it's working fine for me now, despite a big warning saying the game doesn't work with Windows XP....  Maybe steam doesn't know about my trick.

If you are someone who is willing to grind hard and push past obstacles in order to get value out of their time, buy this game. DO NOT, however, buy this game if you are looking for a peaceful PvE survival experience. You should also make sure that you either:
A. have a well-established group of friends who are willing to all put their fair share of time into the game.
OR
B. are willing to join a group of strangers and openly communicate with them.
Does this apply to you? If so, the review below shouldn't have to influence you anymore. Go ahead and buy it.
Tree of Life is a Runescape-esque MMORPG with a heavy emphasis on what sets it apart from its competitors - Clash of Clans style base building and defense in an open factions world. It boasts over 15 different skillpaths, the ability to create
massive guilds with up to 30 members, and medieval-style PvP. Overall, my experience with this game has been good, but that doesn't mean I dont have my gripes with it.
This game is not, will not, and cannot be, without major fundamental changes, a singleplayer PvE game. Though it is technically an option, you're guaranteed to not have fun unless you have less than 80 IQ and enjoy weeks of braindead WORK (not play) plus a hard limit (6 maxed out skills) on what you can do with one character.
I experienced this game with a small guild of 4 regular players including me. With each of us taking up different skillpaths and investing similar amounts of time into the game, we had a great deal of fun for about 100 hours, when it got too hardcore even for the few of us seasoned MMORPG players. We were able to organize and participate in a huge raid consisting of players from different guilds, which I consider one of the highlights of my time playing. Moments like these lead me to believe that Tree of Life is a game that strives on large groups / communities. Guilds aren't called guilds for no reason. When you max out yours with 30 people, they feel and work like, well, guilds.
Like every other review on this page says, the game has a great amount of potential. At the moment, I don't see the devs taking any risks while they try to satisfy the community, fresh off the game's 1.0.0 release, but I do believe it's a future possibility. Though many of the people I've talked to have said that the devs are loose cannons, I was able to observe them add guards to the newbie areas after backlash. It seems like a step in the right direction to listen to the playerbase.
Soundtrack is pretty good. It's nutty at times, but it definitely fits the aesthetic and adds positively to the game.
I have no problems with the PvP mechanics. Tree of Life embraces its simplistic, Minecraft-esque combat with just enough aspects to make it interesting. I do have a problem, however, with the weaponskills. Every weapon has a special effect, but in the end they all deal the same damage. Other than that, spears don't even hit enemies and bows do little to no damage at all.
Game progression seems and feels clunky. I can't quite put my finger on why, but I'm guessing it has to do with some skills requiring a disproportionate amount of work compared to others.
Considering the abnormally high amount of firewood needed to do anything, literally everyone that plays will get their Logging level to 50, which they will, in turn, need. Even after this happens, cutting down trees will still take too long to account for how much wood you require. Logging (and by extension Mining) should simply be removed from the game, instead having trees be affected by how strong your weapon is.
The game's optimization is terrible. Even though I think the game's graphics are, in their simplicity, refreshing, I do not think that I should be getting 25 FPS in the beginner area with all settings on low on a GTX 765M. The game is not Early Access anymore. There are no excuses.
If you're an avid MMORPG fan with a good group of friends, or if you're willing to make a few new ones, Tree of Life will definitely pan out to be an interesting and unique experience. Did this game frustrate and bore me at parts? Yes, but they say that negative things impact you two times as much as positive things, and despite that I came out remembering my positive experiences much more vividly.

This game isn't one of the "main" Mighty Switch Force games (obviously, since to my knowledge those are Nintendo-published); it's actually a port of an iOS spinoff game, unfortunately. It still has the same great art and music, but instead of being a platformer with the switch mechanic, this game is a sliding puzzle game where you have to slide blocks with gaps in them to align them in ways that let you spray water from the bottom left corner into the grid to put out fires and rescue people. It's a small, rather short, puzzle game where you can only control the blocks in the map and shoot with Patricia.
This is a charming little puzzle game, I've been always longing to play one of the Mighty Switch Force games and although it is VERY different from the platform-puzzle games that Mighty Switch Force 1 and 2 are, this is far from a disappointment and is a solid addition to the series.
The difficult curve is mostly fair, but some levels, especially from World 3 onward, may take a good deal of thinking to beat. Nothing particularly horrendous or unfair, though.
This is a fairly straightforward game: douse the fire and you'll proceed to the next level.  The final level of each world requires you to save one of the Hooligan Sisters as well.
Sounds simple? It is. That's why this game is good for people who just want a relaxing experience. But...
I'm sure completionists will have a REAL rough time figuring out how to beat each Par time. While the game itself is not hard, several levels can be very difficult even to figure out-- let alone beat the Par time and get that star.
I said it's a short game, right? It has 50 levels in total and as of this writing I've clocked almost 10 hours in it to get the Par time right in the normal levels.
Of course, if you are just wishing a run without caring for that the game still can last long hours. The difficulty can really get brain teasing on World 4 onward, so be prepared for not-so-easy to figure puzzles.
While it's a good game, Mighty Switch Force! Hose It Down! biggest problem is it's (simple) controls.
Dragging the pipe blocks can be a little clunky, unresponsive, and that alone can severely affect your Par time every once in a while, particularly irritating in levels you must make a lot of block moving. You must slide in a perfect line or else the pipe block won't come with you; you also cannot slide it diagonally when it would save a lot of time.
Mighty Switch Force! Hose It Down! is a good game. It's fun, challenging for both casual and challenge gamers. It's well worth its modest price and as mentioned by the developer, Mighty Switch Force HD (Hyper Drive) WILL be coming to Steam.

Endless Legends has been an RTS game that has made me want to play RTS again and the last RTS I was this addicted to was Starcraft 1. I was never a fan of the civ type games, but the fantasy environment that endless has really draws me in and has gotten me hooked. I've played the game a lot now and feel comfortable giving my insight on it. My main experience comes from playing the Ardent Mages (Favorite empire) and secondly the Necrophages. I've dabbled in the other empires but mostly play those two.
Pros:
+ Unique, distinquishable factions that all have a preffered playstyle
+ Graphics/Art is beautiful
+ Gameplay is smooth
+ The combat is completely unique (Fighting RIGHT THERE on the map huge +++)
+ Customize not only Heroes, but your actual units. And the equipment VISUALLY changes on them.
+ Linear quest system unique to each faction
+ Create your own faction
+ Multiple ways to win games
+ Extensive world generator options
Cons:
- Crashes [11/2/2014] Since the latest patch, there has been significantly less crashes I can actually go a game without it doing it now, but they're still present sometimes
- AI Decisions: I feel the AI still feels really robotic (ironic?) and doesn't really make human-like decisions. Example: I walk one hex into their territory, they close borders immediately when there was no threat presence. I've had the Vaulters end peace next turn right after THEY established it for no reason.
- Diplomacy: The diplomacy is by far the most irritating thing and my biggest con factor in the game for me, I feel its the hardest thing in the game to get anything out of the AI. You could simply ask for a minisquel amount of a resource they have abundance of and no use for, and they'll require all the gold in the world for it. Especially research trading. I sometimes find it impossible to trade for a few things. It would also feel more immersive if they inititated trade with me, rather than me always initiating with them.
What I hope to see:
+ Combat Depth: I like the combat the way it is currently, the only thing I wish that would change is if you could assign MOVE orders WITH the ATTACK orders, especially for ranged units. Otherwise I sort of feel like I'm playing Clash of Clans hoping my units behave how I want them to.
+ Improved AI Diplomacy: See above in Cons
+ More options in the Custom Faction list. I'm tottally fine with the "Affinity" attribute meaning you pick a faction for your custom faction to LOOK like, but currently I feel like the custom factions are just little add-ons/drops from the original faction rather than truly being one of my own.
+ Ally Support: It would be nice to extent what it means to be in an alliance with another empire by allowing aid in combat. I may be wrong and this could already be in the game, but I've yet to see it exercised. I've been next to battles where I'm "At Peace" with that empire, but couldn't join the fight, I hope its the different if you're in an "Alliance".
+ Mods: This is incoming there's even an option in the start menu for it, but I'm curious to what the mods will be.
+ The Marketplace: I'd like to see the marketplace be a bit more meaningful and more player oriented rather than be a "bank" for the game. The supply vs. demand that is currently there is fine, but the marketplace should be more affected when players are buying/selling than it currently is. Almost as if an indirect way of trading with each other. The BIG one though, is I think that the Heroes market should either only be your empire type of heroes, or at least offer more heroes that belong to your empire. This is just immersion for me, I don't want to buy heroes from another empire I'd rather stick with my own affinity but there's almost never a hero from my empire in the list (Roughly 10 heroes are always up for grabs)
+ Passing Turn: Something that definately needs adjusted is that when you're allied or have vision on a large portion of the map, passing turn takes A LONG TIME because the game has to process all the information and visual that you're able to see. Example: I'm in a game with 8 empires and I'm in an Alliance with 3 or 4 of them (So I get vision on their empire). The game stalls for a good while as it processes all the info and moves all the units instantaniously and simultaniously, sort of taking the immersion out of viewing the AI's actions. It'd be a nicer experience if I saw the AI make their moves as the back-end processes that information so it seems like a smoother "Turn Pass"
That's all I can think of right now, I'll update my review as updates come.
