I loved to play this game back in the late 90s because of the summer solstice like atmosphere of the Age of Riven. The experience of going through transitions between islands is like something you'd want to see on a virtual roller coaster ride. The complex numerical system was and is still complicated. Despite that, the experience is rewarding. The Wildlife can be considered the most iconic in the series. Cyan should recreate this game like they did when they made RealMyst and RealMyst Masterpiece Edition, replicating every bit of scenery and texture from the original. It's nice to relive this classic. However, I ran into a few glitches where the game crashed on me a few times and some of the sound has skipped. That's another reason I have my hopes up for a remake.

Ok so I should say right out of the gate - this game is buggy as hell on modern systems. No way around it. It's an old game and just doesn't play nice with modern OS's. Plus - and this sounds kind of nuts, most modern computers are too fast for the experience to be the same as it used to be. What I mean by that is that even the slowest modern gpu/cpu combos will cause the transitions to happen about 600% faster than they did on Win95/98. Even if you have the transitions on the slowest/fade. The result is that you are simply not going to get the original experience.
So - what we have here is a buggy mess that can barely play and when it works - still doesn't deliver the slow/atmospheric experience that it gave us over a decade ago. I would recommend following the progress of the Starry Expanse Project, which is aiming to re-build the game in a 3d engine ala Real Myst. It won't be done any time soon, but playing that when it's done will likely get a lot closer to the original feel than wasting money or time on this.
It makes me immensely sad to down-vote my favorite game of all time... but such is the reality of this product in 2015.

This review is coming from someone who's introduction to the Elder Scrolls world was Skyrim.
In short, I really, really like Oblivion. The graphics were hard to get used to at first, and the controls and game mechanics are also different from Skyrim, but a few minutes spent remapping the controls and reading up on how the skill system works before creating a character was all the prep I needed to do. The rest of the unfamiliar mechanics were easy enough to pick up on.
I found the main questline rather slow and even boring to start, but luckily you do not ever have to complete it if you don't want to (it started to pick up for me about a quarter of the way through it, just FYI). Most of the factions present in Skyrim are present here, and they have their associated questlines. I found the Thieves Guild frustrating, the Dark Brotherhood incredible, the Mages Guild slow (but worth it), and the Fighters Guild boring (but I've never liked the Companions either). As well, the DLC adds Knights of the Nine and Shivering Isles questlines, and while I haven't played the latter yet, the former is absolutely worth it. I would say the rest of the DLC is, too, as Mehrunes Razor is really fun, and the rest add a number of useful locations and tools. There are enough miscellaneous questlines to keep you busy for a long time.
My biggest complaint might be the Oblivion Gates. They are a really cool mechanic that help a lot with driving the main quest forward, and the aesthetic of Mehrunes Dagon's plane of oblivion is hellish. The other hellish thing about them is how difficult and time-consuming some of them are to close. The saving grace is that, of the maximum of 60 will open during the course of the game, there are only 3 you must close as part of the main quest, and another 6 that are optional during the main quest.
In the end, I would strongly recommend this game to any and all Elder Scrolls fans. The lore is insane, and if you're willing to put in the time and effort to adjust to an older game, I think you will find that it's more than worth it.

Overall (9/10): A great Civ-style game with an interesting take on combat and a diverse set of races that all have unique playstyles.
Combat (7/10): The turn-based aspect of battles is okay and you can sometimes pull off a clutch defense or an upset victory.  Battles progress in two phases, the command phase and the resolution phase. Both parties issue commands to their units which are then carried out during the resolution page in order of highest to lowest initiative. I would have preferred a more AoW3/Classic style turn-based combat but can't blame the devs for trying something new. Most likely you will end up auto-ing most combats, I know I do.
City Management (9/10): The population system is a dynamic and powerful tool for your faction when managed properly. Also bonus points for having a faction which can sacrifice its population for happiness.
Diplomacy (?/10): Haven't delved too far into the diplomacy yet but seems standard-ish.
Research, Resources, and Military (9/10): Bunching all these things together because I am lazy. Research trees are large with some unique research options depending on your faction. The resources both strategic and luxury have strong impacts on gameplay and are well implemented. Military management is a very strong aspect to this game where you are allowed to customize your troops with different armor, trinkets, and weapons which affect their rolls in combat and over all abilities.

Cookie cutter, copy paste, same-same.
These are all words that have been used to describe many, many 4x strategy games in recent years.
For those few that are not in the "know", 4x stands "eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, and eXterminate". In the past the 4x genre was an interesting and innovative hybrid of strategy games. Unfortunately many have been taking the "safe" route. (Read UNinteresting and UNinnovative.)
Then Endless Legend walked into the room like a boss, announced that it didn't like the tried and true. It told us that it didn't care what people thought of it.
And it truly doesn't, and I love it for that.
It brought us many new or semi new features, some that it came up with on it's own, some that it borrowed.
The first thing that comes to mind, is the region system.
Gone are the days of spamming cities on every open piece of dirt, whether valuable or not, (Cough-Civ series-Cough) Now every section of the vast continents of land is divided up by regions in which only one city may settle upon. Certain factions are even penalized for expanding onto them too quickly.
It creates an atmosphere that makes each and every one of the cities in your kingdom seem more unique and important.
Instead of thinking of it as just another city, now I think of it by its name and history.
Speaking of regions, there are a wealth of resources in them, both strategic and luxury that can implemented in different manners. Sell and trade them or use them as boost for different affects. They apply different bonuses for your cities, troops and for you kingdom overall.
Resources not enough for you? How about natives? Each region has different native populations that can be assimilated, either by force, bribery or peaceful means. Different species bring interesting boosts to the region and can even be recruited. Ever felt like fielding an army of wolf/human hybrids? Now you can.
---
All layers of the standard 4x are here, diplomacy, economy, expansion and combat. All are done well.
I really enjoyed the diplomacy, and that happens to be a vastly overlooked feature in most strategy games.
But not here. My only wish is that many of the features were not locked behind technology research.
Now that I mentioned technology, Endless Legends has its own view on research trees. It is rather standard with only a few minor twists, there being 6 different ages, all bringing new technologies to research.
Sometimes it seems cluttered and sometimes big decisions must be made. I'm not a huge fan and I hope they rework it through patches.
But it's not big enough of a problem to really detract from the game overall.
---
That's racist.
With only 8 different races to choose from, it may sound like their aren't a-lot of options there.
But instead of 40 different copy-paste races with a few minor bonuses to switch things up with, Endless legends 8 races all play vastly different from each-other and make each play-through seem like you're playing a different game altogether.
In the wise wise words of Lloyd Christmas, "I like it alot".
---
Troops and heroes. The backbone of every 4x, at first glance it appears that this is one of the down failings of Endless Legend, when in fact it is a strong point.
Your standard kingdom only has 4 different soldiers, which sounds like a bummer. That is until you realize that they can be upgraded in many different ways and the aforementioned native and independent troops that can be bought, traded or assimilated into you kingdom. All customizable.
True, they aren't as customizable as some games have striven to make theirs, but in Endless Legends, your choices on each piece of gear is strategically important.
My only complaint here is that upon equipping a new piece of armor, one cant visibly see a difference in the character sprite, that is slightly disappointing and will hopefully be patched later on.
On to heroes! While they can be leveled up, perks and bonuses chosen, extra gear and and gadgets equipped, they seem rather dull.
Don't get me wrong, they are very important to a successful army, just the heroes themselves have no real personalities or real distinctiveness, which in a unique game full of personality, it really sticks out like a sore thumb.
---
Music and graphics.
While these two are less important for a strategy game, they really do need mentioning.
Rarely have I seen or heard such a beautiful game. The graphics are georgeus and relay a real sense of immersion. I believe this may be the most graphically lush 4x I've ever played.
The music is phenomenal. I've never bought a game's soundtrack before, but I will this one.
The music is rendered in the up-most quality, I can't say I've heard such a soundtrack since Arcanum. and that is the biggest complement I can fathom.
---
Overall, I give this game a high recommendation for any fan of 4x strategy games. It managed to pull me deeper than many of its peers in the gaming market. I do not regret this purchase in the slightest, and that coming from a poor man, well that means a-lot.
There are some balancing issues here and there, but with Amplitude-Studios track record, it's safe to say that they will be fixed shortly. That and the addition of modding support, the only direction this game is going, is up.
I've seen what dedicated moders can do with the proper support and that has the potential to add years and years of playability.
If your into 4x and you want something that doesn't come from an assembly line, you couldn't do better than Endless Legends especially for the price.

I'll preface by saying that in spite of my negative vote on this one, it's not a bad game. In fact, it's very well executed. The maps are very pretty, I like the unit editor, and also all of the customization options for setting up a new game.
The problem is that pretty much all of the gameplay is nothing I haven't seen before. The tactical combat is pretty much the same as Heroes of Might and Magic, but not as diverse. For example, units don't have very many abilities, and there are also pretty much only 4 types of units, excluding your hero unit. You can hire mercenaries or "assimilate" minor cultures into your own empire, but they will only give you one new type of unit, and you can only assimilate a few minor cultures at a time.
The strategic gameplay is just Civ 5 reskinned. You build cities on a hex grid, choosing placement based on the amount of gold, food, production on the grid (though it is a little different in that you can't just plop down a city anywhere--only one city per "region"). You queue up buildings, units, and research in your cities. You use your units to destroy roaming enemies (i.e. bandits) or attack other cities. You collect various strategic resources which are necessary for research and production. All pretty standard faire.
Again, I think it's done fairly well. My main issue with the game is the lack of a story. There's a sort of blurb for each culture about why they're doing what they're doing, and you can also perform a "main quest"; however, most of the quest objectives don't really have any relevance to any sort of story. I.e. "Go kill this thing" or "build this building" or "Have X amount of gold in your treasury," that sort of thing. Not particularly compelling. The AI is also pretty passive for the most part, and diplomacy has very few options (declare war, close borders, form alliance). The enemy cultures will also have absolutely nothing to do with any sort of story, so I didn't feel any reason to like/dislike them. They were essentially just mindless opponents, my rivals by sheer virtue of the fact that they were on the same map as me.
In the end, I found myself bored after a couple hours. I hate that I got bored, because I spent a fair amount of money on the game--but I just can't see myself being particularly interested in playing it again, or even finishing the game I started.
So that's why I don't recommend it. If you like 4X games just because they're 4X games, this one is pretty decent. But that's about all there is to it. It's a generic fantasy 4X game.

This is a game where 4 players playing as varied cute chibis battle to get to level 6 before anyone else. How you get there can change as the situation warrents it. You can go the pacifist mode and gather stars and reach a base panel as quickly as you can without losing your hoard. You can go the battle route and collect wins to fulfill your goals. You can pick off your fellow players and steal their stars. You can use cards and blow everything away. Absolute Chaos FTW!
This is a very interesting game that is very well balanced because everything ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING is based on a roll from a D6 (a six-sided die) and each character has modifiers that can change these rolls. However, no one character is overpowered. The way they're balanced is that they can only nudge the rolls one way or another based on their overall character traits. However, even 1 or a 2 modifier is immensely powerful considering rolls are only 1-6. Health is also incredibly well balanced, with most characters only having about 4-5 hp. (There are other characters that go beyond, but they have a balancing mechanic built into them)
The playing field is essentially a somewhat circular grid path that players travel around with multiple branches. Roll the d6 and move that many panels. If your character encounters a branch, you choose which direction you want to move. There are yellow panels that give you stars (d6 roll multiplied by your level). Blue panels that drop your stars (d6 * lvl). Red panels are encounters where you fight a creature (and sometimes a boss). Green panels that let you draw a card. Purple panels that randomly warp you to another warp panel. Cyan panels that give you a bonus move. White panels are just blank panels that do nothing. And then there are the Base Panels (starting locations for the players). The Base Panels are also important because they heal your character by 1 HP and you can turn in your current goal once it has been met.
Battling encounters or other players is fairly simple. The attacker rolls and adds their atk modifier (can be negative). The defender chooses between defense and evasion, then rolls and adds the appropriate modifier. If defending, you reduce the damage by your roll with a minimum of 1 (you ALWAYS take damage). If evading, your roll must be HIGHER than the attack and you take NO damage, otherwise you take the full damage. Depending on your character, you may be more well suited to being incredibly aggressive, defensive, or evasive, or a combination of them. This does not mean you cannot use all of them, it depends on the situation.
There is a deck-building element where you build a deck of 10 cards and these cards are mixed with the decks of the other players'. They can range from boosts that you use at the start of your turn to help you directly, to traps that you drop on the panel you are on, to battle cards that you use in a battle. However at the end of your turn you can only hold 3 cards, so you have to discard any excess. Between games you can buy card booster packs with in-game currency and tailor your decks for your characters.
Leveling up is the only mechanic for winning the game. When you get to level 6, you win. Simple as that. However getting there is tough, as you need to land on a base panel to do so and turn in your current goal. Goals are 1 of 2 things, gather Stars or Wins. When you level up, you have to choose your next goal of gathering the required number of stars, or winning a number of battles, and this goal cannot be changed. So choose carefully. Landing on a base panel is the next step. However when you pass by your own home Base Panel, you have the option to stop there instead. Or if you pass by another player is standing on a base panel you can elect to fight them instead of continuing on your way. If you survive, you count as landing on that spot.
Essentially this is an very tactical COMPLETELY RANDOM Party game that is very fun to play with friends over skype or voice chat. Someone on a winning streak can very quickly lose a lot of progress from getting knocked out and losing their stars, or just being prevented from reaching a base panel. There are probably a lot of other mechanics in the game that I am missing, or glossing over, so I'll leave you to discover them. I am just trying to give you readers a nice overview of how the game goes.

Crusader Kings II allows you to choose any medieval ruler, but it doesn't allows you to actually feel any difference. There is little distinction between Welsh or West African, Spanish or Slavic ruler: they all have the same text in a handful of random events with a very small choice, like "Being a Bad King" or "Being very unimaginative King Okay".
For example: you can face the event in which you make a delegation to other ruler. The ruler is determined semi-randomly without your choice. Let's say out player is a 8th century Slavic chief, and he will visit some Khazar ruler.
In this event there will always be the same text:
. The game doesn't bothers to react that story happens in time and place where people were pretty happy about eating with bare hands.
This seems like an exception, but this immerse-breaking is a core mood of the game. You can buy DLC to play as a pagan ruler, but when you'll make summer feast, the game will assume that you are christianised European king:
. That will happen strictly every time, even if running naked on summer celebrations is your main obligation.
The whole problem summarises as
. You can be a ruler, but it's likely that
is impossible here. The game gives the player opportunities to do taboo things, but it lacks the options to be, I don't know, a good parent for your children, it just does not realized in this game. I see it only as an emulation of politically hurting people. Complexity – yes. Depth – no.
It doesn't matter how much DLCs will be created: they never pursue the goal to let you decide or feel flavour of your play, even "Way of Life" doesn't make the job done. There is no hope on fan modifications, either: even if they add some new flavour, most of them will have especially poor quality (
), and/or will be out of style.
Every now and again I read about Celtic kings, or Byzantium rulers, or some castles and think: "Gosh, I'd really like to play just any game that allows me to see and feel it". This game isn't worth money, it's worth your time. And boy was it a waste.
If you make a puzzle/adventure game, the puzzles should make sense. And a wonky script mixed with bad voice acting makes figuring out what to do in tight situations a real pain in the butt. Especially when it seems like you're supposed to be paying attention and looking for some philosophical message or whatever among it all. But it's all disjointed, irrelevant, and in the end, meaningless. The first several puzzles aren't clear and don't lend any help to the player.
FIRST FAULT: HIDDEN TYPING PROMPTS
Who'd a thunk you need to TYPE stuff into this game? Because there's no way for the player to know from the interface that you sometimes have to type junk. This threw off my friend who first mentioned the game to me. It's stupid and interesting at first, but seriously, that's terrible game design.
SECOND FAULT: BAD PLATFORMING
Is your surreal adventure game going to have platforming challenges? Or mazes? Invest in a good engine. Having the player run and jump and slide in slow motion only makes them hate the adventure that much more. Especially when it involves tiny platforms that are high up.
THIRD FAULT: IRRELEVANT STORY TELLING
I thought this was a game about a guy who goes to a party. It is. Eventually. But the entirety of the game up until the last 2 minutes is too surreal to even connect to anything without getting super super deep about it. Which it isn't deep. All of the stuff Vinnie rants to you about is just drug-induced mania. And that useless information mixed in with crucial puzzle details makes the experience lousy and annoying.
FOURTH FAULT: BAD STORYTELLING
I won't spoil the ending but if you manage the patience to get there, you'll agree with me that that's not how you end this kind of game. I expected some other wishy-washy drugged-out philosophical crud, but it's even worse- a complete shift in mood and tone. And not in a tragic or pleasant way. With really innappropriate music.
OVERALL REVIEW: 2/10.
It's a playable game that I was able to finish in 2 sittings. I wanted to see the game to the end, and I was sorely disappointed from start to finish. Bad platforming mixed with incomprehensible storytelling and cryptic puzzle design make this game not worth your time, but thankfully you saved a few bucks, right?

Riven is the second entry into the Myst series and the sequel to the original Myst game, both of which were extremely well received and achieved massive commercial success, selling millions of copies and being available across a spectrum of platforms including;  Mac, Saturn, Windows, Jaguar CD, 3DO, CD-i, PlayStation, AmigaOS, PSP, Nintendo DS. Riven takes place immediately after the events following Myst in which you play the role of yourself, sent to Riven to free Atrus's wife and capture Ghen, a power hungry lunatic who was banished to Riven.
Riven, like the original and the others in the series is a puzzle based adventure game in which you will need to traverse across islands, explore them carefully and elaborately and solve puzzles. Riven like Myst is extremely hard, these are probably the hardest puzzle games on the market yet at the same time are logical and fair. I first experienced these as a child but had no idea what I was doing and gave up pretty shortly then went back to playing Duke Nukem 3D, now that I am older and wiser was finally able to appreciate these games, to call Myst and Riven masterpieces would be an understatement, these are works of art in every regard. I have yet to try Myst III and upwards and can’t wait.
Riven features tough puzzles, has an amazing soundtrack, brilliant plot and some of the best art work in gaming that will leave you in awe, while this may be picture-based there are some scenes which feature real actors and are done very well. Riven has an atmosphere so thick you’d need a steak knife to slice through it, an insane amount of attention to detail was put into consideration when designing every square millimetre of this game, everything is done so well.
I hope they remake this along the line with a new engine so more people and future generations will be obliged to give it a shot as this is a piece of artwork that everyone should experience.

The TLDR Summary - this is an arcadish version of Arma that can drop your FPS to single digits while looking like an early 2000 era title.
If this had been released around 2000, it would have been a decent title.
In 2017, with titles such as Arma 3 and Squad, this is a laughable attempt to give the player a seamless and believable combined arms experience with adequate system performance.
For a game with graphics this dated, you would think it has stellar perfomance. Instead you get FPS in the single digits just playing against the AI in a skirmish. If your system is used to running Arma 3 with 60+ FPS, expect a stuttering, laggy mess when you play Call to Arms..especially in the first person mode.
The gunplay and physics is akin to Duck Hunt for Nintendo. Mechanics that we're used to such as bullet drop and intertia seemingly disappear in this game, and what's left is an Arcade experience that is worthy for the original Playstation.
If you can get past all of that, which would be commendable, you have to suffer through a complicated UI and control system that isn't intuitive or user friendly.
Perfoming the simplest commands is punishing to the player and detracts from the experience you're supposed to be having fun with.
This title has a long way to go until it's deserving of any DLC purchases. Keep in mind it's still in early access...but they're selling DLC for it anyway.
Save your cash and play Arma 3 or Squad instead. You'll have a much better time.

DISCLAIMER: I don't usually write reviews but after seeing the bad reviews for this game I had to speak up. Scroll down if you just want pros-cons and no detailed story.
After reading the reviews for this game I was a bit hesitant to buy, but when I saw it was on sale for like $15.00 I told myself might aswell give it a try and if I don't like it within 2 hours I can always go for a refund.
Needless to say I passed the 2 hour mark and so far i'm quite impressed, I started the game completely blind I didn't even look at a video for the game. The game is pretty good for explaining things it gives you a makeshift quest tutorial to teach you some basics (you will have to learn a lot on your own it doesn't hold your hand through everything{BUT the community is great and will help if you ask, will explain more later})
I've seen  quite a few people complain about the PVP in the game, which I can understand as it takes a while to set up protections in your base especially if you are alone. BUT just recently last night they added ghosts that protect the noob zones (novice areas) which should help deter any PVP in the starter zones to help new players get a head start SO if you read any previous reviews stating you will get attacked early and wont be able to start that is no longer the case as of today.
As for the rest of the game, the graphics are pretty decent, the attack system is very OS Runescape which I loved runescape back in the day for its simplicity.
The thing that I probably like the most about the game is the community, everyone in the community seems to be willing to help, such as this one time I was wandering out to explore the map (which is pretty damn massive) and found a bull and I tamed it but then found out i'd have to carry it home (you move damn slow when you are carrying a large object) I made it about 1/4 of the way back and ran into another faction member who laughed that I was just carrying a cow. He then asked if I wanted a cart (me being new I didn't know you could use a cart to carry large objects such as animals or logs) I said yes and he gave me his cart and I was able to make it back to my base in 1/10 of the time. That is just one instance, i've had only good interactions with other faction members giving me stuff and helping me out.
PROS AND CONS
Pros
-Decent price tag
-Awesome community
-Simple fighting mechanics (kinda like OS runescape)
-Market system
-Cool skill system (some may not like that you can't max every skill but I like it due to you needing others to get other skill items)
-Guild system (Grab a couple of friends make a guild and build the base together)
-Protected novice zone to help noobies get started (NEWLY implemented)
-Can move your entire base from one area to another (I think this is awesome because you can start in the noob zone build a base then move your base as you level up without having to destroy and rebuild)
CONS
- Cannot repair items? Correct me if i'm wrong but I have not found a way (you can sell broken weapons to the ghost for same price as non broken, kinda odd but whatever)
- Wish they had a level over monsters to tell if they are gonna kick your butt or not have to walk up and see if they do 1/2 your hp in one hit or do nothing, seems to be a large difference in monsters of the same area
-Durability of items seems to be relativlely low for my liking
Overall it's a pretty awesome game and deserves a try!

I'll preface by saying that in spite of my negative vote on this one, it's not a bad game. In fact, it's very well executed. The maps are very pretty, I like the unit editor, and also all of the customization options for setting up a new game.
The problem is that pretty much all of the gameplay is nothing I haven't seen before. The tactical combat is pretty much the same as Heroes of Might and Magic, but not as diverse. For example, units don't have very many abilities, and there are also pretty much only 4 types of units, excluding your hero unit. You can hire mercenaries or "assimilate" minor cultures into your own empire, but they will only give you one new type of unit, and you can only assimilate a few minor cultures at a time.
The strategic gameplay is just Civ 5 reskinned. You build cities on a hex grid, choosing placement based on the amount of gold, food, production on the grid (though it is a little different in that you can't just plop down a city anywhere--only one city per "region"). You queue up buildings, units, and research in your cities. You use your units to destroy roaming enemies (i.e. bandits) or attack other cities. You collect various strategic resources which are necessary for research and production. All pretty standard faire.
Again, I think it's done fairly well. My main issue with the game is the lack of a story. There's a sort of blurb for each culture about why they're doing what they're doing, and you can also perform a "main quest"; however, most of the quest objectives don't really have any relevance to any sort of story. I.e. "Go kill this thing" or "build this building" or "Have X amount of gold in your treasury," that sort of thing. Not particularly compelling. The AI is also pretty passive for the most part, and diplomacy has very few options (declare war, close borders, form alliance). The enemy cultures will also have absolutely nothing to do with any sort of story, so I didn't feel any reason to like/dislike them. They were essentially just mindless opponents, my rivals by sheer virtue of the fact that they were on the same map as me.
In the end, I found myself bored after a couple hours. I hate that I got bored, because I spent a fair amount of money on the game--but I just can't see myself being particularly interested in playing it again, or even finishing the game I started.
So that's why I don't recommend it. If you like 4X games just because they're 4X games, this one is pretty decent. But that's about all there is to it. It's a generic fantasy 4X game.

Despite Endless Legend's stark differences from more traditional turn-based strategy games like Civilization and Total War, the game is endless *heh* fun, and it really is these differences that set it apart from other turn-based games. Each faction has a different playstyle, forcing the player to adapt to the dramatic differences between each group and generating the need for a different mindset regarding expansion, scientific research, economic growth, and militaristic might. Endless Legend's ingame features make it exciting to play, from assimilating nearby villages into your nation for bonuses, exploring ancient ruins for long lost treasure, to conquering the forces of nature to survive the harsh winters. With this in mind I would absolutely recommend this game to any fan of turn-based strategy who is looking for a fresh take on the genre, because it doesn't get much more exciting than this.

You know Mario Party? Well, this isn't that game. But it is quite similar. (Just no aggravating minigames). This is 100% Orange Juice, and is a Party game. You don't really want to play against the CPU (they cheat).
This is a game where 4 players playing as varied cute chibis battle to get to level 6 before anyone else. How you get there can change as the situation warrents it. You can go the pacifist mode and gather stars and reach a base panel as quickly as you can without losing your hoard. You can go the battle route and collect wins to fulfill your goals. You can pick off your fellow players and steal their stars. You can use cards and blow everything away. Absolute Chaos FTW!
This is a very interesting game that is very well balanced because everything ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING is based on a roll from a D6 (a six-sided die) and each character has modifiers that can change these rolls. However, no one character is overpowered. The way they're balanced is that they can only nudge the rolls one way or another based on their overall character traits. However, even 1 or a 2 modifier is immensely powerful considering rolls are only 1-6. Health is also incredibly well balanced, with most characters only having about 4-5 hp. (There are other characters that go beyond, but they have a balancing mechanic built into them)
The playing field is essentially a somewhat circular grid path that players travel around with multiple branches. Roll the d6 and move that many panels. If your character encounters a branch, you choose which direction you want to move. There are yellow panels that give you stars (d6 roll multiplied by your level). Blue panels that drop your stars (d6 * lvl). Red panels are encounters where you fight a creature (and sometimes a boss). Green panels that let you draw a card. Purple panels that randomly warp you to another warp panel. Cyan panels that give you a bonus move. White panels are just blank panels that do nothing. And then there are the Base Panels (starting locations for the players). The Base Panels are also important because they heal your character by 1 HP and you can turn in your current goal once it has been met.
Battling encounters or other players is fairly simple. The attacker rolls and adds their atk modifier (can be negative). The defender chooses between defense and evasion, then rolls and adds the appropriate modifier. If defending, you reduce the damage by your roll with a minimum of 1 (you ALWAYS take damage). If evading, your roll must be HIGHER than the attack and you take NO damage, otherwise you take the full damage. Depending on your character, you may be more well suited to being incredibly aggressive, defensive, or evasive, or a combination of them. This does not mean you cannot use all of them, it depends on the situation.
There is a deck-building element where you build a deck of 10 cards and these cards are mixed with the decks of the other players'. They can range from boosts that you use at the start of your turn to help you directly, to traps that you drop on the panel you are on, to battle cards that you use in a battle. However at the end of your turn you can only hold 3 cards, so you have to discard any excess. Between games you can buy card booster packs with in-game currency and tailor your decks for your characters.
Leveling up is the only mechanic for winning the game. When you get to level 6, you win. Simple as that. However getting there is tough, as you need to land on a base panel to do so and turn in your current goal. Goals are 1 of 2 things, gather Stars or Wins. When you level up, you have to choose your next goal of gathering the required number of stars, or winning a number of battles, and this goal cannot be changed. So choose carefully. Landing on a base panel is the next step. However when you pass by your own home Base Panel, you have the option to stop there instead. Or if you pass by another player is standing on a base panel you can elect to fight them instead of continuing on your way. If you survive, you count as landing on that spot.
Essentially this is an very tactical COMPLETELY RANDOM Party game that is very fun to play with friends over skype or voice chat. Someone on a winning streak can very quickly lose a lot of progress from getting knocked out and losing their stars, or just being prevented from reaching a base panel. There are probably a lot of other mechanics in the game that I am missing, or glossing over, so I'll leave you to discover them. I am just trying to give you readers a nice overview of how the game goes.

First things first CK2 is an excellent introduction into the world of Paradox's grand strategy games. Though not as easy as Hearts of Iron 4, CK2 provides a good platform for Paradox newbies to begin on, war is not the backbone of the game in the same way as it is for other Grand strategy titles which puts a unique and interesting spin on how you play the game, naturally though I feel that war is paced well in the game and when fighting for specific land or titles you really feel as though you have a right- a just cause- to fight for them. Crusades are obviously a fun experience, though they never hold too much sway over how the game is played you do get to see plenty of interesting events, treasury finds and bonuses for your character, being the namesake of the game you'd think there would. Strictly speaking a lot of the fleshed out, flavoured and funny parts of the game come from DLCs, as is the case in most paradox games, if you are unwilling to buy them for simply can't afford them the game is still certainly playable, however I strongly suggest that if you want more flavour that you buy the DLCs, personally I feel that they are over-priced but they do add more content to an already good game. My favourite feature is that the game is very personalised to the player, after an hour or two of playing your dynasty, and their cause, will become very personal to you, overtime you'll watch the warrior that ruled from his teen years grow into a slowly weakening old man and then watch as the torch is passed on to his heir, strictly speaking this game is not about making your country great, it is about making your dynasty- your family- great, to me at least it seems the game can quickly go from a struggle for glory to a medieval sims, which I find entertaining. I can't make you buy the game, and I certainly won't make you buy the pricey DLCs, but if you are looking for an enterance to grand strategies then I would at the very least reccomend this to you. TLDR: Decent starter strat for newbies, 6/10.

When I was a young lad, my dad and I would play this game called Myst. It was addicting, puzzling, and all around beautiful. We've beaten the game several times, and to our dismay, it ends on a cliffhanger of sorts. So when I heard that there were FOUR MORE Myst games. I had to take serious action. I brought Riven for 4 bucks and its been worth every cent.
Not only does it resurrect many of the old timeless features of Myst, (Click on the hidden objects etc.) but adds new ones as well. The graphics, (while a bit outdated) are stunning. Considering they were made with the modern technology of their time. The puzzles never cease to confuse me. Which I suppose is what you look for in a good puzzler. Overall, the game play mechanics, the beautiful images, and the brilliantly designed puzzles, makes Riven live up to the good name Myst erected.
However, the game doesn't work perfectly on Windows 7 unfortunately. Frequent crashes and game freezes aren't unheard of. But I suppose it wasn't really designed for an operating system as complex as Windows 7. ;-;  To avoid loosing your precious game progress, I recommend saving whenever you get the chance. Trust me, I've had my share of rage quits from a game-progress-deleting-crash. (GPDC)
GPDC aside, I recommend a pen and paper, an event-less lazy weekend, a bag of chips, and occasional breaks. To fully enjoy this masterpiece of a game.
Since this game wasn't designed for Windows 7, i'll put aside my crashing con. Aside from that, there's not that much else wrong with this game. I'll give it a  9.8/10

Shtriga is a storyless string of tedious item hunts and great hidden object scenes, but at least those scenes are good enough to recommend this game to anyone who likes some traditional HOG goodness.
Shtriga: Summer Camp feels like a memory game wrapped in a hidden object game. Unlike most any HOGs, it uses two large hub areas, which means it is easy to get lost among its countless sub-screens and even easier to forget where to use any of the key items.
It does not help that there is zero story (there are some notes about missing kids and a witch, but in the end, they lead to essentially nothing), so players feel even less motivated to play hide and seek with the adventure game mechanics.
Considering these design flaws, it is a small miracle that the hidden object scenes are incredibly good. They feel a bit dated even for the game’s original 2014 release, as they are nothing more than static list-based searches, but there are tons of them and their balance is superb. They are, in fact, so good that it is the only reason I am giving this game a thumbs-up.

This is one of the best games you will ever play, and it will take a bit to explain why.
First of all, there is little in the way of 'gameplay': it is a point-and-click adventure game, with no reward given to reflexes or hand-eye coordination. That's not the kind of game this is. The controls are there; they do what they need to do and nothing else. It won't detract from your enjoyment, simply because you'll never feel the need to shoot at something or jump over a pit of lava.
Second of all, you need to play Myst first, and Myst isn't the best game ever made. Myst will do two things for you: it will start you off with the story and the concept of linking books, and it will warm up the parts of your brain that you'll need to solve Riven. Unlike Myst, there is so much lore and eyecandy in Riven that you won't know what notes to take and what you need to remember, and you won't know a puzzle even when it's staring you in the face. Yes, sometimes you'll find a combination lock or something traditional like that, but you'll also encounter obstacles that you won't even know are solvable. It is one of the hardest puzzle games ever made, but it does it the right way: No pixel hunting and no subversive ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
Third of all, the Steam version and the GoG version are both broken. Get yourself a copy of the DVD version.
With that all in mind, go fiddle your way through your favorite Myst remake, and then sit down with a pencil and paper and have your mind blown. Right here is where the universe blossoms, right here is where the blunt story of a peculiar family suddenly shows it's true depth, right here is where you disover that there is thousands of years of history behind you, right here is where you discover that the Miller brothers are two brilliant and crazy motherfrakkers.
And if you look up the solution to a puzzle online, you'll ruin the whole thing. Reach out and poke someone on Steam for a hint. Don't spoil the greatest ocean of atmosphere and intrigue ever made.

Sometimes I can be a weird person.  When someone says something is bad, I have a sick fascination to find out why. That’s why I decided to play
and while it isn’t a horrible game it sure isn’t a good one. In this hidden object adventure game you play an unnamed female detective who is searching for a missing boy. However, the case quickly takes a supernatural turn and things become more dangerous than initially expected. The game was released in 2014 and it shows; the plot is paper thin, there is no voice acting and there is no map, which is a pet peeve for me. The game does have nice artwork and plays well but it’s an easily forgettable title.

A distraught mother seeks out the main character’s help in finding her missing son which leads the player to a haunted summer camp. There isn’t much else to the story besides that, the main character barely has any thoughts or observations of the world around her and there aren’t any other characters to speak to really. The villain is an evil witch, Shtriga, who steals children for their energy. Not much is known about her either, I can only remember two in game notes pertaining to her. An interesting fact is apparently she’s a powerful witch who can transform herself, turn people into stone and isn’t above killing those that get in her way; except for the main character. Shtriga has many chances to kill the detective but never does, instead putting up annoying roadblocks. Sure, it’s a game so dying would not be fun but it makes no logical sense. In the end, the lack of a story or any character development had me very disinterested, I didn’t even feel any sense of accomplishment when I saved the boy, let alone beat the game.

Two things saved this title for me, the first being the gameplay. The game plays perfectly fine as you would expect a hidden object game to be. Point and click controls, interact with objects, collect what you need, solve puzzles, and play hidden object scenes. It meets the basic requirements and has fun moments, however, it doesn’t do it as well other games in this genre especially more modern ones. As mentioned before, there is no map so you can’t see where you’re going and where you’ve been, you also can’t fast travel so be prepared to backtrack if you missed something. The puzzles were overall rather easy but the hidden object scenes were fun. You will visit each scene twice, but when you revisit a scene all of the items reset as if you’ve never been there before. It’s minor but I don’t like that. The game also doesn’t do the best job of letting you know what to do next, but there is a hint feature. Sadly, if you’re after Steam achievements you won’t be able to use the hint feature if you want a certain achievement which may result in some frustration on what the game needs you to do to progress.

My second positive note about the game is the artwork, it’s lovely. The scenes are well done, everything has a great spooky atmosphere. However, due to the lack of a map and much story I didn’t always know where I was. The summer camp parts made sense but then I believe you leave that general area and land who knows where. But still, everything looks good save for the character animations. The music is fine, it suits the mood of the game well but nothing I would add to my playlist. The game does lack voice acting, sadly. While this isn’t vital to a game it really helps immersion for the whole story, and I’m used to these titles having some voice acting. This isn’t a deal breaker for me but it would have been a nice addition.

Overall, I can’t recommend
unless you get it at a very good price or in a bundle or as a gift. It’s not a bad game but it’s just not good either. There are so many other hidden object games to play that are better than this that I don’t think it would warrant seeking it out purposefully. On Steam it does have trading cards and achievements to collect so that might be motivation for some, but to me that’s not a draw. I did find some enjoyment playing this but not enough where I think others should go out of their way to try and play it,

It seems there is an abundance of misinformation which I need to disagree with. Here is a breakdown of each criticism I have seen and why I disagree.
1) "the game is grindy" yeah, not really. I got a skill to max in 4 days. Some skills will of course take longer than this, but that is a good thing. A game where everyone is maxed out in the first two weeks of release would be stupid. I would say the same for the criticism that mid to high level crafting materials are hard to find. Good! Then people will have a reason to play in a few months time.
2) "I keep getting griefed" if this an issue, it should be easy to fix. Build you base directly adjacent to a high level ally. That way, both bases will benefit from each other's defenses. As a low level base, you may be required to coordinate as a faction- I have no problem with that. Also, for what it's worth, my base has been raided once so far, and realistically it caused 30 mins worth of damage.
3) "hackers & devs ignoring players". Have no personal experience with this, but I find it really unfair that all these reviews came pre-release.
Here are my criticisms:
There are some features that haven't been implemented yet, such as individual trading (I.e independent of the market system), personal messages and a friends menu. Despite  this, these things fall under the category of nice-to-have, and the game is functioning well without them.
TL;DR/Conclusion:
take the criticisms with a grain of salt. The game would benefit from a few extra featutures. Work as a team in this game.

Compared to DoS: EE, the sequel severely seems to be lacking in story. Everything feels bland, the character interactions seem strange, some plot twists feel forced. The origin characters have strange situations in which they seem to act completely opposite to their personalities.
Combat wise, Divinity 2 is completely superior, although lacking in difficulty. As someone who played the original, and the enhanced encounters mod for it, it completely lacks the edge. The actual difference between Classic and Tactician seem almost ridiculous. Atleast in the first game Tactician added increased difficulty to battles with additional enemies, slightly enhanced AI and extra factors on the battlefield, such as exploding corpses, or immunity auras. In Divinity 2, tactician only slightly increases combat stats, which barely seems to make a difference. This will hopefulyl change in the future, when the enhanced encounters mod will be released for the game! (very much looking forward to this)
Other than difficulty, Divinity 2 offers superior options for builds, with more variance between skills and races, and combining skill trees. Trying out seemingly stupid builds seems rewarding, and making them work is the most fun i¨ve had in a while.  Due to how easy the combat feels, it also allows for less optimal builds to work easily even in tactician.
Even with the story feeling lacking, the combat has been enjoyable for the entire duration of the game and is the best feature of the game (other than the end). Setting the entire battlefield (and everyone in the party)  on fire never gets boring.
During the 156hrs i spent playing the game, there was only one point that felt completely frustrating and very poorly designed. The final battle forces the player into a dialogue that instantly starts the fight, without giving you any chance to position your party in your favour (and that strategy is an important part of the game), and you're forced to watch your party get completely♥♥♥♥♥blasted with aoe cc & spells with no counterplay. By no means would the fight be under normal circumstances difficult, the forced difficulty comes entirely from the way the fight starts.  It was a very annoying and extremely unfun ending to an otherwise great game.
Still, the game is great, and really shines with its combat and build options 8)

TAURONOS is a dark and gritty dungeon crawler where your goal is to progress through a giant trap-ridden labyrinth while being being hunted by the Minotaur. Grab upgrades that increase your stamina and other attributes and stay one step ahead of the beast.
It's difficult to get a sense of how much tension and atmosphere TAURONOS creates while skimming over the screenshots or videos on the store page. The game uses a bold retro pixel atheistic but it's the music and SFX that do most of the leg work when it comes to building tension and atmosphere. The voice acting is better than I thought it would be and helps the game flow from level to level.
TAURONOS isn't an easy game and later stages are particularly tough, traps become more abundant, the Minotaur levels up and begins to hunt you at a much faster rate. There were plenty of times where I had to think on my feet and decide to run for the exit or risk it all and make a dash for an upgrade. The latter more often than not, led to my bloody demise.
There are some interesting areas that focus on Greek mythology and lore that break up the bulk of the labyrinth crawling, keeping the core game play fresh and enjoyable.
Occasionally character movement becomes clunky, diagonal movement fails and your character just stops. This led to my death a few times and a total game over at least once. Doh!
Collision on some of the corners, objects and traps could be better.
The game sound dropped out a few times, leaving me with no game sound at all. I had to restart the game to fix this. I tested the game on my Surface Pro and my gaming PC set up, it happened on both set ups.

The gameplay is seen from a isometric view, and the controllers are simple, so you will not have any problems to master them. But remember, you start “naked”, be careful, also be curious.
The game has 6 chapters, and exploring in each one of them is essential for you to have a fighting chance against the abomination. And there’s some surprises along the way, bad and good, but don’t worry, you have 5 lives from the beginning.
“And what happens when those five lives are out?” Well, here’s one of the bright of the games: Permadeath. You’ll start from scratch and have to do it all over again. But don’t worry, there are some hidden lives as well, so you won’t freak out when you die.
The voice acting of the game is pretty good, blending with the ambient sound of the game. There’s almost not a song playing (minus when you find upgrades) so you can keep your ears up to listen to everything that’s happening around you.
If you like a challenge, Tauronos is your game. You’ll love to explore the labyrinth, even dying to the beast or traps to find the exit of a stage. And also there’s more that the eye can see (can’t say what because it’s a spoiler) in this beauty.
I’m sure to give it a six with two horns, so please buy this marvelous game and enjoy it as much as you can. And if you didn’t know the original tale, well you can play anyhow, it’s addicting as hell. Cheers!

ABOUT THIS GAME
Men of War: Red Tide is a sequel to the critically acclaimed RTS Men of War. Red Tide introduces a new story driven campaign based on the writings of Soviet scribe Alexander Zorich, it also includes dozens of new or upgraded units and weapons.
Men of War: Red Tide is a stunning mixture of RTS and a third-person action that introduces a new fighting force known for its brutal efficiency during the height of World War II. Played out across more than 20 missions, Men of War: Red Tide allows to take command of the feared "Black Coats," the nickname given to Soviet Marines, an elite combat group specializing in engagements near the shoreline.
The player has direct control of new game units including the Black Coats, tanks, self-propelled guns, armored trains, landing craft, artillery and new enemy emplaced weapons to capture and use. New air support options include fighters, bombers, hydroplanes; cruisers, destroyers and gun boats which provide naval fire support.
Fighting during the Black Sea Campaigns of WWII, history buffs and WWII aficionados will recognize theaters of battle such as Odessa, Sevastopol, Theodosia, Eltingen, Nikolaev and Constanta.
23 missions - Soviet, German, Romanian and Italian forces
Six intense historical battles and landing operations during 1941-1945
Over 100 different military units: tanks, artillery, armored cars, planes (fighters, bombers, transporters), war ships and boats (cruisers, torpedo boats, gunboats)

If you're looking for a decent story to follow and something profound to reflect on, I would steer clear of this game. The writing is poor yet tries desperately to appear deeply introspective, the characters are shallow, and the ending falls into a deus ex machina to clean up it's many loose ends, yet still does a terrible job of it all-the-while. I also found it hard to sympathize with the protagonist due to his use of homophobic and sexist slurs. Don't get me wrong--I can see the value of of doing this to build character and chart growth and development (or lack there of) for the sake of the story line, so I really did withhold my judgement until the end. But upon reaching that point, I was left dissappointed and unimpressed with his 'moral repertoire'. Instead, the insults felt thrown in there without intention, which seems to normalize their usage instead of providing any context to the already suffering plot.
That being said, the graphics are impressive (especially for an inde title) and some of the puzzles were fun, though I felt like I had done them before in other games... But neither of these things were able to overcome my chagrin for the poor writing. A lot of people seem to have a 'wtf' reaction to this game, and if that is a reward in-it-of-itself you'd be interested in, then give it a try. But if you hope to find substance in this quagmire of random philosophy references and juvenile humor, you'll be disappointed.

This game has a lot of cool aspects to it, but unfortunately the bad aspects outweigh the good ones.
This game needs some serious tuning up, or I don't think it will last very long.
I thought after being in early access for two years and finally officially launching, that it would feel more finished.
_The Good______
-Art Style is very pretty. Characters are cool looking, world scenery is beautiful.
-Open world gives a real sense of freedom and sparks the desire to explore.
-Building a base manually in an open world MMO RPG feels cool. Not many games in the genre allow you to alter the world itself for other players to see.
_The Bad______
-Weapons/tools/armor break WAY too quickly, and can NOT be repaired in any way. (You will always on the grind to make more. Always and forever. Or you'll just deal with being naked all the time and looking like an idiot like everyone else.) Almost everyone you see playing is naked, even in high level zones, because gear breaks too fast/is too costly to make. It really sucks to spend hours grinding/gathering/building so you can make the next tier of your weapon, only to find out that it breaks nearly as easily as the last one you were using. The higher tier the weapons get, the harder and more costly it is to craft them, and they break nearly as quickly as the cheap ones. Who the hell decided that was a good idea?
-Monsters literally can't hit you if you just walk away from them. This removes ANY sense of danger for being in high level zones, and makes things feel very lackluster. Even if you're fighting one and see that you can't win, you simply walk away and survive. You can go anywhere you want in the game, as soon as you jump in, and there's zero percent chance of being killed, even if you're literally naked with no weapon to defend yourself from monsters.
-Terrible animations. The animations are laughably bad. The majority of weapon attack animations and emotes look super robotic and poorly animated, and it's a real shame because the style they chose for the characters is fun and cartoony.
-The game is SEVERELY grindy, and I mean that in a bad way. Sometimes grinding is fun, but it's not in this game. I've played games where it's fun to grind mobs for hours just because the combat feels epic/entertaining. This is not a game like that.
-There aren't character levels, just levels for different skills. (Like weapon skills, and job skills such as carpentry.) Because of this, there is no option for on-screen experience bars to gauge how close you are to leveling. If I wanted to see how close to leveling I was in sword skill, I have to open up my menu and hover my mouse over the icon for it, since the circular filling bar seems flawed and doesn't display an accurate amount compared to the numbers. This makes the boring grind even worse, and you will constantly be checking how close you are to leveling a skill.
-Leveling a weapon skill takes WAY too long, and is very backwards. Every time you hit something with a weapon, you gain one exp for it. This means that always using the cheapest and weakest weapons that swing the fastest is the only way you should be training up a weapon skill. Want to use the cool new two handed axe you finally unlocked the ability to craft? Too bad, you shouldn't, that's stupid. Use the one handed starter axe instead.
-Fighting NPC enemies is really only useful for gaining anatomy skill, which gives better crit. Since you only get one exp per hit, and want to hit as many times as you can, you'll use your fast swinging/weak weapon to train on weak enemies and fall asleep IRL while doing so. Why fight stuff that hits harder? Your gear will only break faster, and you'll have to consume more food and bandages to heal up after each fight. Just find a spot where tons of low level♥♥♥♥♥♥spawns and grind there, in the starter zone, infinitely.
-Severely limited character customization aesthetically. (And no way to change your looks after a character is made.) I'd love to see more races in this game, or at least more customization for the characters. There is a real lack of hairstyles, eye colors, hair colors, beard options, etc, to choose from. Everyone looks very similar, and in an MMO many people love being able to feel unique and make their own stylistic choices.
-There are no vanity slots for armor/clothes, and when your gear breaks it turns invisible and you appear naked. (It stays in your equip slots, but is useless for anything since you can't repair. (Unless you want to sell it to the ugly ghost NPC for a few copper.)
-PVP seems to be the focus of the game, since PVE is broken and bland, but even the PVP is terrible. I ran all over the world map to discover zones and have fun exploring/gathering, and even when I got into the opposing faction starter zones and  had four people chasing me at once, there was no way they could kill me. We all had similar gear and skills I'm sure, but none of them could catch or hit me because we had the same walk/run speeds and there's no way to stun other players. It literally just became a 15 minute chase which ended in them giving up when I swam off the island.

Oblivion was my first Elder Scrolls game, and I loved it so much that I fell in love with the franchise almost immediately.  It's got an engaging storyline, lots of sidequests to keep you occupied for a good long time, and a nice open world design.  Combat takes some getting used to, but it's not nearly as boring as some folks like to claim that it is.  You just have to adapt your combat strategies in real time, learn how and when to block and so on, and be prepared to take a few hits if you get staggered (and chances are you WILL get staggered).
There are a few gripes I have about this game, though, and despite the fact that Bethesda is well known for buggy games, the bugs really aren't that big of a complaint for me.  What bothers me most about this game is that enemies scale up with you whenever you level up.  It's as if the whole wide world basically revolves around you.  At level 1 you're fighting wolves and bandits wearing cheap fur armor, but around level 6 you're fighting bandits in enchanted steel plate armor and every other bandit you encounter has magic... and then there are the trolls that you cannot kill because their health regenerates so ridiculously fast.  It's unnerving and it also really breaks any immersion that you might have gotten early on in the game.
Thankfully, there are mods you can get for this game that will allow you to tone down the problems a bit, the Unofficial Patch is a definite must with this game as it takes out most of the bugs that Bethesda never dealt with.  There are also mods that will make the game more balanced.  The only gripes I have about mods is that installation tends to be a lot more complicated than with newer moddable games like Skyrim, and that mods on this game don't seem to work as well on the Steam version as they do on the retail version.
At the same time, though, the fact that there actually is a retail version that doesn't require a Steam account is a definite plus, especially given the problems with mods on the Steam version (and there are other problems I've encountered on the Steam version as well, usually having to do with the Steam Overlay).
So in short, Oblivion is a great Elder Scrolls game.  For a game that originally came out in 2006, it's aged pretty well, and while I do recommend this game I do so with a caveat: if you want to mod this game, buy the retail version instead of the Steam version.  You'll have a lot better time installing mods and getting them to actually work on the non-Steam version than you will on the Steam version.

is a middle-of-the-road HOG that does everything right, yet doesn't manage to stand out from the pack.  It feels the work of competent and experienced HOG developers, but churning out their product with an eye to haste.
Graphics and sound are fine, but not exceptional.  There's occasionally some visible lines where the image isn't stitched together quite right.  Puzzles and HO screens are rather easy, but they are plentiful.  HO scenes are each repeated once, with respawning items, of which I disapprove, but it's still quite tolerable, as they go quite quickly.  Loclalization was hasty, so there's some grammatical errors, and one point at which the text is still in Cyrillic characters.
If it all feels a little bit uninspired, at least it offers a hefty pile of scenes and puzzles.  That's a reasonable offering for this genre.

Note:  I got the game for free, but from a kind Steam friend, not from the developer.
So...not a crowning achievement of the Hidden Object genre, but it's still worth playing.  :)
In general, I'd say this is one of the easier HOGs I've played.  As such, it's a good choice for somebody new to the genre or for a younger player.  There were two puzzles that took some work (including a dreaded 4x4 slide puzzle), but the rest were pretty straightforward.  The HO scenes were similarly straightforward:  no crazy camouflage jobs, no "never heard that word before" terms, and only the standard double-meaning words (e.g. plane).  Also the HO scenes were not particularly densely packed with throw-away, overlapping objects.
A few more things to note:
-- There's not a lot of backtracking, but neither is there a map.  But most of what you need is only a scene or two away.
-- There's no voiceover to the (infrequent) cutscenes.
-- Once you start a puzzle, you can't back out except via the Main Menu, which will reset your progress.
-- I had experienced what I believe were one or two minor bugs, but nothing major.
-- The story?  Fine I guess...standard HOG fare, maybe a click below average.
-- Easy achievements as long as you don't use hints or skips.  You probably won't need one.
-- The graphics?  Probably below average, but this game is from 2014.  It didn't distract from the experience.  The game is in a 4x3 aspect ratio, though you can stretch it to widescreen.
Like most games on Steam-- and virtually every HOG in existence-- don't pay full price.  It was recently bundled and was even free for a time somewhere.  But all that aside, the game is worth playing!  :)

This game succeeds in so many ways it deserves to be declared a MASTERPIECE.

It offers several game modes for both single player and multiplayer (online and local coop) where you face very different challenges (highest climb, longest run, collect coins, etc.) by controlling the sticky body.
The aesthetics are remarkable but the heads and bodies are customizable and there is even a 'safe for work' mode in case you find the original skins a bit too spicy ;)
Play multiplayer to split your sides, learn some techniques and make a fool of yourself; or play single player to practice or compete on the leaderboards. As it's physics based, there is always room for improvement, you never master it completely.
This is one of those games for a lifetime (and it's only $5 !!).

Endless legend does alot of things right, and a few things wrong. The overall experience is however masterfull and a joy to behold.
Firstly the things it does wrong:
-The game has a tutorial that goes as far as explaining the tried and tested tropes of the genre. It fails to explain the intricacies of what Endless Legend offers beyond this. Adding layers of complexity where little external resource exists to fill you in. The steam copy of the manual is actually usefull for once, but Learning to play a modern day game especially one that innovates in so many ways, shouldn't involve reading a 70 page pdf.
-The difficulty and overall balancing is out of wack. This only time will heal, and it will, knowing amplitudes excellent track record with supporting their tittles post launch. The best way to play this game at release is with other human beings who are as fallable and new to the experience as you.
-The combat system removes power from the player in an attempt to streamline what is often the most tedious part of the genre, player agency is important in all game genres and unless I as the player have explicitly surrendered it, it should never be taken away.
-The quest system feels pinned on to the experience the game already offers, and doesn't stand up as it's own thing, You can tell the potential and desire to enhance it was there by the devs but to date it's been squandered.
Now quickly the things that it does right:
-A slick, clean, effective, forward thinking and wholly PC interface. No big picture or touch screen nonsense here tyvm.
-Asymetrical faction design. Making each and every one of the different faction play in a unique and different way. This adds to the multiplayer joy, a 30 hour trade war mirror game where the players can't declare war on each other? priceless. An expansion faction versus a tall single city empire? totaly legit. The options are there and out of the hands of the AI totaly viable.
-It's beautifull. I've never liked blur in video games before, but whoever designed the art style of this game knew all the right things about lens shifting and lighting. And a niche love of papercrafts maybe?
-Combat. Yes it in part removes player agency forcing you to fight for control but other innovations make up for this. The combat the most arduos part of this genre is hastened by spontanious (or double spontanious) turns and a 6 turn turn limit. Combat never feels obtrusive and is actualy worth investing time in thanks to these design decisions.
-Tile exploitation and cities. This one is probably preference and others may disagree with me, but the way cities expand and exploit the FIDS resource system is very rewarding, feels organic and empowers the player. You'll learn to love triangles and spiral patterns in a weird way I swear.
-Soundtrack and art. The word eargasm doesn't exist. But it should for this very reason. The ost captures the hybrid fantasy lowtech sci-fi setting brilliantly as does the art.
Is it worth buying? I judge a games worth if I enjoy playing it over it's price in £ converted into hours. I got my copy cheap as part of a subscription service to IGN, but it retails at around £30. Check my hour count and you'll see that I can wholeheartedly recommend this game.
~Litany

Although it is a classic 4X game at its core, Endless Legent manages to bring a lot of originality and unique gameplay elements to the genre. Those new elements do take a bit of learning and adjustment (especially because each race plays very differently from the others). Tried the 1 hour CIV:BE demo. Too much of the same. So some people were recommending Endless Legend from the creators of Endless Space. I didn't like Endless space at all but this game is different.
It's very much like Civ5 in a fantasy setting and lots of extra stuff added and annoyances removed.
You can choose from 8 totally different factions or build your own one, based on an existing one.
You get side quest, faction questlines, wars that feel reasonable paced, customization for your heroes.
The present AI feels challenging and is exploiting your weaknesses. The autosaves for the last 5 turns may not be enough to save the day.
There are some things I didn't like.
In the late game the performance wasn't that great. Some infrequent crashes here and there plus balancing issues that can make the game much more hard/easy if played wrong/right.
The information overflow or the lack thereof by hiding crucial information, because you didn't know it existed, takes some time to get used to.
Overall if you're looking for an alternative for your typical 4X game, give this game a try. 8/10

Aside from that, the voice actors themselves are really unclear in what they're saying, and there's no subtitles option. It's certainly a unique game, but it's an unsatisfying one and I feel more like the unique part of it is just the developers trying to disguise that they don't know what they're doing.
