Lame duck AI, quick to declare war, throws all it's units at you, they die, then you walk into their undefended cities.  Thanks for the free cities!
I have played through two complete games at the "serious" difficulty level and both times war was forced on you and it was a cakewalk to win.  Not a builders game, not a warmongers game.  Just an exercise in beating up weaklings.
The combat system is goofy too.  You give your units basic orders ("attack that guy") then watch the round play out.  Too often units sit there with a thumb up their butt because their target is already dead.  The AI battle moves are entirely too predictable and so it becomes a puzzle in predicting how the round will play out and giving orders accordingly.  Add to that a set of attack/defense stats that pretty much just end up randomly doubling or halving damage (you always "hit" just for zero, half, normal, or double damage) and the combat is not at all compelling.  Considering the game is always a combat free for all, that's doubly problematic.
Finally, this game series is very focused on multi-player.  If you are a solo player (like me), a lot of how the systems work end up being clunky (like battle).  If Endless Space is any indication, the developers will continually tweak for multi-player and make the AI even more brain dead as they won't be able to handle the changes in the systems (Endless Space became totally unplayable for me as the patches evolved).  I can already see it starting here.
If you are a multi-player all of this might work for you.  For a solo player, I recommend waiting for a sale as this game will likely have a short shelf life.

Hey everyone,
I don't know if I've ever written a review before but I think this game warrents one.  I've been playing for about a week now and 95% of the time this game is great.  Great feel, environment, strategy... but there are some odd bugs that leave me shaking my head.
First the negatives because there are just a few:
1. Game crashes every 20-30 turns after I press "end turn" (Not a huge problem because of the autosave but sometimes I do end up just playing another game instead)
2. I wish the end of the turn load cycle had a better notification.  Sometimes I end up sitting there thinking its still loading because if there was no "event" the only notification is a soft bell sound and brief flash on the button. Again, not a huge problem but def an improvement I'd like to see.
3. The AI in battles drives me a little nuts sometimes.  It seems that the enemy AI "reacts" to your moves when there moves should be based on the same positions you based your own moves on.  For instance, they'll make a move that wouldn't have even been possible if you hadn't chosen to do something with your own units.  This does make the AI seem "smarter" but is clearly just a gross disadvantage for the human player.  This does get balanced out by the extreme strength of a hero(especially with upgrades) but I'd rather see a better balance in power and move advantages.
4.  The last piece that actually made me alt-tab to write this review was the area of effect attack on some units.  A few units get the bonus that when fighting a unit they do dmg to the other units around that unit(ex, Ice Wargs).  Others have a bonus (ex, Haunts) that have a chain attack.  The chain attacking leaping over cliffs makes sense since its traveling in the air.  The Wargs counter (sweep attack or something) should not be traveling to units that have a cliff in between them and the warg.  It makes no sense and destroys the whole point of incorporating terrain into your strategy.
5. Coming back to this review... there needs to be more readily available information about the differences between the races and how they function.  i.e. how the troops regain health.  One upgrade says that you get a discount on the instaheal for heroes but then that race doesn't offer it...
One race uses gold to heal and I use another and I can't seem to heal them unless I'm in battle.  That's great but TELL ME THAT BEFORE I PLAY THEM!
That's my two cents...
On a positive note...

I'm a fan of making my own fun in games. Pursuant to that end, when I realized that every bit of grinding and progress I'd managed in my first ten hours was basically for nothing, my homestead had been looted and fallen apart in the twelve hours I was away from the game, and (despite the fact that I had progressed as far in several professions as the materials of Newbie Island allowed) my top-tier newbie weapons couldn't scratch the "Outlaw Zone" enemies, I resolved to cross the world to drown myself in the ocean on the other end of the expansive, if utterly bland, game-world. There's no way to drown yourself in Tree of Life. I didn't care.
I collected a Green Poison Frog in a putrescent green swamp. I hauled that frog from that swamp, deciding to bring him in on my suicide pact. I had to put him down at one point to get a running leap up one of the sheer, vertical cliffs that dot the impassable landscape; terrain-humping in a manner that I'd perfected in Skyrim, I managed to scale the cliff, but had to leave my companion of nearly two in-game days behind. I collected a bull to replace him. I called him Bangs McCoy. Bangs and I made the trek across the Desert which for...reasons...abuts a dark and misty forest. We crossed the game's equivalent of the Alps... and finally made it to the sea. Bangs and I waded out into the ocean and hopped our way to the edge of the world.
This was far more satisfying than the mind-numbing grind. In every conceivable way.
I crossed the continent acquiring woodland critters, in a futile attempt to drown myself in a virtual ocean. And I went one further...I bunny-hopped across the water to the very edge of that ocean, hoping to simply fall through a hole in this cel-shaded hell. I couldn't do it. I hung there on the edge of oblivion with Bangs, treading water.
And that's kind of an apt metaphor for this game: "Treading water on the edge of oblivion."
Do not play Tree of Life. It is folly. They have my money. They don't deserve yours.

This game is simply about higher-level tactics. Military units are highly abstracted and become a statistical machine of the state. Fortune, luck and being intensely precise at the right times and being a long-term strategic thinker will heavily come to bear if you want to succeed at gaining long-term leverage and power. A lot of the game comes down to maintenence rather than expansion, though if you are going to want to expand you will need to learn how to balance expansion with maintenence, that is, keeping your vassals happy, killing the right people at the right time, marrying the right people, etc.
Though few players place much importance on the prestige system, I am one of those few people who care. There's something I autistically appreciate about the prestige system. It rewards elegance and symmetry in your game play, and it rewards you for game intuition and makes you play the game exquistely rather than brutishly. However, the game is a sandbox and if you want to play like a boorish savage then you are completely free to do so: you can revoke titles, go to war willy-nilly, usurp titles, imprison tyranically, gobble up cash whenever people throw it at you, fabricate claims, etc.
In that sense then the game forces you to think at a meta level, to think beyond and to explore more diplomatic options. You might want to join that war that your mother is fighting because you are the heir to her titles and if she wins her wars you stand to gain from her accomplishments, plus you will gain more prestige for being an indirect participant in the war. This is just one example out of many where thinking at a higher-tier is vital to the success and power of you dynasty.
With the Clausewitz engine at hand you are given the opportunity to put some military theory to the test. Few people have defined what grand strategy really is. Here's a wiki definition and some more information on grand strategy games:
[T]he role of grand strategy – higher strategy – is to co-ordinate and direct all the resources of a nation, or band of nations, towards the attainment of the political object of the war – the goal defined by fundamental policy.
Grand strategy should both calculate and develop the economic resources and man-power of nations in order to sustain the fighting services. Also the moral resources – for to foster the people's willing spirit is often as important as to possess the more concrete forms of power. Grand strategy, too, should regulate the distribution of power between the several services, and between the services and industry. Moreover, fighting power is but one of the instruments of grand strategy – which should take account of and apply the power of financial pressure, and, not least of ethical pressure, to weaken the opponent's will. ...
Furthermore, while the horizons of strategy is bounded by the war, grand strategy looks beyond the war to the subsequent peace. It should not only combine the various instruments, but so regulate their use as to avoid damage to the future state of peace – for its security and prosperity

Calling this game a Civ clone doesn't really do it justice.  It falls shy of Civ's greatness, but brings plenty to the table that civilization can't touch.  My favorite thing that stands out from this release is the style. No faction is cookie cutter, compared to say, Heroes of Might and Magic.  In that series, you have the noble knight guys, the elf guys, the undead guys, the demon guys, etc.  In Endless Legend, each faction borrows from some of the tropes but does a lot to break away from them, also.  For instance, where you might expect to find a "Wizard Faction", Endless Legend grants you the Ardent Mages, a cabal of wizards who unleash their magic through personal torment, and who learned their powers in the grip of those who once enslaved them.  To maintain their power, they torture themselves.  Or perhaps the "Noble Knight" faction who is actually the Broken Lords, a society of ghosts locked in empty suits of armor.  They harvest the worlds magic resource, "dust", to stay alive.  That is, until it's discovered they can gain power much more easily by drinking the souls of living beings.  The game takes the keen style and applies it to every aspect of the game.  Even the hex-by-hex descriptions and bonuses are intriguing.
The gameplay stands up, also.  It doesn't get bogged down as much in the later stages as Civ does, but at the same time setting goals and acheiving them for your empire seems cumbersome.  This is partially due to the increasing frequency of Winter, which comes and lasts for a few turns and first, and then becomes more common as the game progresses.  It's an interesting design decision, but generally halves just about everything you do, from movement to land bonuses.  I'm not sure the game is better off with it.
I'm still playing, and if you aren't already, you should start.

Huge thumbs up so far.  I've played through all of the races on easy, obtaining all of the victory types at least once.  This game is quite complicated and takes some getting used to.  Don't lose patience.  Knowing how Endless Space works is also very helpful - I have about 500+ hours on record in ES.  I've moved on to the higher difficulty settings now, and am finding a rewarding challenge to most/all aspects of the game.
For Endless Space owners leery of purchasing Endless Legend, I will recommend Endless Legend for one huge reason.  They kept ALL of the great things about ES intact (FIDS, race diversity, anomalies, plots & challenges) but got rid of the ONE huge annoyance with ES which was "AI fleet spamming."  It's very possible in EL to win the game with a few garrisson units protecting each city, and maybe one to two invading armies.  Sometimes even less than that.  At no point have I felt that the AI has infinite units to throw at me, so military does not have to be an 'all in' proposition.
Also, in deference to other 4X games such as Civ 4-5 and Endless Space, it is NOT critical in Endless Legend to expand as quickly as possible.  In ES, rapid early expansion is required, and in the Civ games you either have to commit to early expansion or one uber-city for the majority of each campaign.  However EL does a fabulous job (best I've ever seen actually) at letting the player expand early, late, or not at all, and still have a great time with commerce, science, culture, and growth.  The burrough system enables you to maximize one or a few cities, or you can expand as quickly as you desire across the map and find success there too.
Graphics are positively beautiful but the root mechanics of the game are near flawless.  The racial and map diversities ensure massive replayability.  The AI is very good (much improved over ES IMHO), and the story lines are surprisingly intricate while super easy to follow.
Constructive feedback for future releases:
I would like to see more racially specific tech options in future updates.  Races have delightfully diverse affinity effects, however the tech trees are relatively congruent; not many special buildings, etc.  Would also like to have a few more music tracks, but what's there is nice.  When you log as many hours as I do in these games, it's nice to mix it up.  Bugs are clearing up quickly thanks to Amplitude's impeccable customer service and response time.

I cannot tell you enough how much I love this game. I've put 40 hours into it in the last 2 weeks, with almost 120 in the last two months. I'm seriously in love. It is just such a rich, story driven, engaging, deep game. There is so much to do, so much to see, so much to explore. The content is endless.

The combat is incredibly deep and varied. There's a plethora of different ways to handle combat situations with a million different spells to use. The enemies are all extremely varied and I never felt like things were getting old or that they were recycling the same enemies too many times.

Multiplayer is also a blast. If you have friends, definitely play it with them! :)

Once again I find myself in the minority.
- The camera system is archaic and claustrophobic. I can't even think of a similarly styled game that didn't utilize edge of screen orientation in the last 20 years. What is this, 1991? Having to use the home and delete keys to look around severely impedes immersion. Furthermore, it doesn't zoom out enough.
- No option to always run. In all the games I've played over the years, there was never a time where I wanted the avatar to just "mozey" to the desired destination. And because the camera is so claustrophobic, you have to click near the edge of the viewport to initiate the run sequence, even though you may not wish to run all the way to the edge.
It's akward and un-natural, and that destroys any chance for immersion for me personally. I'm going to try for a refund.
As for the story so far, it's cliche to the point of agitating. You start off in bondage. Have to escape. Whoah side quest go backwards and rescue poor helpless people. Yada yada. That's 8 out of 10 story lines. I just don't see how this game commanded the overwhelmingly positive reviews it has.

I loved Divinity Original Sin Enhanced it was quiet the Experience.  It was this sort of magical, funny, serious world that reminded me of Fable as an isometric 3d game.
The battles were incredible!    It was damn fun and evolving, and my first game was 222 hours.
When Divinity Original Sin II(I was part of the kickstarter) came out I waited a bit before I decided to dive in and play it.
Just to make sure most bugs were gone.
My playing time through Divinity Original Sin II is 240 hours.   Once again we have a very deep evolving game.
Divinity Original Sin II has probably one of the best Battle setups of any RPG as Turn base Combat.   You can, like Divinity Original Sin Enhanced, use the enviroment to your advantage and use a plathora of skills, and spells.
This time the game tries to be bigger then the first one.   This time the characters try to be deeper and more part of the story.
One thing Divinity Original Sin II does well is keeping all the characters and stories including smaller quests connected and part of the larger Whole, which is Large!
The Game has many parts each one a Chapter that you play through.   Each Chapter will have something to do with the chapter before.  There are tons of Quests on the sidelines you can finish or not finish.    These chapters connect the whole story to the end and it's very wel done!
Divinity Original Sin II asks for a new Divine is that your Goal then to be the New Divine?  You have to play and see!
The Graphics have been improved over the first one and the game looks beautiful!  Very beautiful with great lighting fx!
Once again there is all voice acting like Divinity Original Sin Enhanced and that voice acting really works at enhacing the world and story.
It also has some nice ambiant music, and few good themes.
Does well to arrange and create varations of the theme as a recuring theme for the game.
I has interesting characters that are part of the story that you will meet on your adventure.
The battles are deep, hard, and fun!
Divinity Original Sin II tries to be little more serious little more darker then Divinity Original Sin Enhanced.
It's a success yes but it also has that Grin in the background, not taking it's self to seriously through out even with it's darker undertones.
If you like Role Playing Games then you need to buy this!  It's very long romp through a world that is more serious and darker then first one.   With a well connected story and some deep characterizations.
An upgrade if you will to an already successful formula that made Divinity Original Sin Enhanced a Smashing Success!

tree of life has a lot of cool mechanics and ideas going into it. it's a runescapey/sandbox game where you just grind and progress for the sake of it. the combat's simple, the crafting's simple, and the game doesn't hold your hand much, and that feels great.
however, the game has completely lost direction and the developers *regularly* ignore their playerbase. they basically do whatever they want and don't bother to fix bugs or prevent hacking. as of the official release, the game absolutely favors griefing and picking on new players. there is NO penalty for robbing and killing people. if you decide you want to go kill new players and steal all their stuff, you can and they can't do anything about it. unless you have a very active, very large group of people, your guild will get destroyed very quickly as soon as you leave the starting area. after spending about 5 hours in the starting area, i decided to move my guild of two people to an area adjacent to the starting area, and within 5 hours it got robbed 12 times and then completely destroyed twice. it's very easy to avoid the defenses that someone can build in their guild, and very easy to destroy the whole guild.
i loved this game in early access. people didn't ♥♥♥♥ with you and there was even a neutral faction where you and your guild could be pvp protected so you could just enjoy your grinding. the pvp factions just happily fought amongst themselves and everyone else relaxed. long ago the game was very pve focused, but now the pve content is just for building up your guild defenses to protect yourself from griefers. now there's absolutely no way to be neutral, and these features were removed for absolutely no reason. it's what i mean by "the developers basically do whatever they want".
some people will probably enjoy the game as is, but everything that made me interested in this game is gone. i guess that's what you get with early access. i won't be playing the game again until these features get restored, or i can at least spend an hour offline without my guild and all the defenses i can possibly build getting destroyed.

Sonic Mania takes the series back to its roots with some good old fashioned 2D sidescrolling platforming.
Pros:
Gameplay (9/10):
The gameplay in Sonic Mania feels just like the old Mega Drive/Genesis games. Smooth, responsive, and no input lag. There's also a new move called the Drop Dash, which executes a short spin dash when you hit the ground after jumping. The level designs are well made, and have various paths to take. The special stages are also pretty cool.
Soundtrack (10/10): Very rarely I give anything a perfect 10 out of 10 score, but this soundtrack deserves it. Every track in the game is wonderfully composed by Tee Lopes, who did such an amazing job at creating some epic, catchy tunes. I'm absolutely addicted to the music in this game, and could listen to it for hours on end.
Graphics (9/10):
The graphics in Sonic Mania are very reminiscent of the older style games from the Mega Drive/Genesis era. The graphics are colourful, vibrant, and overall very pleasing to look at. The low poly 3D models really fit the Saturn era aesthetic well too.
Cons:
I can't think of any cons gameplay wise, but as many other people have said, the game uses Denuvo DRM. Why this is necessary in a single player game I have no idea. However, I'm not going to let it ruin the game for me, it's just a minor inconvenience.
Overall score: 9/10
Despite the the inclusion of Denuvo DRM, Sonic Mania is still an amazing game, and one of the best Sonic games ever made. If you enjoyed the classics, you will absolutely love this.

Time for yet another update. Firstly, I'm quite excited about the new Starstorm Map. Let's see what the Devs cooked up for us. Secondly, I have the impression that the almighty Matchmaking got both, better and worse. Why both you might ask?
Well, 'better' because I have the impression skill levels among teams are not so damn skewed anymore. Seems more even. I have to admit I am enjoying a lot more matches recently. Also, I noticed an increase in crazy comebacks. Boy, did we wreck that one team last night after our base got down to one bar of HP :)
Actually, I am close to changing this review into "Thumbs up".
BUT (Don't be discouraged by the long text below, stay with me here):
'Worse' has gotten the amount of RQs (Rage Quitters). Understandably so. You (not me of course ^^) join a match, 15 minutes in against a "premade team", 3 turrets down. Why waste time on that, right? Just leave, or go afk or feed, it usually won't matter. You'll lose anyway, get your ranking decreased etc. This is the stuff Rage is made of. Don't get me wrong, I've been there, done that. But that just seems weird. Somebody RQs, he gets punished. Then you take his place. Whether you RQ or stay, it is very likely that you also get punished and lose ranking anyway. And the infinte loop of RQ - late join - RQ continues. And now it gets even worse: Imagine, if you so will, the following: You and your team harmonize, you dominate or simply put: YOU PWN YOUR ENEMIES. Now, somebody decides to RQ, is temporarily replaced by a bot, then by another players. Good so far. BUT: remember that "late-join" bonus? Yeah, it's insane. Now lets continue that train of thought: One RQ: no problem. Two: meh, I can handle it. Three or more (and believe me it's more common than you might think): YOU WILL PROBABLY LOSE. All of a sudden, all the late-joiners accumulate a MASSIVE amount of bonusses. Seriosuly, its not even funny. They will simply out-bonus you. Even if you dominated earlier, RQs result in a massive shift in resources. And that♥♥♥♥♥♥is simply broken.
Short version of the above: RQs beget RQs, leading to Bonus town, USA.
Minor stuff I'd also like to nag about:
Premade vs. solo : C'mon devs, still? At least show me that I am playing againt pres.
Lag: pew pew .......................................death
Don't get me wrong here, I like this game (got a couple of in-game hours). But would I recommend it to new players? Probably only to those who are willing to live with minor and major flaws. Then, go ahead, grab the game and hop in, it is fun. If you are prone to anger? Look elsewhere.
Have a good day, everybody.

Okay, first thing's first:
I really hate them. The fantasy/myth/RPG styled theme, all the nonsense you need to cram into your brain faster than forgetting to study for a test and doing it last minute (I personally can tolerate that kind of stuff, but not with MOBAs) and the hostile communities make me hate them. Hate's a strong word, too.
However, Awesomenauts is a significant turn for the better. Although the online multiplayer has its share of issues, Awesomenauts stands out from the rest and is what MOBAs should be like.
The graphics are cartoon-like, with a cheerful (yet dark at the same time) atmosphere. No fantasy stuff here, Awesomenauts is a sci-fi theme and that's something worth seeing after the same old MOBA. I love the visuals for the game, and I see nothing wrong with them.
The gameplay is simpler at first for the rookie MOBA player. Shoot stuff, (attacking without abilities has a bit of a meaning now, hooray!) use your abilities to get an edge over the other 'Nauts, and much more. But then, when you get into it, you'll start analyzing your playstyle to suit your needs with that 'Naut, how to take on the opponent in a one-on-one, and more. Although I did experience significant amounts of lag that costed me quite a few deaths and also really bad matchmaking, the gameplay is still solid to me.
The story is simple and straightforward. You play as an Awesomenaut (or Lonestar in the tutorial) and you need to destroy the enemy's Solar drill. Solar is crucial to your employer for an unknown reason, and you need to destroy the drill so you hinder the enemy's Solar supply. MOBAs are known for their lore, and although this game lacks lore compared to other MOBAs, Awesomenauts doesn't fit in the category of a fantasy/RPG world like this.
The audio is probably the key point to the game. The music (especially the theme song, just play the trailer if you haven't done so already) is outstanding, and the themes really get into your head. My personal favorite themes are Froggy G, Yuri, and the new character Scoop. The voice actors did an OUTSTANDING job with playing the characters and don't seem all bold or shrouded like most MOBAs do. Each one has their own personality that makes them unique from the others, and if I'm not mistaken, popular Youtuber TotalBiscuit even voiced one of the characters (Vinnie and Spike I believe) which I found pretty interesting. The audio overall to this game is near perfection, and I feel empty inside without those "
" songs.
The replayability is pretty massive. I don't want to touch up here much because it's a MOBA. Its easy to get hundreds of hours logged onto a MOBA.
For one thing though, Awesomenauts has some major pros that don't fit into any of the five main categories. The developers are dedicated, for one. They constantly release updates and even do some charity work. Check out Lonestar's Private Mels (?) skin. A kid came in from the Make-a-Wish Foundation and made his own skin for his favorite Awesomenaut. The updates keep on rolling in, and the most recent (as of this review anyway, 2.7 in case you're wondering) introduces Scoop, buffed every character in the game, gained a new main menu, and so much more it's better I keep my mouth shut. One more thing though that sets Awesomenauts apart from the rest is that the community is
You don't get yelled at for screwing up, you actually GET help when you need it, and so Awesomenauts makes me feel comfortable when I get on.
In the end, Awesomenauts may be in my least favorite game genre, but who cares? Awesomenauts still got a thumbs-up from me. Aside from a few online flaws, Awesomenauts is a game that fails to disappoint me, and is one amazing adventure not worth missing.

I am an empire builder. The Civilization series is one of my favorite of all time. About one year ago, I bought Endless Space (made by this company), and it completely redefined the genre. Amplitude Studios does an excellent job of creating new 4X games with a spin. You will spend a minimum of 50 hours playing each faction to mastery, and you will still not know it all. Endless Legend has yet again redefined what I think of the 4X genre.
Pros:
-Factions vary greatly yet are somehow balanced to a degree.
-Absolutely gorgeous world. I have spent 20 minutes looking at the planet Auriga.
-Incredible lore. Who are the Endless? Where did they go? Will we ever find out?
-Tech tree redefined. Technology is non-linear, but gated by 'eras' for balance and interesting civilizations.
-Real-time economic marketplace. Prices for resources change based on player and AI consumption.
-Fluid combat. Battles are highly strategic.
-Reactive AI. That battle you just won with 6 archers? Well the AI created 6 cavalry with bonus damage to range.
-User-based city evolution. You decide WHEN and WHERE your city expands (one of my personal favorite features).
-Breathtaking soundtrack.
-Equippable units and heroes. Complete customization of your army with different resources.
Cons:
-Sometimes game saves are corrupted, but the game autosaves every turn so you just lose 1 turn.
-AI movement happens during your turn, so you can cheese the AI and move twice before they move.
-Embarking units requires a tech which can easily be missed. This is really only a problem for novices.
-Flying and support units so far seem lackluster, making infantry, cavalry, ranged my go-to choices.
-You can annihilate a faction within 20 turns if you rush them. Of course, you can just choose not to do this.
I will edit this list as more ideas come my way.

I want to start off by saying, I was not impressed by Endless Space. So going into this game I was highly skeptical and I felt that Age of Wonders 3 was going to be a superior game in all aspects. Also, if you'd rather watch my review rather than read it, well, here you go:
Thankfully, I was horribly wrong. Endless Legend is a refreshing 4X Fantasy Turn-based Strategy game that has a beautiful aesthetic, simply beautiful music and an incredibly immersive world. Artistically, you can see where Amplitude was trying to create it's own world rather than copy and paste the Civ Map and formula with it's interesting terrain design, huge assortment of resources and even its graphical style. Exploration in this game is an absolute treat and you will find yourself scouting out the various corners of the world with glee; meeting new races, looting abandoned ruins, and solving the mysteries of this ancient world. Amplitude continues to flex is development muscle with it's intricate Unit Customization tools which are incredibly simplistic yet allow for all sorts of loadout variants for your troops and heroes.
What's wrong with the game you ask?
The worst thing (which isn't even that bad) is the combat system. From the time I have put into it, it really seems like it plays itself, just like Endless Space. Essentially, I spend far more time autoresolving the battles rather than playing them. The tutorial is also not incredibly effective at explaining a lot of the economic portions of the game or even explaining the finer points of the battle system.
All in all, this game is freaking awesome and has proved to be one of the best modern 4x games to date! Hats off to Amplitude, you've made a fan out of me.

Endless Legend is an extremely addictive 4X simulation game with a great story and excellent gameplay features. I haven't been this excited about a game in quite a long time, and as a long time 4X veteran - (all the CIVs, Alpha Centauri, Colonization, Master of Magic, Master of Orion, Fallen Enchantress), this game is definitely a stand out.

I have NEVER written a review before, I normally don't think  it's necessary even if I like a game or not, but Tree Of Life [ToL for short] is a game that I have sunken a lot of time into and stuck around for many different versions of the game. None of them are as bad as the newly released-not-in-bata version or whatever you want to call it.
Before I start really complaining about how quickly this game went down the drain for me, i'd like to explain the game as whole. If you enjoy logging into a game and knowing that most of your time will be filled with chopping trees or wondering around looking for a resource until your inventory is full with said resource so you can craft 100 of an item you may or may not need in order to level up a certain skill, then you wouldn't mind the grind of ToL. The first time I ever played this game I was dumped off at a beach by myself 0 information and they weren't many people around to help. I was truly alone to explore and venture freely and I loved it. I wouldn't say that this game is something you should play solo, I 100% suggest finding at least one other person to play with because you only have so many skill points to invest into your tree and although certain skills aren't nearly as important as others, it's nice to be able to dabble into different things.
When I first joined, everything was open PvP and that didn't bother me all too much, I got killed a few different time, stolen from on occasion and lost a few buildings from time to time, which I would easily deal with. Once I was more settled, I rarely had anyone mess with me. Eventually the factions came out. Three PvP centered ones and then one neutral faction that couldn't be affected by the other three. I personally am not one for PvP, but it was also good for new players to get on their feet before choosing to cross over to anther faction. It was super reassuring to me that I could play this game in much more laxing way. In all honesty, ToL is a very relaxing game without having to worry about the PvP. Most people did not enjoy the PVP system at the time because it was centered around fighting over relics, which gave out buffs to whichever faction owned them. So, people would just swap factions for the buffs and no one would actually fight.
Which is why I think the devs didn't really think about the new PvP system enough. People complained that no one was fighting because there nothing to really fight for when you can just join the faction with the most power and didn't need to fight. So now, your dumped off on a shore, but unlike before you can't really just go anywhere because they made certain things level capped.. I mean you can leave your faction's newbie area but the mobs are super strong and hardly worth killing in the higher leveled areas.So it's really not worth leaving, even more so because they took away the neutral faction so not only do you have to worry about giant spiders ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on your chest, but some random enemy faction, at any level even the starting area can come on over, kick your♥♥♥♥♥ steal your stuff, break your buildings and kill your live stock. You can't log out for more than hour with out anything I just mentioned in the last sentence happening to your stuff. If you don't have the time to stay logged in to protect your stuff then there really is no point in playing. Plus everything is so packed tight with people right now, that resources are scarce so being stolen from so early on is honestly tough. Even with what's considered your guild's protection; an arrow tower. It shoots arrows out at red named people [enemy factions], but all they have to do it step out of your guild's bounds and heal up before going back to kill your tower and they rinse and repeat this process until the towers dead and you have nothing left when you log back on.
I can't keep up with the theft game this MMO has become. It's sad really, I wanted more out of this game. I really wanted to enjoy it. Everyone is just out to beat up on the newer little guys and it's a♥♥♥♥♥♥show since there really isn't anything else to fight over. Just everyone scewing each other for no REAL purpose other than ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-ier.

One of the best 4x games I've played. It has a few mechanics that take a little getting used to, but really fit the setting and lore well.
Settling a city claims an entire pre-defined region. No other faction can use that region.  Cities work tiles by having those tiles be within or adjacent to a "district" which can be built as the city grows in population.
The tech "tree" is not a tree at all, but simply 6 ages worth of techs. You unlock the next age by researching enough from previous ages. This really gels with the lore of the game, because much of discovery is re-discovering lost knowledge of the Endless.
Combat takes place between armies (stacks of units), while you can auto-resolve, the real joy is playing out a mini 6-turn battle between armies. The mini battle takes place on a small section of the grid surrounding the armies curret locations. The battle is similar to those you might find in "tactical strategy" games, except you have a little less control. Overall pretty satisfying.
The last cool mechanic is how units are improved. You will research improvements for weapons, armor, etc, and then design upgrades for your current units (or brand new units).  You can then retrofit existing units with those upgrades.
This game runs so damn smoothly that the AAA developers should use this as an example how the game should perform.

Rating: 8/10
Pros:
- Beautiful Scenery that you actually enjoy looking at (with thankfully the option to view a more 'map' perspective if you dont want the visual clutter).
- Variety of Factions with unique abilities to supplement faction units
- Province System prevents the game from being about mass spam of cities, forces consideration on where in a province a city should be placed, and can also encourage more battles.
- Open ended tech tree with no pre-reqs (beyond having enough tech to reach the next tech age) is very nice and allows a lot of flexibility and creativity.
Cons:
- With only 3 units per faction, you're a little limited on choices. The Factions do exist to provide variety, but you have to side track yourself to get enough slots to have more than one of those  factions units available for supplementing your forces.
- Game can be a little tedious as it gets later
- Ai is terrible at city planning and positioning.
- Ai also tends to be very passive
- The above issues mean that, if someone joins your multiplayer session after it started (or had internet issues and reconnect a bit later), they're usually in a terrible position
- Multiplayer matchmaking is poor, often showing only 1-6 games available, even when there are more games online (often had issues where people I know make a game and I can't see it, forcing me to get an invite from them).
In Conculsion: While the game has a lot of flaws, it's still ultimately fun to play, and a nice casual game you can easily spend an afternoon playing. I don't know if i'd recommend it for veteran strategy gamers, but it's definitely good for newbies or moderately skilled players.

Oh boy, where to start?  In the past, I've played the original Divinity, multiple GOTY RPGs such as The Witcher III and Skyrim, along with playing Dungeons and Dragons for years.  After beating this game on classic difficulty, I've realized it is my favorite game of all time, trumping those previously mentioned.
Divinity 2 is the closest I've ever seen a video game get to DnD, near perfectly emulating the freedom of the players.  Notice how I didn't say sense of freedom or illusion of freedom.  Other games try to decieve you into thinking your actions matter, when in all actuality, they make little to no difference.  Here, the game responded multiple times to actions I had done dozens of hours prior.  Not only in simple little references, some had astronomical impacts.  There are also 4 different endings with significant, world-changing differences. You can try to kill anyone, try to steal anything, and have to live with the consequences.  It doesn't hold your hand, and because of that, it makes every decision and discovery you make feel like your own.
Divinity 2 is also a huge step up from the previous game, mainly in terms of overall polish.  The original game was great, however there was an incredibly boring starting zone, poor music, sub par graphics, and nonexistent character in your party.  This sequel does what any true sequel does and improves on the old, in nearly every way, while adding new elements.  Upgraded music, graphics, along with the introduction of origin characters with some of the best writing I have ever seen help breathe more and more life into an already thriving world.  The developers also streamlined the combat system while keeping the depth that make it the king of tactical rpgs.
One of the things that stood out to me was how good the story was and told.  With a lot of big, AAA games such as destiny, there is an amazing story, but the delivery is mediocre, turning a great concept into a meh grind.  Here, everyone is fully voice acted well.  You can tell from talking to people in game that this was a labor of love.  The actors poured their hearts and souls into their performance and it really shows.  The story is also brimming with twists and turns that you never see coming, which caused me on occasion to stop in shock, before yelling at the monitor or tearing up.  There is also one origin story character quest (Lohse's) which really hit me hard.  Never have I ever been so happy for a character before.
Then there is the multiplayer.  This game was a full and satisfying package on its own.  But on top of that, they added drop in and drop out multiplayer, so you can experience on of the best games ever with your friends.  There's an arena mode for pure combat.  AND A GM MODE TO CRAFT YOUR OWN GAMES.  This is huge.  The fact that I can run a Pen and Paper RPG for my friends through a medium such as this opens the floodgates to opportunities normally nonexistent if it was just a normal game of DnD.  It also gives people who host online games the option to give their players the  impression of a more living, breathing world.
The only negative aspect of the game I have experienced are the bugs.  They are few and far between, only amounting to a rare crash, or the voice acting not loading or being delayed.  However, Larian studios are hard at work and have been continually sending out patches to address these issues.
Best game I have EVER played.  I finished the game in 85 hours, doing everything I could along the way, and it's not even $60!

I remember learning about the Elder Scrolls series from my older brother, who purchased Morrowind on the original Xbox. I was never really interested in playing it because I was 7 years old at the time, but I always liked watching him play. About 3 years later, a friend of my brothers brought over another Elder Scrolls game, this one called "Oblivion". We all played it together, and I participated this time. And I fell in love with it. I still remember times from when I was 11 years old, all the lights turned off in my house, nothin' but me and my Xbox in my living room, playing Oblivion for 6 straight hours. Time well spent...
Elder Scrolls, for those who are unaware, is an Action RPG. Imagine Fallout set back in Medieval times, but way better because there's swords and magic! There's not a single complaint I have about Oblivion; it's damn near flawless, at least in my opinion. There's a bit of bugginess here and there, such as getting stuck on mountains, disappearing items/NPC's, etc. But that's a Bethesda game for you! Jokes aside though, the number of times those kinds of glitches have happened to me are few and far between over 7 years of playing this game. The level-up system is fantastic, combat is so good, great set of sidequests, and you can even go to literally HELL.
The one Elder Scrolls game everyone knows is Skyrim. But for those who have only played Skyrim and no other Elder Scrolls game, I strongly encourage you to give Oblivion a fair try. You will not be disappointed.

I have to be honest, when I first installed this game, I just went to the Store page, clicked Free-to-play and wandered around searching for games to lollygag on. I was pretty confused when I saw some screenshots of "Only If" in the store page, because it was single player, wasn't riddled with micro-transactions and was a puzzle game. Something I'd not expect from a free to play game.
Then, a second thought occurred into me: it must be some sort of small project, an experimental one, probably by a "one man team" where they did all the coding, texturing, etc.
Thankfully, I was wrong. I was expecting somewhat outdated graphics, stretched textures, terrible movement, possibly an open world "Get X before Y catches you" sort of formula, average or no music/ambience at all but instead I was presented with gorgeous soundtrack, truly beautiful graphics, a solid storyline which most games lack and great movement (the crouching is a bit odd, but it must be that I'm not used to it).
I played about 75 minutes (probably because I rushed the thing or found just one ending, if there are more) and only found possibly one bug/glitch of sorts which is the lack of collision on the trees, but I guess it is a signature "feature" of the Unity Engine. I truly enjoyed playing this game and some of the tricks the game presented (not saying any as I'm trying to keep this spoiler-free) made me shout "Why didn't I think of that in the first place?!" or "How in the seven hells can I be this dumb?!". One thing that I think is missed here is probably subtitles, it might be nitpicking or even a personal preference, but sometimes the voices of the characters are shadowed by other sounds, music or even the fact that you might be too far away to hear them clearly. As a result, I lost some of the speech and sometimes wandered randomly not knowing what to do.
Moreover, I was astounded that this game was free, I wouldn't expect this amount of work for a game distributed free. Great voice acting, great characters (althought an intro of sorts would be nice; but I may have missed it completely) mainly Vinny, which is not the usual neutral-voiced narrator. Instead, he has his wit which I do adore.
In conclusion, it is a great game and its well worth the 75 minutes I've spent playing and the 1,34 gigs it occupies in my hard-disk. I have to apologize if this review is kind of messy because I haven't written a review that wasn't longer than five words. But either way, thank you Creability (if I'm spelling this right) for this game and I hope you can continue doing these type of games.

Riven has to be one of the most beautiful games ever made, hands down the visuals and ambiance are just wonderful, even now years after its release.  What is Riven though?  Simply put, it is a puzzle adventure game, very laid back and methodical, it is one of the last classic point and click adventure games.  All the environments are pre-rendered image montages and it features a few live action cutscenes.  The story has you as a mysterious stranger, who has been recruited by the writer, Atrus, and tasked you with rescuing his wife from his megalomaniac father, Gehn… both Atrus and Gehn mastered a technique called ‘The Art’ which basically allows their writing to physically create worlds, called Ages… Gehn has taken Atrus’ wife to his collapsing Age of Riven, where you must navigate and solve puzzles in order to find her and Gehn before it is too late.  The game is huge, the puzzles ranging from simple to mind boggling world spanning contraptions.
Unlike anything ever.  It has no peers.  It is genre-defining and genre-reigning.  Only sad part is, you really should play Myst first, and Myst is a tad bit outdated in graphics and puzzle-gameplay.

You are trapped in the world of Riven and must explore and interact with objects to find a way to escape.  You are not alone in this world, and you are not the only prisoner.  There is no combat, there is no time limit or urgency, and there is no way to die in error.  There are alternate endings.
This is an exploration puzzle game, and if you finish without any help you're a genius.  The game had gorgeous graphics and animations for its time, but if you play it in its unstretched, native resolution now it's about the size of a 5x7 photo.  Still, that didn't stop me from being able to complete the game and puzzles (with some help) and it still looks good.  What little music the game has is great too, but most is ambient.
What makes the game so difficult is a combination of trial and error, clues being very cryptic or difficult to decipher, and many objects you interact with that feel like they may be related to solving a puzzle aren't.  Crashed on me several times in Windows 7.

What makes this Sonic better than the other Sonic games you ask? In short, the fans.
You see there have been some who have complained that some of the Sonic games were not as good as some the classic games (and I can see what they mean with some of those games). So some people decide to make fan games which players would want to play. Those players played those games and the Sonic Team noticed this. It was then they realised they could get the same people to create a new Sonic game.
This is what the game is, a game made by fans for the fans. Do you miss some the iconic levels in Sonic 1-3? This game has some of the best choices. Does it have new levels which are as fun as the classic levels? Yes. Does it have the 2 player split screen like in Sonic 2? Yes it does.
In short, this game is made for those who loved the classic Sonic games while adding a nice new touch to it.

tl;dr version: buying base is good enough, lots of fun and potential salt, DLC just makes the game more fun IMO.  Paywall is kinda funky, not too expensive, and is totally optional.  8.5/10, would trigger friends and rip hair out of salt again :^)
This game makes me feel one of two emotions: complete and utter rage/salt, or absolute guilt over how much of a scumbag I can really be at video games.  The cartoony exterior hides a very well done multiplayer board game, much similar to Mario Party.  However, the main objective of the game is to reach the requirements for missions, which are either "Collect X amount of stars" (stars replace coins in this game) or "Defeat X amount of opponents," then you turn in those missions at "home spots," which are the panels that have signs posted on them, to increase your mission rank.  The first one to complete and turn in six missions is the winner.  The game uses cards that every player brings to the game, and all the cards in a player's deck is added to the main deck in which everyone takes from, aside for some cards that only certain characters can use.  Each card has a value where you use the stars that you collect as you go across the board  There are 4 types of cards (5 if you have the Acceleration DLC pack):
Event (which can be activated before the start of the movement roll)
Battle (which can be used before a battle, the mechanics of which I'll go into later)
Trap (which, like Event, can be used before the start of movement, but instead of being actively used at the moment, you place it on your current panel and is triggered when someone ends their movement on that spot)
Blaster (basically, unique cards that only the character your playing can use).
(The 5th would be the Gift Type, which is introduced in the Acceleration Booster Pack DLC.  This type is basically a curse type of card, where you activate it and pass it on to another player, who then incurrs the effect)
In the board, there are 7 panel types to land on.
Blank (Gray): nothing happens, but this spot is highly uncommon on board maps in this game.
Bonus (Yellow): when landed on, this spot gives you stars based on your current mission level and die roll.
Battle (Red): when landed on, this spot forces a battle encounter with a board enemy, which are just a chicken, a seagull, and a weird robot ball thing.  Upon a player reaching mission rank 4, certain battle spots will turn into Boss spots, which will force a high powered monster to fight you.  Don't expect to one-shot the boss.
Warp (Purple): when landed on, this spot teleports the player to another random Warp panel on the board.
Drop (Blue): basically the opposite of the Bonus panel, based on your mission level and die roll, you will lose stars when landing on this spot.
The main distinction between this game and Mario Party is the way competition between players is done.  In Mario Party, you had minigames and would even sometimes fight against the board's unique bullcrap, like with board-specific Bowser events and such.  In this game, the board-specific events are either benefical to everyone, like allowing all players to draw cards, or inconveniences that range from slight to totally annoying, like random warp or having everyone lose 1 HP at the initiation of the event.
Replacing the minigames is a battle system that relies on the roll of a die and boosts/deductions of offensive/defensive stats.  The attacking player can only attack and can use Battle cards to boost their stats or reduce their opponents, and from there, the attacking player will roll a 6-sided die to determine base damage, which is boosted/reduced based on their character-specific stats.  The defending player can either Guard, which will reduce damage by the difference of the attacking roll by the Guard roll and will deal a minimum of 1 damage even if the Guard roll is higher than the attacking roll, or Evade, where the defending player must roll higher than the attacker; a roll equal to or lower will result in the player receiving the full attack roll as damage.  This battle system can lead to some strategy in when and where to stop movement and attack a player.
The campaigns are just short little stories about why each character is in the game.  Most character campaigns consist of about 6 episodes, which have you play on a board, sometimes with certain conditions.  Completing these campaigns also grants the ability to buy more characters at the shop.  Certain characters, such as the board minions (chicken/seagull/robot) and even the board bosses, are purchasable after reaching a certain level in the online mode.  Lowkey, I really want to play as the chicken or the seagull.
While the game is super fun even with the base content, there is still one or two things that bother me a bit.  My only gripe is how exclusive some of the content is.  Of course, you have your DLC packs and such, which isn't too much to be honest.  However, some content, like certain characters, are only accessible if you own certain titles done by Fruitbat Factory.  If I happen to buy at least one of these titles, I'll make an edit on whether or not you get your money's worth, but at the moment, its up in the air.  Another issue I have is the lack of a local multiplayer mode.  The game is pretty cheap, even when not on sale, being only 6 dollars, but it'd be nice to have a local multiplayer, kinda like a pass-and-play system, for when you have company over.  Hopefully, that type of system is being worked on.
Regardless of these slight discrepancies, the game is loads of fun.  The base game alone has loads to do and can bring back similar moments of triumph and salt that Mario Party would bring.
Score 8.5/10, Would trigger friends and rip hair out of salt again :^)

This is the kind of game that will forever top the "best ever" lists of grand strategy as long as the genre continues to exist. Especially when you consider the absolutely mammoth dragon horde of add-ons that have come out since the game first hit shelves years ago. CK2 up to this point is probably 6 times the scope and breadth it was when it started, and it just keeps getting bigger.
So what is it?
Well, to put it bluntly, it's whatever you want it to be. The best way to describe it would be a Royal Dynasty simulator. With all the intrigue, betrayal and surprise of a Game of Thrones episode (don't believe me? Check out the insanely great GoT mod that has been made for this game). You can pick and play any ruler (or Duke, or Count) of significance throughout the entirety of medieval history. With all the addons you can play a game that spans nearly 1000 years. Guiding your dynasty as a lowly count, backstabbing, scheming and marrying your way to the crown.
Marrying is important. When your character bites the dust (and there are soooo many hilarious ways for this to happen...my most recent King♥♥♥♥♥♥himself to death) you can continue playing as your heir.
Ack. It's damn hard to explain the insane depth of this game. If you put in the time to learn all the mechanics, you can lose hours as your imagination runs wild, while you plan your next move towards the crown...or the crown next door!

This game does a lot of things I respect.  It is difficult but always gives you a chance to survey the challenges ahead of you instead of killing you off unfairly.  And the combat requires alertness and reaction, not button mashing.
Unfortunately, the fun is completely drained by some incredibly asinine design choices.  You have four lives to complete the game from start to finish.  There is no saving, not even the option to temporarily save and quit.  Nor is the options menu accessible mid-game, so if you want to take a break you either have to keep listening to the game's music or mute your entire computer.  Although the game is reportedly short, I don't appreciate my progress being held hostage when life interrupts.
You'll find multiple weapons, but they're all the same sword with different damage and 3 or 4 magic effects that can proc randomly.  However, I couldn't see any way to tell whether a sword was enchanted until after I picked it up.  So it's never a good idea to pick up a sword that deals less damage than your current sword, because you can't pick up your previous sword after you find out its true properties.
The level design is non-linear, but in the most obnoxious way.  After completing a room you will frequently find branching exits.  However, you still have to take those exits in the order the game intended, otherwise you will find a locked door for which you haven't yet obtained the key and have to backtrack so you can pick the other path.  Why lie to me by telling me I have a choice when I'm just going to get punished for making the choice I wasn't supposed to?
I love difficult games, but I hate having my progress wiped away and being arbitrarily forced to do the same opening challenges over and over.  When I hit a difficult part and get a game over, I don't want to spend ten minutes fighting my way back to that point, I want to keep practicing that room I figure out how to proceed.  This game is deliberately wasting my time and I cannot respect that.
And to anyone who thinks I'm just a scrub who couldn't handle a difficult game, I beat it on the fourth try, total playtime less than 90 minutes.  There are only two difficult rooms and they're the exact same challenge copy-pasted.  There is zero replay value either, just some achievements that don't look any fun.
I've seen people compare this to Dark Souls, and I hope those people are joking.  Dark Souls encourages exploration, has varied environments rich in backstory, scores of interesting enemies, multiple viable character types and fighting style, and lets you try challenges as many times as you want.  This has none of that.
Don't pay more than a dollar for this game.

First, you're competing with a great many people for resources. There are no chests to be created like in MineCraft, and instead there are survival tents. Which some people see as fair game to raid while you're off trying to grind those same resources to actually do anything. Eventually, you can make a Warden Tree, but it can only be planted if you're in a guild as it, along with survey stakes, will mark out a territory for your guild which will actually prevent anyone from taking your stuff - for seven days. Then you have to pay a 6 silver fee (which seems to be the equivalent of 600 copper, but I could be wrong since I never reached the silver coins) to extend that protection. Not good nor fun if you want to play solo, and it reminds me a great deal of just a fancier version of the Empire app games where you have to keep shelling out money to protect your stuff or you get wiped out by one of the bigger empires out there. I had people going through my stuff while I was right there working on various other things, taking my hard won resources.

Definitely would only recomend it to anyone who enjoys those Empire app games, but for an MMORPG experience, it falls flat.

After putting in 35 hours into Endless Legend, I can say that it is a pretty solid game (8.5 to 9.0 in my opinion) if you are into 4X type games.
Pros: The multiple factions give every race a unique spin on how they play, research and interact with other main factions (and minor factions). The art, graphics and music of this game are one of the best of the 4X genre (in my opinion). Having the main story quest and side quests during the game also help keep the player engaged throughout a play through which is something that I believe the Civ games could learn from. The tech options are numerous enough that you will most likely not be able to research them all which adds to the importance of which ones to research based on how your race (or you) plays. Another important highlight to be aware of would be separate interface that a player can use to manage the multiple cities and armies, I found this to be very helpful when I would get into the late game and would have large amounts of cities and armies to manage. The city manager even gives the player a quick look about the special resources in that particular zone, where the workers are assigned in regards to basic resources as well as a building queue that a player can add buildings/units to. Also, being able to customize your hero and army units whenever you get past a Research Era or research an armor/weapons upgrade technology adds more flavor and tactics that the player can adjust to their liking. For example I prefer longbow men over crossbowmen, so I would change out gear to represent that style. Also upgrading your armies to the newly assigned gear is easy by simply clicking “Retrofitting”.
Cons: Even though this game is a very good game, there can be some improvements. The diplomatic process between the major factions could be improved. In Civ 5, there is an option to basically ask the AI “How can we make this deal work out?” That is an option I would like to add because it can be useful when you are trying to set up trade routes between your cities and the AI’s cities. Continuing with the AI, I would suggest that they add some difficulty to the AI as well as be able to start as allies during the set up screen. As I mentioned before, the main quest and side quests do add something mildly important for the player to do in order to gain rewards and information on their faction’s story. I would suggest that Endless Legend takes that further and add a campaign for the factions or story-related scenarios. The last thing I would say about the game would be the combat system. As mentioned in the review the combat is solid, but could be improved especially if you are a micromanager as myself. There were times I would get frustrated because I would be unable to move into a location AND then cast a support spell on my unit. Instead my unit would move to a title then attack an enemy or just cast the support spell and not move. Adding more depth to the combat mechanics would definitely make this game the best 4X games so far.

Easily one of the best 4x games in recent years, Endless Legend adds new innovations to the genre and improves on old ones. It has all of the staples of the 4x genre - eXplore, eXpand, eXploit, eXterminate and it executes well on all of those with perhaps eXterminating being the weakest of the bunch.
New innovations like wildly different tile yields combined with one city per zone makes even the placement of a new city a challenging decision. The lore is different and imaginative and each faction really requires a very different play style. Playing as certain civs in this game actually is like trying to re-learn how to play the game - they're that different (and this is a good thing). Other innovations are cool, like a more innovative tech tree. Other things may seem small but add to the enjoyment like goodie huts providing quests but these things help to provide a player some direction and the satisfaction of achieving a short term goal.
I really love the graphical style of the game. It looks very different than anything else and it is very attractive. It's bright, colorful and the terrain can be used to your advantage. Music/sound is
OK but nothing to write home about.
Some players hate the winter because it's almost a forced "down time". This is somewhat true. But it also provides a sense of urgency to achieve your goals before the next winter sets in. And if you really plan correctly you can make the winter really the factor that weakens your biggest rival, making them easier to destroy the next summer.
It's by no means a perfect game. Combat is kind of dull, there's no esponiage (since fixed in an expansion), the AI can be dumb (improved in expansions) and a few other minor issues like some late-game boredom. But these don't get in the way of a truly enjoyable playing experience.
Highly recommended for anyone with a passing interest in 4x games.

I bought this game on hype. I kept hearing it was Game of the Year material and the best RPG ever made (or one of the best). Usually when I buy games on hype like this I am disappointed but not with DoS 2. They're right. It is game of the year material. It's as good as everybody says it is.
Think of all of your favourite classic (and more recent) isometric RPG games such as Baldur's Gate, Pillars of Eternity, Neverwinter Nights and so forth. This game is like those except much bigger and with the most fun combat imaginable. There are so many different ways you can execute a battle, so many things you can use to your advantage, from spells and potions in your inventory to the actual environment. One party member may have oil in their inventory (or a spell that leaves oil on the ground) and another party member can ignite that oil using a fire spell, or a bomb, or a flaming arrow, causing burn damage to whatever is in the fire. Or one party member might put water on the ground (from a water ballon, or a water spell, or whatever the hell you have on you that causes water) and another can electrify it, causing electrical damage. You can build a magical party member that weakens and manipulates your enemies, or one that does raw magical damage, or one that causes poison damage and raises dead corpses to fight on your side, or a mixture of everything.
There are classes that use magic, swords and shields, bows, crossbows, rogues, healers... and there are hybrid classes that use pretty much everything and are still just as useful as pure damage/healer classes. The ways you can execute a battle, with a mixture of so many types of damage and utilities and objects, is immense. Your archer character can dip his arrows in any substance nearby and give his arrows added damage of that element. If he's standing next to fire he can dip his arrows in the fire and shoot fire arrows.
The crafting system is... massive. Just combine things and craft things. Pretty much everything can be used. Combine a stick and a crappy knife to make... a crappy stick knife sword.
All the dialogue is voiced. All of it. Even the narration.

Can't sing this game's praises high enough. I begrudgingly bought it, largely out of principle, having heard of it being brilliant and that it was independently developed and published, thinking that I might not like it or give up on it. But I didn't, and now i'm here telling you to buy it.
I started the game up and thought it felt too slow, too cumbersome and somewhat bloated, with just the first area taking near enough half an hour to an hour to fully explore and understand what's going on. It got even worse when I got to the next area. "god this drags on" I was thinking, "when's the proper fighting and loot fest stuff gonna happen?" I thought. In hindsight, I definitely didn't understand the pace of the game and the focus of it at all. After having put in over 50 hours I can now say that this game, for what i've played, is a masterpiece.
It shares similarities with games like diablo or torchlight, but with mechanics and design choices that make you consider every little move you make, this game manages to scratch at more and more layers of depth and forces you to explore options you wouldn't otherwise if not for the firm but fair difficulty. The AI is clever. It doesnt just bash at you with anything/everything, it picks and chooses what it needs to do to take you down. It picks off the weak, avoids the strong and weakens the immovable by using the environment and the creatures therein to it's advantage. For instance, there is a skill in the game that let's you kill an enemy if your character dies. Having cast this, the enemy's allies, themselves unaffected by this skill, will avoid killing your character but WILL proceed to weaken and immobilise you so that when it wears off they can take you down. They work things like this out and have clear strategic formations you need to counter.
It's one of the most rewarding experiences: coming into a fight fully unprepared, as the underdog, only to walk out the other side the victor. You know it was because YOU made the critical choices needed to win that battle against the odds and against a genuinely THINKING cpu opponent. It's fantastic.
The way the game feels to play when you're fully invested is unparralleled. There is an absolute deluge of content if you seek to complete it all and the way the game gives you utter freedom to do whatever you want/need/can do is both daunting and refreshing at the same time. The difficulty is fine tuned to perfection, where small mistakes can be cleverly worked around but rushing can easily get you killed.
Take your time, learn the ropes and think about each and every move as if it's your last, that's when the game is at it's best.
BUY IT

This is the kind of game that will forever top the "best ever" lists of grand strategy as long as the genre continues to exist. Especially when you consider the absolutely mammoth dragon horde of add-ons that have come out since the game first hit shelves years ago. CK2 up to this point is probably 6 times the scope and breadth it was when it started, and it just keeps getting bigger.
So what is it?
Well, to put it bluntly, it's whatever you want it to be. The best way to describe it would be a Royal Dynasty simulator. With all the intrigue, betrayal and surprise of a Game of Thrones episode (don't believe me? Check out the insanely great GoT mod that has been made for this game). You can pick and play any ruler (or Duke, or Count) of significance throughout the entirety of medieval history. With all the addons you can play a game that spans nearly 1000 years. Guiding your dynasty as a lowly count, backstabbing, scheming and marrying your way to the crown.
Marrying is important. When your character bites the dust (and there are soooo many hilarious ways for this to happen...my most recent King♥♥♥♥♥♥himself to death) you can continue playing as your heir.
Ack. It's damn hard to explain the insane depth of this game. If you put in the time to learn all the mechanics, you can lose hours as your imagination runs wild, while you plan your next move towards the crown...or the crown next door!

I remember learning about the Elder Scrolls series from my older brother, who purchased Morrowind on the original Xbox. I was never really interested in playing it because I was 7 years old at the time, but I always liked watching him play. About 3 years later, a friend of my brothers brought over another Elder Scrolls game, this one called "Oblivion". We all played it together, and I participated this time. And I fell in love with it. I still remember times from when I was 11 years old, all the lights turned off in my house, nothin' but me and my Xbox in my living room, playing Oblivion for 6 straight hours. Time well spent...
Elder Scrolls, for those who are unaware, is an Action RPG. Imagine Fallout set back in Medieval times, but way better because there's swords and magic! There's not a single complaint I have about Oblivion; it's damn near flawless, at least in my opinion. There's a bit of bugginess here and there, such as getting stuck on mountains, disappearing items/NPC's, etc. But that's a Bethesda game for you! Jokes aside though, the number of times those kinds of glitches have happened to me are few and far between over 7 years of playing this game. The level-up system is fantastic, combat is so good, great set of sidequests, and you can even go to literally HELL.
The one Elder Scrolls game everyone knows is Skyrim. But for those who have only played Skyrim and no other Elder Scrolls game, I strongly encourage you to give Oblivion a fair try. You will not be disappointed.

I got this game a while ago and thought today's the day I'd give it a real play. Before I had read some reviews about the ai and the difficulty. Thinking "I play rts and strategy games all the time, how bad is it really?" Today I also learned this game has mods, like for WW2 and a Star Wars one is getting updated on the next game update. I found it funny how with the success of Battlefield 1 there wasn't some WW1 mods. Then I launched a game against some ai, and realized why: As soon as you and your allies start popping off shots at the enemy, a very defined line forms, and everywhere between becomes no-mans land. I send 5 Abrams to get rid of some machine gun trucks and push forward. Thankfully my ai allies are compitent enough to take advantage of the progress. Then 3 minutes later they all get massacred by a couple of infantry squads and the lines form up again. I actually count this as a plus because I like having to fight tooth and nail for every inch of land, but I don't like b.s overpowered ai. I move up a heavy sniper team to the frontlines and I personally start lining up headshots against the ai out in the open. Normally I'd say I just missed in these situations but after 3 shots to the head coupled with blood spurts and the target has enough brain left to take cover? Or when 2 squads of seals in cover get dessimated by a lone squad that happened to bum rush? Okay so I finally take a point and have my men hunker down. At that point just forget them. Yes they take out squads easy but if you move them up, they get slaughtered, if you move back you lose the point and the position. The enemy ai is unconsistantly overpowered. This is on normal. One thing that you probably figured out: You can control your units, and the control is VERY strange. The controls definitely take some getting use to and aiming is a struggle. I must admit though, it can be funny at some points. I sent some apcs to help another sniper team capture a point. I take control to try and take some out myself when out of nowhere my apcs barge through the trees and just wreck havoc. I swore I heard the Team America theme song in the background. All in all, I'd give it a 6/10. Expect to be somewhat entertained, but not a fair fight.
