The reason for my No Recommondation is because in its current form the game seems incomplete in content, balance,  stability issues AND because it is not exactly what they appear to be selling.  This doesn't mean it isn't playable or engrossing, during beta it was the first time in a long time I'd found myself playing until the wee hours of the morning since like - Civilization II.  But come live...well it's not exactly living up to the promotional web page
or what is posted in the stream item description.
Despite what I am listing below, I am still interested in this game and am going to give it patience and time for it was enjoyable during the couple days I played it during beta.  There is a LOT of potential...
But...if you came here because of what it said in the promo you are going to be disappointed.
"Make your own village, anytime, anywhere.  Thinking of building your own village to show your workmanship?"
You can, but not as an individual as it alludes to.  Though you can be a guild of 1, only guilds can have territory that is protected by a Warden Tree - that which makes your structures permanent.  This is the ONLY way you can built not just your permant 'Village', but to have any form of storage that is NOT on your person.  ANd unless you are a guild of 1 or the guild master...there is NO personal/private storage.
"Be anyone...make your own character as you like"
To a degree that is true.  But when the game went live that option has been SEVERELY limited.There are 2 skill groups: Combat (10 Masteries for a total of 500 Points) and Living (11 Masteries for a total of 550 Points) but are now LIMITED to 320 Points Combined.  I can understand a need for limits, but it should have been 320 per group perhaps - might not still have mastered everything, but it wouldn't have limited you the way it does now....
At the barest, you're going to need 50 for a Weapon (Sword, Axe, Hammers, Daggers, Spears), Add 50 more if you want to use a SHIELD; Maximum HEALING = 50 more; 50 ANATOMY to maximize Criticals; and then 50 ARMOR if you want to wear the best.  Combined that's 200-250 Points which doesn't leave much for crafting or versatility on the battlefield.
Now unless you have a dedicated group where someone is supplying arms, armor and ammo if you use a bow - well it is going to be impossible now to simply do that.  MINING and LOGGING,, 100 points right there, are nearly prerequisites for anyone, but that only gets you the base materials.  You've still got CARPENTRY, TAILORING, and BLACKSMITHING for making the armors, weapons, and ammo not to mention the specialized building for making those items.
My point here is this...the promo suggests you can do it all.  Maybe it was duirng beta, but that is No Longer the case.  It suggests co-operative play, but doesn't make it seem mandatory.  It also suggests combating other players, but doesn't even come close to indicating the open world PVP that exists with the only limits I can see being the ability to place a bounty - and oh, too bad, so sad for any time and effort you put into building what you did before it was destroyed while you were offline.
Yup...you can repair things, but there is only one way to make coin - selling items to a roaming NPC called Mr. BoBoo.  Other than looted weapons/armor, the only thing you can csell is the stuff you craft (or was crafted) though there are a few harvestable items that sell too.  It should be noted that these coins are an inventory item and are apparently subject to being destroyed/dropped when killed.  Like there is enough space to keep your coins split into smaller stacks so you don't chance losing it all.  And if you want to be a decent "5-Star Chef" - if you don't have a supplier you're going to need FISHING, FARMING, COOKING, and possibly RANCHING or another 150-200 points.
Other little pet peeves:
- There is a slot for placing your mount, but no associated hotkey to call it.  Instead you have to place it on your hotkeys (only have 6) leaving said equipment space empty.  And apparently no way to dismiss it in which case it is constantly using up the food you have to feed it to maintain it's viability.
- For as simplistic graphics as the game has, it is a major resource hog and you'd better have more than even the recommended specifications it asks for - otherwise you are in for a lot of crashes.
- Can't always reset controls and no way to back out of the option short of termination the program - which seems to have a habit of resetting all items to their default setting.

Pros:
-Very easy to set up a multiplayer game, either online, via LAN, via splitscreen, or even a mixture of all three!!!
-Full controller support
-Full splitscreen support
-Several different levels with different turret (tower) and critter arrangements, as well as traps and bonus mob spawners
-Gorgeous 2D graphics
-Great voice work
-Great music
-Regular updates
Cons:
-AI is very challenging! Difficulty can be adjusted however.
Conclusion:
A solid investment, whether you get it on sale or not. A really good LAN game for 2-6 players, and the AI fills any gaps in the player count without it feeling like a disadvantage. I really appreciate the splitscreen in particular, which has been executed extremely well. It allowed me, the wife and a buddy to all play together with only 2 PCs and a controller with literally no tweaking whatsoever.

Still pay to win, there are many other choices that allow for "Free" advancement and use a more balanced tier-based progression model. Characters are locked off unless you buy DLC. Dlc characters are arguably better as they combine aspects from your standard characters. Trying to progress is like playing Call of Duty in a Moba. The game purposely inhibits you in order to "teach" you how to play the game and rewards you for grinding through while lacking critical abilities. Imagine trying to use Aeris in FFVII without any Magic Materia.
Other Moba games that I would recommend (these are free):
Dota 2: Archetype of the entire genre, complex gameplay, rpg/easter egg hidden effects(can be game changing), business model is based on aestheic items, all characters unlocked from beginning
League of Legends: Easier gameplay, easter egg effects are designed to be noticed yet provide bonuses not worth mentioning, business model based on quickening the rate at which you progress in your account level & character roster, playable characters must be purchased with in-game currency and characters are frequently enabled to everyone for a period of time
Smite: Mythilogical/diety based theme, Over the shoulder perspective, same business model as "League of Legends", you are given an initial roster of characters, characters are also temporarily enabled on rotations, still being developed yet it stands on its own two or more feet (depending on the diety)

You know those games that are just a few tweaks away of greatness? The original Original Sin was that kind of game.It had modernised CRPG mechanics,great combat,lots of choices on how to get on with the world,wonderful crafting yet cumbersome UI and a muddled story (even with the Enhancements later released)
Original Sin 2 tries to rectify all those mistakes.
+For starters, it has a more straightforward and darker storyline and writing.
+The UI has been refined and is a lot more accessible
+Character creation, customistaion, companions are all great.
+General gameplay is still solid packing deep environmental interaction(in&out combat),fun crafting and exciting turn-based combat with good animations.
+Classes are varied and many and balanced very well
+Pretty much all lines are voice acted and they do a decent job.Same with the soundtrack
+Challenging Tactician difficulty in which the game should be played (Normal being too easy)
+Game Master mode for PnP RPG simulation and co-op is fun as always
+Game looks great with a more grounded art style this time around
+Mod Support
-I felt the streamlining of RPG attributes and skills from the first game is a bit of a let down (Although they allow less trial & error playthroughs)
-The crafting seems to have been downplayed this time around.They have taken out the skills related to crafting and some fun recipes
-Normal difficulty is way too easy,at least in the first chapter.
-Tactician mode felt cheap in some aspect like when it gives enemy ridiculous amount of physical and magical armor.In the first game,higher diffiiculty meant more enemies and smarter A.I.
TL:DR Orignal Sin 2 easily takes it's place as one of the greatest CRPGs ever along with Baldur's  Gate,Fallout,Wasteland,Planescape:Torment etc and at the same time possess mastery over it's technical aspects something the afforementioned games never did possess.

Once upon a time, there was a small swedish videogame publisher called Paradox Interactive. Their games weren't pretty to look at, but the love they put in them, gameplay depth and apparent dedication made up for all of it. Their pro-consumer, community driven policies meant that, we the customers, could go hand-in-hand with the developers in improving the games. Even dictate whether we wanted an expansion or not!
And indeed, I and many others, spent countless hours on paradox forums discussing, contributing, putting forward changes suggestions and script ideas to better the games. The devs were on there too - it was a unique approach I haven't experienced before. They listened to everything, paid attention in detail, greatly supported and encouraged modders.
Is it then a wonder that a company with such dedication and love for its community, prospered and turned into a very successful publisher ? It is well deserved I can tell you that much.
Unfortunately in recent years Paradox have shown that the community is no longer a family. That money is the sole driving factor for their games. Expansions that come out on a conveyor belt, sometimes as tiny as a few megabytes costing as much as a full-priced indie game. And when the game is then REBALANCED to adapt to the new expansions, you are left no choice but to buy them.
It is a real pity that it has come to this.
I loved CK and EU2/EU3. Played these games for years on and off. Sadly I can no longer recognize the company that made you feel like part of a big family rather than a cash cow for them to milk.

An absolute masterpiece of 4X gaming. It takes a very well established genre and changes it enough to make it unique unto itself.
I got hooked in the first few minutes. The game is beautiful, both graphically and mechanically. It plays extremely well, and the focus on cities and their districts as opposed to rushing out and expanding it very good.
Each race is wholly unique onto themselves. Each with their own unique units ,play styles, race quests, and of course appearances.
This means you really need to pay attention and get around to trying them all if possible. it makes dealing with them later on much easier. Even so there are several independent and unique NPC races as well. Each can be pacified and assimilated into your empire granting you unique bonuses there as well, along with units.
Add in some very lite RPG mechanics in the form of heroes, which can be levelled up and have unique items made for them, or found through quests and the game adds more depth and fun.
Similar to Alpha Centauri you can customise units' items and weapons. All those can be researched and upgraded through strategic resources as well. Which you can then use to later retrofit your older armies.
Combat is interesting as well, unlike Age of Wonders, you're not transport to a specific combat map. Instead the work map is quartered off into a mini strategic map. It's topography remains. You then start off with a deployment phase, arguably the most important phase. Here you position your units, and once happy you click deploy and enter music turn base combat.
interestingly enough each city can have militia garrisons as well, which can function as reinforcements to your army if they're fighting close to a city.
The game is just good, and going into detail would mean around ten thousands words are needed here at least. Hence my video.
I would easily recommend this to any fantasy 4X fan.

I've played 3 games, with 3 difficulties, 3 different factions, and 3 different victory types, and it's a blast. The game runs at a nice pace, I did have some crashing issues which were fixed by switching to 32-bit version, so that was easy enough.
The combat is more involved than Civ 5, for example, with a turn-based-semi-autonomous battlefield similar to Final Fantasy Tactics, i.e. a small-grid-map type with all the units from your army. But the combat is also skipable, or you can just spectate. The diplomacy is nice and I like the empire plans, giving your faction a bonus for some turns.
I really like the soundtrack too.
Two things I would like to see are more hotkeys, and being able to queue up actions. The mouse controls are great, but I would like to be able to input commands a bit quicker. e.g. using multiple stockpiles in one turn. Also with regard to queuing up actions, would be nice to be able to give commands to a unit while it's moving, instead of having to wait for it to finish. Especially once units have 6+ movements.
Neither are essential but it would be nice for QOL for me in the game.

Pros:
★ Create and manage your family even as lowly as a count and raise your family to glory and become emperor!
★ Characteristics in players more in-depth than Rome Total War.
★ Create your own adventure and choose your decisions.
★ Customisable character interface and family options to assist with immersion.
★ Historically and geographically accurate.
★ Restore the roman empire or any other failed empire for that matter.
★ Kickass council management that can have you install your horse 'glitterhoof' to chancellorship.
★ Invite your rivals wife to bed you and get her pregnant ONLY to have your illegitimate son/daughter become ruler of his lands!
★ No shortage of new events or feeling of repetitiveness from this game.
★ Become greater than Charlemagne himself, or live only to end your family name to syphilis or smallpox.
Cons:
✖ Steep learning curve to those that aren't used to Paradox games.
✖ Suffers from the same fate as most Paradox games being that you won't feel that you have a full game without buying all of the DLC.
✖ Multiplayer can be horribly unstable.
Crusader kings is a game where instead of trying to land-grab or own the world as quickly as you can like you do in games such as Civilization or Europa, has you managing a family in an RPG sense. Your character is thrown many different event chains that will have you ruling over your people as a benevolent ruler or a mad king bent over destroying anything they touch. There is no end to the options of how you can raise your ruler and the actions they take. You can choose for a leader to be a militaristic genius or a temperate cassanova wishing to only live in a hedonistic lifestyle.
The game is very hard to get bored over. There is always new challenges to face or paths to take and several starting locations that will have different local objectives for you to complete. You can drive the islamic arabs out of Africa or convert all of Europe to Hindu.. the options are endless. Saying this, because this game was created by Paradox be aware that you may not feel like you are playing the full game because you do not have all the DLC. I highly recommend only purchasing the DLC when it goes on steam sale or if it is advertised on humble bundle. Once you learn the ropes of this game you'll not want to put it down.

Once upon a time, there was a small swedish videogame publisher called Paradox Interactive. Their games weren't pretty to look at, but the love they put in them, gameplay depth and apparent dedication made up for all of it. Their pro-consumer, community driven policies meant that, we the customers, could go hand-in-hand with the developers in improving the games. Even dictate whether we wanted an expansion or not!
And indeed, I and many others, spent countless hours on paradox forums discussing, contributing, putting forward changes suggestions and script ideas to better the games. The devs were on there too - it was a unique approach I haven't experienced before. They listened to everything, paid attention in detail, greatly supported and encouraged modders.
Is it then a wonder that a company with such dedication and love for its community, prospered and turned into a very successful publisher ? It is well deserved I can tell you that much.
Unfortunately in recent years Paradox have shown that the community is no longer a family. That money is the sole driving factor for their games. Expansions that come out on a conveyor belt, sometimes as tiny as a few megabytes costing as much as a full-priced indie game. And when the game is then REBALANCED to adapt to the new expansions, you are left no choice but to buy them.
It is a real pity that it has come to this.
I loved CK and EU2/EU3. Played these games for years on and off. Sadly I can no longer recognize the company that made you feel like part of a big family rather than a cash cow for them to milk.

I love the concept of this game. There is a serious lack of quirky and perverted video games, and this one is just that. It's bizarre, and the simplicity of the menus and the game itself make sure that none of this bizarre world of phalluses competing to plunge into the♥♥♥♥♥♥of other phalluses is ever explained.
So I love the concept, but right now that's all that you're getting when you buy this game. The gameplay itself is extremely fast and simple: traditional mode involves plunging into and being plunged by other players. The party mode is a fast combination of different mini-games. I haven't been able to try the new date night mode due to lack of online players and the buggy lobbies..
Although this game is meant to be confusing and strange, the menus are a bit too esoteric and the complete lack of instructions makes me feel like I'm always missing something. There is supposed to be an "announcer" according to the options (I assume they will sound like the one in the trailer), but so far that announcer isn't heard anywhere. The COMPLETE lack of single-player mode is a shame. Obviously this type of game is meant to be multiplayer, but the single player mode would be a nice way to wrap your head around the game before playing with others. Also, it shouldn't be hard to make a decent AI given how simple the game is. The ability to add AI would also help to fill out the very empty online servers.
Speaking of online servers, the multiplayer lobbies (which are the only place you'll go if you aren't playing offline co-op) are currently quite buggy and laggy. Sometimes I enter a room and I am unable to move (p.s.: you have to move your phallus into a slot to enter the game). Sometimes I can't even see the other players. This is all really problematic since the game relies entirely on multiplayer.
At the moment, the "early access" tag on this game is VERY IMPORTANT. I personally think that the game should have been way further in development before even letting players try it, because the bugs and the lack of content make me want to return it at the moment. However I love the concept and the execution of that concept, so I really hope that the developers are working towards turning this into a proper game.

You have 10 lives, and it uses one to respawn you at the last checkpoint every time you die. Well, As I'm sure you have seen, the main gripes people have with this game is the clunky UI, non-customizable characters, lack of voice acting, less capable AI, and essentially being infirior to sonny 2, which is free, in every way. I don't share those grivances quite so much, but my issue is more with the loss of the semi-abstract artstyle, the humor being "dumbed-down" and the dissapearence of several areas and encounters that I found likeable in the orignal, such as the first beach not being haunted by ghosts, and keep in mind, I gave up pretty quickly, but I think they may have cut the baron, one of the most interesting bosses in the first two games, forcing you to think about your strategy due to his health pool being the largest in each game, and mostly being drained by an NPC who you have to keep alive in the first game, and by himself when he runs out of focus in the second.
I noticed a lot of complaints about the Veradux AI not healing people when they are low on health, and I think I noticed in my short time with this game what was going on with it. it prioritizes debuffing higher than survivabilty, and is overall much more debuff oriented.
Now I will have a short section where I will complain about some story changes from the first game. Louis is no longer blind, the enemies on the ship are more generic looking, with more generic names. Veradux didn't steal his armor from the ZPCI etc. etc.
Another issue I have is that bosses have too much health, and aren't challenging. in the old games, bosses would have around one to five thousand health early game and up to ten thousand late game, unless there was a special method to deal with them. here, bosses START with ten thousand and twenty thousand health, and move up rapidly, and damage dealing used to be harder in the old games, where it was rare to take down a full health enemy in one hit, and rare to be dealt more than half your health with one hit.
However, this game's biggest problem is that it has no soul, no heart, no joy. when you play it you think, eh this isn't that bad, it isn't great, but it's not terrible. then you turn it off, and do somthing else for a bit, then you think about the game for a bit, and you hate it more and more as you look at all the issues. even as a standalone game, ignoring the flash games, this feels like a flash game, but you have to pay for it. it would be like paying for a youtube video so you don't get an advertisement at the start. I rated this game a 5/10 at the start of playing it, but that has since dropped to a 4.1/10. it's good to see flash developers working towards full releases of their games, but this is one of the games that failed to deliver on its full release.
Edit: I thought of a better description of this game. in sonny 2, deep in the mining tunnels, as the party is hallucinating from the noxious fumes, they see an apperation that looks like sonny called shunny. the apperation has over five thousand health, looks like the basic sonny, and is very easy to beat. this game is that one fight in many ways, being slightly off, looking the same all the time, everything having far more health than it has any right to, and being far to easy with the speed at which you win being fairly random. this game should have been called Shunny.

In short:  A great civ style game by the makers of Endless Space.  A lot of fun interesting concepts/mechanics are introduced to the genre.  The game as a good, clean look, and fun execution.  A game on normal speed concludes faster than most entries in the genre, without feeling rushed.  I highly recommend this game to fans of the genre.
Some of the those interesting concepts/mechanics worth mentioning:
The map is divided into regions, and only one city can be built per region, but gives control of the region, allowing harvest of all the strategic and luxury resources therein.  Luxury resources are accumulated and an amount based on number of cities are consumed for a 10 round buff that is different for each resource.
Military units are grouped together into armies with an optional leader hero, and move as a group.  Combat arrays the units of opposing armies against each other.  You give each unit directions at the start of a round of combat, and every unit acts.  Combat takes place on the world map, and nearby armies and cities can provide reinforcements which trickle into combat on subsequent rounds.
Rather than having a series of ever increasingly powerful military units to research, each faction only has a couple to research.  Instead equipment is researched which can be equiped on units increasing their industry cost, and sometimes requiring strategic resources.
Each region contains 1-3 minor faction villages which will occasionally generate roaming armies.  Pacifying villages (through combat, spending dust (money), or doing a quest for them will halt army generation.  Pacified villages in a colonized region can provide increased population in the city and can be assimilated into the empire allowing production of that type of military unit and also providing a passive bonus, such as increased science, increased health regeneration on armies, or a reduction in cost for building construction in cities.
An influence resource which is generated in cities can be used every 20 turns to set policy for the next 20 turns, giving options like increased attack on military units, increased dust generation on trade rounds, or extra science generation.
Rather than a tech tree, technology is divided into tiers.  Each tech researched increases the cost of all further technologies, and each tier is unlocked based on the total number of technologies researched.
A few negatives to counterbalance my gushing enthusiasm:  Early military conquest is perhaps to easily available as an option (at least against AI - I haven't played vs.).  A successful early military campaign pretty much trumps any other strategy.  Co-operative play isn't supported - no allied victory and all diplomatic actions, including trading tech and resources, cost influence.  District leveling mechanics are not explained in the tutorial.  A quick google search will lead to an explanation, though adding to the confusion, one of the top results is from the beta indicates that districts above level 2 are possible*, which is no longer true.  A proper understanding of district mechanics is critical for the mid and late game, and a lack of a clear explanation is disappointing.
*As an aside, one faction, the cultists, can reach level 3 on their districts.

In my opinion,
is a ludicrously underrated game. It is incredibly simple in concept but it is executed incredibly well making it a huge amount of fun, the really simple but highly polished graphics also give this game a great charm to it.
is a blend of Tower Defense and Real Time Strategy, something that can be very difficult to balance but
does it relatively well. There are a nice variety of units to chose from and an eclectic selection of official & community-made maps that give this game a lot of playability in both single and multiplayer games, this is a great game to play either alone or with friends.
Another thing that I love about
along with it's simplistic but great graphics is the brilliant soundtrack, it may be minimal in variety and some tracks sound like remixes of others but there are some really good pieces that fit perfectly into the games art style.
The hardest thing to achieve in any Strategy or Tower Defense game is balance, and even though
does it fairly well, it also has some unfortunate flaws; they aren't necessarily global flaws as the problems only seem to occur on certain maps, but the issue is still there. This is the fact that there is one particular strategy that works 95% of the time said maps, mainly some of the earlier ones but is also prominent on the later/more advanced maps too. If you rush the enemy spawning towers with basic infantry early on, it can be incredibly easy to dominate the rest of the game by pumping more and more infantry to that location. Like I said, this doesn't happen on
maps, just a handful, it is also my only real problem with this game.
Another flaw is that some infantry can feel fairly redundant such as Freds or Sids whereas other infantry like Grills, Flints and Rickys can dominate the grid most of the time in large numbers. This is again the balancing issue that lurks in these kind of games, it's a very difficult thing to overcome but non-the-less, it is nice to have a selection of units to chose from, especially since it doesn't clog up the interface and use minimal space.
So as this game is fairly cheap and is practically given away during sales, I would suggest trying it out if you're a fan of Tower Defense or RTS games. I believe some of the reviews that this game has recieved are relatively harsh and undeserved, sure, it has some issues but what game doesn't? This game and it's sequel are a lot of fun so if it's going for cheap or is in a bundle, I highly recommend it! I'm looking at you, my Command & Conquer buddies.

Just when you feel like you're doing really well, the enemies ramp up and get harder. So this is a pretty challenging game, but it's also very satisfying.
I really enjoy the different builds and the ability to reset your character. That means that if you get bored with a play style or run into a really difficult section, you can respec. As soon as I beat it, I will likely play through it again as a lone wolf.
There were a few bugs that I ran into, but reloading and doing something else first would fix it. For example, if interacting with a certain object causes the game to crash, travel to another area, do some trading, then come back. Or use a different character.
I have only two major complaints. The first is inventory management. Moving things around is tedious. I like having the Wares system, which is where you can move an item into this category called "Wares", then sell all your wares at once to a vendor. Saves time with the vendor, but not placing them into wares. I also had my strength hero be the pack mule. So I'd have to move the item to the Red Prince, then right click and move to wares. Tedious, but manageable.
The second complaint is the persuasion system. It seemed like I failed literally every persuasion attempt for the first half of the game. I gave up on making it work. See, I would see an Intelligence-based persuasion attempt and would say, "Ok, I'll use my dude who has maxed intelligence." FAIL. What the heck?! Turns out that not only do you need high intelligence, you need high persuasion, which is a stat you can level up. Later, when I had more points to spare, I maxed out persuasion on two characters, one finesse based, one int based. That way, I always have someone who can win that persuasion. It was minor and I was able to live with failing literally every persuasion attempt.
Anyway, I give this game a 9/10. The only reason I don't give it a 10/10 is because my summoner can't have more than one summon out at a time! I want to summon my spirit wolf, summon my incarnate, and summon a bone widow from my summoner main! But alas, you can only have one summon out at a time.

One of my most favorite, if not my favorite, games of all time. You can be anything from a Viking to a Buddist, reforming the Roman Empire or having great holy wars against the Catholics as a Germanic Pagan (aka Norse). There are many different mechanics with the game, along with various ways to play the game. You can play as a powerful general, that leads armies, a diplomat that everyone loves, or a sneaky noble that deceives and backstabs others to get what he wants. Every game won't be the same, mighty kingdoms might form, some will fall. The only thing that matters is leaving your dynasty with the best possible chance of survival when you die, and you get to play as your heir after your current character dies. Then you start all over again, trying to keep the peace within your realm, make alliances, expand your religion and your kingdom/empire.

This game has a pretty hard learning curve but once you get past that you are in for a long ride. Whether it is creating your own merchant republic or bringing down those darn muslims or even defending against hundreds of thousands of aztecs from god knows where, this game will keep you engaged. BEWARE: The greatest enemy of them all will be those overpriced, sometimes underdeveloped DLCs that Paradox Interactive loves to keep releasing. Only a few of them actually add any meaningful changes to the game and you are better off without some of them. If you can get past the commpany's greedy business scheme, you will enjoy this game very much, otherwise, don't expect much love from the company.

I love the concept of this game. There is a serious lack of quirky and perverted video games, and this one is just that. It's bizarre, and the simplicity of the menus and the game itself make sure that none of this bizarre world of phalluses competing to plunge into the♥♥♥♥♥♥of other phalluses is ever explained.
So I love the concept, but right now that's all that you're getting when you buy this game. The gameplay itself is extremely fast and simple: traditional mode involves plunging into and being plunged by other players. The party mode is a fast combination of different mini-games. I haven't been able to try the new date night mode due to lack of online players and the buggy lobbies..
Although this game is meant to be confusing and strange, the menus are a bit too esoteric and the complete lack of instructions makes me feel like I'm always missing something. There is supposed to be an "announcer" according to the options (I assume they will sound like the one in the trailer), but so far that announcer isn't heard anywhere. The COMPLETE lack of single-player mode is a shame. Obviously this type of game is meant to be multiplayer, but the single player mode would be a nice way to wrap your head around the game before playing with others. Also, it shouldn't be hard to make a decent AI given how simple the game is. The ability to add AI would also help to fill out the very empty online servers.
Speaking of online servers, the multiplayer lobbies (which are the only place you'll go if you aren't playing offline co-op) are currently quite buggy and laggy. Sometimes I enter a room and I am unable to move (p.s.: you have to move your phallus into a slot to enter the game). Sometimes I can't even see the other players. This is all really problematic since the game relies entirely on multiplayer.
At the moment, the "early access" tag on this game is VERY IMPORTANT. I personally think that the game should have been way further in development before even letting players try it, because the bugs and the lack of content make me want to return it at the moment. However I love the concept and the execution of that concept, so I really hope that the developers are working towards turning this into a proper game.

I desperately wanted to give this a thumbs up and tried so hard to like this game, but to no avail. I love the sonny series and was absolutely ecstatic when I found this remake. I instantly bought it regardless of my friends all begging me not to waste my money on it. I wanted to give one of my favorite game series a chance. Well, I was extremely disappointed and now i've gone past 2 hours and can't refund the game.
PROS:
- New engaging storyline
- New playable characters
- New abilities and Sonny forms
- Tons of items and customization for RPG loadouts
CONS:
- Barely any voice acting. Even the original flashes had more voice acting than this game!
- The visuals are horrid. They're immobile cardboard cutouts and it feels like you'd get a better experience from physically moving actual cardboard with your hands and using your imagination.
- The ally AI is literally the worst in this series yet. The older versions allowed you to control them if you wanted to and use them better, but now all allies use AI and never do anything you want or need them to do. It's as useless as having a lvl 1 Smash Bros bot on your team while fighting tournament champions.
- The Achievements are far too difficult for those who are new to the game. Even a veteran of this series like myself found them a bit harsh to even attempt.
- Some enemy effects are absolute garbage. They ruin the gameplay and sap the fun right out of the game entirely. Sure, it might be fun to have them in a higher difficulty setting, but at least give people the option to either enjoy the game or torture themselves.
Overall, I'd rate this game a solid 3 / 10   because of how buggy it is, how much it lacks QUALITY content, how cheap the battles are, and how much they definitely didn't put their heart and soul into this game like they did the original ones.

Having played the first two original flash games, I really wanted to like this reboot. And I did enjoy it very much. Most of the complaints about this game seem to involve the AI and design changes, but I was impressed by both. Allies follow-up on the main character's tactics logically with their skills, and they're dependable healers when their skills are on cooldown.
Voice acting is partial but still great when it's there (I'm gonna knock you silly!) and animations/weapon and armor skins no longer exist. The palate swaps for Sonny's classes are cool though, and I think the improved art style is a worthy trade-off.
HOWEVER, there are some dissapointments even if you welcome those changes.
There are technical issues, about as many as you might expect from a flash game, though the devs seem to be active trying to address them. I overwrite the same save slot with a new game and I think that caused it's corruption, so I had to start over. Sometimes exiting a screen makes it permanently dim out, justifying a force quit.
I had fun until the end. Which is pretty much the story of the first two games combined, then it seems like he ran out of ideas so he just slapped on some villain that was a thinly veiled Trump parody. It's subtle at first, he seemed like a Lex Luthor type villain in design but it is revealed at the end he's a "big bully" like Trump. Then it's no longer subtle, and it seems like the creator is whining through the game. And it really sucks to have a bunch of political garbage shoehorned in and trying to be passed off as a climax. There's also nothing to do after beating the game except for playing it again, as far as I know.
I hope this isn't the last game this person makes though.

It's taken a long time for me to think of the correct words I wanted to use to describe Oblivion.
I first played Oblivion on my friends Xbox 360 and was immediately hooked - I went straight to our local game store (Our town still had one in those days) and in there was a guy who was being made by his parents to sell all of his games to cover his ridiculous phone bill that he had wracked up, it was hundreds of pounds. I got his copy, a battered old case with a cigarette burn on the cover. And I loved it. It was probably the game I spent most time on, ever, on my good old 360. Now that I have evolved into one of the PC master race, it was time to do it all over again.
Now, I will start here with Oblivion's flaws. For as much as I like it, it does have them and it would be unfair not to mention them. As the game world itself is huge, of course the associated bugs and glitches come with them. There are hundreds, and I suspect not all of them have been found. Some of them are quest breaking and some of them are literally game breaking, so they can be highly frustrating. On PC, this is not so much of an issue due to the all godly console commands.
Combat is clunky, and especially in melee combat - you can get stuck in a hit cycle from multiple enemies and just have no way of defending yourself. The voice acting in itself is quite literally a cultural phenomenon. Yahtzee (our lord and saviour from Zero Punctuation) was 100% accurate when he described characters talking, to themselves, about the shop, owned by themselves. Its a solid attempt at a procedurally generated NPC conversations but it just falls short of the mark. The speech skill/persuasion is baffling in this game, and often I just ended up bribing people to tell me what I wanted.
It hasn't aged terribly well in line with modern RPGs, but this does not matter to me so much - however, this could be an issue if graphics are your marker of a good game. The upcoming Skyblivion mod will seek to remedy this, and good luck to the development team on this - if you're ever in the UK, I'll buy you a drink. It does occasionally crash for no reason, but that could just be my particular set up.
I could sit here and write pages about why I love Oblivion, so I won't. Its not just a game, its an experience. It is a lush, huge world with many different areas to wander, and has hundreds of dungeons, forts, caves, even shipwrecks to explore.  The quests and quest writing is miles above other Elder Scrolls games, the guilds in particular are fantastic - The Dark Brotherhood blows Skyrim's out of the water. I've never managed to complete all of the quests, I still find new NPCs, locations and quests to this day.
It has a good chunk of DLC available - including the much derided horse armour (Seriously, give it a search - it was a bit of a mess). However, the available content also includes the legendary Shivering Isles DLC, often considered to be one of the best ever DLC packages made. It adds well over 30 hours of new content, and its not just new weapons or armour but an entire new world to explore, set in the Alice in Wonderland-esque realm of Sheogorath. That, Bethesda, is how you should be doing it.
I'll stop gushing now.
Seriously, if you let it drag you under - you won't come out for weeks.

In short - Endless Space, now with advanced, fun and tactical combat, fantasy setting mixed with few sci-fi elements, faster gameplay and fractions actually really different from each other.
Game provide few interesting changes in mechanic, compared to standard fantasy 4x titles and Endless Space - surface is divided by regions, with only one city each (which makes cities positioning much more important) and minor fractions villages, providing bonus citizens (and unique units to produce and bonuses, like +5% science production for each village, once assimilated into your empire) after pacification/bribery/completing quest, cities expand by building districts (which can "level up" once they connect with enough other districts - important, since each new one actually decrease happiness in city, while claiming new titles for exploitation), combat takes form of turn-based skirmishes, where you dont directly control each unit, but rather select primary targets and tactic (aggressive, defensive, holding position), world market allows to hire and sell heroes, units and resources (strategic, luxury and "stockpiles" of food/production/science, for boosting new and existing cities), technologies are divided by eras (where to advance you need to research certain number of technologies from previous eras - since cost increase with each new tech, selecting proper ones to boost your gameplay style is important), each fraction have their own quest-line providing background story, along with sidequests, seasons switch between summer and winter (first reducing movement and food/industry/dust production - as turns pass, winter gets longer and players suffer much more penalties, as planet is slowly "dying") and many more.
Plus, like before, units are customizable, just like fractions. FIDS is still there as well, working great (now allowing to manually attach citizens to certain tasks, boosting productions of selected resources, along with titles and improvements production).
Game have flaws, however - you can create new units, but only based on existing ones, equipping them with weapons/armors/accessories researched so far (with different bonuses, based on which material they were made from), which limit your army flexibility a bit. AI have problems with acting way too aggressive and number of technologies is limited. Of course, it helps maintaining balance for multiplayer games, but, much like in most other 4x games, you still develop nearly the same technologies each game (with occasional differences - Broken Lords does not use food, operating only on Dust, so technologies increasing Dust production are priority, while not so much with others). Also, game sessions takes rather short time - around 8 hours each, on normal game speed and difficulty. In theory, game should end in max 300 turns - longest I had lasted 240, but most people would end theirs near 200 or maybe even 150. Before starting, I want to say that I WANT to like this game. It looks visually appealing to me and I'm interested by the setting. I wanna know what went wrong there and what the player character is going to have to go through to fix it.
Speaking of, I do think that with a small number of tweaks, the game could benefit greatly and become more of a skill-based game than what feels sometimes like a bag of cheap tricks (speaking about combat being so unpredictable).
The Good:
1. Shield is automatically up if you are not attacking or moving (duck to block lower. don't duck to block upper). This reminds me of Zelda 2 a lot.
2. You can also attack lower and upper areas of enemy. This provides some challenge/mix in the enemy approach and I'm sure offers some options for AI (difficult enemies could switch more often, etc)
The Bad:
1. Anticipation frames are either too short or non-existent (perhaps this was a mistake on the dev's end?). These are the animation frames that queue the player into knowing what the enemy is doing next with enough time to react. Dark Souls, for example, bakes this into every enemy, every move. Because you cannot anticipate the actions of these enemies, you cannot overcome the possibility of being damaged even with enough practice and skill... and this is really a deal-breaker for a game that's around 98% combat system. Don't believe me? Here's what I mean: In a game where the emphasis is on skill, one could easily go 30 minutes straight of watching, anticipating, and blocking the first skeleton you encounter without taking a single hit. A newbie couldn't do this, but skill could. And I don't mean weeks of skill. This should be possible as soon as you're done learning about the enemy (maybe a dozen minutes?) and are perceptive. The problem is that I don't believe this is actually possible on a consistent basis as the game currently stands.
2. You receive damage when an ememy touches you. This wouldn't be so bad if enemies weren't constantly approaching during a fight, but they are. Because of this, you are forced to either jump backwards or shove the enemy back with your shield very regularly. The shield shove isn't a bad idea - I think it's great! But making it so that I have to press this button almost as much as I press attack just feels... cheap?
3. You cannot shove with the shield when crouched. Some of you are probably thinking that this totally makes sense.. and it does. Could you imagine shoving someone from a crouched position in real life? No way. But this isn't what I'm talking about. I mean the Shove Button is DISABLED when crouched! So if you're in a pinch, you have to not only press [shove], but you also have to remember to first let go of [crouch]. This can be overcome with practice, but it seems like a design mistake: like he knows it works this way, but has been playing his own game so long, he doesn't realize this is actually not a great experience (especially for first time players yelling wtf at their screens when the moment of truth costs them another precious bar of life).
4. You start the game with 3 lives (well, +1 for the live you currently are using), but if you lose a life, you are instantly reset to the starting sword/shield. This is widly frustrating for Bad Reasons #1 & #2. I completely understand this for a roguelike, but I would NOT classify this game as a roguelike.
Recommendations
1. I think the anticipation frames should be increased... maybe start by adding 1 extra frame and see how long you can last in testing without getting hit... you are the dev, so you'd be better than anyone at this (though this is assuming that you're using a random number generator for the actions the skeleton will take next). If 1 extra frame isn't enough, then maybe try 2 or 3 and so on. If you feel like the game is too easy once you reach this point, try testing it out on someone new! You may be surprised to find that it still takes time to master and is definitely not reducing the quality of the experience.
That's my only recommendation. This kind of adjustment would mean that it's totally realistic for a skilled enough player to never die once in your game. So that takes care of Issue #4... Issue #2 will feel more like a valued mechanic than an annoyance since you don't run the risk of trying to shove right before the enemy issues a leg attack or something.

Shadowcrypt is a semi-challening combat focused platformer that takes obvious influence from classics like Castelvania and Zelda.  Unfortunately it is missing a few things that would make me recommend it.  The lack of content for the price is the biggest issue here and if the game was a quarter of the price then I would perhaps look at the game differently.
Like arcade games of old, death will put you back to the beginning of the game.  The dungeon is not procedurely generated, so death will mean you will be playing through the same dungeon over and over.  This isn't a problem if the level you are forced to repeat is enjoyable.  Unfortunately in Shadowcrypt, many rooms are empty and encounters are separated through backtracking which becomes tedious very quickly.  Most of my playtime was spent jumping through empty rooms that look almost identical.  More encounters and some new designs to make areas fresh would have worked wonders.
Combat is quite enjoyable, certain enemies require patience and if you try to hack and slash your way through everything then you will most likely die.  Again though, lack of content means that the combat isn't as good as it could have been.  Swords and shields are great, but to limit combat to only these weapons with some slight variations based on damage is just poor.  I would have loved a staff with limited usage or a slow and heavy battle axe to crush certain enemies under their shields.  The lack of content just pops up time and time again.
Repetitive encounters, environments and a focus on backtracking just make Shadowcrypt more of a chore than it should be.  At the moment it is too expensive for the content and you will be able to find much more enjoyable experiences for less money.  If you are a fan of classic arcade platformers then maybe put this one in your wishlist and wait for a massive sale.

It’s not a *bad* game.  The concept is novel, the graphics feel pretty polished, and the team obviously cared about the game they were building.
But the sign of a great strategy game is balance.  Unfortunately Cubemen lacked this in 2 important ways.
1) The  strategy to beating every Defense level is the same.  I thought the game was extremely hard at first when I was trying to sit back and defend, but then I discovered that if you rush the spawn point with the 2 basic units, you can win nearly every Defense level.  A few of the 35 levels did require some thought, particularly the last one, but really only in the early game.  But even these ultimately came down to the same strategy, it was just harder to do immediately: surround the spawn point, then wait for the win.
2) The wide variety of units doesn’t really matter.  This piggybacks off #1.  You can win every level (except the last one) with just Grills and Flamers (maybe even just Grills).  If you have enough to build Rickies, you probably are going to win anyway.  This made the game fairly one-dimensional.
I think this aspect actually drives people away from the multiplayer; they get a sour first impression and can’t get over it.
Best of luck to the team in their future projects, at any rate!  I know there has since been a sequel;  I may give that a spin to see if some of these things are addressed there.

It's taken a long time for me to think of the correct words I wanted to use to describe Oblivion.
I first played Oblivion on my friends Xbox 360 and was immediately hooked - I went straight to our local game store (Our town still had one in those days) and in there was a guy who was being made by his parents to sell all of his games to cover his ridiculous phone bill that he had wracked up, it was hundreds of pounds. I got his copy, a battered old case with a cigarette burn on the cover. And I loved it. It was probably the game I spent most time on, ever, on my good old 360. Now that I have evolved into one of the PC master race, it was time to do it all over again.
Now, I will start here with Oblivion's flaws. For as much as I like it, it does have them and it would be unfair not to mention them. As the game world itself is huge, of course the associated bugs and glitches come with them. There are hundreds, and I suspect not all of them have been found. Some of them are quest breaking and some of them are literally game breaking, so they can be highly frustrating. On PC, this is not so much of an issue due to the all godly console commands.
Combat is clunky, and especially in melee combat - you can get stuck in a hit cycle from multiple enemies and just have no way of defending yourself. The voice acting in itself is quite literally a cultural phenomenon. Yahtzee (our lord and saviour from Zero Punctuation) was 100% accurate when he described characters talking, to themselves, about the shop, owned by themselves. Its a solid attempt at a procedurally generated NPC conversations but it just falls short of the mark. The speech skill/persuasion is baffling in this game, and often I just ended up bribing people to tell me what I wanted.
It hasn't aged terribly well in line with modern RPGs, but this does not matter to me so much - however, this could be an issue if graphics are your marker of a good game. The upcoming Skyblivion mod will seek to remedy this, and good luck to the development team on this - if you're ever in the UK, I'll buy you a drink. It does occasionally crash for no reason, but that could just be my particular set up.
I could sit here and write pages about why I love Oblivion, so I won't. Its not just a game, its an experience. It is a lush, huge world with many different areas to wander, and has hundreds of dungeons, forts, caves, even shipwrecks to explore.  The quests and quest writing is miles above other Elder Scrolls games, the guilds in particular are fantastic - The Dark Brotherhood blows Skyrim's out of the water. I've never managed to complete all of the quests, I still find new NPCs, locations and quests to this day.
It has a good chunk of DLC available - including the much derided horse armour (Seriously, give it a search - it was a bit of a mess). However, the available content also includes the legendary Shivering Isles DLC, often considered to be one of the best ever DLC packages made. It adds well over 30 hours of new content, and its not just new weapons or armour but an entire new world to explore, set in the Alice in Wonderland-esque realm of Sheogorath. That, Bethesda, is how you should be doing it.
I'll stop gushing now.
Seriously, if you let it drag you under - you won't come out for weeks.

If Civilizations and Age of Empires had a baby, it wouldn't be nearly as bodacious as Rise of Nations. That being said, the combination of the two well-known strategy games - one turn-based the other RTS - does give a foundation to form a basic description of this classic strategy title. It is *not* comparable, however, to another game of a similar title called Rise of Legends - a fantasy based RTS with no progression of ages.
The progression of ages. A time-tested technique mastered by Sid Meier's Civilizations franchise through a multitude of wildly successful (and less successful) grand strategy titles. This game takes what is good about Civ (what isn't good?) and transmogrifies it from turn-based to real time fast-paced action. That being said, there are some differences including a greater emphasis on combat and diplomacy that is less diplomatic. But fortunately for us and the more sensitive individuals at Dhruva Interactive, Ghandi won't be declaring war on anybody on turn eight and using nukes several centuries of "non-violent" war later. No, you do not take control of notable historical figures, at least not in standard skirmish.
There are, however, several historical-based grand map campaigns not dissimilar to those of the Warhammer 40K Dawn of War title released in 2004. Napoleon's short-lived crusade or the wars for the Americas, the span of history this game covers is quite vast. As for graphics this game has aged well. While the steam release date is 2014 the game saw it's original nativity in 2003. Today, it remains one of the greatest RTS games available, competing easily with any of today's alleged DLC bloated triple-A titles.
If you enjoy the game or are looking to expand your strategy collection, check out Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. The greatest space RTS in existence.

As with many others, I have been playing the original Rise of Nations long before I got the Extended Edition, so my playtime is far greater than what Steam lets on.
This is easily one of the best RTS games I've ever played. The list of highlight for me are:
-Age progression spanning from ancient settlers to the Information Age
-24 Nations built upon the same basic framework but given variety through unique National Powers and Units
-Every Unique Unit is based off of actual historic warriors, soldiers and technology used by that Nation
-Your cities actually produce National Borders that affect where you can build and can also passively damaged unsupplied enemies
-You capture cities and add them to your territory instead of outright destroying them
-Infinite resources limited only by the rate you can gather them and a cap on said rate (that you can increase through research)
-Nuclear Weapons with cleverly incorporated consequences (only so many can be detonated before a game over where everyone loses, encouraging their use as a deterrent rather than an actual option just like in real life)
-Build Wonders of the World that actually provide really handy bonuses
-Risk-style Conquer the World campaigns where you take parts of the World via RTS battles
-'Quick Battle' mode has a lot of options to fiddle with, including starting the game with a few citizens who have to build your first city or restricting the game to a certain Age or Ages
-Mod Support, complete with an in game menu to select which one you want to use. And with Steam Workshop support!
I pretty much retired my copies of Age of Empires when I got this game. The Extended Edition serves as a nice bundle of the core game and it's Thrones and Patriots expansion, with some graphical updates here and there. And Steam Workshop. Definite must for any RTS fan.

Crusader Kings isn't that much about playing a country, other than the other Paradox grand strategy title, it is more about a centuries-long session of Medieval Murder Simulator. Playing a string of characters that might start out as lowly counts in Aquitaine and end up being Kings of England or some other wicked chain of events, the game is about scheming to elbow rival characters out of the way just as much as trying to paint the map your personal color. Ever wondered what life was like for Zoroastrian rulers in Central Asia at the height of the Muslim conquests? This is your game to play. Replayability is almost endless, covering every nook and cranny from blistering hot Northern Africa to the frosty hells of Finland, and from Ireland all the way to India. Play kind, play ruthless, take what you want by force or by cunning, be a man of honor, one of the church, or - heck - a woman of the church. Just keep your dynasty alive, so don't forget to procreate at every opportunity.
And yes, the complete game costs about as much as a kidney, but nobody forces you to buy at full price. It is 75% off often enough. Bananas pricing doesn't make it a bad game.

This is a wonderful game that does nearly everything right. I enjoy how it looks, how it feels. The UI could be a bit more friendly, but I can get used to it. The diplomacy system needs to be redone, simply not that intuitive. Converting over from Civ V so it's a welcome change from someone other than a AAA game producing machine.

It's quite enjoyable but I keep finding little details that really sour the experience, usually in the form of AI tactics. To me, it seems like the AI operates in a way that intentionally griefs the player (things like racing to settle territories adjacent to your starting territory and then getting mad at you for being too close to their empire). It seems to me that the AI plays exactly as if Endless Legend were a competitive game which is technically true, but draws a lot away from the immersion of being an empire and not a 'team'.
I like the strangeness of the game, specifically in making the world and the empires you can play as different from 'vanilla' empires as possible. Everyone has a significant quirk and is the master of one aspect of the game, which makes them a threat in one way or another. Yet still, simple land grabbing and military domination is the most potent of these quirks and most games will tend towards this behaviour simply because there isn't enough reason not to.
My favourite part of this game is getting to personalize my hero and military units with gear that I build or otherwise loot from treasure tiles. I get the feeling that they are significant to me and not just pieces on a table, which is important because your units will level up a lot through combat and you will want to be able to outfit them for what ever scenario you will need them for.
It's good, but it's not Civilization good. The face value is honest but with some bad bits too, so if you are still keen on purchasing, not much will change your opinion of doing that.

As far as classic games go, Sonic 3 & Knuckles was a damn solid game. It's miles ahead of Sonic 1 and 2 in terms of level design and gameplay, and I usually recommend everyone to play it at least once. Sadly, it's not really the Sonic game that people remember when talking about classic Sonic.
Now, with Sonic Mania, everyone has the opportunity to see what was so good about classic Sonic. And with many modern improvements over it's predecessors, it shows that the formula still has something worthy to show. A big GOTY contender for me.

This game is a match made in heaven between fan mod creators and Sega, resulting in the end product of Sonic Mania. The classic Sonic gameplay from the Sega Genesis trilogy of games is faithfully recreated to almost-perfection here. The game has a combination of remixed old levels from Sonic 1/2/CD/3&K as well as a small handful of new levels with original tropes. In my opinion, some of the classic levels remixed in Sonic Mania are even better than their original counterparts, such as the levels that return from Sonic CD. This game is very obviously an intense labor of love from the fans, not only in the obvious areas such as the gameplay, but also in the lesser obvious areas such as fan-service Easter Eggs (which I will not spoil here).
If you loved the classic Sonic games, I cannot recommend this game highly enough. In more ways than one, this game triumphs the quality of Sonic 1/2/CD and even stands toe-to-toe with Sonic 3&K.

I agree with people saying it's too expensive. I played it a little before getting a refund for it.
I like the difficulty and the general idea of the game, but the advertised non-linearity, as said in other reviews, just leads to lots of running around aimlessly. Which is even more awful given the repetitive design. It's not like you're aimlessly wandering around through beatiful and unique landscapes. Which makes it even harder to remember which door you took last time and which you have not tried yet.
The combat is ok. I really hate it, though, when I am locked into an animation in a game where very quick reaction times are asked of the user. If I cannot attack because I might have to block an enemy attack which may or may not come, all the while the enemy moving in on you (which is bad because you lose health if an enemy runs into you without even attacking) makes for some really frustrating experiences.
Then there is the absolute randomness of drops that may make the game really easy or really hard, purely depending on your dropluck. You can get a 12dmg sword off the very first super easy enemy and then breeze through the game for quite a while or be stuck with your starting sword, finding it almost impossible to beat harder enemies who have absurd amounts of health. Which also ties in with the terrible decision to make you lose any swords/shields you have picked up when you die, basically dooming you.
Item drops should get progressively stronger as you progress through the game and you really should not lose the items you gathered when you die. That's just a super bad design move as it leaves you with barely any damage on enemies with extremely high health later in the game.
I may pick it up again when it's a lot cheaper than the 5€ I got it for on the sale, but I'd really appreciate some changes to the game to make it a little more friendly. The game is hard enough through the combat patterns and limited lives. You don't have to ♥♥♥♥ people over even harder by stripping them off their gear on death and way too slow attack/shield bash animations.

Visuals: Awesome. A good retro feel, but in no way low budget.
Gameplay: Combat is quite simple, but overall extremely challenging.
The multitude of weapons with different effects, aren't always just "better". This forces you to choose between them, which is nice.
So... what is missing? Oh yeah, I'm not having fun! The extreme difficulty means you will go back to the beginning a hundred times at least. This would be fine, if not for the fact that the levels NEVER CHANGE. You go through the beginning stage again and again, and after a while it just stops giving you any satisfaction.
Also, you have three lives, and you can pretty much die four times before getting a game over and going all the way back. But you know what? You might as well just have 1 life. Because the fist time you die, you immediately lose the weapons you picked up thusfar. And when that happens, your (ahum) butt is grass. You might as well restart. The further you got into the game, the more this is the case.
I've heard someone say to not be "discouraged by this", but honestly; the ONLY way you can beat the rest of the game is by killing all the enemy in extremely cheap ways. Waiting instead of skillfull fighting, and some room lay-outs make even THAT impossible. That, I'm sorry, I cannot see as a good gaming element.
In the end; this game, I feel, does not use it's full potential. It would do the creators very good to take a page out of the "Binding of Isaac" game mechanics, where every time you restart the game a new stroy is ahead of you. Intead of what i can only discribe as a tedious waste of potential.
I will not recommend this game, BUT if you are into hardcore challenges, like retro games and don't mind the repetition, I would tell you to buy this.

tldr; If you get this on a good sale it can be worth it (I got it for $5 on steam sale), and especially so if you played this as a kid or have fond memories of playing it from a long time ago. OVERALL I don't particularly enjoy the game because of "The bad and the ugly" listed below, which kill the fun for me. Lots of customization of options relating to the game, but
The Good:
It holds up okay in some respects still, despite being very old. The economy system is pretty good and for me is by far the most fun aspect of the game. It has a lot of good functions such as hotkeys for every building, finding your army, finding idle workers, and of course the numbers can be hotkeyed to whatever you want such as all of your barracks on 6 for example so you can quickly create whatever units you want. There are also a wide range of nations with varied nation powers, strengths and weaknesses. There are spoken commands/taunts depending on what you type, from 0 - 100 typing just a number will trigger a sound file to be played. This can be fun and even helpful, though I just used voice chat to communicate with the friends I played the game with. The game lobby is pretty good, you can set a wide range of variables there, such as starting age, ending age (if you only want to play the game up to the medieval period you can do so
The Bad: The music is unbearably loud and your only solution is to check the box which turns the music off. Even moving the volume slider to its lowest will not help for long, the volume resets itself at seemingly random times. The combat sucks....Despite the large variety of army units every game I've played has lasted around 50-75 minutes and always ends up at the information age and nukes galore. You can have a large advantage over a computer player and still not be able to kill their forces quickly despite overwhelming army forces. It can be very frustrating especially when you're an age ahead. For example massing main battle tanks should be able to kill most groups of lower tier enemies with ease, but can struggle (especially with..;)
The Ugly: The pathing in the game is pretty attrocious. Your units if near a border will run headlong into battle chasing enemies until they themselves are killed, or you tell them to come back (they will immediately run back again unless you hit the stop command, which can get them killed easily by siege weapons if you're not careful, since after telling them to stop they will not move unless told to. It's a mixed blessing that the command is there). Your units will also bunch up if you have many of the same type, they'll have to go around the forests and can sometimes split your army very disadvantageously for you if you're not careful with clicking the minimap. If you're attacked, it can be very difficult to move the few civilians who are in danger because if you try to draw a box to select them, you'll prioritize your army and thus be unable to select the civs. If you double click the civ, it will select all civs on your screen (when usually you want the majority of them to continue what they were doing). The game is also a huge time sink, as you can be in a game for an hour long but essentially lose it 30 mins into it without knowing, but you think you still may have a chance so you stay in a little longer, and longer....
It's one of those games that I play a few matches every now and then and have fun until the battles happen, because the combat system in this game is quite bad, which is a shame because everything else is quite well thought out in my opinion. I flip-flopped a few times between recommended and not recommended, but ended up choosing "not" because the game is actually very expensive when not on sale ($25+ CAD), and overall I'd probably have given it a 55/100 to begin with, for reasons stated above

Crusader Kings isn't that much about playing a country, other than the other Paradox grand strategy title, it is more about a centuries-long session of Medieval Murder Simulator. Playing a string of characters that might start out as lowly counts in Aquitaine and end up being Kings of England or some other wicked chain of events, the game is about scheming to elbow rival characters out of the way just as much as trying to paint the map your personal color. Ever wondered what life was like for Zoroastrian rulers in Central Asia at the height of the Muslim conquests? This is your game to play. Replayability is almost endless, covering every nook and cranny from blistering hot Northern Africa to the frosty hells of Finland, and from Ireland all the way to India. Play kind, play ruthless, take what you want by force or by cunning, be a man of honor, one of the church, or - heck - a woman of the church. Just keep your dynasty alive, so don't forget to procreate at every opportunity.
And yes, the complete game costs about as much as a kidney, but nobody forces you to buy at full price. It is 75% off often enough. Bananas pricing doesn't make it a bad game.

Adorables is a collection of 6 mini games which starred a group of cute creatures called "Adorables". The game can only be played with a mouse although you can use keyboard to navigate through the menu.
The music sounds pleasant and reminds me of world cup's song. Maybe this is influenced by the game which has a lot of ball games in it (and one mode with Europe cup theme).
The graphics are decent, although the settings page can be quite annoying. It took several clicks just to go back to main menu after you buy eyes, mouth, or hat parts. Although you can costumize all of your Adorables appearance (even its body shape and color), most of the hat parts cover the Adorables' face although i love seeing their cute faces. More variation for the hat parts which doesn't cover the Adorables' face would be appreciated.
There are several modes in the game, which are:
-
, where you will be playing with CPU in 1 round
-
, where you will be playing soccer game in a bracket preliminaries mode and then moving to tournament mode in 7 rounds total
-
, where you will be playing single type game in a tournament elimination mode in 4 rounds
-
, where you will be playing all game in 1 round each, totalling in 6 rounds
-
, where you'll be playing in multiplayer with internet connection
-
where you will be playing with your friends locally
Although there are lots of game mode in this game, you'll mostly play either Continental Contest or Tournament because they will give you coins which can be used to customize your Adorables.
The Online feature is terrible as you have to input the host IP to join a game. It also lag endlessly when i try to host a game, which forces me to restart my computer.
There are several games in this game, with 3 being ball games and 3 being non ball games. The ball games work the same way like each other (move the ball to the goal), except that the ball has different size and weight with a different goal placement. The Ice Hockey game can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because the AI will act weirdly whenever the puck is going behind the goal. The small puck size also makes the game to be hard to finish, as the game will be finished whenever a team scored 3 points.
The game is played in turn, where you will be given a chance to move your three Adorables by using your mouse to drag them to move to the said location with a certain speed (the longer the line you drag, the faster it will move). After you finished positioning them, you can confirm your selection and the round will start. The game will keep on continuing until one team scores three points first (or based on time limit, if you are playing Continental Contest in bracket preliminaries) for the ball game. For the non ball game, the objectives will depend on the game. For Last Adorables Stand, you'll win if your team is the last one to stand. For Capture The Flag, you'll win if you place enemies' flag in your place before your enemies do the same thing with your flag. For Mummy, you'll win if at least one of your team survive from the mummies.
If you think that the turn based move is too slow, you can activate a speed mode, which will remove the turn based mode and change it to real time based. However, you'll get a disadvantage, especially in ball games, because the AI will be able to move three Adorables at once while you only can do once (unless you can figure out how to click and drag at three different points in the screen at once). The mechanism that your Adorables will get stunned if they are hit by other Adorables also can make it worse. However, the game will end faster in this mode, which could make the game to be lively.
Although the game might be frustating at first, it will be enjoyable as soon as you learned how to play it. However, the game can be boring soon after that because it mostly will do the same thing (especially if you played it too many times at once).
Pros:
- 6 game modes
- 6 game types
- Customizable Adorables
- Speed mode to fast things up
Cons:
- It can be boring when it's played too often
