Overrated game with potato-faced NPCs, convoluted level up rules and not much atmosphere.
In less than an hour after posting my first review of this game, some fan boys with several hundreds of hours playtime had added backseat driver comments already. Guys, if you don't point out anything essential, I won't change my mind. I've had another look, though, but stopped eventually because of boredom again.
The game is surprisingly unstable with Windows 7.
It crashes spontaneously, such as while exploring the wilderness. I've also had some weird  savegame corruption, where entire houses in the city of Chorrol became invisible except for their doors. I could move through the invisible buildings and had to revert to an older savegame file.
The game also crashes always when quitting. The so-called Unoffial Oblivion Patch doesn't fix that either. I don't feel like investing a lot of time on installing a growing number of mods, mod managements programs and extra runtime dependencies.
The game manual only touches the surface.
That may be okay for some casual playing, but the included documentation is not detailed enough when you want to do some real planning or when you want to avoid pitfalls, such as leveling up too fast and too inefficiently.
And the level up procedure is everything but intuitive.
Whereas using your major skills repeatedly -- say heavy armor, a shield and a single-handed sword or axe -- leads to leveling up, using a wider mix of major skills leads to lower attribute bonuses when you level up. With some of the prebuilt classes the game offers, simply walking slowly (not even running) while exploring the wilderness or a city, leads to increasing the Athletics skill and reaching the next level eventually without increasing your fighting skills and their related attributes. You can only avoid inefficient leveling with a multitude of tricks and boring meta-gaming, such as by not using some skills and restricting yourself to a small subset of skills that are governed by the same attribute, such as jumping around steadily to advance Acrobatics or letting your own summons attack you so you can train shield usage. Boring. In forum topics about that, the fan boys ask others to "do their homework", which involves non-intuitive playstyles described in guides in the community's Wiki, such as the "Efficient Leveling" guide or the "Creating an Awesome Character" guide.
To make it worse, enemies in the game get rebalanced as you level up, even if you may have
advanced non-combat skills mostly. The enemy scaling makes some quests much easier when you are at a low level and requires more effort or even meta-gaming when your level is higher -- such as the Odiil farm quest - took me several retries at level 4 to keep the two sons alive, because they stay weak while the enemies get stronger. Obviously, the fans and meta-gamers figure out when to go where as to retrieve special items as early as possible and other rewards as late as possible, because - d'oh! - item rewards get upgraded depending on your level when you finish a quest. Various guides recommend waiting for level 30 before completing some quests to get better rewards. Meta-gaming hell or a metagamer's wet dream. Take your pick!
Cannot say the story would be uninteresting. It's okay. You get a main quest with a next goal
and enough motivation, but it seems to be a bad idea to focus on it, since you don't know how capable you need to be when you want to advance the main quest. On the other hand, how much time to spend on exploring and searching for side-quests, no idea. I've completed a few quests and interactions with NPCs and have started various quests to learn a bit about them, but clearing one very similar cave after the other isn't exciting stuff.

I'm giving this game a provisional thumbs up because I did enjoy playing it -- for a while.  It has a lot of cool gameplay elements.  First and foremost is its "quest" mechanic, which as far as I know is unique in a 4X game.  It also has an interesting one-city-per-province limitation that really forces you to consider your city placement carefully.  The map that smoothly fades to a lower level of detail as you zoom out is also pretty neat.  And another feature I've never seen in a 4X game before is that combat takes place directly on the strategic map: the view zooms in and your units are placed in nearby locations on the map for tactical combat resolution.  What a great  idea!
But it's not without its problems, either.  City-building is lackluster, and the strategic-level campaign becomes monotonous pretty quickly: the early game (which heavily features the aforementioned quests) is fun, but the mid-game is only so-so, and the end-game is just tedious.  Once you reach a certain tipping point, your eventual victory is a foregone conclusion, but you still have to slog through dozens of turns to get there.
I enjoyed this game for 20 or 30 hours, which I think gave me my money's worth.  That's about a dollar per hour of entertainment -- which compares quite favorably to, say, a night out at the movies.  And that's why I give it a thumb's up; but I probably won't ever play it again once the new Civilization comes out in a few weeks.

First off, let me say that I'm not a fan of Endless Space. As a huge 4x fan I wanted to like ES badly, but the game felt very flat. I thought the galaxy was lifeless, military strategy is just an r/p/s guessing game and each play through feels pretty much the same after about the first 20 minutes.
I mention that because this is what made me hesitate about buying Endless Legend. I need not have worried. EL is wonderful. It has all of the life and character that ES lacked and much, much more.
Picking a "best thing" about this game is tough, but I would agree with many that it's the faction design. The factions don't just have a few different units or stat bumps, they obey entirely different game mechanics. They have their unit trees and city plans. You can't play the same game with two different factions, it just won't work. And that's awesome.
Above everything else, Endless Legend is original. The regional cities, tech tree "eras," expressing influence directly as a resource, redesigning units like you would in a space 4x, they make this game feel like something I haven't seen before. In a field that has been competing to become the next Master of Magic or Civ fantasy for the last 20 years, that's a breath of fresh air. Endless Legend is fun, it's original and it's incredibly worth buying.

No 4X game has grabbed me quite as Endless Legend. The Presentation is almost flawless. With beautiful artwork, an awesome soundtrack and an interface, that lets you have all necessary information in an instant. The Factions are maybe the biggest plus of this game, because they REALLY change how you play in a big way... just how fantasy-factions should. There are still issues with game-balance, but the Developers are really engaged in ironing those out.
The fighting system, although often criticized, is very solid in my opinion, because it gives you a sense of combat, without wanting to be a RTS-Minigame.
Also, the City-Management and the minor factions are really good own concepts, that manage to keep the game fresh and apart from it's 4X-Brothers. One thing that is worth mentioning is the missing campaign, so anyone playing this as a Singleplayer might not get a much fun out of it.
in Conclusion:
+ vastly different factions
+ great User Interface
+ great artstyle
+ cool new twists on genre-standards (semi RTS-battles)
- AI can be ridiculous at times
- Naval system needs to be expanded
- no Campaign
Concerning the Addons:
Guardians:
This Addon adds one-man-army-Units (the guardians) to the game. Even more important however are the new wonders and deeds, that add a new level of competition between empires and give every round a new twist.
Shadows:
Adds Spying to the game. Also, you get a new, spy-based faction. Great Addon, especially if you are playing with friends, since mind games are alwasy better against real people.

A very nice take at mining resource manager. Not unique in itself, but indeed an achievement.
Difficulty-wise - it sits between outpost (original one, not godawful sequel) and industry giant 2.
The thing is - it's not as difficult as outpost. It's more on par with alien legacy or reunion, albeit doesn't have exploration element of alien legacy, or gorgeous in-between cutscenes of reunion.
It doesn't even has a story to speak of either.
You are one of the executives (of mining division) of a corporation which does space mining. Objective is to balance resources and money between selling resources, building ships, maintaining your colonies and, if the allegiance breaks, assault enemies via various means.
Core gameplay loop is satisfactory enough that you will, at the very least, get 3-6 hours out of single mission (if that mission is easy), more so out of multi-racial missions with agressors and active diplomatic routine.
There is no research system to speak of - you just pay to tech company to deliver you blueprints for better swag, which increase your performance.
The first part meat of the game is searching for new asteroids to mine, protecting them, optimizing production (mainly by buying new stuff) or staring at the stars (no, seriouisly, space'y soundtrack does give it meditative qualities); the other part of the meat is warfare. You have your standard Fighter/fighter missions, planetary bombardment, and missle command which you use to launch missles with various effects. Then there is also chemical/biological warfare, which is, in all honesty - a welcome sight, as it is usually omitted in most of the games about corporate warfare. Although it is punishing, if you use it and then get discorvered by your own federation, which will most likely execute you (i should try it to be sure).
The main beef i have with this game - is that there are no objectives side to it outside of all-out domination.
It is very open-ended indeed, and whenever you abort/end game - it will count in things you've done and score you.
It did had mutiplayer, but setting that up will probably be a pain.
Overall - I enjoyed experience, and will probably play a bit more of it. Although i still wish it would've had some sort of campaign with fixed objectives to achieve.

Cubeman is a very barebones strategy game. The idea is pretty simple: You're given a variety of nondescript cubic soldiers, all of which require a certain amount of resources to be summoned, and are tasked with positioning them on the battlefield in a way that will give you control over your opponent. All units perform a different task and all of them do better under certain conditions, so choosing where to place each of them is vital to your victory.
The gameplay, albeit solid, can be kind of slow and boring at times. Its basic nature makes it so that there isn't a lot of room for strategy in it: Position your units correctly, and soon you can start spamming heavy-hitters, giving your opponent little to no room for recovery. It feels more like a slaughterfest than it does like an actual strategy game. The online community is pretty much dead, and after you figure out the game mechanics, beating the AI opponents isn't too hard.
Graphically, there isn't much to say: They don't suck, but they're not very appealing either. I give the designers credit for giving you the option to customize how your soldiers and the levels look. A+ for going the extra mile.
The soundtrack is actually pretty good. It's not something I would listen to on my free time, but I took notice of it when I first started the game and was very pleased with it while I played. Deserves a special mention because of that.
In the end, I think cubemen will appeal more to those who aren't very into the RTS genera and looking for something simple that will help them get into it. It's a very solid game and it can definitively be a lot of fun if you have a friend to play with. For its low pricetag, it’s definitively a worthwhile deal.

Excellent game for anyone looking for a game that's simple but challenging.
Shadowcrypt feels very retro in all the best ways: Simple controls, a manual with valuable game knowledge, no long tutorial, and the best part: its replay value comes from not the length of the game or a plethura of features and modes, but the sheer challenge of finishing the game (and getting achievements).
To clear things up:
This is a combat-based platformer, meaning that if you don't learn the timing and dynamics of the combat, you won't get very far. Understanding that this is by design and is meant to be adapted to is essential to enjoying and completing Shadowcrypt.
The description may sound like the game has procedurally generated levels, but it does not. This isn't a bad thing though, once you get into the game you learn to embrace it. The levels are technically non-linear, but at the end of the day, they're linear. They just involve exploration and remembering where to go; the crypt is confusing and a bit maze-like, but that's a part of the game. Getting lost in the crypt is also part of the game. You'll see.
You get three lives, and when you lose them all you start over from the beginning. A complaint I hear a lot is people saying once you lose your first life you're screwed because you lose all of your gear (which is an important part to progressing). To these people I say: Don't get discouraged! You can beat this game with the starting crappy weapons, as impossible as that may sound. If you're good at fighting in this combat-based game, you will move forward. And there will most likely be a weapon or shield drop or a treasure chest. Just keep going, don't give up!
Final verdict:
This is one of the BEST games I've played this year. It took me a long time to beat it and I appreciated the mood, the music, the excellent character animation, the sound of the dungeon doors opening and closing, and especially the challenge. It's old school and feels like you picked it up from the SNES bin at the local game store, and I love that.
I'd love to see another game like this from One-bit Punch, or a sequel. I'd love to see more weapons, more levels, and more boss fights. I couldn't tell you how much money I'd pay for another, longer, more expansive version of this exact game.
It's grindy, it's retro, it's moody, it's a real challenge. I'll be playing it more in attempts to get the ridiculously challenging achievements. I highly recommend this game. 10/10

There's two big reasons, two different types of people who play games. There are people who play video games to unwind, because they had a hard day at work and they want to let loose and not have to think, people who want to have fun without the worry of being stuck or presented with obstacles.
Then there are those who love punishment, people who live to play games like Journey to Silius, I Wanna Be The Guy or the more recent Dark Souls series. Diehards who don't want their hand held and want to be beaten mercilessly over and over until they finally learn what they've been doing wrong this whole time.
Shadowcrypt is absolutely a game for the latter, and I'm proud to say I'm one of these deranged masochists. This is a game that presents players with a big question; are you in touch with your roots?
As the torches of the title screen begin to flicker around the ominous skull decorating the entryway the haunting chants of the intro music beckon you to the dank and dark depths of the most brutal arcade platformer I've had the pleasure of playing.
Shadowcrypt is all about the combat. The bleak and claustrophobic level designs of the game only lend to your unbridled focus on the task at hand. All of your attention will be drawn to the beautifully crafted sprites and their precise animations as you slash and bash your way to the heart of the Crypts in pursuit of the wicked Necromancer.
Only 4 rooms into the game my mysterious cowled hero crumples to the floor dead..again..for the third time. "I-I'll just try this again later.." I whimper to myself, tucking my gamepad away and walking away to make a sandwich to hopefully forget about this brutal game that just made me it's slave. Not even a minute later, I toss my condiments to the ground and declare "Eff that, I can do it!" and find myself rushing back to the computer where I give these beckoning crypts another go. I feel that same kind of determined spirit I held in the Famicom days.
The gameplay with it's visceral combat and the insane amount of concentration needed exceed my expectations, it's almost a little overwhelming. I've heard people call other games "the Dark Souls of 2D gaming" before many times in the past but Shadowcrypt is probably the first title I've played to actually match and truly capture the punishing and calculated approach to combat Dark Souls has, where every little move you make has a huge impact and consequence.
Even more-so are the striking similarities to what seems to be the developer's hugest influence, Zelda II, from the candle finding objective needed to progress to the highly memorable and iconic shield-wielding Iron Knuckle battles that the combat here seems to inspire from heavily. It's the refreshing change of pace I've been waiting for since the golden-era of games.
While I can see a lot of less patient players outright quitting in frustration the moment they die and are reduced to the starting 3-7dmg sword prior to a strong foe, the more retro-minded of players will remember this sort of challenge from our earlier and most important days of gaming. We'll stick with it and experience something exceedingly rewarding. You'll die often, but everytime you start again you'll feel better, stronger, and make it a little bit further. And when you do finally beat those rooms? Holy crap, it feels
.
Though the system of losing your only reliable weapon will feel almost too brutal for newcomers, it's what gives Shadowcrypt the refined gameplay it has. To give a sense of real distress in every confrontation and to make death that much more consequential.
The punishing nature is extremely familiar to the first Castlevania titles where dying would lose you your chained whip, sticking you back with the puny leather alternative in the midst of a tough level. Konami in general were masters of this formula, as my other favorite series Gradius was very similar in nature with deaths reverting you back to the almost useless pea-shooter.
That fear of losing what was making me do better in those classics caused a much higher level of awareness and addiction to the game. To succeed in Shadowcrypt you will need to adapt and get into the motions of the combat. You will block, dodge, and bash your way through enemies, you will learn to stand face-to-face with your most feared adversaries. Eventually, things just start to 'click' with the player.
The game is certainly short and decidedly so. It requires a level of focus that if prolonged would just cause player fatigue on unmanageable levels. The short, sweet, and very to-the-point approach gives a lot of breathing room for the hectic and chaotic nature of the player's progression.
Shadowcrypt is composed of one lengthy stage or "level" roughly the size of the original Castlevania, but the amount of practice and dedication required in order to pass even a small section will have most players retrying for days before they're able to conquer nearly all of the evils within.
You will get no breaks nor will you receive any hand-holding, it's a game by the hardcore for the hardcore. Unfortunately that may drive the less strong-willed of players away, but it's that determination in presenting the game how the creator intends which is extremely admirable and is exactly what draws me to the titles I have the fondest memories of.
When video games are developed by people who genuinely love the culture and obviously grew up with a passion for them it's always a breath of fresh air, and Shadowcrypt is the kind of game I and probably many others have wanted to play since the late 80s as kids.

I bought this game simply for the combat system. It looked precise, fast, and not too complicated. I was not dissapointed. Everything in this game is very precise; jumping, attacking, ducking, and bashing. To put it simply, this is very much a game where you will only die if it is your fault. So far the game has been very fair, but still difficult.
This game is not randomly generated rooms. It does not advertise randomly generated rooms. Every playthrough will have the same rooms with the same enemy and trap placement. The only thing random about this game is the item drops and on-hit modifiers. Some people might want randomly generated rooms (and it is appealing to subsequent playthroughs for some games) but this game is in the mindset of Legend of Zelda II, Castlevania, and classic arcade games. Every encounter is carefully crafted, not generated.
The combat is precise, simple, satisfying, and difficult but fair. When you are not moving or attacking, your shield automatically blocks hits. Enemies can do damage to you with attacks or by walking into you. If enemies didn't deal damage from walking into you the game would be very easy. Some enemies have no good way to counter you if you just duck and stab. Ducking doesn't let you shield bash, but dodges high attacks and blocks low ones, making you extremely defensive. If they couldn't walk into you to deal damage, every encounter would end with you ducking and stabbing their ankles to death while taking no damage. Doing hit and run tactics by constantly running and stabbing is sort of viable, but not nearly as fast, satisfying, or viable as just keeping enemies back with a shield bash. It's the superior tactic. The javelins help in terms of dealing damage from a range, but you have a limited supply and they don't deal a lot of damage. Attacks and shield bashes hit all enemies in front of you which helps make groups manageable, though so far I haven't had more than two people attack me at once. Again, if you take damage in combat, you only have yourself to blame.
This game does not advertise itself as an RPG or a rogue-like. It is very much an action game, and a very tactical, precise one.
The atmosphere is nice, but nothing special. You trek through a fairly standard dungeon with nice pixel graphics and a fitting soundtrack. It's decent, but nothing to scream about. The pixel lighting is very nice though and adds a whole lot, though.
EDIT:
Simply playing the game for a bit longer showed me what each element and shield does. Fire for damage, ice for stun, and lightning for knockback and piercing javelins. Defender has a chance to stun, Avenger for damage, and Hammer for extra knockback. It is a fairly short game, but a fun one that I can see myself replaying a lot. The only thing that takes away from this game is it's relatively short length and everything that comes along with that. The story is minimal, but not really important in this type of game. If this game was ever expanded or used as a basis for another game, I would like to see pretty much more of everything. More kinds of enemies, more traps, more weapons, more elements, more shields, more rooms, and more areas. The number of these things in Shadowcrypt itself suffices for its scope, but there really is only room for improvement.

A cute little remake of Cestos (which itself was likely a remake of something), but flawed in its current state.
Like Cestos, the basic thrust of this game revolves around sliding little blobs around on a playfield and bumping them into each other. One mode - Last Adorables Standing - is exactly like Cestos, in that you're trying to knock the other guy's blobs off the edge of the playfield, except there's only one map here, which is a bit of a disappointment - it's not like these playfields are terribly complicated to come up with once the basic engine is written.
Three of these modes (Soccer, Volleyball, and Ice Hockey) involve a "ball" and a "goal". The only difference between Soccer and Volleyball is that in Soccer, the ball is slightly smaller, and your players can be knocked through the goal and off the map. Ice Hockey reduces the friction a little and puts the goals slightly closer together to create some "dead space" behind each goal, but it's generally the same concept.
The two remaining modes are a bit different: Capture the Flag is, well, Capture the Flag, where touching a flag-carrier in the central section of the map "steals" the flag. "Mummy" is best described as "Zombie tag" - an AI-controlled Mummy tries to knock into both players' blobs, and once a blob is touched by the Mummy it becomes a Mummy too, targeting whatever blobs remain. Unfortunately, the asymmetrical map here gives one side a permanent advantage. The Capture the Flag map is also asymmetrical, though it's slightly harder to decide which side is favored.
Games can be played as "practice" (skirmishes), a "World Cup" event where you play the Soccer mode using World Cup rules (group stages, then I assume a tournament), a "Tournament" mode where you can choose the game mode, and a "Story" mode which is pretty much just one skirmish after another. Online and hotseat multiplayer modes round out the bill.
So, that's the basics, so far so good, for the most part. However, now the problems begin to surface.
There is no matchmaking for online play. I don't just mean that there's no ELO or similar system to organize balanced matches - I mean that there's not even a server browser. Unless you and your friend(s) share your I.P. addresses, there's no way to play anything other than single-player or hot-seat.
Single-player is also flawed - for the most part, the A.I. just simplistically charges at the nearest valid target. In some modes (particularly Capture the Flag), this is randomized a bit, but it's still pretty basic. With such a variety of game-modes, many of them organized around the concept of "teams", it would seem natural to vary things a bit - some teams aggressively charging, other teams focusing more on repositioning themselves to secure an advantage. As far as I can tell, this isn't happening, and each A.I. team plays pretty much the same.
Customizing your little Adorables is done from a separate menu at the start of the game, with various cosmetics unlocked with in-game currency earned from winning matches. Customization is nice, but I think it's a bit of a missed opportunity - my Practice Soccer team will look the same as my Tournament Volleyball team, and changing the looks requires backing all the way out to the main menu. I think it might be more interesting if the non-practice modes had their own separate player-teams, so a Story mode team starts off as just a bunch of generic Adorables and earns their own unlocks separately from the default team.
The sound is atrocious. A five second loop of background noises (birds for soccer, crashing waves for the ship setting of the Capture the Flag and Last Adorable Standing modes, and so on), with occasional sped-up "oh no!" "goal!" and similar vocalizations.
The GUI is a bit finicky - you navigate by clicking on a "<" and a ">", but the hitboxes for those symbols only cover the intersection. If you click too far to the "open" side, you just end up selecting whatever mode is currently highlighted. Probably just as bad on the touchscreens this game is clearly designed for.
Finally, as far as I can tell, none of the longer modes saves your progress. If you want to play the World Cup mode, I really hope you love soccer, because you're going to have to play a crapload of matches in one sitting. Does your friend want to play a quick match? Too bad, you can't start up a quick multiplayer game without losing all your progress.
The individual modes themselves also suffer from various less-obvious game-design flaws - for instance, the timed modes run off an actual continuously-running timer, rather than a set number of turns, which has the consequence of encouraging players to not actually click "ready/end-turn" and just wait out the turn limit timer so they can milk the game clock. I imagine this would be really tiresome when playing online multiplayer. The "speed mode" tries to alleviate this, but really just turns the game into frenzied clicking instead, desperately trying to set move orders - any move orders at all - in the tiny window of time you're allowed. Really, a turn limit (game ends in X turns) rather than time limit (game ends in X:XX) is the way to go with this.
All in all, there's potential for fun here - especially for those of us who loved Cestos back in the day - but it's still a major update or two away.

This game tries really hard to be the Stanley Parable, but ends up failling due to a few reasons.
While the puzzles are pretty decent, they are presented in a format that screams "MESSAGE." While I applaud a game for trying something new, trying to imbue meaning into something that is rather shallow ends up looking bad. This is especially true for the vase jumping part. It tries hard to make the vases seem like drugs, but the ingame message is that the vases are good, powerups. This relays the message: Drugs are good, without adding anything to that idea.
The worst part is the story, which revolves around Anthony and Vinny. Vinny drugs anthony and all of the story takes place in his dream. None of the continuity is explained and it becomes a mess by the end while we wonder what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on.
We are supposed to like Vinny as a character based on how he is charismatic and funny, but he acts downright evil in the windmill section. Was him trying to kill you part of the dream? If so why would he act so nonchalant during the final scene. This "it's all a dream" excuse ♥♥♥♥s with the story way too much in that you might as well ignore it and just go with it by the plays.
The splitting off part was a stupid move by the creator as it meant that a huge section was barred off from the main playthrough. Splitting resources like that for the sake of an artificial choice is stupid in triple A games and it's stupid here.
With the dumb choice forced in and the omnipotent narator it almost feels as if the creator was going for a Stanley Parable vibe. If so, then he failed. It wound up feeling just about as interesting but a hell of a lot less satisfying.
Despite the rawness of this critique I actually kind of enjoyed the game. It was interesting and varied and it tried something new with a new aesthetic that is rare from games like this. It was free to play after all, a choice I admire from the creator, and the puzzles were pretty engaging at times. I'd recommend this to a friend for the sake of having a conversation about it. It is the kind of game that invokes thinking and that's always a good thing.

Honestly, I don't feel as ripped off as most people here, I just think this game got really confused as to what it was supposed to be somewhere in development, just sort of in general. Does it want to be a sequel to Men of War set in the Modern Era? Great, thats what most of the old fan base wanted, a developer led version of some of the great mods for Assault Squad that were already on offer that could do that same thing, hopefully with the polish that a developer could bring. But its not really that.
Is it a FPS/RTS hybrid? Direct control has always been a big part of Men of War, but this time you can use it to even go down into an infantrymen's perspective directly, and with FPS controls! While an interesting idea... it isn't really that either. The direct control mechanics for Men of War worked because it was the ability to momentarily fine control an RTS unit led to further strategic thinking and fun "oh wow I didn't think that would work" moments. This the camera and the controls just make it clunky, and shifting perspective means you suddenly lose the grand picture for a moment in order to fine control something on the ground, which means you will inevitably lose ground or an important bit of kit in the meantime. So again, no its not really an FPS/RTS hybrid.
Is it a fully featured paid game? Well, you definitely can buy a "full" version of it, but with the increasing in microtransactions, the season pass being put up already, promises of future DLC content even before the Early Access logo disappears, are you really truly getting everything you can be? And considering how a lot of that microtransaction stuff is currently there for cosmetic multiplayer reasons, while the multiplayer stands mostly idle due to this general genre and game confusion... do you really even care if its "full" when there is no one else to play it with?
On and on it goes. This really should not have been that difficult. Digitalmindsoft made Men of War. They have that engine still I'm sure. They updated it for this game, but they came up with the concepts that we wanted to see in this game, the original direct control, all of that was their idea to begin with. All you had to do, was replace panzers with T-55s, halftracks with IFVs, and call it a day really. I think most fans would have been perhaps a bit disappointed it didn't go into further depth in some areas if they took that approach, but all in all I wouldn't have minded really. New toys to play with is always fun. Instead, what you get is a confused mess of a game that doesn't even have some of the quality of life improvements that Assault Squad 2 introduced later on.
Stick with Assault Squad 2. For better or worse, and that game has a few flaws of its own, but it is still leaps and bounds better, and less confused than this game.

First let me say that I don't think this is a bad game. Its very polished, looks great, the menus are intuitive, and its easy to get an understanding of what your empire is doing in a quick look.
However, this game bored the ever living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me.
My biggest problem was the combat. I read reviews and from what I understood, combat was going to be like Age of Wonders 3. And while they share similarities, Endless Legend dumbed it down big time. In this game, you don't individually move your units and attack. Instead, you give a very, VERY general set of instructions. You tell a unit to attack an enemy, no matter if the unit can reach the enemy or not, and thats it. Your unit does its best to get within range and attacks if able. Automatically. There is no tactics, no skill. Its purely who has the most units, who has the smartest units, and who has the best equiped units.
No special powers, no tactical positioning to flank an enemy cause there is no bonus for such things. You can't select one unit, move it out of the way so another unit can move to its spot and attack. You can't even really tell your unit where to go in most cases. While it is true that you can tell your unit to move to a specific place next to an enemy and attack, if that enemy moves before that unit, the unit isn't going to do anything except move because now the enemy isn't where you told your unit to move.
Combat in this game has been dumbed down to "Everyone attack this one guy! And if he dies, then attack whatever guy you feel like! But be sure to trip over yourselves trying to get within fighting range!" You make sure the red lines are all pointing towards one guy, hit play, and watch your units try their little hearts out to attack whatever the red line pointed at.
My next issue is equiping and upgrading your units (I.E. the RPG aspect of this game)
First, I have an issue with having only one infantry, archer/support, and calvery unit per race. In order to get more units, you have to convince a minor faction (Either by destroying their village in your region then rebuilding it, bribing them, or completing a quest for them) to be assimilated into your faction. Then you get their one unit. Which I must admit, was pretty lame to me. I like to have multiple units with different abilities so being restricted to less than a hands count sucked.
I was fully expecting to find magical gear like powered up swords or armor and having to choose which units or heroes to give it to. Instead Endless Legend makes you choose between having your one racial infantry unit hold a sword or spear (Doing extra damage to infantry or calvary respectively) and just getting the next "Tier" of armor your technology level allows.
I will admit, I liked being able to upgrade or "Retrofit" as the game calls it my units after adding my newly researched better armor to them immediately. But again, the upgrade itself is nothing more than equiping the next level of equipment rather than making any real choice as to how to upgrade them.
The heroes was something I liked however. Your heroes have a skill tree with 3 different trees with abilities that can affect them if they are the general of an army or the mayor of a town. Or both in some cases. It did make you have to choose if you wanted a powerful unit or to give a city huge bonuses.
The city building was interesting. Its a mix between Civilization and Heroes of Might and Magic 6 I believe. Maybe 5. I don't remember. But you build a city anywhere you want in a region, which are randomly cut out areas on the map. But you can only have one city per region so once you build a city, that region is considered yours. Along with everything in it. So enemy players can't build a city directly next to your land and take it via influence like in Civilization.
I'm not a real fan of the thumbs up or down method steam uses to rate games because this game itself isn't bad. It was just incredibly boring to me which is why I cannot recommend it.

Number one on my list is the combat system. It is much too hands-off. You can give units an attack, defense, or hold ground order, and you can direct units to target enemy units. There is the ability to move units to certain hexes, but it's not very reliable for making them attack a given unit. After setting the orders, you then play the turn, and they move in order based on their initiative. What this results in is units often not doing what you want them to, and making stupid moves that leave the unit (e.g. ranged unit getting too close to a melee) or your whole squad (e.g. attacking the wrong unit and not killing the immediate threat) exposed. On the one hand, you could say that this takes the focus off the tactics and placed more on the strategy. But on the other hand, it feels like a cop-out or a tease: simply with added controls, I can definitely say the combat would be a solid experience. All of the mechanics for a good tactical system are already there, it just needs more player control. I'm hoping Amplitude makes this happen, or a combat mod comes along.
Number two - I did not know there was a manual. You don't really need the manual, as I learnt the game by trial and error without it, but there are many things that were not obvious to me as someone who has not played Endless Space or any other 4X game before, such as... you need more citizens in a city if you want to build additional districts. It took me a while to figure that out, and I was stuck on the "build a city centre or district to level 2" part of my faction quest for quite a while. But basically there's some crucial information that should be visible but isn't. For example, a simple tooltip that says "next district available at 8 citizens" or something like that would have been great.
Number three - the early game, especially on the harder modes, can be slow - dangerous too, if you have aggressive neighbours (I have been wiped out in the first 30 turns more than once). I learnt the game on Newbie mode, and it wasn't so bad. On harder modes (currently playing Serious), incomes are reduced, so getting additional workers, building city upgrades or expansions, and recruiting new units, takes longer. Long enough that often you're stuck clicking "next turn" a few times without making any meaningful changes or choices, simply waiting for things to happen. Researches, too, are critical, and you have to wait not only for those to finish researching (which takes a lot of time), but also for the city improvements that are unlocked from them to finish building, before you gain the benefit from the research. All of this waiting time is mitigated to some extent by the exploration and questing side of things, but when you start with a small number of units that can only move four hexes per turn, and equipping them with the move bonus item costs precious resources, and healing them after a battle takes time or resources, the 'distraction' is only limited. There will still be several turns where you'll do nothing but click Next Turn. I don't know how they would fix this side of things. - Make early constructions and researches cheaper? Have a temporary income boost in the first several turns? Have a small stockpile from the start of the game? Make exploration/questing an even bigger part of the early game by making it more accessible?
Number four - the endgame. It just sort of... ends. You can play on if you like (to finish your faction quest for example), but it'd be nice to have some more closure, or a challenging final objective to complete the win condition.
If Amplitude Studios improved on these things, it would make an excellent game perfect. But make no mistake, it is an excellent game, and I'll reiterate what I said at the start: You should play this game.

Before you read the review, know this. I was/am a fan of the original Sonny 1 and 2 so this  review is a bit biased.
Sonny is a turn-based RPG that tells the story of a zombie named Sonny and his path of finding out who he is. If you want to find out then play the game, the story is good. Not great but good. Why is just good? Because it removed Sonny 2's story completely making the game sort of confusing for fans of the original. The ending and story overall is good and was pretty much what I had expected.
The combat is different from the classic games. There is a bar called "Focus". The first character that fills it up first moves first. All abilities cost 100 focus, making all abilities balanced in terms of resources. Combat is fun, adrenaline packed and overall very well suited for a TB RPG. However I do have some complaints about it. For example, some units will simply be much faster than you, so fast that they can attack twice before you can, that's not really fair. But what's even worse are some boss fights and specific creatures. Some of the battles feel like the odds are completely stacked against you. Not in the way that it's difficult, but in the way that it's completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. Like one character having 2 abilities that can completely drain your focus, a silence ability and an ability which makes you 200% weak to all attacks. WTF is that? So yeah, several fights will definetly be keyboard-breaking level hard, but they are definetly possible to do.
The soundtrack is awesome! The tracks are mostly taken from the other Sonny games. They are remastered and let me tell you they literally pack you with adrenaline for the whole fight. 10/10 even purchased the track from the maker of it - David Orr.
The leveling up system is very fun to use, dozens of options and also provides a lot of replayability. About 1/5 into the story you will be allowed to get a new strain of abilities, having them along the physical abilities you start with. You can also reset the abilities if you don't like them or they are not suited for that specific battle.
I did hear that the game has technical issues, but by the time this review is written most of them are patched. The only one I ever encountered is when the screen goes dark and you have to press the escape button twice to reset it, but other than that I never saw anything else. Oh, one more thing. It's hard to believe that free flash games are fully voiced and an 8 euro game isn't. It does have some lines in it, but the games feels weird, sometimes the character will say what they are supposed, but mostly they won't. Hopefully this will be patched somehow later on. Please, you either fully voice a game or you don't do it at all, your choice.
I would say this game is definetly a 7/10, needs some fixing and balancing but other than that it's good.

A very lovely old real-time strategy game. Looks great (well, you may need to play around in the dosbox .conf file to get it to look great on modern machines -- see the community hub discussions -- but it's well worth it :P) and the gameplay is lots of fun. The game's designers obviously put a lot of attention to detail into this title, and it shows. There's tons to do, and the game can get quite hectic and fast-paced, depending on the settings you choose. Reading the in-game "fluff" during the quieter moments shows that quite a lot of thought went into the world-building, too, which isn't a big deal in itself, but just goes to confirm again that this game was a labour of love. It has the odd bug and design flaw, but it's also more than the sum of its parts, and provides a joyful and very positive experience to any strategy fan. Plays a little bit like a mix of Sim City and Master of Orion; however, this game has a quite unique feel and style to it, so it is a bit difficult to directly compare to any other major title. If you're a fan of classic strategy games, I'd say this one is definitely worth a try. I have lots of happy memories of this game -- and thanks to this Steam release I'm still having lots of fun playing it now!

There was a time when I was still playing demos downloaded via dialup internet connections. This was the time when I found this game on sale at Best Buy (back in those days when you had to get your games at the store).
The game places you as the leader/executive of a mining operation as an employee of Tetracorp. As part of the company, you will engage in competition with other races who are also trying to get a share of the asteroid belt. The story is that a Federation treaty that was signed ended the war between the races, but that the "trade war" has continued between the races (but these battles are governed by "rules").
The game has a very well developed economy, with rising and falling mineral and goods prices. When things get hectic, you can hire some managers to help with the running of your asteroid colonies (so you can focus on war production and combat). There is a surprising amount of depth to this game (research, diplomacy, espionage, black market, employee morale).
You can customize your ships with different modules. You can build masses of weenie ships or a fleet of capital ships (or both, like I do). You can build a variety of different missiles to launch them at your enemy (or buy some illegal weapons and use them, at risk of being fined by the Federation).
It's one of the few games I know where after you spend time building up a missile bank and giant fleet, and you can finally sit back and watch in satisfaction (from a spy satellite) as your missiles fall down and make fireworks of the enemy asteroid. It is also hilarious to send asteroids crashing into your enemy.
For a game that is about 20 years old it holds up surprisingly well. Try watching some demos or videos and see if it's your kind of game. I highly recommend it.

the game is very simplistic and linear. i would not recommend this to anyone unless they assign very little value to their dollar and want to play a difficult game that uses poor mechanics to accomplish its level of difficulty.
you must travel through the exact same dungeon each time you play. there is no random generation, there are no alternate routes, there are no interesting environments, there are no pacing mechanics. when you die you lose all your gear, meaning that upon your first death you will most likely save significant time by just ending your run immediately instead of trying to stab skeletons with the basic sword 30+ times in a row. there is a significant amount of mandatory backtracking through empty rooms each time you play the game. approximately 40% of your time spent on a run will consist of walking back through a long series of already cleared rooms.
the combat gives you very little to work with: jumping can potentially provide you with an extra attack due to frame reset upon landing, but makes you very vulnerable. ducking makes you stationary, resulting in it being a worthless mechanic. enemies don't follow the rules of the game: they ignore damage from traps, and in addition to attacking you will also harm you upon contact while constantly walking forwards. this means that all forms of "normal" combat (ducking, blocking, parrying) are thrown out the window since you can not backstep their approach during all of these maneuvers. instead, you must backstep-stab-repeat ad nauseam in order to guarantee defeating an enemy safely.
there is very little content. every sword is identical in usage except for the randomly varying damage ranges and the possibility for 1 of 3 elemental enchants that have a 10% chance (RNG? in a game where "quick reflex and timing are key"?) to trigger a minor effect. there are also 3 shields in the game with chances to trigger minor bonuses. that is all of the "gear" in the game.
you will quickly grow tired of going through the exact same basic rooms time and time again, fighting the same limited collection of simple enemies.

-art assets that are inferior to the base game assets (why does that child look 20? Have the normans evolved to homo-sapiens yet?)
-sound assets that are repackaged songs from the base game (literally the base songs with viking beats)
-sub-systems that werent good enough to be in the base game (SHUT THE GATES...ok open them...SHUT THE GATES...ok open them...omg fun....)
-"min-max your way to greatness" the dlcs generally considered "required" or "necessary". Theyre not, they just make a tough game easier via min-maxing.
-timeline dlcs that extend the timeline (ok, but a normal game takes tens of hours for me, so this is not needed)

Rise of Nations was ahead of its time when it came out over a decade ago. The Extended Edition bundles the whole game up with a few new extras. Despite its age, it’s still tons of fun to play. If you’re an RTS fan who missed it the first time, go grab it on Steam! Now’s your chance to see what the fuss is about.
Unlike many RTS games, the focus in Rise of Nations is on all of human history, from people throwing rocks at one another all the way up to modern stealth bombers and cruise missiles. Despite this wide focus, the game flows well from era to era, and each phase of the game feels meaty.
Rise of Nations is also unbelievably polished. There are shortcut ways to do almost everything, like hotkeys that select often-used buildings like the library. You can set up an infinite build queue at any unit producing building, which can replenish an army that is engaged in active combat in the field. Everything in the UI is streamlined towards long play sessions

Classic Sonic was always one of my guilty pleasures... no, scratch that, Classic Sonic rank among the best as one of the (if not the) greatest 2d platform games of all times. Speaking of scratching, Sonic Mania has scratched that itch for a new Classic Sonic title.
The guys who made this went above and beyond in a labour of love towards the franchise, delivering a consistently fun game with suprises around every loop and turn. The animation is suprisingly fluid, detailed, and pops out to the eye.
Gameplay-wise, the trio handle just as well in the original titles. Sonic's new ability, the dropdash, is a great move that allows the player to keep the momentum moving. The level design is great as well.
There are, of course, cricitisms. There are only 3 original levels in the game, the rest being taken from previous classic-series games. Green Hill and Chemical Plant return yet again. Despite the creative, and fun takes the team takes on them in their Act Twos, (not spoiling anything, but that CPZ Act 2 boss tho) it is clear they were limited by being forced to shove these levels into this game. In the future, retire these levels- almost all you can do with them has been exploited. The Bonus Levels, despite being a wonderful callback to the S3 special stages, get tiring after awhile (especially when you try to go for the platinum tokens). After you 100% them, there is no reason to do them anymore, most likely driving you to groan once you accidently jump into a bonus level.
Back to the positive, the Special Stage is perhaps the best special stage in any classic series game. Featuring a low-poly landscape that harkens back to Sonic CD, it emphasizes the best parts of playing the game regularly - going fast, and fun fluid gameplay. The super forms return, with Sonic of course being able to transform into Super Sonic. However, Knuckles gets to use his Super Form after years since S3, keeping his pinkish flair. Suprisingly, Tails can go super now - without the requirements of the super emeralds. Unfortunaly, there are no hyper forms - thus no broken jumpdash, nor the devasting flicky army.
All in all, this is a solid game, and it's clear that with the love and dedication put into Sonic Mania that this is one of the best Sonic games to come out to date. What I mean by this, is that there are no large chunks of gameplay that make me go, "Not Again",  or altogether frusturating. Indeed, in a rare occasion for the Blue Blur, all the pieces of the puzzle fit together! The entire game is, as I previously said, consistently enjoyable, even euphoric to yet again play though the unique platforming gameplay Sonic previously touted.

I'll try to keep this simple.
There's good points to the game, I like the concept, and building up a little town with your friends or guildmates. The graphics are cute, although not very impressive.
Unfortunately the bad points really killed it for me. Like many games of this kind, it ends up being crowded very quickly.  Wanna build a fort? Yeah, well so does every other player, and they'll take up any decent space. You end up with scattered little junky player tents everywhere and no sense of order.
Getting resources to build anything takes AGES, and worst of all, other players can exploit your work. I had several times where I spent a while cutting down a tree, only to have another player run up and last-hit it, and thereby steal all the resources.
Which brings me to the next bad point, the community in the game seems as likely to kill you or rip you off as to say hello. I had guilds in small in enclosed areas shooting at me simply for trying to run by, plenty of people trying to last-hit resources on me, etc.
Finally, it's just boring. The whole game is a long, slow grind. Combat isn't really fun, it's about as generic and dull as it gets. Try playing an MMO where all you can use is your basic attacks. It's something like that.
At it's core it feels like there was some potential here, but the execution is so bland, slow, and exploitable that it just isn't fun. If you're in a large guild of people dedicated to the game and grind, you might have some more fun with this. Otherwise, there are better games out there that are more worth your time.

You should play this game.
The list of things that is good about this game are too numerous to list. It is almost perfect, but it does have some flaws:
Number one on my list is the combat system. It is much too hands-off. You can give units an attack, defense, or hold ground order, and you can direct units to target enemy units. There is the ability to move units to certain hexes, but it's not very reliable for making them attack a given unit. After setting the orders, you then play the turn, and they move in order based on their initiative. What this results in is units often not doing what you want them to, and making stupid moves that leave the unit (e.g. ranged unit getting too close to a melee) or your whole squad (e.g. attacking the wrong unit and not killing the immediate threat) exposed. On the one hand, you could say that this takes the focus off the tactics and placed more on the strategy. But on the other hand, it feels like a cop-out or a tease: simply with added controls, I can definitely say the combat would be a solid experience. All of the mechanics for a good tactical system are already there, it just needs more player control. I'm hoping Amplitude makes this happen, or a combat mod comes along.
Number two - I did not know there was a manual. You don't really need the manual, as I learnt the game by trial and error without it, but there are many things that were not obvious to me as someone who has not played Endless Space or any other 4X game before, such as... you need more citizens in a city if you want to build additional districts. It took me a while to figure that out, and I was stuck on the "build a city centre or district to level 2" part of my faction quest for quite a while. But basically there's some crucial information that should be visible but isn't. For example, a simple tooltip that says "next district available at 8 citizens" or something like that would have been great.
Number three - the early game, especially on the harder modes, can be slow - dangerous too, if you have aggressive neighbours (I have been wiped out in the first 30 turns more than once). I learnt the game on Newbie mode, and it wasn't so bad. On harder modes (currently playing Serious), incomes are reduced, so getting additional workers, building city upgrades or expansions, and recruiting new units, takes longer. Long enough that often you're stuck clicking "next turn" a few times without making any meaningful changes or choices, simply waiting for things to happen. Researches, too, are critical, and you have to wait not only for those to finish researching (which takes a lot of time), but also for the city improvements that are unlocked from them to finish building, before you gain the benefit from the research. All of this waiting time is mitigated to some extent by the exploration and questing side of things, but when you start with a small number of units that can only move four hexes per turn, and equipping them with the move bonus item costs precious resources, and healing them after a battle takes time or resources, the 'distraction' is only limited. There will still be several turns where you'll do nothing but click Next Turn. I don't know how they would fix this side of things. - Make early constructions and researches cheaper? Have a temporary income boost in the first several turns? Have a small stockpile from the start of the game? Make exploration/questing an even bigger part of the early game by making it more accessible?
Number four - the endgame. It just sort of... ends. You can play on if you like (to finish your faction quest for example), but it'd be nice to have some more closure, or a challenging final objective to complete the win condition.
If Amplitude Studios improved on these things, it would make an excellent game perfect. But make no mistake, it is an excellent game, and I'll reiterate what I said at the start: You should play this game.

I've played several 4X and RTS games in my time: From Civ 5 to Fallen Enchantress to Gal Civ, Age of Wonders series, Warlock series etc.
If there's one thing I'm good at, it's fantasy 4X games.
So I bought Endless Legend in early access, and the following are the reasons why I am still attracted to this game:
1- The aesthetics. The art is unique and fresh. It is a masterpiece to look at. Simple and elegant color schemes. The environments look "alien" and yet realistic at the same time.
2- The sci-fi + fantasy combination, which is something I always wanted and very few games have it
3- The story. I love each and every faction and all their themes. I seriously feel like I want to write a novel based on this game. And if you are a player who actually enjoys reading some text, you will definitely love the story.
4- The customization (I want more of it). I play this game to relax! to bounce some ideas around and try new things
5- Innovations: the cliffs and elevation mechanics in the terrain, the Influence resource for diplomacy, and terrain variety, less micromanagement in combat, each faction has a unique questline for them only in addition to normal quests, the very dynamic economy system, 1 city per each province, summer and winter seasons... Other developers are taking notes right now.
6- the community: I don't mean to patronize, but I just love the atmosphere in the forums. Everyone has interesting ideas and experiences. The experienced players are very helpful. The devs are reasonably responsive to the audience. I'm having a great time chatting and playing with everyone. At some point, multiplayer will greatly raise this game's popularity, if they do it right and fix all the bugs.
The main weaknesses for this game as of early October 2014, after full release:
1- Overly simplistic (easy to understand) but unique combat system. Still needs some more balancing and more features to make it less boring
2- Weak AI: Amplitude studios have had a few problems with AI programming in their other games as well, but the other good aspects about the game make you forget about the AI altogether... and Amp usually fix the AI issues over time with player feedback.
3- Like most 4X games, EL needs to work a little more to keep the end-game interesting
As long as the developers and community continue to cooperate together, this game will definitely be remembered for a long time to come, at least for the innovations.
Before you make your decision about buying this game or not, one last thing I will say:
If you are a social gamer who likes to jump in to a community and participate, you will be amazed by the warmth of the Amplitude forums. Trust me, you will not regret your participation. There is something for everyone there. Your suggestions, complaints and bug reports will all be taken into consideration. If you appreciate the aspects I mentioned above and you want to try a unique 4X Strategy experience, I recommend Endless Legend to you.
8/10

Never played the first, but I've been loving everything about this so far. I've always enjoyed the style of game that feels pseudo pen-and-paper D&D (Baldur's Gate, Icewind Dale, Neverwinter Nights, etc.). But with those, and even D&D itself, I have a similar gripe with special moves and spells, which tend to work on a very limited, "x uses per day" system. Divinity 2 has a similar feel to those kinds of games, but most abilities and spells have a turn cooldown.
Also, where the default in those other games mentioned was real-time with options to pause on triggers, or to manually pause and unpause, combat in this is solely turn-based. Battles tend to feel a lot more strategic as a result. Also a bit chaotic, as elemental effects get thrown across the field all the time. The important thing to note is that all of your characters are likely to get set on fire or be poisoned in most battles. It's inevitable.
I haven't played multiplayer, but it's been great playing single player because of the character stories. A full party of 4, and I'm really wanting to know more about all the pre-made characters. While you
make a fully custom character, I recommend playing the first time with one of the characters that has a backstory. It's really adding to the lore to have a character with a much more fleshed out backstory than I'm used to seeing in these kinds of games, and it's been adding another layer of fun to not just roleplay, but try to roleplay my character (in dialog, you'll get prompts for why a certain option is choosable, and you'll sometimes have your character's name next to an option to show it's choosable because of their backstory, which I don't think you'd get if you made a fully custom character).
If you've enjoyed other cRPGs then all I can say is two thumbs up -- would recommend.

Amazing game. Don't listen to the negativereviews, they are solely about the price of the dlc, this is an amazing game. The base game is more than enough on its own.
As for the DLC, no matter what you google, what you read on reddit or steam, what other gamers tell you, NONE OF THE DLC IS NECESSARY OR REQUIRED. So basically they suck unless your goal is to create easy mega-empires, which isnt the point of this game.
Buy this game, play it and have fun. Then decide if you want the DLC.
The DLC can be broken down into categories:
-art assets that are inferior to the base game assets (why does that child look 20? Have the normans evolved to homo-sapiens yet?)
-sound assets that are repackaged songs from the base game (literally the base songs with viking beats)
-sub-systems that werent good enough to be in the base game (SHUT THE GATES...ok open them...SHUT THE GATES...ok open them...omg fun....)
-"min-max your way to greatness" the dlcs generally considered "required" or "necessary". Theyre not, they just make a tough game easier via min-maxing.
-timeline dlcs that extend the timeline (ok, but a normal game takes tens of hours for me, so this is not needed)
-race dlcs that give you access to new races (also ok, but the hindus are a blatant cash grab and never should have been in this game, they just slow it down)
My absolute favourite game. The DLC makes it more fun but it can be played without it despite what other reviews say. If you can afford it buy it,

Playing Crusader Kings and Crusader Kings II for a long time and it gets better with every expansion. I usually wait for some pricing reductions to get the newest expansions and the waiting is no problem at all because there are so many expansions - so when a new one comes out, you can get the latest before that, most of the time between 70-50%. The Game:

This game got a lot of negative reviews at first, which I think were for the most part unfair and nostalgia-fueled. Yes, some features from the previous Sonny games were removed, but others were added and all in all, the experience of playing this Sonny game is arguably superior (though I still prefer the original ones) with a much more streamlined story and characters, memes and pretty innovative combat mechanics. I prefer the way classes are handled in this Sonny game, being able to choose a) 2 classes and b) to do so at different points in the game really gives the ability to make a character yours.
The games biggest flaw by far is it's lack of replayability, there is no new-game plus or arena, all you can really do is... replay the campaign, starting from scratch everytime. I think this is a true shame because by the end of the game, your character isn't perfect, there is room for improvement both in terms of loot and skills, and not being able to perfect and then playing with your perfected build is ridiculous to me.  This game will probably never get this fixed, and I think that's a shame because it would increase it's replayability tenfold.
All in all the game is worth it, but it isn't perfect, and if you come from the flash games you will have mixed feelings at first, but the game is decent, and it is a real Sonny game and not some shoddy-rehash. I'm more exited to see how all of this will be built on rather than what this game actually is. A lot changed in the production for this game compared to the flash games, and those changes will only help Krin bring more quality content in the future.

The game:
GCI is a team-based shooter just like others you've seen, It features a decent amount of game modes and customization (clothes, weapons, profile, etc.) and works on the basis that on particular levels you can unlock something.
It's kind-of like TF2 but with no set classes, and Batman V Joker based (don't play this if you hate either, as you'll be forced to play as them half of the time).
Tutorial teaches you some of basics, but proves insuficient once you start the real thing (it's mostly "stand and do this).
Pros:
+ Fun, fast paced, game
+ Good Customization Options
+ Stupid enough to make you smile
+ Decent amount of game modes (around 5)
+ Doesn't seem Pay2Win, but you really have to know what you're doing with your first unlocks (or save them).
+ Good balance of weapons, however as I mentioned you will need to level if you want access to any non-starting weapon.
+ Cool movies, but weird ones, what did you expect?
Cons:
- Only one game mode is playable (Team Deathmatch), seriously, I queued every other game mode 3-5 times with no success.
- Matchmaking doesn't exist, first online game (level 1), level 120 or so on the other, not even kidding (there's no stat boost or anything, but he has access to a lot of equipment and has a lot of exp that a new player just doesn't). My side had a level 90, rest of us were 1-8.
- Both things might be because of this, but not many people play this. (Dead game).
- You can only play as Batman or Joker. No Robin, No Catwoman, No Riddler (I'd love to play as Riddler, so it was a huge letdown) or any character you'd like to play as.
- Only 6 maps. Yup, that's right, 6. Each of the game modes can be played on any map as far as I know though.
- You can't change video options in-game, so you won't know if the configuration you picked runs smoothly until it's too late.
The opinion:
As a light game or mod, this could be great, however as a full-blown game, with barely enough players that only allow for the simplest game mode, not worth the disk space.
Don't get me wrong, it's fun, will keep you really entertained for a while, but you'll get bored sooner than later.
The rest:
If you want something stupid, go find another fun multiplayer game.
If you want something FPS team-based, go find another game.
This game has a correct balance between both, but doesn't excell in any for it to be truly destacable.
Nothing sticks out really, it's just a mixture of everything we've seen in MMOFPS., nothing original (apart from the funny disguises).
Recommendations:
* More promotion, no players kills this game instantly.
* More maps.
* More disguisable characters, only 2 makes it boring. (Just change the name to order v chaos or something).
* Joker small part of the tutorial (maybe in-field to help you get the hang of it?)
* Altough it has a great start, still needs a little "unique" thing for it to be a game on its own and not just "the same game, but stupid and with batman"
* Maybe in-game option change? That only screws you the first couple times you play, but could potentially screw you up a lot...
* Rest is really good.

Oblivion makes some arguable improvements over Morrowind, as well as some massive steps backwards. Some of these mistakes would be fixed in Skyrim, while others will be ignored or worsened in some sense. As a full experience, Oblivion is a big open, sometimes annoying, technically and gameplay wise, but still mostly enjoyable overall. However, unlike Morrowind, where if you looked past the graphics now you could likely get immersed, Oblivion has numerous barriers preventing it from matching Morrowind.
Compared to Skyrim, the combat feels somewhat choppier. It is faster at some points, but it manages to feel a lot more simplistic. I definitely prefer non-magic combat over Morrowind's dice roll simulation however, as combat finally feels responsive. Magic crafting also returns from Morrowind, and still feels very powerful at higher levels. However, I actually, for whatever reason, prefer magic in Morrowind to Oblivion. Learning a school of magic however, unlike Skyrim, is still worth doing regardless of playstyle due to the ability to cast regardless of whether both hands are occupied or not. Oblivion is, combat wise, the halfway point between Morrowind's more traditional style and Skyrim's faster combat, so benefits and pros of both apply here. I don't actually mind it, as like I said, magic feels superior to Skyrim, while in most other areas, combat feels more responsive than Morrowind.
Location-wise and graphically, Oblivion is very green and bright. It has a better colour pallet than non-modded Skyrim, and there are definitely graphical improvements over its prequels. However, the location itself is generic. It's all greens and old elven architecture and medieval towns, rather than the alien lands of Vvardenfell's plains or Skyrim's cold mountain ranges. My main problem with Bethesda worlds has always been the very small population, and the Imperial City, although more populated than anything in Skyrim, still feels empty, and the NPC's all have very funny looking faces. Character models in Bethesda games always feel like the lack, and Oblivion is a prime example here. What feels like a let-down is that the beast races no longer have unique animations either for movement. This is more an immersion thing, and animations never affect your gameplay experience, but if you had played Morrowind before Oblivion, you'll likely notice it.
The soundtrack is quiet and peaceful. The scores are always nice in Elder Scrolls games, and although I don't have anything in this game I prefer over Morrowind (which Bethesda seemed to like as they were re-using the compositions even before the Dragonborn DLC in Skyrim), the music all fits and helps build on the games atmosphere, which is all you need a soundtrack to do.
The guild quests in Oblivion are some of the best in the series. Although the main quest becomes a bit of a drag, the Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood in particular have some of Bethesda's best quests and plotlines to them. Highlights include the Gray Fox and his final heist, and The Dark Brotherhood as a whole. There aren't any quests in Skyrim that compete with the quests here. The Fighter's Guild also has a few interesting ones and the Mages Guild suffers from the same problem that the College of Winterhold suffers from in that you can be hopeless with advanced magic and become the archmage in a few days of joining. The Arena is a massive missed opportunity, as fights never feel that big and the questline can be dusted off in about 30 minutes, which is massively disappointing. Guilds are definitely stripped back from Morrowind, due to the removal of skill barriers between the low and high ranks. Although this means that the player will be able to see everything, it means that unless you force yourself to roleplay, you can see everything on a single character. This is something even Skyrim dodged with its Civil War questline. This becomes even more self-defeating if you originally played it on the XBOX 360, and you were allowed to pick up every achievement on a single character.
The Shivering Isles expansion included is brilliant. You have to play it more than once to see everything, and although a bit short, gives a far more varied world than Cyrodiil to explore, and Sheogorath and the residents of the isles have fun, over-exaggerated personalities that fit perfectly with the theme of madness and misery the expansion is going for.
Overall, Oblivion has very nice ideas. The best ideas of Skyrim seemed to appear here, albeit somewhat under-developed, and although not as focused as Morrowind, it still maintained the RPG gameplay that Bethesda seems glad to phase out more and more as they release more games themselves. Worth a buy, and with mods, just like all the other popular Bethesda games, if it doesn't crash, you can go on and on, possibly even fixing your own personal problems with the game.

Oblivion is the worst TES game ever. Then Skyrim came around and a good half of the TES community kinda changed its opinion. Turns out that Oblivion's actually a pretty good game.
Almost as soon as you get out of the prison you realize just how different this game is compared to Morrowind. A lot of people hated this, but this is not actually a bad thing - even Morrowind kinda gets boring after a while, so a change in the setting keeps this game varied. Especially since Oblivion is good at doing what it tries to do, which is to be a game with a pretty comfy medieval fantasy atmosphere. However, it's mostly Jeremy Soule's soundtrack that does this because the game's graphics are incredibly lame and make this game look like the painting world from one of the sidequests. Speaking of sidequests, they're actually better than Morrowind's. They're a lot more interesting and a little bit more varied, so they almost become these short self-contained stories. I personally think that Oblivion has some of the best guild questlines in TES games ever. Dark Brotherhood is simply amazing and Thieves Guild was also pretty cool and Thief 1-like, with a really neat final quest to boot. Other guilds were not that great, sadly, because there was almost no improvement to the way quests are structured in this game. For some reason, Bethesda thinks it's really great to do this thing where they give the guild quests a storyline that becomes clearer the more quests you do, but then start throwing you off the trail by giving you lame tasks. I found the sidequests to be the real icing on the cake, because the main quest was pretty lame and brought nothing unique to the table. Overall, the base game is actually pretty good. Sure, some things got dumbed down compared to Morrowind, but it's also not cool to hate this game anymore, so there you go.
Then Shivering Isles came out. "And, behold, it was very good". It almost feels like more effort was put into this expansion pack rather than into the ginormous base game. It was very interesting to be in this weird world, meet all those strange oddball characters who, this time around, had actually good and almost unique voiceovers, and do these bizzare quests. And, of course, who could forget Sheogorath? It's worth playing the expansion for the single purpose of hearing his amazing voiceover and reading his hilarious dialogue. Sadly, I can't say that all quests and sidequests in this expansion were great, but it's still worth to play Oblivion simply for Shivering Isles only. By the way, it's an actually good expansion pack done by Bethesda -  that's one for the books!
Knights of the Nine is also supposed to be an important thing. However, it's not. It's painfully average and incredibly short. It's supposed to consist of 11 linear main quests, yet a good 60% of them can be done in a matter of 30 minutes. The writing is almost nonexistant, but the armor and the bossfight in the sky were cool. If you think that's not too bad, then just remember the fact that this pathetic excuse for an "expansion pack" used to cost 10 or 20 buckaroos when it just came out.
Don't buy Skyrim, buy this.
