One of the best RPGs I have ever played, Divinity: Original Sin 2 truly is a work of art. From character creation to waking up in the prologue, the player will experience a familiar and welcoming feeling similar to creating a character for a tabletop RPG. This is pen-and-paper put into video game form in the truest sense.
Character creation is simple, and handled rather well. Though there is a slight lack in customization where one must choose face x through y and skin color x through y. Although the amount of races to choose is actually impressive. Alternatively, rather than playing a custom character, the player can experience the story from the perspective of one of the six, well-written, story characters. The races are vast and different in their own right with Human, Lizard, Dwarf, Elf, and Undead to choose from. They each face their own difficulties but all have unique boons or bonuses. Each class is just a combination of skills, a preset of gear and skills to start the player off with as customization and 'build-your-own' is heavily emphasized soon after the prologue. The player even has a choice to select a pseudo-background for their customized character of anything between a noble, mystic or barbarian with plenty more to be earned through the Roleplay elements.
Combat is very in-depth and ties in well with character customization. Skill trees and the skills, themselves, interract with the world differently in, sometimes, unexpected ways. The way combat feels is amazing, satisfying as it is turn-based combat done well. Abilities and spells, positioning, and the wide range of items make it one of the best features in this game, though one that is difficult to master. Spells can set the ground ablaze, clouds of poison can be created, and a combination of thing A and thing B can create explosions, electrified hallways, and giant spiders made of bone. Feedback, something important for combat, feels good. Powerful spells feel powerful and two-handed weapons feel weighty and hit hard. An overall enjoyable experience.
For those less combat-savvy, there is always the option to talk yourself out of a situation. The Rp elements are some of the finest done that I have seen in recent years. Skyrim has nothing on this. Each conversation and attempt at persuasion can change the experience of playing through the game. Accidentally anger a skeleton? Talk her to death- Yes, that was a thing that happened. Got caught stealing? Convince them otherwise! Need help solving a theft? Talk to a rat! The conversations and interractions with NPCs around the world are some of the best I've ever seen. From sad tales of a family lost to the hilarity of a cow attempting to tell your future. Or, simply murder them all if you can. There is freedom here that is just waiting to be explored.
On top of all of this, however, is the fact that this game has a co-operative feature of up to four players. Each player can choose to create a customized character or take the role of one of the story characters. While it is set up for an enjoyable single-player game, the ability to enjoy the full game with friends or family is also very welcome. The party is able to split up completely and roam the world if desired. There are also ways to troll your friends by Dying poison red, and giving it to them as a gift. Or, of course, you can all become Heroes.
The storytelling in this game is deep and rich as is player choice and freedom. The combat system is well thought out and satisfying. Even the character creation, simple as it is, gives the player more freedom than in most games to change almost everything stat-wise. It is easy to see that this game is made with love, and the developers have shown it clearly enough through this game that I regret not being able to support it on kickstarter. I cannot recommend this game enough. It is a gem and a must-have, even if you are not a fan of turn-based strategy games. This is, first and foremost, an RPG. If you have ever played D&D, Pathfinder, or any other table-top game then Divinity: Original Sin 2 is for you.

It's tough for me to review this game and sound in any way even-handed because I love this, and the previous game, about as much as it's possible to love a game.  The story, the gameplay, and the world.  I love it all.  So, what the heck is it?
Divinity Original Sin 2 is a strategy RPG with a deep and engaging story that encourages its players to use the tools presented as creatively as possible to overcome obstacles.  With the ability to combine elements (electricity causes liquid to become charged and causes electrocution, fire can be combined with poison or oil to cause really fun explosions, etc...) you can often trick your opponents in entertaining ways and the more clever you are, the better.
The game's only flaw derives from its greatest strength, and that's player freedom.  The lack of rails sometimes result in you playing out the later part of a quest before you even know what you're doing, which then causes the game to become confusing.  Additionally, there are a few bugs that will cause missions to remain in your queue because you didn't complete things in the right order.  I find these flaws to be a minimal distractions and mostly chalk them up to the complexity of allowing so much choice.
Finally, a very wierd warning because I got chewed out by a friend:  BEWARE DOG LOVERS...our beloved canines do not fare well in this world and their stories will likely tug at your heartstrings.  You have been warned!!!

I have played a lot of Endless Space back in the day and, having enjoyed the overall feeling of the game, decided to get Endless Space early access. Having played the full version now, I must say I'm disappointed.
To keep it short: it's not a bad game. Yet, it's not great, either, and for your buck and time's sake, there are much better similar games out there (chiefly Civilization V).
My biggest problem with the game, and this is more on the subjective side, is the interface. I find it unecessarily complicated and just plain ugly, and while it worked in Endless Space, I find it very intrusive in Endless Legend. Small things, like checking your research progress, assigning skill points to your hero or even assigning him to other armies seem too complicated (and this is from someone who plays, and loves, Europa Universalis IV). Things like figuring out what the quest objective is is also overly complicated, having the game provide you with a bunch of useless info and buttons while leaving the important quest objectives cluttered on the side. An example of unecessary complication is exploring ruins: whereas in CIV V you just have your army move onto the ruin's hexagon, here you have to click on it and, everytime, select the option to "explore" manually. The fact that the ruin doesn't leave the map after also annoys me, and is just another intrusive icon on an already overconvoluted interface.
Most of the game's good ideas - equiping the troops, minor factions - ultimately don't seem to make a difference in the long run (and this was also a problem with Endless Space). Despite the different factions and all, it all seems to boil down to the same gameplay style, whereas in CIV V, for exaple, you could play totally differently going for an Economic or Diplomatic victory.
If you're a big fan of 4X games and want to try something with a different flair, Endless Space might provide you that. If you just like 4X games and want the biggest bang for your buck and for your time, I'd suggest looking elsewhere.

This game is in unacceptable condition.  I have given it every opportunity to succeed, and am now done.
They had people participating enthusiastically in early access, yet they have released a beta-quality product.  There are multiple game breaking bugs, and I did not spend my money for the privilege of submitting crash reports.
The AI provides no challenge (other than its tendancy to declare wars it can't win.)  The diplomacy system consequently is pointless, since AI behavior is not engaged.
The basic game systems are even broken; in no game that I have played have any of the luxury goods past level one ever spawned (which means that world generation fails consistently.)
The final failure is that you are really playing against the game mechanics, instead of against the AI.  The existing challenges are not provided by the other factions, but by the hard limits coded into virtually everything.
-For instance, Winter, which comes unpredictably (why??) simply limits movement and productivity.  So you work to prepare for winter, which is a much bigger obstacle than the other 7 factions, even on hard.
-And there is unhappiness, which happens for every additional borough (city tile) and every new city you add.  I get the fact that the designers want to limit my expansion, but why would my very successful citizens want me to fail?
-Those boroughs have an undocumented requirement for upgrading which is extremely fussy and even the forums don't explain it properly because it has changed so much during recent development.
-And technology: every tech I have increases the cost of every subsequent tech, even those on lower levels.  That is like saying that inventing the telephone made inventng the wheel harder.  I understand the devs want to slow down my progress, but it is done hamfistedly.  Diminishing returns requires some logic.
-And the faction quests: they sound fun, but instead they just create arbitrary tasks that go on and on without any clear benefit.  After so many crashed games, I still don't know what prize I would have achieved in the end.  Yet it had me forced to declare war on cities on the opposite side of the planet just to move it forward.  (Given the poor AI, it was simply a logistical chore.)  Then the quest required me to upgrade city tiles without instructions (see above...).
The results are an enormous disappointment.  The game looks good and intriguing, but the gameplay is nonsense.

It's basically a turn-based football with 3 players on each side. Despite this being a tablet game obviously, it's cute, easy and may catch you for a while, but I can't really imagine why you would want to launch this on your PC.

- You control a team of 3 players, where the aim is to beat the other team. You do this by specifying in each turn, how you want your 3 players to move.
- There are a few different game types to choose from: e.g. soccer, ice hockey, capture the flag, escape the mummy, knock your opponent into the water, etc, and you can choose to play in practice mode, online vs, hotseat, world tournament, etc.
- The goals of each game differ depending on the type of game you select. E.g. In "capture the flag", you must get to the other team's home base, steal their flag, and bring it back to your base, while making your own flag isn't captured first. And in "escape the mummy", you must try to make the mummy turn all the players on your opponent's team into mummies themselves, while making sure you have at least 1 player still alive on your own team.
- Movement is free anywhere within the game board as long as there are no obstacles in the way.
- On each turn, you can specify 1 linear direction in which you want your player to move, as well as the amount of force.
- You can also choose not to move any of your players per turn.
- If players bump into objects (i.e. game board items and other players), they will rebound.
- I had no problems at all playing this game using my mouse, on my laptop.
While kids may enjoy the cute graphics & sound and appreciate the simple physics involved, more mature players soon realise that, in order to win, you have to take into account how the other team is going to move, and also in which direction all players will "rebound" when they hit stuff.
Different game types require different methods of strategising. E.g. In "capture the flag", you may find it beneficial to not move 1 of your players and have it permanently stationed at your home base instead.
This really is an
game that I would recommend to both kids & adults alike. I can see kids enjoying the colourful, cute characters and interface, and adults having fun thinking up various strategies to beat each game type.

I hesitated buying this because I wanted either Cossacks 3 or Age of Empires 2, but I went with AOE and RON - refunded AOE (even though I used to play it so much as a little kid, it was among many that got me into RTS - and proved that I was a sore loser) and stuck with RON because this game encapsulates both the mechanics from AOE (base building, war mongering RTS) and the economic management of Civ V.
The gameplay is familar to RTS fans: build buildings to generate resources; expand to generate more resources and increase your national borders; spend resources on technology; build an army; attack. But it's the middle of the game where the meat is at; the rising tension of who is going to attack first and "how best do I attack? Do I use a decoy army to confuse him? Or shall I go all in? How about I trickle cavalary units every so often to annoy him?" The object of the game is to defeat your enemy by conquering his capital city (or if the timer runs out, most of the map)
Moreover, the combat has a depth to it that makes it more than just "whoever has the biggest army wins", because the player can select a single type (such as cavalary) and target the enemy's archers with it (destroying them easily) or fleeing them from the brutal heavy infantry. The rock, paper, scissors mechanic (while certainly not new) prevents the game from becoming stale even though the player might have an increadibly large army.
Furthermore, the economic management adds a light depth to the game when the player is not at war because he needs to constantly build new cities in order to increase his revenue and national borders (he cannot build outside his borders); tech is also needed to be able to upgrade units, increase caps and build new cities.
In addition, the campaign mode resembles Europa Universalies or Total War (a turn based style map where the player picks his next target to wage war) and a selection of historic campaigns such as Alexander the Great or Napoleon. There is also an option to conquer the whole Earth.
To conclude this short review (I have certainly left a lot out because I haven't played a lot of it - games are always more fun with friends - and I have non) I just want to mention a few negatives of the game because I think that many neglect this in their reviews and it infuriates me. Firstly, the graphics are outdated obviously and the resolution (although I think I read that there is a mod to fix this) is not 1080p; second, the maps (I haven't played many of the maps so take this with a grain of salt) are dull in my opinion because there is a lack of variety in the terrain (just hills, rocks and grass - maybe because it is an old game); third, citizens, when created, automatically (not sure if this can be turned off) go to work so I lose track of them and just end up having to pull citizens out of jobs if I need one to build something.
Other than that, I can't fault the game as I find it fun, even on singleplayer. Games usually last 1 hour and can quickly be turned around if the palyer manages to repel a large enemy force. So don't give up!

Oblivion makes some arguable improvements over Morrowind, as well as some massive steps backwards. Some of these mistakes would be fixed in Skyrim, while others will be ignored or worsened in some sense. As a full experience, Oblivion is a big open, sometimes annoying, technically and gameplay wise, but still mostly enjoyable overall. However, unlike Morrowind, where if you looked past the graphics now you could likely get immersed, Oblivion has numerous barriers preventing it from matching Morrowind.
Compared to Skyrim, the combat feels somewhat choppier. It is faster at some points, but it manages to feel a lot more simplistic. I definitely prefer non-magic combat over Morrowind's dice roll simulation however, as combat finally feels responsive. Magic crafting also returns from Morrowind, and still feels very powerful at higher levels. However, I actually, for whatever reason, prefer magic in Morrowind to Oblivion. Learning a school of magic however, unlike Skyrim, is still worth doing regardless of playstyle due to the ability to cast regardless of whether both hands are occupied or not. Oblivion is, combat wise, the halfway point between Morrowind's more traditional style and Skyrim's faster combat, so benefits and pros of both apply here. I don't actually mind it, as like I said, magic feels superior to Skyrim, while in most other areas, combat feels more responsive than Morrowind.
Location-wise and graphically, Oblivion is very green and bright. It has a better colour pallet than non-modded Skyrim, and there are definitely graphical improvements over its prequels. However, the location itself is generic. It's all greens and old elven architecture and medieval towns, rather than the alien lands of Vvardenfell's plains or Skyrim's cold mountain ranges. My main problem with Bethesda worlds has always been the very small population, and the Imperial City, although more populated than anything in Skyrim, still feels empty, and the NPC's all have very funny looking faces. Character models in Bethesda games always feel like the lack, and Oblivion is a prime example here. What feels like a let-down is that the beast races no longer have unique animations either for movement. This is more an immersion thing, and animations never affect your gameplay experience, but if you had played Morrowind before Oblivion, you'll likely notice it.
The soundtrack is quiet and peaceful. The scores are always nice in Elder Scrolls games, and although I don't have anything in this game I prefer over Morrowind (which Bethesda seemed to like as they were re-using the compositions even before the Dragonborn DLC in Skyrim), the music all fits and helps build on the games atmosphere, which is all you need a soundtrack to do.
The guild quests in Oblivion are some of the best in the series. Although the main quest becomes a bit of a drag, the Thieves Guild and Dark Brotherhood in particular have some of Bethesda's best quests and plotlines to them. Highlights include the Gray Fox and his final heist, and The Dark Brotherhood as a whole. There aren't any quests in Skyrim that compete with the quests here. The Fighter's Guild also has a few interesting ones and the Mages Guild suffers from the same problem that the College of Winterhold suffers from in that you can be hopeless with advanced magic and become the archmage in a few days of joining. The Arena is a massive missed opportunity, as fights never feel that big and the questline can be dusted off in about 30 minutes, which is massively disappointing. Guilds are definitely stripped back from Morrowind, due to the removal of skill barriers between the low and high ranks. Although this means that the player will be able to see everything, it means that unless you force yourself to roleplay, you can see everything on a single character. This is something even Skyrim dodged with its Civil War questline. This becomes even more self-defeating if you originally played it on the XBOX 360, and you were allowed to pick up every achievement on a single character.
The Shivering Isles expansion included is brilliant. You have to play it more than once to see everything, and although a bit short, gives a far more varied world than Cyrodiil to explore, and Sheogorath and the residents of the isles have fun, over-exaggerated personalities that fit perfectly with the theme of madness and misery the expansion is going for.
Overall, Oblivion has very nice ideas. The best ideas of Skyrim seemed to appear here, albeit somewhat under-developed, and although not as focused as Morrowind, it still maintained the RPG gameplay that Bethesda seems glad to phase out more and more as they release more games themselves. Worth a buy, and with mods, just like all the other popular Bethesda games, if it doesn't crash, you can go on and on, possibly even fixing your own personal problems with the game.

Oblivion is the worst TES game ever. Then Skyrim came around and a good half of the TES community kinda changed its opinion. Turns out that Oblivion's actually a pretty good game.
Almost as soon as you get out of the prison you realize just how different this game is compared to Morrowind. A lot of people hated this, but this is not actually a bad thing - even Morrowind kinda gets boring after a while, so a change in the setting keeps this game varied. Especially since Oblivion is good at doing what it tries to do, which is to be a game with a pretty comfy medieval fantasy atmosphere. However, it's mostly Jeremy Soule's soundtrack that does this because the game's graphics are incredibly lame and make this game look like the painting world from one of the sidequests. Speaking of sidequests, they're actually better than Morrowind's. They're a lot more interesting and a little bit more varied, so they almost become these short self-contained stories. I personally think that Oblivion has some of the best guild questlines in TES games ever. Dark Brotherhood is simply amazing and Thieves Guild was also pretty cool and Thief 1-like, with a really neat final quest to boot. Other guilds were not that great, sadly, because there was almost no improvement to the way quests are structured in this game. For some reason, Bethesda thinks it's really great to do this thing where they give the guild quests a storyline that becomes clearer the more quests you do, but then start throwing you off the trail by giving you lame tasks. I found the sidequests to be the real icing on the cake, because the main quest was pretty lame and brought nothing unique to the table. Overall, the base game is actually pretty good. Sure, some things got dumbed down compared to Morrowind, but it's also not cool to hate this game anymore, so there you go.
Then Shivering Isles came out. "And, behold, it was very good". It almost feels like more effort was put into this expansion pack rather than into the ginormous base game. It was very interesting to be in this weird world, meet all those strange oddball characters who, this time around, had actually good and almost unique voiceovers, and do these bizzare quests. And, of course, who could forget Sheogorath? It's worth playing the expansion for the single purpose of hearing his amazing voiceover and reading his hilarious dialogue. Sadly, I can't say that all quests and sidequests in this expansion were great, but it's still worth to play Oblivion simply for Shivering Isles only. By the way, it's an actually good expansion pack done by Bethesda -  that's one for the books!
Knights of the Nine is also supposed to be an important thing. However, it's not. It's painfully average and incredibly short. It's supposed to consist of 11 linear main quests, yet a good 60% of them can be done in a matter of 30 minutes. The writing is almost nonexistant, but the armor and the bossfight in the sky were cool. If you think that's not too bad, then just remember the fact that this pathetic excuse for an "expansion pack" used to cost 10 or 20 buckaroos when it just came out.
Don't buy Skyrim, buy this.

The map is spacious, packed full of dungeons and small, and usually interesting quests. And best of all, the game never gets "too easy". Some may dislike the leveling scale system, and while it may be merciful early on, enemies get tougher as you reach higher levels. Morrowind and Skyrim are very, very easy after a certain point in the game, but this game holds its own against you. Even after maxing my strength, blade, intelligence, and destruction skills, and a boatload of restore/fortify magicka potions, enemies still prove a challenge. I have a boatload of memories with this game, and each playthrough is a flashback to my better, happier days.

Honestyl, I'm incredibly disappointed in this new addition to the Sonny series. The original Flash-based Sonny and its sequel were both incredibly rich strategy games where every fight felt like a boss fight, each one felt different and had different mechanics, and the trick was always to find the best way to counter what the enemy was throwing at you. The game was filled with respecs as you try out new strategic builds, learn the boss' patterns, find the right time to throw out your conters, etc.
This one just doesn't have that depth. The character choices are far more limited and don't feel particularly different from one "class" to the next. There's zero control over whether your allies play offensively or defensively, if they focus on attacks or heals, etc. You fight much of the same mobs over and over on each stage. All in all, the game just feels like it's lacking content. Add to that the extra-long narrative, and the game just drags.
Other problems with this version: the voice acting is only partial. The previous games were fully voice acted; this one you're mostly reading the dialogue while the character makes vaguely contextual audible grunts. The art stills are more impressive, but none of the characters are animated. You gain equipment, yet you never get to see what your character looks like in the new equipment, because it's the same art still throughout the whole game.
This is to date the only Sonny game I haven't absolutely loved, and I honestly barely enjoyed this one at all. I often found myself just getting tired of it and setting it aside for a day or two, and normally I binge my way through games. Go play the originals - for free. Don't spend your money on this disappointment.

What is Sonny exactly? Sonny is a turn based RPG based of the original Sonny 1 and 2 that is primarily focused around challenging combat and strategy.
You can't just grind an area an expect to win, this game requires strategy.
You will definitely need to be switching around things such as allies, equipment, and skills in certain areas in order to progress and make proper use of those when in combat.
Compared to the original Sonny games this definitely has its ups and downs.
Now of course I need to address the elephants in the room. The lack of combat animations/no displaying armor/weapons and fully voiced dialogue.
I understand that this installment of the franchise focused more on the mechanics of the game during the development and that this topic has been gone over on several occasions,
but it still impacts the game greatly in my opinion, it feels odd to have "frozen" characters that constantly stay in the same pose and to never change. As Well as the lack of fully voiced dialogue just feels off putting to me.
Now that that's out of the way I'm going to give a list of pros and cons.
Pros:
+ The prologue is a nice homage to the previous games and allows for both old and new players of the franchise to enjoy it.
+ The strategy involved in gameplay is a nice change of pace compared to other games forcing you to think about your actions and to use your abilities tactically
+ The visuals and designs in this compared to the others is a major step up and still manages to capture the personality of the characters.
+ Even though animations are not in this one, it did allow for different designs of characters allowing for more uniqueness among them.
+ The music in this one is great, The combination of redone old themes and new sounds makes the game more fresh with some nostalgia.
+ Although I personally like the old story more, this one is completely new after the prolouge and much bigger, it introduced a lot more characters and zones making the universe seem bigger and more populated.
+ Mutations of Sonny and his ability is a good concept that allows for variation in gameplay, keeping things fresh.
+ The characters have their own personal goals and thoughts, adding to the immersion of the game.
Cons:
- The AI can be a little aggravating at times by not picking viable moves also not being able to control allies.
- You can tell this game was primarily developed with mobile gaming in mind, The UI feels a bit to odd for PC
and I can think of a few good ways to localize it. (Able to slide items and abilities, more of a similar combat
hub like in Sonny 2 with the debuffs displaying near the health bar, ability highlights, and making it a bit smaller.)
- The lack of atmosphere in the hub makes the game feel a bit less immersive.
- One of the most annoying things in the game has to be the attack time bar in combat,
It'll always get to the point where the enemy will debuff me and get 3-5 hits in before I even get in 1.
- The music in the training area is the same as the hub which makes it feel slower in pace.
- Not being able to change the difficulty is a bit annoying.
- And finally my biggest complaint of all is not enough of "Ima knock you silly".
Although it's not Sonny 3 overall it's a really fun, enjoyable game that can be played in a multitude of different ways.
whether you're a veteran of the Sonny franchise or just looking for a new RPG to play i'd definitely recommend giving this a try.

A turn based RPG based almost entirely around the combat. There is no world map to explore or treasure to find like in traditional JRPGs, there are just options to fight the next battle or manage your skills and inventory. The battles move fairly quickly and are hardly ever tedious in the way a lot of RPGs become after you've seen the attacks dozens of times.
The game is very much focused on strategy, rather than grinding to become overpowered. The game is fairly difficult in spots, which I found to be a nice change over most turn based RPGs where you usually can power through the whole game without ever dying. Some fights seem downright impossible until you adjust your gear, skills and tactics. There's no penalties for death so trying out different strategies is never punishing.
I have not played the flash Sonny games and am judging this game purely on its own merit. Animations and equipment models are nothing but fluff, this game is a very solid strategic turn based RPG that I would recommend over any of the RPGmaker drek that's on Steam.
-Playtime-
A good 8 hours for the initial play through. Additional play throughs for achievements take less time as you can skip any cut scenes and you know what you're doing at that point.
-Achievements-
A few one-off achievements that usually have you defeating a boss in some special way that added a bit of challenge. Unless you get it on your first run you will have to repeat the game at least once to get the "only use the physical skill tree" achievement. Another achievement requires that you have evolved a skill from each of the 5 elements, requiring you to at least play a 2nd run about half way through.

Plays like a more in depth Civilization.  Which is awesome!  Consider any Civ game to be your pretutorial, then play the tutorial included with the game, and then you're all set!  So far I am absolutely loving it!  Barbarians and citystates have been fused to make "minor factions".  You can either use diplomacy and do some stuff to gain their favor or use military might to subjugate them.  The factions seem quite diverse, though I have only played with the Necrophague.  The terrain plays a large role in warfare, and battles can be micromanaged whereas you decide which unit does what.  I really can't recommend this game enough if you enjoy strategy games.  If you don't, I'm not sure this will win you over.  Then again, I doubt any strategy game would.  For: people who like Risk, Civilization, Heroes of Might and Magic          Not for: people who do not have patience

1) There's a role-play of the civilization you pick. It also plays into Endless Space (and maybe the other Endless game, but I don't have it). That is a neat feature and I love it
2) Visuals for the most part. The map is gorgeous but sometimes it's hard to find that there are lootable sites on it. The unit appearnces and animations are poor, however
3) The ability to see tile yields
4) The neat way resources are harvested and a part of the game
5) Many quests and different ways to approach the game
What I don't:
1) The super long lag between selecting an action and something happening (no longer a problem - seems like the game is better optimized)
2) Encountering units early on that wipe out yours. Particularly because I can't determine the strength of enemies until too late (due to my lack of knowledge. I've learned a LOT through trial and error)
3) The long build times for anything. It has the Civ V keep advancing turn 'cause nothing is happening' problem (not as bad as it was when I first got the game - maybe something better optimized)
4) Poor Man-Machine-Interface. Too many clicks to accomplish things (nowhere near as bad any more, again suspected to be caused by tweaks to the game)
Overall, worth having, but I probably won't play it often. If I see updates, particularly optimization/speeding up things, I might be more patient with it. But a minute plus load time (fast machine, mind you) and then about two minutes from the setup to playing do not a happy ninjaGhost make.
[EDIT] Since writing, there have been multiple DLC releases, which greatly improved the game. The load times are still really long, but the feature that allows the player to speed up combat mechanics is very nice and prevents the long delays during fights. Now, this is my favorite city builder ever (just nudged Civ IV out of top billing.

Don't let my hours on Steam fool you, I have played this game for thousands of hours on various platforms, (PS3, 360, and Disc PC). I started out on PS3 and I absolutely adored it, at the time it was revolutionary and amazing. I have 1,200 hours on just my first character on PS3, and that was without doing some questlines.
Main Story:
Oblivion's Main Story is what to be expected from games of this sort, especially Bethesda. Hero has to go from place to place and kill that or learn that and eventually face the main bad guy at the end. Of course it's more complicated then that but I don't really wanna spoil anything. I personally much prefer Oblivion's main quest to that of Skyrim's but that is all personal taste. Don't expect anything amazing but you can get immersed in it and remember it for years to come.
Side Quests:
The game features such amazing side quests for every type of player. Assassin's having to sneak into a pirate ship to having to systematically kill off every guest in a mansion. Thieve's having to steal various items. From a Robin Hood take from the rich and give to the poor mentality but also from a pure selfish gain alike. Fighters getting their fair share of killing this and protecting that and fetching that. Mages doing various tasks from killing rogue necromancers to fetching enchanted rings that weight almost 200 pounds. And of course misc side quests that vary from sleeping on a boat only to wake up and find pirates have abducted the crew and sailed into the ocean. To having to solve why an entire village's population have randomly turned invisible all of a sudden. And the amazing Daedric quests I will not spoil.
Guilds:
I felt it correct to give the Guilds it's own secton since it has suge a huge prescence in the game. The guilds in this game are insanely good. If you were impressed by Skyrim's guilds they don't hold anything on Oblivion's. I was frankly disappointed by Skyrim's guilds compared to Oblivions. The Mage's Guild, Dark Brotherhood, and Thieve's Guild especially are really good. And Oblivion even has minor (guilds) you can join such as the Knights of the Thorn, White Stallion, Order of The Virtuous Blood, etc. Every thing I've mentioned so far you can avoid and not even play, most people won't even come across all of the guilds in their first or second or even third playthrough.
Expansions:
Oblivion's expansions add a lot, Shivering Isles is known as one of the best expansion packs ever, and I can't deny that. Knights of the Nine is also really good. And the housing DLC I don't mind but rarely find myself ever using. And the Horse Armor dlc is just... Why Bethesda?
Modding:
The humongous modding community Bethesda games is now known for started becoming huge with this game, there is an abundance of great mods. From new weapons, armor, quests, cities, and even entirely new guilds and dozens of hours long quests. The modding community isn't as big as it is for Skyrim, but it still has an overwhelming amount of mods.
The World and Graphics:
This game feels like a vibrant, breathing, real world. (Although a little bit on the derpy side.) No other game I have played have I felt like I can live inside of a city inside the game. Many people claim Oblivion is one of the most compfy games to exist, to which I have to agree. Everything is just where it should be. Although the graphics are slightly dated they have a charm to them, the faces are ugly and the landscapes look a bit like a painting more than a game, but in my honest opinion the landscapes in this game hold up better than even Skyrims. It looks gorgeous, (save for the characters and some dated textures).
Gameplay and Ai:
Now onto the gameplay, Oblivion features the standard mediocre combat to expect from Bethesda. With hits that feel like you're using a nerf sword, except for one exception. The magic in Oblivion is extremely fun and diverse, unlike Skyrim it doesn't take up a hand. You can be a battleaxe using, fireball casting, robe wearing assassin. You can also make your own spells in Oblivion.The dynamic AI is both amazing (at the time it came out), and absolutely hilarious. Every NPC in the game can have a conversation with every other NPC in the game, and this can result in some hilariously stupid conversations. Although it is funny and stupid and doesn't work how the Devs intended it, I still think it adds to the world. Hearing people have dynamic conversations as you walk through a city going on a quest or to the inn is very immsersive and adds so much more.
Character Customization:
The character creation is what to expect from Elder Scrolls, various facial customization, (except beards... C'mon Bethesda really?) and all the races. And let's not forget what Skyrim left out, classes. There are preset classes and custom classes you yourself can make and name. They don't restrict what you can do or use. They just enhance your starting attributes and skills, and make certain attributes and skills easier to level up in.
Conclusion:
Overall Oblivion is an amazing RPG and an amazing game in general. Even though it's graphics and voice acting have aged poorly it is still very very good. I would recommend it to almost anyone.

This is my attempt at a genuine review. I'm not trying to be funny nor am I trying to protest against external business decisions (except the ones that affect gameplay). Please read the full length of the text for insight.
If you are going to buy it anyway, I recommend these DLCs as a starter pack (from highest priority to least):
Fundamentally a good game at its core. Becomes a mixed bag (at least for me) and borderline abusive relationship when you're a veteran. I don't mind the DLCs. I just have a problem with the quality of the DLCs.
-------------------------
It's hard for me to thumbs down this game.
I'm not denying that CK2 is a good game. In this instance, I believe that either buying the game or not buying the game are both good choices. The qualifying argument that I wish to convey below is simply why I (personally) cannot advocate this game. They have forgotten the old ways of making good quality content over emplacing mechanics that may annoy you unless you buy their DLC. Often, even their good ideas are also poorly executed. They make you ambivalent because they add good ideas, but convolute it with bad ones.
It's hard to roll back to an earlier patch that I favor, because often times there are genuinely good things that newer patches add: bug fixes, balancing issues, more options, etc. However, some features can't be turned off or are simply poorly thought out: merchant republics, secret religions (not secret cults - you can turn those off), broken retinue triggers (as in certain tactics don't pop as often as I think they should), bugged out inheritances, the frequency in which most states become
over time (possibly fixed; haven't checked), etc. The good changes come with the bad, whether you agree with them or not. Recently they've been getting better at addressing the issues by allowing you to change the initial settings, but my problem with Paradox is thus: the tendency is that features they have added come with more problems than they can fix and a lot of my gripes cannot (typically) be addressed with initial settings. The way they've been churning out more content instead of addressing very annoying issues indicate to me that they're cashing in the faith of their customers out for money at the expense of quality.
Even though I'll probably be playing this game for at least two hundred more hours (close to 600 at the time of writing), I can't recommend the game to newcomers. I wish to convince you to not play the game to save you the trouble. Even though I love this game, my central issue with
of their games that I’ve played including EU4 and Stellaris is thus:
Why should you buy a game where the developers consistently execute really half-baked ideas to a fundamentally good game, then charge you as if it were worthy of your money, but at the same time devoid yourself of content if you choose to reject? It's hard to pinpoint and explain to people who all but seek entertainment: t but you would understand if you had played hundreds of hours of this game.
It's as if a friend gave you gifts that were practical, but all distinctly smelled of butt. It's nice and useful, but it's still butt. It's hard to parse the butt-gift from its scent, so you may try to put on a mask or put perfume onto it to cover it up. Though you get utility out of it, either two things will happen: you will get use to the smell or start going insane, wishing that the butt smell would go away. Ultimately, your friend was an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and shouldn't have given you the gift in the first place.
If you're the sort of person that cautiously guards their heart, don't buy this game. For me, it's too late. The die has been cast.
Listen to my advice so that you can avoid the headache of falling in love with maiden Paradox, only to have them undeservingly rifle your coinpurse. This is not exclusive to CK2 either, and, mind you, that my decision to
recommend this game is not because I'm "against" DLC's (I'm not). It's the
of the DLCs with which I have a problem and the manner in which they try to
the DLCs. The
of several minor issues DO build up, and I think they're just not willing to look at issues past a certain date so the hopes of them getting fixed is dim.
Lady Paradox is trouble. Don't fall for her. Go elsewhere. Find someone that will treat you right. You deserve better.
So is it worth it? Yes and no. I certainly spent a lot of time on this game, but it leaves a bad taste in my mouth after a while. Think ME3's ending.
Also for the record, I don't have anything against Paradox. I judge them by their content, and I find their lack of quality disturbing. They really do need to consolidate their effort into QA instead of spitting out DLCs rapid fire and fixing it later. Time will tell if they fall from their prestigeous position from the community, but, at least at the moment, they have a -50 opinion modifier from me.

Pros:
Steep learning curve rewarded by intricate mechanics.
Community are super helpful - if you're stuck with anything steam, paradox and reddit forums offer heaps of help.
Ludicrous scope from quaint Duke to god Emperor.
Historical accuracy for once! No appropriating, no blending of cultures etc - if you've studied, or simply enjoy, medieval history then you'll probably love this.
Roleplaying aspect is simultaneously fun as it is making you think of your actions, reminds me of The Witcher decisions except less harrowing.
Cons:
Some aspects are behind a DLC pay wall. These don't make the game unplayable, but they add aspects that flesh out the base game considerably. For example: it's community consensus that "Way of Life" is a must have; don't expect to play as  a Muslim without "Sword of Islam" etc - most of the DLC is great, or at least builds upon what is already a great game, but can feel quite expensive for what it adds. Alongside that is a recent price hike for many regions, so for the 'full' game is very expensive.
The tutorial could do with a rework; whilst it teaches somethings it totally misses other basics and makes the game out to be less fun that it actually is.
For me it's one of the best stategy games out there. Don't be put off by the UI, it takes some getting used to but it's far more interactive than first appears - and don't be put off by not being able to do anything for a while, it makes it all the more rewarding when you're pillaging, usurping, murdering, seducing, bribing your way to glory.
Also for everyone grilling Paradox recently - they are one of the few developers that still tweak their games years after it's release, and as much as patches take away gameable aspects overall I'd say they've done a really good job with balancing CK2 - remember it's supposed to be accurate, there are meant to certain biases. Admittedly the price hike doesn't seem necessary, especially as it doesn't even allign with inflation, but the product itself is top quality.
9/10 - the amount of work in the game is ridiculous, and the developers derseve to be rewarded for their efforts, however the price can be a bitter pill to swallow - definitely pick up in a sale (like now for example!) and don't add all the DLC at once.

I were, and still am, an avid fan of Paradox games. HoI 3, Vicky, Vicky 2, EU 3, EU 4, CK, CK 2. I played those games for countless hours, yet I cannot in honesty say that I recommend them. There is little fun and passion anymore in those games.

I have been a long time user of Paradox games, since Europa Universalis 2. They are great, the best historical strategy games out there. However, from the launch of CK2, their DLC policy is completely out of hand. Paradox used to issue free patches now and then for their games, that helped to sort out problems and improved some mechanics, along with more comprehensive old style expansions, that were really worth it and changed the game so much that it was almost a new game. Then, DLC model came. At first, DLCs were ok, a little like the old expansions, but the model degenerated into what it is now, more like a money grabbing scheme.
It has gone bad. Some DLCs look rushed and unbalance the game or just add content for the sake of it. Mods have been a very important part of the Paradox experience, however, now it seems like modders have a hard time keeping pace with the DLC updates. If you want to use some of the best mods, you need to get the DLCs. The base game looks hollow in comparison, so it is not like you can just buy it and get the full experience. I played a lot this game at the beginning (I had it on Gamersgate before they migrated it to Steam), but I stopped playing in frustration at the inability of getting a "finished" product and a "finished" game experience, if you know what I mean. I got frustrated when half way down my campaign a new DLC would come altering the game mechanics and my favourite mod updated to it, somehow making necessary to buy the new DLC.
It is sad to me to say so, as I loved Paradox games, but I cannot reccomend this game. If you buy it, you are likely to be bound to buy more than 100 euros worth in DLCs for the full game experience. I can only warn you about that. Five years after release, they keep coming. As consumers and gamers, no one should contribute to these policies that degrade the market and our hobby. They have only gone worse with their new games. Paradox, change your ways. A reckoning is coming.

As I expected, the vast majority of negative reviews here are incredibly silly.
Just to get the two most common aesthetic complaints out of the way:
1) Yes, the partial voice acting is annoying. It's awkward to hear bits and pieces of dialogue while you're reading text; it should be all-or-nothing. I like the system of having a simple voice-acted reaction that summarizes the text (like Kara's "awww" when you meet the zombie wolves), but occasionally voice-acting entire sentences throws it all off. That said, this is a minor complaint.
2) It's mind-boggling to me that people think a game MUST cover up all of its characters with a bunch of equipment you've picked for mechanical use rather than for appearance. The character sprites are well drawn and I'd much rather be able to see them; in Sonny 1 & 2, characters were hidden under layers of armor and robes, and it was extremely unappealing. This complaint makes no sense to me.
As for the actual combat...it's pretty neat. There are five classes with extremely different playstyles, for a total of six skill trees (including the basic one all classes get), and the limited skill slots make you choose your options very carefully while preventing a lot of the absurd brokenness that Sonny 1 & 2 enabled. Mid-combat skill boosts offer a very unique mechanic that allows you to alter your skillset on the fly in order to adapt to new threats. I take a little issue with the fact that the enemy wave system means you'll sometimes have two characters ready to act as soon as the new wave comes, or sometimes all be sitting on empty turn meters and max cooldowns. But other than the game's occasional incentives to leave enemies alive longer (which feels bad in any game when it happens), everything else about the mechanics really is stellar.
For anyone who's considering this game and is being turned off by the negative reviews, please read them carefully to determine how much of their complaints actually matter to you, and how much the reviewers actually played the game. Chances are that both answers will be "very little".

Huge Sonny fan. Played 1 and 2 countless times with different difficulties and builds. While this new game is very questionable. I would throw a neutral vote if i could. So without much saying i will just gonna list most of pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Very good visuals and desighns. Everything looks zombie-futuristic-mecha-mutated and stylish overall.
+ Great music. A little reworked old themes that still sounds fresh and active.
+ New and bigger story. Lots of new characters and story telling. Bunch of stuff reworked completely.
+ Longer. 8 zones , enemies mix ups , unique bosses/minibosses and encounters.
+ Dialogs and storytelling. Characters are different, with their own motivations and thoughts. Good jokes from time to time.
Cons:
- Animations removed. While not so catastrophic, removing all animations from characters aint looking so nice.
- Not everything voiced. In this game we dont have full audio for dialogs. There are some phrases thrown from here to there, but not much.
- Same start. While you can still have different abilities and builds. You start with same options every game and can change into something different only later on.
- Dumb AI. You cant control them at all. Some moves can be absolutely random.
- No little clickable things in safe zones. You could click on merchants or just on stuff around to get some special atmosphere going on.
- No end-game content. When you complete the game, you complete the game.
Overall while having some major cons, game turns out to be pretty decent and enjoyable. While animations is gone, good art style completes the game just alright. And new story is pretty good too (while the main villain is kinda weak for me). If you are a Sonny fan or just want to spend some time in turn based rpg you can grab this game for sure. A fair game for its prize.
P.S. I will never forgive you Baron rework.

I've never written any reviews before, I haven't even finished the game yet but I'm so determined to write one because I desperately want to nominate this game for the “Even Better Than I Expected” Award.
I'll go ahead and discuss my reasons for nominating a little bit and then some details to help you know the game better.
Being a Sonic fan has been really hard in these recent years and so I'd got a little pessimistic towards Sega, but when I saw the trailer for the first time, I got completely blown away by how epic the whole atmosphere of the game was. Speeding through absolutely well-made stages filled with tiny little details here and there, focusing on each character's core and the style they were born to be played as, amazing soundtracks etc. And the whole attitude of setting things right of Sega really touched my heart. Deep down a hope was born inside of me, Sonic can be great again.
So I went ahead and pre-ordered the game as soon as I could and played it soon as it was released and did it feel so good! It brought back my childhood memories right in front of my eyes. How could I ever imagine a classic Sonic game can get great to this extent?! Pacing through the levels, trying special stages and fighting bosses... there was nothing that felt even a bit faulty or wrong; it was pure fun! It was even far beyond my expectations as a devoted Sonic fan.
I'll go to the details right away, hope it helps in your decision of whether this game is good for you or not.
Note: Please consider that I haven't finished the game yet, my list will be updated as I progress in the game.
Gameplay:
-More advanced levels compared to the classics with lots of different ways to finish each level. Meaning you won't get bored by just beating the game once or even a couple of times.
-Redesigned old stages + epic and fun new stages.
-Lots of new elements; a new item that stack rings when they fall, a fun and useful new skill for Sonic, very creative ways of transport in each level, some nostalgic cameos and etc.
-Since its a fast-paced game I recommend this game to people who enjoy or at least are ok with fast and hyper gameplay.
-Two challenging special stages which one of them can be taken a couple of times in the middle of each level for a change of mood and ofc more bonus!
-A somewhat good pointing system as many elements are considered such as combos, time and the rings you collect.
-The ability to collect Chaos Emeralds which leads you to different endings. So the way you play somehow matters.
-2P support both in game and as a competitive mode.
-Playing on a low-end pc, I haven't noticed any lags when only the game is running.
Soundtrack:
-Epic as always.
Graphics:
-Smooth and swift graphics.
-Beautiful or detailed stages filled with eye-catching details every here and there.
Story:
-Haven't beaten the game yet but looks promising.
-Like notable other Sonic games, I find fighting against evil for freedom and rescuing tiny little animals really enjoyable.
As a con I see people arguing about denuvo quite often. Unfortunately I don't have enough information about it but I personally haven't encountered any problems in either software or hardware of my pc.
As for other cons I have to beat the game at least once to realize what the game lacks or what is needed to make it better, that's why I'm sorry if this review sounds one-sided. Will be updated as soon as possible.

One of the best single player RPGs I ever played. The best turn based combat I ever experienced in a RPG. The quests, the way just about every quest can be completed in different ways and have different outcomes depending on what you do, the world design, the many secrets and hidden stuff, the puzzles, the character customization, the story, plenty of different stuff you can experience or miss depending on the choices you make, the openness, the freedom with how you approach and deal with things, the variety you experience throughout the whole game, all the unique encounters and stuff that happens, just everything in the game, its all great. The graphics and soundtrack are great. Pretty good voice acting. Not only does the game have a great PC-centric interface, it also has a great and separate console-centric interface for if you want to play with a gamepad on a bigscreen while sitting on a couch. The game doesn't hold your hand at all, you really got to figure things out. The game is so open that it never slaps your hand away and tells you "no, can't do that", instead you can do crazy and over the top stuff to solve things and succeed in combat, regardless of how hilarious and goofy it ends up being. The game really rewards creativity. While this is a great game on its own, its also an example of a sequel done right, because unlike modern sequels to Bethesda and Bioware RPGs, this game takes everything the first game did while improving plenty of stuff and adding plenty of new stuff. The co-op mode doesn't play like a standard co-op game such as Left 4 Dead, Diablo or something, its like a digital version of a D&D campaign, so if you have a buddy you play pen and paper RPGs with then this is a co-op game you'll enjoy together. The game has full mod support. I haven't tried the PvP mode, so I can't comment on that.

After fourteen hours and one run through down. I sit here trying to type out a quick review on my thoughts on the game. So to pirate one of my favorite game reviewers, here is my take on
.
So graphics are up first. I have to admit I did really enjoy the new artwork. The basic sprite designs, the new backgrounds, the comic still cinematic, are all very good quality. They are worthy of being in a graphic novel.
But then we run into the next bit that probably is one of the main turn offs for returning fans of the series. There are
attack animations to speak off. Well, there are, but minimal at best.
During battle, the character sprites sit in their default poses the whole game. If melee attacks are used, the sprites move towards the target. But it’s like watching a cut-out jump from its position to ram into the enemy cut-out. Not unlike how a child would simulate action heroes in hand-to-hand combat.If ranged move is used, the projectile will go flying and hit the target. The sprites don’t flinch, there are no stationary animations. This is kind of a step back from the flash games, sadly.
Another source of ire is a little superficial. And it’s the fact that there are no visual representations of equipped items on your character. This is not much a problem for me, but after looking over the previous Sonny games, this is also brings the thought of “one step forward, two steps back”.
For game sounds you can feel the ‘whumps’ and ‘thwacks’ of physical based moves, the ‘crackle’ and spine tingling ‘crinkle’ of energy and frost based abilities do give a good bite when used. It’s not fantastic, but it gets the job done. But seeing that its a PC port, a better sound quality on these effects could’ve added more weight to the game’s quality.
Next is music. The music in this iteration is very reminiscent from the older the games and with the leap of technology and recording, the quality does sound better now than it did then. But that’s just my opinion. Unfortunately, the music pieces are few, and eventually you’ll be gauntleting through the same pieces over, and over, and over again by the end of the tutorial level.
And that’s only if you play the story/campaign based fights. The moment you hit those training fights, get ready for several rounds of the main interface screen that’s dreary and accompanied by character grunts and attack effects.
Last for this section are the voices. Now, the voices are of better quality than previous iterations. That much is certain. However, speaking lines are very few and in between. The longest running voice-over lines we get are at the end of the game. It’s a shame though as the voices do capture the character’s personality, from Sonny’s dry British lilt to Vendara’s Punisher-esque military voice. Heck, even the bosses like Farsight had good voiced lines, the little that there was.
For those not familiar with Sonny, the game acts like a JRPG. That’s the most basic explanation in a nutshell.
Other mechanics include buying/grinding equipment for your characters and spending those ability points from those level-ups to activate new moves for you to use. But do keep in mind, the only character you have any total control over is Sonny. After purchasing his skills you can activate them by putting them in his combat wheel which allows the moves to be usable during fights. The wheel is limited in slots. Unfortunately, passive effects also need to be equipped on the wheel for them to kick-in. This reduces your number of options during a fight if you wish to use some of the passive abilities (like life steal or speed buffs).
During fights when Sonny’s turn to activate comes up, all you need to do is tap your target and tap the skill you want to use on said target.
This now brings me to the next point of irritation that people may bring up, the UI. The UI for Sonny (2017) is really clunky. Though do keep in mind that this game was intended for mobile devices at the beginning.
You want to remember what skill does during battle? Just tap and hold the skill icon. You want to immediately equip your shiny new loot that you just bought? You have to exit the shop then equip the item. There are so many breaks between actions that it disrupts the flow of the gameplay experience. Not to mention that during fights, there’s this constant camera movement which may give those with weaker constitutions a bad case of motion sickness.
Though to be fair, it looks like the development team is heeding the criticisms and are trying to work in patches to help streamline the UI.
Next, character growth. Now, I’ll be honest, the skill development, management, and investment were a big draw of the Sonny games to me. Each fight felt more like a puzzle where not only did you have to figure out how to fight your opponents, but what moves would be the most effective to use.
And I’m happy to say that some of these moments are in the game. The game does force you to choose your move sets and you can re-spec Sonny later on if you hit a wall against a particular fight -looking at you, Baron!- but you still must try to find the means for victory with the stuff you got. There are no take-backs once you’ve chosen your sets, not unless you want to restart your run.
As a side note, the new mechanic is a nice touch.
Moving on, you also have party members that become available as your progress through the story, each one with their own particular move set.  This adds a little variety, but your choice who you want to bring along is largely determined by how you spec Sonny out.
This now brings me to the guys you fight. They are a little varied but eventually, through repetition, you will figure out their attack patterns and plan accordingly. But I’ve noticed that there may be an issue in difficulty escalation. The game only has one setting for difficulty.
In the beginning, you’re tearing through monsters, left, right, and center. By mid to late game, the fights become so intense that the difficulty curve might as well be a straight line up. Eventually, with deep pockets (equipment and the cost of redistributing ability points) and LOTS of point redistribution, I managed to eke out victories but it took a while plus a couple hours of grinding to do so.
It was nice to see the Sonny game out and about again. It brought back memories from my childhood. And for the time I’ve sunk in so far, I’ve enjoyed it thus far. But I wouldn’t recommend this game to just anyone.
The player has to willingly look beyond the faults and the gripe to see the jewel. The seeds for a good series are there and past work models can be implemented in a sequel, and test beds for UI development can be done in patches to the current game.
If you want to support the makers and try to give them a reason to continue this series, I would suggest you buy the game and try the challenges provided. But if the listed faults above –and in other’s testimonies- turn you away, then there’s nothing else I can do to convince you.
The creators mentioned that this would be a different iteration of the Sonny series. And this is what we got. Now, we can lament about how much better the previous versions are. But that doesn’t change the fact the developers are trying something new with this I.P. And who knows where this may go. We can only hope that the next step is a better and more polished game.
Peace out!

I've played both the original Sonny and Sonny 2 shortly after each came out. So after waiting for such a long time for this game to come out, I had high expectations from this game. And while I will admit that all of them were not met, what I got from this game certainly was quality.
This game is basically a reboot of Sonny's original story, and I must say that I very much love how things turned out. I'm not gonna go into spoilers territory, but I like how the game justified Sonny's newborn powers with his zombie taint. I was initially disappointed with Veradux being retconned as a human, but at least this justifies both why he always has his armor and how his powers are nowhere near Sonny's. While the direction the story takes is drastically different from that of the original games, a lot of elements mentionned in the original games were incorporated into this new story (including the infamous tape), and they fit quite nicely. So both old fans of the games and newcomers get to enjoy this story for different reasons.
Gameplay-wise, I was initially disappointed with how the mechanics of the game were simplified and how the skill trees are a lot smaller, but it does make it more easy to get into for newcomes. The original skill trees had 40 abilites when you only had 34 skill points at most (in Sonny 2 at least, in the original you had even fewer points), so most of those were redundant anyways. The new ones are simpler and easy to look over to see what you deem most important. My only big complaint about the gameplay is how you only get your second skill tree a quarter of the way in, and you cannot go back on your decision unless you restart everything over. It makes sense from a story standpoint, but still... The equipment system was also made simpler, although I wish there were more choices in the way of equipments we can choose from the stores. The game's difficulty is also still like the older games: the beginning is very easy, and the difficulty curve is not too steep until the final areas. There is no post-game area, but the final area very much makes up for it. My only real complaint is how we can't fight bosses a second time like in the original games. I would love it if this could be patched in. Otherwise, this means we have nothing to do except train once the game's over on a specific file.
In the way of the game's aesthetic, I am very much content. A lot of people complain about both the attack animations and sprite variations being gone, and honestly, I don't think it's that big of a deal. While it's true that it could have looked much better with the game's new graphics, there are a few good things that come out of both: no attack animations mean the gameplay's much faster (and honestly, you won't be thrilled by those animations anymore after seeing them 100 times, I know I wasn't back in the original two games...), and no variations in the characters' sprites based on their equipment mean they always "look good". By that I mean that they're still recognizable in their own way and it also makes sense from a story standpoint (how would Veradux get around without his MechSuit ? Or How would Kara fight with a shovel instead of a gun ?). Otherwise, the characters' sprites look pretty good (for the budget of course).
To conclude, I'd say that this game is definitely worth considering wherever you come from. If you're a newcomer to the series and like strategy-oriented RPGs, you'll definitely have a lot of fun on this game. If you're a veteran of our favourite zombie's adventures, while you might be initially discouraged by the changes made to the game, I can guarantee as a fellow veteran that you will find your share of amusement in this game. Krin, I'm looking forward to you continuing Sonny's adventures !

Sonny is a game that might have gotten a mixed bag of reviews. According to some, including the hardcore flash players who have followed Sonny's lead developer Krin since his first foray into flash games, they may be right. This new "soft reboot" of Sonny definitely is missing features or details that added a level of charm to the sonny franchise that is rarely seen. However it feels like most of the reviews also stem from miscommunication, and this can be verified by the extremely limited playing time of most reviewers. To kick this review off, here is a summy of what you are getting in this 6-8 dollar game:
- A cartoon-style visualization of characters in a turn-based style combat system similar to games like the Final Fantasy series.
- 3 different classes for you to level as the game moves on, with in-combat levels gained the longer the fight persists that allow you to temporarily level individual skills to your advantage.
- 8 stages with each stage possesing anywhere between 7-12 encounters that function in waves of enemies with different weaknesses and resistances.
- A streamlined inventory system that, unfortunately, is similar to most IOS style games but still somewhat in-depth enough from the sacrifices you will have to make to improve one stat over the other. There is no be-all end all armor set in this game, and part of the fun is balancing your stats through equipment. Unfortunately Levels do not give you extra stat points, however. Levels only help increase your skills.
- A comic book style telling of a story though limited voice interaction and still cutscenes.
However, the most important thing that people have yet to realize, is that this, is not the original Sonny. This game is trying new styles and new concepts, and  that definitely rubbed people the wrong way, since it was under a beloved flash game brand that has tens of millions of playthroughs.
Despite this, however, the game still delivers in it's own way. All the items above combine to create a solid gaming experience that, in my opinion, is worth 6 dollars. The different classes (that are unlocked after various stages later in the game) have enough variety and potential combo ability that you can spend an hour or two simply trying to find out the best class combinations. Along with that, the ability to specialize into multiple different classes could create interesting depth.
The combat is fairly solid as well, as the turn-based style system requires a fair amount of strategy, especially on the later encounters. The Evolution system further increases the strategic level of combat, however this is still somewhat blunted by the fact that evolutions are somewhat random.
While the different characters are somewhat cliche', there is enough personality to create distinction between characters to allow some attachment, and the dialog between characters is OK (with references and even some 4th wall jokes getting thrown in.)
The biggest draw is that there are no character animations, no full voice acting, no control over AI teammates frustrating certain encounters, and the evolution system is somewhat blunted by the sheer randomness of what evolutionary traits you can pick. However, the combat is still very solid and reminescent of classic Sonny games, and the elongated and more fleshed out storyline means that there is more to come back for.

It's a good game. Get ot if you're interested in an MMO that pits you with powers on different planets, killing baddies, and finishing missions. That's as simple as you can get.
Going into more detail, the amount of things you can do in this game is vast. You can get your own pets, play any level you want as long as it's unlocked, heck, there's even a PVP mode you can get into if you are feeling pretty competitive.
Most of the game does revolve around PVE, especially in the beginning, where it's not as good to play PVE, since you don't have as many things unlocked. I've only played the PVE side of the game, so I can't get into much more detail than that, but if you want more detail on some other gameplay, just look below.
Not necessarily. It's more of pay 2 advance, as it can speed up progress of the game, but overall, you have to put time and effort into the game in order to get things, and there's only so many things you can get with paid currency. Everything is available to grab as a F2P, it just requires time and effort.
Weapon crafting requires ingredients that you can get in a variety of ways, usually by getting resources from different planets, or by crafting weapon parts, but it really just depends on the blueprint.
You get blueprints by playing certain missions, by buying them off the market, or by buying them off the pay store.
Upgrading is simple; you gain upgrades through playing the game, and put them on your weapon. There's only a certain amount of points you can use, and there's different types of upgrades that can get buffed or nerfed depending on what weapon you use.
Warframes can be obtained by buying using paid currency, crafting, or through certain missions.
In order to craft Warframes, you need to craft the body parts (there's normally 4), so there's 5 blue prints you need to obtain. You usually obtain these through relics.
-----------------------------------------------------
Upgrading is simple (yes, I copied the text from the weapons, it uses the same system); you gain upgrades through playing the game, and put them on your warframe. There's only a certain amount of points you can use, and there's different types of upgrades that can get buffed or nerfed depending on what warframe you use.
I give this game an 8.5/10, since there were rare but noticable points where the game becomes a little less like a game and more like a work, so if you're playing this game for the fun, you're not gonna get to endgame unless you push yourself, since once you get to midgame, the game becomes more of a major grindfest.

Adorables is a very simple physics ball game with nice graphics and cute little "Adorables". You can change the color of your characters at the beginning of the game. After you've won some money, you can change the shape of your adorables , buy a different eye and/or mouth and also buy a hat, bow or horns. There are severals different sporting events, Soccer, Beach Soccer and Ice Hockey. There is also Capture the Flag, Last Adorable Standing, and The Mummy. Your 3 Adorables are controlled by assigning each a direction in which to launch via an arrow attached to them. The speed and distance in which the Adorable will launch is decided by how long or short you stretch the arrow. They can also be banked off the sides, knock each other and the ball around, kind of like playing pool. Its a fun little game, but can become repetitive. If you like very simple physics games, I'd wait to get it on sale or in a bundle.

At first, you play on the new-players servers. So much fun! People just whacking away occasionally accidentally killing their own teammates & looking silly while doing so then everyone laughing about it while you respawn.
However, after a certain level - based on how much you play, not your skill - you are banned from the new-player servers. I understand what they're going for, but if you want to control the game as in to make it fair, why not to automatic match-making as an option?
As many other reviews have mentioned, the fighting becomes really, really stupid once you begin to take the game seriously. There are all sorts of tricks that allow you to swing a sword in a 360-degrees on three axises simultaneously essentially sending out a burst of death around you.
I highly recommend this game to someone who wants to get about 10-20 hours of really truly sincerely hillarious and fun gaming. Really, that's a lot more than most games can offer! However you should be ready to quit as soon as you're no longer allowed to play on the new-player servers. Go play Mount And Blade Warband instead! That has both a much better combat system possible to use on a massive multiplayer scale as well as singleplayer RPG.

I am quite glad I got the new version instead of the old one.
That having been said, this game provides a nice balance of fighting, building and economy that keeps you on your toes without being too difficult. Its the little things that make it stand out, like the way a worker, if they where working at something nearby before building, returns to doing that thing when they are done building! There are a lot of more 'advanced' games that don't think of these kinds of things. There are also alternate victory types, which is a nice touch.
Unforutnately, there are two weaknesses, the big one is that the tech tree advances the exact same way no matter who you are playing, while a good balancing measure it means who you play doesn't matter quite as much as it should.
