I really wanted to like this game I really do, but the current state it is in makes me want to tick off the mark off the wishlist considering that I have finished playing sonny 1 and 2 in armor games since 13 y.o . I don't want to sound like an old man reminiscing the good ol'days of the war and stuff like that, but the truth is, the flash version of the game is more immersive and enjoyable than what they have released on steam and iOS. Like all before me that have tried the game and give a bad review, the main problem with it is the UI, animation and gameplay. You couldn't see what you are equipping and it really puts me off, because it is an RPG, and kinda reduce the value if you get cool equipment but cannot see it on your character during battles. Animation it seems also receives less attention, as your melee attack pretty much do the same animation, while on the flash version you can see different sound effects and physics with each group of attacks. Regarding the gameplay, you get some new skills in this version and is quite unique in their own way, and the evolution system is interesting enough, though at times a little bit annoying. The problem though lies with the ability system. In the flash version you got 8 ability tabs and when you unlocks a passive you dont need to equip it to the tab in order for it to activate, while in this version, you DO need to equip passives in tabs in order to make them "actives", while you still get the same number of tabs as the previous one, which when you progress to face higher level enemies, combat easily became frustrating. How so? Well higher level enemies will deal more CC's, get more turns(increase in speed) and more DoT, so its hard to experiment with classes when you have limited option regarding abilities, and it will feel at times that enemies are getting stronger, while you are not. I have managed to finish the game through sheer luck(The warlock at the last stage didn't one shot kara that time). The upside of the game though, it has more in depth story I suppose, and more detailed regarding the environment, skills, and etc. Though  I would like to suggest one more thing. Please bring back the class system such as biological, hydraulic, assassin, guardian, or assimilate those classes into something new, but please let us choose classes. If there is no class to choose from, people would less likely to repeat the game after they had beaten it once, because the class system is what makes the game repeatable. I know you have said that it will be hard to implement these changes, but please for the sake of your fans, just do it. I would gladly pay more than its current price if you would apply these elements to the game.
EDIT: It seems the skill tree opens up later in game, though class options is murky because the game's poor explanation. In my opinion its not an upside, rather another downside to the game. Why? Well considering that you can't turn off autosaves and make new saves in the middle of the game manually, this really explains the term "do or die" perfectly. Meaning if you chose a class that you are not comfortable with, or you thought it was bad, you really have to pull through until you finishes your game. In order to make a new character with a new class, you have to start over from scratch doing about 10-20 battles(training not included) again to choose a new one. I don't know about you, but to me its really tiring doing that just so you could have a class that fits your gameplay.

I hate to say bad things about this game, since I've been waiting for Sonny 3 for years. The original two were my favorite flash games of all time. I was guaranteed going to buy this no matter what the reviews said. I wish I didn't, honestly. I also wish that the developers of Sonny (2017) stuck to it's original style. When I say style, I mean EVERYTHING. They changed almost EVERYTHING in this game. There are no animations, making the static sprites slide around with no polish. The items you equip on your character don't show up at all, which wouldn't be a big deal, if Sonny and Sonny 2 worked in that feature, which blew me away as a kid. Speaking of the inventory, they reduced the equipment options from 7-8 slots to 4. So it made it feel like every other iOS RPG on the market. They removed the voice acting, which was sometimes cheesy in the originals, but I really think it brought charm and character to the games. They completely took away the class selection (although they did implement a strain system, which is sort of like classes, I guess.) and made each stage have a smaller selection of enemies. The enemies can range from weak basic ones that go down in a few hits to big hulking monsters that will kill you and your friends in one hit. I never had to keep respecing my abilities that many times in the original ones. I wanted to beat the game before I wrote this review, but honestly I got stuck in diffferent areas multiple times, even the TRAINING areas (you know, the ones you go to so you can level up and face an easier challenge?), they all seemed to be just as hard as the story battles. This game is worse than the original two. And it hurts me to say it, as the developers (especially Krin) have been nothing but excited and positive about this game. It HURTS to write a negative review for something I've been looking forward to since the mysterious ending (which I guess will never be expanded upon?) to Sonny 2. I would pay more than eight dollars for the first games on Steam than this disappointing sequel.
Go play Sonny and Sonny 2 instead.

PROS: The game itself feels like a love letter, intent on drawing old fans back and new fans in.  The controls are tight, with an engine designed to have flow in movements.  The simple design is made for fast movement, but also exploration if one wants to try and find secrets.  The soundtrack is a mix of old and new, designed with an aesthetic in mind, rather than a limitation of older hardware.
CONS: A fair amount of the cons, such as the lack of a 'transformation' button, have been fixed through patches,  But there are two things in particular that weigh this game down a bit.  First, the levels.  Only a third of the levels in this game are new, and while I do understand that was more a decision against the wishes of the gamemakers, the fact that we're retreading ground covered so recently in Generations, it does feel a little tiresome.  Although I love certain levels, there's a limit to how many times I want to travel through Green Hill again.  The second is the DRM, Denuvo.  Let's set this on the table right now: DRM does not enhance, protect, or benefit a game.  All it does is punish consumers who purchased your product.  As such, I will always consider this a con for a game.
ACHIEVEMENTS: A fairly simple runthrough, with a few challenges here and there to test your abilities.
FINAL:  Sonic Mania is a good game.  Not a good Sonic game, a good game.  It's atmosphere, control, and experience are all something platformer fans will enjoy.  I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who wants a solid experience to how these kinds of games can march into the future.

I can't recommend this game because it is fundamentally a game of chance with a bit of strategy (the same way that poker is), although there are good things about it too.
When I first played it, I was completely lost as to what the hell was going on. Once I figured it out, I actually found freeplay games to be fairly enjoyable. It's basically a game of chance, but you do make strategic decisions that can help you to win. This makes it a good casual game, since it mostly plays itself aside from your decision making.
The campaign mode, however, makes it very clear that this is fundamentally just a random numbers game and absolutely nothing more. For some reason, AI characters in this mode will have very good luck while your rolls actually seem to be nerfed. This sucks the fun out of it completely since the only fun of the Free Play mode was that everyone has an equal chance to win if they play their cards right and get a few good rolls. The "final boss" of the campaign is just a character with extremely high rolls on both offense and defense, and your "allies" on the board don't actually work with you (you can lose to them). But if you are really curious about the game, or you like the idea of a card and board game with a bit of strategy, then the Free Play mode does offer some worthwhile timekilling. A game with simple mechanics like this needs to at least be pretty, and luckily the visuals are charming and the audio is well done too. There are cards, characters, and boards to collect with the stars you earn in game (even when you lose a round) which adds another layer to it, although some of the content is paid DLC.

50% Skill-based Card Game, 50% Chance-based Board Game, 100% Orange Juice.
Think of Mario Party, you're using a dice to run around a board, collecting stars, while trying to battle each other away from any chance of winning.
Replace the mini-games with short battles, somewhat reminiscent of the Pokémon TCG, each with your own Hit Points, Attack and Defence, even throw in some cards to help you / manipulate your chance of coming away with a more favourable outcome.
Almost every tile has an action. Sometimes this is positive like collecting cards or additional stars, negative such as losing stars, or varied by switching up your positions on the board.
Each player can place trap cards on any square they are stood on, with the next unfortunate soul to land on it either benefiting the trap-placer, or giving them a disadvantage.
The whole package is a charming, animé-style board game that can keep you amused for hours.
It's not the most complex or taxing of games, so it's good fun to relax and take your mind off things when you need some time to wind down.
That said, this game is no pushover either, and despite it's simple appearance, does know how to frustrate you with some seemingly impossible stages and achievements that will keep you playing it for hours just to get it to 100%.
When all said and done, it is an adorable game with cutesy characters, and there are a hell of a lot more expensive games that would get less engagement and hours than this has done.
So with it's price-tag, I'm just saying, there's a lot worse you can spend your fiver on.
Give it a chance, you won't regret it!

This is my attempt at a genuine review. I'm not trying to be funny nor am I trying to protest against external business decisions (except the ones that affect gameplay). Please read the full length of the text for insight.
If you are going to buy it anyway, I recommend these DLCs as a starter pack (from highest priority to least):
Fundamentally a good game at its core. Becomes a mixed bag (at least for me) and borderline abusive relationship when you're a veteran. I don't mind the DLCs. I just have a problem with the quality of the DLCs.
-------------------------
It's hard for me to thumbs down this game.
I'm not denying that CK2 is a good game. In this instance, I believe that either buying the game or not buying the game are both good choices. The qualifying argument that I wish to convey below is simply why I (personally) cannot advocate this game. They have forgotten the old ways of making good quality content over emplacing mechanics that may annoy you unless you buy their DLC. Often, even their good ideas are also poorly executed. They make you ambivalent because they add good ideas, but convolute it with bad ones.
It's hard to roll back to an earlier patch that I favor, because often times there are genuinely good things that newer patches add: bug fixes, balancing issues, more options, etc. However, some features can't be turned off or are simply poorly thought out: merchant republics, secret religions (not secret cults - you can turn those off), broken retinue triggers (as in certain tactics don't pop as often as I think they should), bugged out inheritances, the frequency in which most states become
over time (possibly fixed; haven't checked), etc. The good changes come with the bad, whether you agree with them or not. Recently they've been getting better at addressing the issues by allowing you to change the initial settings, but my problem with Paradox is thus: the tendency is that features they have added come with more problems than they can fix and a lot of my gripes cannot (typically) be addressed with initial settings. The way they've been churning out more content instead of addressing very annoying issues indicate to me that they're cashing in the faith of their customers out for money at the expense of quality.
Even though I'll probably be playing this game for at least two hundred more hours (close to 600 at the time of writing), I can't recommend the game to newcomers. I wish to convince you to not play the game to save you the trouble. Even though I love this game, my central issue with
of their games that I’ve played including EU4 and Stellaris is thus:
Why should you buy a game where the developers consistently execute really half-baked ideas to a fundamentally good game, then charge you as if it were worthy of your money, but at the same time devoid yourself of content if you choose to reject? It's hard to pinpoint and explain to people who all but seek entertainment: t but you would understand if you had played hundreds of hours of this game.
It's as if a friend gave you gifts that were practical, but all distinctly smelled of butt. It's nice and useful, but it's still butt. It's hard to parse the butt-gift from its scent, so you may try to put on a mask or put perfume onto it to cover it up. Though you get utility out of it, either two things will happen: you will get use to the smell or start going insane, wishing that the butt smell would go away. Ultimately, your friend was an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and shouldn't have given you the gift in the first place.
If you're the sort of person that cautiously guards their heart, don't buy this game. For me, it's too late. The die has been cast.
Listen to my advice so that you can avoid the headache of falling in love with maiden Paradox, only to have them undeservingly rifle your coinpurse. This is not exclusive to CK2 either, and, mind you, that my decision to
recommend this game is not because I'm "against" DLC's (I'm not). It's the
of the DLCs with which I have a problem and the manner in which they try to
the DLCs. The
of several minor issues DO build up, and I think they're just not willing to look at issues past a certain date so the hopes of them getting fixed is dim.
Lady Paradox is trouble. Don't fall for her. Go elsewhere. Find someone that will treat you right. You deserve better.
So is it worth it? Yes and no. I certainly spent a lot of time on this game, but it leaves a bad taste in my mouth after a while. Think ME3's ending.
Also for the record, I don't have anything against Paradox. I judge them by their content, and I find their lack of quality disturbing. They really do need to consolidate their effort into QA instead of spitting out DLCs rapid fire and fixing it later. Time will tell if they fall from their prestigeous position from the community, but, at least at the moment, they have a -50 opinion modifier from me.
Buy it when it's on sale if you have the time and personality to allow yourself for long-drawn out rewards with huge pay offs, but also be aware of the issues I have stated above. Also, if you only buy the base game, be aware that you're essentially paying for a demo.
I genuinely love this game, but I also have to be honest with its current flaws. I suspect that many people will disagree, and that's fine. But this review is not for them. This review is for newer people, and I hope this helped.

Pros:
Steep learning curve rewarded by intricate mechanics.
Community are super helpful - if you're stuck with anything steam, paradox and reddit forums offer heaps of help.
Ludicrous scope from quaint Duke to god Emperor.
Historical accuracy for once! No appropriating, no blending of cultures etc - if you've studied, or simply enjoy, medieval history then you'll probably love this.
Roleplaying aspect is simultaneously fun as it is making you think of your actions, reminds me of The Witcher decisions except less harrowing.
Cons:
Some aspects are behind a DLC pay wall. These don't make the game unplayable, but they add aspects that flesh out the base game considerably. For example: it's community consensus that "Way of Life" is a must have; don't expect to play as  a Muslim without "Sword of Islam" etc - most of the DLC is great, or at least builds upon what is already a great game, but can feel quite expensive for what it adds. Alongside that is a recent price hike for many regions, so for the 'full' game is very expensive.
The tutorial could do with a rework; whilst it teaches somethings it totally misses other basics and makes the game out to be less fun that it actually is.
For me it's one of the best stategy games out there. Don't be put off by the UI, it takes some getting used to but it's far more interactive than first appears - and don't be put off by not being able to do anything for a while, it makes it all the more rewarding when you're pillaging, usurping, murdering, seducing, bribing your way to glory.
Also for everyone grilling Paradox recently - they are one of the few developers that still tweak their games years after it's release, and as much as patches take away gameable aspects overall I'd say they've done a really good job with balancing CK2 - remember it's supposed to be accurate, there are meant to certain biases. Admittedly the price hike doesn't seem necessary, especially as it doesn't even allign with inflation, but the product itself is top quality.
9/10 - the amount of work in the game is ridiculous, and the developers derseve to be rewarded for their efforts, however the price can be a bitter pill to swallow - definitely pick up in a sale (like now for example!) and don't add all the DLC at once.

I have been a long time user of Paradox games, since Europa Universalis 2. They are great, the best historical strategy games out there. However, from the launch of CK2, their DLC policy is completely out of hand. Paradox used to issue free patches now and then for their games, that helped to sort out problems and improved some mechanics, along with more comprehensive old style expansions, that were really worth it and changed the game so much that it was almost a new game. Then, DLC model came. At first, DLCs were ok, a little like the old expansions, but the model degenerated into what it is now, more like a money grabbing scheme.
It has gone bad. Some DLCs look rushed and unbalance the game or just add content for the sake of it. Mods have been a very important part of the Paradox experience, however, now it seems like modders have a hard time keeping pace with the DLC updates. If you want to use some of the best mods, you need to get the DLCs. The base game looks hollow in comparison, so it is not like you can just buy it and get the full experience. I played a lot this game at the beginning (I had it on Gamersgate before they migrated it to Steam), but I stopped playing in frustration at the inability of getting a "finished" product and a "finished" game experience, if you know what I mean. I got frustrated when half way down my campaign a new DLC would come altering the game mechanics and my favourite mod updated to it, somehow making necessary to buy the new DLC.
It is sad to me to say so, as I loved Paradox games, but I cannot reccomend this game. If you buy it, you are likely to be bound to buy more than 100 euros worth in DLCs for the full game experience. I can only warn you about that. Five years after release, they keep coming. As consumers and gamers, no one should contribute to these policies that degrade the market and our hobby. They have only gone worse with their new games. Paradox, change your ways. A reckoning is coming.

For a start, this game is more sophisticated and complex than it seems at the first blush. Game mechanics are deep and many-sided, so it's always interesting to build your empire from scratch again and again.

That's what I always loved this game for: you develop a great power through its entire history like in Civilization, but battle as if you were playing AoE. Fighting enemies demands a lot of awkward micro-management tho' and I consider this a weak side of Rise of Nations.
Every nation is well-balanced and extremely enjoyable to play for every country has its unique abilities (e.g. the Egyptians are impossible to compete in a wonder race, the Germans get their crucial industry upgrades earlier etc.). These elaborate features of nations enhance replayability many times.
OK, disadvantages of the game are:
1) slightly depthless diplomacy
2) difficult to micro-manage units in battle
3) getting units through the water is pain
Nevertheless it's the best RTS I have ever played :)

Cannot recommend. It does not live up to either of its predecessors really anywhere. Aesthetics are too bright and detailed, there is neither animation nor, oddly enough, full voice acting. The design is more of a Marvel reboot style, wich is acceptable. The UI is not informative and often not intuitive, and gameplay and combat are really not fun to execute. In general it doesn't feel like a full Sonny game, and you'd be better served playing the free Flash games.
The most damning issue is combat. It is neither solid nor intuitive, and quickly escalates past a manageable point without aggressive re-spec'ing of your skill trees and equipment.
For starters, turn order is a combination of speed and "focus". The notion of "turns" goes out the window in a heartbeat. Attacks use up focus, which counts for your "turn", then your focus regenerates while other allies or enemies take their turns. Problems arise out of the fact that you're never really told how much focus you regain per action, and if you don't regain enough focus you don't take a turn. It's not very well explained. In addition, some enemies have attacks which immediately give them full focus for another attack, and when chained can wipe your party outright without a chance to counter.
Comparing this to the flash versions, where turn order was determined by speed, and focus acted like mana to power skills, the flash interpretation is preferable.
Enemies quickly develop abilities and skills that outstrip your own skill development and ability to counter them. Combinations of these enemies become frustrating to deal with in very short order. Enemies can have abilities which make them stronger the more damage they take, can completely disable melee characters, some can even chain stun. The list gets worse and worse, and while the enemy composition is not random per battle, there is usually more than one enemy type.
For instance, there are "time bomb" enemies that will wipe at least one of your party members after a set number of turns. (The game never tells you how many.) These require prioritization, but are often paired with other time bombs or enemies that can heal the time bombs, get stronger each turn, et cetera. Some time bombs also have abilities that can target your entire party. If they can't be destroyed in time, goodbye ally. Often the time taken to destroy the time bombs lets the other enemies get more powerful or melt your team's health to the point where it becomes prohibitive to fight back against them.
Add into this scenario the wave mechanic, where a new field of enemies appears after the first or second field has been defeated. This means you can fight even more time bombs, or another combination of enemies with crazy skills, but this time your abilities are on cooldown and your health isn't full.
The bosses or named enemies quickly become virtually impossible to handle. The point where I gave up was Inquisitor Leon, who has an ability to get two attacks off before anyone else's turn, and can sacrifice one of his minions to gain 300% stat boosts. This buff makes him almost completely unhittable, and allows him to pull off multiple fatal or near-fatal shots before you or your team can do anything. Instead of long wars of attrition, major fights devlove into desperate frenzies to kill specific targets before the enemies wipe your party in two turns, while simultaneously praying your AI is smart or lucky enough to not die in the meantime.
Speaking of AI, you don't have the ability to adjust your allies' behavior like you could in Sonny 2. You are completely reliant upon their whims as to whether they heal or attack. Your team Medic and first ally, Veradux, is also seemingly less effective at his listed job of healing than in previous installments.
You also cannot train any of your stats like you could in the flash Sonnys. The only way to adjust your stats is through the use of armor and weapons. If you want high speed, your only recourse is to use speed-boosting armor, which may or may not have any other benefits. You cannot compensate for deficiencies in your stats on your own.
Your skills have the chance to "evolve" over time, granting them battle-specific new effects. This is of very questionable utility, as some battles don't last long enough to even gain evolution, and the effects granted are most often not the same each time. This mechanic cannot be relied on in most fights, and only serves as a curiosity.
Another issue, the UI is generally awful, especially in combat. Status effects are not shown on enemies apart from visual cues, the target in question has to be selected to find out what buffs or debuffs are active. You have to further select those debuffs to see turns remaining. Selecting a target zooms in on said target, and applies a whole-screen shaky-cam. Not only is this effect visually jarring and rather pointless, it can throw off your mouse pointing. The camera also zooms in on fighters to show attacks or effect changes. It's a rather poor altenrative to showing the entire battlefiled.
The Marvel reboot aesthetics and story are forgivable. The lack of full voice acting, armor customization and animated fighting, while very questionable, don't kill the game. What does sink it is the combat difficulty, lack of polish, and general failure to meet the standards of the already existing Sonny games, which are free.

Okay. So.
First and foremost, i'm going to outright say that YOU SHOULD NOT play this with the idea that it'll be as great as sonny 2. In fact, overall, its a downgrade even from sonny 1.
That being said; Its a LOVELY "alternate universe" kind of game. Its set sort of like a retelling of the original story, and I was iffy on the "soft remake" idea, but it works for me in the end.
There are things that this game does BETTER than the original, and things that the originals do better. IMO, worth the 15% off it is atm (though if you're a super hardcore fan of sonny/sonny 2, wait until a better deal) and you'll DEFINITELY get what you have been missing for the past decade. Its nostalgic, and maybe it'll even make you go check out the flash games. Its NOT going to be greater than the flash games but I can't say that I PERSONALLY am offended. I like this iteration and I understand why a LOT of people are fairly upset about it, but I will happily recommend this game to ANY fan of the series. I don't expect everyone to enjoy it, especially in comparison to the flash games, but if you take this game as it is; sort of like playing Halo CE versus the Anniversary edition, you'll enjoy it. You'll be reminded of what made you like it in the first place and maybe, you'll even enjoy it anyways.
AUDIO: 7/10 - Its kinda... there. Sound effects are meaty and "accurate" if that makes sense, and they're well worth the first 5/10, but the music is neglible. I listen to my own stuff tbh.
VISUALS: 8/10 - VERY few animations, but VERY VERY PRETTY. Still fairly similar to the original, but better detailed, well done and high resolution.
STORY: 8/10 - While not QUITE as enjoyable PERSONALLY, as the original, it holds many similarities and works quite well if you take it as an "alternate universe" or even a "retelling" of the original.
MISCELLANENOUS DETAILS: Invokes nostalgia, but DEFINITELY leaves you wanting more. Difficulty is pretty throttled, depending on RNG, basic CC/Heal skills, and working around your abilities on your rather limited action bar.
OVERALL - 5/7 perfect game

Pros:
-Map has elevations, allowing for cliffs, slopes, and requires that you take the geography into account before moving units and build cities, which adds on another layer of strategy on the game.
-Units and heroes are customizable, allowing a player to tailor an army to his needs.
-Resources and Anomalies on the strategic map are extremely diverse and interesting to discover, each with their own buffs to production.
-Can assign population (workers) of a city to focus on producing a resource (food, science, money, etc), adding a layer of city management to the game.
-Battles between armies can be played out manually, rather than left up to chance (like Civ does), allowing for more strategy/player involvement in each individual battle.
-Absolutely fantastic Diplomacy system. Utter genius. In order to initiate in diplomacy, you need to spend influnce points, which is made by your cities, but if you don't spend these points, then you could use them to buff your empire. Dimplomacy is NO LONGER something you do willy nilly to suit your needs at the time. Declaring war is a big deal, trying to dissolve your alliance is not a simple decision, and you can even buy (in late game) units which appear "factionless" to attack your enemies (or allies), but suffer no repercussions!
-Seasonal system is perfect. Spring and Fall are useless. Summer and winter is all anyone cares about.
-Graphics are very well done, and the fact that tiles are not perfect hexagons make the world considerably more realistic.  (toggleable for those of you who like your shapes)
-Each faction has a really cool storyline with quests to go along with it. Really makes you want to play them all, just to learn about them.
Cons:
-Once you have a large number of cities, the worker micromanaging gets to be a little much, but you've probably won by the time you have that many cities, so you can generally ignore them. (It's more of an early game buff).
-Ranged units are extremely overpowered. Entire melee armies can be nearly wiped out by an army of 3ish ranged units, if you play manually. Cavalry units are meant to counter this, but will still take heavy losses.
-Very few units to choose from. A ranged, melee, support, and cavalry are the only 4 units (which don't change for the whole game), so the only difference between 2 units of the same type are their equipment, speaking of which...
-Types of weapons/armor you can equip to units are very limited. Only 2 types of builds: High attack or high defense. Research tiers let you improve the weapons and armor, but there are still only the 2 types.
-Would be nice if you had a few more factions to choose from. Even if they didn't have a really cool Storyline.
-Will suck up massive amounts of your time, when you SHOULD BE STUDYING FOR TESTS AND QUIZZES!

**Edit 10/2/2014: A bit of information on the tech tree and my feelings on it added.**
Having played an ungodly amount of Endless Space, I of course was looking forward to Endless Legend. And overall, I'd have to say my experience has been a positive one-- but not without numerous potholes.
First, the positives: The graphics are gorgeous. Just totally amazing for a 4X game. Units move fluidly, resources sparkle invitingly, and the transition from summer to winter and back again is just lovely to watch. Then there's the level of customization you can get into with your armies.
It's basically the massive level of outfitting you could do with your ships in Endless Space... but with people! Mix-n-match older tech with new, or just put everyone in the shiniest stuff you can find, and upgrading is nice and easy (if ludicrously expensive sometimes). And the game is definitely engaging; my first playthrough was of the "okay, one more turn and THEN I go to bed-- oh, wait, I just won a score victory. Huh. That was 300 turns?" variety.
The quest system keeps things fairly fresh throughout the game as well, as it gives you something to actually work towards instead of just the standard "build stuff, build armies, kill everyone" or "build stuff, research things, wait for end of game" ideas. You have a series of tangible goals, with rewards, and can even get massively advanced technology through them. And it can make pacifying those locals with parley much more of a rewarding endeavour than just beating them until they stop moving.
However, there are a fair amount of balancing negatives to look out for: Remember those gorgeous graphics? Yeah, I'm going to be turning those down for my next playthrough. The transition effect for the season change is lovely, true, but it also causes some lag when you've got the graphics maxed out. And maxing the graphics also doesn't help with the next complaint...
There's no mini-map. At all. You would think that a mini-map would be standard for a 4X game, yes? Well, you don't get one. In order to move around the map, you can either drag the viewpoint around (which, on high graphics settings, causes the aforementioned lag), or zoom all the way out to the 2D map representation, scroll to where you want to be, and then zoom back in. A total waste of time that could be avoided with a simple mini-map somewhere.
Battles are also...odd. After playing through several of them, I fail to see why anyone would use anything other than ranged units. For any battle. Ranged units with high enough initiative, on high ground, can slaughter anything else. Even if not on higher ground, they're still going to take out most of the opposing army before anyone else even gets a turn. It just seems fairly broken. I acknowledge this may need more playtesting on my part, though.
Then there's the problem that Endless Legend has with giving you information on how to actually PLAY it. Don't feel like reading the manual? Then you, my friend, are going to have a VERY hard time playing this game. "But the tutorial will tell me everything I need to know, right?" Wroooong. The tutorial completely leaves out several important things, not least of them the highly important district/city center upgrade procedure, how trade routes happen, how to use ANY of the special abilities for the various races (And no, they're not particularly self-explanatory. For instance, the Vaulters information in-game just says that they can designate a Holy Resource. Several techs say they need a Holy Resource. Nothing bothers to tell you that you have to activate a booster effect on a resource to designate it as "holy".), and the rather important bit of information that only one city can be placed per region, so you'd better be dang sure that you're putting it in the right spot. Or even what a "region" is, other than just referring to them.
And if you try to open up the Archives in-game, thinking it's the equivalent of the Civilopedia? It minimizes the game and takes you to the Endless Legend Wiki. And that may or may not have anything useful for you.
There's one more major thing that I've decided counts as a negative, and it's enough to warrant an edit to my original review. I originally just thought that the tech tree idea was "original, but a bit rubbish", and not terribly impressive, but after further thought and a few more tests, it is my opinion that it really does need an overhaul. Now, I realize that many players treat the tech tree as an afterthought, merely a way to get their new weapons to beat other civs over the head with, but to me the tech tree is one of the main parts of the game. And Endless Legend downright punishes you for using it.
The tree is split into six ages. You start in Age 1, obviously. After nine technologies are researched, you advance one age. This seems all well and good, but there's a catch; it's not just "nine technologies from the previous age." It's ANY nine technologies. Research nine technologies from Age 1, unlock Age 2, and then want to get the rest of Age 1 that you haven't researched yet? Congrats, you're progressing towards Age 3! That may not seem so bad at first, but then you hit the second catch: every time you advance an Age, the technologies from the PREVIOUS ages become MORE EXPENSIVE. Yes, that's right. Suddenly, in the more advanced ages, it becomes harder to learn how to make more primitive things.
Now, I'm guessing they put this feature in to make sure that people couldn't rush to the Sixth and Final Age just by researching lower-end techs, but you know what would've been an even simpler fix? Make it so that the nine techs you have to research to advance an Age can only come from the Age directly prior to it. Not particularly difficult to implement, one would think. And it would allow you to have a little more time to actually get all of the techs your civilization needs, rather than having to rush through and try to pick out nine per Age before they skyrocket in price.
Now, you may have noticed that one of those negatives is fixed by reading the manual, another is (potentially) fixed by turning the graphics down, and another may not be a problem if more playtesting reveals other strategies to work better than just all-ranged-all-the-time. So yes, overall I'm rather happy with Endless Legend. It's no Endless Space, and it's no Civ V, but it is something sort of halfway between the two. I'm not terribly impressed with how they messed up the technology tree, and I'd like quite a bit of refinement with things like starting position and a few other minor gripes, but overall it's a good way to spend the time until Civ: Beyond Earth comes out.

100% Orange Juice is a charming, yet simple, card board game using a lot of characters from different games of this game producter.
The graphics are cute and beautiful, with anime stylized characters from different games. The board is nicely drawed and it's lively and colored.
You mount your deck and you start the campaign or the free mode and you'll get some currency game based on your results during the game. This currency can be used to buy some items, including booster packs with one random card each, to improve your deck and better your chances of winning.
The game is not complicated, however you received no help in game, so you need to play (and probably lose) sometimes first to try learning until you get the hang of the things. Even knowing how to play is not enough, because some mechanics of the game are lucky based. However, skill alone gives you the upper hand most of the time.
In the board, you take turns with 3 more characters and each one rolls a dice and advances at the board. Depending of the panel you land, you have different results. The orange one earn you stars, the blue panel take off stars from you, the green one earns you a random card outside your deck, the purple teleport you to another random purple panel and the red panel makes you fight a monster. There's also the goal panel (it has a flag on it), which you need to go each time you fulfill a objective. You need to fulfill a objective 6 times, I guess, to win the current game. And it's not easy to do it.
The audio is a happy one, like you would expect from a game of this type. There's also some voices from the characters, which are nice, too.
The game has a silly story, which is not important, because it's only a prelude to a battle against 3 other characters and probably that's all the game main campaign. I can't say for sure because I barely advanced at the game.
It's a relaxing card board game, for every gamer that needs to play a casual game. That's why every gamer can give it a shot. I would recommend.

I bought Tree of Life back when it first came out and played it for a bit on and off for months. Recently though I had to stop playing due to changes made to the game by the Devs. When originally offered the game was billed as an open world pvp game with systems in place to prevent griefing and to penalize those who killed or robbed too often. This system worked, the game was alive, people fought, betrayed, worked together and the server had a healty population. Of late however they have switched to a four faction system, with the faction you start in being invulnerable to any type of pvp and the other 3 being dedicated war factions. Thius has caused quite a change in the health of the game, with a large part of it being a much more inactive player base.
In a large part this can be attributed to what they created in exchange for open world pvp, a faction pvp game with 4 factions, one pve only and invulnerable which was in a way needed since the game was rife with glitching griefers and being offline was a death setence to any camp, the other 3 being war factions which are the only guilds allowed to pvp. This has led to a system by where one faction has 11 guilds in it (The max number of guilds a war faction can have out of a total of nearly 2000 guilds on the US server currently) and the other two are empty as trying to join the other factions is a death sentence as the map shows the locations of every guild, allowing the 11 guild faction to rush you and destroy you. This has imbalanced the pvp of the game so badly its become unplayable. On the EU and Asia server 2 of the war factions have 0 guilds, and on the US server one has 0, one has 3, and one has 11. Along with this the introduction of a invulnerable faction with nearly 2000 guilds has resulted in the player trade market becoming nearly obsolete. Back when I first started playing there were shops everywhere selling all sorts of items, now your lucky if one out of 10 guilds has a shop. I myself am not a huge pvp player but even I can tell the faction change was made with poor research and understanding of what goes into a faction game.
On top of that, they added relics that buff the faction that has them. This means the 11 guild faction always owns all of the relics, granting a large boost to their players in pvp on top of the massive number difference. Again, poor research and understanding on the part of the Devs.
Along with this change, the game itself has stagnated, with little movement made in the way of adding new content. Currently most mobs in the game are simply renamed/re skinned versions of their lower level form, resulting in a constant flow of goblins, kobolds, and mermen when exploring. These two things combine to make the pve aspects increasingly tedious.
Oh and did I mention cash shop items have been added instead of content? 25$ mount anyone?
Over all if you have any interest in this game, I would warn you away from purchasing it and suggest you try a different game. Perhaps in another year or two they may have fixed some of these issues, but if their history is anything to go by, that is unlikely.

Quite literally, this game - nay, experience - is something that saved my life on innumerable occasions. It's best to not compare it to anything else - even other games in the series - and instead focus on it as a separate entity that provides a wondrous realm of vivid storytelling and escapism. Lose yourself in the bloom-lit ethereality with Jeremy Soule's transcendent soundtrack as a companion, and endless discoveries hidden just over that next green hill. Not all of us know how to appreciate Oblivion for what it really is, but enough of us understand it's essence to respect it in a way that presents the game as an escapist classic. I explored the rich and beautiful lands in this game on my Xbox 360 for several years, and it provided a profound sense of solace and reflection, strangely enough.
Anyone in search of an experience or a portal to a place to simply lose oneself in (in a good way) should at least give Oblivion a try. For me, this will always be the best entry in the series due to that special, undefinably brilliant magic that's embedded in it and how it provided endless hours of whimsy and solace to me during times when I needed it most. And if you can't quite get what all my ramblings and praises represent, perhaps you haven't given the game enough time to let it get into your head (or, perhaps you're a longtime Morrowind fan who understandably detests the changes made in this entry). The DLC expands upon the game even moreso, and with select mods you can do no wong with taking a step back into this wondrous title.
It feels like an entire era - a golden age in itself - that will forever be timeless. Just ignore the potato-headed NPCs and look beneath the surface of this game. There's magic there.

I originally bought Oblivion because I couldn't afford Skyrim when it first came out, and this was on sale. I was immediately sucked into Tamriel, and I can honestly say that this game has aged immaculately. I did go on and play Skyrim for a long time, but Skyrim requires so many mods to fix lackluster questlines and glitches. Oblivion's only con is that the people's faces look like potatoes, but it's really not that big of a deal. The Oblivion quests that are available are so much more interesting; you really feel like you're there. It's so immersive and the writing is incredible. You don't have to force yourself to feel empathy for the Emperor, and this game is never too easy. I don't find myself looking for ways to make this game more immersive or interesting; I don't find myself searching for mods to fill the void left by poorly written quests and plotholes.

Adorable is a casual/strategy/sports/online game for all ages. This game will offer you five modes to test your skills with these adorable creatures across three different sports: Capture the Flag, the Last Adorable Standing, and the Mummy Events. The sporting events are Football (Soccer for my Aussie and American friends), Beach Football and Ice Hockey. In these sports you have to score three goals to win the game. You have to capture your opponent’s flag three times to win in the Capture the Flag game. In the Last Adorable Standing (please use a slightly Austrian accent when reading it), you will be on a platoon and you will have to get rid of the three adorable opponents by sending them off for a swim. In the Mummy Event, all you have to do is to make sure your Adorables are not touched by the Mummy.
How do you control your Adorables? Well, it is like a turn base setup. Let’s take the example of the Football. Each turn you will assign each Adorable in which direction they will travel via an arrow attached to them. You can choose how fast your Adorable will travel by stretching the arrow as fast as you can toward the direction. When you are ready to end the turn, all Adorables (yours and your opponent’s Adorables) will launch themselves towards their specific directions and you might think you are playing a game of billiards.
Every time you win a game, you will be awarded with coins which you can use towards customizing your Adorables, from body shape, mouth and eyes to different colours.  The only option missing is the ability to save your progress or just have auto save.
The graphics are cute and adorable. Catchy music (cute) and the controls are easy to use and master.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Adorable graphics
-	6 modes to play including online
-	Fun customisation
-	Fun and addictive
-	Good price point
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~

-	No Saving options
-	Repetitive

Let me start off that I normally am not one to write reviews, as I feel I'm very very poor at doing them. That said, I feel that the "hatred"/flak directed at the game right now is sadly not deserved.
I too was a fan of the originals and of Krin's works, like Sinjid. Those were games I loved to play years ago while growing up, on the age where animators and game designers trekked and bloomed in fields of their craft in sites such as Newgrounds, Armor Games and Kongregate. They were brilliant back then, and they still are to this day.
I'm not gonna beat around the bush and say that yes, sadly, some things that I loved from the original Sonny's were removed, such as the AI tweaking on party members, the animation of the battle sprites to static effect and, of course, the lack of not being able to see the gear you're wearing on your character.
Also it is true and no hiding the fact that the overall asthetic of the game, both UI and functionality, are cathered and organized towards a IOS/mobile frontline, which is of course where this game first was released.
But tossing the nostalgia bias aside and the small gripes I have from comparing it to the originals, what I've found so far is a very solid game, that while being a remake, offers a complete experience and familiarity towards those games we love and grew up with.
The AI so far has proved to be very capable, even without being able to tweak it at will, getting cues by your skills and as the battle goes on if they should provide a more agressive and supportive role. Same can be said towards enemies, that try to support each other and find ways across your weaknesses, trying to pick low HP targets on your party apart.
I'm still yet on chapter 2, still early on the game of course, and having that somewhat "familiar yet different" kinda feeling from it, makes it that much more enjoyable to see what it brings to the table. The combats are fluid and challenging, and revisiting old characters given new life and meeting new ones is simply a joy.
Overall, what I'm saying is that i understand that some people where expecting Sonny 3 out of this, and understandably might be disappointed that this is a fully finished remake with some things stripped from what the originals brought to the table... and that is fine :) But if you're on the fence about getting it, and can take your nostalgia glasses aside for a fun tactical RPG and enjoy the game for what it is, I think you'll be pleasantly surprised to enjoy it.

The best of the Iceberg games.
Playing this game is immediately familiar to any player of 4x games. At the same time, this game does excels at feeling fresh, with an enviroment fitting its medieval fantasy setting. I would love to see future 4x games, from anyone, copying some of what this game has.
These are the bad things:
The game could use more quests. After playing a few times, you start to know at a glance what quest you've just been offered. About half the quests are genuinely worth doing, so there's still reason to get excited, but it is never as exciting as the first few games.
The enemy AI [and the friendly AI] could be better. More than once, I've seen the chief enemy power grow strong by picking off one nation after another, and the other nations simply doing nothing about it. When I move in, I find the largest power has hardly any military, and take provice after provice from them. Yet the AI would just let them keep growing. The AI isn't dumb, but I would like it consider the world a bit more throughly. As well, the automated units often will move in a way that prevents your other units from moving in to attack. Each unit takes the best path for that individule unit, without thinking about the other units that will be active. It would be nice if the AI did consider such things.
The game could also be a little more clear on what the unit stats mean. Attak: "oh, damage, no that's 'damage,' so, accuracy? But units only rarly miss, so, is that is what it is?" It's just a bit hard to know what to actually expect from a unit.
Er, those are pretty much my only real complaints. Maybe the graphics could be better, too?
The game is just fun to play.
It plays much faster than Civilization, or most other 4x games. Which is just a nice change, to have a 4x game you can sit down to play, and actually play a whole game of it. At the same time, the game does not feel like it's playing really fast. You can really enjoy exploring and building up your lands.
The tech system is well designed, and each game can evolve differently from what you choose.
The use of a season system adds challenge to each part of the game. I would love to see more games with a season system, and with even more seasons; I think that would just be great. The depth put into it in this game really makes you feel the fear people in the medieval era must have felt from winter, as you never really know what you should expect from it. I hate when winter arrives, but I love that it's in this game.
The factions are all quite different from one another. While I have a favourite, I really want to play as all of them. I would still like to see more of them, but there's a good amount for this sort of game.
It's a really fun game. The choices you make on each turn are important, and deciding what choices I should make keeps me coming back for game after game. It's a game I'll enjoy playing for a long time, and I'll always be hoping for another game like this one.

Update 4/17/2015: Many stability and AI issues were resolved since I wrote this. Relevant text removed.
Endless Legend isn't totally without flaws, but it's nonetheless a great fantasy 4X that's well worth your time and money. It's one of the most creative strategy titles I've seen in a long time.
Pros:
- The battle system. Battles in this game play out on a grid laid on top of the area where the armies met. Each side then gets 6 turns to destroy the other in a TRPG-esque battle. Dramatically more powerful armies are still practically guranteed a win, but the extra level of control is nonetheless appreciated versus the random chance combat common in other titles.
- Faction creativitiy. All of the games 7 distinct factions (The Mezari and Vaulters are just a reskin) have very different playstyles and interesting traits. The Roving Clans, for instance, are unable to declare war, but are able to unilaterally ban opponents from global trade and to pick up and move their cities. Other creative abilities include the Ardent Mage's productivity boosting temporary towers, the Draken's forced diplomacy, and the Vaulter/Mezari teleport.
- The Summer/Winter system. The game world has two seasons that alternate in inexactly predicted intervals. Summer has no effect on the game, but Winters penalize nearly every aspect of the game and grow increasingly harsher and longer as time progresses. They're completely capable of destroying your economy or wrecking a military action if you don't plan ahead during the summer.
- The tech tree. It isn't actually a tree. The game is instead divided into eras. When you're in an era, every tech in it or an earlier one is immediately researchable. Advancing to the next era requires discovering a number of technologies significantly lower than the number you have available, and each tech discovered increases the cost of every other one. This creates a very interesting dynamic where equally advanced players can have almost no shared technologies. Choosing what to research and when is extremely important.
- The UI. Anyone who's played other Amplitude games was likely expecting this. They've once again done a fantastic job in making everything quickly accessible without over cluttering the screen or making anything too small. Other devs could learn a lot from them.
- Lots of other mechanics I can't adequately describe here. City management, diplomacy, graphics, and sound are all quite nice.
Cons:
- The AI. I'll edit this after playing at higher difficulties, but so far it's inconsistent. AI players can be very dangerous for score or expansion victories if left alone, but they're pretty useless militarily. Diplomatic relations with some factions are seemingly random. Update: The AI is still kind of crap at war, but diplomacy is much better now. Higher difficulties can be challenging.
- The tutorial. It gets the basics across, but a lot of the more minor mechanics aren't explained at all. Some of it is intuitive, but there's more than a few things that won't make sense until your first game is over.
Overall it's a very fun strategy game. If you liked Endless Space this is a must-buy, and even if you didn't I still highly recommend it.

You also get the basic foot soldiers that will mindlessly attack the enemy base every round. The wide variety of maps make up the majority of the difficulty differences, along with a couple other changes. This is a great little game and well worth the couple bucks it costs.

So, the actual review: Sonic Mania is a pleasant return to form, just as everyone and their cat has mentioned, and while these sentiments are overused, the game itself is deserving of them. Christian Whitehead and Co. have went all out on recreating as classic a Sonic 'feel' as possible - the physics are very similar to the first 2-D Sonic titles, and the levels themselves have returned, akin to Sonic Generations.
The soundtrack is on point, with each classic levels Act 1 having a small remake of their original music, with the Act 2 music being a true revamp, yet still fitting in the same motifs as the original. The sounds are, like the rest of the game, recreated for this game.
The bosses? While I won't go into spoilers, regardless of how long the game has been out for, they have brand new bosses for most, if not all of the zones, breathing some more fresh air into the old zones, especially the second zone's boss. Well played, Christian, well played.

100% Orange Juice. This game is very interesting, is an Anime themed take on a classic board game but with different changes to it that make it interesting and enjoyable. I was only able to play to the end of the first level before my game crashed apon Alt-Tabbing out. The main objective I have found is to complete challenges as you travel around the board collecting stars or beating enemies before you then land on your home base to do another set of challenges until you reach the highest level achievable.
The first level has a safe lane and a dangerous lane, the dangerous lane has a boss at the end of it that can either wipe you of most of your stars (Which you collect throughout the level) or you beat them and win a wholesome collection of stars for yourself. Either of which can add or detract from the challenge you choose when you reach your home base for the first time. You can also come across other players which you can then choose to fight or leave as you travel around, if you are beaten you have to roll a certain number before you are revived. Every failed attemp lowers the requirement.
The soundtrack is annoying after a while and the gameplay is repetitive but still enjoyable, mixed up between the challenge choices and grabbing cards to activate (I only used 1). All in all, if you enjoy playing board games and fancy trying some new and ANiMe then this is worth a try.
Tl;dr, Enjoyed it more than expected. Someone out there will enjoy this more than me.

One of the best RPGs ever made! One of my favorite games of all time. Seriously..
Definetely worth every penny even if you buy it for the full price.
I don't believe there are any other RPG out there that makes the class system so obsolete. You can play with your character any way you like, literally.. Wanna play a melee pyromancer mage? An elementalist who controls every element? A baddass ranger who is also a dual wielding rogue? A Warrior with a big♥♥♥♥♥weapon who flies (yes, with wings) around the battlefield while shooting laser rays out of his/her♥♥♥♥♥ Go ahead, no one is stopping you. Your own imagination is the only limit in this case.
Multiplayer is also fun, nothing beats when your friend uses a poison bottle (combined with red dye to look like a healing potion) in combat and dies without knowing why or how. You can play with up to 4 players online or even play local co-op if you have 2 controllers.
Also, speaking with animals? PRICELESS! A powerful wizard who happens to be a rooster, known by the name of Magicockorel, teleports you away if you make the mistake of not believing in him and call him a liar. The conversations are so good that I felt like speaking to a dog or a chicken. What else to say?
But to be honest there are some flaws in the game, especially in the inventory management and crafting sections. I wish the developers had implemented some basic UI options like a simple "search" bar to ease dealing with the overwhelming components, ingredients and foods that keeps piling up in the inventory page. Minor bugs in quests are also present that sometimes prevents a quest completion.
Nevertheless, it's a GREAT GAME.

*Potential spoilers*
Only If in itself, is a very unique, story-driven game. You follow the story of a man named Anthony Clyde, who, after, shall we say, having a bit too much fun at a party, wakes up in a bed that is seemingly unfamiliar to him. After eventually composing himself, he walks through the only door in the room, only to find himself engulfed in a black smoke upon doing so, he then follows a blue light to, again, end up in a room he is unfamiliar with. It is after this that we are introduced to the game's main "antagonist" (and I use that term loosely because it depends how the player chooses to see him). This leads me to an interesting point in the games story telling mechanic. The antagonist (who I will not name so as to not ruin the experience any further) communicates with Anthony through a radio, constantly harassing him depending on what choices you make throughout the game, leading to some sometimes humorous, sometimes unsettling dialogue at times. That's right, this game has multiple endings, adding to the replay value of this game, on top of 10 achievements (currently) for any achievement hunters out there.
The gameplay of this game is pretty much a straightforward first person puzzle platformer. You will jump from platform to platform, solve the game's cryptic riddles and puzzles, find some secrets if you explore enough and at the end of the day question whether or not you made the right choice, and that alone makes this game worth checking out or the low price of free.

The game looks excellent for a game running on the unity engine with some sometimes gorgeous views, the visual style of this game is very pleasing to the eye, and if you take the time to take a good look around at some places I'm sure you'll appreciate it just as much as I did.
Only If is one of the most unique indie experiences I've had on Steam (and I haven't had many so don't quote me on that) and I highly recommend you give this game a try if you have the time.

“Sonic has never had a good game,” this or a variant of this statement has been made by numerous games media individuals in the past few years. No one knows why this revisionist and simplistic belief has become popular in recent history, but if there's one truth to be garnered from this, it's that those people are ♥♥♥♥ing idiots. If Sonic has never had a good game, then why is Sonic Mania getting so much praise and attention for being a true successor to the Genesis games, from the same asshats that have been lambasting the series no less? Either they're hypocrites, or they just spew♥♥♥♥♥♥in order to garner clicks.

Sonic Mania comes out as the de facto successor of the Genesis era formula, featuring the trademark sense of linear speed as well as a constantly rising complexity to its structure. It comes out at just the right time to show people that Sonic is good, that playing Sonic is good. It hits that sweet spot where you experience the feeling of going fast and the accomplishment that going fast had meaning behind it. It's pure nostalgia bait, and it's real ♥♥♥♥ing proud to be one.

The translation from Genesis to Mania is not exact, but still respectful to the momentumn-based gameplay found in the originals. Other Sonic games in the past have been unsuccessful in replicating the way Sonic moves from moment to moment, and usually you'll end up either barreling at a constant speed or come to a dead stop. Mania delivers on this by ensuring that no matter which path you take in a level, you're going to be looping and zipping about like on a roller-coaster ride, with varying degrees of speed to ensure that when you actually do hit max it actually feels like you're going way too fast.

The new Drop Dash solves a lot of the problems the old era had by letting you keep your momentum high going from platform to platform, so you no longer have to sacrifice speed for precision and thus you can continue through the level without any breaks, but ensures you won't abuse it by inserting tricky platforming sections or sneaky enemy placement throughout the level. It's the type of mechanic that a lot of good sequels add without straying too far from the original's formula. And it is evoking these memories and experiences of the originals that plays a constant theme throughout the game, while at the same time introducing little changes here and there in order to justify a brand new existence.

These levels are much more complex than they appear, even Green Hill Zone, the first level in the game, has been sized up so trying to plan a route through it is like how the levels are arranged in Shadow the Hedgehog. You have incentive to get out there and explore as much as you want without feeling pressured to do so like you would in CD, while reward those willing to take those extra steps to seek out what Mania has hidden in store for them. Taking the default path laid out for you in Flying Battery Zone is relatively safe compared to the outside path you can go through, being buffeted by the hard winds and having to make use of turbines and spinning fans to avoid being tossed off into the void rather than hopping over fire-spitting springs and running through loops both vertical and horizontal.

The real treat however, comes from the presentation. This is what makes the game for me. Every zone has two acts, and with every act comes new scenery and new music to jam out to. Just when you finish clearing one the next one begins immediately, the cycle repeats at a fast pace to match Sonic's and you are constantly bombarded with stimulation that enhances your playing experience. The levels both before and after contrast heavily to ensure that what you see next will be fresh and stimulating. 95% of the graphics in the game are brand new, hand-made sprites arranged so you never grow bored of seeing the same small section of landscape in a level over and over on repeat playthroughs.

For one the game uses a lot of sprite rotation, which wouldn't be an issue if it wasn't constantly used on large, prominent elements where it shoves its ugly jagged♥♥♥♥♥mess in your face. The level choices the game uses is questionable because as far as the overall content goes, it doesn't throw in enough of the new stuff out there. Only about a quarter of the game has you going through new stages with new gimmicks, the rest is comprised of the old♥♥♥♥♥♥or slightly changed old♥♥♥♥♥♥ your enjoyment of which depends on if you like playing through Chemical Plant for the umpteenth time.

It's a game that's meant to be taken in its entirety and one to be taken several times. Repeat playthroughs aren't going to diminish the value in the game, but choosing only to play certain bits of it is doing it a disservice. Sonic Mania is the most consistent, and most balanced Sonic game a person can find. Its faults can be chalked up to personal opinion and it does a great job to make even the oldest experiences in the series feel new again. It is definitely worth playing in my opinion even if you've never played a Sonic game before, and for those who are coming back to the series after a long hiatus you're going to spend a lot of time appreciating all the small details the game throws your way. Even after you beat this game, you're going to find yourself coming back to it again and again and again just to relive that experience. It's that good.

So, Sonic Mania. Where do I even start here?
Well, first of all, it's probably the most beautiful Sonic game I have ever looked at. No, I'm serious. The amount of effort and professionalism put into the sprites in this game are jaw-dropping. I don't think I've ever seen such fluid movements for pixelated characters and environments. Not to mention the music and sounds are as retro and smooth on the ears as ever!
Gameplay wise? Well, it depends. It's not impossible, but it's certainly not a cakewalk and I noticed some flaws. First off, you get to go pretty fast and you run into a few traps here and there and those springs that completely throw you off but make you laugh at the same time because BOI-W-W-WOING! Anyways, the first bosses aren't too difficult following the end of each act, but they should get worse if the game is still following traditional Sonic formula. Then you'll move into a more challenging place.
The Chemical Plant Zone.
I've been stuck in this zone since I got the game and it's a little infuriating, but I've been adjusting how I play to get into the vibe of it. What did I do? I had to slow way down and this put me off a bit. It was hard adjusting a character with fast physics into a zone full of precision, timing and slow movements. Especially considering the fact that I'm on PC, the movements felt really... wonky, to say the least. I'll probably get better as I go, I'm just not as used to Sonic games as I was back in, like, 2013 or so.
So overall I'd rate this game a 9/10 because while it can be a little unforgiving at times, the artstyle and genuinly fluid pace of the game makes up for it. I'd definitely recommend it for people who want a little challenge and adventure or just want to kill time since they're burnt out on other games. Totally worth the money.

Never thought that bad UI could spoil the fun from the otherwise good game, but well, here we are. Solid gameplay and interesting plot, terrible UI port from mobile which drastically decreases pleasure from playing. It might be worth it if you can overlook the UI flaws (but I could not).
When you hear about the game “Sonny” some of you probably remember your teens: that was a really popular flash game. The same goes for me: I still have fond memories of playing it. This game on Steam, however, is not exactly a direct sequel of sonny1/2 from flash to PC. It’s a port from the iPhone game, made by the same author, based on the plot of the first game. It’s a turn-based RPG where you clear stages with your party, acquiring new skills and items in the process. You can only control your character, but this feels more like a feature that you need to play around, rather than a limitation. To sum it up, characters from both sides take turns hitting each other and you control only one of them. When you clear the “room” – a next one opens, followed by a dialogue / plot advance.
•	Content is decent. Lots of items, engaging plot (who does not like zombies?)
•	The combat system is well thought out: it’s easy to learn but hard to master, offers a solid challenge
•	Talent tree + possibility to evolve your abilities during battle, adjusting to your playstyle and improving the ways to defeat your enemies
•	Combat feels well polished: there’s really no attack animations for the character sprites, but hitting the enemies feel really good: lots of flashy numbers and colorful effects.
•	Solid and colorful graphics overall.
•	Sounds/music are good
•	All cons for me are essentially associated with UI/UX. The game might be ported to PC in terms of graphics, but UI/UX is still kept from Mobile. No difference between left / right / middle clicks in battle: if you want to see ability descriptions, you have to hold your CLICKED mouse button on them which screams “touch” from mobile. No skill hotkeys. The first flash game had similar mechanics, but it did not open a new window when you clicked the skill for description. That makes a huge difference. Here, when you want to check your skill out during the battle, you’ll also need to close the window with description (in case you don’t want to use it).
•	By the way, using right click on skill upgrade window teaches your character skill instantly in your talent tree. Learned it the hard way. So yes, there is a way to read about the talent, you just need to LEFT click it. The inconsistency is killing me.
•	Shop: no buy-and-equip at once. You have to buy your item, close the shop window, go to inventory window and equip your item there.
•	Hovering on stats does not explain them. There’s “Stat” info button that explains basic stats.
•	Big one: some debuffs are not visibly displayed on your character (you can find out that he’s debuffed only by clicking on him). Might not seem like a huge deal, but there’s literally a debuff that kills you when you attack.
Essentially, it feels like a good mobile game that tries to find the way to PC. By itself, there’s nothing bad in the fact, but the laziness in adjusting the UX for decent use on PC really breaks the experience. The game screams “mobile” right now. Endless Legend isn't totally without flaws, but it's nonetheless a great fantasy 4X that's well worth your time and money. It's one of the most creative strategy titles I've seen in a long time.
Pros:
- The battle system. Battles in this game play out on a grid laid on top of the area where the armies met. Each side then gets 6 turns to destroy the other in a TRPG-esque battle. Dramatically more powerful armies are still practically guranteed a win, but the extra level of control is nonetheless appreciated versus the random chance combat common in other titles.
- Faction creativitiy. All of the games 7 distinct factions (The Mezari and Vaulters are just a reskin) have very different playstyles and interesting traits. The Roving Clans, for instance, are unable to declare war, but are able to unilaterally ban opponents from global trade and to pick up and move their cities. Other creative abilities include the Ardent Mage's productivity boosting temporary towers, the Draken's forced diplomacy, and the Vaulter/Mezari teleport.
- The Summer/Winter system. The game world has two seasons that alternate in inexactly predicted intervals. Summer has no effect on the game, but Winters penalize nearly every aspect of the game and grow increasingly harsher and longer as time progresses. They're completely capable of destroying your economy or wrecking a military action if you don't plan ahead during the summer.
- The tech tree. It isn't actually a tree. The game is instead divided into eras. When you're in an era, every tech in it or an earlier one is immediately researchable. Advancing to the next era requires discovering a number of technologies significantly lower than the number you have available, and each tech discovered increases the cost of every other one. This creates a very interesting dynamic where equally advanced players can have almost no shared technologies. Choosing what to research and when is extremely important.
- The UI. Anyone who's played other Amplitude games was likely expecting this. They've once again done a fantastic job in making everything quickly accessible without over cluttering the screen or making anything too small. Other devs could learn a lot from them.
- Lots of other mechanics I can't adequately describe here. City management, diplomacy, graphics, and sound are all quite nice.
Cons:
- The AI. I'll edit this after playing at higher difficulties, but so far it's inconsistent. AI players can be very dangerous for score or expansion victories if left alone, but they're pretty useless militarily. Diplomatic relations with some factions are seemingly random. Update: The AI is still kind of crap at war, but diplomacy is much better now. Higher difficulties can be challenging.
- The tutorial. It gets the basics across, but a lot of the more minor mechanics aren't explained at all. Some of it is intuitive, but there's more than a few things that won't make sense until your first game is over.
Overall it's a very fun strategy game. If you liked Endless Space this is a must-buy, and even if you didn't I still highly recommend it.

Endless Legend is the prequel to Endless Space and Dungeon of the Endless. Like both games, it has elements of science fiction in it. But the setting for the game is mostly medieval fantasy. You can see it in the terrain, the map that your armies march on,and your cities expand on. There are many geological anomalies, and interesting objects, artifacts, specimens, that you find while traversing the terrain with your heroes. You lead them to it, and many turns later or maybe even very soon, you decide you want to setlle in that area for resource benefits, or find out later that the mineral can be harvested for technological innovation.

Even the minor factions have units and stats that while they don't seem like much, when assimilated and uplifted into your nation, properly equipped, and enhanced with newfound technology, can change the way you expand and fight.
