Endless Legend is like Civilization but not really.
It does use the same hex tile map system as Civ does but the gameplay itself is rather different. For instance, the combat is not just command unit here, numbers decrease and something dies.
You get the option to command your individual units as they fight and the battle itself takes place on the world map. The commands themselves are rather limited but still involving and your decisions may change the course of the battle since the AI is a bit questionable at times. Or you could just select autoresolve.
The factions are also interesting. Every single faction is unique in aesthetic and lore and each comes with their own questline which you can complete or ignore. Their story is told through the questing and is done in a way which adds to the gameplay; you are not punished if you don't complete the quests but you are rewarded if you do. The quests also break the monotony somewhat by giving you a goal to build toward.
Asymmetric gameplay is also implemented very well. All factions have handicaps and bonuses, some of which seem rather extreme at first glance and yet, if one plays them skillfully, each has an equal possibility of winning.
The main complaint that I have with this game is the learning curve. Certain mechanics are not explained very well like the district levelling system where your city districts level up when there are three or more districts built adjacent to it. I only found that out after doing a little reading on the Amplitude Studios forums. And at the time of writing, I still haven't figured out how to traverse the oceans even though I know there are ships in the game.
In summary, I would definitely reccommend this game if you enjoy a good Civ style 4X turn-based strategy game or would like a Civ style 4X strategy game but found it a little too dull.

Endless Legend has made a very good first impression on me. I've spent less than 10hrs with it at the time of writing this, but I already love everything about this game.
Graphically, it's a just a joy to look at - Everything has a soft hand-painted look to it, the UI is amazingly sleek and clean, and the way the map dynamically changes as it's revealed, as well as when you zoom in/out, never gets old.
The addition of hero units, quests, and other RPG mechanics is executed very well, and is definitely a highlight of the game. They've also made some smart changes to the design/mechanics of traditional 4x games, which let you spend less time micromanaging different aspects of your cities, and more time exploring and completing quests with your hero units.
If you're a fan of 4x and strategy games, I'd definitely recommend Endless Legend.

If you enjoy a well crafted 4X game and don't mind what is currently a generally weak and inconsistent AI (particularly militarily) then Endless Legend is highly recommended.  If your 4X play style is solely military this game may seem too easy at the moment.  However, hopefully Amplitude will improve the AI in coming patches with some changes made already and a track record of good community engagement.
I've found the game immersive enough to play for 80 hours already using different factions with different styles of play, units and quests.  I'm completely hooked at the moment!  There are still a few factions left to play, so while longevity will be limited until the AI is improved, the game represents a good investment.  The professionalism of the games development stands out in many ways.  The user interface is easy to use, the music is terrific, the graphics are beautiful for a 4X game and the tactical combat is vastly improved over Endless Space. I've had no crashes or seen any bugs with a material impact.
Amplitude have developed a really good 4X game.  I only hope that they deliver AI Improvements in patches and also give the AI far more focus before their next release.

This review is based on the version of the game that Launched on August 17th. I was an early access player a year ago, and came back for launch.
Tree of Life is a skill-based, crafting, sandbox MMORPG with survival elements. It has more in common with the great MMO's of the 90's than modern survival games. If you like games where you can have your own property, farm, breed livestock, explore, craft, and the possibility of a good fight, then this is the game for you. It is a virtual world with a complex economic system (with permanent item decay as a gold sink) and your character is living in. Fans of SWG, Glitch, Ultima Online, and ArcheAge will rejoice.
First, I must say, if you were curious about this game in the past but turned off by the PVP aspects that now is the perfect time to check it out. There is still PVP in the game, but they recently added NPC guards to patrol the starter zones. These NPC guards attack enemy faction players, meaning if you build your base in the Novice Zone you don't have to worry about it being raided. You can still be attacked once you leave the Novice zone, however.
With that out of the way, let me get to the Good, the Bad, and the Neutral.
The Good:
- There have been many changes since Early Access. When you first start there is a little achievement tutorial that teaches you the basics of the game. It can be confusing your first couple hours but once you get the hang of how the controls work it all comes together quite intuitively.
- Graphics have been updated and the world size has greatly increased. You don't have to worry about the world being too crowded. Right now the only crowded area are the novice zones, but as long as your walls are upgraded your base is relatively safe out in the world.
- The Dev's are very responsive right now, and we've gotten a big patch and hot fixes shortly after launch with promises of more content to come.
- The community is surprisingly helpful. New players who ask questions in Faction/Global chat get answers right away. There are still the usual suspects for an mmo's chat, but the good outweighs the bad so far.
- You can take things out of your inventory and set them on the ground for other players to pick up.
- The Average player age seems to skew older than most games.
- There is permanent item decay, taxes to be paid, and repairs that cost coins making your items and currency truly valuable.
- You can terraform the world and every resource in the game has a life cycle: trees, animals, rocks. If you leave it alone it will grow larger and contain more resources. If you kill it, it will die and new resources spawn in its place. If you pick it up and move it, if will transplant to the new area. If trees never get chopped down they will eventually fall over and die of old age (uncommon due to wood demand but does happen).
- Your base can never be truly destroyed. The most enemy players can do is get the durability of everything down to zero, at which point you have to pay coins to repair it.
- If you want to be a peaceful player who plays the game like 3d Farmville you can do so and not only have a good time but become profitable.
- If you want to delve deep into politics and partake in EVE-online style schemes that is also possible.
The Bad:
- The game is very grindy. I noticed a few players becoming frustrated with the grind and quitting. If you don't like grinding, you won't like this game. Every skill tree has its own grind, and you will have to grind for each one. If you find an activity you like, this won't be bad, because you'll be having fun as you level up.
- There are no quests and you have to make your own fun. For some players this is an issue. If you are reading this, and you are one of those players, I don't recommend getting the game.
- As part of the PVP overhaul, there is now a 3 faction system. The faction you choose determines your starting area, and that's about it. There's a brief lore blurb on the character creation screen but for the most part the differences are arbitrary.
- You can only own territory in a guild, and the guild shares territory for all members. At higher levels of crafting you are able to make chests that have different ownership permissions based on guild rank, but for the most part everything is shared between guild members.
- There are too many solo guilds at the moment.
- The server gets laggy due to all the living things and buildings on it. If you go to a less populated area the lag gets better.
- The world is huge, but after a while all the zones get a bit samey. There is potential for more content to fill up all this space, but for now you can expect to see the same mobs with different challenge ratings.
- There are no big bosses or mini-bosses to fight.
The Neutral:
- There are 3 shared servers, separated by region: America, Europe, and Asia. However, this designation seems to be based more on language rather than server location. I play in and live in America and my ping gets really bad sometimes.
- Even with this designation, you will find many non-English players in the America server. This can be an issue for some people. Expect there to be times where no one is speaking English in Faction chat.
- The PVP system is more balanced than it was in the past but it's not state of the art combat.
- There is a cash shop mount and cash shop bags that never lose durability. You can also achieve these items in-game through crafting, but the crafted versions lose durability and will break over time. I have purchased both the cash shop mount and cash shop bags. I feel that for the box price of this game, and no monthly subscription, you get a lot of content and I didn't mind paying a little extra for the developers. The only downside to this is that it kind of renders mount-crafting obsolete, which is a shame since the mount system is really cool.
- You can break into another player's base and lock pick their chests. If you are successful, you will loot 1 to 4 items. I think this is cool, but some players don't like PVP so I'm making this a neutral point.
- If you have a group of friends and work together you can progress much faster than smaller guilds or players playing alone. The upside to this is that it takes a LONG time to reach max in anything, and even if you do the item decay prevents any one guild from dominating the server.
For all its faults Tree of Life is one of the only MMO's that allows this type of freedom and control over your own character and the shared virtual world. Your actions matter and affect other players. The box price is low, and I recommend all fans of the virtual world genre, and old school MMO's check it out.

“Sonic has never had a good game,” this or a variant of this statement has been made by numerous games media individuals in the past few years. No one knows why this revisionist and simplistic belief has become popular in recent history, but if there's one truth to be garnered from this, it's that those people are ♥♥♥♥ing idiots. If Sonic has never had a good game, then why is Sonic Mania getting so much praise and attention for being a true successor to the Genesis games, from the same asshats that have been lambasting the series no less? Either they're hypocrites, or they just spew♥♥♥♥♥♥in order to garner clicks.

Sonic Mania comes out as the de facto successor of the Genesis era formula, featuring the trademark sense of linear speed as well as a constantly rising complexity to its structure. It comes out at just the right time to show people that Sonic is good, that playing Sonic is good. It hits that sweet spot where you experience the feeling of going fast and the accomplishment that going fast had meaning behind it. It's pure nostalgia bait, and it's real ♥♥♥♥ing proud to be one.

The translation from Genesis to Mania is not exact, but still respectful to the momentumn-based gameplay found in the originals. Other Sonic games in the past have been unsuccessful in replicating the way Sonic moves from moment to moment, and usually you'll end up either barreling at a constant speed or come to a dead stop. Mania delivers on this by ensuring that no matter which path you take in a level, you're going to be looping and zipping about like on a roller-coaster ride, with varying degrees of speed to ensure that when you actually do hit max it actually feels like you're going way too fast.

The new Drop Dash solves a lot of the problems the old era had by letting you keep your momentum high going from platform to platform, so you no longer have to sacrifice speed for precision and thus you can continue through the level without any breaks, but ensures you won't abuse it by inserting tricky platforming sections or sneaky enemy placement throughout the level. It's the type of mechanic that a lot of good sequels add without straying too far from the original's formula. And it is evoking these memories and experiences of the originals that plays a constant theme throughout the game, while at the same time introducing little changes here and there in order to justify a brand new existence.

These levels are much more complex than they appear, even Green Hill Zone, the first level in the game, has been sized up so trying to plan a route through it is like how the levels are arranged in Shadow the Hedgehog. You have incentive to get out there and explore as much as you want without feeling pressured to do so like you would in CD, while reward those willing to take those extra steps to seek out what Mania has hidden in store for them. Taking the default path laid out for you in Flying Battery Zone is relatively safe compared to the outside path you can go through, being buffeted by the hard winds and having to make use of turbines and spinning fans to avoid being tossed off into the void rather than hopping over fire-spitting springs and running through loops both vertical and horizontal.

The real treat however, comes from the presentation. This is what makes the game for me. Every zone has two acts, and with every act comes new scenery and new music to jam out to. Just when you finish clearing one the next one begins immediately, the cycle repeats at a fast pace to match Sonic's and you are constantly bombarded with stimulation that enhances your playing experience. The levels both before and after contrast heavily to ensure that what you see next will be fresh and stimulating. 95% of the graphics in the game are brand new, hand-made sprites arranged so you never grow bored of seeing the same small section of landscape in a level over and over on repeat playthroughs.

Now I've just been blowing my load all the time but just like its predecessors it's not a perfect game, it has its share of mars and downcomings. For one the game uses a lot of sprite rotation, which wouldn't be an issue if it wasn't constantly used on large, prominent elements where it shoves its ugly jagged♥♥♥♥♥mess in your face. The level choices the game uses is questionable because as far as the overall content goes, it doesn't throw in enough of the new stuff out there. Only about a quarter of the game has you going through new stages with new gimmicks, the rest is comprised of the old♥♥♥♥♥♥or slightly changed old♥♥♥♥♥♥ your enjoyment of which depends on if you like playing through Chemical Plant for the umpteenth time.

It's a game that's meant to be taken in its entirety and one to be taken several times. Repeat playthroughs aren't going to diminish the value in the game, but choosing only to play certain bits of it is doing it a disservice. Sonic Mania is the most consistent, and most balanced Sonic game a person can find. Its faults can be chalked up to personal opinion and it does a great job to make even the oldest experiences in the series feel new again. It is definitely worth playing in my opinion even if you've never played a Sonic game before, and for those who are coming back to the series after a long hiatus you're going to spend a lot of time appreciating all the small details the game throws your way. Even after you beat this game, you're going to find yourself coming back to it again and again and again just to relive that experience. It's that good.

So, Sonic Mania. Where do I even start here?
Well, first of all, it's probably the most beautiful Sonic game I have ever looked at. No, I'm serious. The amount of effort and professionalism put into the sprites in this game are jaw-dropping. I don't think I've ever seen such fluid movements for pixelated characters and environments. Not to mention the music and sounds are as retro and smooth on the ears as ever!
Gameplay wise? Well, it depends. It's not impossible, but it's certainly not a cakewalk and I noticed some flaws. First off, you get to go pretty fast and you run into a few traps here and there and those springs that completely throw you off but make you laugh at the same time because BOI-W-W-WOING! Anyways, the first bosses aren't too difficult following the end of each act, but they should get worse if the game is still following traditional Sonic formula. Then you'll move into a more challenging place.
The Chemical Plant Zone.
I've been stuck in this zone since I got the game and it's a little infuriating, but I've been adjusting how I play to get into the vibe of it. What did I do? I had to slow way down and this put me off a bit. It was hard adjusting a character with fast physics into a zone full of precision, timing and slow movements. Especially considering the fact that I'm on PC, the movements felt really... wonky, to say the least. I'll probably get better as I go, I'm just not as used to Sonic games as I was back in, like, 2013 or so.
So overall I'd rate this game a 9/10 because while it can be a little unforgiving at times, the artstyle and genuinly fluid pace of the game makes up for it. I'd definitely recommend it for people who want a little challenge and adventure or just want to kill time since they're burnt out on other games. Totally worth the money.

Endless Legend is like Civilization 5 with less gravity and more character.
Less Gravity - The status quo in Endless Legend is very fragile. Cities can be captured quickly, and faster still if you choose to automate combat. A single technology can catapult you ahead of the game, and customizable hero units sway the tide of battle with their powerful skill trees. There are lots of fun game mechanics to interact with, and when you properly exploit them, there's this wonderful feeling of getting away with a clever trick.
More Character - A beautifully rendered world map with named provinces is yours to conquer. The soundtrack is top notch, and has a sort of mythical, tribal feel to it. Each faction is dramatically different from the others. One can uproot and move their cities, and another that can teleport their units from city to city. Still another ignores food and consumes Dust (the game's currency) to reproduce and heal. Each faction also has a unique quest that you follow throughout the game, and it can interact with your neighboring factions in surprising ways if they accidentally get in the way of your goals. Each playthrough feels like a unique story, and that adds a lot of longevity to a game you're meant to replay many times.
The devs are still doing some patching and bug squashing, but the game is exciting, fun, and complete. If you dig 4X style turn-based strategy, don't pass it up!

Sonny is a reimagining of the original flash game released almost ten years ago (still available online)
So, what the heck is Sonny about?  Well, you play as the titular character, "Sonny",  zombie that is sentient for some reason (and suffering from a bad case of amnesia). You're rescued by a mysterious man named Louis, not long before the ZPCI (a zombie extermination group) tries to kill you and Louis. You take out the squad, but Louis is mortally wounded and gives you a tape right before he dies. Thus, Sonny must explore the world, gain new allies, and figure out who he is.
As for the game itself, it's a turn based RPG with a combat system similar to that of Grandia. Sonny has access to various attacks and passive buffs (that he can acquire and upgrade whenever he levels up) and can attack when his "focus" gage fills up. You can only equip a limited amount of skills and passives at once, so you do need to figure out how you like to play (though you can always respec at a cost). Unlike the original games, the game runs at a smooth framerate constantly. The combat itself can be pretty enjoyable, especially because of the great auditory feedback of the abilities. However, the screen wobble does get annoying and can make some people nauseous, so I'm disappointed that there wasn't an option to turn that off.
Outside of combat, there's the occasional conversation, inverntory management, and shopping. Truth be told, there's not much to do outside of combat.
However, as a reimagining of the original Sonny games, I gotta say I'm disappointed. It's far less in depth. Gone the ability to customize the party AI, level up specific stats, specific types of elemental piercing, the mana bar (and the focus system really isn't a sufficient replacement), etc. I do like the addition of the evolution mechanic, as it gives some very interesting buffs to your abilities in drawn out fights, but in shorter engagements, it might as not well be there (since it takes a while to build up)
The skills themselves are a step down from Sonny, and especially Sonny 2. Sonny 2 had some of the most interesting builds in any RPG I've ever played and were really creative for the most part. You had a hulking brawler that would deal insane melee damage, but had to constantly conserve his mana in order to do so, or a Shadow mage who used buffs and debuffs on himself and enemies alongside DOTs/HOTs to deal heavy sustained damage.
EDIT: There are 5 different strains that Sonny can pick from as a secondary class, and you cannot repick them (Shadow, Fire, Ice, Frost, and Nature), which does add more depth to the skill system, but the initial skill tree leaves a bad impression since it is incredibly bland and incredibly basic. Playing as the Lightning Strain is far more of an interesting experience, though it's not as fun as the builds in the second game.
In fact, the visuals took a step down. While the comic bookesque cutscenes still look great, the in-game visuals go for a more generic anime look. They're not bad by any means, but they lose out a lot of the rough character that the first two games had. The combat animations are incredibly basic (your characters just shuffle along a plane, not even raising their arms to attack or cast spells, which the original games had). Despite what weapons and armor you equip, you'll always see the same half-naked Sonny (whereas the original game had full armor customization that would change the way your character looked), though selecting a strain does change your appearance.
Oh, and the game isn't fully voice acted like the original games, which is a shame.
As for the PC version, it's functional, but not brilliant. You can choose between windowed or fullscreen and have a limited number of resolution options (and the game doesn't support anything higher than 1080p). There's no keybinding/hotkeys as well (which isn't terrible, since the game is fully mouse driven).
Overall, you're looking at a remake with less depth and character than a game released 10 years ago. While the game itself is actually pretty decent, it's a shadow of what the original games were. Considering that the original Sonny games are still playable and are free, this game is a hard sell at its current price. I'd probably wait for a 50-75% off sale and play the original games first to see if you like this one.
EDIT 2: I've gotten significantly further in the game and it's become extremely frustrating. Enemies have lots of heals, CC, high damage abilities, buffs/debuffs, etc. It often feels like a battle against RNG (especially with the incompetent allied AI) and you constantly have to respec and mess around with your items in the hopes that you can progress.So far, CC is king. You can't really be creative with builds since stuns and slows are all but required in most encounters.
For example, there was a boss encounter where one enemy can heal and buff its own damage/heal every turn (and its turns are significantly faster than yours), will always deal 50% of the damage you deal back to you, and the other one gets +200% damage resistance to the last used damage type, can heavily damage you while slowing you down, and have a 50 TURN silence affect your entire party while heavily damaging them.

Well, I hate to say it, but the negative reviewers are right... and then some. All the issues they mentioned exist, plus a few more.
I am not some big fan of the Sonny series. Hadn't even heard of it before I bought this, but I saw all the negative reviews praising the original flash game and thought to myself "Maybe it's good, huh?"
I played it, thought it was pretty neat, but still, I decided to buy this game... just in case. I mean really, pff, so what if your characters don't make a flashy animation when they attack, and so what if you don't see their clothes change?
In actuality, that was the minor stuff. Here's the bigger stuff I noticed between my two hours of Sonny 1 and the 20 minutes with this game.
1. Sonny 1 allows you to choose a class at the start of the game. You get four choices. In this game, you get none.
Edit: You may choose 'one' strain later on in the game. The problem is that you have to play through quite a chunk of the game first, reducing replayability and increasing the 'starting grind' as I like to call it.
2. The UI for this game, which I REALLY thought would be a big selling point... is actually worse! In battle, all you get for your attacks are icons. You'd better have a good goddamn memory because you can't right click them or find out what they do before you click attack. I kept mixing up the 'stun' attack with the 'speed dash' attack.
EDIT: You can click and hold to view descriptions. Dunno who thought that was a good idea when hover-descriptions are obviously superior, but it's a thing. Still bad design even if they are included.
3. Speaking of skills in battle, wow you have so much fewer! Sonny 1, from the few hours I played, had 4 massive skill trees, and every skill felt cool. This game has maybe... 16 skills? I didn't count them, but they felt more limited. Maybe they'll open up later on, but they feel worse for now.
EDIT: The skill tree does open up later on and you can choose other classes. The game did a poor job explaining that for long-time fans though, but I can still subtract it as a negative point. The other stuff still stands.
4. Sonny 1 was 'snappy'. You clicked the items screen, you were there a moment later. This game fades every screen change in and out. With all the changing of screens you'll be doing, it gets rather annoying.
5. Inventory and equipment management feels way more limited. You had 7 pieces of armor to equip in Sonny 1, plus an 8th if you dual wielded. Here, you have 4. That's it.
6. As others have said, your attacks have no flashy animations and your armor doesn't change when you equip new stuff. Fairly minor in my opinion, but it's a thing.
7. I thought Sonny 1's voice acting, from the bit I played, was cringey and bad. Somehow this game is worse, because instead of fully VA'd lines, you get Fire Emblem Awakening/Fates style 'grunts' where characters just say the first word in their dialogue. CRINGE.
There's actually a lot more, but the biggest thing for me is the complete dumbing down of strategic depth, the infinitely worse UI, and the major steps back in voice acting and character customization.
I'm not saying Sonny 1 was an amazing game. I thought it was kinda grindy but definitely strategic and fun overall... this game is anything but. The problems in this game will not be fixed with any minor or major patches, it literally needs a total overhaul.

I´m not quite sure what to think of this game. On one hand it has some pretty visual designs here and there, and a few puzzles are actually really well made. It did keep me interested enough to play through it - or should i say "experience it" - ONCE. And it is completely free, so even if one doesn´t like it there´s no real loss other than the time spent on playing the game.
But certain design choices and technical flaws really do bring this game down. Lack of subtitles being the biggest one for me personally. The audio levels were all over the place, making dialogue often hard to hear. Not a very good thing, especially when some puzzles require listening to the characters. The controls were simple so there´s not much to say about that, but interaction with the games environment was sometimes a bit iffy. I´m still not sure if the games "save" system - if you can call it that - was made like it is intentionally or merely due to technical limitations.
And finally the story. It does make you think, or alternatively scratch your head in bewilderment. I can´t in all honesty say that i personally liked it, but i guess it created a perfect backdrop for the crazy locales and puzzles.
But despite all that, Only If does show promise. It is a proper (indie) game, even if a short one. And since playing it doesn´t even make a dent in your wallet, why not give it a try.

I was very excited about this game back when it was on Greenlight, but now that's it out, I'm dissapointed in a few aspects of the final product - enough that, even at free, I wouldn't outright reccomend it.
First, on the plus sides, the graphics are amazing, the atmosphere is very unique and has a LOT of varaiety, the two entriely different story paths is a nice feature, and the voice acting and dialogue, I thought, were pretty top-notch.
Now for the downside: the gameplay mechanics, outside of the puzzles, suck. At it's core, Only If seems to be a puzzle game: and the puzzles are done pretty well. They're not particularly difficult, admittedly (though I might include that I play a LOT of adventure/puzzle games), but they're interesting at the very least. Unfortunately, the developer decided to include a lot of non-puzzle mechanics, and sadly, all they seem to accomlish is making the game tedious. Cases in point:
1. There are, on the "White Pawn" story path, a couple of platforming levels. Platforming in first person is usually not very good, and here's it's downright awful - even a slight graphical bump (which, thanks to the great graphics, some slower cards will probably have) can get you killed and make you have to start all over, and while I'd like to say a nice card will fix that, the controls aren't really responsive enough for platforming anyway, maing the entire level a pain that you'll be begging to be done with (or you'll cheat and skip it, or just quit).
2. Also on the White Pawn path is a shooting mechanic - which, as there is no crosshair and while you CAN aim down the gun's sight doing so proves useless as that's NOT where the bullets end up (you actually need to aim around the middle of the grip) it is just a tedious process. Best part? You actually need to use the gun on a platforming level, so you can get BOTH of the horrible mechanics at once!
3. On the Black Pawn path, which I have yet to finish because of this very reason, there is a quick time event mechanic. A long one. That you actually have to move around while doing. That consists of either bashing or holding one button (I'm not sure which, and both seem to work equally poorly) over and over until you get lucky or a combination of poor response time, lack of being sure what to do, and the fact that quicktime events are the worst kill you (what kills you in-game is not 100% clear here) and you have to start the level over again. And again. And again. Until you get sick of starting the whole sequence from the start and go play a game that's more...well, fun.
Major complaints done, I've got a few minor ones that alone wouldn't make it a bad game, but combined with the game-ruiners above add insult to injury:
a. Steam acheivements don't really seem to work right. Every once in a while you'll get one, but others seem to get skipped or ignored for no explainable reason. The forums indicate this is a common issue.
b. The "Continue Game" mechanic is a bit of a pain, as you need to type in level names that include spaces when given to you but do NOT use spaces when loading (as space leaves the continue screen), and you can't see what you're typing or use backspace, which is a little annoying.
c. Some levels it's a bit unclear what to do - usually in a puzzle game, esp. a surreal one, this is fine, but there was at least one level I passed with literally no idea what I was supposed to have done or if a puzzle was even there (for those who have played it, it's the "Inception" moment), and all I really did was stand around until it was over. Another level I misheard the word "peas" for "bees" which, while admittedly prolly my fault, kept me failing for quite a while. Again, though, some of this may be expected from this type of game.
d. It is, in fact, possible to get stuck and be unable to move on a level (I did this on a couple of the platforming ones) and have to quite and restart. Which is a pain.
So there you have it - again, great looking, interesting story, awesome atmosphere, and good voice acting, but the major problems above simply ruin what should be a killer game.

I love this game.  I have almost 1,000 hours played.  It is out of love that I leave this negative review.
Five years ago when Crusader Kings II was first released, the "Paradox model" was great.  DLC was released regularily and affordibly.  It expanded the game significantly for both those that chose to pay and those that didn't.  For example, The Old Gods DLC opened up centuries of new playtime and features everyone and still allowed people to pay for more content without making those that chose not to pay feel locked out or left out.  It was definitely a delicate balance, and it felt like Paradox was nailing it.
However, in recent years the balance has been distrupted with DLC and direction decisions that punish those that choose not to pay while simultaneously angering the paying players because the content is empty, unpolished and uninspired.  A trend that has begun to spread to other Paradox titles.
The DLC model can only function if both ends of the game, the player and the publisher, hold up their end of the deal.  In other words, players will continue to pay for DLC and additional content only if the publisher maintains the quality and consistency of the offerings.  Once either end of the "agreement" is broken, the entire model falls apart.
I truly hope that Paradox takes this criticism to heart and chooses QUALITY over QUANTITY in both future CK2 releases as well as their other games.
Players will only pay for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DLC for so long.  Once they see no value in spending additional money on an already purchased game, the entire Paradox model is doomed to failure.  But it doesn't have to be this way, please Paradox, take a step back and look at the long term of the DLC pricing model.

I guess I put off putting a review up for this game long enough.
100% OJ is an ensemble game featuring characters from titles developed by the doujin group Orange Juice. They're primarily known for shoot-em-up titles, (some of which are also available on Steam!) but 100% OJ offers something quite different. The game is a multiplayer board game focused on dice rolling and using cards to inhibit various effects. It's very simple to learn, and easy to get into even if you know nothing of the characters and the games they originate from.
Easily the best thing about the game is its accessibility. It's very cheap, especially when put on sale, and there is a lot of value to be had from playing with friends and pubs alike. The community majority is very friendly, and creating/joining lobbies is hassle-free.
The base game offers single player campaigns, a number of default characters, and a few free to play unlockables. Unfortunately, most of the game has expanded by way of DLC, however it's worth the investment if you enjoy the game enough and the additional characters and cards add a lot of flavor.
Games are relatively short (maybe 20-30 minutes), but it can depend on the stage. The game is largely RNG based being a dice-rolling game, but there are subtle elements that can increase your chances of winning. It's an interesting dynamic that lets you play about as seriously as you want, although few things pan out perfectly. There are lots of really fun plays you can make by combining different cards and characters, these give the game some depth without making it too complicated.
A lot of people compare the game to Mario Party, but I think that's a bit of a loose analogy. While they're both video board games, 100% OJ plays a bit more like a gambling/fighting game in terms of choices and options. There is nothing to learn mechanically, it's really all just knowledge and risk.
The game is pretty well-balanced and offers a lot of replayability. As it's been said, you can easily play with people online. However, the ideal experience by far is playing with people you know, especially if you have voice chat.
The game is certainly not perfect. Although many nuances have slowly been improved upon by the developers, the game could certainly still grow in terms of gameplay. However, as it stands: the game has only gotten better and better. That really shows.
If you want something to just derp around with your friends or to get away from all that "skill-based" nonsense, it's priceless. A hallmark of minimalistic multiplayer and easy fun.

This game has an interesting take on the tower defense type of game by instead of using stationary towers that stay off in the distance, safely killing off the enemy. Instead, you send soldiers down the path to defend your tower. The soldiers that you send out are not invincible, the enemy uses soldiers of their own that fight back, causing you to have to think of defensive positions that you can use in the heat of battle. The first few levels are pretty easy (spamming the lowest level units will easily get you a platinum medal) but then it becomes a real challenge.
There is a multiplayer function as well, with its own different game modes. You can either work with a friend in co-op or go head to head in an intense vs. battle. For the changing the definition of tower defense, the fun multiplayer modes, and wide variety of single player game modes, I give this game a 7/10

Classic Sonic and the gang are back and better than ever.
I grew up with the Sonic games on the Mega Drive so I've been a Sonic fan for as long as I can remember. Over the years there's been a lot of changes to the series, particularly with the 3D/modern Sonic games. Sonic 4 didn't deliver that classic Sonic feel that we all wanted and until Mania Sonic has been mostly 3D, well apart from some of the handheld Sonic games.
While there are a number of classic Sonic levels that have returned in Mania, they have been remade and feel new again. As well as the updated visuals and music in these levels, the layouts have been modified adding additional paths and areas to explore. On top of this there are a number of original levels that still deliver on that classic Sonic feel.
The updated music and graphics are really impressive. With new character sprites and animations plus environments with great attention to detail, Mania doesn't only play better than ever it looks and sounds it too.
Mania plays like a classic Sonic game and yet feels even faster. The drop dash allows you to get around levels so much more quickly as you no longer need to stop as you would when using the spin dash. There's a diverse range of bosses, some inspired by bosses from previous games but no two bosses feel the same. The usual 7 chaos emeralds return which are unlocked via a special stage that feels like a combination of Sonic CD special stages mixed with Sonic R. On top of that you've got the blue sphere bonus stages to complete which can unlock some hidden extras.
Overall, Sonic Mania is an amazing Sonic game, not only is it one of the greatest Sonic games but one of the greatest games of all time.

So I finally bought this shortly after Sonic Forces's release and playing the first three sonic games, excluding CD and I must say, wow.
Even after watching let's plays and listening to the music of the game on youtube, the gameplay and music still blew me away. The level designs are beautiful, allowing for secret powerups and hidden special rings while also keeping you on the right track the entire time. Even with how expansive the levels are and the amount of secrets and multiple pathways, I never found myself getting lost which I did frequently in Sonic 3 and some of the Advance games. Everything rolls smoothly, and some of the speed sections blew me away with how clever they were, especially in Studiopolis and Press Garden act 2.
One bad thing about the level design though is that crushing seems to be more plentiful then any other sonic game, and sometimes it can be really janky.
Never will you encounter lag from hitting enemies with lots of rings and being underwater like in Labyrinth zone and never will you fail a blue sphere stage because the game stuttered. Speaking of bonus stages, the lag fix makes the blue sphere stages oh so more enjoyable and the special stages are the best in the series hands down. You can see whats coming perfectly unlike sonic 2's stages, and no more jank pinball controls of sonic 1's stages. Special stages are easy to get into with a little exploration, and they are VERY fun to play. Usually I dread the special stages knowing I will most likely fail them, but in this game I crave them.
The visuals are great. The pixel art is on point, leaving me staring in awe at some of the backgrounds, particuarly Stardust Speedway, Lava Reef and Titanic Monarch. Personally though, I find Sonic looks a bit strange in this with the bright cyan colors. But knuckles has never looked better in a classic game.
What else can be said about the music other's haven't said already? It's amazing. I listen to the songs all the time. Tee Lopes did an outstanding job with the soundtrack. And some of the stage remixes are better than the originals I would argue. (Hydrocity, Lava Reef).
My three favorite stages in this game would have to be Mirage Saloon (Knuckle's stage especially), Studiopolis, and Stardust Speedway, with an honorable mention to Press Garden Act 2. The way the bumpers push you around and the ice block sliding around the round bits of the stage and back around again at super fast speeds, I was astonished that you could do all these things with stage gimmicks in a classic sonic game.
My only complaint with the game is that well, most of the stages are classics that are remastered. I'd love to see more of the new stuff in a future title if they do go about making a Sonic Mania 2 or whatever they call it. The ending was also... eh. Tying it into forces kinda cheapens the experience I feel like, and it would've been better if they just had a fully fleshed out ending that contained Mania as it's own thing but eh, it doesn't really take away from the whole experience.
I haven't played many 3D sonic games (The only one I've played so far being Sonic Adventure 2, I have Generations but it crashes on startup every time for some reason) so my opinion could change, but from the games I have played, I can definitely say this is the best Sonic game I've touched so far.

The direction of this game has changed drastically since its early release in the Summer of 2015.  While this is to be expected in an early release title, the developers have changed their minds quite significantly in regards to how they want the game setup.  They removed features that they spent  months on during the 25 month Early Access such as PvE Invasions, Relic Wars, an attribute system, free-form building, etc.
Instead of keeping the content, they have made the game much more grind-intensive than before.  I am no stranger to the grind in this game as I was a max lvl tailor and blacksmith for our guild in EA.  However, trying to pursue these professions again is almost impossible.
Most people run around naked because the tailoring requirements are so high on mid-range gear that you will spend hours and hours farming the mats for them only to see them break in less than an hour of fighting.
Massive bugs/design flaws still exist even after being reported over 18 months ago.  One such flaw is the fact that wild tameable animals no longer spawn anywhere in the world.  Killing these animals are required to participate in the excruciating grind.  However, the game is so broken, that you can't even continue to grind because of this bug/design flaw.
The game had great potential, which is why I played for as long as I did.  However, the devs continue to change their minds and they listen to the players mostly with their ears closed.
Even if you like grindy games, stay away.  Because as of now, it is not even possible to grind through certain professions.

After doing some research, it seems that the reason they have all this additional priced content content is because the kickstarter didn't recieved the full backing goal (This abviously provides them with the resources to perpetuate improving and fixing the game onwards)  yet they still decided to continue developing a free element of the game so that people who haven't played men of war could get a feel of what the game is akin to, supplementally for people who have played men of war series can play the game with a modern styilized approach.
Considering that the game has the free-to-play element already contains all the realistic mechanics such as; bullet trajectory, armor piercing, bullet ricochets and weak spots that the base game has alongside with a decent amount of micro management if playing at a high difficulty/level, which sanctions for a more tactical and enjoyable experience overall. In my own anecdotal experience, I've found that I geneuinelly enjoy the free-to-play aspect regardless of me not playing the full version. Sure for the constrained budget they had the game can seem clunky at times with broken path-finding, animations and AI (at times).
Lastly, as I haven't payed/played the full version of the game, this opinion is only derived from my experiences on the free to play element. However, I feel like the with the compatability of steam workshop the players themselves will begin to fix and ameliorate the game regardless of if devs decide to abandon the project. Withal, I'd just like to note that the deluxe edition, ultimate edtion etc. aren't compulsory requisites and just integrate what i'm assuming is: DLC, in-game items and season passes which many games have already done in the past and no-one has complained.
Pros:
- Visually and aesthetically pleasing (Graphics, modernized)
- Tactical features and gameplay elements.
- Very enjoyable when playing with friends.
- Realistic mechanics.
- Impressive first person mechanic (Direct control of units)
- The factions vary to the point of having their own advantages and disadvantages (Unique).
- The cover system is well designed and can make for some interesting fire fights.
- Inventory system (The same system used in MoW)
- Hardcore mode (Makes the game very challenging and realistic)
Cons:
- They same to be using the same engine as MoW (Men of War) which contained many bugs.
- Buggy path-finding (A.I. can seem to get lost at times)
- Lack of content (To be expected though)
- Granade throwing distance seems to be very short and unrealistic.
- A.I. can at times be borderline ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.
Final verdict: 6.5/10

Classic Sonic and the gang are back and better than ever.
I grew up with the Sonic games on the Mega Drive so I've been a Sonic fan for as long as I can remember. Over the years there's been a lot of changes to the series, particularly with the 3D/modern Sonic games. Sonic 4 didn't deliver that classic Sonic feel that we all wanted and until Mania Sonic has been mostly 3D, well apart from some of the handheld Sonic games.
While there are a number of classic Sonic levels that have returned in Mania, they have been remade and feel new again. As well as the updated visuals and music in these levels, the layouts have been modified adding additional paths and areas to explore. On top of this there are a number of original levels that still deliver on that classic Sonic feel.
The updated music and graphics are really impressive. With new character sprites and animations plus environments with great attention to detail, Mania doesn't only play better than ever it looks and sounds it too.
Mania plays like a classic Sonic game and yet feels even faster. The drop dash allows you to get around levels so much more quickly as you no longer need to stop as you would when using the spin dash. There's a diverse range of bosses, some inspired by bosses from previous games but no two bosses feel the same. The usual 7 chaos emeralds return which are unlocked via a special stage that feels like a combination of Sonic CD special stages mixed with Sonic R. On top of that you've got the blue sphere bonus stages to complete which can unlock some hidden extras.
Overall, Sonic Mania is an amazing Sonic game, not only is it one of the greatest Sonic games but one of the greatest games of all time.

Game of the Year Oblivion is a fantastic value for the price.  If you've played Skyrim, but have become bored with the repetitive mediocrity Skyrim offers after a few playthroughs, Oblivion is a shoe-in.  Morrowind was a fantastic game in its own right, but is so different to Skyrim, the "dated" mechanics and graphics might not be what you are looking for.  This is where Oblivion still shines. 
 
Oblivion offers a large number of unique experiences, with a slight difficulty curve; not necessarily in combat difficulty, but mastering the leveling system, and other intricate details.  Initially, to make the most powerful character in the end-game, you have to purposely gimp your skills/classes (depending on playstyle) in the beginning in order to plan each level up you achieve. 
 
The leveling aside, the quests are where Oblivion really shines.  There are no better thieves guild or dark brotherhood quest lines in any other (modern) Elder Scrolls.  The mages guild and fighters guild shine as well, just not as brightly.  To be fair, many of the game's narratives have little to do with the main, or faction quests, but entertain as singular experiences discovered in the wild.  Look no further than nearly the entirety of Shivering Isles, if you enjoy macabre, dark humor. 
 
I can't recommend Game of the Year Oblivion enough, especially at the price it retails for now on steam.  If you are even a little curious, you could do significantly worse with 15 bucks on other forms of media.   
 
PSA: If you are new to modding, be prepared for a bit of a challenge if you want to overhaul the game.  Texture mods are relatively simple, but getting mods like Oblivion Reloaded and an ENB to work together requires learning and patience.  It is not as simple as Skyrim, though support through the Nexus Mod Manager has come a long, long way since release for many mods. 
 
Oh, and with Steam Big Picture, you can play with nearly any controller, just download one of the controller configurations on steam and enjoy!

I'll be going over a the graphics, quests, protagonist, and gameplay in this review, so hold onto your butts, or they might get terraformed.
Like most Elder Scrolls releases, you start the game as a prisoner. In Oblivion, you're a prisoner in the Imperial Prison, for... who knows, really. Considering what kind of person the PC becomes later (Most quests are canon. Vivec wrote this.), you probably should have rotten in there. After some racist and potentially rapey remarks from the prisoner across the hall (no seriously, play as a female dunmer, he wants to shove his muatra in you), the goddamn Emperor himself shows up to go through a secret passage in your cell. Lucky you, right? You tag along with your new Imperial butt-buddy and his posse of weeaboos for a bit, get split up, and then meet up again when the Emperor get's a knife through his back. Aren't you clearly a hero chosen by destiny, with your wrist-shackles and pitful, rusty weapons?
So, after picking a class and all that jazz, you walk out the prison sewers and are greeted with
Cyrodiil. It's your duty to deliver the Amulet and save... nah, I'm just kidding. Now is the time for the real game, where you roam around and do sidequests. Perhaps join a guild, or just delve in dungeons. That's the magic of Oblivion, you're supposed to get lost in the world and do your own thing.
Side quests are the real meat of Oblivion. This is how you're going to be spending most of your time, goofing off, not saving Nirn from Daedra, but instead getting involved in guild politics, reckless thievery, murder, political assassinations, the works. Fun, fun, fun. I'm going to go over each of the major side questlines in a bit of detail.
Fighters Guild: Get a woman's gay son killed inadvertantly, uncover a "evil" Fighter's Guild clone from Black Marsh, get high as ♥♥♥♥ off of alien tree sap (somehow, don't ask questions), and torture someone for information before they kill themself.
Mages Guild: Stop the edgy necromancers from doing some nefarious deeds and kill some jackass impersonating the God of Worms. It's not exactly compelling. But hey, you can make custom spells!
Thieves Guild: Unlike in Skyrim, you actually steal things. A looooot of things. Oh, and you steal an Elder Scroll. Your reward? A stupid mask. Oh, and nobody recognizes you when you wear it, too.
Dark Brotherhood: Join a murderous cult of space worshippers who are constantly getting pranked by Mephala. Probably the most fun questline for the varied assassinations and quests. You are hilariously edgy during it, too.
Knights of the Nine: Don the armor of a genocidal cyborg time traveller who slaughtered elves so you can save Tamriel from those goddamn elves once again. Ayleids, I swear. Also, don't worry, the armor was given to him by planets.
Arena: Slaughter people for the public's amusement. Wow, you're such a hero. Really glad you're spending all this time saving people who only care for bloodsport and greed.
Daedric quests are a mixed bag in Oblivion. You have to complete at least one to finish the main quest, and they're pretty varied in quality. You have fantastic ones, like Molag Bal's, and atrocious ones, like Peryite's. Most of the them involve you doing some reprehensible act so you can get an artifact of unimaginable power. There's a Daedric artifact for every playstyle, really. My personal favorite artifact is Goldbrand, and the quest for it isn't really that bad, if a bit unimaginative. Before I forget, I just want to mention how horrible the Daedric Princes sound. Seriously, go compare Hermaeus Mora in Skyrim to his voice in Oblivion. He sounds like he's stuffing his face with twenty Big Macs while covering his keyboard in Cheeto crumbs.
Alright, let's pretend you actually care about the main quest for a moment. I know, it's preposterous, but hear me out. Maybe you remembered at one point in your murderous, drug-fueled rampage across Cyrodiil that you were supposed to give some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ an Amulet.
Anyways, you give that dude an Amulet, and it turns out he's the Grandmaster of the Blades, the Emperor's eyes and ears. You grab the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ son of the Emperor and drag him to the Grandmaster so he can be Emperor. Well, actually, first, you have to close an Oblivion gate! Honestly, the main quest isn't much to write home about. I won't write more of it, because it's just that boring overall. You're not really even the main hero of the story, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child of the Emperor, Martin, is. However, this isn't actually your main quest. It's the main quest of Martin. Your main quest is...

So I finally bought this shortly after Sonic Forces's release and playing the first three sonic games, excluding CD and I must say, wow.
Even after watching let's plays and listening to the music of the game on youtube, the gameplay and music still blew me away. The level designs are beautiful, allowing for secret powerups and hidden special rings while also keeping you on the right track the entire time. Even with how expansive the levels are and the amount of secrets and multiple pathways, I never found myself getting lost which I did frequently in Sonic 3 and some of the Advance games. Everything rolls smoothly, and some of the speed sections blew me away with how clever they were, especially in Studiopolis and Press Garden act 2.
One bad thing about the level design though is that crushing seems to be more plentiful then any other sonic game, and sometimes it can be really janky.
Never will you encounter lag from hitting enemies with lots of rings and being underwater like in Labyrinth zone and never will you fail a blue sphere stage because the game stuttered. Speaking of bonus stages, the lag fix makes the blue sphere stages oh so more enjoyable and the special stages are the best in the series hands down. You can see whats coming perfectly unlike sonic 2's stages, and no more jank pinball controls of sonic 1's stages. Special stages are easy to get into with a little exploration, and they are VERY fun to play. Usually I dread the special stages knowing I will most likely fail them, but in this game I crave them.
The visuals are great. The pixel art is on point, leaving me staring in awe at some of the backgrounds, particuarly Stardust Speedway, Lava Reef and Titanic Monarch. Personally though, I find Sonic looks a bit strange in this with the bright cyan colors. But knuckles has never looked better in a classic game.
What else can be said about the music other's haven't said already? It's amazing. I listen to the songs all the time. Tee Lopes did an outstanding job with the soundtrack. And some of the stage remixes are better than the originals I would argue. (Hydrocity, Lava Reef).
My three favorite stages in this game would have to be Mirage Saloon (Knuckle's stage especially), Studiopolis, and Stardust Speedway, with an honorable mention to Press Garden Act 2. The way the bumpers push you around and the ice block sliding around the round bits of the stage and back around again at super fast speeds, I was astonished that you could do all these things with stage gimmicks in a classic sonic game.
My only complaint with the game is that well, most of the stages are classics that are remastered. I'd love to see more of the new stuff in a future title if they do go about making a Sonic Mania 2 or whatever they call it. The ending was also... eh. Tying it into forces kinda cheapens the experience I feel like, and it would've been better if they just had a fully fleshed out ending that contained Mania as it's own thing but eh, it doesn't really take away from the whole experience.
I haven't played many 3D sonic games (The only one I've played so far being Sonic Adventure 2, I have Generations but it crashes on startup every time for some reason) so my opinion could change, but from the games I have played, I can definitely say this is the best Sonic game I've touched so far.

Endless Legend is a great surprise for anyone that loves 4X strategies. It can be REALLY slow sometimes, but the replayability through truly endless world generation system, unit customisation, and a bunch of really well-crafted races make it a good alternative to a Civilization or Warlock series of games.

Essentially, this is everything I could have hoped Civilization: Beyond Earth will be and more.
That said, for anyone who has played the Civilization series, this is a bit more abstract. For instance, technically there are only 4 units per race (one of those being a settler unit, which doesn't quite count). You aren't even guaranteed to have one of every type of unit (flying, infantry, ranged, and cavalry). However, you are able to absorb minor native races into your own, granting you access to many new units. Plus, rather than all units being the same, you are allowed to pick and choose items for them, as well as making entirely new styles of a unit based on the basic unit blueprint. So you could have one cavalry meant to move fast and hit hard, while another is meant to soak up damage. So in this way, compared to Civ there is an infinite number of units, in a slightly less straightforward way.
A couple of other features take getting used to, even if you have played Endless Space before (though it does carry on a quite a few things from Endless Space). There are a few things I don't entirely agree with (the diplomacy mechanic could use some work), and definitely some things that need some work or expansion, but based on Endless Space I would say the developer will patch the game quite a bit. Plus the graphics are very, very eye-catching. I think this is the first game I’ve actually paused to look at the graphics.
Edit: Thought I would add this about anyone who was concerned about things that are lacking at the moment. In the forums, they did a Q&A and answered a number of questions about where the game was headed and whether they will continue updating and expanding it like they have done with Endless Space.

Played this game for 5 minutes, the battle system confused me completely, stopped playing it.
However, a few days ago, I'm like "Why not." So I played it for about half an hour. Got to understand the battle system. Now I go to bed, wake up, play this game. Go to work, come back, play this game. I'm addicted. I just can't stop playing it.
There's events in this game for Valentine's Day, Poppo Season (August-ish?), Halloween, and Christmas, where you get special items just for the season. This is something rare to any game, and for it to be a board game is shocking. Props to the devs for this.
Secondly, the character lineup is very likable. The chicken is by far my favorite character, as it just lets you joke around and have fun. There are unlocks for every character, and very numerous ones at that. The replayability for unlocks is really frequent, so this game will last you a while if you're a completionist.
Thirdly, the campaign. This is kind of what people say makes the game fall flat, but I tend to disagree. Its story is very fluffy, and it teaches you how to play the game. Plus, if you beat all campaigns on normal, you get a red crown accessory, and a purple crown for beating theme all on extreme difficulty. (Which requires amazing luck and strategy.) You can use any accessories, outfits or characters you unlock in place of the main scenario character if you think that gives you an edge. (Which it probably could.)
Finally, the multiplayer. This is where the game truly shines. The community is incredibly outgoing, and the game doesn't really lag regardless of where in the world the players may reside. It's a lot of fun. You use all of the accessories, outfits, and characters you unlock via the in-game store that you buy with stars that you earn in multiplayer and campaign and can show them off to your friends and random people in multiplayer. You will get oranges to unlock other stuff by playing multiplayer (though only in matches that aren't CPU-only.) You also have a chance to unlock stuff randomly by finishing multiplayer games.
Anyway, it sounds complicated, but it really isn't. It's a lot of fun, and for a game under $7, I think it's a great worthwhile purchase with a ton of replayability. Go for all the unlocks, and remember to play as much as you can in event times.
Anyway, great game, and you should get it. Rated 9/10 overall, and 11/10 for a game that's under $25.

Cubemen was a strange experience for me. Somehow I had gotten myself a little excited about this game, not sure why, it didn't exactly have much of a hype going for it. But there I was, actually looking forward to this game. And boy was I disappointed.
Cubemen is a Tower Defense game. You place your towers, or cubemen on the map and move them around as necessary to shoot the enemies who will come at you from a multitude of spawnpoints on the map. They use a variety of weapons who's damage potential, type of damage and accuracy varies decently. Unfortunately several easy strategies exist to completely overpower the enemy early and take command of the game to the point where any challenge disappears out the window.
The random accuracy does provide some problems though as an early rush strategy that sometimes wins you the map with no casualties will other times make you lose without killing a single enemy. This randomness, combined with the reliability of camping the enemy spawns makes the strategy very shallow. You never have to spend much time contemplating unit placement or even which units to purchase beyond the first 2 minutes of a map.
The problem is that Cubemen is a very, very simple game. It'll take you five minutes to learn how to play it and ten to master it completely. The economy questions are virtually nonexistent, all enemies and maps can be met with the same strategies and the is virtually no challenge to be found in the game.
Despite the multi-player being cross-platform with mobile devices it is almost completely dead which is probably not a bad thing, considering the broken balance.
It is a game that gives you no reason to continue playing once you've done the first 30 minutes. Only the achievements exist to keep you playing but even that is just a mindless grind.

Call to Arms takes what the MoW series has done, brings it into the modern theatre and then works to further develop old mechanics to create a familiar yet new experience. While some mechanics still need a touch of polish (something the developer has been continuously doing), the overall experience has been pleasant.
Pro's:
- 2 unique factions
- AI which can provide *both* a fun experience and a challenge
- An excellent F2P approach to encourage a bolstered online community
- A new first person direct control camera style for all units that works extremely well (With the exception of a slight lag on weapon movement which is being worked on)
- Interesting maps
Cons:
- The current limit of two factions can allow matches to grow stale (A problem that will eventually be fixed with DLC)
- The bag drop system unfortunately actively discourages players to use player created maps (As bags do not drop when any modded content is used)
- Some polishing still required
- F2P approach has been wildly misunderstood by playerbase
Having bought into early access for this title at a very early stage, I have been impressed with the steady progress the developers have made and I am always excited at each update to see the consistent improvements. I have full confidence in the ability of the development team to have a solid product once CTA leaves early access.
I look forward to future DLC factions (I hope for there to be many beyond those currently announced including *Canada*), and I also hope to see the mechanics developed in this title taken to future titles in different theatres (Such as a return to Vietnam)

This is a love letter to the Genesis/Megadrive era of Sonic.
The overal presentation is fantastic. Smooth animations, tight gameplay, great music, and beautiful backdrops flood this game.
It borrows pretty heavily from old school Sonic games, taking levels straight from them. However, they are not exact duplicates of these levels. Instead, they are added to. New paths, objects, enemies, etc. It isn't uncommon for you to play a level from Sonic 2 that adds elements from Sonic CD for example.
As a veteran who has been playing mostly the old Sonic games since the early 90's, I can say that there's still a good challenge here. The levels you've memorized will help you some, but some paths are drastically altered, making you pay close attention to what's ahead lest you get hit by a badnik or other obstacle.
There will be some challenging bits ahead, however. You won't breeze through this like you would Sonic 3 & Knuckles nowadays.
Some parts can be frustrating, though these sections seem few and far between.
The new bosses are pretty good and some old school bosses are re-imagined pretty well.
There are a few times I've had some unfair deaths, usually by crushing. You will be on a moving platform against a wall and there will be a hidden passage. When the platform moves high enough, you will may get crushed, even if you aren't in the passage whatsoever. Keep a pixel or two between you and walls while on these platforms and you will be fine.
My only real complaint is that there's a few unlockable abilities in the game that you can only use while playing a no-save game. I wish you could switch these up, maybe turn a specific ability on in a new save, but no such luck.
This game is by fans for fans. You won't go wrong here.

This is my first steam game that I've bothered to write a review for simply because, of all the games in my library, I feel that RON is most deserving and in need of it. If you were a fan of this game in the early 2000s like I was, I can assure you, the game's re-release on steam only enhances the original experience. Otherwise this is practically the same game, and more then deserving of your hard earned $20, (in my opinion easily worth $30-$40, yes it's that good). And if you got it on sale, it’s practically a steal.
Now back in the early 2000s this was the only game that was ever able to compete with the giant of RTSs at the time AOE2, (sorry empire earth guys but RON is the better more polished game). And in my opinion is a better game than AOE2. Also while I like the more hardcore Cossacks and American Conquest, RON has certain game mechanics that I personally enjoy and RON has far-less micromanaging without sacrificing all that much in complexity and strategic gameplay.
What makes RON so great is that is combines the mechanics of traditional RTS games like AOE2, with gameplay mechanics from traditional turn-based games like the civilization series, into a polished, triple-A, well-balanced RTS. It also streamlines the management of your particular nation so you don't spend 80% of your time micromanaging workers, and allows you to focus on macro-decisions that determine who will win the game. Don't get me wrong worker placement and the efficient use of resources is huge, but this game has far more to offer then just that and your occasional battle.
The key gameplay mechanic that separates RON from the rest of the genre, is the city mechanic and use of national borders. Anyone familiar with the CIV series will likely be able to easily understand this. On the map there are things like vast forests, mountains full of ore, oil rich plains, and rare resources that will not only give you resources, but bonuses that can give you benefits from the mundane buff, to game-altering keys to a winning strategy. Borders will also damage unsupplied enemy armies in your territory. How do you expand borders, build cities and forts, research techs like religion, and techs like taxation will give you gold, the more of the map you control. You can try to turtle in RON but you will likely not fare so well.
At your senate, choosing your government type is another huge decision, and wonders aren't just a victory type. Wonders grant you amazing benefits and you'll probably want to build some for their buffs alone, even if you’re not going for a wonder victory. Nations have unique units and benefits that make each nation play different. And the game goes from the ancient era to the modern day. Also even for the bland stock unit types and buildings: European, Asian, Middle East, Native American...etc. all have different skins that help with the immersion.
While I'm little rusty and was laugh out of multiplayer queues at first, I've since begun to rehome my RON skills and found new appreciation for this game. Over a decade later it still holds up and is far better than many other present-day RTS that too often tend to be buggy, unfinished cash grabs. The AI is quite good and your allies aren't actually useless. In fact I would highly recommend playing the tutorial and then playing quick battles with diplomacy. Also I prefer to set the research to expensive and slow so as to better immerse myself in each age. Modifying match rules to your personal preferences is quite easy.
The king of old-school RTS style games is back. "Hail to the King baby".

While On Thin Ice was released without fanfare, the original flash game Icycle was at least a little bit known. The concept is attractive: the world has been frozen and a naked man on a bicycle is navigating through the beautiful and bleak environments. I don’t mean that this particular man is attractive, but the concept is. Problem was, the bicycle was not very interesting to use (it could only move towards the right) and the difficulty was brutal and considered unfair. It seems like the lone developer of Damp Gnat learned from this because On Thin Ice is completely free of these issues. By the way, the same person did the coding and the art, which is impressive. Additional help was given for the audio, and that part is good too. Upon starting a level, our naked bloke will sometimes send a high-pitched scream that will echo throughout the frozen landscape. Chilling. Literally, as the poor guy is shivering on his bicycle even in the menu. If that is not enough incentive for you to go through the levels and unlock gear, the secret levels requiring specific pieces of clothing will be an additional motive. Because in these games the levels are so gorgeous that you will not want to miss a single one.
I have been itching to tell you why I think that Icycle: On Thin Ice is an amazing game, and here it comes. Notwithstanding the gorgeous art design, the game level is actually moving as you go along so that the levels transform under your wheels as you progress through them, from platforms rising out of thin ice to trees growing. If you have ever played a game from Vectorpark like Windosill, now imagine actually navigating the thing rather than just prodding it. There are many beautiful themes that serve as background, not just ice. From Magritte’s The Son of Man to a frozen war laden with dangerous bombs, anything goes in this surrealist game. I absolutely loved the experience. I felt like a kid watching marvels with little stars in my eyes. I am a platforming veteran. If a game can make me feel like that, it must be really damn good.
Since I mentioned the platforming, the controls have been vastly improved since the original flash game (which can be unlocked in On Thin Ice). It is now possible to cycle backwards without penalties, and it feels more like Trials without being as technical as the games from this series. Icycle: On Thin Ice feels more like a floaty platformer with a bit of momentum and sliding on the ice. While I usually use “floaty” to disapprove bad platforming feelings, here there is a physicality to the character that works wonders without being realistic. I find it hard to describe, but believe me when I say that the controls are tight and smooth while feeling different enough from other platformers to justify playing this game besides the gorgeous art. I would argue that the “floaty” feeling also comes from the fact that the naked man can deploy his umbrella in mid-air and gently hover in the same vein as Rayman with his helicopter hair. While this is not a unique mechanic, it adds a welcome layer of air control rather than just being a game on wheels. And that control will be well needed, as the levels start to get difficult half-way through the game. Nothing too brutal that a few retries won’t solve, and on top of that each screen is a checkpoint thus the player never has to restart from very far except if all lives were expanded and the (short) level needs to be started over.
The whole game is quite short, the main story can be completed in about two hours. Considering the price of the game and the enjoyment I had, I would say that it is fairly reasonable and worth the price. However, there is more to the game than this as there are bonus levels to unlock, lots of clothes and upgrades to unlock, and alternate objectives to complete in each level. These objectives range from completing a level without dying to finding a secret area. The economy of the game is based around ice cubes to collect in the levels. They are basically coins to pick up, but what is interesting about them is that they are very well integrated as part of the level design. They are either here for an extra little challenge to divert you from a route that is too easy, or they are here to signal where to jump so that you do not get surprised when an iceberg suddenly rises from below. These might seem like details, but it shows the mastery of the designer. For instance, the lums in Rayman are very well positioned and contribute to the pacing, while the gems in Black Forest Games (Bubsy: The Woolies Strike Back and Gianna Sisters: Twisted Dreams) can be an awful distracting mess.
Enough praises, are there any shortcomings? I would say that a few levels towards the middle are not as exciting as the rest, and I feel that the environmental story-telling was occasionally brilliant (the first dream sequence) but then it was a bit too thin. I would have loved to see more of that. Finally, the options menu is essentially non-existent and the controls cannot be changed. WASD and arrows are both supported, however, this might be an issue for foreign keyboards with ZQSD and the likes.
If you have read the rest of this review the conclusion practically writes itself: Icycle: On Thin Ice is a brilliant game. The platforming on wheels feels fresh while being tight and an absolute pleasure to control, while the art design is magnificent. And then these moving levels that morph as you go along? I’m completely charmed. As a veteran platformer player, the game constantly put a big smile on my face and that’s rare enough to be mentioned. Well done! The game is cheap, I strongly recommend it.
