I love this game.  I have almost 1,000 hours played.  It is out of love that I leave this negative review.
Five years ago when Crusader Kings II was first released, the "Paradox model" was great.  DLC was released regularily and affordibly.  It expanded the game significantly for both those that chose to pay and those that didn't.  For example, The Old Gods DLC opened up centuries of new playtime and features everyone and still allowed people to pay for more content without making those that chose not to pay feel locked out or left out.  It was definitely a delicate balance, and it felt like Paradox was nailing it.
However, in recent years the balance has been distrupted with DLC and direction decisions that punish those that choose not to pay while simultaneously angering the paying players because the content is empty, unpolished and uninspired.  A trend that has begun to spread to other Paradox titles.
The DLC model can only function if both ends of the game, the player and the publisher, hold up their end of the deal.  In other words, players will continue to pay for DLC and additional content only if the publisher maintains the quality and consistency of the offerings.  Once either end of the "agreement" is broken, the entire model falls apart.
I truly hope that Paradox takes this criticism to heart and chooses QUALITY over QUANTITY in both future CK2 releases as well as their other games.
Players will only pay for ♥♥♥♥♥♥ DLC for so long.  Once they see no value in spending additional money on an already purchased game, the entire Paradox model is doomed to failure.  But it doesn't have to be this way, please Paradox, take a step back and look at the long term of the DLC pricing model.

Full Disclosure: This review comes from a longtime Sonic fan, dating back to the original Sega Genesis trilogy (Back when the franchise was good, up until about Adventure 2)
Overall I enjoyed most of what the game had to offer. Is it perfect? No, not quite, but it's certainly better than most of the other big-name Sonic offerings of recent years. Who needs a complicated story and a billion new characters to interfere with things anyways? If only Sonic went more of a Mario route in that sense sometimes... Oh well.
I feel like the back-to-basics approach works, and many of the classic zones fit right in, but with a bit of new spice added to many of the Act 2s of classic zones, which was a nice touch. Seeing a Blue Spheres return was much hype indeed. Bonus points for having the elemental shields have a little more interactivity (Notably Flying Battery and Oil Ocean). Most of the bosses had interesting concepts, and a few old favorites return for another go, or with a new spin (Like the Metal Sonic fight)
Meanwhile, the original zones are a bit of a mixed bag overall. I liked Studiopolis (But not the Act 1 boss), Press Garden was pretty forgettable (Though interesting Act 1 and 2 bosses), Mirage Salloon 1 I didn;t really like, but 2 was pretty good. Titanic Monarch felt kind of like a remaned Death Egg, but was okay. The Emerald bonus boss was kinda eh. And the UFO chases were okay I guess, but 5 and 6 proved to be frustrating.
Also, if you're going to do zone transitions like 3+K did, do it for every zone in the game, not just some of them as currently constructed. I would also have liked to seen a  bonus minigame similar to what 3/3+K had to offer too in terms of adding more rings and elemental shields to the other zones.
If you're on the fence or concerned about other issues that have made their way onto the reviews, I'd say pick it up when it goes on sale and see what you think. But if these guys make a sequel to this or more games like Mania, I'd certainly put it on the short list of must-buy games.

This game is a fairly fun game to play if you are run ragged from serious shooters like Call of Duty and Battlefield, but don't want to play Team Fortress 2. While the community is very few, a few of the right people spreading the right word could bring this game back.
It plays like a slightly watered-down Team Fortress 2 with more maneuver options and weapon attachments. You are a poorly-costumed copycat of either the caped crusader, Batman, or his psychopathic arch-enemy, Joker. You join into combat with other poorly-costumed copycats against another team of poorly-costumed copycats and the best team of poorly-costumed copycats wins.
The Good:
-The Customization: You are able to customize how your bat-fake or Joke-killer look with various logos, outfits, and what have you.
-The Payment: The use of money in this game is almost purely cosmetic as you can unlock the same stuff with the proper amount of grind.
-The Maneuverablity: It is really easy to get around the map and get to high points and other advantages. It is also very creative in it's methods. Example: One of my most diffcult choices in the game, mode of transport: Skates or Hangglider?
The Bad:
-The Gunplay: Every weapon does roughly the same damage, barring any attachments added. It eventually goes down to, what I like to call, "rock, paper, scissors" gameplay,
-The Lack of ID: In game, it can get pretty difficult to identify if the person you are shooting at is on your side or not at times.

It's a nice if overrated strategy game, where nukes are underpowered until the Information Era and people still line up to shoot each other like it's the Enlightenment era....but in the Modern era. I give this a very hesitant thumbs up, but if it didn't have a few very awesome features (listed below  in pros) I wouldn't recommend this game.

So, general pros:
-Unique and well-implemented research tree, with cool future tech.
-Attrition damage forces players to have supply lines before attacking enemy cities.
-Kindof a mix of Age of Empires RTS and Civilization 5's focus on cities.
-Naval combat is (mostly) balanced, with it's rock-paper-scissors approach giving it the best combat dynamic in the game.
-Wonders are generally well done.
-Great ethnic skins and unique units; for instance, the Romans for example use German uniforms in the Modern era. I thought that was clever.
-Awesome Cold War campaign; I have yet to see another RTS/Turn based strategy game without a modern-only focus nail this down.
-Nice alt history flavor in Napoleon campaign.
Cons:
-Armies are overly difficult to control, with fast units always outrunning slower units (like supply wagons), leaving them vulnerable to attack. I have to constantly assign them to slow down manually, which is a hassle if your nation has lots going on inside its borders.
-Lots of balancing issues; for example, air power is completely useless in the Industrial era, only effective if the other team doesn't know what a flak gun is in the Modern Era, and OP in the Information era. And that is just the beginning; artillery can't seem to dent infantry, infantry can do enormous amounts of damage to a cruiser, aircraft can't scratch ground targets unless they are from carriers or are large bombers, etc.
-No real army control; you basically always need every unit in the army to win a war, which is annoying because it robs the player of the army-building experience. You can't make an army of armor, artillery, mobile AA and some sparse infantry without getting mowed down by an opposing army because they have bazookas and you don't.
-The government feature is kinda just thrown in; there is no real reason to choose republic. Just go socialist/monarchy in order to have the military bonuses. Only two choices, the second one doesn't really give much.
-The economic waste feature seems broken. It's a great idea but I can let resources breach the cap and it just seems like they just gather faster. Like waste isn't a con at all.
-The campaign maps clearly were not playtested properly (besides the Cold War campaign); I'll give an example from the New World campaigns. I started as Spain in the Caribbean, and decided to first attack Hispaniola--which was not occupied by any nation, and therefore should have been a very easy target. The RTS map is a bunch of islands inhabited by warlords, one of which you ally with and the rest you fight. They had Triremes and galleys while I had sloops and cannon frigates. No matter how many ships I had, no matter if I had sloops or men O wars, their fleets of galleys had MORE ARMOR than my ships and more firepower. It was a ratio of 4:1 at least (4 of mine for every 1 of theirs), making it completely impossible to conquer the map because somebody in the script had nerfed the hell out of European ships and turned the Classical era galleys into dreadnaughts. This issue kept cropping up in the campaigns all of the time.
-Resources are inexhaustible, ruining any potential for resource wars; once you have an oil well, you always have oil. Once you have a forest,you never have to worry about running out of trees. Kinda lame, if you ask me.
-Environment is very stale and lifeless; no wild animals, no beauty in the environment. It all feels stale, unlike other games.
-No WW2 campaign, despite a tutorial with it featured. Or World War I.
-Tactics and terrain never matter, it's just line up and shoot; every time you inevitably clash with another nation, the way of waging war is always the same no matter the era,; Army A approaches target city, hits it a few times, Army B attacks Army A in a chaotic mob fashion, both fight in a blur of explosions, battle ends--OR--Army A haphazardly runs into Army B while en route to target city, all line up and charge/blindly shoot with confusion, battle ends. While there is a flanking bonus, and going behind someone can destroy their wagons/arty, for the most part the game revolves around throwing bodies into the meat grinder and seeing who wins out (or who launches a nuke first). Naval battles have some more depth than this, what with submarines and aircraft carriers, but usually it's the same Fleet A runs into Fleet B/Fleet A provokes Fleet B near a city.
-Air combat is very poorly implemented; while strategic and stealth bombers are death from the skies, when airplanes fight it's virtually impossible to control/direct them in combat. It's just a mess of barely 3d planes strangling each other in some kind of twisted fast-moving soup of metal.
So yeah, very hesitant thumbs up. If the research tree was any worse, or there was no Cold War campaign, I would say look elsewhere. If you want a good Modern Warfare game, stick to the Wargame series. If you want turn-based strategy and RTS gameplay, look to the Total War series. If you want a good RTS, go to Age of Empires. If you want broad strategy along with good tactical warfare, stick with Civilization 5. If this goes on sale for a few dollars, get it if you want.

4X has always been my favorite genre in PC games, luckily it's a popular one that has had a lot to choose from over the years. Plenty of developers try new twists on the standard formulas, with mixed success.
Amplitude, the studio behind Endless Legends, has had some pretty good results with some of their changes. Their "tech web" from Endless Space has clearly influenced Civ:BE, and I think they're on to some really interesting innovations in Endless Legends that we might see pop up elsewhere in the future.
Their region and city-building system is really interesting and complex. It takes a lot of getting used to. They also have fully customizable units - you can really specialize your unit choices to your own needs. It's really well-done. Even their approach to the tech tree is innovative... you'll often choose many important techs each time through, but I can't imagine always using the same optimal path like you would in Civ for example.
Heroes and missions are also interesting and well-implemented. The reliance upon minor factions to round out your army, provide empire buffs, and bolster your workforce is also very cool. And have I mentioned that there are a ton of resources, each with unique qualities, that are actually relevant? It's crazy.
Of course the game isn't perfect. The AI needs some work, it does well at the start but before long the player can easily out-perform the computer. Amplitude was very good about supporting Endless Space and improving the AI and other features, so I am confident in the future. However if you chose to exploit the AIs weaknesses you can run them over pretty easily. Of course, there's also a lot of customization that can be done in the pre-game menu, so an argument could be made that you could set paramaters up enough to hinder yourself and boost the AI... but really that's a big workaround for what should be in the game already.
The game has huge potential but currently (9/28/14) it still has some room to grow. I'd recommend buying it if you're a fan of the genre, although waiting for the AI to improve wouldn't be the worst decision. It shouldn't take too long.

I've sunk many hours into this game ever since I had to take a few days off after getting sick. I've played through several full games as the different factions and found that each of them is very unique. I'd say that this is the biggest thing that the game has over Civilization V. If you're at all interested I recommend you read up on each of these because it would take too long to explain here. The other two big differences are a quest and combat systems. Unlike Civ5's city state quests, they don't involve racing other factions or killing another city state(there are none). So!
Cosmic Leap. The game where you go to space, jump on planets made of (legos, voxels, minecraft blocks, etc.) and fly away in a rocket. Simple right? Well it is but it's one of those "easy to learn, hard to master" type games.
I really enjoyed this game and it's a great way to pass the time. Let me explain...
Gameplay: When a game needs only one button and an analog stick (controller) to play it makes for some pretty simple controls...except said controls are a bit wonky. There's also the fact that I keep thinking if I push the stick left I'll go left when sometimes it takes you right made me slightly frustrated. Again, it's very simple. Jump from planet to planet, don't die and reach the rocket. Plus if you don't take your time you can easily finish this game in under an hour.
Music: I. Love. The music. It fit incredibly well with the games levels. Then again, I love music in general so this might be completely biased :P
Variety: How would you like to be an anthropomorphic rabbit with sunglasses riding a whale into space? You heard me. With around 40 different "characters" which are really alternate skins and different rockets to blast off again in some of my greatest enjoyment was from watching the level finishing animations. Gotta unlock 'em all!
Graphics: WHO CARES?!? I don't. Graphics are nice and all but I'd rather play a good game with terrible graphics than a horrible game with state-of-the-art 3D crap or whatever it is...
Story: Not really needed. It has somewhat of a story but it's not the biggest part of the game. Except the scenes in between worlds with "The Host" which I thought were great...perhaps it's because The Host is wearing a chicken suit...I don't really know.
ACHIEVEMENTS!!! Most of them are easily obtainable through regular gameplay if you can find the secrets, which aren't hidden at all. One achievement does require you to have completed 75 percent of the game but it's not too difficult to get...just time consuming.
My only real gripe is the slightly wibbly-wobbly controls. It gets a bit frustrating when you want to do something and end up doing something else. Other than that, Cosmic Leap is a charming, short, fun, and spacey way to pass your free time.
Now where did I park that space whale...

Note- I was given code for this.
Cosmic Leap is an inexpensive precision platformer with a pretty nice soundtrack, interesting premise, and rather nice voxel art design inclusive of some neat references. With 5 normal and 5 hard mode stages per sector across 10 'sectors', theres a lot of challenge packed in here. The controls can sometimes be a little fiddly, as my video below demonstrates, but it's not a bad deal for a couple bucks.

Cosmic Leap is a planet platformer with plenty of space-based obstacles. The majority of levels can be completed in less than 10 seconds, but that probably won’t happen until fumble your way through the first time. Sounds a lot like every sexual experience I’ve had… Erm, regardless of the small size (dammit) I did have a lot of fun completing my Cosmic Leap review. The controls are absolutely abysmal, but I was pulled right back in by the likeable aesthetic and the bevy of unlockable skins for both your ship and your character. For the small price, Cosmic Leap doesn’t disappoint.
Trying to explain what makes the controls so bad is quite difficult. Running to the left or right is done automatically. However after you’ve stopped, starting again in the correct direction becomes extremely frustrating on both a controller or a keyboard. Planets are divided into quadrants and the controls invert themselves depending on which quadrant you are currently standing in. The wonky nature of the controls were bad enough to effect the both the difficulty and fun factor scores in a significantly negative way. If concise controls are what you’re looking for, Cosmic Leap will leave you in a foaming rage.
Things are not all grim, luckily. The story isn’t extremely developed, but it delivered much more than I expected for a game of this scale. There are plenty of big-brother elements that strike a chord with me. Having such creepy elements done in such a cutesy style only serves to add to the feeling of dystopia. The music is, for the most part, wonderfully on point. The soundtrack features a down-tempo electro sound that I personally can’t resist. The music did lose a point because it didn’t make me feel like I was in space at any point. All I’m saying is there is a surprising lack a theremin music in space games these days.
The massive amount of unlockable skins is what really saved this game in my opinion. If you don’t share the same weakness, you might be disappointed by Cosmic Leap. The levels are tiny, the obstacles are relatively generic, but the wonderful aesthetic and sky-high replayability score lead toward this game having a lot of potential depending on your personal tastes. For me? It came in about average. My first 30 minutes were frustrated by extremely simple levels, but the difficulty did ramp up nicely though mostly because of the botched controls. Still not a bad first game from Michael Hall, and for the price? I’d say it is worth picking up for platforming/speedrunning fans.
Summary: Bite-sized momentum-based platformer with tons of unlockable skins.
Verdict: Not a gem, but for $2 this game delivered a bit more than I’d expect.

You've probably scrolled past my review by now; I don't play you. For those still here, wondering what will happen next,
I will explain why this is a decent to awesome game.
It is good for all audiences. If you love the Sonic franchise, you'll love running through all the stages, finding that quick path and getting the chaos emeralds with the new special stage (although it is kind of like Sonic CD).
If you're new, you'll enjoy it even more and it will cause you to think about past Sonic games. For that crowd, I emplore you to try Sonic 2 and 3. One is good, but it is tough.
No game is perfect and this is not an acception to that rule.
The checkpoint stages (class "stars above the checkpoint pole and play a neat minigame for points and/or rings) are just the chaos emerald stages on Sonic 3 and Knuckles. Even if this is your first Sonic game, they could have done way better. I know, it is so that you can collect medals to get cheats (hold on to those cheat code questions). Lastly, they did regurgitate stages from other series (just the act 1s). Also, Knuckle's stages are hardly unique which is disappointing since they have so much more resources to work with. Again, fine for the n00bs but a disappointment to die hard people like me.
So, cheat codes, right? I am unsure if you can still get achievements with them. Regardless, anything you do with cheats, you cannot use on your saved file. You have to play the "no save" file which is a huge disappointment. This means each time you want to use debug mode and play as "super (insert character name here), you must collect all chaos emeralds again to play in this manner. It can take 2 hours to remember where all the Big Rings are and actually win the bonus stage.
Oh, you want me to explain the cheat codes? Level select, de bug mode, and play as Knuckles&Knuckles!!!
The disappointment is that you can't use cool abilities for your saved file like the Insta shield or Sonic CD tricks like peel out.

I would have liked it to have been more arcade like, but SEGA really knows how to use contrasting and now that they have an option to include high color satuation, it is a true blast from the past.
Why do I recommend this game? Because I had fun playing the damn game. Yes, I have a lot of complaints. This is typical for Sonic games because SEGA cannot figure out what we want in our games. Just be glad it isn't like CoH2 where you have to spend about $1000 to have all of the factions and leaders.   But more importantly,
You don't have to buy it in EA, but any fan of RTS or military games owes it to themselves to at least check out the free version.  If you see yourself playing it for 100 hours or more, pick it up on a sale.  Like
.  With the current drought of good and original RTS games, RTS fans need to support games like this.  I liked Grey Goo, but I want to see new things in the genre.  I doubt very many people are going to play hundreds of hours on the free version without ever wanting to play co-op, single player, or user-created content.  But if they want to, so be it.  You still have everything you paid for.  Just be glad they're trying to bring more people into a dying genre.  For that purpose, it's actually a great model.  I'm willing to pay $20 for the full experience because I love single-player RTS.  Not to mention, because I believe in supporting developers who make games I enjoy.  But I have no problem with F2P models that work, and I could see this model being very successful for an RTS multi-player game.  Would DOTA and LoL be as big without F2P?
I should mention I am aware of the MoW series, so I know that CtA is not a completely new and original thing.  But MoW is how old now?  It's time for an update, and there aren't a lot of developers making a serious effort in the RTS arena.  Even fewer are offering an RTS with direct unit control and seamless transitions from birds-eye to 3rd, and all the way into 1st person camera.  There area a couple of games doing similar things, but none of them are pulling it off in a mil-sim setting like CtA.  The modern mil-sim aspect is something I really appreciate.  Nothing against fantasy or medieval settings, but we don't get a lot of strategy games with a grown-up, realistic feel.  In CtA, the men are proportional to their surroundings, and all of their actions have detailed and specific animations.  For example, when a soldier is bandaging himself, he looks like he's bandaging himself.  When he's taking cover, he looks like he's taking cover.  Etc, etc.  They use weapons and vehicles that are authentic to their real-life counterparts.  Overall it's a very cohesive and authentic look, just needs a bit of polishing.
Another knock against the game I've seen is that it's a "dumbed down" version of MoW.  I don't think that's the case at all.  It may appear that way because it's still in EA, but the unit controls are still plenty deep.  To be honest, I thought the controls in MoW were far more complex than they needed to be, and not very intuitive.  It was the biggest barrier keeping me from playing them more.  The controls in CtA are much more streamlined and intuitive.  I was actually able to jump into a skirmish and play without having to consult the keybindings for 10 minutes.  Granted, I still had to check them in order to be effective, but they are much more digestible.
Caveat emptor, I will say the game still feels like an Early Access game.  But... it is, so I won't thumb it down for that.  There is some work to be done with optimization and generally polishing things up, but the core gameplay is there and it's fun.  I have been starving for something like this, and CtA is doing a great job of scratching a very particular itch.

Quite honestly I was on the fence on whether or not to make the purchase on this game.  The screenshots and overall favorable reviews is what sold it to me.  I'm a huge fan of the 4x strategy games and with that being said, I was NOT disappionted in the slightest way with Endless Legend.
Some of the pros with this game include the graphics.  Great graphics, especially when compared to games like Civ and Fallen Enchantress.  The units and factions are also completely fresh.   There are your typical archers and melee units which are both essential to any 4x game but take my word for it, a lot of units are at least slightly different and most are really cool (Especially on your first few play throughs when you first encounter them).  Another pro for me is the added involvement regarding the city building aspect of the game.  Each time your city gains population you gain a "Worker" that you can place in specific parts of the building/production within your cities.  If you need buildings or units produced more quickly put more of your "Workers" in the production.  Technologies not getting researched fast enough place them into the science slot etc.
With this being said, the game isn't without it's downfalls (In my opinion).  I prefer to have more control over my units during combat.  I would rather control each unit for each move.  This isn't the case in Endless Legend.  When your units are involved in a a battle you basically follow the certain steps.  First off, the battle map is basically a zoomed in portion of the current location of the map that unit is currently on (This for me is actually a plus and definitely a welcomed change).  However, the battle sequence leaves a bit to be desired.  To start you basically have to place your units.  Then you select what you want them to do whether it be to attack a specific unit or if you have a healing unit etc. you decide who you want them heal etc.  The battle then ensues until the next turn where you have the option to change your strategies and the battle sequence proceeds as previously mentioned.  Some may prefer this method as it is simplified but I prefer battle sequences like Age of Wonders 3.
The modifications also leave a little to be desired for me as well.  Personally I love that fact in Fallen Enchantress where you can outfit your heroes with anything and it shows on the character, not only on the character screen but when you see them in the world too.  With Endless Legends this portion is true in regards to the weapon and Shield only.  Any new armor etc can be equipped but you will not see them.
Overall I do recommend the game and it has kept me busy for about 16hrs since purchase and I'll be busy for many more hours because of the differences it offers to the genre.  It is fun and when I want a slight change in units/factions/city buidling I'll be starting this one up!

Note: The following review is for the single-player campaign only, and may not reflect the experience of those who enjoy multiplayer 4x games.
Pro: It feels very clean. The whole thing has a sense of professionalism that is very attractive. From the unified art direction, to the sounds things make when you click them, to the very straight-forward and no-nonsense UI. This is a game that screams: "I'm made by people who know what they're doing!"
Pro: The art is fantastic, and the world-building feels quite epic! The intro cinematics are all entertaining and give you a sense of purpose, while the game map feels very much like a magical miniture board game. It also has a very "Game of Thrones" intro feel. Building your city and exploring the map is very satisfying, and all of the races are visually distinctive from one another.
Pro: The quest system works fairly well to guide the player to victory. Quests are clear, sensable, and come in a wide enough variety of flavors that they won't initially feel too repetitive. On smaller maps the game is a joy to explore, and players will find themselves especially excited when the find that 'perfect' place to plunk-down a new city!
Mixed: While the races all look visually distinctive, they don't play differently enough to provide much replay value. Like Civ 5, there are a variety of different win conditions, but the actual end-game for each race basically amounts to a splash-screen and a standard graph showing the progress of the players over time. More cutscenes scattered throughout the campaign would have been appreciated, or at least something at the end of the game to book-end the experience. The intros for each faction feel like introductions to interesting stories that will, ultimately, never be fully realized.
Con: Manual combat isn't very exciting. It's cleverly done, for what it is, but it just doesn't feel quite fleshed-out enough to make the whole enterprise worth it. Having the animations play at a faster pace with poppier effects, giving units a wider variety of options, and allowing players to more thoroughly craft and customize their own units would have gone a long way to making manual combat more interesting.
Con: Unit customization is dissapointing. Players can choose between different weapons and armors to outfit units with, but the new items do not change the actual appearance of the units (aside from the weapons and shields). Instead of altering the tactics availible to units, items and weapons only really serve to improve that unit's prexisting abilities (increased attack, damage, defense, etc...). This limited approach to customization only ends up feeling like a tease, instead of a valuable addition to the gameplay.
Con: The variety units types is severerly limited, and after the first three or four ages of technology, you'll have unlocked all the units availible to your faction. Minor faction units provide some differentiation, but in combat, they play almost identically to your own units, meaning that those differences are only skin-deep. The archers/marines/soldiers you begin with on turn 1 will be mostly the same units you end the campaign with, just with bigger numbers. The result is a sense of same-ness that proliforates throughout the experience.
Conclusion: Endless Legend suffers from its own successes. What it does well (art, presentation, and gameplay framework) give players a sense of scale and possiblity that the game itself will not deliver. If the game had really doubled-down on the elements that made it unique, it would have been a must-buy, but as it is, it's a title that hesitates too often for its own good. If you're desperate for a new single-player 4x experience, give it a shot, but if you're looking for something that will grab you and not let go... you may be better off saving your money.

Genital Jousting is a fun party game but you'll need to provide your own party.
Its "adult" nature aside, Genital Jousting is a pretty mechanically sound and fun game that pits a number of male genitals in competition where you must wriggle, squirm, penetrate, wrestle and eat (!) your way to victory over your fellow dongs.  It's silly and really fairly innocent aside from the shapes of your players.  They could have just as easily been snakes biting one another's tails and no one would blink.  But the developers went with genitals and it's okay because, at its core, it's a solid and fun game.  Also, wrestling wieners are just funny.
Game play has a traditional mode where you simply enter and be entered for points until the round is over.  It's a good way to learn the mechanics but we quickly switched to Party Mode where you get a quick-fire sequence of contests including wrestling, races, herding li'l doggies and a, erm, Splatoon-style "paint the arena" level. Each mini game happens quickly and most are over within 30 seconds to a minute aside from the occasional wrestling stand-off.  Although the mini games are technically locked, you can unlock them all in the options which is good since playing the same two over and over would get old fast.  After five games, a winner is declared and you start all over.  It's pretty simple and there isn't much depth but the controls are good, the game is colorful and fun to look at and everyone stayed amused for 90 minutes and left feeling good about the game.
A few quick points: One, the mini games could stand to be a little longer. I don't want to spend five minutes eating little blue pills with my butt, but some games are over within seconds and that just makes them repeat that much faster.  Secondly, it's a little baffling that the developers don't offer a 4-game pack because you'll need to bring your own friends and you really want at least three people in a game (four is better).  A 4-game pack instead of trying to convince three friends to buy in seems like an obvious choice.  There's not much in the way of public games and engaging in dong-to-dong combat is best among friends.
If you can round up some friends who aren't above the humor and aren't expecting hours of play at a sitting, Genital Jousting is a surprisingly well made game featuring fast-paced play and lots of laughs for an hour or so at a time.

Nowadays there are a lot of mmorpgs out there. A lot. Not much innovation is really occuring either. Ideas have not moved forward much and neither has implementation of new technology. What I am getting at is that if you plan to release a game of this type to play, there needs to be some sort of extra hook to keep people playing despite not much in the way of new positive change. For Tree of Life the source of this seems fairly apparent in the form of community. This should be driven by decent building that allows for guild creation along with the ability to PvP and wage wars (not only stealing from players, but destroying what you steal). That would be a great hook for this game. Unfortunately on my return visit to ToL that community does not seem to exist anymore. Without it, the game is a currently a very benign, repetitive and frankly boring game. There are some things I like, namely the art style and some elements of the UI, but beyond that, there just was not anything "special" that I could find that will keep my interests. That is the primary reason I am not recommending this game.
A secondary reason and somewhat of a curiosity for me, can be found in the developer short description of their store page. This is an early access title. Thus it is inherently in a state that is not finished. Most if not all players will understand that (though many will still complain). I find it very offputting that in this description section, it does not describe the game. Instead if basically says to not complain because this is not a finished product. That is a red flag for me and another reason I would not recommend paying for this title, at this stage of development.
Wait until it is completed and see what the reviews say then.

Ignore the playtime as I only recently picked this up again on PC after having it on console for many years. This game. I don't even know where to start. If people ask me what my favourite game of all time is, I answer them with this every single time without hesitation. If someone tells you this game is nothing compared to Skyrim, you have my full permission to slap them, because if it wasn't for this game, there wouldn't be Skyrim. You can see some of the ques and mechanics that was in this game that was then polished and refined for Skyrim. You can also see inspiration from Morrowind in Oblivion. Back to the game itself though...
The story, is simply fantastic. The opening in prision drops you into the story perfectly, it allows you to familiarise yourself with the controls and mechanics and lets you know enough about the story by the time you complete your escape to feel immersed and engaged. The main characters are acted superbly with the likes of Patrick Steward, Sean Bean and Terrance Stamp lending their voices. Their roles really add to the grandness of this adventure and you form a connection with the characters.
The world is huge and you will throughly enjoy exploring it. I feel a lot of people also take the radiant AI for granted also. While it isn't perfect, it adds to the immersion so much. There's so much to explore and do with a brilliant veriety of quests that can suit any type of role playing. Want to be a hero of the ages? The main quest line, the Fighters Guild, Arena and if you have it, the Knights of the Nine are brilliant tales. Fancy being a renegade and walking down the path of evil? While the main quest won't exactly cater for it, the Dark Brotherhood, Theives Guild, Vampirism, Daedric and to an extent, Shivering Isles are dark, gritty and utterly brilliant.
I could type about this game for ages, but I don't want to make this too long. If you're and Elder Scrolls fan, play this game. If you've only played Skyrim, play this game. If you like RPG's generally, play this game. Just, stop reading this review and play the game! You will lose hours that will turn into days into it and once you emerge from it, you won't regret a single second of it.

A Classic that brought Elder Scrolls into the mainstream. Unfortunately Oblivion also marks the end of classic RPG setup, as when you play this you will realize that Skyrim in many aspects was stripped to the common denominator in order to appeal to a larger audience. Nevertheless, the story and interface of Oblivion will forever be a monument and reminder to what the genre of RPG used to be. It is showing its age, and in a few more years, may even be near impossible to play, but if you come across this at a cheap price, experience a great RPG

Pro:
- Each level is more or less easy to win, but hard to nearly impossible to master
- I like the school grade measuring system for level success. Makes you want to try it "only one more time" ;-)
- the retro-modern, cathode-ray tube, 8-Bit, pseudo-3D graphics
- Support! The game creator/programmer was able to help me with a specific technical issue within hours. Double plus LIKE!
Neutral:
- the storyline. Not every game must have one. This one fits into the overall game look and feel, but I would not have missed it if it did not have one.
Cons:
- when playing for a while, the music may get a bit monotonous. This is my personal experience, which may not be applicable to other players.

Some of the most broken controls I've seen in a game.
The on-screen character basically keeps running in one direction until the game logic decides to read controller input
, which then produces one of three results: the game either completely ignores what is pressed, stops the character in its spot, or sends it running in the opposite direction.  The response is inconsistent and unpredictable, which is unacceptable.
Plus, the game crashes if the resolution is changed before setting it to full-screen.. then keeps on crashing on each subsequent startup.  A registry edit resolved that issue, however.
But hey, at least the music is nice..
Update: The Dev has been working to resolve the issue, so kudos to them.  I will update or remove this review if in the future these problems are ironed out.

Ultimately, I think I have to vote it down.
Warframe was a game where you take on the role of a tenno, a brand of space ninja of sorts, spun off from an earlier game that had almost nothing to do with this one. As it was introduced to you, the solar system, or Origin System, was laid out before you and you were its ward.
Current world politics and technology sped forward thousands of years left the galaxy with two brands of humans, irredeemable militarists and irredeemable capitalists. Your job was to use small-scale tactical insertions to weaken the two, turn them against each other, and rescue defectors, all while a flood-like species lay in waiting, searching for vulnerability. Unaware of your own history, your only option was to infiltrate and desecrate your own ruins for tools and keys to increase your understanding and ability.
I'm writing in the past-tense because those things are either no longer accurate or are only technically true. The nature of your character has changed, as have the factions, the void, and even your own people. The game has shifted a bit to revolve around microtransaction cosmetics on Steam, prime programs, too many flashy or pricy gimmicks, an overabundance of warframes, an overabundance of weapons, and an overabundance of unique resources you have to spend hours grinding to get. All of these feed into a 'gotta catch 'em all' master leveling scheme that just makes you sink more time in unless you buy your way out.
Certainly colour packs, platinum unlock skins, and prime access existed in 2014 as well and, from experience, I know I will get an endless barrage of comments regarding Warframe being a free game that I'm under no obligation to buy anything in; however, it's simply a good, common courtesy to pay for something you like, and I have sunk hundreds into Warframe against all prevailing financial reasoning. But certainly it shouldn't be so obnoxiously prevalent. So many different aspects of the game have been added and so much of the original theme, mechanics, gameplay, and lore have been rewritten and revised that the game no longer resembles itself. What once felt like a charming indie 1-4 person sortie game has turned into the worst possible thing: a successful MMO, and I was left with the consequences.
Taking a note from Dota or LoL, when you have a first person moba-like hero/champion, and undertake these specific themed missions, you kind of have the intrinsic problem of only being "allowed" to chose from 3-6 ideal characters. In those characters, you are expected to use your gimmick or relevant abilities
and run through the mission at light-speed. In reality, with decent equipment and decent familiarity, you can complete any mission with any warframe. But sometimes this takes patience and that is an instant deal-breaker with the overwhelming majority of the player base.
What fun are any of these hyper-speed, hyper-easy runs? Honestly, you should play difficult missions to see if you, as a person, are able to use your skills and strategy to figure out a difficult situation and feel the reward that comes from succeeding. You should find a warframe that suits your personality and identity and see what the struggles are going to be for that character as you progress through the game. But it's fine if that's the preferences of the player base, I'll just play single player.
And distanced myself from the increasingly weird, neckbeardy playerbase and ended up putting in around 600 additional hours in the less stressful single player missions. But that still didn't stop the game changing around me. Slowly, the gimmicks and mechanics changes started rolling out. Kubrows were added, archwing was added, wall running became bunny hopping, Baro Ki'Teer upped the ante for spending your life grinding, Lotus was installed as official ninjamom with weird implications, and your backstory was changed to be a odd monster, mind controlling a completely mechanical robot out in the field, sitting in a floating away-pod with a zit-popping room.
What game am I even playing anymore?
It feels a bit like a time-sunk fallacy, but I rather disagree with that assessment. The thing about Warframe that I enjoyed was the sort of Minecraft-like idea of returning to something every day, constantly adding more to it. Warframe was about building your character and seeing what kinds of things came next. Unfortunately, the game's development took a turn for the heavy-handed capitalist approach and milked that for all it had. The end result was something that I don't really want to have much to do with, while not really knowing when we got to this point. Some time between 2016 and now, the intense interest I had in this game became a mild repulsion. Would I recommend this game in 2014 or 2015? Hell yes. ♥♥♥♥ yes, without even giving it a second thought.
My review is negative.

It was december of 2002, and I was rummaging in the bargin bin of my local Best Buy. Hard to believe it was 15 long years ago. In these days we did something very silly - we bought software in boxes and drove them to our houses. Ridiculous, i know. This time I saw two game in that larg mesh bin that caught my eye. One was System Shock 2 (a great game), the other was something weirder, and more obscure. 'Divine Divinity'? like.. wet water? dirty dirt? There's an angel on the box? Will this be like bible adventures. I check the pricetag... its cheap. Ok, what the heck. I'ts friday night, its December, its cold, and I'm curious.
This was my first step into Larian's world. It remined me of Arkanum, another relatively unknown and awesome title from the era.  Suffice to say, the game was great. I found myself playing every subsequent game from this (at the time) lesser-known studio. Beyond divinity was next. I recall the voice acting was atrocious in the little demo that came in my PC Gamer magazine. They fixed that in the final. Then some time later, I saw divnity again. Just "divinity" this time, and you could..turn into a dragon? Of course this was even better than the last one.
Some additional time passes, and the next game.. Original Sin. Of course its fantastic. And finally, this. 15 years later from that first step.
These games are all, at their core, well balanced and artfully constructed rpg's that don't deviate far from the genre. They incorporate humor judiciously in the games, giving the game a quirky, 4th wall breaking feel from time to time. Most importantly, they are just quite fun, all of them.
A I reflec ton these games,  I feel like I've been on a long adventure, and each point in this adventure has been throughout my life, and has been growing with me. I'm in my 30s now, and I was in my teens when I started. Its hard to not have a strong sense of nostalgia and excitement for this series now.  I played this game, Original Sin 2 with my wife, and for her it was her first step into this world. Sometimes I'd pause the game and share some backstory, the rest of the time we just played and stayed glued to the incredible plot.
I don't want to reveal too much in this review so I'll mark spoilers. I'll tell you this: the moment when I was a the very end of the game, at the end of all of it, a string arrangement of this games theme sets in; the sound is doused in this ephemeral reverb, that really sets the tone as a battle that spans the ages like a mighty collosus;  your protagonists are set with some incredible and disturbing truths. It's not only big reveal in this game, but in the context of the series its even bigger. It was simply put, beautiful;
.
You don't need to be a long time fan to like this game, but if you are, there's just that much more to like. The game is funny, dramatic, tactical, exciting and even at times charmingly pedestrian. its fully deserving of its overwhelmingly positive rating. Also the music is not only good, its top notch. The composer(s) truly understand how to treat a theme and orchestrate. I'm picky, I write music too. At times I was almost jealous of just how incredible the tracks were.
My only hope is that in the future, maybe I can afford to be a aprt of their next kickstarter and be an even bigger supporter of Larians next project.
I don't know if you read these, Larian - but if you do, I just want to say thank you for enrapturing me with such quality work over all this time. I wish nothing but success for your company, you deserve it.
As for the rest of you, yes this game is a thumbs way-the-hell-up its a great game 10/10. Just buy it, even at full price its so good. Its like 200(or so)  hours of engaging gameplay. The value is there.

I have endless space and although I liked it I didn't really give enough time to fully enjoy it. Lots of people say this is endless space in a fantasy setting. I disagree. Although some of the mechanics are similar this game is different. Its also different and a lot more fun than many other fantasy based 4X titles.
So far I am into my first game and practically did not stop for 14 hours. Yes this game does an excellent job of keeping you in it. The game has a brief tutorial which does a great job of familiarising you with the basics. At first the game does appear a bit daunting with so many options and things to remember. After a couple of hours I became comfortable and then everything just seem to get better as my Empire slowly came to life. Breaking my 4x tradition I decided to start with a faction thats focus is on economy. I have to say  its really been good. It makes a change to buy your way to success instead of relying on churning out a constant army. With this faction I buy my army and its ready in an instant. The game consists of several varied and interesting major factions and then you have numerous minor factions.  Whichever major faction you choose they will have their own unique background story and quests.
Units vary but are basically broken down into heroes, support, infantry, cavalry, ranged and flying. You can even make your own units. To conquer regions you need cities and growing your city is a long process. In fact as your research grows you will enter several different ages unlocking even more ablities for the city. As well as battles this game is very much about resource management. I love the way every single hex in the game produces some kind of resource in different quantities. This makes it especially important when deciding where to place your city.
This game is pretty much all about time and planning. I really like it that at the beginning of the game you will be in whats known as a 'cold war' with all the other factions. At this stage there can be no peace treaties and you are quite exposed if you end up next door to an aggressive neighbour. Diplomacy in endless legends takes a long time to bear fruit. One thing I do like about the AI on easier settings is that it doesn't tend to attack you the moment it stumbles across you. I've played too many 4X's in the past where you literally get jumped on by the AI before you have started. The great thing about endless is that you start off with a limited number of diplomatic options. The others only come later if you research them. All the other AI factions in the game behave in a specific way. Some are expansionists while others are pacifists. This becomes apparent over time when you see how the factions behave towards each other and the size of their territory.
On to the map. Its one of the best and most intuitive I've seen in a 4x. Randomly generated hex landscapes with varied environments from cold wastes to desert. Each will effect how units interact with it. Scattered across the landscape are numerous weird anomalies, exploitable resources, explorable ruins and minor factions. At any point you can smoothly zoom right in and out of the map to get an overview of the empires. The map is big and takes a long time to fully explore. Minor factions play a role in that you need to pacify them early or they will become a threat with their wandering armies. You can even assimilate a limited number of pacified factions which will give you access to one of their units.
Battles are fought on a zoomed in version of the region it takes place on. Then its a simple turned based hex battle which goes through a number of phases before the outcome is decided. The environment your units are in at the time will have an effect. Some may think the battles are too simplified with limited options and no spell books like with HoMM games. To be honest I think it works just fine for endless. After a battle if you win your units will earn experience points and gradually level up. This makes keeping veteran armies alive essential for the later game.
The music score is superb and blends into the game perfectly.
There is a lot more to this game than what I have touched on in this review. Be sure that once its got your attention you will be sinking endless hours into it.

The mechanics of the game feel polished, and the team behind it is hard at work creating new content (the Starstorm expansion is being rolled out right now). I highly recommend you try this game if you enjo platforming, player-vs-player combat, and if you're into other MOBAs of course.
Awesomenauts is quite often on sale on Steam, and is also often included in "bundles" online (like the Humble Bundle), so the price tag shouldn't put you off for long if that's a factor.

The developer responded to me saying the game was not free, to which I respectfully disagreed. Let me break down why, free or not, you should avoid Call to Arms:
1. The actual extended content offered isn't that great. Differing factions don't offer really any unique properties beyond skins.
2. The content available after all unlocks are made is seriously not reflective of what the original videos, images, and descriptions show. It plays a lot like MoW, with little to no content that a typical RTS would have.
3. Bad AI - even on highest difficulty, the typical AI tactic is to spam light infantry and hold easily defended positions, removing a layer of offline play and co-op play online because the AI is so bad.
4. Developer involvement and response - most complaints are overlooked, and some are outright criticized.
5. Poorly implemented progression - Unlock other RTS games that will allow you to use all units and forces in offline sandbox play, Call to Arms gates your unit access behind XP that can only be gained by playing online.

I spent basically 300 hours on this game. As a level 45 sewing character i can finally craft myself some crude linen cloth.
If you know what crude linen cloth is, you will understand my review.
If you don't, let me explain...
When you first start the game and you kill something, you get yourself linen cloth. This can literally be achieved in less than 5 minutes after starting a new game. After you get 6 pieces of linen cloth you can "sew" them into one linen cloth roll. This is the first crafting thing you make for your armors, less than 30 minutes into the game. Consequently this linen cloth roll is bad quality ("crude") because your skill level ("sewing") is only 1 out of 50.
After spending 300 hours you will be level 45-50 sewing. Very high right, there is no way you will make bad "crude" quality linen cloth right? WRONG. 300 hours later you will still make bad quality ("crude") linen cloth rolls.
In other words, you have just wasted 300 hours and your first ever crafting recipe at level 1 is still giving you garbage because the devs are too busy partying in hawaii to care.
The best part? before some update a few months ago or last year you actualy used to be able to get rare items if you were high level. But why reward a 300 hour grind? amirite trololololol

So, basically, think age of empires, but extended throughout recorded history, so you get a wide variety of combat, from slings and arrows to stealth bombers and nuclear icbms, Then throw in deeper concepts from turn based strategy games like borders and an actual (albeit simplified for real time play) logistics system.  Plus a campaign which pefected what we would now call the "metamap" system. I would honestly rate this as one of the best rts games of all time, with the only other real contender for the top spot being maybe the original starcraft.  Certainly the best rts in a histroical setting.
Even if you already own the original, it's might be a little harder to justify, but it does have working multiplayer through steamworks(the original used gamespy, which was terrible and now defunct), and then there's just the convenience of having it in your steam library.  Worth getting during a sale anyway.
If you're a strategy fan who somehow never played this when it first came out, This is absolutely a must buy.

When I saw Sonic Mania, I was hyped like everyone else. When I found that the Steam version was delayed, I was disappointed, but that was it; I decided to keep it & try it out for myself. When I finally got around to playing it, I was more than excited. Already people are saying this is "Sonic 4 as it should be". Are they right? Are they wrong? Well, let's find out.
Pros:
+Great controls.
+ACTUAL SPOT-ON PHYSICS!!!
+Silky smooth sprite animation with twice or thrice or more frames than Genesis/Mega Drive titles.
+Pixel-art is top-notch & higher quality than I expected.
+Frame rate is amazing.
+Lots of memorable music & it's catchy!
+Old ideas used creatively.
+New stages pretty cool.
+Special Stages are a lot more fun than they look.
+Blue Spheres bonus stages are more addicting than they look.
+Level design is just like S3&K again!
+"Mean Bean" is a lot more fun & addicting than it looks.
+Actually FEELS like a Genesis game AND legitimate sequel!
Cons:
-Kind of difficult even with practice.
-Not enough original zones.
-Can only use unlockables, like "& Knuckles" with "No Save".
-A few inconsistencies with story.
-A few levels can drag for too long.
-Finding Special Stage rings aren't as easy as it looks.
Conclusion:
Fans have already proven that they can develop great Sonic games & this is living proof. This is basically what "Sonic 4" "should've" been from the start. Pretty much how you make a real Classic-style Sonic game & do it right! Buy it! You won't regret it!
P.S.: Can we please have a "Sonic Mania 2" but with more original zones? Please??

This game is very much Civ-inspired. Civ V: BnW+GnK, not Vanilla. It's hard not to compare the two because they share so much in common. But that's not a bad thing. It takes what works, and it adds some very nuanced depth to the mechanics.
Faction selection is at the moment 8 choices. They cover most gamestyles you'd expect to find, for the most part they are fairly balanced between each other, with only one faction seen far and away as being UP, and none in particular as being OP. If you don't like any of the factions you're free to take one of the factions as a template, and make a custom faction, with different bonuses costing a set amount of creation points. You can also take some disadvantages to allow you more points to spend on bonuses.
You start the game with a meager military, a hero, and a settler. You can't settle wherever you want, as there are a finite number of regions, and there  can only settle one city per region. Each region has its own host of strategic and luxury resources, who's exploitation is handled with city improvements. This is in addition to minor faction villages, which when pacified and settled, provide you different bonuses depending on which faction it is, and how many of their villages you own.
Heroes are units that can either lead a military stack, or lead a city, providing bonuses to one or the other. For the most part they are slightly stronger than regular unit, but as they level up and acquire skills through a skill tree, they can become quite powerful, but also much more expensive. After researching a certain technology you're free to pick up as money heroes from the mercenary market as your wallet will afford you. You're also free to pick up other faction's heroes at the same time, if you so choose.
Your city planning is handled with city improvements, most of which cost dust (money) to maintain. There are no "workers" in this game so most of your tile improvement is handled with city improvements. You can expand your city with borough expansions, which extends the urban sprawl of your city while adding the surrounding tiles as usable. However this comes at the price of happiness (which can be mitigated as your urban tiles level up by building surrounding urban areas, wiping out the happiness deficit of that particular tile).
Citizen management is a large overhaul from Civ as well, it isn't something that is mostly used to fuel great people or beakers. Citizens can provide any of the basics of a city (food, money, production, research, culture, etc) at any time. Late game especially improvements can allow workers to provide more income than most tiles. Micromanagement of them allows for high level efficiency, but can get tedious towards the end of a game when your empire has a lot of workers, and a lot of cities.
Periodically during gameplay, you'll break from normal weather to undergo winter. Winter for the most part, halves movement, decreases combat effectiveness and vision ranges, and plummits your city growth, production, and income for the (several turns) duration of winter. Most heroes, once leveled high enough, can learn a skill to mitigate or eliminate the effects of winter, on stacks of units, or cities. This becomes essential later in the game when the map becomes permament winter.
Military is handled rather well, but could be expanded upon somewhat with more diversity in selection. Each faction gets 3 military units ranging from cavalry, infantry, archers, flying, and support. Each faction maintains a flavor for their selection of units, and these can later be upgraded and diversified with an rpg-style equipment system, most units carry a selection of at least 2 weapons selections which can change their role significantly, as well as a host of armors and accessories. However none of these change the appearance (save the weapons) of the unit. These 3 units are augmented with whatever units your minor factions can be recruited from. These too can be upgraded.
Combat is handled much differently from Civ. It is not handled with dice rolls (although you are allowed that option). Every engagement is zoomed in on the map and played out in a Fantasy Tactics-type of minigame. You (or you can let the computer manage for you) fight the enemy's stack on the map as is, terrain and all. If the enemy AI was more detailed it would be more enjoyable, but they for the most part tend to attack the first thing they run into. Which (in my experience) means most of my stacks are developed as hordes of archers with 1 or 2 high defense tanks to block the enemy.
As far as diplomacy goes, it's very rudimentary, you start off in cold war, for most factions, which means you're allowed to do anything to them short of outright taking their cities. You can negotiate peace, alliance, and trade settlements, or attack them. They will do the same.
Questing is a big mechanic within the game. Each faction has its own quest lines, which pile your usual quest fair of kill this, and search this location, with more factional specific missions that try to guide you towards playing on the  strengths of your race. Expect conversion and building from the Cultists, trade and money from the trader oriented Roving Clans, etc. These are nice little distractions which keep interest in the game when you aren't actively at war or preparing for war.
AI in general, is very unchallenging it seems, but so was Civ's. If you are fairly experienced with turn-based 4x games, you will most likely find Normal difficulty useful only to be introduced to mechanics or factions. The difficulty factor primarily seems to be from increases on the AI's starting roster, and their increases to research speed, production, and income. They don't seem to handle oceans or seas rather well either, in aggression or in peaceful expansion. So expect to perform better, with more water seperating you from the AI.
Graphics, are stupendous. For a 4x game. The artstyle surrounding the game is also quite good, and maintains a very fantasy/sci-fi vibe. Units have a fair bit of detail to them, along with your cities, and the general tile layouts of the map. It's not hang up on your wall beautiful, but it looks good, doesn't get boring to look at for extended periods of time, and doesn't tax a moderately built computer's resources too much. However it does make initial map seeding take a fair longer than what I'd like, but once the game's loaded it runs without many hiccups.
I have no experience with the multiplayer, but I haven't heard anything bad about it. No news is good news right?
All things said, if you've enjoyed Civ V, EL brings enough new things around that it'll be interesting enough for several games. If you enjoy 4x games in general, it has some rough trimmings about it, but it is already a fairly solid game, with some fairly interesting mechanics bundled with it to make it one to give a shot.

Despite the fact that CCII is in the running for my favorite game of all time, I haven't written a review until now, mostly because there are a number of reviews already highlighting the strengths of the world's greatest incest simulator. I'm not even going to try to top them.
Really, I just want to counterbalance some of the brigading that's going on in the review section. For some reason, people don't like the publisher's DLC policies and are arbitrarily downvoting one of the great games of our generation to protest.
Here's my take:
If you think the game or the DLC isn't worth the price, don't buy it. It's really that simple. I get the hate with money-grubbing companies selling unfinished games and then charging extra for DLC that fixes the base game, but let me be that CCII is NOT one of those games. The base game is well worth $40 in my opinion. The DLC varies in quality (and cost), but none of it is required to enjoy the game. It's extra stuff added to the base game. If Paradox turns around and releases a broken CCIII that is only fun when DLC is purchased, I'll be at the front of the downvote brigade. But CCII is not, so have no fear that you can buy none, some, or all of the DLC and have a good time. The game is really is worth your time if you're into dynastic strategy games.
The bottom line is that if you want to kill your husband, marry your brother, and steal the thrown from your father, Crusader Kings II is the best experience in gaming. Be discerning about DLC (most is good, but quality is uneven), but the base game is absolutely worth it, even if you can't find a sale.

Do you want a cute RNG game to play in your spare time? Do you want to be killed by a chicken? How about a duck? If you said yes to any of these questions 100% Orange Juice is the game for you. 100% Orange Juice is a virtual anime board game. You pick your favorite character, go into a map with a selection of cards, which will be used by all players, and try to achieve the five goals (normas) set to win. You can attack other players, set traps, and use cards to try and bring your friends and foes down so you can triumph over them. How to win, card art, panels, characters, pros, cons, and the small details will be the main focus point of this review.
At the beginning of the game you’re given a card, norma, and a base. To fulfill your norma you have to land on a base. If the base is not yours you cannot land on it unless you battle someone standing on it or roll the exact distance needed to land there. To battle a character you can pass over them and opt to stop and fight or keep going. When battling it’s completely RNG as your offense and defense will be determined by your dice roll. Each character is given base stats that will either subtract or add to your rolls. If you have a battle card that is your level (number of normas you have achieved) you can pay stars (currency) to use them to help try and sway the battle in your favor. The idea of having normas is nothing new to any game and the system is pretty generic. Complete the goal, base, continue. I personally didn’t find any faults in this system, however, at the same time nothing stands out. The card designs are typically very nice, I’ve only seen a couple cards that I didn’t like the design for.
As you’re trying to win the game there will be many spaces you will land on that will change the game. Battle spaces are red and will summon a chicken, golem, duck and later bosses that fight you. The yellow bonus spaces give you free stars based on your dice roll. The blue drop panel works in a similar fashion as the bonus space but you lose stars. The purple spaces teleport you to a random spot on the map which can allow you to have awesome escapes or comebacks. Finally there’s the green spaces which let you draw a card, and the light blue space which allows you to roll to move again. When first playing there is no tutorial to tell you what each of the spaces do, however, the panel art is pretty obvious so you do know what you’re landing on. The panels are colorful and makes the game have a very cheerful and colorful appearance.
Trap cards can be used before you move and will be placed face down on top of your current panel unless otherwise stated (Certain characters hypers act as traps to be randomly placed on the map). When a player lands on the trap card they do the traps action and then the panel action under. If the trap card moves your character you will not do either of the panel actions you land on. Some traps in the game are so infuriating that I want to quit as soon as I land on them, others seem really pointless.
Each character during the game may draw a Hyper Card. These are character based, each character having their own special hyper. These hyper cards are played like regular cards that can either be used for battles or for map control. Hypers can dramatically change the game, with many hypers you can take the advantage of your allies and gain stars, health, or damage them allowing you to swoop in for the kill. With certain deck cards you can either get another characters hyper or your own, this provides you with a way to try and strategize for the win. In my experience I found the battle hypers to be the most useful as you can swoop in and kill someone and take their stars, or kill a boss.
In the game currently there are about thirty six playable characters, some of these characters are unlocked through the store, others are DLC, with other special characters that can be unlocked by purchasing other games on Steam (200% Mixed Juice, Sora, etc). The cast of character all can be found in other games published by Fruitbat factory. If you are a fan of the other games this game is basically a dream come true yet it’s still fine to play the game without knowing any characters coming in (since the storyline doesn’t have any influence or importance in the game).  When starting the game you can play four characters from the start while eight other humanoid characters can be unlocked, as well as the ability to play every enemy character. All the other characters are DLC. While having most character be unlocked through DLC or the purchase of other games may be a turn off, once Steam sales roll around and you have less than a dollar to spare you may find yourself spending it on the DLC.
In campaign mode you play the game following whichever character you select’s storyline. Personally, I skipped the story after the first two scenarios. The story means almost nothing to someone who has not played any games with these characters involved. Overall, playing through campaign can be a huge pain but you get a crown as a reward that you can put on your character for completing it all. If you’re into customization it can be a huge bragging right when playing with friends, otherwise, there is no purpose to campaign. There are seven total story paths each having five episodes and a final battle, two of these paths come with DLC.
Outside campaign there is Free Play with both multiplayer and single player options. In this you can chose the map, and the field events that occur. Field events can range from drawing a card every seven turns to getting bombed and losing 1 hp. Field events either make your game even harder, or help you. Some Steam achievements can be unlocked easier by utilizing these field events.
Pros to this game:
•	Cute characters (And a lot of them)
•	Can play alone or with friends
•	Character balances
•	Spectate system
•	Different difficulty settings in campaign
•	Cheap
Cons:
•	Rage inducing
•	The music can get pretty annoying and repetitive, I mute the game.
•	Bots do get unfair rolls (not always, unless in harder modes, then always.)
•	Profile level can only be raised in multiplayer
•	No tutorial for first time players
•	Campaign has no real impact
Overall, I find 100% Orange Juice to be very cute and fun, and even better once you start playing more with others. I’d give the game an 8/10 because the AI can get pretty unfair, tons of rage, and the music is just too much. (It changes each time someone changes their norma between a track of songs and after hearing all the songs and them getting changed over and over it just gets too irritating.) I don’t think this game is perfect by any means but it isn’t a bad game. I think it’s a game that is worth the original price listed on Steam, and on sale should be purchased by anyone slightly interested in the title. I find the game something I will pick up and play when I don't have tons of time and would like to play without too much thought. It's a game I think anyone with interests in virtual board games and anime should pick up and give a shot. Prepare to be frustrated.

200~ stars. Level 5, almost home, all the other players are far away from you. It's an easy win.
"GG", everyone else says in chat.
You roll.
1 short.
Enemy panel.
"Well, I'm full health, I'll be fine, so let's end this game already", you say to yourself.
A wild Seagull appears!
You roll a 6.
The seagull rolls a 6 in defense.
The seagull gets a 5 for defense.
The seagull survives easily.
The seagull rolls a 6 in attack.
The seagull gets a 7 for attack.
No problem, you're full health, after all.
You roll a 1 in defense.
"LOL", Everyone says in chat.
The seagull then proceeds to destroy you, physically, emotionally, mentally, and financially.
Half of your stars are gone (And half of your will to live, too).
Just as you finish up wiping your tears, you proceed to see the scoreboard, naturally, with Marie Poppo in first, who robbed you as you were down, and rolled onto your home to win.
This is what 100% Orange Juice is like. Do not be fooled by its cute art style and seemingly casual gameplay.
This isn't a game.
This is a future therapy session.
I'd still recommend it. 10/10

I've put off writing this review for a long, long time because I've very mixed feelings about it.
I've played this game since early Alpha release (around July 2015) and have around 1500 hrs in game over two accounts (this takes me up to about 6 weeks after the Beta release).
Firstly I'll start with the good / what I like about the game:
GOOD
1. The game has awesome scope to build a base / castle / home.  You have pretty much got total freedom to make any layout of your choosing and you can design the base for looks or to be safe from raiders / thieves from a strategical standpoint.
2. There are a variety of skills / professions to chose from... around 20 (some not fully completed though at the time of writing this). So for a guild of about 8-10 people, everyone is valued and becomes a valued member of the team, which is important for the social aspect of this game.
3. The environment / different biomes looks great.
4. The crafting variety is very good.
5. The variety of weapons and corresponding weapon skills is quite diverse.
6. The map is relatively large.
7. The community liaison person (OddAlice) is very nice and works very hard.
Here's the bad / what I dislike about the game:
BAD.
i. The lag.  There servers are often laggy when a moderate number of players are online (say 400-500).  There are also random lag spikes and FPS drops for no apparent reason.  Note: I am aware the game is not optimized yet (I'm running a top of the line Alienware rig, so it shouldn't be an issue for this game).
ii. The crafting system is currently a little buggy and its almost impossible to craft higher quality items.
iii. There is a desync when fighting (both PvP and when fighting PvE monsters).  It is almost impossible to hit someone who is moving, so unless you both stand still and take it in turns trading hits, battles are pure frustration and become boring fast.
iv. There are many small bugs that are not very significant but very irritating that have been around since Day 1 and have not been fixed (despite people calling out for them to be fixed on the forums).
v. The developers do not communicate with the player base.  They are silent for long periods and tend to only reply when there is a massive uproar with the players.  Then the response is often vague or scant on content.
vi. The developers appear to be more focused on tweaking existing features / graphics, rather than fixing the small bugs mentioned before or adding new content.
vii. There is practically NO END GAME CONTENT.
viii. The profanity filter on the game chat is overly sensitive, so censors non-offensive words.
iX. At Beta release the developers covered 75% of the map in mist.  You cant view these areas properly and you cant build on these areas.  It's a huge annoyance to everyone who plays.
X. The game is a little too grindy.  I dont mind grinding in a game and this is Korean so I understand and expect it to be a little grindy.  The grind in Alpha was just about right, but in Beta they made it way more grindy.
Xi.  Forever chopping trees... many joke this game is actually a lumberjack simulator.  This is ok when you are in a large guild, but because a serious pain in the a$$ if you dont have 5+ players.
Xii.  The recent milestones released by the developers appear to take the game in a very different direction to how it is currently or how it is referred to in their reviews and promotional videos.  I know this is early access and things change, but this could take the game in a totally new direction.
Xiii.  Mice infect your base if you are offline for about 12 hrs.  After 24 hrs your base starts losing HP.  This is VERY irritating.
Xiv. The devopment team are very small so new content is VERY slow and recent comunication suggests patches for new content will be every 2-3 months.
Xv. Patches / hotfixes to date appear rushed out and untested.  This results in very buggy content and usually every patch is followed up by a hotfix.
TL:DR:
PvP is broken due to the desync.  Its been like this since Day 1 and little has changed in over a year to fix this.  There is no end game content (guild wars etc.)
PvE is currently broken as the crafting is buggy, you cant build on 75% of the map and there is no end game content (like quests / dungeons / bosses etc.)
So all in all I give this one a thumbs down. This is on the basis that over the past year, not a lot of core features / funamentals have been added and major bug fixes are still not dealt with (desync).  Also, the last 2 months of Beta suggest a similar approach will be taken this year.
I suspect the developers dont have the resources to deliver on their promises so I am doubtful this game will make it over the line or it will be realease in much the same state it is in now.
I would LOVE to be proven wrong though...
