Sorry, but I play BF4 on the highest settings without issue. This *should not happen* regardless of the reason.
If they can't fix the net code, then when people have high ping rates (or purposely desyning), they should disconnect them from the server. Something has to give.
Cheating:  Plenty of reports about people wall-hacking into bases, players either not taking damage or taking very reduced damage as well as being able to attack you without turning yellow.
This game has so much potential but the devs don't seem to care. They are hemorrhaging users as the player base has grown tired of the issues not being resolved.

Where things stand currently? Not so much.

This is my favorite elder scrolls/Bethesda Obsidian game and I want everyone to know why.This game captures all of the best elements of these series.Enough fluff though.The story and questlines in this game are AMAZING.EVERY QUEST feels like someone poured their passion into it to make a fun experience.While the modern bethes/idian games are repetitive and fall short in their monotous fetch quests and settlement farming this game deliniates from the pack and succeeds substantialy.The quests in this game feel like they have purpose.Furrthermore the main story of Oblivion is compelling and the Deadra pose a clear and existential threat to Tamriel.Im not going to blow smoke up everyones♥♥♥♥♥and pretend this game isnt without its flaws,They are numerous and can serve to break your immersion but most of the time they are just silly and add to this games unique charm.(Minor Characters having multiple voice actors with very different voices for example)I could go on and on with praise for this game but I'd like to highlight the ways it outclasses its succesors.Oblivion vs Skyrim:Oblivion has a much more interesting main questline and has a much more interesting world imo.The rugged and unsettled terrain has a very stark contrast to skyrims complete overkill of roads and fluff settlements.There is a sense of wonder and suspense walking through the lush woods of cyrodiil not knowing when a minotaur or a unicorn may appear.Another way oblivion beats out Skyrim is in its original gamespace designs.All of the caves and a lot of the settlements in skyrim feel recycled and drab.In oblivion the caves are all quite original and they have a higher variety of enemies I.E:Vampires,Goblins,trolls,Imps,bears,wolves,bandits(need i go on?)On the other hand Skyrim recycles the same "drougre?" caves and enemies like tree hugger trying to reduce its carbon footprint.Skyrims world may be larger and have more areas to explore but they are no where near as fulfilling as Oblivions.I feel the need to list off a few main detriments of the game before i wrap this up.Oblivs main problems are somewhat reppetitive Oblivion gates(Ironic when this is something i criticised skyrim for but the gates in this game at least have quite varied designs and good rewards in the sigils),somewhat dated AI,and an arbitrary level scaling system.While these are problems they arent even close to experience killing.This is getting quite long so im going to end this review here.I just want to let first time players know before they get this game that it is quite dated by modern standards in some ways but it a really compelling story and the quests are always fresh.I havent even played the Shivering Isles expansion yet as i have been too busy with the main game but i have only heard positive things about it so i feel confident in reccommending it.The knights DLC is good though(just annoying trying to keep a positive moral standing so i can wear the armor)This review was off the cuff and out of my passion for the game so i likely left  a lot of things out but i hope this helps you form your decision on whether or not to pick up the game(allthough i realise a lot of my critiques wouldnt make sense unless you have played skyrim...lol)

There are a few bugs here and there, but no game is perfect. I really enjoy how in depth this game goes to make the gameplay last. The races all differ in playstyle, although I am Partial to the Drakken. I like it more than Civ 5 because it has more of a fantasy feel with different types of creatures for the factions and the lore. I know this game type has almost been done to death, but Endless Legend puts a nice spin on it.

I will compare this to Civ 5 since most people will probably have had experience with that title, due to the fact it can be considered one of the most popular 4x games out there right now.
Endless Legend is a 4x game similar to Civ 5 but with many changes and improvments that makes it really stand out from Civ.
First off, I always found the nations in Civ 5 to be really similar to one another. Two things would be differnt between them all, like a unique unit or building and a special ability that most of the time I don't really notice and thats it, everything else is pretty cookie cutter and the same.
Now I can understand why it's like that, human civilizations did develop and have similar technologys at around the same as eachother.
But since Endless Legend is set in a fantasy setting they could develop these really unique factions. They all play and look and feel differnt. For instance, one faction is a cult of creepy living doll like beings who can only build one city,but they can pretty much build it into a super city and can convert minor factions to there cult to do there bidding!
Or how about another faction where you can't really do much diplomatically and you are just one big war mongering swarm of blood thirsty zerg-like insects who spread in a fashion similar to the zombie plauge that feed on your fallen enemies? And on the opposite end of the spectrum, You have the opportunity to play as dragons that use there vast knowledge and prestige to force people to do what you want them to do through the power of diplomacy? And who says actions speak louder than words?
Alot of thought as gone into this game, not just gameplay wise but lore wise aswell. This game boasts a very deep and interesting lore that shares the same universe with 3 other games this developer has well...developed. Not only are the factions histories deep but the worlds is too. It's an absolute joy to read up on the lore of this games and those connected to it. If you like deep lore I am sure you will enjoy what this game has to offer.
The graphics are nice too, they are not next gen or anything, but they are good looking. They use them very well too and make a world that looks very imaginative such as trees shooting blazing flames from its branches, large forbidding pits that lead down to dens which contain giant spider women hybrids. And so on and so fourth. The game also contains 2d art aswell which looks stunning. Some of it is even animated and is very nice to watch.
Some gameplay elements that differ from Civ 5 and this game is that this game got rid of manually telling what tiles you wanted to be worked,now every tile that is in the cities range is automatically being worked on. So instead you can now put your workers into these little check boxes that will increase the amount of resources you gain that that particular check box represents.
Some people may have liked the micro management that civ 5 had in that respect but I personally found it tedious and boring and much prefer this system of doing it which gets you the same outcome but with alot less time wasted.
Another change is the research tree in this game. You dont have to know specific technologies in this game to get more powerful versions of previous ones, or to advance to the next era, you just have to research enough of the current era to advance to the next era.
Battles are differnt too. When units fight they take a small portion of the surrounding map and then have turn based tactical fights going on. Using the terrian is important since it gives you boosts in combat and you have to be weary of your units stats since they matter quite a bit in these skirmishes.
There's alot more to this game that I haven't touched, and it would take a long while to explain it all, but I hope that you get a good idea of what this game is about and its quality. If your a fan of 4x games, fantasy or just strategy games in general I think you wont regret giving this game a try.

I bought this game after reading many 5/5 reviews and being told it's a bit like Civ5.
Well... not quite. The first thing you'll notice is that there's absolutely zero hand-holding in this game. I couldn't find anything like a tutorial, so I had to go on youtube to find out how to play. It's not particularly convoluted or difficult, so you'll probably manage quite well after 10 mins of introduction.
Without going into too much detail here are my problems with the game:
Combat is tedious and not particuarly strategic. Order your units to attack a target and press next turn until done. Often I found my units doing whatever they want during fights even when ordered to specific tasks. There also is an auto-resolve button which skips combat, with the obvious downside of leaving your army at the mercy of the AI.
There is no resource diversity. Everyone starts with Titanite and Steelgrass. There are no auxillary ressources either and all special tiles are basically just fixed boni applied to you when you control it.
Winter straight up sucks. It wrecks every economic or strategic aspect of the game for several turns. On multiple occasions my gold income dropped from around +15 to -130 just because it was winter. I'm not exactly sure how that mechanic is supposed to be played around.
The map is a mess. Everything looks like a super special ressource, but really is just a normal tile. Also the trees' aspect ratios are terribly butchered, making them look like bulldozed over and shot with a shrink-ray.
You can't zoom out without going into brown-map-mode.
The UI is the biggest mess I've seen in quite along time. It's literally indistinguishable which information is important and which isn't. When you put the UI in big mode it feels clunky and too big, and in normal mode the text gets butchered by downscaling.
What I liked:
The hero system is cool, and the equipment makes them very strong and useful.
Many units are very unique and fun to use.
The graphics are quite pretty.
Might have a lot of potential after patches.

This game kind of resembles a fantasy version of Civ in the Endless universe that Amplitude has created. There are a lot of cool tie-ins with their other games which is great if you were also a fan of Endless Space. This game plays a little bit like civ, but instead of trying to force your armies through choke points over a span of countless turns, you can group your units similar to creating fleets in Endless Space. While there is a limit to how many in a stack, this greatly reduces the headache of managing large forces.
This brings me to the excellent combat system. When an engagment occurs, the units stacked in your army get set up in your half of the battlefield. The battlefield is just a part of the map which gets sectioned off for the battle, so the terrain you fight on is still the map terrain itself. Things like height and tile type play a role still but it allows armies to be set up specificially for engagements. The battles use a turn based system which allow you to give orders that more resemble suggestions ( there's a degree to which units will decide what to do when reaching a tile you command them to, or set a default stance when an order can't be completed because of the simultanious turn system ). Despite that sometimes your forces will do things that make you cringe, it has never been a problem for me to take advantage of terrain with smaller forces and win by exploiting it in this system. Additionally, any forces in range will slowly join the battle if you have secondary armies available in the area. This immediately put this game well above Civ in my books. Not that warfare is necessary. It is still usually a large part of the 4x experience.
Also excellent, is that while unit variety is lacking on a per/faction basis. You can buy units from a market from minor factions, or assimilate them into your empire allowing you to customize and train their units. The lack of variety is also made up for by the ability to fit them with weapons and armor to suit your requirements for them ( including multiple fit types on the same unit model ). If it becomes obsolete, when you edit their design you can pay to retrofit just like in endless space. This allows for a fairly wide range of approaches.
If you played Endless Space, a huge difference you will notice is that heroes commanding armies take up arms on the battlefield. They can be combat or support oriented allowing you to play with their tactics a fair bit. They can be equiped with different weapons and armor as well. They will have some stats that influence the entire army ( some equipement serves this purpose as well ) in addition to their more direct involvement. They can be taken down requiring a player to pay to have them revived.
The factions are diverse, but explaining everything would be better left to a guide. That said, you may also customize a faction by picking a base faction then choosing attributes. Most will have a cost associated and you can pick up negative traits to give you a bigger budget for positive ones.
If you enjoy fantasy and 4x games, you can't possibly go wrong with this game. It's a ton of fun with several elements that eliminate some of the minor annoyances I've had in games like Civ. This and endless space will probably remain top of my list regarding 4x titles for quite some time.

I've played a lot of strategy games over the years and this is one of the better ones. A lot of 4x games (not including space 4x) tend to be heavily modeled after the Civilization series, not Endless Legend though. This game is very much its own game.
Pros:
Each Faction plays very differently from each other. Necrophages can't have peace or alliances, Broken Lords don't need food. Drakken can force peace upon another player, Roving Clans can't declare war etc. Each faction truly is a vastly different playstyle.
The game is beautiful. A minor thing that just makes it more enjoyable.
The battle system is interesting. More in depth than Civ's smack two units against each other, but not as in depth as Age of Wonders 3 where you control each unit on the battle field.
The world is very diverse and there are quests, ruins, minor factions etc. that make exploring both profitable and enjoyable.
Unit Customization. You can alter your units with different armor, weapons and trinkets to suit your needs. You take a basic unit from your faction (or assimilated minor factions) and equip them with different equipment to make them stronger or more specialized. For instance you could have a lance weilding Stalwart that does a lot of damage, or one that can take as much damage as you throw at it.
Heroes: Strong units that lead armies or govern cities. Very useful and very cool.
Mixed:
The region system is somewhat strange. When you settle a region with a city, you own that whole region. However, only the tiles directly around your city are worked. You also can only found a single city per region. This means that many areas that would make excellent cities are wasted. On the other hand all the strategic and luxury resources in the region can be harvested by the single city. You also don't get AI settling right next to your city to steal a resource like in Civ.
Cons:
Limited number of Units. Each faction only has 4 base units. You can assimilate different minor factions for their units but there is a limited number of slots to do this. Compared to other games there aren't many units around. However each faction has three unique units (the settler is common to almost all the factions).
AI can travel into your territory automatically and can attack your units outside of your territory without declaring war. You have to declare peace for them not to be able to attack your units and declare closed borders to keep them out of your territory. Both of which cost influence.
Declaring war costs influence. Severely annoying and pointless. The other diplomatic stuff makes sense. This does not. You don't need to influece someone to declare war, you just attack them.

When I saw Sonic Mania, I was hyped like everyone else. When I found that the Steam version was delayed, I was disappointed, but that was it; I decided to keep it & try it out for myself. When I finally got around to playing it, I was more than excited. Already people are saying this is "Sonic 4 as it should be". Are they right? Are they wrong? Well, let's find out.
Pros:
+Great controls.
+ACTUAL SPOT-ON PHYSICS!!!
+Silky smooth sprite animation with twice or thrice or more frames than Genesis/Mega Drive titles.
+Pixel-art is top-notch & higher quality than I expected.
+Frame rate is amazing.
+Lots of memorable music & it's catchy!
+Old ideas used creatively.
+New stages pretty cool.
+Special Stages are a lot more fun than they look.
+Blue Spheres bonus stages are more addicting than they look.
+Level design is just like S3&K again!
+"Mean Bean" is a lot more fun & addicting than it looks.
+Actually FEELS like a Genesis game AND legitimate sequel!
Cons:
-Kind of difficult even with practice.
-Not enough original zones.
-Can only use unlockables, like "& Knuckles" with "No Save".
-A few inconsistencies with story.
-A few levels can drag for too long.
-Finding Special Stage rings aren't as easy as it looks.
Conclusion:
Fans have already proven that they can develop great Sonic games & this is living proof. This is basically what "Sonic 4" "should've" been from the start. Pretty much how you make a real Classic-style Sonic game & do it right! Buy it! You won't regret it!
P.S.: Can we please have a "Sonic Mania 2" but with more original zones? Please??

I remember playing this game all the time back in the heady days of the early Aughts. Maybe it's nostalgia talking, but for someone who's not super into strategy games this one still stands up as one of the best.
It's an RTS, but has a great deal of depth to it. The most accurate way to describe it, I think, is that it's the RTS version of the Civilization series.
You can play as any one of a huge number of real civilizations throughout history and you play them as an expanding empire throughout history, starting out as cavemen and going on to develop space age technology.
The nations you can play as are all functionally the same besides some minor differences in a few unit types and inherent bonuses based on the history of that nation. So the best way to go about it is to play a few matches to figure out what sort of play style you prefer, and then pick a nation that helps out your play style.
Each match takes roughly an hour and a half, which makes it centuries faster than a standard Civilization match, but you still go through all the same motions as you would in a Civilization game. Trying to burn through technologies, pushing out resources, setting up border cities in order to claim territory, and then finally ending the world in a barrage of nukes because the match has been going on too long and you're bored.
If you like the idea of the Civilization series but always hated how slow-paced they are, you'll love this game.

EARLY ACCESS REVIEW:
I've tried unsuccessfully to write a review for Tree of Life for some time now.  I originally added this to my wishlist because I was greatly interested in the sort of "World of Warcraft" style graphics coupled with the idea of an engaging survival game.  Unfortunately for me, the game just doesn't live up to what I was looking for.  In fact, this will probably be my only negative review on Steam so far.  I tried my best to like the game, I really did, but here are some brief points about the game, some positive, most negative:
-Completely abandoned community/island/area.  Nice if you like being alone, but still oddly errie to see hundreds of abandoned buildings.
-Lack of single player, lack of private servers.  This is the main reason I dislike the game.  I like playing alone sometimes, and frankly would like a private server with friends.
-Too much relies on other people.  Not enough options for people who want to form small clans.
-Combat is clunky and broken.
-Music is very good but annoyingly repetative.  Drives me crazy after a few hours, and have to turn it off.
-TONS of typos, TONS of spelling errors, and complete failure in translation.  I give them a break on this since they aren't an English-based developer, but it's so annoying.  The description for the french fries actually made me roll my eyes so hard I fell out of my viking ship.
-Good graphics, good animations, doesn't feel dated.  I like the cartoony feel.
-Game requires WAY TOO MUCH wood.  Everything takes wood, lots of wood.  Game should be called "Tree Cutter Simulator 2016"
-Misty areas/foggy areas can seriously go take a hike.  They provide no value-add at all.
-Mining sulfur makes you want to /wrist.  In fact, mining iron, or any "high tiered" anything makes you want to /wrist.
The list goes on, but yeah, at it's current state I don't recommend this game.  Maybe in a few updates, maybe in a few months, maybe in a year, who knows.

Despite the fact that CCII is in the running for my favorite game of all time, I haven't written a review until now, mostly because there are a number of reviews already highlighting the strengths of the world's greatest incest simulator. I'm not even going to try to top them.
Really, I just want to counterbalance some of the brigading that's going on in the review section. For some reason, people don't like the publisher's DLC policies and are arbitrarily downvoting one of the great games of our generation to protest.
Here's my take:
If you think the game or the DLC isn't worth the price, don't buy it. It's really that simple. I get the hate with money-grubbing companies selling unfinished games and then charging extra for DLC that fixes the base game, but let me be that CCII is NOT one of those games. The base game is well worth $40 in my opinion. The DLC varies in quality (and cost), but none of it is required to enjoy the game. It's extra stuff added to the base game. If Paradox turns around and releases a broken CCIII that is only fun when DLC is purchased, I'll be at the front of the downvote brigade. But CCII is not, so have no fear that you can buy none, some, or all of the DLC and have a good time. The game is really is worth your time if you're into dynastic strategy games.
The bottom line is that if you want to kill your husband, marry your brother, and steal the thrown from your father, Crusader Kings II is the best experience in gaming. Be discerning about DLC (most is good, but quality is uneven), but the base game is absolutely worth it, even if you can't find a sale.

After watching 5 youtube videos I decided I'd buy the game. I picked up a few basics from those videos so I quickly managed to get the basics.
Here's how my first playthrough went (Normal, Pangaea with 6 civilizations) playing as the wild walkers:
I focused on my main city for a bit researching and building until I found myself in a position to expand, which I did. At this point I encountered a neighbour next to me and another a bit far from where I am.
50 turns in one of them declares war on me suddenly with a smaller army than me, but more advanced. I lost my capital. So I reload the save, upgrade my army and still lose it, except he lost most of his as well and was forced to withdraw.
Seeing how I have 3 towns to his 1 I quickly rebuild my army and fight him again. Tie again, and again I rebuild. This time I slowly take ground until I reach his capital, where I notice his army is at sea RIGHT next to my capital. What to do?  I try to negotiate peace but he won't budge. So I start a race to his capital, I attack it about a TURN before he reaches my capital city. BAM I win.
Now I meet some other neighbours. Turns out I'm now at 3rd score (around 400, highest is 600). I make use of this time  to negotiate peace with my first neighbour and focus on trade, research and expansion. Slowly I also build up 2 armies and position them at my borders. I remain at peace for close to 150 turns slowly developing my empire and making sure my armies are a deterrent to anyone who'd declare war. Meanwhile, the 3 remaining players are at war with each other. One of them has a score of 2000 to my 1100 and the others are worn out and remain at 400-500.
At this point, the guy with the 2000 is close to a scientific, expansion, conquest victory and has 50 turns where he'd win. He also conquered one of the players and is waging war with the other to the North (I'm at his East). So sensing the danger, I upgrade all my units, sell excess resources and pump out as much units as possible. I position my 4 armies at the borders with one remaining in reserve. I strategically pick targets whereas he is involved in another frontier. 40 turns left, I declare war.
Blitzkrieg is what happens next. I quickly sweep through his southern and eastern lands and pick off stragglers using combined armies to overrun his better upgraded units. Although he initially had a much better army than me, the tactic I employed significantly crippled him. By the time his northern armies come south I already conquered 3 provinces and I pick them one by one. At this point he is desperate for peace, which I decline. I conquer 3 more provinces and my peaceful neighbor conquers one of his. I decide to plan for the future, so I position 3 armies at the border of my peaceful neighbour and the other 3 to conquer the remaining provinces. Just as I'm about to declare war, what happens? I win.
I literally went from a losing situation to a winning one through good strategy. This is what I'd want in a game, to offer challenges and reward strategic thining. 10/10

This is a great 4x game concept if still a bit rough around the edges.
The good:
* The map is divided into regions, with no more than 1 city/region, with that city having access to all resources in the region--this eliminates city spam.
* Units are grouped into armies, but armies have a max number of units based on current technology--prevents stacks of doom.
* Cities exploit tiles around them by building districts that must be next to the city center or another district--the city gradually works more and more tiles in it's region under player control.
* Armies have something to do even when not at war, exploring ruins, fighting with other factions in neutral regions, and conducting quests.
* Battles are resolved with a decent--but skippable--tactical combat system.
* Tech is non-linear and varied.
* Units are customizable, with new base patterns acquired by assimulating minor factions.
* A number of different paths to victory--military, science, and quest.
* Different factions have huge differences that making playing them basically a completely different game.
The bad:
* Still some significant bugs, including ones that make it impossible to finish a game even from saves.
* No real documentation or tutorial for a lot of the good new concepts--you just have to figure out a lot of things by trial and error.  Though this can also be fun--"Oh, *that's* how that works...."
* The notification system--that a city is not producing anything, or that you aren't researching any tech, is easy to miss, leading to turns of no production and no research unless you remember to check it every turn.
* The AI is pretty weak, and probably always will be, due to the complexity of the options available.
* The UI can be frustrating and confusing.
If you're willing to learn by trial and error as you go, and have a high tolerance for bugs, there are some really good new concepts here.  If not, you might wait a couple of months until some good beginner's guides are written and the game is more stable.
If you do play it now--notifications appear as icons on the right side of the screen.  Make sure you click on every one every turn--they disappear as soon as you hit End Turn.  And the circle around End Turn has an arrow circle icon next to it--click on that every turn to move your armies, or they'll just sit where they are doing nothing.  And use the scroll wheel on your mouse to zoom out far enough that you get the strategic map--that shows you region bondaries, resources, unexplored ruins, etc.

Sometimes, a new game comes out and is in early access/beta testing for a while. You don't buy for early access, even though the reviews are great, mainly because you want to experience the full game. You wait, you buy the game and you are disappointed because the devs have clearly thought "that'll do, it's getting good reviews" They then charge you a fortune for DLCs that make the game up to what it should have been in the first place.
D:OS2 is not like that. It feels complete. The voice acting is superb. The storylines (yes, plural) are great. The combat system has all the things the first game lacked and more. It's different, it's interesting. I am 40hours in and know i've barely scratched the surface. Any bugs (and there are a few, yes) are dealt with and patched really quickly by a super active team.
I almost dont want to talk about the gameplay mechanics or storyline, because i don't want to spoil it, so I'll just say that the variety of character development options is great, the choices in how your storyline goes are genuine and you can basically attack and kill almost any character and the game will deal with it and change the story to suit.
It's a very immersive and enjoyable game. The scaling of difficulty is great, there are so many ways to progress. I can't say enough good things about this game - I paid full price (£30) for this game and it was worth every penny.
One thing does annoy me. Voice acting is great and so immersive, but please please please if you're going to put in a load of (reasonably good) regional British accents then can your actors please learn to say "herbs" like a Brit? It doesn't start with a "U" and it really makes me sad.
Back serious though, if the only downside to a game is one word being said wrong then that doesn't seem bad going to me...

Gotham City Impostors is a competitive multiplayer FPS by Monolith Games, which was enough of a selling point for me, despite admittedly not being much of a multiplayer person. Monolith has been responsible for several of my favorite shooters, from Blood to Shogo to F.E.A.R., and that pedigree certainly comes through in this game. Before I continue, let it be known that the most frequent comparison I've seen has been to Call of Duty, which I've never played multiplayer for any length of time.
First off, the game looks great. The technical side of the graphics aren't phenomenal by 2015 standards, but they more than make up for that in aesthetic. The central conceit is that you are playing street gangs made up of groupies of Batman and the Joker, and as such, the character designs convey the appropriate sense of wackiness. This is met by terrific customization, from weapons skins to individual elements of your character's outfit and body type (The latter serves as the class system, with the chick being fast but fragile and the four male types are various grades ranging from slightly heavier to tank) to their voice pitch and speaking accent. The weapon design feels appropriately sloppy, with bottle rocket launchers and so on. The levels are well designed, and almost all based on trashed urban exteriors, so if that's not your thing look elsewhere. Overall, the maps are all terrific and leave a lot of room for different tactics. Overall, the aesthetic design is unparalleled. Between the psychotic character appearances to the terrific little quips that all of the characters throw out, the theme comes together beautifully. It might be silly for some, but it joins Team Fortress 2 as a great parody of the modern competitive FPS, as well as the Batman mythos.
The shooting feels nice, although the short time to kill doesn't leave much room for error and rewards ambushing tactics. The coolest thing this game does for gameplay is the gadgets. These are movement-oriented items that will serve as your movement technique. The characters move much slower than Quake or UT2K4, but with the gadgets, the speed of the game is increased drastically. I like the Rollerskates, which basically make your character move with the speed and floatiness of a older FPS, although with a little bit less control (It can also lead to ridiculous amounts of knife kills). There's the glider, which does exactly what it says on the tin and also allows you to dive bomb enemies. Another nice one is the grappling hook, which lets you latch on to any surface you can shoot with it. There are a number of these, and the levels are designed with loads of elements that allow you to use them to their fullest, like ramps for the skates or grates with updrafts for the glider. You can tell that this was the focus of the game design, and Monolith did it justice.
The free-to-play model is one of the better ones. The initial loadouts are great and levels come in quick. I haven't spent a dime and I've been competitive against people who are much higher levels than me. In fact, for my light character the starter FPS is fantastic and feels terrific. You'll get plenty of coins for ingame purchases just by playing the game with some small skill.
There are two big things that take away from the game, however. First is the ping. Now, at the time of this writing I currently reside in Hawaii, which is hell for connectivity. In Red Orchestra 2, I have between 150-400 ping. Even so, in Team Fortress 2 and Dirty Bomb, both of which I've been playing recently, I can find 60-90 ping servers pretty easily. In GCI, I couldn't tell you a number. The game rates ping with bars, like a cell phone. When I'm lucky, I get two bars, and most of the time, one. What makes this worse is that GCI there is no server browser that I can find. If the game wasn't so fun, the lack of a server browser would be fatal. It is fun, though, so let me move on.
The second big problem is that at this point GCI is functionally a Team Deathmatch game. There are a number of game types, but no one ever seems to be playing them. It's pretty easy to find a decent TDM game, but it can and will get repetitive for long play sessions and it can really screw over compulsive achievement hunters.
All in all, it's free to play and one of the good ones. The mechanics themselves are excellent, and the Team Deathmatch is always good for a laugh. I recommend it, just don't expect much variety in the modes.

Endless Legend is a continuation (or prelude? The timeline is unclear, in case you are interested in the backstory) of Endless Space and bears distinct similarity with its predecessor. Basically, it is a mixture of Civ5 and HoMaM set in a fantasy world (an industrialized fantasy world).
The game itself is more oriented towards empire building rather than combat; however, you will fight a lot, especially on higher difficulties, where the beefed up AI tends to rush you. EL utilizes the same resource system as ES, also known as FIDS (food, industry, dust, science); this time, we also have an additional resource called "reputation", which you can spend in dealing with other factions, minor factions or on focusing your empire via long time buffs. The strategic and luxury resources are also present - strategic resources are spent on upgrading your units and heroes or building particular structures in your cities; luxury resources, when activated, give a 10-turn long buffs.
The world map is divided into regions you can colonize. Each region can hold only one city and a player in control of such settlement controls the resources in that region. As the city population increases, you have an option to expand the borders of your city (not the region) to make the city more productive. Also, the city sprawl looks very quaint :). There are season changes present in Auriga - summer shifts into Dark season. As you progress through the eras (research and development of your empire), the Dark season ultimately lengthens to a point where summer lasts only a few turns (kind of a soft cap).
Combat is more engaging than in ES, though it is clearly not a main focus of the game. Every turn, you can give orders to your units and when you are done, your minions try to carry those orders. You are unable to interfere when the combat round is proceeding, therefore you need to consider the initiative (the order in which all units act) and terrain - if you order your unit to attack an enemy unit that acts first and retreats, your unit can end up in the middle of enemy army trying to pursuit its target.
Each race can build and deploy three unique units (and a settler); by assimilating a minor race into your empire, you get an option to produce the respective unit (upgrade it, too). If you have enough dust, you can hire mercenaries from the marketplace, but those cannot be upgraded.
Heroes have three skill trees now - army focused (blue), city focused (orange) and general (green). An experienced hero presents a significant boost to your city output (based on the skills taken of course) or for your army. When leading an army, the hero doesn't take a spot in the army cap, but is still deployed on the battlefield as a "free" (an powerful) unit.
Races are quite diverse, with their own unique storylines and special abilities. If you are not happy with the options presented to you, you can create your very own race.
There are currently two big flaws with the game:
1. Optimalization - the game runs smoothly until you attempt Impossible or Endless difficulty on any of the 4-8 maps. The computer tends to stack massive amounts of dust and other resources, along with building large armies. Having a few AI opponents alive doing this results in game freezes, when the game simply refuses to load - I was once waiting for 40 minutes for a safe to load, since it was a scenario on endless difficulty where I was doing well. After said 40 minutes the game still did not load and thus I gave up. Mind you, I have a decent computer that runs smoothly significantly more advanced games. Apparently, this is a known issue, so hopefully a patch will be issued soon.
2. AI - on lower difficulties, AI tends to be sloppy, not building proper defences to its cities, not maintaining decent armies or researching military projects. The AI will still attack you, but if you survive the initial onslaught, you are likely to take all the cities you desire at your leisure. In ES, I liked the fact that in order to conquer a planet or the whole system, you need a large invasion fleet along with your warships - in EL, you are usually opposed just by rather pathetic militia units. In my latest game on serious difficulty, each of my army stacks took one big sprawling city IN ONE TURN, destroying the whole AI empire that had more score points than me in 5 turns.
On higher difficulties, namely Impossible and Endless, the AI is ridiculously buffed. Forget about overtaking the AI economically or scientifically, unless you keep conquering its cities, which is not easy, given the units and heroes are buffed as well. Civilisation used this way of managing difficulty too and I do not like it - it is a lazy way how to provide you with some degree of challenge instead of programming smarter AI.
All in all, a worthy successor of Endless Space; Endless Legend can proudly stand on its own and provide you with hours and hours of good, turn-based fun.

I would highly recommend this game.  It combines elements of a number of my favorite genres into one of the best-looking packages I've ever seen.  I especially recommend it to all my friends who love the Civilization series.
The entire game is gorgeous.  It may not be the most technically advanced game when it comes to graphics (though it makes great use of depth-of-field, and zooming in/out and discovering new areas are impressively smooth), but the visual design is top-notch, and not just with the art for character and environmental designs.  Hands-down, the UI design is the best I've ever seen in anything, period.  The menus look gorgeous and are easy to understand.  Complicated concepts like resources are abstracted and displayed in a way that really pops.  Even when I didn't understand the game, it was fairly easy to learn by doing, thanks to the great interface design.  Whoever did the visual design for Endless Legends should get a medal.  A really pretty medal.
As for gameplay, it's a 4x at its core, with a lot of similarities to Civilization 5.  However, it boils down a lot of the more obtuse and complicated aspects of the genre into something a little more manageable.  A smaller number of meaningful and balanced choices and tradeoffs is the name of the game here, and it makes for riveting gameplay.  The "one more turn" aspect of the genre is in full force here.  Every session so far ends when I finally look at the clock and realize it's 4 in the morning when I thought it was 1 at the latest.
It also adds a nice twist by having an actual battle system.  When two armies meet, their battle isn't decided just by stats.  Instead, you play a tactical turn-based game in the vein of X-Com and Final Fantasy Tactics, where unit positioning and targeting are just as important as the gear and levels you bring to the fight.
Endless Legend also borrows some of the best elements of RPGs.  There are unique hero units you can customize with gear and skill trees as they level, and you can customize every single unit with gear as well.  This allows you to simply upgrade your base units as your technology progresses, or create totally different variations for different purposes.
The game also has a storyline for each of the 8 (or so?) factions you can play as, and it allows you to create custom factions.  Completing the story's questline leads to a victory condition while fleshing out the world and offering a few twists on the way.
Man, this game is really good.  And really, really pretty.  Buy it!

This game is one of the better 4x games that I've ever played. Each faction that I have played has been very different from the ones that came before it, both in aesthetics and gameplay. The world is gorgeous, the art is gorgeous, the diplomacy screens are gorgeous. The game has this unique techno-fantasy feeling going on.
Focus of the game seems to be more on the building than on the heroes, so on the 4x spectrum I would place it closer to civilization than to something like HOMM. The game is a fantasy setting, but there is barely any magic so it also doesn't exactly have the feel of Master of Magic or other fantasy 4x games. Large cities sprawl across the land in a satisfying way, reminding me of what Elemental tried to do but failed at.
Combat is different than other 4x games I've played. It is kind of a tactical/real time hybrid. Each fight is six rounds of issuing orders to your units and then watching the orders resolve. Sometimes the way things play out make slower units unable to carry out their planned orders, so a wrench can be thrown into your movement/attack orders.
I've been playing on standard settings and each game takes about six hours or so. The time just flies away. It's just so damned immersive.

Sonic Mania is, quite honestly, a good game. The level design is, despite what many will claim, something very unique to the Sonic series- a 2D platformer that neither focuses on pure speed nor just platforming. The game's levels can easily be sped through if you're skilled, unlike the actual classic Sonic games, whose levels quickly petered out into very slow and measured platforming. There are also speed sections, areas of the game where Sonic briefly moves at top speed before going back to high-speed platforming. These additions are well spaced out, and do not dominate the game, but help keep Sonic moving quickly across the level, which is really the essence of Sonic- speed and skill, not one or the other.
The only complaint is the bosses. They are, quite frankly, riddled with problems. The sad fact is, they are either very easy, or very hard to figure out the gimmick. This results in the bosses feeling less like challenges and more like a puzzle- what gimmick that goes against normal Sonic gameplay will I have to figure out this time?
My final score: 8/10.

Though the Mania has come and gone like a blue blur of fond memories, Sonic remains eagerly on everyone’s minds with renewed interest and the upcoming game that follows Mania, Sonic Forces. If Sonic Forces is even half-decent of an improvement on Generations, Sonic will truly return to form in 2017—a statement I never thought I would say because, surprisingly, I have never liked Sonic. Even though there have been decent games like the Adventure titles and Generations, no game has truly enraptured me into understanding the admiration of its fanbase than Mania and my recent playthrough of Sonic 3&K.
Prefacing all this information is important because my experience with Sonic is largely due to growing up with his modern games, which, while not as timeless as the classics, are fun in their own shallow ways. This is a statement said not to deride modern Sonic or to create division amongst fans but to build understanding of how to make his 3D games equally in-depth. Mania is more than proof that Sonic can work when done right, and playing it is almost a baptismal event to modern eyes to relearn many design decisions that have become forgotten. In truth, these truths have always been remembered amongst its followers that have inspired the Mania that has created it, and now Sonic Team needs to learn from it to add it to their own games.
In keeping with the religious metaphor (and no, I am not equating Sonic to Jesus), Mania has largely stayed true to form with the teachings of the Genesis titles, and even after twenty-five years these designs remain timeless. These foundations are the cornerstone to what makes Sonic different from other platformers and why, when done right, he can outshine all the others. As with the case of second-hand teachings, these truths have become burdened by misconceptions with time and with different perspectives, and Mania is a true return to form to highlight what has become forgotten.
The first of these misconceptions is the statement that Sonic is about raw speed, not momentum based challenges. Speed is only one component of the Sonic trinity of its design; exploration as well as platforming are also vital to the experience. However, and this is the important part, these elements alone are not what make Sonic great; instead, Sonic is at his best when these three elements are synergized together. This is why the Genesis titles, over time, polished Sonic’s exploration based elements of 1 and CD as well as the speed and the platform-consequences of Sonic 2 into Sonic 3&K that blends everything together. Mania returns to this form by having players utilize speed to reach new heights the modern games have largely forgone as modern Sonic has separated these elements into different playstyles or spectacles of a level rather than keeping them unified.
The second of these changes are the importance of slopes. Modern titles like Generations or the Adventure games largely take away the skill behind slopes with automated loops and speed-boosters supplementing their lackluster physics. Classic titles and Mania fully utilize slopes as a speed/skill challenge players are never forced to utilize, yet, like Sonic’s speed, it’s a double-edge sword that makes his basic platforming more interesting. As Christian Whitehead, one designer of Mania and the man behind the port of Sonic CD, describes in a Rolling Stones article, “It’s all about the natural interaction with the slopes [to enhance Sonic’s basic skillset.] The additional elements that augment that gameplay is what makes a stage novel.” In Mania’s four new zones and remixes of classic areas in their second acts, there is a higher number of slopes compared to the Genesis originals and the modern titles. It’s these elements that add a level of playfulness unrivaled by the conventional Boost formula.
However, as much as slopes are vital to Sonic playing well, the last major feature of Sonic is its level designs. To describe the essence of Sonic at his best is when levels feel like sandboxes where the player never is punished for taking a wrong turn, only rewarded with new areas to explore or new pathways to exploit. Mania’s levels are largely based on areas with no optimal pathway, which encourages a healthy playfulness with its areas on the second, third and even the fourth time. In contrast, modern Sonic stages are more based on Sonic 2 where a player is punished for not taking the optimal pathway with ranks and timers, which heavily discourages exploration. In addition, Mania’s additional characters from S3&K, unlike the different playstyles of the Adventure games, only adds more explorative possibilities rather than restrictions. Levels never restrict players from choosing not to explore nor deny them exploration rewards as neither playstyle is omitted in this manner.
These core tenets are all easy to witness the further you play Mania, and yet it’s so easily forgotten when you return to Sonic’s modern games. These titles choose to pick and choose these elements rather than blending them together. (On top of this issue, no modern Sonic game has solved the dilemma of its lack of camera control, which makes me hopeful that Sonic Utopia will break that barrier.) If these ideas were codified into a modern 3D Sonic game with an emphasis on momentum, slope mechanics and various playstyle environments, then we would truly have a return to the Classic formula that has aged only greater with time.
Never has this line had more relevance today than with Sonic Mania. While Nintendo would rather remove all traces of a fanwork to make their own nostalgia grab, SEGA will utilize the creativity of its fanbase to make nostalgia grabs of their own. Make no mistake about Mania; it is unabashedly a game of pandering to its audience, yet it one-ups itself from being nostalgia bait because the design principles it works on are timeless and they will only become better on introspection in the future. Mania is what new Sonic titles should aspire to be in every regard.
Now the bigger question about Mania is, “Are there any issues with the game itself?” Of course. The pandering can be obtrusive with a few bosses that will show their age due to being uninteresting battles to stand in as obscure references to past games. (However, most bosses are some of the best in 2D Sonic history.) The Drop Dash, a notable inclusion, doesn’t feel as easy to chain together as Sonic Lost World nor the implementation in Sonic After the Sequel DX, and, as a result of its extra button press than simply holding the button like ATSDX, the feature is more of a gimmick than a helpful tool. The unlockable abilities seem like a waste not to make Sonic more interesting to play around with a full ability list with additional buttons and new moves, yet it’s understandable why mechanics like the figure-eight dash are limited to a No Save mode. If Occam told his maturing son how to shave with a razor, he would probably tell him, “Keep it simple, stupid.”
None of these blemishes do not detract from the absolute return to form of Mania, and it is more than simply the result of its hype. Mania will live on by modders who will take all the new sprites to feed into its past games—which is already possible with the conversions available with the addition of the Drop Dash in the Steam Workshop--and into future fan projects that will keep Sonic alive.  Though the fanbase has its share of mania episodes, Sonic Mania is simply a heightened state of euphoria and happiness that never ceases to end until it winds down into an amused smile.

Only If is a free first-person puzzle game. You take control of Anthony, a young man who awakens in an empty bedroom after a long night of partying with his female companion Sam. Soon Anthony is contacted through radio by an angry man named Vinnie and discovers that Sam is missing. Now Anthony has to find Sam and escape the bizarre prison that Vinnie has made for him.
Only If is a game designed to trick and toy with you. The solutions to the puzzles are surprisingly creative. You must scan the environment for clues and use different objects to complete different riddles, allowing you to progress.
The game is divided into two paths. The first path you can choose is well done. Here the game turns full in a dream-like identity.
The second path uses some stealth elements, terribly glitched switch puzzles and environments that never feel fantastic or dream-like.
To finish the whole game with both paths takes something between 2 and 3 hours.
Graphics and voice acting are good, nothing really big to complain about.
Only If has some good aspects but also some bad (second path) In my opinion it is still worth playing, it is free, so why not?

Game with great potential! Very fun as an idea but falls short and I was very hopeful until just now when i read the recent patch notes which didn't address a single one of the following issues.
-The resource gathering is not engaging. No skills or even progression in resource gathering... Skilling up merely allows you to process the next item tier. Everything requires about 10 minutes of farming wood ( bassically clicking trees ) before you can craft with them. Processing these items into something usable takes another 10 minutes... WITH NO QUEUING. This means if you have to make 50 stone bricks or 50 iron Ore or whatever... you have to sit there and click the icon every 15 seconds. Autoclickers help but why do we have to bother with setting any of that up??
-Combat is not engaging. You bassically face your target and click... no skills... no progression. On top of that you have to deal with the terrible lag which means most attacks will not even register because of server desync, and you will have to do all your fighting while standing still.
-Nothing is worth killing... nothing... Bears were for a little while when you need oil and HQ oil... but other than that, nope. Most mobs drop coins which is the currency that is used mainly to repair buildings and you only need to kill about 10-20 things to get enough to repair your base fully. There are however, about 5 items that requires you to farm a specific mob that will require you about 1hour to just get to, kinda cool but bleh that time sink! OH let me say it again... there is no reason to pve in this game. The only pve available is an event that spawns a bunch of mobs to attack your base. Its novel and can be fun but the only reward is bassically resources to build a bigger base to fight against bigger attacks... This is not content, there is no strategy or skill involved in any of it... bassically build more walls and turrets win game!
-Coins(the intended currency) are worth very little. you can buy items from player made shops but since coins are so useless, most shops are not replenished and in the event someone is selling something you want, you have to travel to said shops to buy. Sooooooo.... if you actually do find something you want, this translates to about 30minutes to an hour to run there just to buy it.
-If nobody in your guild logs on, your base will slowly decay. Meaning you have about a week before someone will have easy enough access to pillage literally everything no matter how big your base is. This doesnt mean you simply have to log on but you literally have to be near the base to stop this despawning. Multiple bases or outposts are never ever worth it. Destroyed buildings also only have 24 hours to be repaired before vanishing. So don't ever go on vacation or anything or you lose stuff!
-pvp is bassically impossible because of dsync. Its still kind of fun to clash sometimes, but unfortunately, however good your gear is, it will bassically come down to who has more bandages and ginseng - meaning if someone is prepared to fight you and you are farming... you will always lose. Plus numbers matter... a lot... a lot lot and it doesnt make sense to farm together because resources are spread out, so you will get ganked, and you will probably have no chance
So besides all that, it can be a fun game still, I cleared a lot of hours, albeit a lot of those hours are spent logged in afk waiting for criminal rating to go down. There is great potential here, and if you read all that and still want to give it a try, go for it! If you have a small group it can be lots of fun for a bit but you wont find players to group with in game, and you wont find any end game. You might still get your 20 bucks worth out of it, but I feel you should know these things because there was an update from the devs about long term goals that did not adress a single one of these issues so dont say you werent warned. Gooduck!!
ps. I see a lot of complaints about theives but honestly this is not a huge problem and i'd like to give my 2 cents. If you are smart you will learn how to make yourself a difficult target for them (DO NOT BUILD GATES UNTIL YOU LITERALLY HAVE THE BEST LOCKS, instead just build walls and ladders ). The system does favor theiving, but danger is the only thing that makes this game fun! Safety lies in numbers... do not solo... make sure someone checks your base daily! Use your resources before logging off or log off with rares and you will not experience crippling losses.
pss. They are planning on releasing the game in 6-9 months so expect another wipe then.

Early Access Review: Bought Deluxe edition before F2P version came out.
Off hand I have to say it's a decent little game.
The game has some decent strategy in the single player campaign.
Graphics are good, audio could use a bit of work. (Mission statements being voiced, guns sound a bit off.)
The single player could be fun once it has some work done to it; even in its current state it's playable & feels like a squad based RTS game.
However the single player could really use some tutorial missions. Trying to figure out all the controls on your 1st go is difficult; I had to resort to looking at the key bindings just to figure out how to change the controls of the humvee because I got "stuck" in... direct control I think? I'd call it first person.
Now the part the developers are crying about... the multiplayer.
I don't doubt the multiplayer will be fun (I'll probably never play it as my friends don't play this type of game) since it shows various game modes that typical online shooter games have. Examples are deathmatch or hold flag areas.
It also has built in LAN & AI support... something every game should have & something that will make this game a long lasting game... however I haven't tested it with out internet yet to ensure it doesn't need the central server to start. Dedicated server files that one could download & run separately would go along way in player confidence.
HOWEVER.
The multiplayer is most definitely pay to win. He who holds the most $ will win.
The transactions, and I don't think you can even call them micro, cover all sorts of things... such as emoticons for chat, free experience, clan symbols etc.
Prices range with a quick glance showing prices upwards of $6 CDN.
At this point in time I do think the game is worth supporting; but buy it for the single player & don't bother with playing multiplayer with anyone who isn't a friend... the store takes the equality out of it.
(Also when I tried playing it now the public lobby, which was joined automatically, had 33 players in it... none of whom said anything. Not a lively community off hand.)
Over all: Recommend... get something with single player. Ask developers to post dedicated server files that don't require Steam to use.

I'm going to start this off by saying that Warframe is an INCREDIBLY grindy game, it's a literal farm/grindfest, so of course, this game won't be something nice for lots of people, however, if you decide to stick around, then here is my review of Warframe.
[NEGATIVES]
-Warframe is extremely grindy, as said before.
-It doesn't do a very good job of explaining things to new players, the tutorial will teach the basics of sprinting, jumping shooting, and stuff like that, but doesn't really explain all of it, leaving the player to figure it out for themselves, with this, the best source of information would be the fan wiki, it has everything, to the advanced maneuvers like bullet jumping (crouch+jump) to the drop chance of mods. With that in mind, let's move into the the next thing.
-It will take a while to farm/craft things, farming not as much, since you get a lot of resources from missions, but crafting however will take time, first of all, once you have the right resources to build something, such as an alternate helmet for your Warframe, it will take time, real world time, 12 hours to fully build, after that has gone by, you can than get your helmet, time varies, going from 1 minute to craft a key, to 3 whole days to build a Warframe, don't worry though, it still progresses the time even if you're playing a different game or even offline, so if you have multiple things waiting for you, but have to go somewhere few days, when you come back they'll be done.
[POSITIVES]
-The movement, the movement is part of why this game is so fun to play, you really do feel like a space ninja flying through the air killing enemies with one bullet, the game makes you feel so mobile and swift, you feel like a snail playing something like Destiny or CoD, there's a lot of movement in the game, so that when you watch a new player for the first time, it's weird, because they're not spending half their time in the air or sliding past enemies, you're like "Yep, definitely a newbie"
-Gunplay, the gunplay is so fun because there's a variety of weapons available to you, from scythes to bows to snipers to dual swords to tonfas, the list goes on and on, the only reskins are different variants of weapons but look so cool you forget that their reskins, same with enemies, except for variants, no reskins. All weapons in Warframe will probably make you feel strong, some may make you feel weak, but every gun is still good if you mod it right, including the ones you get at the tutorial.
-Customisation, the sheer amount of customisation is insane, you can spend literally hours doing nothing but colouring your Warframe, ship and weapons, putting decorations up, choosing how those some things are placed, the way they're sized, it's honestly amazing.
-Story, at first, Warframe's story just seems like "Kill all the villains on every planet and bring peace" or something like that, but then, going across the way to unlock Pluto, it says "Complete Quest: The Second Dream", thinking that it's just some Warframe quest or crappy lore quest, you do it, but then it happens, you see that cliched story turn into something amazing, and well, play the quest for yourself and be amazed.
-No Pay2Win Elements, at first you start off with 50 Platinum, the premium currency, going into the Arsenal or Market, everything must be bought with Platinum, you think that you can get it from killing bosses and such, but nothing happens, you see that the only way to get Platinum, is to pay, and one day, going into trading chat, you see something along the lines of WTS [Opticor Acricron] 200p, and you realise, trading, farm for good gear, then sell it to players for Platinum, and so, you realise that this isn't pay to win, this is just grindy.
And there it is, my review of Warframe, in my opinion, Warframe for me is the best Free2Play game released, the community is great and will help out new players, which i forgot to mention, theres so much content in the game its impossoble to beat all of it in at least 6 months, I highly recommend this game it's amazing and I hope you think so too.

Mount Your Friends was released in the absurd indie frenzy, alongside titles like Goat Simulator and Surgeon Simulator 2013. Mount Your Friends is just as nonsensical as those games, but also features simple and suprisingly addicting gameplay.
Its a very simple mechanic; you control the appendages of your players, and you want to climb up a tower and reach new heights. At first the tower is a perched goat, but when the first player "mounts" the goat, he becomes the new vertical record, and then the bodies continue to pile up. By pressing the corresponding buttons for each limb, you "unsticky" that limb from whatever it was attached to and move it around to reach another ledge. Much like other physics-influenced games like QWOP, the controls seem unintuitive at first, but with a little practice you will find yourself flinging your character up the bodies of your competitors.
The single player modes are plentiful but barebones, which is to be expected. There is, however, a surprisingly large amount of multiplayer modes available in Mount Your Friends; the only problem is that they are all restricted to local multiplayer. There are virtually only two modes for the multiplayer lobbies (2-4 players); vertical tower building, and stretching horizontally to create a bridge. There are various settings you can mess with, but these are the only modes available online.
Another big feature of Mount Your Friends is the ability to completely customize your character. If you can create head-shaped images and a collection of images for the stomach, torso, legs and arms, you can add those to the Mount Your Friends custom directory and create a player from those images. But again, the games online functionally is limited because your competitors will have to have the same files with the same file names to see your custom players.
When this game says a gamepad is recommended, it isn't joking. A mouse and keyboard are playable but you are severely limited in which acrobatics you can perform. You will become more proficient with 2 joysticks and 4 instantly recognizable buttons. I know where the WASD keys are, but it still takes me second to remember which one is which.
Despite a few multiplayer limitations. Mount Your Friends is an exceptionally goofy and entertaining game with simple controls that are difficult to master. Buy a 4 pack when you can and enjoy it with a few of friends. Expect a solid 10 hours of fun out of it.

Recommend YES (but also NO)
I bought Crusader Kings II and huge bundle of the DLC during one of the previous seasonal Steam sales. Even then it was on the pricier end of the game scale but I'd heard such great things about the game that I took the plunge.
A quick breakdown:
The game. At it's best it is amazing. Hilarious, intricate and diverting. It's almost as fun to lose as it is to succeed and that is a very impressive feat for a game to achieve. The game designers and writers should be celebrated for their work on the game.
The community. People love this game and pour a lot of effort into it. They are happy to share information and build excellent mods to give the game new and creative life (the Game of Thrones and Avatar: Last Airbender ones in particular).
The developer. Questionable business model and extremely poor relationship with its player base. This is not an understatement. Their players actually HATE them!
I explain this further below.
Even at the time I purchased CK2, the ire was building against Paradox, in particular against a DLC policy that often released DLC when it wasn't ready for market and then charged separately for the aesthetic embellishments that should have been included with the respective DLC (these are the so-called Portrait Packs). Prices for these are generlly more than is justifiable. As a result many players wait for the sales to purchase those DLC add-ons that the community deem worthy (Reaper's Due being the last of these). Sale discounts are generally never better 50% and usually hung at 33% for more recent DLC.
To give context, when I bought this 5 year-old game and the DLC I wanted, even with the 50% discount, it cost me over $60 CDN.
Shortly before the 2017 Summer Sale, Paradox hiked the prices on the base game for several countries, Canada included ($43.99 to $51.99 for the exact same 5 year-old game, with no tangible updates outside of the premium DLC not included).
The price in the US was not raised. Hikes in some other countries were much worse as I understand it.
Paradox claims that this has to do with the "purchasing power of the currency." And this may be so. However, in light of the already poor relationship they have with their players, this has kicked off a huge anti-Paradox campaign. Checking the RECENT REVIEWS, you will see how they have revolted. I don't really blame them.
The CEO subsequently decided to rollback the price hike decision (although not during the Summer Sale — so don't bother buying now unless you want to pay more). He also circulated a letter explaining his error in not being more transparent about the pricing changes and that he would be more upfront in the future (from which we can infer that the price hikes will be back in some form in the future — once they figure out how to do it without the blowback).
There was also some Travis Kalanik-esque beligerence about the DLC model.  All told, it was a kind of "I'm sorry, I'm not sorry" sort of letter. In general, this characterizes most of the communication between the company and the players.
Had these price hikes come from a company not known for nickel-and-diming their player base (ie. charging for aesthetic upgrades that would have been parcelled into the DLC by any other company), it's unlikely the backlash would have been so severe. Hell, if Paradox made the least effort to show their loyal community some genuine love (here's some free stuff people who have blown hundreds of dollars on our products) maybe we'd let them charge us even more. But they don't.
What they do is make you feel BAD about buying a game you like and suspicious of any changes they make to the games or pricing structure. And that's too bad because they make some good games.
CK2 won me over and I have been interested in picking up Europa Universalis and Stellaris (although I hear it isn't quite up to the level of the other two titles). Problem is I don't have much faith or goodwill towards the developer. So, unless I see some unprecedented discount or a significant course change in their player relations, I doubt they'll be getting more of my money. There are other good games out there, where the companies make me feel good about investing in their work.
So YES to the game itself, but NO to the games that Paradox plays.
And because the corporate policies spoil the experience of a good game, several people high up the corporate ladder should be apologizing to the people who made this game and the people who have played it so loyally.

Fantastic game and a masterpiece. While some of the voice acting and graphics are bad and outdated, the storytelling and the gameplay bring out the brilliance of this game. The lore of this game brings you into it's world and makes you feel as the adventurer you are playing as. Gameplay is well engaging except for some problems that affects leveling and monster scaling. Monster scaling was not implemented well, I personally had no problems with it but I know of past horror stories of "facing certain monsters is hard" or "the monsters were too easy once I started leveling". Certain scaling elements slow down the battling but not much that causes this game to be unplayable.
The main story writing is great as it shows how you are not the main character but as the catalyst that brings the Oblivion Crisis forward. Each of the Guild's storytelling try it's best to make you a part of the guild. Each guild has different strengths and helps raise your character for leadership. Each of the DLC's has the Bethesda touch to them. A couple masterful story-based DLC and immersion DLC. A lot of people could argue that the Shivering Ilses DLC is better than the base game.
Each character has their own backstory and motavation that is found out. Dialogue in-game is some of the best writing in any game. Sadly some characters lose their impact because of the voice direction choice, of each race having the same voice character with not many pitch or tone changes. But several characters stand out. The skill and attribute system is somewhat towards the classic RPG feel and actually effects your character in-game. Animations in the game are not super diversed but is immersive. After puttting in a lifetime of hours in Oblivion in all platforms PC is the ultimate tier of playing this game. Not only does PC help strenghten what consoles failed to work with being on PC offers mods. Mods also offer ways to fix the usually Bethesda glitches and mechanics. Mods have been made for more than 7 years now and is still being made today. Any RPG fan should definitely play this game and live through it's worlds.
I could just sit here and tell you what Oblivion did better than Skyrim or Morrowind or tell you what Skyrim or Morrowind did better than Oblivion. But there is no reason, they might be continuations in the series and its lore but each game should be measured by themselves rather than the other games in the series.

I gotta say I'm actually completely surprised with this game. I half-expected a game that only feels like it's jsut trying to be another Civ game, but what I got was a game that does draw inspiration from Civ 5, but doesn't really feel similar.
First off, alot of the things that really annoyed me about Endless Space are no longer here. Actually none of them are.
1. The AI is actually less stupid and basic and WAY less hard to fight at Easy difficulty.
2. The game's combat system uses none of that stupid freaking card crap from Endless Space which is always better to go without in my opinion, making victory more about strategy and less about chance. Combat has about as much chance as Civ 5 or any 4X game has.
3. The game doesn't feel or seem like it's trying to be Civilization 5, or trying to sell itself as such, instead this game feels like it's actually on it's own ground, although connected to Civ 5, that's not remotely bad however.
The UI from Endless Space is the only reason I still occasionally played it, but now that this game is out and has an even better version of it, which has only very tiny differences to make it all the more better, I've got no reason to play Endless Space anymore.
The game's handling of city's makes things much less complicated in one way while allowing more complication in another way.
Each region can only have a single city, but the game is set up into multiple regions. Each city's limits are capped at the edges of a region, and the city limits are expanded using burroughs.
This makes a sort of promise that you'll be spending less time worrying about city placement in relation to the other cities on the map, but it makes he same promise that you'll be spending more time in macro managing your cities over time.
The game (like Civ) has many resources and special tile benefits that (if worked) bestow huge bonuses to a city, and ofcourse in turn, your empire.
Unlike Civ however, there are no gimmicky things which give you bonuses over others or makes your life more difficulty if not utilized, such as Culture, Tourism or Religion, there also is no ability to move over water tiles however as the regions always end after the first water tile of any palce's coast.
The usual difficulties from endless Space are there, and if anything, this game has a bit of a sense that it's like a prequel to Endless Space, most likely intended due to the title of this game and Endless Space.
In my opinion... This game is fun, it's rather challenging with the Minor races sometimes getting very aggressive at random times, the other civilizations seem to be less warmongering (unless you're the Necrophages, you know... the Krogan disease from Mass Effect, only with undead) in comparison to their previous game, and that is honestly really quite nice.
The way the game handles technology is awesome, and I wish other games did such. The game's technologies are split up into 4 Eras. researching 9 in one era will unlock the next and advance you to it, and so on until the 9th (where I imagine techs to get a science victory would be possible.
The game has none of the dead wonders you could find in Space, thank the gods as in my opinion, they detracted and were often not worth restoring unless you could manage 20 turns of getting something that would boost only approval, or would boost science just a bit.
My first game with 5 others took 4 hours and it's not even over yet, I've yet to get past the 2nd Era, but that is mostly due to the fact i spent 100 turns with 1 city, and that's never something you wanna do honestly.
Overall, the game's very fun, original in it's own ways and has enough bits from Endless Space that it enhances what's already there, as certain aspects of Endless Space were already great, and... well why not use what's already great in another Turn-based game right?
There's some things I haven't said like the factions, or how there's heroes and how they're awesomely powerful, but I highly recommend you to atleast play it for yourself, you will enjoy what you see and experience. If you have doubts, then just ask a friend to play their copy, or do some research with gameplays and other reviews.
My final Verdict for this game, is an 8/10, it's honestly one of the most fun 4X games I've played in a while for the first time.

Endless Legend is to Endless Space, as Warhammer is to Warhammer 40 Thousand. Except Endless is actually relative to all the games. They all connect in some way, and they are similar. Lovely UI, look wise
Specific Graphics, sharp edges except for units and some factions
Well science trees and techs, if some are illogical
An EXP system for next to every unit, I think, anyway.
Nuetral
Everything is explained by the magical essense called Dust.
Smart AI
Enough variety that a single strategy may not work every time.
Bad
Quests, sometimes they require you to achieve or do something, that is not actually possible for a very long time. IE, a quest recieved on turn 5 may not be fulfilled until turn 50.
Lore breaking, I suppose? Lore tech- Vaulters survive, and are a faction in Endless Space, which takes place in 3000, EL takes place very early.
Random surroundings. A dirt field having a random tile of sand, or a desert, sand or ice, having water.
