YOu can go through teh screens and menus and get more detailed info but I for one don't like being bogged down trying to discover why something is happening when i just want to play. As for playing the game.... the quest system adds a cool element to the usual explore and expand mechanics these games have and the minro factions with their own motivators are interesting. The different ways you can interact with other empires and minor factions is cool. Kill them, Bribe them or do something nice for them. It allows for differing play styles as opposed to the usual conquer, conquer, conquer cycle that some of these games fall into. I am always impressed by those early access projects that understand a game needs to be fun and playable in order to get good feedback and Endless Legend achieves this easily. The mechanics of the game's system is somewhat similar to Pillars of Eternity, in that your character's stats function in terms of percentages and there is a skill system of sorts that you build from 1 and up. It is an open classless system where, while one selects a few options as a baseline at character creation, one is free to invest in any of a full variety of skills over the course of the character progression. However, it does turn out that, at least from an optimization or min/max perspective, maxing the Warfare skill ends up being the default choice for builds that care about damage. There are a few other potential balance issues with the skills, but that's the big one.
The overall combat difficulty in this game seems to be harder than one has probably come to expect from most new RPG's, even on classic mode (the equivolent of the "normal" setting), though things can get easier as one learns and exploits the system. But, especially when approaching it on my first playthrough, I too often found myself putting it on story mode ("easy") to overcome otherwise tough battles. I dislike doing such a thing in an RPG. It feels cheap, But I found myself doing it. The dual physical and magic defense system is simple and functional, though perhaps it is not the most nuanced or fun basis for combat in the way that it works. Combat becomes a matter of destroying enemy defenses in order to leave the enemy vulnerable to taking damage.
There is an attempt to have a little dialogue depth when talking with companions and important NPC's. I would say the dialogue and roleplay involved in it is okay. Nothing super immersive and detailed, nothing like a Torment game or a Dragon Age: Origins, but it's there more than would be the case in a more pure action RPG. There is some choice and consequence based on certain dialogue choices. Your companions have distinct back-stories and personal goals, and stories of their own that can play out over the course of the game. Further, due to the 4 character party limit, there is a little bit of replayability in terms of playing with different companions.
One of the problems with the game is that there simply is not enough explicit direction for the character to be able to follow or complete quests, since there are no quest markers and not much in the way of detail in the journal. Sometimes this is the case in such a way that breaks certain quests because of timing and choice/consequence issues. In and of itself, I don't object to a lack of quest markers or the idea of having the player have to work for things a little. But while it isn't much of an issue in the early game, by the mid to late game I found myself with a journal half filled with unfinished quests simply because I had no clear idea or memory of exactly where the characters I'm supposed to talk to are, or because I had progressed too far doing other quests and missed a vital quest cue or one-shot oppurtunity.
On a 1-10 scale, I'd give it an 8/10.

This game is profoundly impressive. There is such an abundance of content and ways of just figuring how to approach it. There are so many choices to be made inside the game, whether how I want to build my character's stats and abilities, how I want to approach someone diplomatically, how I want to go about figuring out a puzzle. The game does not punish you for being creative at all and very much rewards it. At one point in the game I was approached with a complex puzzle that involved getting pipes to deliver a certain type of element to special bowls on the ground. Instead of doing the puzzle I just teleported through the barrier and blasted the bowls with spells. It worked.
The game is difficult, in the way quests are handled (Very few quest markers, directions are often more like hints) and the combat (A.I will read your characters like a book and they know how to hurt your team.) Every fight is rewarding and satisfying and if certain fights got too difficult I could just run away and come back better and stronger. I admittedly am a bit of a casual when it comes to games and I love to find the easy way out or give up when things get tough and I felt like that wasn't punished here. I stumbled my way through the entire game and it felt right. I save scummed every encounter and god damn it I was proud to do so.
If you think this game is not for you, I'd tell you you'd have to try it first. I was hesitant to get this game but its reviews and constant praise eventually convinced me otherwise and I picked it up while it was on sale. It was worth every moment, every dollar. I would buy this game again just to say I did. I've just finished my first playthrough and I'm getting ready for my second and I expect a completely different experience.

If you want a quality game without tons of random nuances, please buy the Divinty: Original Sin 1. This game butchered a lot of that game's charm, but quickly cut off its face and wore it around as a facade. Sourcery feels flat and weak, and almost entirely pointless at times due to it just being sucked out of you like nothing by most every enemy you come across (not to mention they're oftentimes weak and eat your AP like no tomorrow when you can do comparable damage or effects for the same amount AP). Some of the combat scenarios you will go through are also just tedious and can take upwards of an hour and a half per fight even when you are spending less than two minutes per character turn.
Slight Edit: The difficulties are also superficial in their differences. Tactician spouts on about in its description about how enemies have special effects and think more about their moves. In truth, the enemies have double your base stats: double vitality, phys. and magic armor, and quite often double your damage. They also commonly outnumber you meaning that you are up♥♥♥♥♥♥creek without a paddle. The first voidwoken you spot upon landing on the beach have "vampire" which lets them lifesteal damage they do. Some enemies have a bonus spell that 'spices' things up (usually a summon or something else of the sort that also has double your stats). It's not even a fair way to play the game, because you often have to abuse game mechanics and essentially cheat with quicksaves and quickloads to get anywhere. I am by no means a noob at this game either. I played a coop save with a friend in the first original sin where we both picked lone wolf, which rendered us locked to a two man party. We functioned as a team and got through the playthrough easy peasy as a first playthrough. That was a fair challenge. This game's difficulties are nothing more than jokes to play on people expecting a tactical difference in how the AI functions.
The biggest kicker, and the most apparent reason for my negative review is that the game is HORRIBLY optimized for Radeon cards. I have an AMD Radeon R9 Fury Sapphire and it absolutely begins to cook under the pressure of this game's coding. Within six minutes of starting the game, mind you this is only at the main menu, my graphics card's temperature jumps from 54 degrees Celsius to 72 degrees. Six minutes. On the menu. I have a water cooling system and near to seven fans in my PC that are all optimized to keep my tower as cool as possible. For comparison, I can play Doom on Ultra graphics at 1920x1080 resolution for hours without my PC trying to become an easy bake oven. The problem persists even on the lowest graphics settings as if it just wants to fry my GPU (once again, something that happens in no other game regardless of graphics settings). This game is absolutely a hog, and even the devs know it because they always talk about needing to remove peripherals from your USB or shutting off all non-essential programs. What is this: a pre-flight check-up? Just program your game better and give AMD cards a fair chance with optimization.
This problem is not just me either. Many other AMD users, based on community posts, support tickets, and forum posts, have had similar issues are just being flat-out unable to play the game because it crashes their graphics drivers. If you are an AMD user, avoid this game and buy its predecessor- a game you will enjoy far more. This might seem like pointless ranting, but as a consumer who has tested multiple things to adjust how this game functions. When I can't even play the game with my friends for more than a couple hours at a time (and at risk for damaging my PC) then this game has serious problems.

Act of War: Direct Action is a military strategy game developed by Eugen Systems. Eugen Systems are the developer of games such as the Wargame series and R.U.S.E. The game is set in an unknown period though seems to be set around the 1990s-early 2000s. A global energy crisis occurs and the uprise of terrorist organisations allow them to use the crisis to their advantage to gain publicity. However, suspense is great as to revealing whether a president of an existing major oil company was in charge of the crisis and the uproar of terrorist attacks. You, the player take control of Task Force Talon to fight back the terrorist threat that is secretly hitting many American nations including San Francisco, Washington D.C. among other worldwide nation states.
The game sounds great on paper but the question of does it live up to that expectation is present. And yes, I can simply say that this game immerses the player into the story through the games mix of in-game cut scenes and a real-life movie. Instead of in-game cut scenes during each mission there will be a live movie playing that continues the story through actors. I really like this approach to the cut scenes because this game was released in 2005 and in-game cutscenes would have been dull at best. Therefore by placing actors to enhance and further the story it allows for more elements and reach in the story compared to in-game cinematics.
According to the game mission selection feature there are 33 missions. These missions are crafted with profound engagement and are relatively simple. The main missions are solid. They progress the story, are intense, and they are entertaining. As the game progresses the missions and story improves in quality. Missions would include taking a stronghold and/or defending your base or secondary missions of destroying field generators to assist in your main mission. The use of secondary missions are substantial as just mentioned as if you complete them they provide benefits. For example, destroying enemy field generators help in limiting the enemy weapons. Or capturing a bank would provide more money for your base to build troops, among others. I completed the game in about 13.5 hours on normal difficulty. Each mission had an appropriate length of completion whilst varying in difficulty.
The gameplay is your typical gameplay for a strategy birds-eye view game. You control multiple units and move them along the battlefield while completing your objectives. It is good at best at times, however the pathfinding can be ridiculous. For one having many vehicular units is annoying because they get caught over little objects like civilian vehicles. Moving the units is annoying as there are no options for formations to move your best units at the front followed by your weaker/more useless units. So other than those two complaints gameplay was good.
The graphics are pretty solid for a 2005 game. They flourish in showcasing the buildings, locations, and capturing the various locations. The sound is pretty annoying including the main menu theme. I liked the dialogue in the game quite a bit. The dialogue is short, sweet, engaging and intense, which improved the quality of the story.
Towards the technical aspect things are not so great. There is no full screen option in the game. The game is capped at 1280x720. However, the limited resolution is understandable for an 11 year old game and there is a mod to allow for higher resolutions. You cannot access steam overlay, which is a real nuisance. Basically if you want to talk on steam or do anything else on your computer while you play you have to quit the game as minimising will not work. It is a major nuisance as specified but if you are playing for multiple hours at a time it does not overly bother you. And there are framerate hitches when moving along the map or selecting other parts of the map.
Lastly the game was recently updated to allow for Windows 10. Fair to say it works like a breeze.
Overall, Act of War: Direct Action is a very unfamiliar game amongst people on Steam judging by its 80 reviews. But for $2.99, I totally recommend this game. You will get a lot of value out of the game with multiple game modes but you will enjoy the story and the gameplay aspect of the game. The rating is low due to its technical issues but I can't penalise it overly due to its age. In saying that, the positives are strong. 6.75/10.

The core concept of this game is fun. It's a pacey shooter with funny costumes, silly sound clips and an overall hilarious setting. Two groups of vigilantes (Joker and Batman inspired ones) fight for objectives or simply shoot, stab, slash and bombard each other with parrots (yes, parrots) until one wins. It's hilarious, doesn't take itself too seriously and creates an enjoyable environment for what could be one of the best casual shooters out there. Of course, it is not - but let's focus on the good things first.
The customization options - from body type to weapon mods - are a nice touch that lets you adjust your character to your play style with more than just a simple gun selection. And then there's the clothes, voice and 'calling card' - cosmetics, but hilarious ones, adding to the overall fun. You unlock everything by simply playing the game and getting experience, levels and costume points, as well as from random drops ingame - provided you're quick enough to pick them up and don't get shot, stabbed or exploded in the process.
The pace is frantic. There's a lot of running, roller skating, trampoline jumping and bat suit divebombing to be done. The maps are complex enough to turn many matches into fast, chaotic chases or endless brawls. Once again, pure fun. The game invites you not to take it too seriously and enjoy yourself, getting a laugh as much from your deaths as you do from the kills. It works, at least for a while.
The game has a cash shop. Yes, yes, cash shops make people cringe - but since you ca unlock pretty much every element that influences gameplay just by playing, the cash shop is mostly a vanity thing, which is brilliant! Love the game? Want to spice it up? Buy funny clothes. Want to speed up your progression just a little bit so you can get a few more unlocks? Get the XP or costume point boost - but don't worry, no matter what you do or do not do, it's your skill and the time spent playing the game (map knowledge and the knowledge what kind of kit to run on a map are key) that make the game. This is in no way a pay to win game - it's a pay to look silly game. And that's GOOD.
Between being able to unlock pretty much everything in the game, the short, frantic matches and its unique humour and cartoony visuals, Gotham City Impostors has everything it takes to keep people coming back, spamming game after game, trying to sneak in "just another match", etc. It's fast, funny, entertaining and while not pretending to be anything other than a casual, quirky shooter, it does what it's meant to do excellently. In fact, I can't remember a single FPS that made me laugh as much in such a short time.
HOWEVER.
There is another side. Certain aspects - most notably, the human factor, but one that COULD be influenced - take away a LOT from the game itself.
Firstly, although the game has several fun game modes (plus single player challenges), you're pretty much forced to play nothing but deathmatch. Only deathmatch. All the time. Why? Because if you want to try other modes, you'll sit in queue and more often than not, give up after 15 minutes or so of not finding a game. And while deathmatch is fun - it's the least original of the game modes. It would be great to play any of the three other modes. Except you can't. Because nobody does. And that's where things get boring. Spamming deathmatch after deathmatch slowly turns this otherwise fun, creative and original game into yet another grindy, generic shooter. I hear you saying "But if it's what the people want..." - yeah, it is. People go for the safe options. But if you offer prizes, achievements and other things to pull them towards other game modes, they may change their minds once giving other options a try. It's a waste of a fun game to spam nothing but deathmatches.
Secondly, the matchmaking. See... all too often I (a miserable level 1, 2, 3...) was matched against a bunch of level 50+ players, or even more. What does that mean? It means more unlocks of course, which means they may have kits better suited to maps. And with a limited number of maps, it also, more importantly, means they know the maps better. And, also worth mentioning, they have hours and hours of experience with the game. So while everyone at around my level or perhaps a little higher is frantically running around, brawling etc., the lv. 90 sits in just the right spot to pick people off with a sniper. Or worse, the lv. 200 systematically runs around, taking out the entire enemy team one by one, again and again, ending with a ridiculous score like a 50/2 when the next highest kdr is 10/5. It becomes frustrating for the lower level player... and it happens over and over and over again. Bad matchmaking has been known to kill good games before.
Thirdly - voice chat. Now, let's be honest. Voice chat is, was and always will be one of the worst, festering, gangrenous cancers lumps ever integrated into shooters. It made games like Counter-strike or CoD the incredibly unpleasant environments that they are today. And once you hear the kiddy voice that can't be more than 10 years old shriek "putaine" (however you spell that) for the umpteenth time, your ears ringing from the high pitch and the rage ridden frenchyness that can only be rivalled by a babbling, fuming, russian, spoken by someone probably frothing at the mouth or gargling vodka mixed with toothpaste, you realise - this adds nothing to the game. You have no idea what they're saying, it's probably something about your female parent unit, and it prevents you from focusing on your play OR on how fun and silly the game is. Voice chat in competitive FPS environments pretty much makes sure that a potentially fun game becomes a toxic cesspit of fecal feeders gargling stale vomit. And once again, yes, the players (used to games that think they gain something - play calling? LOL! - with such systems) may "want" it. But it doesn't have to be implemented and frankly, it ruins the fun whenever someone actually decides to use it.
I give this game a 6/10 overall. Worth trying, but certainly not worth investing money into it via the cash shop because the downsides will likely not keep you hanging around or coming back enough to justify any purchase.

While I originally liked this game and thus you can see how much I have played, recently the developers have made changes which make their claims that this is a sandbox survival MMO into bold faced lies!
Sandbox - a style of game in which minimal character limitations are placed on the gamer, allowing the gamer to roam and change a virtual world at will has been severely limited and seems destined to further restrictions.
Survival -  games start the player with minimal resources in a hostile, open-world environment, and require them to collect resources, craft tools, weapons, and shelter, and survive as long as possible. In ToL the only real danger is other players and now with the faction system there is no more risk, just stay in the passive faction and you can not be attacked.  And you can still roam the map griefing other players without fear of reprisals.
MMO - if and only if, 30-40 people playing in the world after 2 months is massive then this game qualifies, but the total number of players left is less than 100 combined from all 3 servers.  You can run all around and never see another player.
It seems abundantly clear from such things as the DLC's where this $20.00 game has a backpack that costs $15.00 and a mount that costs $25.00; that the developers have no intention on putting together a game meant to entertain players.  Instead they seem to have worked out a clever scam to get players to pay the low introductory price and then con them out of the other $40.00, then alienate the player base and get a new crop of suckers to fall for the scam.

Velocibox is a game that comes with one of the simplest ideas you could ever come up with, a cube, sliding through a rectangular tunnel full of obstacles, with 2 ways to avoid obstacles: steering and flipping.
The game so far is one of the hardest I ever played, never reached level 4 and probably never will (there are 9 total levels...) but even if you fail countless times, playing still is totally enjoyable and flipping the box makes your brain go crazy with directions: when you flip the box from "floor" to "ceiling", reversing everything, it takes quite some time (and countless fails) to get it accustomed to that. I personally like when things mess with my brain preconceptions.
From a technical point of view the game is flawless: no bugs, best graphics they could come up with and perfectly suiting music. Another thing that is perfect is the price: 5€ as base price is what you would expect to pay without discounts for a game like that.
So, to recap I'd recommend this game to everyone, not that everyone will ever even go further level 1, but the fact it messes your brain up is so good and interesting that it's worth trying at least for an hour or so. Not to mention that this runs flawlessly on linux too, much appreciated.

This game has to be one of my all time favorites. Tactical freedom is close to rediculous. From the team you pick, the weapons you choose, the small moments the world interacts with you, or you realize that an entire area's storyline has changed (ever so slightly, but with some weight) because you chose to be a baddy for 3 minutes, the second time. Divinity Original Sin 2 has depth, amazingly fun gameplay. Can be massively challenging and punishes those who run into danger without thinking. I'm currently on my honor run close to the ending of Act 2. This is the hardest difficulty with permadeath. Meaning... when your party dies, you lose your savegame. And no... this is not Xcom where you can Alt-F4 when♥♥♥♥♥♥hits the fan. The second a character dies, the game saves for you. Good luck getting yourself out of that pickle. With good preperation comes great rewards. Fights can be easy at times, but if I think for one second that I'm overpowered..? The game punishes me hard.
And that is what I love. It's like advanced chess, but you don't play "the same pieces", your characters evolve, become stronger. No pure warrior, naaah... give him some heals and necromancy spells to leech the blood out of your enemies. Making him the most dangerous guy on the field at all times. Feel like your character isn't strong enough? Give your archer some support spells to boost each others moves. Now your dangerous guy has the potential to kill four characters in two turns. And who needs a shield when you have a healthpool of 3000 health, hit with 500 dmg per swing and heal 70% of the damage done? One good area attack and you are healthy as an ox. And I know that when my warrior gets nuked with stuns etc? My archer is there with the right support spells to get him out again. And at no time am I really overpowered. Two times I almost lost my savegame because I misjudged a few skills from enemies. The constant struggle to play with the best optimisation and adapt to the game's AI. It's simply amazing.
Don't expect too much from the main story. It has depth, interesting aspects but you buy this game 100% for the gameplay. Do know... you CAN kinda abuse the game at later levels. There are skills that can be abused so you absolutely trash everything with the proper respec. Keep in mind that figuring out how the game works, what spells do etcetera, THAT is where the most fun is.
Some other Pro tips:
- Stealing is great fun, saves tons of money and keeps your party geared up (probably the best tip, do not-not steal).
- Undead are awesome, but start with a regular team, different mechanics can mess your party up if unprepared.
- Stick to either full physical damage OR full magical damage. Trust me on this one, you will thank me later.
- Summoners are overrated. They kinda make fights last 3x longer than needed. Only pick them if you absolutely love the mechanics.
- Figure out how to use stealth in combination with teleportation. You can "cheat" some fights that will otherwise trash your party.
- You can respec shortly after the end of Act 1, which is - on average - 10 hours of gameplay
- Crafting... almost EVERYTHING can be crafted. You only get to see 10% of the recipes that actually excist. Just google a crafting wiki. Thank me later. Don't wait until you find the books. If you want to make something, you probably can.
- Make sure your characters can survive alone as well. If they are too dependent on each other you will have a hard time nearing the endgame.
- Last but not least... Aim to finish about 80% of all the (side)quests. You will need the experience until the middle of Act 2, after that the game becomes a little more flexible when it comes to XP.
Downsides of the game?
It can be buggy, but rarely game breaking. AI can be brutal, feel unfair... but there is a pattern to exploit at all times. Quests can still be bugged out because you did something so complex that the game doesn't really know what you actually did.

Divinity 2 is definitely a game that can hold your attention for a while and you would probably really like it if you haven't played the first Original Sin. The problem for me, though, is that this game feels like a downgrade in nearly every respect from the first. The story isn't as interesting, the locations feel really bland (comparatively), combat is slower and worst of all the party interaction is simplistic at best.
One of the best things about Original Sin was that you and your partner built a relationship and history together as the game went on. You had arguments about what to do in a quest and could discuss the outcomes afterwards. Over time you began to develop your own tropes. It wasn't perfect by any means, but it was far better than what you get with Original Sin 2. This game allows for 4 player co-op, which is awesome. I was really excited when I heard the announcement about that. The problem is, however, that they really had to sacrifice a lot for characterization to accomidate that. All the pre-made characters have their own quest lines and stories, sure. But you have essentially no influence on the character, your dialogues feel meaningless and what you do in a quest is entirely your own decision. There are no group decisions. It's every man for himself, which leads me to the biggest problem.
As I said before Original Sin had you both discuss quest paths and if there was a disagreement, you would do a paper rock scissors minigame to decide who won. Nothing ground breaking, but it worked. Your two characters were partners and worked together for a common goal. It was kind of campy at times, but it made for a really fun and light hearted setting. Enter Original Sin 2. Not only does it not encourage working together, it in fact encourages the opposite. There are options that will only benefit one person. There are plot points that flat out tell you, "Only one person can win." It sets you against one another from the beginning. It might be interesting for some people, but I personally hated it. Coming from Original Sin where I loved the cooperative element, I hated that the game actively encouraged people to put themselves first. It might sound interesting at first, but I guarantee it really sucks to have to play a RPG where people start ignoring the story so that they can loot everything in sight before others get there first.
The tone of Original Sin 2 is much different from Original Sin. In fact, the exact opposite. Original Sin had a pretty light hearted campy feel to it. Pretty much every option felt like it had a good enough outcome if you put in the effort to get it. Original Sin 2, however, is a bleak and depressing setting. The people in the world are generally terrible and there are very few happy moments ever available. There are many quest lines that actually just turn a sad situation worse even if you go through all the effort to finish everything. The story feels completely hopeless and it eventually had me choosing to do as little as possible for questing.
As for the combat, they made magic a bit more accessible to people. There are more schools of magic and more abilities for you to choose from. It's interesting enough. But once again they made it worse, I think, from Original Sin. They basically halved your action points (AP) in this game. So you have less moves available in a turn. Then they added two types of defense. Physical and Magic. In order to do health damage, you have to bring one defense down to 0 and then hit with an attack of that damage type. So if you want to kill somebody with a sword, you have to get their physical armor to 0 and then hit them. Or if you want to kill somebody with a fireball, you have to get their magical armor to 0 and then hit them. All of this is done so that certain status ailments cannot be applied while certain armors are up. For instance, burning will first reduce magic armor before it takes health away. Same with stunning and knockdown. All this does is make combat feel like a chore. Before you can do anything to hurt anybody, you have to get their defenses down. But your moves are severely limited so you can maybe attack twice if you stand completely still and have max AP. It's slow and much less fun.
Most of this review was comparing Original Sin 2 to Original Sin and saying 'the first one was better.' And I think it was. If you haven't played Original Sin then you will probably really enjoy Original Sin 2. But for me Original Sin 2 was a huge letdown compared to the first. This is a good game but it's a big step back. I love this studio and I really, really hope to see an Original Sin 3 or some other CRPG from them in the future. With the success of Original Sin 2, I'm sure we will. I just hope they manage to bring back all the good they did with the first Divinity Original Sin.

2D platform game, an official but fan-made sequel to Sega's Sonic the Hedgehog games of 1991-95. You use momentum, reactions and precision to control a vividly coloured anthropomorphic animal around a vast world full of robots, traps, hidden rewards and opportunities for massive bursts of speed.
If you like any 2D action games, Sonic Mania is pretty much essential. I'd also recommend it to those who enjoy movement-intensive 3D games like Quake or Unreal Tournament, as the satisfaction comes from mastering a versatile physics system. It's suitable for all ages, but younger players may have some frustration.
If you don't like fast games, this one probably isn't for you. I heartily recommend tea-drinking and Backgammon.
A new player should manage a single playthrough in about two hours. Replay value is added by three characters with different abilities, local multiplayer modes, lots of unlockable features, and the sheer number of routes you can take through the levels. If you're familiar with Sonic games, Mania is a bit longer than 3 & Knuckles, and there's more to do.
It really does feel like a true sequel. The game's presented in a slightly pixellated 1990s style, but feels modern due to the widescreen format, resolution options and high framerate - and the sheer amount of detail.
The physics are an exact emulation of Sonic 3 & Knuckles, and Mania retains that game's combination of vast multi-tiered levels, lots of high-speed sections for adrenaline junkies, precise platforming tests, and concealed routes or items for explorers. Tails and Knuckles have their full abilities, Sonic just lacks his insta-shield (which you can re-enable via an achievement or modding) in favour of an instant spin-dash after landing from a jump.
The levels are absolutely crammed with references to the original series. Even Knuckles' Chaotix gets a look in. Some levels you flat-out revisit - eg. Green Hill and Oil Ocean - but they have new layouts, and incorporate mechanisms from other parts of the series (eg. Flying Battery has Wing Fortress' badnik emplacements and fan platforms, and Death Egg's antigravity). There's more that's familiar than pioneered in Sonic Mania, but it's so mixed together that it feels fresh and solidly designed.
If you know the old games inside out - or have dismissed them out of hand as child's play - it may be a surprise to come to Sonic Mania and find just how challenging it is. Despite the speed, careful play works best, and continual rushers rarely do well. Some of the difficulty is from obtuse design decisions though. A few stages are so enormous that they're tough to finish in the 10-minute time limit, and it's rarely clear how to take down bosses without hurting yourself (hell, it's often not clear when they're hittable). The Special Stages, which unlock the good ending and an invulnerable Super mode, are particularly difficult (until you master the technique, after which they're easily the most fun Special Stages in the series).
The only significant issue for me is the tone. Sonic Mania isn't particularly serious, whether you're looking at Sonic and Knuckles' unusually bright palettes, the cheerful expressions, use of Dr Robotnik's goofier eastern name Eggman, the irreverent cutscenes, the happy boxart, or the (admittedly great) soundtrack inspired by the Japanese version of Sonic CD that gives the game an upbeat disco mood. This all misses the cool factor that Sonic had in the early '90s, particularly the subtly edgier canon that made it to the West. Sega has gradually been making Sonic a more anime-ish, try-hard and childish property over the years, and while we're thankfully spared Sonic's 1998+ redesign in Mania, the easy coolness of the Megadrive/Genesis era isn't quite fully realised here.
When you're getting into that level of nitpicking, though, you know you're looking at a great game.
While Sonic Mania is a throwback to an increasingly distant time, don't let that fool you, this is the sort of game that's inherently fun, and easy to pick up. The original games haven't *really* aged, because 2D platforming reached its apex during that period. So being a proper sequel, Mania feels fantastic.
Is it
fun to play as Sonic 1-3K? I'm not sure. The level design certainly aids replayability a lot more, with multiple routes pretty much everywhere (whereas even Sonic & Knuckles confines you to a singular path more often than you might realise). But Mania's areas are so long and complex that some of the later, harder levels wear out their welcome. Sonic 3 may be a lot simpler, but there's maybe more joy in that. Mania is in the same league though, and far more fun than series side-projects Sonic CD and Chaotix.
There are also arguably minor issues in Sonic games' original design. The elaborate levels make you want to explore, but the gameplay dynamic doesn't incentivise this. One mistake loses you everything you've found, and most of the pickups don't have a lasting effect. It might seem sacrilegious to tinker with a dynamic that's sold millions of games since 1991, but another sequel could be improved by lowering the punishment for exploration, or amping the rewards.
Wrapping up though. Mania is a game I've been waiting 23 years for, a great platformer as well as a worthy sequel.

Just finished my playthrough of Act of War: Direct Action last night.
However did play the GOG version as the steam version isnt fully updated with Win 10 support yet.
That beeing said, the steam version should support upto Win 7 so if you have that then do not fear from buying it on steam!
So that is over with, now to the game.
Act of War is a RTS from 2005 that follows the "purest" RTS form with build basing and lots of unique units for every faction. The single player playthrough is fun and gives you quite a few headshakes even for a old school RTS players like myself, every unit has it´s strenght and weakness which is amazing and makes it impossible to just take a huge bunch of tanks and win the game, every unit has a counter and even footmen the most basic unit in every RTS is in fact valuable in end game.
The story itself isnt much to talk about, it does the job and drives the game forward in a good speed and in a way that makes you want to continue, it is made with on old Red Alert/C&C formular with greenscreen recordings and real action videos, this gives you a more insightfull way to follow your missions and why you need to do what the mission states, it is overall a better story than most RTS`s i´ve played and it really keeps you stuck in many ways.
Gameplay wise Act of War has everything you could wish for in a RTS and more. That it starts with the entire lineup from any classic RTS, footsoldiers, light tanks, tanks, special units and ofc super weapons. Now that is all like any other and that is what we enjoy, but hold on, there is a lot more, like capturing prisoners of war for money, counter super weapons, off screen airplane control, usage of heli´s to save your wounded soldiers and tanks across the battle field and much much more.
All in all Act of War is a great RTS that has been overlooked by many as it came out while there was other more famous RTS`s on the market which is a shame as it is diffenetly worth buying and worth playing.

After more than 40 hours I can honestly say:
The worst part about the game are is the beginning. You'll be stuck with the same Frame (pretend it's a class) and weapons for hours after you are immediately pushed into making the choice the minute you start.
You can make an edjucated guess which is most fun to you, but it's sure to get boring.
However, once you unlock the second and third planet you start getting blueprints for new weapons you can try, then slowly master and further customize through mods.
Apparently every planet has one assassination mission you can farm for 3 Frameparts and the needed blueprint to craft a new Frame.
Which takes 12 or 24 hours, but I am not mad, seeing that it takes so long gets me away from the game once in a while...
Though I am kinda annoyed when I get a blueprint for a weapon which I can still not craft, because ONE required resource can only be found several planets down the line....
You do have the option purchasing blueprints for ingame credits on the market or the desired item through platinum right away. Keep an eye on required crafting items, there is no use buying the blueprint if you won't get all the items soon enough ;)
The beginning has a long grace period. It's easy to go stealth, headshotting and ambushing npcs. However you might as well go all out berserker and just whack away on the enemies
My computer is far from being good, but the game still manages to look stunning at times on all settings right down the middle.
I HIGHLY recommend getting friends to play with, as you can play the way you like and get more loot(mods). The game doesn't really require you to talk tactics, so going with randoms is not that bad, but everyone has different playstyles and chances are you will get annoyed.
Also, I don't really care the Platinum for real money system. It's a good game and in the end it's worth as much as you want to put into it. It's free to play and they have to get money in somehow without putting adds into it :D
